Welcome - How to Use This Dart Guide

0.1 How this guide is organised0.2 The right mindset0.3 Tools and the command line0.4 What compiles where

Dart is the language behind Flutter, and a genuinely good general-purpose language in its own right. This guide teaches the language itself, then covers the four platforms it compiles to.

Dart 3 is a null-safe, strongly typed, class-based language with sound null safety, pattern matching, records and sealed types. It compiles ahead of time to native machine code for mobile and desktop, and to JavaScript or WebAssembly for the web. That combination is unusual and it is what makes one codebase target four platforms.

0.1 How this guide is organised

The three parts of the guide, and where to start if you already know some Dart.

  • Part I (Ch. 1-7) - the language: types and null safety, functions, classes and immutability, collections, the Dart 3 pattern-matching features, and error handling. This is the core, and it is where most of the value is.
  • Part II (Ch. 8-12) - doing real work: async, isolates for concurrency, packages and pub, files, sockets and serialization, plus FFI and native interop.
  • Part III (Ch. 13-16) - shipping: compiling for Android, iOS, desktop and the web, testing, performance, and a reference appendix.

Every chapter ends with exercises. Dart's type system is best learned by being corrected by the analyzer, so write the code and let the errors teach you.

How to read a chapter

Each section follows the same four-part shape, and it is worth knowing what each part is for before you start, because the tables and the prose are not saying the same kind of thing.

PartIsRead it for
The opening lineOrientationWhether this section is the one you need
The code samplesThe referenceThe syntax, in the order you would meet it
The tablesDecisionsWhich of several options to take
The closing paragraphsThe reasoningWhy the language is shaped this way

A guide that is only a reference is a dictionary, and a dictionary answers the question you arrive with rather than the one you will have next. The last part is what turns a listing into an explanation: it is where the trade-offs live, and it is the part worth reading even when you already know the syntax.

Read the samples as examples rather than as snippets to copy. Dart's type system is checked at compile time rather than at run time, which means most of the sample lines that could fail have been made impossible by the compiler instead — so a sample tells you what is legal, not what is likely.

// the habit worth forming early: read the error, then the type
void main() {
  final List<String> names = ['Ada', 'Grace'];
  names.add(42);          // ERROR: The argument type 'int' can't be assigned
                         // to the parameter type 'String'. dart_analysis_server
                         // reports it before main() ever runs.
}
// the same mistake in dynamic code
void main() {
  final names = ['Ada', 'Grace'];   // inferred as List<String>
  names.add(42);                   // still an error - inference fixed the type
  final loose = <dynamic>['Ada']; // explicitly dynamic
  loose.add(42);                   // COMPILES, and throws at run time
}
// which is the whole argument for the static type system in one comparison:
// the same line is caught in one case and deferred to production in the other
// only if a human writes `dynamic`, and `dynamic` is visible in the source

0.2 The right mindset

Four habits that separate idiomatic Dart from Java or JavaScript translated into Dart syntax.

  1. Null is a type, not an exception. Dart 3 has sound null safety: the compiler proves a nullable value is checked before use. When you fight that with !, the bug you were avoiding becomes a runtime crash instead. Chapter 2 is entirely about doing this properly.
  2. Prefer immutability, and make it the default. final for variables, const for compile-time constants, immutable classes with final fields and copyWith. Almost every "spaghetti" codebase is a consequence of too much mutable shared state.
  3. The analyzer is the compiler and your best tool. Run dart analyze constantly. It catches nullability errors, unused code, dead branches and lints before you run anything. Never suppress an error without understanding it.
  4. Everything heavy is an isolate. Dart's single-threaded event loop means any long synchronous computation blocks everything - including the UI. Long work goes in an isolate, and communication is by message. Chapter 9 is the single most important performance chapter.

What Dart is trading, and for what

Dart is not trying to be the most expressive language available, and it is not trying to be the fastest to compile. It is optimising for a narrower and more unusual target: a language that compiles to native on a phone, to JavaScript on the web, and to something in between for the desktop, with one type system and one set of semantics across all three. Almost every design decision follows from that sentence.

DecisionBoughtPaid
Sound null safety, no implicit dynamic escapingA compiler that can prove a null dereference is impossibleA migration cost, and no null-means-absent shortcut
A single type system across web and nativeOne codebase, and no dart:html / dart:io divergence in the coreSome platform APIs must be behind abstractions
Tree-shakeable icons and AOT compilationA binary that contains only what you reachReflection at run time is not free
Fast incremental compilationThe edit-compile-run loop stays sub-secondNo whole-program analysis on every build
Sound typing everywhere except dynamicThe compiler can generate efficient code for any typeGenerics are reified, so a generic type is part of the value

Two of those deserve more than a row. Sound null safety is the reason a Dart program cannot have a null-pointer crash that the compiler did not already rule out — which is a different and stronger claim than "has optional types". And tree shaking is why the same source can produce a 4 MB Android binary or a 60 KB web bundle: the compiler can only remove code it can prove is unreachable, which is a direct reason to avoid reflection.

// what "reachable" means, and why it constrains your code
import 'dart:mirrors';                    // NOT available on every target
import 'dart:io';                         // not available on the web at all

// this is why a JSON decoder is usually written by hand or generated:
// json.decode reaches code through string keys, so the compiler cannot see
// which branch is live, and tree shaking has nothing to remove
Map<String, dynamic> decode(String s) => json.decode(s) as Map<String, dynamic>;

// whereas a sealed hierarchy with a switch is fully analysable
sealed class Result {}
class Ok extends Result { final int value; Ok(this.value); }
class Err extends Result { final String message; Err(this.message); }

String render(Result r) => switch (r) {
  Ok(:final value) => '$value',
  Err(:final message) => message,
};
// the compiler sees both branches, checks both, and tree shaking keeps both -
// because both are reachable and both are handled

// the practical rule this produces
//   `dynamic`         pays for itself only at a true boundary: JSON, a plugin,
//                      a platform channel
//   `Object`          an unknown value you cannot call methods on
//   a concrete type    everywhere else, and the compiler will tell you when
//                      you have guessed wrong

The mindset to bring is that a Dart type annotation is not documentation, it is an optimisation hint and a proof obligation that the compiler discharges. Writing final everywhere costs nothing and enables the compiler to skip the wrapper object entirely for a final local of a known type — so the type is not only a safety feature, it is usually also a speed one.

0.3 Tools and the command line

The commands you will run every day, and what each one is for.

// install
# Dart SDK alone (needed for command-line/server/library work)
# Flutter SDK bundles Dart, so Flutter developers skip this

// every day
dart --version                the SDK version
dart create -t console my_app scaffold a project
dart run bin/main.dart        run a program
dart analyze                  static analysis: errors, warnings, lints
dart fix                      apply the automated safe fixes
dart format .                 the formatter; non-negotiable
dart test                     run the tests
dart run build_runner build   run code generation
dart pub get                  fetch dependencies
dart pub add http             add a dependency
dart pub outdated             see what can be upgraded
dart pub deps                 the dependency tree
dart doc                      generate API documentation

// compile
dart compile exe app.dart -o app            a native executable
dart compile js   app.dart -o app.js        JavaScript for the web
dart compile wasm app.dart -o app.wasm      WebAssembly for the web
dart compile aot-snapshot app.dart          an AOT snapshot for Flutter

// profiling
dart run --observe bin/main.dart           attach the VM service
dart --profiler --timeline                 record a CPU timeline
dart pub global activate dev_tools          a browser-based debugger

Run dart format . on save, and commit the result. The Dart formatter is non-negotiable and deterministic: nobody argues about formatting because the tool decides. Disagreements about style are wasted time, and this tool removes them entirely.

The toolchain, and which command answers which question

The Dart SDK ships with everything needed, and the commands divide cleanly into four groups. Knowing which group a problem is in is most of knowing which command to reach for.

GroupCommandsAnswers
Build and rundart run, dart compile, flutter runDoes it work, and how big is it
Analyse and formatdart analyze, dart formatIs it wrong, and is it conventional
Dependenciesdart pub get / add / upgrade / outdated / depsWhat is installed, and is anything stale
Test and profiledart test, DevToolsWhy is it slow, and why did it break
// the five commands you will actually use daily
dart pub get                  // install from pubspec.yaml + pubspec.lock
dart analyze                  // the analysis server over the whole package
dart test                     // run the suite, in every target that compiles
dart format .                 // the formatter, which is not negotiable
dart run bin/main.dart        // run one entry point

// and the two that answer questions the others cannot
dart pub deps --style=compact   // the resolved dependency tree, flattened
dart pub outdated                // what a new version would change

// `dart analyze` is not a lint run - it is a static analysis server, which
// means it keeps state between invocations and is fast enough to run on save.
// The distinction matters for CI: a lint is a style opinion, an analysis
// error is a correctness claim.
dart analyze --fatal-infos     // CI: treat an info as a failure
dart analyze --fatal-warnings

// and what the formatter does and does not do
dart format --output=show lib/a.dart   // print, do not write
dart format --set-exit-if-changed .    // CI: fail if reformatting is needed
// it normalises indentation, line breaking and trailing commas, and it
// does NOT reorder imports, rename anything, or change semantics. Which is
// why "the formatter did it" is a complete explanation for a diff that
// touches only layout - and why a diff that does not is worth reading

Two habits pay for themselves on a project of any size. Run dart format before every commit, so that a diff is a diff of logic — a formatter fight in review is pure noise. And keep analysis_options.yaml in version control with its strictness raised over time: include: package:lints/recommended.yaml to start, and add rules as the codebase earns them.

// analysis_options.yaml - the file that makes quality a build setting
include: package:lints/recommended.yaml

analyzer:
  language:
    strict-casts: true        # no implicit dynamic->T, ever
    strict-raw-types: true    # every raw generic must be instantiated
  errors:
    todo: ignore               # or: do not leave them in main
  exclude:
    - "**/*.g.dart"
    - "**/*.freezed.dart"      # generated files are not ours to lint

linter:
  rules:
    - prefer_final_locals     # a local that is never reassigned should say so
    - avoid_dynamic_calls     # the whole point of the type system
    - prefer_const_constructors
    - unawaited_futures       # a Future nobody awaits is a silent bug
    - use_build_context_safely

Reading the version, and what it commits you to

The SDK constraint in pubspec.yaml is the most consequential line in a Dart project, and it is the one most often left to whatever dart create generated. It is worth reading deliberately rather than accepting, because it decides three things: which language features you may use, whether your package can be depended on by modern code, and how often your users hit a resolution conflict on pub get.

// the constraint, and the three questions to ask of it
environment:
  sdk: '>=3.4.0 <4.0.0'
// ...1. What does the LOWER bound buy me? `>=2.12.0` buys sound null safety;
//    `>=3.0.0` buys records, patterns and class modifiers. Every feature you
//    use below the bound means a user on the lower bound gets a compile error
//    when they consume your package, not when you wrote it.
// 2. What does the UPPER bound buy me? `<4.0.0` buys the promise that Dart 4
//    will not break you — which is the convention, not a guarantee. Pub treats
//    a major-version bump as breaking and will refuse to resolve a package that
//    omits the bound.
// 3. Is the lower bound actually NEEDED? Raising it is how you exclude users for
//    no benefit. If you do not use a 3.0 feature, `>=2.19.0 <4.0.0` is a
//    strictly better line.

// the diagnostic that makes the answer obvious, and it is worth running
$ dart pub publish --dry-run
// ...reports "Package has 0 warnings" or names each one. The SDK constraint is
// checked there, along with the LICENSE, the CHANGELOG, the description and the
// dependency graph. For a library this is the single most useful command in
// the toolchain and it costs about a second.

// and the constraint on the RUNTIME version, which is a separate line
$ dart --version
// Dart SDK version: 3.4.0 (stable) on "stable_linux_x64"
// ...`dart run` runs on YOUR sdk; `dart compile exe` freezes the output for the
// target. So a bug that reproduces locally and not in production is often
// explained by the SDK versions differing, and `dart pub global run` pins one
// per tool for exactly that reason.

The commands you will actually use daily

Most of the Dart toolchain is commands you need once. Three are commands you need every day, and it is worth being precise about what each one is for, because the overlapping responsibilities are a common source of running the wrong one and concluding the codebase is fine when it is not.

// 1. dart analyze — static checks. The one you run on other people's code.
$ dart analyze                              # whole project, human output
$ dart analyze --fatal-infos                # what CI should run
$ dart analyze --format=machine | jq .      # for tooling and dashboards
// ...covers the compiler's errors PLUS 200+ lints (unused_import, prefer_const,
// avoid_print, depend_on_referenced_packages). Two lints worth promoting to
// errors because they are always defects:
//   unused_import            a dead import hides a real dependency
//   depend_on_referenced_packages  you import a transitive dep directly; pub
//                                  allows it, and it breaks when the
//                                  transitive dep changes
// ...and one to leave as a hint, because promoting it produces noise on hot
// paths: prefer_const_constructors.

// 2. dart format — the formatter is NOT configurable
$ dart format .
$ dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed .   # the CI form
// ...it takes no options: no line length, no bracket style, no indent size. It
// fixes every one of those from the language's own grammar. This is deliberate
// — the point is that formatting is not a matter of taste, so it never
// produces a diff that is about style. Consequences worth knowing:
//   - a long string literal is never wrapped, because wrapping changes it
//   - a long parameter list is wrapped at 80 columns, and a trailing comma
//     forces one-argument-per-line
//   - `// dart format off` exists, for a genuinely hand-aligned table, and is
//     almost always a mistake
// ...so a formatting diff is never ambiguous: it is exactly what the tool
// decided, and rejecting it means arguing with the grammar.

// 3. dart test — the test runner
$ dart test                                 # everything
$ dart test test/widget_test.dart:42        # one test by LINE NUMBER
$ dart test -n "isolates"                   # by name substring
$ dart test --coverage=coverage              # writes coverage/
$ dart test --concurrency=4                 # default is half the cores
$ dart test --platform vm --platform chrome  # run in a browser as well
// ...running one test by line number is the feature that makes TDD practical in
// Dart, because the cycle is edit -> `dart test file:42` -> read -> edit. A
// test runner without it forces a full run per cycle, and full runs are how
// TDD attempts die.

// 4. and the two that are one-off but not optional
$ dart pub get                   # resolve the graph
$ dart pub outdated              # what a newer version would change
$ dart pub deps --style=compact  # where a transitive dep came FROM
$ dart pub global activate cli   # install a tool, pinned to a version
$ dart pub cache repair           # after a corrupted download — rare, real
$ dart pub publish --dry-run     # the only full package validator
$ dart doc                       # generate API docs (built-in, no dartdoc pkg)
// ...`dart pub deps --style=compact` is the tool for "why do I have this
// package", and it prints the dependency chain, so it is the answer to a
// question you will ask when a supply-chain advisory names a package you never
// installed directly.

// and what is NOT built in, which is a frequent surprise for newcomers
// ...there is no linter bundle to install (dart analyze has them all), no test
// framework to add (dart test wraps package:test, which IS a dependency), and no
// build runner. If you need codegen, a CLI, or a server, add them explicitly:
//   dev_dependencies:
//     build_runner: ^2.4.13      // codegen
//     lints: ^4.0.0              // the lint rule set, referenced as
//                                 //   linter: rules in analysis_options.yaml
//     mockito: ^5.4.5
// ...and `lints` is worth adding even though analyze works without it, because
// without it you get the default rule set rather than the recommended one.

Two habits make the toolchain pay for itself. First, put the four checks in a single script so that "did I check everything" is never a question: dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed . && dart analyze --fatal-infos . && dart test && dart pub publish --dry-run, with the last one conditional on being a library. Second, run that script in CI from day one rather than adding it when something breaks — a check introduced during an incident is a check that gets disabled during the next incident.

0.4 What compiles where

The four targets, what each can and cannot do, and which APIs are platform-specific.

//                    native    web      what it is
//
// Android            AOT       -        arm64/x64 machine code, in the APK
// iOS                AOT       -        arm64 machine code, in the IPA
// macOS              AOT       -        arm64/x64 executable
// Windows            AOT       -        x64 executable
// Linux              AOT       -        arm/x64 executable
// Web                -         dart2js  JavaScript, loaded by a browser
//                                    (or dart2wasm: WebAssembly)
//
// KEY CONSEQUENCE: dart:io exists on native, and does NOT exist on the
// web. There is no compatibility layer, deliberately: a filesystem and
// a TCP socket have no meaning in a browser sandbox.
// the standard library splits cleanly

// available EVERYWHERE (dart:core, plus a growing shared set)
List, Map, Set, String, num, int, double, bool, Iterable, Stream
Future, Stream, Duration, DateTime, RegExp, Uri, JSON, math, convert

// native only (dart:io)
File, Directory, Socket, HttpClient, Process, Platform, stdin/stdout
Random access files, signals, isolates, FFI

// web only (package:web, or dart:html)
DOM, window, fetch, Canvas, WebGL, ServiceWorker, WebAssembly
IndexedDB, localStorage, Notification, Clipboard

// therefore: abstract the platform boundary behind an interface
// and provide two implementations. Chapter 13 shows the pattern.

This split is the single most important thing to internalise before writing a cross-platform Dart program. The moment you import dart:io, the program is no longer web-capable - and the error only appears when you try to compile for the web, often long after you wrote the line. Decide your platform strategy in chapter one, not at the end.

Exercises 1

  1. Install the Dart SDK, run dart --version, and scaffold a console project.
  2. Write a program that imports dart:io, then run dart compile js on it. Read the exact error. This is the platform boundary, and seeing it once makes it memorable.
  3. Run dart analyze on a file with a deliberate type error and read the message carefully. The analyzer is worth learning to read closely.
  4. Write down your platform strategy for a project you have in mind: native, web, or both, and what follows from it.

Five targets, and they differ in more than output format

Compilation targets are usually presented as a list of file extensions. That framing is misleading, because the important difference between targets is not the format of the output file but how much of the Dart standard library is available. dart:io exists in every native target and in none of the browser targets, and that single fact explains most of what you cannot port.

The targets are: native executable (dart compile exe), kernel snapshot (dart compile kernel, for AOT-on-device and for embedding in another runtime), JavaScript (dart compile js), WebAssembly (dart compile wasm), and Flutter's own targets, which use the engine's compiler rather than the standalone one.

TargetOutputRuns ondart:ioChoose it when
exeSelf-contained binaryOne OS/archYesA CLI, a server, a deployable
kernel.dillThe Dart VMYesTesting, embedding, iOS/Android via Flutter
aot-snapshot.aotOne OS/arch, needs the VMYesSmaller than exe where the VM is already present
js.jsAny browserNoWeb apps needing a wide support floor
wasm.wasm + .mjsModern browsersNoCompute-heavy web apps
FlutterApp bundle6 platformsPartlyAny app with a UI
// the same program, three targets, and what changes
// lib/app.dart — ONE source file, no conditional compilation anywhere
import 'dart:math';              // portable: available on EVERY target
void main() { print(pow(2, 10)); }
// $ dart compile exe  lib/app.dart -o app.exe   -> runs, no runtime needed
// $ dart compile js   lib/app.dart -o app.js    -> runs, 1.8 MB
// $ dart compile wasm lib/app.dart -o app.wasm  -> runs, needs the .mjs too

// now add ONE line that breaks two of the three targets
import 'dart:io';                // NOT available on js or wasm
void main() { stdout.writeln(File('x').path); }
// $ dart compile exe  lib/app.dart   -> OK
// $ dart compile js   lib/app.dart
// Error: Dart library 'dart:io' is not available on this platform.
// lib/app.dart:1:8: Error: Dart library 'dart:io' is not available.
// ...ONE line, and the failure is at compile time with a file and a line. Not
// a runtime "not supported in the browser" and not a silently undefined
// behaviour. That is the design: a target either supports the whole program or
// refuses to build it.

// and the conditional import, which is the only supported escape hatch
// lib/io_client.dart     — the dart:io implementation
// lib/web_client.dart    — the package:web implementation
// lib/client.dart        — the interface both implement
import 'client.dart';
export 'client_stub.dart'
    if (dart.library.io) 'io_client.dart'
    if (dart.library.js_interop) 'web_client.dart';
// ...three branches: the stub is the default and exists so the file parses on
// a target that matches neither, and it should throw
// UnsupportedError('no implementation for this platform') rather than silently
// doing nothing. Silent stubs are how a browser build ends up with a working
// login form and a non-persisting session.

// and how to find out what you have got wrong BEFORE deploying
$ grep -rn "dart:io" lib/ | grep -v "_io.dart"
// ...every hit outside a platform-binding file is a line that will break a web
// build. This is a three-second check and it belongs in CI for any project that
// ships to more than one target.

Two consequences follow that are worth stating before you start, because both are discovered late otherwise. First, a browser build is a different standard library, so any program that reads a file, opens a socket, or spawns a process cannot be compiled for the web — it can only be restructured so the I/O happens in a platform binding. Second, Flutter's target set is a third thing: Flutter apps compile to AOT for mobile and to JavaScript or WebAssembly for web, and a plugin that uses dart:io works on mobile and fails on Flutter web for exactly the reason above.

1 · The Dart Language Core

1.1 Your first program, and the two entry points1.2 Variables: var, final, const, late1.3 The type system1.4 Numbers and the int/double split1.5 Strings and interpolation1.6 Lists, Sets and Maps1.7 Control flow1.8 Imports, libraries and main

The syntax and the type system, with the Dart 3 defaults that differ from what you may know from other languages.

1.1 Your first program, and the two entry points

A console program, a library file, and the two places main can live.

// bin/main.dart - a console program
import 'dart:math';

void main(List<String> args) {
  final random = Random();
  var total = 0;

  for (var i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    final value = random.nextInt(100);
    total += value;
    print('roll $i: $value');
  }

  print('total: $total');
  print('args: $args');
}
// main can return a Future, and awaits work correctly
import 'dart:io';

Future<void> main() async {
  final sw = Stopwatch()..start();
  final contents = await File('data.txt').readAsString();
  print('read ${contents.length} chars in ${sw.elapsedMilliseconds}ms');
}

// a generator-style main, for tests and long-running processes
Stream<int> main() async* {
  for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    yield i;
    await Future.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 100));
  }
}

Dart requires a semicolon-terminated statement and is fully typed by default in Dart 3. Type inference is applied where it is unambiguous, so you do not write types everywhere - but you do write them in public signatures, where they are documentation and a contract.

What actually happens between the file and the process

A Dart program's journey from source to running process has more stages than most introductions admit, and each stage is a place where a confusing message comes from. Knowing the stages turns "the compiler said something impossible" into "the front end accepted it and the back end rejected it", which is a much shorter distance.

The front end parses and resolves, producing a kernel (.dill) file. The kernel is a whole-program intermediate form that contains every library your program imports, including the SDK's own. dart run then hands that kernel to the runtime, which JIT-compiles it to machine code for the current CPU and OS and executes it. dart compile skips the second half: it AOT-compiles the kernel to a native executable ahead of time, so the machine code is already correct for the target when the process starts.

// the four stages, and what each one can tell you
lib/hello.dart          SOURCE      .dart  — what you write
  |  front end (CFE)     PARSE       resolves imports, infers types, reports
  |                                        errors WITH source positions
  v
build/hello.dill        KERNEL      .dill — whole program, untyped-ish IR
  |  back end (DVM/AOT) COMPILE     machine code, CPU-specific
  |  runtime (JIT)      EXECUTE     or: dart compile exe skips this stage
  v
a running process

// ...which is why there are TWO error formats, and both are legitimate
// $ dart run lib/hello.dart
// lib/hello.dart:5:9: Error: Method not found: 'pritn'.
//   pritn('hi');
//   ^^^^^^
// ^^^^^^ line:column, from the FRONT END, with the caret under the token

// $ dart compile exe lib/hello.dart
// Internal problem: Transforming lib/hello.dart failed: DDC error
//   Unexpected type: Null
// ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ from the BACK END, which does not always have a position
// ...so a message with no line number came from the second half of the
// pipeline. It is rarer, it is often a compiler bug, and the workaround is to
// reduce the program until it stops. Knowing which half spoke saves an hour.

// and the intermediate stage you can actually inspect, which is the tool that
// makes this concrete
$ dart compile kernel lib/hello.dart -o hello.dill
$ dart --observe=8181 lib/hello.dart      // then attach DevTools
// ...`.dill` is a binary file, but `dart compile kernel` plus a decompiler in
// DevTools lets you step through the program's whole-program form, including
// inside the SDK. Debugging "why is this null" in library code is only
// possible at this stage.

The two entry points, and why the difference matters

Dart has a traditional main() and an main(List<String> args), and they differ in exactly one way that matters: whether the program reads command-line arguments, and whether the return value reaches the shell. Most of the design decision is in the argument parsing, not in the signature.

// 1. THE NO-ARGUMENT ENTRY POINT. Nothing to read, and nothing to report.
void main() {
  print('hello');
}
// ...`dart run lib/hello.dart` works. `dart run lib/hello.dart --flag` ignores
// the flag silently, which is the trap: an unrecognised argument does not
// produce an error, it produces a program that behaves as if the argument were
// not typed.

// 2. THE ARGUMENT-FORM ENTRY POINT. The signature is not the difference; the
//    RETURN TYPE is.
int main(List<String> args) {
  if (args.contains('--verbose')) { ... }
  return 0;                 // ...this 0 is the process exit code
}
void main(List<String> args) {
  ...                        // ...and THIS ONE is always exit code 0, however
}                             //    the program ended. A `void main` that throws
                              //    exits 255; a `void main` that catches the
                              //    throw exits 0 and looks successful.

// 3. ASYNC. `Future<void> main()` is legal, and it is what almost every real
//    program uses.
Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  final server = await HttpServer.bind('localhost', 8080);
  await for (final req in server) { ... }   // ...runs until this completes
}
// ...`dart run` awaits the returned Future and only then exits. So the process
// lifetime is the Future's lifetime, which is why a `main` that starts a server
// and returns immediately exits immediately. There is no "keep running" —
// either something is awaited or the process is over.

// and the exit code, which is the only channel between your program and every
// shell, CI system and supervisor that will ever run it
import 'dart:io';
void main(List<String> args) {
  final file = File(args.first);
  if (!file.existsSync()) {
    stderr.writeln('not found: ${file.path}');
    exit(2);            // 0 = ok, 1 = generic failure, 2 = usage error
  }                        // ...and 128+n for a signal, which is a convention
}                         //    worth knowing so you do not invent a code for it
// ...the rules that follow from this being the only channel:
//   - print diagnostics to STDERR, results to STDOUT, so `prog > out.txt`
//     captures only results and errors still reach a human
//   - choose a small, documented set of codes and be consistent, so a caller
//     can branch on them
//   - never signal success by NOT failing. `exit(0)` after catching an error is
//     a lie, and CI will report a green build over a broken deployment.

// ...and the shebang, which makes a Dart file directly executable
#!/usr/bin/env dart
// ...saved as lib/tool with a +x bit, `./lib/tool --help` then works. `dart run
// lib/tool` also works and needs no permission bit, which is why the shebang is
// optional and why CI prefers the second form.

1.2 Variables: var, final, const, late

The four declaration forms, and choosing correctly between them.

// var: a mutable variable, type inferred at first assignment
var count = 0;              // int
count = 3;
count = 'three';            // ERROR: the type was fixed to int
// the fix: declare it as dynamic or Object, which is almost never right

// final: assigned once, at declaration
final now = DateTime.now(); // cannot be reassigned
// final List<String> names = [];
// names.add('ok');          // allowed: the list contents can change
// names = ['new'];         // ERROR: the reference cannot

// const: compile-time constant, deeply immutable
const pi = 3.14159265358979;
const appName = 'Field Notes';
const List<int> primes = [2, 3, 5, 7];
// primes.add(11);          // ERROR: even the contents are fixed
const Map<String, int> ports = {'http': 80, 'https': 443};

// late: assigned later, but exactly once, before first read
late final String token;    // read before assignment -> runtime error
late String? cached;        // late + nullable: the honest version

class Service {
  late final Database db;   // initialised in an async method
  Future<void> open() async {
    db = await Database.connect();
  }
}
// the rule that removes most Dart style debates
//
//   default to final
//   use var only when the type is genuinely inferred and obvious
//   use const whenever the value is known at compile time
//   use late only for genuinely deferred initialisation
//
// the analyzer will tell you when a const is possible: it offers the
// `prefer_final_locals` and `unnecessary_final` lints. Turn them on.

late is genuinely useful and genuinely dangerous. It is the right tool for a field your constructor cannot supply synchronously - a database handle, a parsed config. It is the wrong tool for avoiding a null check. If you find yourself writing late on a field that could simply be nullable, use the nullable type and handle the absent case honestly.

Choosing between the four

This is the single highest-leverage decision in the language, because it is the one the compiler reads. var is not "untyped" and it is not "dynamic" — it is infer the type from the initialiser and then hold it, which is why a var assigned twice with different types is a compile error.

FormType isSetCompile-time constantUse for
varInferredAny timeNoA local whose type the initialiser makes obvious
finalInferredOnceNoThe default for a local — 90% of cases
constInferredAt compile timeYesA value known at build time
late finalInferredOnce, laterNoA value computed on first use
T / final TStatedOnceNoA field, or where the type is not obvious

The Dart style guide is explicit: use final by default for locals, and omit the type where the initialiser makes it obvious. Both halves matter. var rather than int when the initialiser is an integer literal, because the annotation adds nothing and the two must be kept in sync. An explicit type where the initialiser does not make it obvious — an empty list, a literal with mixed element types, anything from a generic call.

// the three decisions, as they appear in real code
void main() {
  // 1. obvious: infer. The annotation would repeat the initialiser.
  var count = 0;                  // int - and assigning a String later fails
  var name = 'Ada';               // String
  var sum = 0;                    // int, inferred from the literal 0

  // 2. NOT obvious: state the type, because the initialiser cannot.
  var empty = [];                 // List<dynamic> - and dynamic calls with it
  final List<String> names = [];  // List<String> - what you meant
  final config = <String, dynamic>{};  // Map<String, dynamic>, not Map
  final result = json.decode(s);  // dynamic - so say what it should be
  final parsed = jsonDecode(json) as Map<String, Object?>;

  // 3. computed later: late final, which allows ONE assignment anywhere
  late final User user;           // no initialiser
  user = fetchUser();             // ...but exactly one, and the compiler knows
  print(user.id);                 //   how many times the read can happen

  // and what is NOT allowed
  late var count2;                // ERROR: `late` requires final or a type
  late const x;                   // ERROR: nothing to defer, it is already constant
  final int n;                    // ERROR: a final must be initialised
  final int n = f();              // ERROR: not a compile-time constant
  const int m = f();              // ERROR: ditto
}

A final variable cannot be reassigned, but the object it points at can be mutated — final List is an immutable reference, not an immutable list. And const is not simply "more final": it is canonicalised at compile time, so two const lists with equal contents are the same object, which is why const cannot hold a non-const value and why a const collection is genuinely immutable all the way down.

// final: the binding is fixed, the value is not
final items = [1, 2, 3];
items.add(4);                     // fine - the list grew
items = [9];                      // ERROR: the binding cannot move

// const: both are fixed, and the object is canonical
const frozen = [1, 2, 3];
frozen.add(4);                    // ERROR: UnmodifiableListException at run time
const a = [1, 2];
const b = [1, 2];
identical(a, b);                  // TRUE - the compiler made one object

// which is what makes const usable as a map key or a default value
const defaultPageSize = 25;       // legal as a default parameter value
const emptyNames = <String>[];    // legal, and canonicalised
void paginate({int size = defaultPageSize}) {}

// and the rule that catches people
const now = DateTime.now();       // ERROR: not a compile-time constant
const fromApi = 42;               // ERROR: not constant either
// so `const` is for values the COMPILER knows, which is almost never a value
// read at run time

1.3 The type system

Static typing, soundness, and the type hierarchy you need to know.

// Dart is statically typed and soundly null safe.
// A value of type T is guaranteed to behave as T - no runtime surprises
// from a type system that lies.

Object        // everything except null
  +- num
  |    +- int
  |    +- double
  +- bool
  +- String
  +- Function
  +- Symbol
  +- Type
  +- Iterable<E>
       +- List<E>
       +- Set<E>
       +- Queue<E>
  +- Map<K, V>
  +- Future<T>
  +- Stream<T>
  +- Enum
  +- Record
  +- Pattern
  +- Function type          (using the (T) -> R syntax)

// everything is an Object, so this is always legal
void describe(Object value) {
  print(value.runtimeType);   // what it actually is
  print(value is String);
  print(value.hashCode);
}
// static vs dynamic vs Object
var a = 5;                       // int        - inferred, checked
dynamic b = 5;                  // dynamic   - NO checking, escape hatch
Object c = 5;                   // Object    - checked, but no members

b.toUpperCase();   // ERROR at compile time: dynamic has no members
c.toUpperCase();   // ERROR at compile time: Object has no members
a.toUpperCase();   // ERROR: int has no toUpperCase either, but the
                   // point is you get a useful error either way

// dynamic is almost always a mistake in application code.
// it is justified in exactly three places:
//   1. JSON decoding into a shape you validate afterwards
//   2. a reflection-based or generic-bridge layer
//   3. interop with a dynamically typed host (JavaScript)
// generics
List<int> ids = [1, 2, 3];
Map<String, List<int>> byUser = {
  'ana': [1, 2],
  'bo': [3],
};

// a generic function
T firstOr<T>(List<T> items, T fallback) {
  return items.isEmpty ? fallback : items.first;
}

final name = firstOr<String>([], 'unknown');   // String
final count = firstOr<int>([1, 2], 0);          // int

// bounded generics
T maxOf<T extends Comparable<T>>(T a, T b) {
  return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b;
}

maxOf(3, 7);          // 7
maxOf('a', 'b');      // 'b'
// maxOf(3, 'a');    // ERROR: String does not satisfy Comparable<int>

What sound typing buys, concretely

Dart's type system is gradually typed — sound at the boundary, inferred everywhere — and the practical effect is that the compiler can generate specialised code for any type it can prove, while still accepting a boundary that is genuinely dynamic.

AnnotationChecked atAllows callsCost at run time
A concrete typeCompileYes, checkedNone — specialised code
ObjectCompileOnly Object's membersNone
Object?CompileAfter a null checkNone
dynamicRunAnything, checked at the callA dynamic dispatch
voidCompileNothingReturn value discarded
// the boundary is the point, and it is narrow on purpose
Object parseId(Object raw) {          // says: I accept anything
  if (raw is int) return raw;          // and narrow before using it
  if (raw is String) return int.parse(raw);
  throw ArgumentError('cannot be an id: $raw');
}

int useId(Object raw) {
  // a promotion: after `is` and inside the branch, `raw` is int, and the
  // compiler REWRITES the access. No cast, no runtime check, and it works
  // on a local variable only - which is why this does not compile:
  if (raw is! int) throw ArgumentError('bad');
  return raw + 1;                     // raw is int here - promoted
}

// why promotion is local-only, and the two workarounds
Object? box;
if (box is String) { box.length; }    // ERROR: `box` is a field, so it could
                                      // change between the check and the use
// 1. take a local - which is the idiomatic fix
final b = box;
if (b is String) print(b.length);     // fine - `b` is a local, and final

// 2. use a pattern, which binds rather than narrows
if (box case final String s) print(s.length);

// 3. or declare the field non-nullable, so there is nothing to narrow
class Session { final String token; Session(this.token); }

The promotion restriction is the most common surprise for anyone coming from a language without flow analysis, and it has a clean rationale: a field could be changed by any other code between the check and the use, so a compiler that assumed otherwise would be wrong. Taking a final local is a one-word fix and is what the style guide recommends.

// generics: reified, covariant, and bounded
T identity<T>(T value) => value;
identity(42);            // T is int
identity('x');           // a SEPARATE instantiation - T is String

class Box<T extends Object> {
  final T value;
  Box(this.value);
  T? get maybe => value as T?;      // note: nullable needs an upper bound
}

// the bound matters: without `extends Object`, T can be int? and the
// nullable case needs a where clause
class StrictBox<T extends Object> {}
StrictBox<int?>();      // ERROR: T cannot be nullable with this bound

// covariance in Dart is per-use, which is why List<Animal> is not a
// List<Dog> - it is unsound, because you could append a Cat
final animals = <Animal>[Dog()];
animals.add(Cat());                    // legal, and unsound
final dogs = animals as List<Dog>;   // compiles, and throws if a Cat is there
// so the sound approach is an immutable view or a sealed hierarchy, not a cast

// and where `dynamic` is genuinely the right answer
dynamic plugin;                         // loaded at run time, unknown here
final result = plugin.invoke();         // the compiler cannot help - correct
final safe = result as int;             // and the cast is the check, here

Sound null safety is a mode, and the mode is set by a version

Dart's type system is not uniformly typed or uniformly sound. It is a gradual system with a language version, and the version decides which guarantees apply. This is the single most useful thing to know about Dart types, because it explains why code you have seen has ! operators and late and code you wrote this week does not, with no other difference between them.

The version is a per-library opt-in, set in pubspec.yaml and expressible in a file, and the opt-in happened in Dart 2.12. A library on 2.12 or later is sound-null-safe: nullable types are accurate, promotion works, and a non-nullable type is a guarantee the compiler can rely on. A library below it is legacy: int may hold null at runtime, so every non-nullable type in it is a hint rather than a promise.

// the opt-in, and where it lives
name: my_app
environment:
  sdk: '>=3.4.0 <4.0.0'
// ...this is what puts the library in sound-null-safe mode. There is no
// per-file flag and no per-declaration flag: it is one version for a whole
// package, and it is why a package's null safety is stated in its pub.dev
// score rather than inferred.

// a legacy library cannot be depended on soundly, and pub warns about it
//   Because my_legacy 1.2.3 depends on some_legacy ^2.0.0 which is not
//   null-safe, the following users of my_legacy must be null-safe
//   (your package is NOT null-safe)
// ...the migration is therefore not purely per-package: a sound library cannot
// use a legacy one without either migrating it or living with the unsound
// boundary.

// and what the mode changes, concretely
void legacy() {
  String? s = maybeNull();
  print(s.length);      // legacy: COMPILES. s.length is 0 if s is null, because
}                       //          legacy code has an implicit `s ?? ''`
void sound() {
  String? s = maybeNull();
  print(s.length);      // sound: COMPILE ERROR
}                       //        - 's' can't be used as 'String' because it
                        //          could be null.
// ...and that error is the entire value proposition: a mistake that used to be
// a runtime "NoSuchMethodError: The method 'length' was called on null" is now
// a compile error at the line.

// and the four places promotion deliberately does NOT apply, because each is a
// situation where the value could change between the check and the use
class Box {
  String? get value => throw UnimplementedError();   // ...a GETTER: promotion
}                                                       //    does not survive a
Box? b;
if (b != null) b.value.length;   // sound: ERROR - `b.value` is String?, because
                                 // the getter could return something else on a
                                 // second call. Capture it instead:
if (b != null) { final v = b.value; print(v.length); }

// ...a WRITE, because the compiler will not assume no other code runs between
int? x;
if (x != null) print(x.isEven);   // sound: ERROR - x is captured by a closure
x = null;                          //    somewhere and could change. Write
                                  //    `final y = x;` before the check.

// ...an OVERRIDABLE member, because a subclass may override the getter
class A { int get v => 1; }
class B extends A { @override int get v => 0; }
A a = B();
if (a is B) a.v;         // sound: ERROR - `v` is overridden in B, so the
                         // compiler will not use the promotion

// ...and a TYPE PARAMETER, because promotion to a type variable is not sound
T first<T>(List<T> xs) {
  if (xs.isNotEmpty) return xs.first;   // ...T is `T?` inside the check, and
  throw ArgumentError();                 //    promoting it would need T to be
}                                        //    covariant, which it is not

// ...the pattern that works for all four: capture into a local, which is a
// single read of a value the compiler then knows cannot change
if (b case final v?) print(v.length);   // ...`if-case` does this in one
                                        //    statement, which is why chapter
                                        //    16 prefers it to `is` on a field

The type system and the runtime are the same system

Dart has one type system, not two. There is no separate compile-time and runtime type system that disagree — is, as, generics and reified types are all real at runtime, which is unusual for a statically typed language and has a specific consequence: a generic cast can fail at runtime, and List<int> and List<String> are different runtime types even though both are List.

That is what makes unsound casts possible at all, and it is why as is a promise the compiler makes you keep rather than a check it performs. The consequence you meet in practice is a TypeError thrown at a distance from the mistake, and the discipline that avoids it is to use is (which checks) rather than as (which asserts), and to use pattern matching when you need both a check and a binding.

// reified generics: the type argument survives to runtime
List<int> ints = [1, 2, 3];
List<String> strs = ints as List<String>;   // TypeError, not a warning
// ...`ints is List<String>` is false, and so is `ints is List`. Dart's
// runtime check for a generic type tests the TYPE ARGUMENT too, unlike Java or
// C# where `List<int>` and `List<String>` erase to the same runtime
// class. So a cast between two `List<T>` with different T throws, which is
// stricter than the JVM.

// the practical rule: never cast a collection to a different element type
// ...it throws. Cast the ELEMENTS instead, which is what you meant:
final strs = ints.map((e) => e.toString()).toList();   // correct
final wrong = ints as List<String>;                 // throws at runtime
final alsoWrong = List<String>.from(ints);           // ALSO throws

// and the safe downcast, which is what `as` is actually for
abstract class Shape { double get area; }
class Square extends Shape { Square(this.s); final double s;
  @override double get area => s * s; }

double total(List<Shape> shapes) {
  var sum = 0.0;
  for (final s in shapes) {
    if (s is Square) sum += s.s;    // ...narrowing to a SUBTYPE, which is
    else sum += s.area;             //    always safe if the test passed
  }
  return sum;
}
// ...`as` is for downcasting a supertype to a known subtype after a test that
// did not narrow: `if (o.runtimeType == Square) (o as Square).s`. It is not
// for reinterpreting data as something else, which is what most misuse is.

// and soundness, which is a property of the whole program rather than of one
// declaration
void soundnessBroken() {
  final a = <Object>['x'];
  final b = a as List<int>;   // TypeError
  b.add(1);
}
// ...two rules define soundness for a given program, and they are worth being
// able to state:
//   1. every unsound assignment / cast to a parameterised type is a RUNTIME
//      error. Above is the failure: the cast succeeded because `Object` and
//      `List` are related, and the list turned out to hold a String.
//   2. null is not a value of a non-nullable type.
// A library with sound-null-safe enabled can still violate (1) through `as`,
// which is why `as` is described as UNSOUND: it can take a sound program and
// make it unsound at runtime. The compiler allows it because it is sometimes
// necessary, and it names the soundness hole rather than pretending it does not
// exist.

// and what you give up by choosing dynamic, which is the honest trade
dynamic d = 'a string';
d.length;             // sound mode: allowed - dynamic suppresses checks
int n = d;             // ...and throws at runtime if d is not an int
// ...`dynamic` is `Object` with all static checking on that expression
// disabled. `Object` instead keeps the checks and only allows any non-null
// value. So:
//   Object   checked, non-null, type must be a subtype of Object
//   dynamic  unchecked, may be null, any type
// ...prefer `Object` when you want type safety and `dynamic` only when you are
// genuinely talking to code whose types you cannot know — a JSON blob you have
// not validated, or a JS interop value. `dynamic` in a domain model is a type
// error you have chosen to make.

1.4 Numbers and the int/double split

Two integer widths, one num parent, and the conversions that catch people.

// int  - a signed 64-bit integer on native, a JavaScript-safe number on web
// double - a 64-bit IEEE 754 double
// num  - the common supertype; arithmetic on it is allowed but loses type

int a = 7;
int b = 2;
print(a ~/ b);   // 3   - integer division
print(a / b);    // 3.5 - true division, returns double
print(a % b);    // 1
print(a.isEven);
print(a.abs());

double c = 7.0;
print(c.floor());  // 7   - int
print(c.ceil());   // 7   - int
print(c.round());  // 7   - int
print(c.toInt());

// int and double do NOT implicitly convert
double d = 3;          // ERROR: an int is not a double
int e = 3.0;           // ERROR
int f = 3.0.toInt();   // correct, but be explicit about the rounding
int g = 3.9.toInt();   // 3  - truncates toward zero, it does not round
int h = 3.9.round();   // 4  - what you usually want
// FIXED-WIDTH types: integers that do not wrap silently
import 'dart:typed_data';

final b = Uint8List(4);           // 0..255,   wraps modulo 256
final i16 = Int16List(4);         // -32768..32767
final u32 = Uint32List(4);        // 0..4294967295
final f32 = Float32List(4);       // 32-bit float, half the memory of Float64
final f64 = Float64List(4);

b[0] = 255;
b[0] = b[0] + 1;   // 0 - it wrapped, as documented

// these matter for binary formats, image and audio data, FFI, and
// interop with native buffers. For counting, plain int is right.

print(1 << 62);   // 4611686018427387904
print(0xFF);        // 255
print(0b1010);      // 10

On the web, int is a JavaScript number: a 64-bit float, so it holds integers exactly only to 2^53. That is not a theoretical limit - a 64-bit database id will not survive a round trip through the web build. Use int for values under 2^53, and a String for identifiers that might be larger.

The 64-bit decision, and what it costs

Dart's int is a 64-bit signed integer on every platform, including the web, where JavaScript numbers are doubles. That single decision removes an entire class of bug from code that has to behave the same on a phone and in a browser.

TypeRangeNotes
int−263 … 263−164-bit signed, everywhere including the web
double±1.8 × 10308IEEE 754 binary64, like a JavaScript number
numEitherThe abstract supertype; an escape hatch, not a choice
BigIntUnboundedArbitrary precision; a separate runtime and library

The consequence worth internalising is that num is not "a number". It is the union of two types with different arithmetic, and a num variable can hold an int on one line and a double on the next, with the compiler unable to help because you have told it not to.

// an int literal that does not fit in 64 bits is a BigInt, not an error
const small = 42;                     // int
const big = 100000000000000000000;    // BigInt - inferred from the literal
big.runtimeType;                      // BigInt
big + 1;                              // works - arbitrary precision

// but an int literal inside a double context is a double, and loses precision
// above 2^53, which is where JS integers start losing it too
print(9007199254740993);              // 9007199254740992 - the last digit is gone
const exact = 9007199254740993.0;     // the same value, as a double

// num is the union, so it inherits the worst of both
num loose = 3;
loose = 3.5;                          // legal - loose is num now
loose.floor();                        // only available on num, not on int
final int strict = loose;             // ERROR: num is not int

// so the rule is: name the narrow type you mean, and use num only where you
// genuinely accept either. A parameter typed num is a parameter that cannot be
// reasoned about by the compiler or by a reader.

// and the division asymmetry, which is the bug that actually happens
7 / 2;                     // 3      - int division, truncated
7 ~/ 2;                    // 3      - the same, spelled explicitly
7 / 2.0;                   // 3.5    - a double operand makes it real division
7 % 2;                     // 1
-7 % 2;                    // 1 in Dart, 1 in JS - non-negative, unlike C
(-7) ~/ 2;                 // -3     - truncation toward zero

// money and quantities: never a double
double cents = 19.99 * 100;   // 1998.9999999999998
int cents2 = 1999;            // the correct representation

Conversions, and the two that are not conversions

Dart has no implicit widening between int and double, which removes a whole category of bug that JavaScript has. What it has instead is an explicit num type that sits above both, and three conversions worth knowing by their exact names.

ExpressionResultNotes
2.0.truncate()intToward zero: (−2.9).truncate() is −2
2.9.round()intHalf away from zero
2.9.floor() / ceil()intDown / up
2.9.toInt()intTruncates — the same as truncate()
2.toDouble()doubleExact up to 253
2.9 as intintTruncates — and throws if it cannot
int.parse("42")intThrows FormatException on bad input
int.tryParse("42")int?Returns null instead of throwing
2.9.toStringAsFixed(2)String"2.90" — for display only
// parse and tryParse: the pair to reach for at every input boundary
int.parse('42');            // 42
int.parse('4.2');           // FormatException
int.tryParse('4.2');        // null
double.tryParse('4.2');     // 4.2
num.tryParse('1e400');     // null - it is not representable

// so a boundary is:
final id = int.tryParse(req.params['id']);
if (id == null) return badRequest('id must be an integer');
// rather than a try/catch, which costs an exception on every bad request

// fixed-point money, which never touches a double
const PRICE = 1999;                       // cents
String format(int cents) =>
    '${(cents ~/ 100)}.${(cents % 100).toString().padLeft(2, '0')}';
format(PRICE);        // 19.99
format(5);            // 0.05    - and this is the case that catches people
format(-50);          // 0.-50   - so handle the sign explicitly

// the arithmetic that is not exact, and why it does not matter here
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3;              // false
0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3 < 1e-10;     // true - and for money, still wrong
// because a tolerance is a guess. Integers have no tolerance.

// and the conversions that throw rather than truncate, which is safer
const n = 2.9;
n as int;                       // 2 - silent
num.parse('x');                 // FormatException
int.parse('3.0');               // FormatException - strict about the format

// so: `as int` on a double you control, `int.parse` on a string you do not,
// and `tryParse` at a boundary where rejection is ordinary

The 64-bit int also means the classic int-is-32-bits bug cannot happen, which removes an entire genre of overflow report from a codebase that ships to phones. What replaces it is subtler and just as real: a value that fits comfortably in 64 bits but not in a JavaScript number, so a Dart API that returns an int and is consumed from JavaScript through dart2js or through a JSON channel silently loses precision above 253. That boundary is far higher than people expect and far lower than they assume, and it is the one number worth writing down when choosing between int and BigInt.

The other asymmetry is division. Integer division truncates toward zero, which matches every language except JavaScript, where -7 / 2 is -3.5 and there is no integer division at all. Code ported from JavaScript into Dart — and Dart is often reached through JavaScript — is where this shows up: a loop bound written as n ~/ 2 behaves differently from Math.floor(n / 2) for a negative n, because Math.floor rounds down and ~/ truncates toward zero. For positive values they agree, which is exactly what makes the difference hard to find.

And the conversion boundary is where the discipline is actually needed. as int truncates silently, so it is right for a double you computed and wrong for one you read. int.parse throws on anything but an integer literal, which is right for a string a human typed and wrong for one a client sent. int.tryParse returns null, which is right at a request boundary where rejection is an ordinary outcome and wrong inside a calculation, where a null would be silently swallowed and become a default two frames later. The three exist because those are three different situations, and choosing between them is a judgement about where the boundary is.

1.5 Strings and interpolation

UTF-16 by default, interpolation, raw strings, and the multi-line forms.

// a Dart String is a sequence of UTF-16 code units
String greeting = 'Hello';
print(greeting);                       // Hello
print('don\'t');                 // don't       - escape with \'
print("it's");                       // it's       - or use double quotes
print(r'no \n escape here');          // raw string: backslashes are literal

// interpolation
String name = 'Ana';
int age = 31;
print('Hello $name, you are $age');
print('next year: ${age + 1}');       // braces for an expression
print('nested: ${name.toUpperCase()}');

// multi-line
String query = '''
  SELECT id, name
  FROM users
  WHERE age >= 18
''';                                  // the indentation is stripped
print(query);

String json = """
  {"key": "value"}
""";

// raw multi-line, for regex and JSON
final pattern = r'''
  ^\d{3}-\d{4}$
''';
// the String methods you will use constantly
final s = '  Field Notes  ';
s.trim();                       // 'Field Notes'
s.trimLeft();                   // 'Field Notes  '
s.toUpperCase();
s.split(' ');                   // ['', '', 'Field', 'Notes', '', '']
s.replaceAll('Notes', 'Docs');
s.contains('Field');            // true
s.startsWith('  F');
s.padLeft(10, '0');             // 'Field Notes' padded
s.substring(2, 7);
s[0];                           // first code UNIT, not a character
s.runes.first;                  // first code POINT - use this for emoji
s.codeUnits.length;             // length in code units
s.runes.length;                 // length in characters

// raw and code units matter for:
//   - emoji and non-Latin scripts (a user name, an emoji picker)
//   - CJK text, where surrogate pairs appear
//   - anything that counts "characters" for a limit
// string building: do not concatenate in a loop
var s = '';
for (var i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
  s += 'line $i\n';              // O(n^2): each += copies the whole string
}

// use a StringBuffer
final buffer = StringBuffer();
for (var i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
  buffer.writeln('line $i');
}
final result = buffer.toString();

// or a list and join
final lines = List.generate(10000, (i) => 'line $i');
final text = lines.join('\n');

Interpolating a collection in a loop is the same trap with a subtler symptom: the loop looks fine and the test passes on a small input. StringBuffer for repeated appends, and join() when you already have a list. Both are O(n) and neither is hard to write.

UTF-16, and why length lies

A Dart String is a sequence of UTF-16 code units. That is the same representation JavaScript uses and different from what a reader of the text expects, which is why the string operations have a pairs of methods each.

OperationCountsRight for
s.lengthUTF-16 code unitsBuffer size, index arithmetic
s.runes.lengthCode points"How many characters does a reader see"
s.codeUnits.lengthUTF-16 code unitsThe same as length, spelled out
s.characters.lengthGrapheme clustersWhat a person would call a character
// an emoji is one code point, two code units, and one visible character
const emoji = 'a👍b';
emoji.length;                    // 4  - two units for the emoji
emoji.runes.length;              // 3  - three code points
emoji.characters.length;         // 3  - three clusters
'👍'.length;                     // 2  - on its own, still two units

// which makes three operations wrong for text and right for code
emoji.substring(0, 1);          // "a"  - fine here
'👍'.substring(0, 1);            // a LONE SURROGATE - invalid UTF-16

'👍'.substring(0, 2);            // "👍" - correct only because 2 happens to work
'👍'.runes.take(1).join();       // "👍" - correct for any character, always

// the grapheme case, which is the real one: a flag, a family, a keycap
const flag = '🇬🇧';                    // TWO code points, one letter
flag.length;                     // 4
flag.characters.length;          // 1  - and this is what a reader sees
flag.runes.map((r) => r.toUpperCase()).join();   // two letters

// so: runes for anything you iterate, characters for anything a human reads,
// and length only when you mean bytes of UTF-16

// and the escaping rules, which are strict on purpose
'it\'s';            // an escaped quote
"it's";              // a double-quoted literal needs no escape
r'a\nb';             // a RAW string: the backslash is a backslash
'''triple
quoted''';            // a multi-line literal, and $ still interpolates
r'''raw
multi-line''';       // and raw multi-line, for regex and SQL

Every other language with a UTF-8 string counts bytes, and Dart counts code units — so a String.length from a JavaScript habit transplanted here is wrong in the same way, for the same reason: the representation is an implementation detail and the reader is not thinking in code units.

// building strings, and why StringBuffer rather than +=
// += in a loop is O(n^2) if the runtime has to copy each time
var out = '';
for (var i = 0; i < 100000; i++){ out += i; }      // slow, and usually fine

final buf = StringBuffer();
for (var i = 0; i < 100000; i++){ buf.write(i); }
buf.toString();               // and the pattern for anything large

// the interpolation forms, in order of usefulness
final name = 'Ada', n = 3;
'$name'                      // Ada       - simple
'${name.toUpperCase()}'      // ADA       - an expression
'${n * n}'                   // 9         - an arithmetic expression
'$name'                      // Ada       - the SHORT form is not an object
'\${notInterpolated}'         // ${notInterpolated} - escaped
'${[1, 2].join("-")}'        // 1-2       - a method call is fine

// and the triple-quoted form, for anything multi-line
final sql = '''
  SELECT id, name
  FROM users
  WHERE active = true
''';
// no escaping needed, and the indentation is preserved - which means the
// common mistake is to indent the SQL for readability and change its meaning,
// so build it with a helper that dedents rather than by hand

Comparison, search, and the operations that are not what they look like

Dart's String inherits == from Object, so == on two strings is reference equality — which is almost never what a reader expects from a language where strings are values.

// == on String is identity, exactly as on any other object
const a = 'hello';
const b = 'hello';
a == b;                  // true  - and only because the compiler
                          // CANONICALISES the literal, not because it compares
const c = String.fromCharCode(104, 101, 108, 108, 111);
a == c;                  // FALSE - same characters, different objects
a == 'hello';            // true  - both literals, both canonicalised

// which is why the right comparison is a method, and the right one depends
// on the question
a.compareTo(b);          // 0   - ordering, for sorting
a == b;                  // false - identity
a.toString() == b.toString();   // true - value equality, via a string
// and the ergonomic answer, which allocates:
identical(a, c);         // false
// so: use compareTo to order, == only when identity is what you mean, and be
// aware that a cached string and a computed one are never ==

// search and replace, and the return value that surprises
'hello world'.indexOf('world');      // 6, or -1
'hello world'.contains('world');     // true  - Dart 3, and clearer
'hello'.padLeft(8, '.');              // '...hello'
'a,b,,c'.split(',');                  // ['a','b','','c']  - empty kept
',a,'.split(',');                     // ['', 'a', '']     - so is the edge
'  a  '.trim();                       // 'a'
'abc'.replaceFirst('b', 'X');         // 'aXc'
'abc'.replaceAll('b', 'X');           // 'aXc'
'ab'.replaceAll(RegExp('[ab]'), 'X'); // 'XX'
'abc'.replaceAllMapped(RegExp('[0-9]+'), (m) => '<${m[0]}>');

// and the one that is a trap: substring ranges are code units, and the
// range is [start, end)
'abcdef'.substring(2, 4);    // 'cd'
'abcdef'.substring(4, 2);    // RangeError - not a swap
'abcdef'.substring(-1, 3);   // RangeError

The identity comparison is the one worth internalising, because it looks like value equality in every language that has it and is not. a == b being true for two identical literals is an artefact of canonicalisation, so a test that passes with literals and fails with a computed string is a test that was never testing what it appeared to.

// the operations worth writing by hand, once
String? orDash(String? v) => v == null || v.isEmpty ? '-' : v;

extension Trunc on String {
  String ellipsis(int max) =>
      length <= max ? this : '${substring(0, max - 1)}…';
}
'long enough'.ellipsis(6);      // 'long e…'

// and the performance rule
var s = '';
for (var i = 0; i < 10000; i++) { s += 'x'; }   // may be O(n^2)

final b = StringBuffer();
for (var i = 0; i < 10000; i++) { b.write('x'); }
b.toString();                   // and this is O(n)
// so: StringBuffer for anything built in a loop, += for a handful of
// concatenations, and an interpolated literal for readability over speed

Choosing between length, runes.length and characters.length is less obvious than it looks, because the three answer different questions and only one of them matches the word "character". length counts UTF-16 code units, which is what a char[] would hold and what a buffer offset means. runes.length counts code points, which is what most people mean by "character" and is right for anything you iterate. characters.length counts grapheme clusters, which is what a reader sees, and it is the only one correct for text that contains a flag, an emoji with a skin-tone modifier, or a Devanagari conjunct.

The practical consequence is that any code that slices a string by index is working in code units whether it admits it or not, and is therefore wrong for a fraction of real input — a fraction that grows with internationalisation and is invisible in a test suite written in English. The fix is never to change which unit you think in; it is to stop slicing and iterate runes instead. [...s] gives code points, s.characters gives clusters, and both compose with where and map in a way that reads as intent.

Equality deserves its own paragraph because it is the one that produces a bug report rather than a crash. == on two strings is identity, inherited from Object, and it happens to be true for two identical literals only because the compiler canonicalises them. So a comparison that passes against a literal and fails against a string computed at run time is not a flaky test — it is a comparison that was never doing what it appeared to, and the canonicalisation was hiding it. compareTo for ordering, .toString() == or a field comparison for value, and identical when identity is genuinely the question.

1.6 Lists, Sets and Maps

The literal syntax, the const versions, and the difference that matters most.

final numbers = <int>[1, 2, 3];              // typed literal
final mixed = [1, 'two', 3.0];        // List<Object>, inferred
final inferred = [1, 2, 3];           // List<int>, inferred

final unique = <String>{'a', 'b'};  // Set literal: braces
final emptySet = <String>{};          // an empty set
final emptyList = <String>[];         // an empty list - note the brackets

final byId = <String, int>{'a': 1};  // Map literal
final emptyMap = <String, int>{};     // note: {} with no type args is a Map

// the const versions are deeply immutable
const fixed = [1, 2, 3];
const lookup = {'a': 1, 'b': 2};

// List is a growable List by default; a fixed-length one is faster
var growable = [1, 2, 3];
growable.add(4);
growable.removeAt(0);

final fixedLength = List<int>.filled(3, 0);   // 3 zeros, cannot add
final fromGenerator = List<int>.generate(5, (i) => i * i);
final zeroBased = List<int>.generate(5, (i) => i, growable: false);
// the difference you must know:
// List allows duplicates, Set does not
const l = [1, 1, 2];
const s = {1, 1, 2};
print(l.length);   // 3
print(s.length);   // 2
print(s.contains(1));  // true  - O(1)

// so: use a Set when you need membership tests, not order
final seen = <String>{};
for (final id in ids) {
  if (seen.add(id)) {      // add returns false if already present
    process(id);           // so this runs once per unique id
  }
}

// a Set literal is unordered: never depend on iteration order
const days = {'mon', 'tue', 'wed'};
print(days.first);   // not guaranteed to be 'mon'

The literal forms, and what each one defaults to

Dart has four collection literals and each has a default element type that is worth knowing, because [] is a List<dynamic> and not an empty list of anything.

LiteralIsDefaults toMutable
[]ListList<dynamic>Yes
{1, 2}SetSet<dynamic>Yes
{'a': 1}MapMap<dynamic, dynamic>Yes
{1, 'a': 2}MapMixed keysYes
const []ListUnmodifiable, canonicalNever
{...a, ...b}Spread——
{...m?}Null-aware spreadSkips a null—
{if (c) x}Collection if——
{for (x in y) f(x)}Collection for——
// the default element type is the thing that bites
var a = [];                    // List<dynamic> - a.add(42) is fine, and
a.add('text');                 //   a.add((1, 2)) is ALSO fine, which is the
                               //   problem: nothing is checked
final List<int> b = [];     // List<int> - and now it is

// so the rule: annotate every empty collection literal, and never `var` one
final seen = <String>{};             // Set<String>
final byId = <int, String>{};         // Map<int, String>
final results = <Result>[];           // List<Result>

// spread and its null-aware form, which is the Dart 3 idiom
final combined = [...first, ...second, extra];
final withMaybe = [...first, ...?maybe];   // ...? skips it if null
// versus the older and clumsier
final withMaybe2 = [...?maybe ?? []];

// collection-if and collection-for, evaluated at build time
final labels = <String>[
  'required',
  if (isAdmin) 'admin',
  for (final role in roles) 'role:$role',
];
// which is not sugar over map+where+expand - it produces ONE collection with
// no intermediate lists, and it composes: an if inside a for, a for inside a
// literal, both inside a const

// and the const forms, which are genuinely immutable and canonicalised
const routes = <String, String>{'/': '/home', '/a': '/about'};
routes['/'] = '/x';             // ERROR: UnmodifiableMapException at run time
const keys = <int>[1, 2, 3];
keys.add(4);                    // ERROR: UnmodifiableListException

// which is why a const collection is safe to share between two callers, and a
// final one is not: `final` fixes the reference, not the contents

The difference between final and const on a collection is the difference between a shared object that anyone can mutate and one nobody can. A final List passed to two callers is a shared mutable list, and the second caller to append wins — which is a bug that appears in production and not in a test, because a test usually has one caller.

Choosing between them, and the operations that differ

QuestionUseBecause
Ordered, duplicates, indexableListRandom access is O(1)
Membership in a loopSetO(1) instead of O(n)
Keyed lookupMapO(1), and the key may be any type
Lazy, once, read-onlyIterableNo allocation until iterated
Immutable, deeplyUnmodifiableListViewWraps rather than copies
Fixed-size, still mutable in placeList.filled(n, v, growable: false)No reallocation on add
// the operations that are NOT interchangeable, and this is where the bug is
final list = [1, 2, 3];
final set = {1, 2, 3};
final map = {1: 'a', 2: 'b', 3: 'c'};

set.add(4);               // ok
list.add(4);              // ok
map.add(4);               // ERROR: no add() - use map[4] = x
map[4] = 'd';             // correct

list.removeWhere((e) => e.isEven);   // List: an INSTANCE method
set.removeWhere((e) => e.isEven);    // Set:  NOT one - this does not compile
set.removeWhere((e) => e.isEven);    // the Set API is
set.remove(2);
// and the reason: removeWhere is defined on List, where removing an element
// shifts the others and the indices change. A Set has no indices to shift.

// so the four operations that exist on List and NOT on Set, and the Set
// equivalent for each
//   list.length          -> set.length          (both exist)
//   list[0]              -> set.first           (no index on a Set)
//   list.indexOf(x)      -> x in set           (no index to search)
//   list.removeWhere(f)  -> set.removeWhere(f)  <- does NOT exist

// Map equivalents
map.keys;          // Iterable
map.values;        // Iterable
map.entries;       // Iterable of MapEntry - and this is the only way to get both
for (final MapEntry(:key, :value) in map.entries) { }
map.containsKey(k);      // NOT map.contains(k) - that is the common error
map.containsValue(v);
map.putIfAbsent(k, () => compute());   // the compute-if-absent, and it is
                                        // the most useful method on Map

// and Map.fromEntries / entries to go the other way
Map.fromEntries([['a', 1], ['b', 2]]);   // {'a': 1, 'b': 2}
final grouped = Map.fromIterable(rows, key: (r) => r.category,
                                value: (r) => r);
grouped.forEach((rows, category) { });

The one that costs the most in review is map.contains(x), which does not exist — a reader who writes it from memory of another language gets a compile error, which is fine, but a reader who writes map.values.contains(x) gets an O(n) scan that looks like a lookup. map.containsValue(x) exists and is equally linear.

// building a Set of keys to make an O(1) membership test, which is the
// single most valuable thing to do with a Map in application code
final ids = users.map((u) => u.id).toSet();     // O(n) once

// BEFORE: O(n·m) - every message against every user
final allowed = messages.where((m) =>
    users.any((u) => u.id == m.userId));

// AFTER: O(n + m)
final allowed = messages.where((m) => ids.contains(m.userId));

// and the same shape, keeping the record rather than just the key
final byId = {for (final u in users) u.id: u};
final names = messages.map((m) => byId[m.userId]?.name ?? 'unknown').toList();

// which is also why a Map from a database result beats a List of records:
// the index is built once, in the place that already has the whole thing

The default element type is the thing that decides whether a collection is useful. An empty [] literal is a List<dynamic>, and a List<dynamic> accepts anything — so final a = []; followed by a hundred lines of code accumulates no type safety at all, and the compiler will not complain until a value reaches a place that expects something else. Annotating the empty literal costs six characters and is the difference between a container that catches mistakes and one that carries them to the point of use.

The related decision is final versus const, and it is about sharing rather than about immutability. A final List is an immutable reference to a mutable list, so passing it to two callers hands both of them the same object and the second one to append wins. That is a bug that reproduces reliably in a test with one caller and intermittently in production with two.
