A const List is immutable all the way down and canonicalised by the compiler, so it is safe to share and can be a default parameter value — at the cost of not being able to hold anything the compiler cannot see.

The third thing worth internalising is that the four collection types have genuinely different APIs rather than a shared interface with four implementations. removeWhere exists on List and not on Set, because removing an element from a list shifts the indices of everything after it while removing from a set does not. Indexing exists on List and not on Set for the same reason. So "which collection" is not only a performance question — it is a question about which methods you will have, and choosing the wrong one removes the operation you need rather than making it slow.

1.7 Control flow

Dart's control flow, including the case expression from Dart 3.

// if / else, with a ternary
if (age >= 18) {
  print('adult');
} else if (age >= 13) {
  print('teen');
} else {
  print('child');
}

final label = age >= 18 ? 'adult' : 'minor';

// for, with an index, a range, or a collection
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) print(i);
for (var i = 0; i < names.length; i++) print(names[i]);
for (final name in names) print(name);
for (final (i, name) in names.indexed) print('$i: $name');
for (var i = 3; i > 0; i--) print(i);

// while and do-while
var n = 0;
while (n < 3) { n++; }
do { n--; } while (n > 0);

// Dart 3: switch as an EXPRESSION, exhaustive without default
enum Status { active, suspended, closed }

String describe(Status status) {
  return switch (status) {
    Status.active => 'currently active',
    Status.suspended => 'paused, can be resumed',
    Status.closed => 'permanently closed',   // no default needed:
  };                                        // the compiler knows it is total
}

// pattern-based switch, also exhaustive
String describe2(Status status) {
  return switch (status) {
    Status.active || Status.suspended => 'open',
    Status.closed => 'shut',
  };
}

// break and continue
outer:
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  for (var j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
    if (j == 1) continue outer;
    if (i == 2) break outer;
    print('$i,$j');
  }
}

// assert: debug-time only, stripped in release
assert(age >= 0, 'age cannot be negative');   // only in debug builds

assert throws in a debug build and does nothing in a release build. That makes it right for internal invariants and completely wrong for validating user input. A user-supplied value must be checked with an if and a real error, because the release build will not check it for you.

Switch, and the two forms

Dart has a statement switch with optional case bodies and fall-through blocked by default, and a switch expression that is an expression because it has no case keyword. The expression form is the one to reach for.

StatementExpression
Syntaxswitch (x) { case 1: … }switch (x) { 1 => … }
Returns a valueNoYes
Needs a breakYes, per caseNo
Must be exhaustiveNoYes, over a sealed type
Usable in an argumentNoYes
Pattern matchingYesYes
// the expression form, and why it is the default choice
String label(String status) => switch (status) {
  'draft'     => 'Draft',
  'published' => 'Live',
  'archived'  => 'Archived',
  _           => 'Unknown',        // required without a sealed type
};

// exhaustiveness is checked by the compiler over a sealed hierarchy
sealed class Shape {}
class Circle extends Shape { final double r; Circle(this.r); }
class Square extends Shape { final double s; Square(this.s); }

double area(Shape shape) => switch (shape) {
  Circle(r: var r) => 3.14159 * r * r,
  Square(s: var s) => s * s,
};
// add a third subclass and this STOPS COMPILING until the new case is handled
// which is the entire value: the compiler proves the switch is complete

// the statement form, where break is mandatory and non-empty case falls
// through silently - the classic Dart bug
switch (command) {
  case 'add':
    addItem();
    break;                      // WITHOUT this, 'add' also runs 'save'
  case 'save':
    saveItem();
    break;
  case 'quit':
    exit(0);                    // no break needed - it is the last case
}

// and the guards, which replace a chain of ifs
switch (pair) {
  case (1, 2):
    print('one and two');
  case (int x, int y) when x > y:
    print('descending');
  case (int x, int y):
    print('two ints, ascending');
  default:
    print('something else');
}
// the loops, and the one that is a mistake
for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) { }      // C-style, when the index matters
for (final x in list) { }              // the default: iterate a collection
for (final entry in map.entries) { }   // a Map needs .entries or .keys

while (cond) { }                      // cond first
do { } while (cond);                  // body first - runs at least once

// and the loop that belongs in a function, not a loop
for (final row in rows) {
  if (row.isHeader) continue;
  if (row.isBlank) break;
  process(row);
}
// every iteration of the outer loop is a full list scan, so this is O(n·m)
// and the fix is to build an index once, outside the loop:
final index = {for (final r in rows) r.id: r};
for (final row of refs) {
  final target = index[row.targetId];
  if (target == null) continue;
  process(target);
}
// which also reads better, and the reason it reads better is that it is
// correct - which is usually the reason something reads better

// labelled break, for nested loops
outer:
for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) {
  for (var j = 0; j < n; j++) {
    if (grid[i][j] == target) { break outer; }
  }
}

// and the collection-for equivalent, which needs no label
for (final row in grid) {
  for (final cell in row) {
    if (cell == target) break;         // breaks the INNER for only
  }
}

The control flow that is not a loop

Three constructs carry most of the weight in idiomatic Dart code, and none of them is a loop: a switch expression, a cascade, and a collection comprehension. Choosing them over the loop they replace usually removes nesting.

Instead ofWriteReads as
A chain of if assigning a variableA switch expressionA single expression with a value
A temporary variable built by mutationA cascadeOne statement, one target
for building a listA collection literalData, in one place
if (x != null) return x; then using x?? or a guard clauseThe happy path first
An early return in a loop bodyany or firstWhereOrNullThe question, asked
// a cascade, which is a statement form for configuring one object
final buffer = StringBuffer()
  ..write('a')
  ..write('b')
  ..writeln();
// reads top to bottom, targets one object, and needs no temporary

// versus
final buffer = StringBuffer();
buffer.write('a');
buffer.write('b');
buffer.writeln();
// ...which is four lines and three chances to write `buffer` twice by mistake.
// The cascade is not shorter for its own sake: it makes it VISIBLE that
// nothing else is touched.

// and the conditional cascade, for a configuration that may not apply
final builder = Builder()
  ?..name = name          // applied only if builder is non-null
  ?..size = size;
final plain = Builder()
  ..name = name           // unconditional - a NullPointerError if null
  ..size = size;

// the collection comprehension, which is data rather than steps
final byStatus = <String, List<Task>>{};
for (final t in tasks) {
  byStatus.putIfAbsent(t.status, () => []).add(t);
}

// versus
final byStatus = <String, List<Task>>{
  for (final t in tasks) t.status: [
    ...?byStatus[t.status],   // read the map being built - legal but subtle
    t,
  ],
};
// so the comprehension is the right tool for BUILDING a new collection from
// another, and the wrong tool for accumulating into one you are mutating -
// which is the case putIfAbsent exists for.

// and the early-return-in-a-loop question, asked directly
tasks.any((t) => t.isOverdue);              // true if at least one
tasks.every((t) => t.isOverdue);            // true if all
tasks.where((t) => t.isOverdue).length;    // how many
tasks.firstWhereOrNull((t) => t.isOverdue);  // which one, or null
tasks.firstWhere((t) => t.isOverdue);       // which one, or StateError
tasks.sort((a, b) => a.due.compareTo(b.due));  // returns void - do not chain
tasks.where((t) => t.isOverdue).forEach(remind);
// ...note the last one returns void, and forEach on a lazy where re-walks the
// predicate per element, so filter-then-loop is often the honest version

The pattern worth adopting is: ask the question with the collection's own method — any, every, firstWhereOrNull — rather than writing a loop with a flag variable. It removes the flag, removes the nesting, and reads as the question rather than as the mechanism for answering it.

The statement switch and the switch expression differ in ways that are easy to state and easy to forget. The statement form requires a break in every non-final case, and omitting it produces fall-through — so a case that handles one command silently handles the next too, and the only symptom is that something happened twice. The expression form has no case keyword and no break at all, because each arm is an expression that yields the value, so fall-through is not expressible.

That is the reason to prefer the expression form even when exhaustiveness does not force it. It removes a class of bug by construction rather than by review, the same way an exhaustive switch over a sealed type removes the "someone added a subclass and forgot a case" bug. Both are cases where the language can make a mistake impossible instead of merely discouraged, and both are worth preferring over the alternative even though the alternative is shorter to write.

The third thing is the nested-loop exit. A break inside an inner loop breaks the inner loop, and the outer loop continues — which is usually not what a reader assumes when the loops are both for and there is no label nearby. The two honest answers are a label, or restructuring so the nesting is not there: a collection comprehension, a where, or a firstWhereOrNull for the "find it and stop" case. The second is better, because it also removes the flag variable the loop needed.

1.8 Imports, libraries and main

Import syntax, the part/part of rule, and library privacy.

// four forms
import 'dart:math';                      // the core library
import 'dart:math' as math;              // with a prefix, for conflicts
import 'dart:math' show max, min;        // only these members
import 'dart:math' hide Random;          // everything except this
import 'package:http/http.dart' as http; // a package: URL
import 'src/models.dart';                // a relative path

// conflicts are the usual reason for a prefix
import 'package:flutter/material.dart' as ui;   // not used here, but the
import 'package:my_app/ui.dart' as mine;        // pattern is identical

// library privacy: a leading underscore is private TO THE LIBRARY
// src/parser.dart
class Parser { }                 // public: other files can use it
class _Token { }                // private: only parser.dart can see it
int _cache = 0;                 // private

// one file can be several libraries with `part`
// src/service.dart
library service;                 // optional and deprecated; a plain part
                                // comment is now the convention
import 'dart:async';
part 'service_io.dart';
part 'service_web.dart';

// src/service_io.dart
part of 'service.dart';          // shares the imports and scope above
class Service { }
// package structure that scales
// lib/
//   my_app.dart              the public API: what others import
//   src/
//     models/
//       entry.dart
//       entry.g.dart          generated
//     data/
//       repository.dart
//       local_db.dart
//     platform/
//       storage.dart          the interface
//       storage_io.dart       the dart:io implementation
//       storage_web.dart      the web implementation
//     ui/
//       screens/
//
// bin/main.dart               the executable entry point
// test/                       tests
// test_driver/                 integration tests
// example/                     a runnable example, kept compiling

Keep lib/my_app.dart a thin barrel file that exports what is public. Everything under lib/src/ is conventionally private, which means you can restructure freely without breaking anyone. The underscore gives privacy within a file; the src/ convention gives it across the package.

Exercises 2

  1. Write a program that declares variables with var, final and const, and trigger each error the analyzer gives when you break the rule.
  2. Prove the int to double conversion is not implicit, then write the correct version and the rounding-aware version.
  3. Build a string from 10,000 lines first with +=, then with StringBuffer. Time both.
  4. Write an exhaustive switch expression over a three-value enum. Delete a case and confirm the compiler complains - that is the point of the feature.
  5. Create a package with a lib/src/ structure, a barrel file, and a private class, and confirm the privacy rules hold.
  6. Write a function using the wrong base property and observe what runtimeType reports. The bug is the same in every language.

Libraries, parts, and the three ways to share code

FormMergesUse for
importOne libraryThe normal case
import … as pOne library, under a prefixTwo libraries with clashing names
import … hide XOne library, minus namesTaking only what you use
import … show X, YOne library, plus namesWidening a hide
exportRe-publishes a libraryA barrel file, or a facade
part / part ofSame librarySplitting one library across files

The distinction that matters: import gives you a namespace, part splices the file into the same library. A part file has no imports of its own, shares every private name with its parent, and cannot be imported by anything else. Using it to split a library is legitimate; using it to organise a package is a mistake, because the files are no longer independently meaningful.

// import: names come in, and a prefix renames the whole namespace
import 'dart:math';
import 'dart:math' as math;
import 'package:collection/collection.dart' show UnmodifiableListView;
import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;      // the idiomatic use of a prefix
final res = await http.get(uri);

// export: a barrel, so consumers import one thing
// lib/models.dart
export 'user.dart';
export 'order.dart';
// then
import 'package:acme/models.dart';      // and get both
// export supports the same show/hide, which is how a facade narrows a
// package's public surface:
export 'package:http/http.dart' show Client, Response;

// part: one library, several files
// lib/parser.dart
library parser;                        // optional in Dart 3
part 'lexer.dart';
part 'ast.dart';
// lib/lexer.dart
part of 'parser.dart';                 // shares parser.dart's scope
// so a private name in parser.dart IS visible in lexer.dart - which is the
// point, and also the risk: a part file cannot be tested or reused alone

// deferred import: load a library later
import 'package:acme/heavy.dart' deferred as heavy;
await heavy.loadLibrary();             // the network or disk cost happens HERE
heavy.parse(text);
// which exists for the web, where a deferred library is a separate chunk -
// and is almost never worth it on native, where the whole binary is loaded
// anyway and the deferral buys nothing but complexity

// and the two rules that are not negotiable
// 1. imports are relative to the FILE, not the package root
import '../models/user.dart';          // correct from lib/parser/lexer.dart
// 2. never import 'src/...' - it is not in the package's public surface, so it
//    breaks the moment the internals move
import 'package:acme/src/impl.dart';   // WRONG: works locally, breaks for users

2 · Null Safety in Depth

2.1 What sound null safety buys you2.2 Flow analysis and promotion2.3 late and the definite assignment gap2.4 The ! operator, and when it is acceptable2.5 The ! and ? operators side by side2.6 Null-aware members and collections2.7 Refactoring to remove nulls2.8 Designing an API that avoids null

The most important chapter in the language. Sound null safety moves a whole class of crashes from runtime to compile time, and this chapter is about working with it rather than against it.

2.1 What sound null safety buys you

The guarantee, and the single change that makes it true.

// before null safety, this compiled and then crashed at runtime:
String s = getName();        // returns String? at heart
print(s.length);             // Null check operator used on a null value

// with sound null safety, the same code does not compile:
String s = getName();        // ERROR: String? cannot be assigned to String
print(s.length);             // the error moves to the assignment

// the guarantee: if a variable's static type is non-nullable, at every
// point where it is read it is definitely not null. No exceptions.
// That is what makes the check cheap AND the crashes impossible.

// the price: the migration. Every `T` that can be absent becomes `T?`.
// That is the whole cost, and it is a one-time, mechanical change.
// the rules, in full
//
// 1. the type `T` means "always a value"; `T?` means "a value or null"
// 2. `T?` is a SUPERtype: T is assignable to T?, not the reverse
// 3. the default value of a nullable variable is null
// 4. a nullable variable must be checked before use
// 5. `late` declares a non-nullable variable with a deferred assignment
// 6. flows (`..`, `?.`, `!`) capture a value at a point in time
// 7. `!` asserts non-null and throws if wrong
// 8. the top type `Object?` includes null; `Object` does not

Sound null safety, and what "sound" buys

Before Dart 2.12 a type said nothing about nullability: String could hold null and the compiler said nothing. Sound null safety makes the type total — every non-nullable type is guaranteed non-null at every point the compiler can see — and that is what allows a compiler to emit code with no null checks at all.

LegacySound
StringMay be null; every use uncheckedNever null; a runtime check is unnecessary
String?Same as aboveNullable; the compiler forces a check
dynamicAnythingAnything, checked at run time
Null dereferenceA crash at run timeA compile error, unless the value is dynamic
Generated codeNull checks everywhereNone for a non-nullable type
// the whole guarantee, in one function
String lengthOf(String s) => s.length;   // s.length can never be a null check

// the compiler rewrites a nullable access into a check plus a throw
String? maybe;
// maybe.length;          // ERROR - the operator does not exist on String?
final n = maybe?.length;   // int? - the ?. short-circuits to null
maybe!.length;              // throws at run time - assert non-null, and the
                             // compiler now trusts it for the rest of the scope

// the three ways to establish non-nullability, and what each costs
final a = maybe ?? 'default';              // a fallback, always safe
final b = maybe?.isNotEmpty == true;        // a guard, as a bool
final c = list.firstWhere((e) => e.id == id);  // throws if absent
final d = list.where((e) => e.id == id).firstOrNull;   // null if absent

// the flow analysis, which is what makes it tractable
String f(String? input) {
  if (input == null) return '';
  // input is promoted to String HERE, and stays promoted for the rest
  return input.toUpperCase();
}

// the promotion rules, and where they stop
void g(String? input) {
  print(input?.length);      // fine - no promotion needed
  print(input.length);       // ERROR - not promoted yet

  if (input != null) {
    print(input.length);     // fine - promoted
  }

  final copy = input;        // copy is String? - a new, unpromoted binding
  print(copy.length);        // ERROR
  print(input.length);       // fine - input itself is still promoted
}

The phrase "sound" is doing real work: it means the guarantee holds for every execution, not merely that the compiler checked the code it could see. A dynamic value inside a sound-null-safe program breaks the guarantee — which is why dynamic is the boundary where the discipline has to be re-applied by hand.

What it costs to migrate, and what it buys at run time

The migration is a single flag and a mechanical set of errors, and it is worth doing in one pass rather than gradually: a half-migrated package has both rules in force and the compiler reports two different messages for the same mistake.

// enabling it, and the flag that gates the migration
// pubspec.yaml
environment:
  sdk: '>=3.0.0 <4.0.0'

// the three errors the migration produces, and what each means
// 1. "The operand can't be unconditionally null because of the type"
//    -> a nullable value is used where a non-null is required
String bad(String? s) => s.length;             // add !, ??, or a check

// 2. "The argument type 'X?' can't be assigned to the parameter type 'X'"
//    -> a nullable argument to a non-nullable parameter
render(fetchMaybe());                           // fetchMaybe() returns T?

// 3. "The method 'x' can't be unconditionally invoked because the receiver
//     can be null"
//    -> the same, through a receiver
node!.children

// the migration tools, which do the mechanical part
dart migrate                       // rewrites what it can, comments the rest
dart fix --apply                   // the lints that have codemods
dart analyze --fatal-infos         // CI gate

// what it buys, concretely
// before: every field access on a String carried a null check
String f(String s) => s.length;
// after:  the compiler knows s is non-null, so it emits the field offset
//         directly - no branch, no call to a helper
//
// so the win is not only safety: it is that the generated code for sound
// code is smaller and faster, which is what makes the migration worth doing
// for performance reasons alone on a hot path.

// and what it costs
// - every public API's signature changes, so it is a breaking change
// - a caller in unsound code still gets dynamic behaviour, so the guarantee
//   is only as good as the boundary where dynamic is introduced
// - generics from Java or C# arrive nullable, so interop needs a shim
// the boundary, and it is narrow
// Everything on the way IN is checked; everything on the way OUT is trusted.
class Api {
  // IN: nullable, because the wire may omit it, and validated immediately
  static Order? parse(Map<String, Object?> json) {
    final id = json['id'];
    if (id is! int) return null;
    return Order(id, json['total'] as num? ?? 0);
  }

  // OUT: non-nullable, because the rest of the program has proved it
  final List<Order> orders;    // never List<Order?>
}

// and the two ways the guarantee leaks, both of them visible in review
// 1. a dynamic value in the middle
final x = json['total'] as num? ?? 0;   // fine
final y = (json['total'] as dynamic) + 1;   // UNSOUND: dynamic breaks it
print(y);                                  // and no check happens

// 2. an unsound generic from another language
// Java's String maps to String? in Dart, because Java allows null
void render(String name) {}
render(javaResult);          // ERROR: String? to String
render(javaResult!);         // what every interop shim does, on every field

// so the discipline is: accept dynamic or nullable AT THE BOUNDARY, convert
// immediately, and never let either past the constructor. Everything
// downstream is then operating on a guarantee rather than on a hope.

What soundness actually buys is a guarantee about every execution rather than about the code the compiler could read. A compiler can see that a local is non-null on one path and fail to see it on another, and the difference matters: a tool that checks "does this expression ever evaluate to null" is giving a weaker answer than one that has proved the type total. Dart's claim is the stronger one, which is why the emitted code for a non-nullable field access is a field offset rather than a branch.

The cost is concentrated at one place: the boundary. Every value arriving from JSON, from a plugin, from a platform channel or from Java is dynamic or nullable, and everything downstream is sound only to the extent that those values were converted at the edge. A program that lets a dynamic value reach the middle has opted out of the guarantee without saying so, and the failure will be a run-time error in the one place where nothing was checked.

Which is why the migration advice is to do it in one pass rather than file by file. A package with some files migrated and some not has two sets of rules in force, the compiler reports the same mistake two different ways depending on which file it is in, and the review argument about "is this file done yet" costs more than the mechanical work. dart migrate plus dart fix --apply handles the mechanical part, and the judgement calls are the ones worth spending review time on.

2.2 Flow analysis and promotion

The feature that makes null safety ergonomic: the compiler tracks what you have already checked.

void example(String? input) {
  // ERROR: the method 'length' can't be unconditionally invoked on
  // a nullable receiver
  // print(input.length);

  // promote with a null check: after this, input is a String
  if (input == null) {
    return;                  // early return narrows the rest of the block
  }
  print(input.length);       // no error: input is promoted to String

  // or use &&, which narrows only in the right-hand side
  if (input != null && input.length > 3) {
    print(input[0]);         // still promoted
  }

  // the pattern form, which also works on properties
  if (input case final String s when s.isNotEmpty) {
    print(s.toUpperCase());
  }

  // and the assertion form
  assert(input != null);
  print(input.length);       // promoted by the assert
}
// promotion does NOT work for:
//  1. a local variable captured and modified by a closure
//  2. a getter (it could return something different next time)
//  3. a top-level or static field (any code could change it)
//  4. anything behind a non-nullable reference that might be mutated

class Cache {
  String? _name;
  String? get name => _name;         // a getter: no promotion

  void bad() {
    if (name != null) {
      print(name.length);   // ERROR: a getter result is not promotable
    }
    // the fix: capture it in a local first
    final n = name;
    if (n != null) {
      print(n.length);      // fine: a local is promotable
    }
  }
}

void closureExample() {
  String? value = 'a';
  void modify() { value = null; }

  if (value != null) {
    modify();
    // print(value.length);  // ERROR: modified by a closure
  }
}

When promotion is refused, the fix is almost always to capture the value in a local. That is not a workaround, it is better code: a local cannot change under you, so the rest of the function reasons about a fixed value. The compiler is telling you that your assumption was not guaranteed.

Promotion, and the four things that stop it

Type promotion is the compiler rewriting a variable's type from T? to T inside a branch where it has proven it non-null. It removes null checks from the generated code, and it is why Dart does not pay the cost soundness promises.

Blocked byExampleFix
A fieldif (f != null) f.xTake a final local
A global or top-level variableif (g != null) g.xSame
A write in betweencheck, then assign null, then useReorder, or copy to a local
A closure before the checkcaptured, so it could be reassignedCheck inside the closure
class Box {
  String? name;
  String? get label {
    if (name != null) return name.toUpperCase();   // ERROR - name is a field
    return '';
  }
}
// the reason: any code could have set field to null between the check and the
// use, so a compiler that promoted it would be wrong

// the fix, and it is one word
class Box {
  String? name;
  String? get label {
    final n = name;              // a local, and final
    if (n != null) return n.toUpperCase();   // promoted
    return '';
  }
}
// or a pattern, which binds rather than narrows
String? upper(Object? o) => switch (o) {
  final String s when s.isNotEmpty => s.toUpperCase(),
  _ => null,
};
// or null-aware access, when promotion is not worth arranging
print(name?.toUpperCase());

// the version to recognise: a getter or a global
int get cached => _cache != null ? _cache!.length : 0;   // _cache! on every read
// which is correct but noisy, and the local-copy version is not
int get cached2 {
  final c = _cache;
  return c != null ? c.length : 0;
}

// and what promotion does NOT do: it never changes the declared type
void h(String? s) {
  if (s == null) return;
  print(s);              // s is promoted to String HERE
  s = null;              // and the promotion is invalidated by the write
  print(s.length);       // ERROR again - the assignment reset it
}

Promotion in closures, loops, and the places it silently fails

// a loop variable promotes, and stays promoted, because it is a local
void f(List<String?> names) {
  for (final name in names) {
    if (name == null) continue;
    print(name.length);        // fine - promoted, and `name` is a local
  }
}

// a field does not, because anything could change it between the check and
// the use - and the compiler is right to refuse
class Repo {
  List<Row>? rows;
  int count() {
    if (rows != null) return rows!.length;    // the ! is necessary
    return 0;
  }
  int countClean() {
    final r = rows;              // one extra line, no assertion
    return r != null ? r.length : 0;
  }
}

// an assignment invalidates the promotion
void g(String? s) {
  if (s == null) return;
  print(s.length);               // promoted
  s = null;                      // ...and here the promotion is gone
  print(s.length);               // ERROR
}

// a closure does not, because it may run later
void h(String? s) {
  if (s == null) return;
  print(() => s.length);       // ERROR - s is captured and could change
  final f = s;                   // a final local CAN be captured
  print(() => f.length);       // fine
}

// the false positive, which is the version that reads as a compiler bug
void i(List<String>? names) {
  if (names == null) return;
  names.add('x');                // ERROR - and correctly: names is a PARAMETER
  // ...which cannot be promoted because a parameter could be reassigned
  // inside a closure the compiler cannot see. The fix is non-obvious enough
  // that it is worth knowing:
  if (names == null) throw ArgumentError('names required');  // still an error
  // so for a parameter, promote into a local:
  final n = names;
  if (n == null) throw ArgumentError('names required');
  n.add('x');                    // fine
}

// and the pattern form, which binds rather than narrows, and has no
// restriction on locals only
final len = switch (value) {
  final String s when s.isNotEmpty => s.length,
  _ => 0,
};
// the bound name is a new local, always non-nullable, always in scope only
// inside the pattern - which is why it composes with closures and with `when`

Promotion's restriction to locals is not conservatism — it is soundness. A field or a parameter could be changed by any other code between the check and the use, so a compiler that assumed otherwise would generate code that crashes. The one-word fix, a final local, is worth knowing by heart because it appears in almost every "the compiler says this is null but it isn't" report.

The restriction of promotion to locals is the part that generates the most confusion, and it is worth being precise about why: a field or a parameter can be changed by code the compiler cannot see — a closure, another isolate's callback, a subclass overriding a getter — between the check and the use. A compiler that promoted it would be generating code that is correct for the code it read and wrong for the program it is part of. Since Dart's claim is soundness rather than approximate analysis, refusing is the only consistent choice.

The consequence is that a final local is the single most useful idiom in the language for this, and the pattern is worth recognising mechanically: any time a promotion error appears on a field, copy it to a final local and use that. The copy is one line, it costs nothing at run time, and it reads better than the ! it replaces because it states the assumption rather than asserting it.

Two related cases behave differently and are worth separating. Promotion does not survive an assignment, because the compiler is right that the value changed — though a value assigned inside the same scope and not captured is often a sign the flow is doing something the author did not intend. And promotion does not cross a closure boundary, but a final local does, because a closure over a final local captures the value rather than the variable. That difference is why the fix works for asynchronous code and for callbacks, not just for straight-line flow.

2.3 late and the definite assignment gap

When late is the right tool, and the four ways to initialise it safely.

// late: "this will definitely have a value by the time you read it"
class Api {
  late final String baseUrl;         // assigned once, in configure()
  late final Future<Client> client;  // assigned in main()

  void configure(String url) {
    baseUrl = url;                  // in source order
  }
}

// 1. field declaration with a computed value
late final int startTime = DateTime.now().millisecondsSinceEpoch;

// 2. lazy, computed on first read
late final RegExp pattern = RegExp(r'^\d+$');

// 3. assigned in main() after an await
late final Database db;
Future<void> main() async {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  db = await Database.open();
  runApp(const MyApp());
}

// 4. in a test
late final Fixture f;
setUpAll(() async { f = await Fixture.load(); });
// the failure mode, and how it presents
class Service {
  late final String name;
  void init() { name = 'x'; }
}

final s = Service();
print(s.name);        // throws LateInitializationError
                      // with a clear message - better than a null crash,
                      // but still a crash

// rules for using late safely:
//   1. exactly one code path assigns it, and it always runs first
//   2. never assign it in a method that can be called later
//   3. final: the compiler stops you reassigning it
//   4. if the value can genuinely be absent, use T? and handle it

Do not reach for late to silence a nullable field. late String x and String? x are different contracts: the first says "always there", the second says "sometimes there, and you will handle it". Turning the second into the first does not remove the null check, it moves the crash from a helpful compiler error to a LateInitializationError at an unpredictable moment.

Three ways to defer initialisation, and what each is for

FormAssignedReads before assignmentUse for
Nullable fieldAny time, any number of timesForced to handle nullIt genuinely has no value yet
late finalOnce, lazilyThrows LateInitializationErrorYou can guarantee one assignment
Nullable local + ??——A computed default
A factory constructor——Deriving it from arguments
// 1. the nullable field, and the discipline it requires
class Config {
  String? endpoint;
  String resolved => endpoint ?? 'http://localhost:3000';
  void use() { print(endpoint.length); }    // ERROR - and that is the point
}

// 2. late final: assigned once, on first use, and the compiler stops asking
class Session {
  late final User user;         // User, not User? - no null checks downstream
  Session(this._token);
  final String _token;
  // ... somewhere much later, in an initState or a hydrate method:
  void hydrate(User u) { user = u; }
}
final s = Session(token);
print(s.user.name);        // LateInitializationError: Field 'user' has not
                           // been initialized - a clear message, at the read

// late final cannot be reassigned, so it is the strongest of the three
late final int cache;
cache = 1;
cache = 2;                 // ERROR: 'cache' can't be set as it is final

// 3. the lazy getter, which is the idiomatic answer for a computed value
class Report {
  final List<Row> rows;
  Report(this.rows);
  int? _total;
  int get total => _total ??= rows.fold(0, (n, r) => n + r.price);
}
// the `??=` on a nullable field gives: compute once, remember, and the
// declared type stays non-nullable, so callers never handle null

// 4. late on a LOCAL is an error, which is right
void f() {
  late int x;                // ERROR: locals do not need it - just assign
  print(x);                 // ERROR: used before assigned
}
// a local is initialised on the path that reaches it, and the compiler
// already proves that; `late` on a local would suppress a check that is
// currently useful
Prefer a lazy getter over late wherever the value is derivable from state you already have. A late final field makes "has this been set yet?" a run-time question the type system cannot answer; a getter with ??= behind it makes the same value available with no possibility of the uninitialised state at all.

The order late initialises in, and what throws

// the initialiser runs LAZILY, on first read - not at construction
class Expensive {
  Expensive() { print('constructed'); }
  late final data = _load();      // not printed yet
  static String _load() { print('loading'); return 'x'; }
}
final e = Expensive();             // "constructed" only
print(e.data);                     // "loading" - now

// which is the point, and also the trap: a late final that throws does not
// retry. The second read throws the SAME error, because the initialiser is
// not re-run after a failure. That is a deliberate difference from a lazy
// Map cache, and it surprises anyone porting one.
late final parsed = jsonDecode(text);   // throws FormatException on first read
                                      // and again on every read after

// if you want retry semantics, use a nullable field
String? _parsed;
String get parsed {
  try {
    return _parsed ??= jsonDecode(text);
  } catch (_) {
    return '';                    // or rethrow, or return an error
  }
}

// and the three exceptions it throws, which are distinct and all confusing
late final a;                     // LateInitializationError on read
late final int b;                 // LateInitializationError
// a late FINAL cannot be read before assignment at all if the compiler can
// see the write - so the error is reserved for the write-after-use case:
//   late final int x;
//   print(x);                     // ERROR: used before assigned - a COMPILE error
//   x = 1;
// so a compile-time error where the compiler can prove it, and
// LateInitializationError where it cannot - which is a field written from
// another method.

// and the field-initialiser order, which is a real bug source
class Ordered {
  final String a = _a();
  final String b = _a() + 'b';    // runs AFTER a's initialiser
  static String _a() => 'a';
}
// Dart runs field initialisers in DECLARATION order, before the constructor
// body - the same rule as most languages, and worth knowing because a
// derived field must be declared after the one it derives from
// the three-way choice, once
class Widget {
  // A. genuinely may not exist yet
  final Widget? child;
  Widget(this.child);

  // B. exists, and you can guarantee one assignment - but lazily, because
  //    computing it in the constructor would be expensive or would need
  //    something the constructor does not have
  late final LayoutNode layout;
  void attach(LayoutNode n) { layout = n; }

  // C. exists and is derivable - and this is the one to prefer, because the
  //    uninitialised state cannot exist at all
  final String _raw;
  String get title => _raw.trim().isEmpty ? DEFAULT : _raw.trim();
  String get normalised => _normalised ??= _raw.trim().toLowerCase();
  String? _normalised;
}

// B is the one that reaches for `late` and regrets it. The compiler cannot
// prove that attach() is called, so the type system has nothing to say about
// whether layout is safe to read - and the error arrives at the READ, in a
// different file, from a caller who never knew about attach().

The property that distinguishes late final from a nullable field is the compiler's belief about how many times it can be assigned. A nullable field admits null, which means every read downstream has to handle it, and that handling is what spreads the uncertainty. A late final field has a non-nullable type, so downstream code reads it without a check — and the price is that "has it been assigned" becomes a question the type system cannot answer and the run time has to.

The price is also paid in a way that is easy to overlook: the error arrives at the read, in a different file, from a caller who has no idea an assignment was expected. A field written by an attach() method in one file and read in another is invisible at the read site, and the resulting LateInitializationError names the field rather than the missing call. That is a poor diagnostic for a mechanism whose whole purpose is to defer work.

So the ordering of preference is worth having explicit: derive the value where you can and use a getter, because then the uninitialised state cannot exist; use a nullable field where the value genuinely may not be there yet, because then null is honest; and reach for late only where the value exists for certain but computing it eagerly would be wrong — a constructor that lacks a dependency, an expensive computation needed only if some property is read. The third case is real and worth the trade, but it should be the third case.

2.4 The ! operator, and when it is acceptable

The null assertion, and the honest accounting of what each use costs.

// ! asserts "this is not null" and throws if it is wrong
String? maybe;
print(maybe!.length);     // throws at runtime if maybe is null

// when it is genuinely correct:
//   1. a value the compiler cannot see the source of, and you have
//      checked by other means
//   2. a value proven non-null by an invariant the compiler cannot see
//      (e.g. checked in a factory constructor)
//   3. after a null check on a DIFFERENT reference to the same object
//   4. an `!` on a just-initialised local in a test setup

// acceptable: after a check
final raw = input.text.trim();
if (raw.isEmpty) return;
final value = raw.length > 0 ? int.parse(raw) : null;
print(value!);            // hmm, still risky - prefer narrowing

// acceptable: an invariant enforced in the constructor
class Point {
  final int x, y;
  Point(this.x, this.y)
      : assert(x >= 0, 'x must be non-negative'),
        assert(y >= 0, 'y must be non-negative');
}

void use() {
  final p = Point(1, 2);
  print(p.x + p.y);       // safe, and provable by inspection
}

// NOT acceptable: silencing an error you have not investigated
// final rows = query.result!;   // what if result is null?
// final el = document.querySelector('#x')!.innerHTML;  // not in the DOM?
// if you must, prove it with a test rather than a comment
import 'package:test/test.dart';

test('init() always sets baseUrl before use', () {
  final app = MyApp()..init();
  expect(app.baseUrl, isNotNull);
  expect(() => app.request(), returnsNormally);
});

// the honest count: audit your own code
//   grep -c '!' src/          non-comment, non-!=
//   every one should be justifiable in a code review

A good rule: ! is acceptable when the invariant is enforced somewhere you control - a constructor assert, a factory that validates, a null check three lines above - and unacceptable when it is papering over a case you have not thought about. The test is whether you could explain, in a review, exactly why it cannot be null.

The three operators, and when the ! is right

// ?.: short-circuits and yields null
final len = maybe?.length;              // int?
final n = maybe?.length ?? 0;           // int

// !: asserts non-null. Throws if wrong.
maybe!.length;                          // safe ONLY if you can prove it

// ??: the left operand if non-null, else the right. Not `||`.
final n2 = a ?? b;
// the difference, and it is not cosmetic:
0 ?? 99;        // 0    - zero is a value
0 || 99;        // 99   - zero is falsy
'' ?? 'x';      // ''   - the empty string is a value
false ?? true;  // false
// which is why `??` is correct wherever the falsy value is legitimate, and
// `||` is a bug whenever a legitimate value happens to be 0, "", or false

// the compound forms
a ??= b;               // assign b if a is null - not if a is falsy
a ??= compute();       // compute() runs only when needed, which is the point
cfg.port ??= 8080;     // the common shape: a default for a field

// and the combination that reads as "or else"
final user = session.user ?? throw StateError('no session');
final port = env['PORT'] ?? '3000';

// what ! actually costs
class Config { String? host; }
void connect() {
  final h = host!;       // Throws LateInitializationError or a cast error
  print(h);              // if host is genuinely optional
}
// the compiler records that h is String from the ! onwards, so every use of h
// skips a check - which is the optimisation, and also the risk: ! converts a
// compile-time question into a run-time crash with no static trace back to it

// so the rule: ! when the invariant is enforced elsewhere and is true by
// construction; ?? when null is a legitimate state; a null check when it is not
class Buffer {
  final List<int> _bytes;
  Buffer(this._bytes);
  void write(int b) => _bytes.add(b);
}
Buffer.of(List<int> b) : _bytes = List.of(b)..ensureCapacity(b.length);
// ...where the constructor guarantees it, so a ! inside the class is
// unnecessary and a ?? would be wrong

Where ?? and ??= differ from what you would write

// the falsy-vs-nullish table, which is the whole point
int? a = 0, b = 1;
a ?? 99;      // 0    - nullish coalescing: 0 is a VALUE
a || 99;      // 99   - short-circuit: 0 is falsy
a ?? b;       // 0

String? s = '';
s ?? 'x';     // ''   - an empty string is a value
s.isEmpty;    // true  - and THAT is how you check for it
'' || 'x';    // 'x'  - wrong if empty is legitimate

bool? flag = false;
flag ?? true; // false
flag || true; // true  - wrong

// so the rule, precisely:
//   ??  when null is the only thing you want to replace
//   isEmpty / isZero / isNegative  when falsy is what you mean
// and mixing them is the bug: `page ?? 1` is correct and `page || 1` silently
// turns page 0 into page 1, which is a valid page.

// ??= computes the default only when needed, which ?? does too
int cost() { print('computing'); return 10; }
Map<String, int> m = {};
m['x'] ??= cost();     // "computing" - because the key was absent
m['x'] ??= cost();     // silent - because the key is present
// and the evaluation-order trap
final list = [];
list.first ??= [];     // ERROR: the left side of ??= must be a property
                        // or an index, not a method call
m['a'] ??= m['b'] ??= 0;   // right-to-left: m['b'] first, then m['a']
// which is the opposite of the reading order, and worth knowing

// and the combination that replaces a guard clause
void f(Map<String, Object>? opts) {
  final timeout = opts?['timeout'] as int? ?? 5000;
  // ?. for the absent map, ?? for the absent value, as for the type - and
  // three questions answered in one expression with no branch

// the versions to watch for in review
//   a ?? b ?? c          correct, and the idiomatic chain
//   a?.b?.c ?? d         correct
//   a ?? b!              pointless - the ! throws on exactly what ?? catches
//   a!.b ?? c            the ! throws before ?? is consulted - often a bug
//   a ??= b ?? c         assigns b ?? c when a is null - correct

The `a!.b ?? c` case is the one that survives review, because it reads as "use the default if there is no b". What it actually does is throw if a is null, before ?? is ever consulted — so the default is unreachable in exactly the case it was written for.

// the assignment forms, and what they are for
class Config {
  int port = 8080;
  String? host;
  Map<String, String> headers = {};

  void apply(Map<String, Object> env) {
    host = env['HOST'] ?? host;              // correct: null means "unset"
    port = (env['PORT'] as int?) ?? port;
    headers['Accept'] ??= 'application/json';
  }
}

// versus the initialiser form, which is shorter and states the default once
class Config2 {
  int port;
  String host;
  Config2({this.port = 8080, required this.host});
  // and this is the shape to prefer: a default belongs in the signature,
// not in a body that assigns it
}

// and where ??= genuinely earns its place: a cache
class Store {
  final _cache = <String, User>{};
  User user(String id) => _cache[id] ??= _fetch(id);
}
// which works ONLY because _fetch is pure with respect to the id. If it can
// return null, this assigns null, caches null, and calls again next time - a
// silent repeated call that no test catches.

Nullish coalescing is not a stylistic preference, it is a different question from short-circuiting, and the difference shows up the first time a legitimate value is zero, empty or false. A page number of zero, a search term that is the empty string, a feature flag that is off — all three are values rather than absences, and || treats all three as absent. That produces a bug where the default silently replaces something the caller meant, and it is invisible until a user is on page zero.

The compound assignment form earns its keep for a different reason than the plain one. a ?? b evaluates b every time, which is fine for a literal and wasteful for a computation. a ??= b evaluates it only when a is null, which is what makes it the right form for a lazily computed default and for the caching idiom. It is also the form that reads most like the intention: "set it if unset".

The case worth watching in review is a ! on the left of a ??, because it inverts the order of operations. a?.b ?? c asks for the default when the value is missing; a!.b ?? c throws when a is missing, before the ?? is ever consulted, so the default is unreachable in exactly the case it was written for. It reads correctly and means the opposite, which is the profile of a bug that survives review.

2.5 The ! and ? operators side by side

Cascade, null-aware access, and the operators that trip people up.

class Config {
  String? host;
  int? port;
  final Map<String, String> headers = {};

  Config? backup;
}

final c = Config()
  ..host = 'api.acme.com'      // cascade: .., runs on the SAME object
  ..port = 443
  ..headers['Authorization'] = 'Bearer x';   // cascade into a nested object

// the null-aware variants
final host = c?.host;              // null if c is null
final port = c?.port ?? 8080;      // null-aware + null-coalescing
final set = c?.headers['x'] = 'y'; // ERROR: ?. is not assignable

// the difference that catches people: ?. short-circuits the whole chain
final a = c?.backup?.host;         // null if EITHER c or c.backup is null
final b = c.backup?.host;          // throws if c.backup is null, and c is
                                    // non-nullable here so that is fine

// for a long chain, a local is clearer than nested ?.
final conf = c;
if (conf != null && conf.backup != null) {
  print(conf.backup!.host);
}

// ??= assigns when the current value is null
c.port ??= 8080;                   // same as: c.port ?? (c.port = 8080)
// collection null-aware, with the type you actually get
Map<String, int> scores = {'ana': 10};

scores['bo'] ??= 5;         // adds bo: 5
scores['ana'] = null;       // ERROR: the value type is non-nullable
// scores['ana'] = null;    // the correct shape, if nulls are possible:
Map<String, int?> nullable = {'ana': 10};
nullable['ana'] = null;     // the key now maps to null

// which iterable methods need null awareness
final List<int>? maybeList = [1, 2];
print(maybeList?.length);              // int?
print(maybeList?.where((e) => e > 1).toList());   // List<int>?

// for (final x in maybeList ?? []) is the safe idiom
for (final x in maybeList ?? const <int>[]) {
  print(x);
}

Flow analysis, and the three questions it answers

Dart's flow analysis is what turns sound null safety into something writable: it works out the set of possible values at each point, and uses that for promotion, exhaustiveness and definite assignment. Those are three separate jobs from one analysis.

AnalysisQuestionUses
Type promotionIs this non-null here?Removes the null check from the emitted code
Definite assignmentWas this definitely set?Errors on a read before a write on every path
ExhaustivenessIs every case covered?Errors on a non-exhaustive switch over a sealed type
Type inferenceWhat is this?final x = 42; is int
ReachabilityCan this run?Marks dead code, and removes it
// definite assignment, which is the one that catches the most bugs
int f(bool cond) {
  int x;
  if (cond) { x = 1; }
  return x;                  // ERROR: x might not be assigned
}
// the three fixes
int f1(bool cond) {
  int x = 0;                 // a default - and the honest one if 0 is valid
  if (cond) x = 1;
  return x;
}
int f2(bool cond) {
  if (cond) return 1;
  return 0;                  // return instead of assign - clearest
}
int? f3(bool cond) {
  int? x;
  if (cond) x = 1;
  return x;                  // nullable, and the caller decides
}

// definite assignment for a final, where there is no default
final String id;
if (condition) {
  id = compute();            // ERROR: not assigned on the other path
} else {
  id = fallback();           // ...and now it is, because BOTH paths assign
}
// which is why a final field assigned in a constructor body or an initialiser
// list works: the compiler sees both.

// reachability, and why it matters
bool impossible(int v) {
  if (v < 0) return false;
  if (v > 100) return false;
  if (v < 0 || v > 100) {   // the compiler knows this is dead
    throw StateError('unreachable');
  }
  return true;
}
// it does not error, but it warns as dead_code and removes the branch from the
// output - which is a free proof that a guard was written correctly
// where the analysis stops, and what to do about it
class Repo {
  List<Row>? _cache;

  // across a function boundary: no promotion, because the value is re-read
  int count() {
    if (_cache != null) return _cache!.length;   // the ! is needed
    return 0;
  }

  // across an async gap: promotion does not survive `await`
  Future<int> countAsync() async {
    final c = _cache;
    if (c == null) return 0;
    await Future.delayed(const.ms(1));
    return c.length;        // fine - `c` is a local, captured by value
  }

  // a closure that runs later: the captured variable is not promoted
  int countLater() {
    final c = _cache;
    if (c == null) return 0;
    return () => c.length;()();      // fine - c is final
  }

  // and the version that does not work
  int countBad() {
    if (_cache == null) return 0;
    return () => _cache!.length;()(); // works but needs the ! every time
  }
}
// the general answer: a `final` local captures its value, so every closure
// over it sees the promoted type with no assertion at all

Definite assignment, and the constructor case that catches people

// the rule: a local must be assigned on EVERY path that reaches the read
int f(bool c) {
  int x;
  if (c) x = 1;
  return x;                          // ERROR: might not be assigned
}

// which the compiler proves for both branches of an if/else
int g(bool c) {
  int x;
  if (c) { x = 1; } else { x = 2; }
  return x;                          // fine
}
// and for a switch, which must be exhaustive over a sealed type
int h(Status s) {
  int code;
  switch (s) {
    case Status.ok:   code = 200; break;
    case Status.fail: code = 500; break;
  }
  return code;                       // fine - both cases assign
}
// but NOT over an enum, because an enum can gain a value later
int i(Status s) {
  int code;
  switch (s) {
    case Status.ok:   code = 200; break;
    default:          code = 500; break;
  }
  return code;                       // fine, because of the default
}
// ...and this is why an exhaustive switch expression needs no default:
// it cannot be non-exhaustive over a sealed type, so there is nothing else it
// could return

// the field version, and the error people hit
class Point {
  final int x;
  final int y;
  Point(this.x, this.y);            // fine - an initialiser list
  Point.origin() : x = 0, y = 0;    // fine - explicit
}
// and in a BODY, which is legal but error-prone
class P2 {
  final int x, y;
  P2(int a, int b) { x = a; y = b; }   // fine
  P2.origin() { x = 0; y = 0; }         // fine - but it is an assignment,
}                                        // not an initialisation, so the
                                         // final is genuinely assigned
// the error:
class P3 {
  final int x;
  P3(int a) { this.x = a; }              // fine
  P3.bad() { this.x = 1; print(this.x); }  // fine here, but...
}
// the real error is a field used before assignment in an initialiser:
class P4 {
  final int x = compute();
  final int y = x + 1;                  // fine - initialisers run in order
  final int z = y * 2;
  static int compute() => 1;
}
// reachability, and why the warning is worth reading
bool f(int v) {
  if (v < 0) return false;
  if (v > 100) return false;
  if (v < 0 || v > 100) return false;   // dead_code: the compiler knows
  return true;
}
// it does not error, and it should not - but dead_code means a guard is
// written correctly, which is a free proof, or that a branch was moved and
// one copy was left behind.

// where the analysis gives up, and what to do
Future<int> g() async {
  var x = 0;
  await Future.delayed(const Duration(ms: 1));
  return x;                            // fine - x is definitely assigned
}

Future<int> h(bool c) async {
  int x;
  if (c) x = 1;
  await Future.delayed(const Duration(ms: 1));
  return x;                            // ERROR - and here the compiler is
  // RIGHT: a closure or a caller could have observed the uninitialised x
  // during the await, because Dart's isolates share no memory but an
  // async gap is still a suspension point.
  //
  // the fix is the same as for the synchronous case: give it a value.
}

// and the pattern that removes the question
class Config {
  final int port;
  final bool debug;
  Config._(this.port, this.debug);
  factory Config(Map<String, Object> raw) {
    final port = int.tryParse(raw['port'] as String? ?? '');
    if (port == null) throw const FormatException('port');
    return Config._(port, raw['debug'] == true);
  }
}
// the factory validates, so the private constructor can take non-nullables -
// which is the shape that makes the type system do work rather than
// restate a fact

Definite assignment analysis is the least discussed of the three and the one that catches the most real bugs, because an uninitialised value is a defect that produces a plausible answer rather than an error. A local read on a path where it was never assigned returns whatever happened to be on the stack, and a field likewise — so the failure is a wrong number in a report rather than a crash, and it survives testing because the tested path happened to assign it.

The fix is nearly always to give the variable a value rather than to prove the path unreachable, and that is worth saying plainly because the alternative — restructuring so the compiler can see every path — is often the better fix but is not always available. A function that reads a local assigned in one of two branches has three honest shapes: a default in the declaration, an early return from each branch, or a nullable type that forces the caller to decide. All three are better than a suppress comment, and the first is usually right when zero is a valid value.

Flow analysis gives up at two boundaries, and both are places where the reasoning has to be redone by hand. It does not follow promotion across an await, because between the two points other code can run. And it does not analyse a field or a getter, because anything can change them. In both cases the same answer applies — take a final local — and in the async case that answer has the side benefit of capturing a value into the closure rather than a variable.

2.6 Null-aware members and collections

The operators applied to real code, and the default-value patterns.

// defaults, in order of preference
final port = config.port ?? 8080;            // null-aware: use if null
final port2 = config.port ?? 0;              // 0 can be a real value: careful!
final port3 = config.port != 0 ? config.port : 8080;  // explicit about 0

// for a collection
final tags = entry.tags ?? ['untitled'];
final count = entries?.length ?? 0;

// a call
final result = cache?.get('key');            // skip entirely if cache is null
final result2 = cache?.get('key') ?? compute();  // compute only if null

// a cascade on a nullable
config?.host = 'other';     // ERROR: ?. is not assignable
// the correct forms:
final cfg = config;
if (cfg != null) cfg.host = 'other';
config ??= Config();       // create if absent, then assign
config!.host = 'other';     // acceptable after the ??=

Four operators for absent values, and when each is right

OperatorReadsTriggerUse for
??Right if left is nullLeft is NullableA default
??=Writes if left is nullLeft is NullableA default, assigned
?.Short-circuits the chainAny link is nullOptional chaining
...?Skips a null iterableThe iterable is nullCollecting possibly-absent values
?..CascadesThe target is nullChained configuration
!.postfixNothing — asserts—An invariant you can prove
// ?? vs ??= : the difference is whether the default is computed
int retries = config.retries ?? 3;          // always evaluated, cheap here
config.retries ??= computeDefault();        // ONLY if null - which is the point

// ?. short-circuits the whole chain, so the middle link matters
print(a?.b.c);       // safe if a is null OR a.b is null? NO - a.b.c still throws
print(a?.b?.c);      // safe - and note the difference from the one above
// which is the mistake that survives review: one ?. on a two-link chain

// the collection forms, which are the ones people forget
final all = [...maybeList];           // TypeError if maybeList is null
final all2 = [...?maybeList];         // empty if null - and this is right
final map2 = {...?maybeMap};          // same, for a Map
final set2 = {...?maybeSet};          // and for a Set

// the argument-spread form, which takes a MAP not a list
final m = <String, int>{...};
call({...?...m});                     // conditional map spread

// and the two operators that have no analogue anywhere else
// ?.. is a conditional cascade: everything after applies only if non-null
final builder = Builder()
  ?..name = 'x'
  ?..version = 2;
final b2 = Builder()
  ..name = 'x'
  ..version = 2;         // unconditional - the ordinary cascade

// ?.[] and ?.() for index and call
print(map[key]?.length);
print(maybeCallback?.());      // null if the reference is null

// and the combination that replaces most defensive code
await Future.wait([
  if (a != null) loadA(),
  if (b != null) loadB(),
]);

The ...? spread is the one with the largest effect on how the code reads. A nullable list used to force a guard at every use site; with [...?list] the guard moves to the boundary where the value arrives, and every downstream line is written as though it were non-null — which is usually what the author meant and could not previously express.

The collection and cascade operators, which are Dart 3 additions

Four of the null-aware operators exist because nullable values became ordinary: optional chaining for reads, the null-aware spread for collecting, and two cascade forms that skip the whole expression when the target is absent.

WrittenEquivalent toNull-aware?
a?.ba == null ? null : a.bYes
a?.[0]a == null ? null : a[0]Yes
a?.b()a?.b == null ? null : a.b()Yes
[...a]List.of(a)No — throws
[...?a]a == null ? [] : List.of(a)Yes
a..b()cascadeNo
a?..b()conditional cascadeYes
// the spread, which is the one that changes how code reads
final withNull = [...maybeList];       // TypeError if maybeList is null
final without = [...?maybeList];       // [] if null - and usually what you want

// a set and a map, too - all three were given the ...? form in Dart 3
final s = <String>{...?tags};
final m = <String, int>{...?base, 'extra': 1};

// and the argument-spread, which is a MAP rather than an iterable
void call({String? a, String? b}) {}
call({...?maybeArgs});                   // spread a map's entries as named args
call({...?maybeArgs, 'c': 'always'});    // and combine with literal entries

// the cascade, and the three forms
final b = StringBuffer()
  ..write('a')
  ..writeln();

// conditional - everything after the ?.. applies only if non-null
final b2 = StringBuffer()
  ?..write('a')
  ?..writeln();

// and the one that reads as a null check but is a cascade
final b3 = maybeBuffer
  ..write('a');      // NOT a null check - throws if maybeBuffer is null
                     // ...which is why ?.. exists, and why a cascade on a
                     // nullable value is almost always a bug

// the mistake that costs an afternoon: mixing them
maybe?.method()
  ..another();       // ERROR: ?. returned a value, and .. is a cascade on a
                     // receiver - you cannot chain a cascade onto ?. result
                     // unless it is non-null, and the type is nullable
// the fix is a local, which is promoted
final t = maybe;
if (t != null) {
  t
    ..another()
    ..third();
}

The ...? spread is the highest-leverage of the four, because it moves a null check from every use site to the boundary where the value arrives. Once a list is non-nullable, every downstream line reads as though it always will be — which is what the author meant, and what ...?list finally lets them write.

The four null-aware operators exist because null became ordinary rather than exceptional, and each one removes a check from a specific position. Optional chaining removes the check on the receiver, the null-aware spread removes the check on a collection being accumulated into, and the conditional cascade removes the check on a whole configuration block. Together they are the difference between a guard at every use site and a guard at the boundary where the value arrives.

The one that changes how code reads most is the null-aware spread, because it makes "possibly absent" expressible inside a literal rather than as a branch outside it. [...?maybe] reads as "and whatever is in maybe", which is the domain statement, where the equivalent guard reads as a concern about a variable. That matters for review: the first is checkable by reading the expression, the second requires tracing where the variable came from.

The mistake the cascade form invites is worth naming, because it looks like a null check and is not. maybeBuffer..write('x') is a cascade on maybeBuffer and throws if it is null; the conditional ?.. is the form that skips. Both read as configuration, and the difference is whether the object is expected to be there. Using the unconditional form on a nullable value is almost always a bug, and the compiler will not flag it because cascades are not null-aware by design.

2.7 Refactoring to eliminate nulls

Four techniques that genuinely reduce nullability rather than papering over it.

// 1. an empty collection instead of null
//    BEFORE: List<String>? tags;
//    AFTER:  List<String> tags = [];
List<String> get tags => rawTags ?? const [];
// now every caller works, and `for` over it is safe

// 2. a sealed type instead of a nullable enum + string
sealed class Result<T> {}
class Ok<T> extends Result<T> { final T value; Ok(this.value); }
class Err<T> extends Result<T> { final String message; Err(this.message); }

// usage is exhaustive and readable
switch (result) {
  case Ok(:final value):
    print(value);
  case Err(:final message):
    print(message);
}

// 3. an early return, which is usually the simplest fix
String describe(String? input) {
  if (input == null) return 'no input';
  if (input.isEmpty) return 'empty';
  return 'got ${input.length} chars';     // input is a String in here
}

// 4. a non-null with a documented default, at the boundary
double readDouble(double? raw, {double fallback = 0}) {
  return raw ?? fallback;
}
// the antipattern, and why it spreads
class User {
  String? name;         // nullable...
  String? email;
  int? age;
  // ...and now every consumer needs a check
}

void greet(User u) {
  if (u.name != null) print('hi ${u.name}');
  if (u.name != null && u.name!.isNotEmpty) {   // and the ! comes back
    print(u.name!.toUpperCase());
  }
}

// the better shape: validate once, at construction
class User {
  final String name;
  final String email;
  final int? age;                 // genuinely optional

  User({required String name, required String email, this.age})
      : name = name.trim().isEmpty ? 'anonymous' : name.trim(),
        email = email;

  void greet() => print('hi $name');   // no checks needed
}

Early return, guards, and the shape of an error path

With nullable types in play, the interesting design question is no longer how to check but where to check. Every null check placed at the point of use spreads one uncertain condition across the whole function; placed at the boundary it is handled once.

// the wrong shape: every line has to cope with the uncertainty
String describe(User? user) {
  if (user != null) {
    final name = user.name;
    if (name.isNotEmpty) {
      final parts = name.split(' ');
      if (parts.length > 1) {
        return '${parts[0]} (${parts.length} names)';
      }
      return name;
    }
  }
  return 'anonymous';
}

// the right shape: convert once, then write the logic plainly
String describe(User? user) {
  final name = user?.name.trim();
  if (name == null || name.isEmpty) return 'anonymous';
  final parts = name.split(' ');
  return parts.length > 1 ? '${parts[0]} (${parts.length} names)' : name;
}
// same behaviour, one nesting level instead of five, and the reader is
// looking at the logic rather than at the null checks

// the pattern, named: normalise at the edge, then work with a total function
User requireUser(Session? session) {
  final u = session?.user;
  if (u == null) throw const Unauthorized('no session');
  return u;
}

String label(Order o) {
  final customer = requireUser(o.session);   // total from here on
  return '${customer.name}: ${o.total}';
}

// which is why "early return" beats "single exit" in a language with a
// meaningful return type: a guard clause makes the happy path read top to
// bottom, and the error cases collect at the top where they can be scanned.

// and the one place a single exit IS right: resource lifetime
List<Row> readAll(String path) {
  final h = File(path).openSync();
  try {
    return h.readAsLinesSync().map(Row.parse).toList();
  } finally {
    h.closeSync();       // exactly one close, and it runs on every path
  }
}
// the construct that expresses this directly
sealed class Outcome<T> {}
class Ok<T> extends Outcome<T> { final T value; Ok(this.value); }
class Err<T> extends Outcome<T> { final String message; Err(this.message); }

Outcome<Config> load(String path) {
  if (!exists(path)) return Err('not found');
  final parsed = parse(path);
  if (parsed == null) return Err('unparseable');
  return Ok(parsed);
}

// and the caller is forced to handle both, because the switch is exhaustive
final msg = switch (load('c.toml')) {
  Ok(:final value) => 'loaded ${value.keys.length} keys',
  Err(:final message) => 'failed: $message',
};

// which is the alternative to a nullable return, and it is strictly better
// where the failure has a MESSAGE: `Config?` loses it, and `String` conflates
// a failed parse with a legitimate empty string.
//
// so the ladder, in order of preference
//   1. a total function over a normalised input  - nothing to handle
//   2. a sealed Result with a message             - the compiler enforces it
//   3. `T?`                                     - fine when absent is normal
//   4. a thrown exception                        - when failure is exceptional
// ...and the choice between 2 and 4 is whether the failure is part of the
// ordinary range of outcomes or an exceptional one

Three shapes for handling a fallible call

The decision is not stylistic: it determines whether the caller can forget a case, whether the failure carries information, and whether the failure is part of the ordinary range of outcomes.

ShapeCaller mustCarries a messageFailure is
T, throw on failureNothingYes, in the exceptionExceptional
T?Handle nullNoOrdinary
Sealed ResultHandle both, forcedYesOrdinary
Either<L, R>Handle both, forcedYesEither side is normal
// 1. throw: the caller is not expected to cope
Config load(String path) {
  if (!exists(path)) throw FileSystemException('missing', path);
  return parse(File(path).readAsStringSync());
}
// right when failure means the program is broken: a bad config file, a
// corrupt database. Catch it once, at the top.

// 2. nullable: the caller decides, and absence carries no explanation
User? find(int id) => rows.where((r) => r.id == id).firstOrNull;
// right when "no such user" is an ordinary answer to a question - and note
// the loss: `find` cannot say WHICH id was missing, because there is nothing
// to put it in.

// 3. a sealed result: the compiler enforces the handling
sealed class Parsed<T> {}
class Valid<T> extends Parsed<T> { final T value; Valid(this.value); }
class Invalid<T> extends Parsed<T> { final List<String> errors; Invalid(this.errors); }

final msg = switch (parse(input)) {
  Valid(:final value) => 'ok: $value',
  Invalid(:final errors) => 'errors: ${errors.join(', ')}',
};
// right for validation, for a result the user can act on, and anywhere the
// failure is a normal outcome with detail the caller needs.

// 4. the early-return version, and where it fits
Future<String?> fetchName(int id) async {
  final user = await api.user(id);
  if (user == null) return null;        // ordinary absence
  return user.displayName;
}
// the version that is usually right, because it is the one that reads
if (user == null) return null;
return user.displayName;

// and the rule of thumb
//   failure means BUG      -> throw, catch at the top
//   failure means ANSWER   -> Result, and let the caller read the message
//   absence means "none"   -> nullable, and lose the explanation knowingly
// choosing wrong is not a style error: a nullable return that callers treat as
// exceptional produces a null-dereference crash three frames from the decision,
// with nothing in the stack trace pointing at the choice.

The shape of an error path is a design decision with three observable consequences, and only the first is usually considered. First, the caller can forget a case: a thrown exception and a nullable return are both skippable, while a sealed result is not. Second, the failure carries information: a nullable return cannot say what went wrong, and losing that is what turns a useful error into a silent default. Third, the failure is classified — as a bug, as an answer, or as neither — and that classification is what determines where it should be handled.

The normalisation pattern is what makes all three achievable at once. Converting an uncertain input once, at the top of a function, into a total value produces code that reads top to bottom with no nesting, because the guard clauses at the top are the only place the uncertainty appears. Everything below the conversion is ordinary code that could be lifted into a pure function and tested with a literal.

Which is the practical test for whether an API has been designed: write the caller you would want, and see whether it needs a branch it does not have a name for. If handling the failure means checking a condition you cannot express as a single expression, the failure is carrying detail that a T? has nowhere to put — and that is the signal to reach for a sealed result or an exception with a message rather than adjusting the caller.

2.8 Designing an API that avoids null

Signature choices that keep nullability out of every call site.

// 1. prefer an empty collection over a nullable one in the signature
//    BAD:  List<String> getTags()          // what if null?
//    GOOD: List<String> getTags()          // never null, may be empty
List<String> _tags = [];
List<String> get tags => List.unmodifiable(_tags);

// 2. return a Result rather than a nullable
//    BAD:  User? findUser(String id)
//    GOOD: Result<User, UserNotFound> findUser(String id)
//    the caller must handle both, and the compiler enforces it

// 3. a default parameter value handles the optional case
Future<Response> fetch(String url, {int retries = 3, Duration? timeout})
    async { ... }

// 4. do not accept null unless you handle it differently
//    BAD:  void onSave(String? name)
//    GOOD: void onSave(String name)   or
//          void onSave({String? name, bool isClearing = false})

// 5. nullable fields with a getter that never returns null
class Timer {
  final Duration? _duration;
  Duration get duration => _duration ?? Duration.zero;
  bool get hasDuration => _duration != null;
}

The goal of null safety is not to eliminate the ? from your source - some data genuinely is absent. The goal is that every ? is a deliberate decision you made, and that the compiler holds you to handling it. A codebase with nullable types but no ! and no unhandled late is a well-designed one.

Exercises 3

  1. Take a function with three nullable parameters and refactor it so each has an early return. Count the ! before and after.
  2. Write a class with a getter returning String? and watch promotion fail, then fix it with a local capture.
  3. Implement late initialisation in four different ways and confirm the final version rejects reassignment.
  4. Replace a String? field with a validated non-nullable one and see how many call sites simplify.
  5. Build a sealed Result type and write three exhaustive switches over it.
  6. Grep your codebase for ! (excluding != and comments) and justify or remove each one.

Designing a null-safe API

The signature is the design. A parameter that is nullable is a promise to every caller that they must handle absence, and the cost of that promise is paid at every call site — so the question is not "can this be null" but "who decides".

SignatureSaysCost to callers
void f(String s)Required, non-nullNone — the compiler checks
void f(String? s)Required, may be absentEvery caller handles it
void f([String? s])OptionalSame, plus a default to invent
void f({String s = 'x'})Optional with a defaultNone, and the default is documented
void f({String? s})Optional, no defaultEvery caller supplies or handles it
// the pattern: separate the two concerns so neither is nullable
// BAD: one method that does both, so one parameter must be nullable
Future<void> save(String path, String? content) async {
  if (content == null) { await File(path).delete(); return; }
  await File(path).writeAsString(content);
}

// GOOD: two total functions, and a nullable parameter that is never awkward
Future<void> remove(String path) => File(path).delete();
Future<void> write(String path, String content) => File(path).writeAsString(content);

// the caller reads as the domain does
await remove(p);
await write(p, text);
// rather than
await save(p, null);          // what does null mean here? delete? skip? clear?

// and the builder form, where the absence is a state rather than a value
class HttpOptions {
  final Duration timeout;
  final Map<String, String> headers;
  final String? body;
  const HttpOptions({
    this.timeout = const Duration(seconds: 30),
    this.headers = const {},
    this.body,
  });
  bool get hasBody => body != null;
}
