// `hasBody` reads better at the call site than `body != null`, and it gives
// the check a name that can carry a doc comment

// the return type is the same decision
User? find(int id)              // fine: absent is an ordinary outcome
Config load(String path)        // throws on failure: fine if it is exceptional
Future<Config> load(String path)   // rejects: the async equivalent

// the anti-pattern, and what it produces at the call site
class Api {
  User? user;                    // public mutable nullable field
  void setUser(User? u) { user = u; }
  void send() {
    if (user != null) {
      final id = user.id;
      if (id > 0) {
        final body = user.toJson();
        if (body.isNotEmpty) {
          post(body);
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
// five nested guards to reach a value that is either there or not, and every
// one of them can be forgotten by the next person to touch this file.

// the three properties worth designing for
// 1. INVISIBLE INVALID STATE: a public nullable field can hold null while an
//    invariant elsewhere says it cannot. Make it private and expose a getter.
// 2. ABILITY TO REQUIRE: a builder that produces an incomplete object cannot
//    construct it at all.
// 3. ABILITY TO TELL: "absent" and "present but empty" must be distinguishable,
//    or every caller guesses. null and the empty string are not the same
//    thing, and an API that uses both without saying which is which is a bug
//    with a delayed fuse.

The recurring lesson is that a nullable parameter spreads uncertainty through the caller, and the fix is almost never a null check at the use site — it is a signature that does not need one. Split the method, or move the default into the signature, and the guards disappear along with the nesting they caused.

3 · Functions, Closures and Callbacks

3.1 Declaring functions3.2 Optional and named parameters3.3 Function types and typedef3.4 Closures and captures3.5 Tear-offs3.6 Higher-order functions you actually use3.7 Extension methods and extension types

Dart treats functions as values, which makes higher-order programming a matter of course rather than a technique you have to reach for.

3.1 Declaring functions

The forms, and return types that include void and Never.

// the full form
int add(int a, int b) {
  return a + b;
}

// inferred return type
int add2(int a, int b) => a + b;      // the single-expression form

// no return value
void log(String message) {
  print(message);
}

void log2(String message) => print(message);

// returning a function
int Function(int, int) get adder => add;
final op = add;
print(op(1, 2));   // 3

// Never: the function never returns normally
Never fail(String message) {
  throw Exception(message);
}

Never _unreachable() {
  throw StateError('unreachable');
}

// dynamic return, for genuinely dynamic code
dynamic legacyLookup(String key) {
  return _cache[key];
}

The two lists, and why Dart needs both

Dart's { } on a parameter list brackets a set, and [ ] brackets an ordered list. Required parameters go inside the braces; optional ones go inside the brackets, in the order they can be supplied positionally. That one distinction is the whole syntax, and it is unusual enough that a reader arriving from any other language gets it wrong on the first attempt.

ParameterDeclaredNamed at the callNullable by default
Required positional{ }NoNo
Optional positional[ ]NoYes
Required named{ } + requiredYesNo
Optional named{ } with a defaultYesYes, unless required

Named parameters are the important half. Positional parameters make the call site a sequence of values whose meaning is carried entirely by order and by the reader's memory of the declaration; named parameters make the call site a set of labelled values that can be read out of context, reordered, and partially filled. Once a function has more than three parameters, named is not a preference — it is the only form in which a caller can tell which argument is which without opening the declaration.

// positional: the caller must count
String greet(String name, String greeting, int punctuation) =>
    greeting + ', ' + name + '!' * punctuation;

// three booleans at a call site, and no way to know which is which
render('Ada', 'Hello', 3);

// named: the caller can read it
String greet2({
  required String name,
  String greeting = 'Hello',
  int punctuation = 1,
}) => greeting + ', ' + name + '!' * punctuation;

render2(name: 'Ada', punctuation: 3);      // greeting defaults
render2(greeting: 'Hi', name: 'Ada');      // order is free
render2('Ada');                            // ERROR - a named arg needs its label

// optional positional, for the rare case where order genuinely is the API
String greet3(String name, [String greeting = 'Hello', int punctuation = 1]) =>
    greeting + ', ' + name + '!' * punctuation;

greet3('Ada');            // fine
greet3('Ada', 'Hi');      // fine
greet3(greeting: 'Hi');   // ERROR - cannot skip the first to name the second
// which is the reason optional positional exists but should stay rare: it
// cannot be combined with named, and it punishes anyone who reads the
// signature from the bottom up

The other thing the declaration decides is whether a parameter may be null, and it does so in three different ways that are easy to confuse. A parameter with a default is implicitly nullable, because the default is the fallback for absent — so a caller who omits it gets your default and a caller who explicitly passes null gets a null, and the function has to handle both. Adding required removes the default and therefore removes the implicit nullability. Adding an explicit ? alongside a default keeps it nullable but changes what null means.

// four declarations that differ in a way that matters
void a(String s);                          // required, non-null
void b(String? s);                         // required, MAY be null - two cases
void c({String s = 'x'});                  // optional, defaults; implicitly String?
void d({required String s});               // required named, non-null
void e({String? s});                       // optional named, null, no default

// so a and d are total: the compiler proves every use
a(''); d(s: '');

// b has two distinct cases, and the difference is invisible at the call site
b(null); b('x');

// c's type is String?, which surprises people who assume a default makes it
// non-null:
void c2({String s = 'x'}) {
  print(s.length);         // ERROR: s is String?
}
// the fix is a late local or a non-null assertion at the point of use, and
// the honest fix is to decide whether null is a real input:
void c3({String? s}) {
  final v = s ?? 'x';      // one default, stated once
  print(v.length);
}

Two more rules are worth internalising before the first surprise. First, optional parameters must come after all required ones, in both lists — there is no way to have an optional parameter followed by a required one, because positional order would then be unsatisfiable. Second, a named parameter marked required cannot also have a default, which is not a contradiction but a statement: "the caller must choose a value" and "there is a value to use when they do not" are different claims about the same thing, and a function cannot honestly make both.

The two lists, and why Dart needs both

Dart's { } on a parameter list brackets a set, and [ ] brackets an ordered list. Required parameters go inside the braces; optional ones go inside the brackets, in the order they can be supplied positionally. That one distinction is the whole syntax, and it is unusual enough that a reader arriving from any other language gets it wrong on the first attempt.

ParameterDeclaredNamed at the callNullable by default
Required positional{ }NoNo
Optional positional[ ]NoYes
Required named{ } + requiredYesNo
Optional named{ } with a defaultYesYes, unless required

Named parameters are the important half. Positional parameters make the call site a sequence of values whose meaning is carried entirely by order and by the reader's memory of the declaration; named parameters make the call site a set of labelled values that can be read out of context, reordered, and partially filled. Once a function has more than three parameters, named is not a preference — it is the only form in which a caller can tell which argument is which without opening the declaration.

// positional: the caller must count
String greet(String name, String greeting, int punctuation) =>
    greeting + ', ' + name + '!' * punctuation;

// three booleans at a call site, and no way to know which is which
render('Ada', 'Hello', 3);

// named: the caller can read it
String greet2({
  required String name,
  String greeting = 'Hello',
  int punctuation = 1,
}) => greeting + ', ' + name + '!' * punctuation;

render2(name: 'Ada', punctuation: 3);      // greeting defaults
render2(greeting: 'Hi', name: 'Ada');      // order is free
render2('Ada');                            // ERROR - a named arg needs its label

// optional positional, for the rare case where order genuinely is the API
String greet3(String name, [String greeting = 'Hello', int punctuation = 1]) =>
    greeting + ', ' + name + '!' * punctuation;

greet3('Ada');            // fine
greet3('Ada', 'Hi');      // fine
greet3(greeting: 'Hi');   // ERROR - cannot skip the first to name the second
// which is the reason optional positional exists but should stay rare: it
// cannot be combined with named, and it punishes anyone who reads the
// signature from the bottom up

The other thing the declaration decides is whether a parameter may be null, and it does so in three different ways that are easy to confuse. A parameter with a default is implicitly nullable, because the default is the fallback for absent — so a caller who omits it gets your default and a caller who explicitly passes null gets a null, and the function has to handle both. Adding required removes the default and therefore removes the implicit nullability. Adding an explicit ? alongside a default keeps it nullable but changes what null means.

// four declarations that differ in a way that matters
void a(String s);                          // required, non-null
void b(String? s);                         // required, MAY be null - two cases
void c({String s = 'x'});                  // optional, defaults; implicitly String?
void d({required String s});               // required named, non-null
void e({String? s});                       // optional named, null, no default

// so a and d are total: the compiler proves every use
a(''); d(s: '');

// b has two distinct cases, and the difference is invisible at the call site
b(null); b('x');

// c's type is String?, which surprises people who assume a default makes it
// non-null:
void c2({String s = 'x'}) {
  print(s.length);         // ERROR: s is String?
}
// the fix is a late local or a non-null assertion at the point of use, and
// the honest fix is to decide whether null is a real input:
void c3({String? s}) {
  final v = s ?? 'x';      // one default, stated once
  print(v.length);
}

Two more rules are worth internalising before the first surprise. First, optional parameters must come after all required ones, in both lists — there is no way to have an optional parameter followed by a required one, because positional order would then be unsatisfiable. Second, a named parameter marked required cannot also have a default, which is not a contradiction but a statement: "the caller must choose a value" and "there is a value to use when they do not" are different claims about the same thing, and a function cannot honestly make both.

3.2 Optional and named parameters

The three parameter kinds, and why named parameters are the default choice for anything with more than two arguments.

// 1. required positional
String greet(String name) => 'Hello $name';

// 2. optional POSITIONAL - order matters, use sparingly
String greet2(String name, [String? title, String? suffix]) {
  final t = title == null ? '' : '$title ';
  final s = suffix ?? '';
  return '${t}Hello $name$s';
}
greet2('Ana');                 // 'Hello Ana'
greet2('Ana', 'Dr');           // 'Dr Hello Ana'

// 3. NAMED - the Dart idiom
String greet3(
  String name, {
  String? title,
  String suffix = '!',
  bool formal = false,
}) {
  final t = title == null ? '' : '$title ';
  final body = formal ? 'Good day' : 'Hello';
  return '$t$body $name$suffix';
}

greet3('Ana');
greet3('Ana', title: 'Dr', suffix: '.', formal: true);   // readable at the call

// 4. required NAMED - forces the caller to be explicit
Future<void> save({required String path, required List<int> bytes}) async { ... }
await save(bytes: data, path: 'out.bin');   // order does not matter

// 5. combining all kinds
void configure(
  String name,          // required positional
  int version, {
  String? description,  // optional named
  required bool strict, // required named
  int retries = 3,     // optional named with a default
}) { ... }
// the rule: two or more parameters of the same type, or a boolean
// flag, means named parameters.
//
//   fetch(url, headers, timeout, retries, cache)   -> unreadable
//   fetch(url, headers: h, timeout: 5s)           -> obvious
//
// a boolean positional parameter is nearly always a mistake:
//   process(data, true)        // what does true mean?
//   process(data, overwrite: true)   // now it is obvious
// default values must be compile-time constants
void a(int x = 1) { }                     // fine
void b([List<int>? items]) {}         // fine, null is allowed
// void c(List<int> items = []) {}    // ERROR: [] is not a const
void c([List<int> items = const []]) {}   // correct

// nullable vs optional, precisely
void f({String? a}) {}      // a may be absent, or explicitly null
void g({String? a = 'x'}) {} // a may be absent, defaults to 'x'
void h({required String a}) {} // must be provided, cannot be null
// void i({required String? a}) {}  // must be provided, but MAY be null

Defaults, required, and the nullable consequence

The rule that surprises people most is that an optional parameter with a default is implicitly nullable. The type of {int n = 5} is int?, not int, because a caller who passes nothing explicitly gets null as far as the type system is concerned before the default is applied — and the compiler applies the default inside the function body, after the type has been established. That single fact explains a large fraction of "why is this parameter suddenly nullable" reports.

DeclarationStatic typeNull at run time?
f(String s)StringNever
f({String s = 'x'})String?Only if explicitly passed null
f({required String s})StringNever
f({String? s})String?Yes
f({String? s}) with a null testpromotes to StringNo, after the test
// the implicit nullability, and the error it produces
void f({int n = 5}) {
  print(n.isEven);         // ERROR: n is int?
  print(n?.isEven);        // fine
}

// the two correct forms, and they say different things
void f2({int n = 5}) {
  final v = n ?? 5;        // "absent and explicitly null are the same here"
  print(v.isEven);
}

void f3({int? n}) {
  if (n == null) return;   // "null means the caller did not choose"
  print(n.isEven);         // promoted
}

// and the required form, which is the one to prefer when there is no default
void f4({required int n}) {
  print(n.isEven);         // fine - no default, so no implicit nullable
}
f4(n: 3);                  // the caller must supply it

// the difference between "optional" and "required named" is not cosmetic
g(n: 1);                   // optional named: omissible
g4();                      // ERROR - n is required
// ...which is the correct signature for anything the function cannot
// meaningfully proceed without

// and null is always allowed to be passed explicitly, even to a required
// non-nullable parameter? no - that is a compile error:
f4(n: null);               // ERROR: null is not assignable to int

The practical rule that falls out of this is about which of the four declaration forms to reach for. If the function cannot work without the value, mark it required and get a non-nullable type for free. If the function has a sensible default, give it one — and be aware the type is nullable, so convert once at the top rather than at every use. If null is a distinct input the function must treat differently from absent, say so with an explicit ? and test it. If the value is only needed sometimes, prefer an optional positional parameter or a separate overload, because a named parameter with a null default is usually a sign the API has collapsed two ideas into one.

// the anti-pattern: one parameter standing in for two meanings
Future<void> save(String path, {String? content}) async {
  if (content == null) {
    await File(path).delete();
  } else {
    await File(path).writeAsString(content);
  }
}
await save(p, content: text);   // what it means - fine
await save(p);                  // delete it - surprising at this call site

// two functions, each total, is better in every way
Future<void> write(String path, String content) =>
    File(path).writeAsString(content);
Future<void> remove(String path) => File(path).delete();

await write(p, text);           // reads as what it does
await remove(p);                // ditto

// and the version that looks equivalent and is not
Future<void> save2(String path, {String? content}) async {
  if (content != null) await write(path, content);
  else await remove(path);
}
// identical behaviour - the point is that the caller above could not tell
// which of the two it was asking for, and neither can a reader of the log

There is one further wrinkle worth knowing, because it changes what a default can be. A default value must be a compile-time constant, so it cannot be the result of a computation, a call, or a reference to a mutable object. That is why a default of const Duration(seconds: 30) works while a default of Duration(seconds: now) does not, and why a default collection literal is const. It also means a default cannot depend on another parameter — for that you use a nullable parameter and a ?? in the body, or a redirecting constructor, which is the idiomatic answer for a default that depends on the arguments.

// what a default may be
void ok({int n = 5, String s = 'x', List<int> l = const [1, 2]}) {}
// a const literal, a literal number, a literal string - all compile-time

// what a default may not be
void bad({List<int> l = []}) {}          // ERROR: not const
void worse({List<int> l = build()}) {}   // ERROR: not a constant
void alsoBad({int n = compute()}) {}        // ERROR: not a constant

// the fix, for each
void fixed({List<int> l = const []}) {}  // const makes it legal
void viaBody({List<int>? l}) {
  final v = l ?? build();                    // compute inside
}

// and the constructor version, which is the elegant answer for a default
// that depends on other parameters
class Point {
  final double x, y;
  Point(this.x, this.y);
  factory Point.polar(double r, double a) => Point(r * cos(a), r * sin(a));
}
// because a redirecting factory has no body, so nothing in it needs to be
// constant, and it returns a fully built object

3.3 Function types and typedef

Writing function types, naming them, and the generic cases.

// the type of a function: parameters in, return out
int Function(String) parse;
void Function(int, {bool strict}) process;
Future<List<int>> Function(String path) load;
void Function(int) callback;

// name them with typedef
typedef Parser = int Function(String);
typedef Transform<T, R> = R Function(T value);
typedef Predicate = bool Function(String);
typedef Reducer = int Function(int a, int b);

final Parser p = (s) => int.parse(s);
final Reducer sum = (a, b) => a + b;

// a class with a callback field
typedef OnProgress = void Function(int completed, int total);

class Downloader {
  Downloader({required this.onProgress});

  final OnProgress onProgress;

  Future<void> run() async {
    for (var i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
      await Future.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 100));
      onProgress(i, 10);
    }
  }
}

// a typedef that carries state: a closure is usually what you want
typedef Formatter = String Function(int value);
String dollars(int v) => '\$$v';
String percent(int v) => '$v%';

void printAll(Formatter f) => print(f(50));
printAll(dollars);   // $50
printAll(percent);   // 50%

What a typedef actually is, and what it is not

A typedef is a name for a type. That is the entire mechanism, and everything else follows from it: because it is only a name, using one costs nothing at run time, it can alias a generic type with its parameters partially applied, and it cannot add behaviour. What it does buy is the ability to name a type that has no good name otherwise — a callback signature used in four places, a long collection type, a domain type that is structurally a Map but means something specific.

// 1. a function type, which is the common case
typedef IntMapper = int Function(String source);

// without it, every declaration repeats the signature
String parse1(String s) => s.length.toString();
String parse2(String s) => s.length.toString();

// with it, the signature is written once
typedef Parse = String Function(String source);
Parse parse3 = (s) => s.length.toString();

// 2. a generic alias, with some parameters already applied
typedef Handler<T> = void Function(T event);
typedef ScoreMap = Map<String, int>;          // two fixed, none free
typedef Rows = List<Map<String, Object?>>;

// 3. a type with a name that carries meaning the underlying type does not
typedef UserId = int;
typedef Meters = double;
typedef Cents = int;

void move(Meters d) {}
void charge(Cents amount) {}
// which is not decoration: it makes move(3) a compile error, where
// move(3) on a bare double would be legal and meaningless

// 4. a union, for "one of these" - and this is where typedef earns its keep
typedef Outcome = Result<User, String>;
typedef Id = UserId;
typedef Bytes = Uint8List;

// a sealed result, aliased
sealed class Result<T, E> {}
class Ok<T, E> extends Result<T, E> { final T value; Ok(this.value); }
class Fail<T, E> extends Result<T, E> { final E error; Fail(this.error); }

Result<User, String> load() => Ok(User(1));
// ...and the alias lets a signature read as a domain statement
Outcome fetchUser() => load();

The limitation that matters is that a typedef cannot be a class. It has no fields, no methods, no constructors and no identity, so it cannot carry invariants and it cannot be used with is to distinguish two uses of the same underlying type. Two functions taking UserId are taking the same type; nothing about the alias makes them different, and a value of one can be passed where the other is expected. That is the trade: readable signatures in exchange for no new type safety.

// typedef does NOT create a distinct type
typedef UserId = int;
typedef OrderId = int;

void f(UserId id) { print(id); }
f(42);                 // fine
f(999);                // also fine

OrderId oid = 7;
f(oid);                // fine - and this is the point AND the limitation
// a distinct type needs a class:
class UserId { final int value; UserId(this.value); }
class OrderId { final int value; OrderId(this.value); }
void g(UserId id) {}
g(OrderId(7));         // ERROR - and now the compiler catches the mistake

// so the decision
// typedef when the intent is DOCUMENTATION or COMPRESSION
//   typedef Cents = int;        // reads correctly, catches nothing
//   typedef Rows = List<Row>;  // shortens a long generic
// class when the intent is PREVENTION
//   class UserId { ... }        // catches a real bug at the call site

// and a mixed approach, which is what most codebases converge on
class UserId {
  final int _v;
  const UserId(this._v);
  int get value => _v;
  @override
  String toString() => 'UserId($_v)';
  // so it reads well in logs AND enforces at the boundary
}

Two practical notes on where typedefs belong. In modern Dart, records cover most of the cases a typedef once served, so a typedef Pair = (int, String) is usually better written as an inline record type (int, String) — records carry field names, so (count: 3, label: 'x') is self-describing in a way Pair is not. And a typedef for a function signature is worth aliasing at the point of use — as a variable or field type — rather than only as a global name, because a local alias gives the reader the name without the indirection of finding the declaration.

// the modern equivalents, and when each is better
typedef Pair = (int, String);        // opaque
(int, String)                        // inline, and a reader sees the shape

// a named record type, which is what typedef wanted
typedef User = ({String name, int age});   // still a type alias...
({String name, int age})                  // ...but the shape is visible
({String name, int age}) u = (name: 'A', age: 3);
u.name;      // named access - a plain typedef of a tuple would not have this

// a local function-type alias, via a variable
void process(List<String> lines) {
  typedef Line = String Function(Map<String, Object?> row);
  final handlers = <String, Line>{};
  handlers['csv'] = (row) => row['id'].toString();
  // the name appears in the type of the map's values, so the reader knows
  // what shape the callbacks take without looking anything up
}

// and the one place a typedef is documentation rather than abbreviation
typedef Millis = int;      // all durations in this package are milliseconds
void sleep(Millis ms) {}
sleep(500);                // and 500 is now self-describing

3.4 Closures and captures

What a closure captures, and the loop-variable rule that changes in Dart.

// a closure captures the variables of the scope it was created in
int counter() {
  var count = 0;
  int increment() {
    count++;         // captures and mutates count
    return count;
  }
  return increment;
}

final next = counter();
print(next());   // 1
print(next());   // 2

// the same, as a class
class Counter {
  int _count = 0;
  int increment() => ++_count;
}

// returning a closure that remembers its parameters
String Function(String) prefixer(String prefix) {
  return (value) => '$prefix$value';
}

final hi = prefixer('Hi, ');
print(hi('Ana'));   // 'Hi, Ana'
// THE LOOP VARIABLE: Dart creates a new binding per iteration
final callbacks = <void Function()>[];
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  callbacks.add(() => print(i));
}
for (final cb in callbacks) cb();   // prints 0, 1, 2 - correct!

// in JavaScript this prints 3, 3, 3, because var is function-scoped.
// in Dart, `for (var i...)` in a collection-for or a plain for creates
// a fresh variable per iteration. There is no equivalent bug.

// final vs var in the loop
final mutable = <int>[1, 2, 3];
for (final x in mutable) {
  if (x == 2) continue;
  mutable.add(99);          // ConcurrentModificationError
}
// never modify a collection while iterating it: iterate a copy
for (final x in List<int>.from(mutable)) { ... }

One case where the copy is required even in Dart: a for-in over a list you are filtering, which reads better as a loop than as a chain. Use List.from() or a where chain. The ConcurrentModificationError is the analyser telling you the iteration order was not guaranteed, not that you got unlucky.

Lexical scope, capture by value, and the loop variable question

A closure in Dart is a function that captures the scope where it was created. It reads and writes the variables that were in scope at that point, not copies of them at that moment — so a closure over a mutable local observes later changes to it, and a closure over a loop variable sees whatever the loop variable holds when the closure runs, not when it was created.

// capture is by REFERENCE to the variable, so later writes are visible
int x = 1;
void bump() { x = x + 1; }
final counter = () { x++; print(x); };
counter();      // 2
counter();      // 3
print(x);       // 3 - the same variable

// ...which is how a closure-based counter works, and why it is not the same
// as a local variable
class Counter {
  int _n = 0;
  int call() { _n++; return _n; }     // a method: `this` is the receiver
}

// with an explicit closure it is the same object, captured
final makeCounter = () {
  var n = 0;
  return () { n++; return n; };
};
final c1 = makeCounter();
final c2 = makeCounter();
c1();     // 1
c1();     // 2
c2();     // 1     - a separate captured n

// the loop variable, and the bug this used to cause
final fns = <Function()>[];
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  fns.add(() => i);      // what do these capture?
}
print(fns.map((f) => f()).toList());   // [3, 3, 3] in Dart, per iteration
// Dart has PER-ITERATION loop variables since 2.0: each iteration of a
// `for` loop gets a fresh copy, so this is [0, 1, 2]. This was not true
// before 2.0, and code ported from JavaScript may rely on either.

// for (var i in ...) is the same - a fresh binding per iteration
for (final x in [10, 20]) {
  fns.add(() => x);
}
// [10, 20] here too

// but a variable declared OUTSIDE the loop is one binding
var j = 0;
final fns2 = <Function()>[];
while (j < 3) {
  fns2.add(() => j);
  j++;
}
print(fns2.map((f) => f()).toList());   // [3, 3, 3] - one `j`
// so the rule is per-ITERATION binding, not per-loop-statement

The distinction between a closure over a variable and a copy of its value is what makes closures useful for callbacks and dangerous for anything that outlives the creating scope. A callback that runs later — an event handler, a timer, a future's then — sees the value the variable holds at that later moment. So a handler that increments a counter captured from an enclosing function works, and a handler that records "which item this was" does not, unless the item itself is captured per iteration.

// the fix for a value that must not change
var i = 0;
final fns = <Function()>[];
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  final captured = i;              // a per-iteration local
  fns.add(() => captured);
}
// or in Dart 2.0+, `for (var i = ...)` already does this

// callbacks that fire LATER need the same care
final handlers = <String, void Function()>{};
for (final name in names) {
  handlers[name] = () => print('hello $name');   // fine - per iteration
}

for (var k = 0; k < names.length; k++) {
  final key = names[k];
  handlers[key] = () => print('hello $key');     // correct explicitly
}

// the closure returned by a method has access to `this`
class Repo {
  final List<String> _items = [];
  void addAll(List<String> items) {
    for (final item in items) {
      _items.add(item);           // `this` is captured implicitly
    }
  }
  List<void Function()> removers() => [
    for (final item in _items)
      () => _items.remove(item)   // captures this AND item
  ];
}

A closure also carries the this of the scope it was created in, which has an observable consequence for a very common pattern. Extracting a method into a variable produces a tear-off that keeps the receiver, and a closure written inside a method also keeps this — so passing either to a callback that expects a plain function will still hold a reference to the object, and cannot be used with static or in a context that requires no receiver. Dart 2.17 added this.-less static tear-offs for exactly this, but the general answer is that a method value is a bound function, and a bound function holds its receiver alive.

// a tear-off is a bound method: it keeps the object alive
final f = [1, 2, 3].map;         // tear-off of List.map
f(2);                            // works, bound to the list

// a closure from inside a method captures `this`
class Widget {
  final String id;
  Widget(this.id);

  void schedule(void Function() work) {
    Timer.run(work);              // the closure holds `this`
  }

  void bad() {
    schedule(() {
      print(id);                  // fine - and it holds the Widget
    });
  }

  void good() {
    schedule(() {
      print(id);                  // same
    });
  }
}

// and the version that does not, which is what a pure function should be
int double(int x) => x * 2;            // static - no receiver
final g = double;                        // a plain function value

// using a method where a plain function is wanted
class Api {
  Future<User> fetch(String id) async { /* ... */ }
}
final f = api.fetch;             // bound to `api`
// so a tear-off can be stored and reused, but it is not equal to a top-level
// function and will keep the Api instance reachable for as long as it exists

}

final c1 = makeCounter();
final c2 = makeCounter();

c1();     // 2
c2();     // 1     - a separate captured n

// before 2.0, and code ported from JavaScript may rely on either.

// for (var i in ...) is the same - a fresh binding per iteration

// [10, 20] here too

for (final name in names) {

}

for (var k = 0; k < names.length; k++) {

  handlers[key] = () => print('hello $key');     // correct explicitly

// the closure returned by a method has access to `this`

  void addAll(List<String> items) {

A closure also carries the this of the scope it was created in, which has an observable consequence for a very common pattern. Extracting a method into a variable produces a tear-off that keeps the receiver, and a closure written inside a method also keeps this — so passing either to a callback that expects a plain function will still hold a reference to the object, and cannot be used with static or in a context that requires no receiver. // a tear-off is a bound method: it keeps the object alive
final f = [1, 2, 3].map;         // tear-off of List.map
f(2);                            // works, bound to the list

// a closure from inside a method captures `this`
class Widget {
  final String id;
  Widget(this.id);

  void schedule(void Function() work) {
    Timer.run(work);              // the closure holds `this`
  }

  void bad() {
    schedule(() {
      print(id);                  // fine - and it holds the Widget
    });

// and the version that does not, which is what a pure function should be
int double(int x) => x * 2;            // static - no receiver
final g = double;                        // a plain function value

// using a method where a plain function is wanted
class Api {
  Future<User> fetch(String id) async { /* ... */ }
}
final f = api.fetch;             // bound to `api`
// so a tear-off can be stored and reused, but it is not equal to a top-level
// function and will keep the Api instance reachable for as long as it exists

3.5 Tear-offs

Referencing a function without parentheses, and the three places it makes code cleaner.

// a tear-off: the function value, without calling it
void greet(String name) => print('Hello $name');

final fn = greet;        // a tear-off
final fn2 = greet;       // identical; greet() would CALL it
fn('Ana');               // Hello Ana

// 1. as an argument
final numbers = [3, 1, 2];
numbers.sort();                 // needs a comparator
numbers.sort((a, b) => a.compareTo(b));
// a tear-off cannot be used directly here because compareTo has a
// different signature, so the lambda is correct

// 2. as a method reference
class Repo {
  void save(String v) {}
  void load() {}
}
final r = Repo();
final saver = r.save;     // a tear-off, bound to r
saver('x');              // r.save('x')

// 3. in a Stream or callback
final timer = Timer.periodic(const Duration(seconds: 1), _onTick);
void _onTick(Timer t) { print('tick'); }
// where tear-offs genuinely read better
final list = [3, 1, 2];

// by name
list.sort((a, b) => a.compareTo(b));
list.sort(compareToInt);              // a top-level comparator

class IntCompare {
  static int byValue(int a, int b) => a.compareTo(b);
  int compare(int a, int b) => a.compareTo(b);
}
list.sort(IntCompare.byValue);       // a static method tear-off

// and for callbacks
Future<void> main() async {
  final data = await fetchData();
  print(computeHash(data));
  await Future.wait(items.map(processItem));   // a tear-off in map
}

int computeHash(List<int> d) => d.length;
int processItem(int i) => print(i);

Tear-offs, and where they differ from a lambda

A tear-off is a reference to a function's body without a call — f for a method, string.length for a property, SomeClass.namedConstructor for a constructor. It has a function type, so it goes anywhere a function value goes, and the difference from writing a wrapper lambda is that there is no wrapper: nothing is allocated per call and no extra frame appears in a stack trace.

WrittenTypePer call
(s) => int.parse(s)int Function(String)One closure call plus one target call
int.parseint Function(String)One call
(n) => n.toDouble()num Function(num)Wrapper
doublenum Function(num)Tear-off of the double property
User.newUser Function(...)Constructor tear-off
User.namedSame shapeNamed constructor tear-off
// the four kinds
final a = int.parse;                    // static method
final b = list.length;                  // instance method, bound to list
final c = double;                       // a top-level function
final d = User.new;                     // unnamed constructor
final e = User.fromJson;                // named constructor
final f = int;                          // the type itself, used as a constructor

// passing them where a callback is expected
['1', '2'].map(int.parse);              // tear-off: one frame
['1', '2'].map((s) => int.parse(s)); // lambda: two frames
// both are correct; the tear-off is measurably cheaper in a hot loop and
// produces a stack trace that names the real function

// instance tear-offs, and the receiver
final repo = UserRepo();
final find = repo.findById;             // bound: find(1) works, no repo needed
final unbound = repo.findById;          // same thing - it IS bound
find(1);                                // correct

// constructor tear-offs, which are how a factory takes a builder
typedef Json = Object Function(Map<String, Object?>);
List<User> parseAll(List<String> rows, Json fromJson) => rows.map(fromJson).toList();
parseAll(rows, User.fromJson);

// and static tear-offs on an enum, which read well in a switch
enum Colour { red, green }
Colour parseColour(String s) => switch (s) {
  'red' => Colour.red,
  _ => Colour.green,
};

// a tear-off of a method used as a callback in a widget
onPressed: handler.handleTap          // bound to handler, not to `this`

Two Dart-specific details make tear-offs more useful here than in most languages. The first is that a tear-off carries a precise type, so list.map is not Function but Iterable<E> Function(int Function(E)) — which means the compiler checks the argument you pass to map against the method's real signature, and a mismatched lambda is a compile error rather than a run-time surprise. The second is that Dart 2.17 added static tear-offs, so a generic function's tear-off can be instantiated at a specific type argument, which is what makes the pattern below type-safe.

// generic functions and instantiation expressions (Dart 2.15+)
T first<T>(Iterable<T> items) => items.first;

final strings = ['a', 'b'];
final firstString = strings.first;      // a property tear-off - String
final asString = first<String>;      // an instantiation expression
asString(strings);                      // String, checked

// ...which is what you need when a function expects a value, not a call
final List<int> Function() makeLen = () => strings.length;
final parseIt = int.parse;              // inferred as int Function(String)

// the inference rules for a bare tear-off
final f = print;                        // dynamic Function(Object?)
final g = print.toString;               // String Function()

// where a tear-off is wrong: needing a different arity or an argument
// (s) => int.parse(s.trim())          // this must stay a lambda - it is
                                        // not a tear-off of anything
final h = int.parse;                    // the tear-off
final i = (String s) => int.parse(s.trim());  // the wrapper

// and the case that looks like it works and does not
["1", "2"].map(int.parse);      // fine
["1", "2"].map(int.parseInt);   // ERROR if it does not exist
// ...and a common near-miss:
['1', '2'].map((s) => int.parse(s));     // equivalent, one frame more

// where the tear-off is a bound METHOD and the receiver matters
class Cache {
  final Map<String, Object> _m = {};
  Object get(String k) => _m[k]!;
  void put(String k, Object v) => _m[k] = v;
}
final c = Cache();
final getter = c.get;                  // Object Function(String), bound
getter('a');                           // works
// and this is why a tear-off of an instance method is not equal to the
// method: two tear-offs of the same instance method are equal, but a
// tear-off and a lambda wrapping it are not

The other detail is that a tear-off is immutable in a way a closure is not. Two evaluations of repo.findById produce equal tear-offs, because a tear-off's equality is defined by receiver and function; two evaluations of () => repo.findById(1) produce two closures that are not equal. That matters in one place specifically — as a widget key, in an == test, or in a deduplication set — where a lambda makes every call look like a new object and a tear-off looks the same every time.

// equality, and where it is observable
final a = [1, 2, 3].map;
final b = [1, 2, 3].map;
print(identical(a, b));      // false - different list instances
print(a == b);               // false - receiver is part of equality

final c = repo.findById;
final d = repo.findById;
print(c == d);               // TRUE - same receiver, same function

final e = () => repo.findById(1);
final f = () => repo.findById(1);
print(e == f);               // false - two different closures

// so for a key or an identity test, use the tear-off
final handlers = <int, void Function()>{
  1: ctl.save,              // equal across calls
  2: () => ctl.save(),    // a new object every time
};

// and for a callback that closes over a value, use the closure - there is no
// tear-off that captures a parameter
for (final id in ids) {
  buttons[id] = () => ctl.delete(id);   // must be a lambda
}

3.6 Higher-order functions you actually use

The standard combinators, and when a plain loop is clearer.

final numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];

// transform
numbers.map((n) => n * 2);                 // [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12]
numbers.map((n) async => await fetch(n));   // Iterable<Future>!
numbers.where((n) => n.isEven);             // [2, 4, 6]
numbers.any((n) => n > 5);                 // true
numbers.every((n) => n > 0);               // true
numbers.contains(3);                          // true
numbers.firstWhere((n) => n > 3);          // 4  - throws if none
numbers.firstWhere((n) => n > 3, orElse: () => 0);   // safe
numbers.reduce((a, b) => a + b);            // 21
numbers.fold<int>(0, (sum, n) => sum + n);  // 21, with a typed seed
numbers.join(', ');                           // '1, 2, 3'
numbers.take(3);                              // [1, 2, 3]
numbers.skip(3);                              // [4, 5, 6]
numbers.reversed;                             // [6, 5, ..., 1]
numbers.expand((n) => [n, n]);              // flatten one level
numbers.toList();                             // List<int>
numbers.toSet();                              // Set<int>
numbers.sort();
numbers.reversed.toList();

// a real chain
final summary = entries
    .where((e) => e.updatedAt.isAfter(cutoff))
    .map((e) => e.title.trim())
    .where((t) => t.isNotEmpty)
    .toSet()
    .toList()
  ..sort();

// THE ASYNC PITFALL: map with an async callback gives Futures
Future<List<String>> naive() async {
  return items.map((i) async => (await fetch(i)).name).toList();
  // returns List<Future<String>> typed as List<String> - a bug
}

Future<List<String>> correct() async {
  // for a Future, use Future.wait
  return Future.wait(items.map((i) async => (await fetch(i)).name));
}

Future<List<String>> ordered() async {
  // for sequential, use a for loop
  final out = <String>[];
  for (final i in items) {
    out.add((await fetch(i)).name);
  }
  return out;
}

The map-with-async bug is the most common Dart error there is, because it type-checks: Iterable<Future<String>> is assignable to what you declared if you are not careful, and you get a list of unresolved futures at runtime. Write the for loop, or Future.wait, and never map(async).

// when a loop is better than a chain
// a chain is better: one pass, one expression, reads as a pipeline
final names = users.map((u) => u.name).toList();

// a loop is better: early exit, multiple statements, no allocation
for (final user in users) {
  if (user.isBlocked) continue;
  if (user.attemptCount > 3) break;     // a chain cannot express this
  final name = user.name.trim();
  if (name.isEmpty) continue;
  active.add(name);
}

First-class functions, and the shape of a pipeline

Dart functions are values: they can be stored in variables, passed as arguments, returned from other functions, and held in collections. That is what makes the iterator protocol in dart:core possible, and it is why where, map and fold take callbacks rather than taking a block the way a Ruby method would.

MethodTakesReturnsIterates again?
mapT f(E)Iterable<T>Yes, lazily
wherebool f(E)Iterable<E>Yes, lazily
expandIterable<T> f(E)Iterable<T>Yes
foldT f(T, E)TOnce
reduceT f(T, T)TOnce
any / everybool f(E)boolStops early
firstWherebool f(E)EStops at a match
sortint f(E, E)voidEager, in place
// the pipeline, and the laziness that makes it safe
final words = 'the quick brown fox'.split(' ');
final lengths = words.map((w) => w.length);      // Iterable<int>
lengths.take(3).toList();                          // [3, 5, 5] - only 3 words
                                                    // were examined
// so a map over a lazy where RE-RUNS the predicate per element, which is
// the reason this is slower than the eager version:
final n = words.where((w) => w.length > 3).length;   // one pass, 3 matches

// the eager equivalent, when it matters
final eager = words.where((w) => w.length > 3).toList();
eager.length;                                      // 3

// fold for a running total, and the three-argument form for a map result
final total = prices.fold(0, (sum, p) => sum + p);
final byCategory = rows.fold(
  <String, double>{},
  (m, r) => m..update(r.category, (v) => v + r.amount, ifAbsent: () => r.amount),
);

// reduce, and why it needs an identity only when the collection may be empty
final sum = [1, 2, 3].reduce((a, b) => a + b);      // 6
[].reduce((a, b) => a + b);                          // ERROR - StateError
[].fold(0, (a, b) => a + b);                         // 0 - the identity

// sort, and the comparator contract
items.sort((a, b) => a.name.compareTo(b.name));       // returns void
// ...so it cannot be chained, and a comparator that returns a bool is a
// compile error rather than a silently wrong order
final sorted = [...items]..sort((a, b) => a.n.compareTo(b.n));
final desc = [...items]..sort((a, b) => b.n.compareTo(a.n));

A callback that takes another callback is where the interesting decisions start, and the two that go wrong most often are the difference between a synchronous and an asynchronous callback, and the difference between a "call for each" and a "call once at the end". Both are invisible in a lambda's syntax, because (x) { ... } looks the same either way — the type of the parameter is what tells you which one you have.

// SYNC callback: void f(T item)
void each(List<String> xs, void Function(String) f) {
  for (final x in xs) f(x);            // called now, in order
}
each(names, (n) { print(n); });         // fine

// ASYNC callback: FutureOr<void> Function(T)
Future<void> eachAsync(List<String> xs, FutureOr<void> Function(String) f) async {
  for (final x in xs) await f(x);      // must await, or they overlap
}
eachAsync(names, (n) async { await save(n); });

// the mistake: an async callback passed to a SYNC parameter
each(names, (n) async { await save(n); });   // compiles!
each(names, (n) { save(n); });                // compiles!
// ...and the first one silently does not wait: each() returns before any
// save completes, so the ordering guarantee the caller assumes is false.
// FutureOr<...> exists so the parameter's type can accept both, and it
// still cannot make the caller await.

// a "collect" callback: called once, with the finished collection
List<T> build<T>(T Function(List<T>) f) => f([]);

// a "transform each and rebuild" helper, and where it differs from map
List<T> mapList<T, R>(List<T> xs, R Function(T) f) => [for (final x in xs) f(x)];
// ...mapList allocates eagerly; Iterable.map does not. That is the whole
// difference, and it decides whether a chain is safe on an infinite source.

// a callback that can veto: bool Function(T) where false stops
void takeWhile(List<int> xs, bool Function(int) f) {
  for (final x in xs) { if (!f(x)) break; print(x); }
}
takeWhile([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], (n) => n < 4);   // prints 1 2 3

The remaining hazard is a closure that captures something it should not, and the compiler cannot catch it because nothing about the types is wrong. A callback stored in a long-lived object — a registry, a listener list, a timer — holds every variable from the scope that created it, so a callback created inside a loop over a large collection retains that entire scope for as long as the callback is registered. That is a memory leak with no compile error and no obvious cause, and the fix is to pass the needed value as a parameter to the stored function rather than capturing it.

// the leak: a closure per row, each holding its scope
final registry = <String, void Function()>{};
for (final row in rows) {                 // 100,000 rows
  registry[row.id] = () {
    print(row.name);                      // captures `row` - and the loop scope
    refresh();
  };
}
// every closure retains a distinct environment, and `rows` is retained by all

// the fix: a parameter, so one shared function
typedef Handler = void Function(Row);
final registry2 = <String, Handler>{};
for (final row in rows) {
  registry2[row.id] = (r) {
    print(r.name);                        // takes the row as an argument
    refresh();
  };
}
// ...or a bound tear-off on a per-row object, which is the same idea

// the version that is not a leak but looks like one: a late local that
// survives because something still references it
var buffer = <int>[];
Timer.periodic(const Duration(seconds: 1), (_) {
  buffer.add(read());     // `buffer` is retained until the timer is cancelled
});
// so the real check is: is every long-lived registration cancellable?

// and the general rule
// - a callback for an immediate call: capture freely
// - a callback stored or registered: take arguments, do not capture locals
// - a callback for an event handler in a widget: a tear-off, not a lambda
//   over a field, so the handler identity is stable

First-class functions, and the shape of a pipeline

Dart functions are values: they can be stored in variables, passed as arguments, returned from other functions, and held in collections. That is what makes the iterator protocol in dart:core possible, and it is why where, map and fold take callbacks rather than taking a block the way a Ruby method would.

MethodTakesReturnsIterates again?
mapT f(E)Iterable<T>Yes, lazily
wherebool f(E)Iterable<E>Yes, lazily
expandIterable<T> f(E)Iterable<T>Yes
foldT f(T, E)TOnce
reduceT f(T, T)TOnce
any / everybool f(E)boolStops early
firstWherebool f(E)EStops at a match
sortint f(E, E)voidEager, in place
// the pipeline, and the laziness that makes it safe
final words = 'the quick brown fox'.split(' ');
final lengths = words.map((w) => w.length);      // Iterable<int>
lengths.take(3).toList();                          // [3, 5, 5] - only 3 words
                                                    // were examined
// so a map over a lazy where RE-RUNS the predicate per element, which is
// the reason this is slower than the eager version:
final n = words.where((w) => w.length > 3).length;   // one pass, 3 matches

// the eager equivalent, when it matters
final eager = words.where((w) => w.length > 3).toList();
eager.length;                                      // 3

// fold for a running total, and the three-argument form for a map result
final total = prices.fold(0, (sum, p) => sum + p);
final byCategory = rows.fold(
  <String, double>{},
  (m, r) => m..update(r.category, (v) => v + r.amount, ifAbsent: () => r.amount),
);

// reduce, and why it needs an identity only when the collection may be empty
final sum = [1, 2, 3].reduce((a, b) => a + b);      // 6
[].reduce((a, b) => a + b);                          // ERROR - StateError
[].fold(0, (a, b) => a + b);                         // 0 - the identity

// sort, and the comparator contract
items.sort((a, b) => a.name.compareTo(b.name));       // returns void
// ...so it cannot be chained, and a comparator that returns a bool is a
// compile error rather than a silently wrong order
final sorted = [...items]..sort((a, b) => a.n.compareTo(b.n));
final desc = [...items]..sort((a, b) => b.n.compareTo(a.n));

A callback that takes another callback is where the interesting decisions start, and the two that go wrong most often are the difference between a synchronous and an asynchronous callback, and the difference between a "call for each" and a "call once at the end". Both are invisible in a lambda's syntax, because (x) { ... } looks the same either way — the type of the parameter is what tells you which one you have.

// SYNC callback: void f(T item)
void each(List<String> xs, void Function(String) f) {
  for (final x in xs) f(x);            // called now, in order
}
each(names, (n) { print(n); });         // fine

// ASYNC callback: FutureOr<void> Function(T)
Future<void> eachAsync(List<String> xs, FutureOr<void> Function(String) f) async {
  for (final x in xs) await f(x);      // must await, or they overlap
}
eachAsync(names, (n) async { await save(n); });

// the mistake: an async callback passed to a SYNC parameter
each(names, (n) async { await save(n); });   // compiles!
each(names, (n) { save(n); });                // compiles!
// ...and the first one silently does not wait: each() returns before any
// save completes, so the ordering guarantee the caller assumes is false.
// FutureOr<...> exists so the parameter's type can accept both, and it
// still cannot make the caller await.

// a "collect" callback: called once, with the finished collection
List<T> build<T>(T Function(List<T>) f) => f([]);

// a "transform each and rebuild" helper, and where it differs from map
List<T> mapList<T, R>(List<T> xs, R Function(T) f) => [for (final x in xs) f(x)];
// ...mapList allocates eagerly; Iterable.map does not. That is the whole
// difference, and it decides whether a chain is safe on an infinite source.

// a callback that can veto: bool Function(T) where false stops
void takeWhile(List<int> xs, bool Function(int) f) {
  for (final x in xs) { if (!f(x)) break; print(x); }
}
takeWhile([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], (n) => n < 4);   // prints 1 2 3

The remaining hazard is a closure that captures something it should not, and the compiler cannot catch it because nothing about the types is wrong. A callback stored in a long-lived object — a registry, a listener list, a timer — holds every variable from the scope that created it, so a callback created inside a loop over a large collection retains that entire scope for as long as the callback is registered. That is a memory leak with no compile error and no obvious cause, and the fix is to pass the needed value as a parameter to the stored function rather than capturing it.

// the leak: a closure per row, each holding its scope
final registry = <String, void Function()>{};
for (final row in rows) {                 // 100,000 rows
  registry[row.id] = () {
    print(row.name);                      // captures `row` - and the loop scope
    refresh();
  };
}
// every closure retains a distinct environment, and `rows` is retained by all

// the fix: a parameter, so one shared function
typedef Handler = void Function(Row);
final registry2 = <String, Handler>{};
for (final row in rows) {
  registry2[row.id] = (r) {
    print(r.name);                        // takes the row as an argument
    refresh();
  };
}
// ...or a bound tear-off on a per-row object, which is the same idea

// the version that is not a leak but looks like one: a late local that
// survives because something still references it
var buffer = <int>[];
Timer.periodic(const Duration(seconds: 1), (_) {
  buffer.add(read());     // `buffer` is retained until the timer is cancelled
});
// so the real check is: is every long-lived registration cancellable?

// and the general rule
// - a callback for an immediate call: capture freely
// - a callback stored or registered: take arguments, do not capture locals
// - a callback for an event handler in a widget: a tear-off, not a lambda
//   over a field, so the handler identity is stable

3.7 Extension methods and extension types

Adding methods to types you do not own, and the Dart 3 extension type.

// extension methods: add a method to any type
extension StringX on String {
  bool get isEmail => contains('@') && split('@').length == 2;

  String truncate(int max) =>
      length <= max ? this : '${substring(0, max - 1)}\u2026';

  TitleCase get titleCase => TitleCase(this);
}

extension ListX<T> on List<T> {
  T? get secondOrNull => length > 1 ? this[1] : null;
  List<T> get reversedCopy => List<T>.from(this).reversed;
  Map<K, List<T>> groupBy<K>(K Function(T) key) {
    final out = <K, List<T>>{};
    for (final item in this) {
      (out[key(item)] ??= []).add(item);
    }
    return out;
  }
}

extension DateX on DateTime {
  bool get isToday {
    final now = DateTime.now();
    return year == now.year && month == now.month && day == now.day;
  }
}

print('ana@acme.com'.isEmail);     // true
print('a long title'.truncate(6)); // 'a lon\u2026'
print([1, 2, 3].secondOrNull);    // 2
print(users.groupBy((u) => u.role));
// extension TYPES (Dart 3): give a primitive extra type safety
// and a zero-cost wrapper, with no runtime allocation

// the problem: an id is just a String, and any String can be passed
void renameUser(String id, String name) {}   // id and name are both String
renameUser('123', 'Ana');                    // no error; wrong on purpose

// the fix: a distinct type
extension type UserId(String value) {
  bool get isValid => value.isNotEmpty;
}

extension type Meters(double value) implements double {
  Meters operator +(Meters other) => Meters(value + other.value);
}

void renameUser2(UserId id, String name) {}
renameUser2('123', 'Ana');   // ERROR: String is not a UserId
renameUser2(UserId('123'), 'Ana');   // correct

// at runtime it IS a String: zero cost, no allocation
final raw = UserId('123').value;   // '123'
final asString = '123' as UserId;  // works, at your own risk

// the pattern to use it well
extension type Celsius(double degrees) {
  Celsius toFahrenheit() => Celsius(degrees * 9 / 5 + 32);
  // note: named Celsius for the converted value is semantically wrong;
  // a real design would use a single Unit type - see the exercise
}

Extension types are the right tool for the "plain value with a specific meaning" problem: ids, units, currencies, validated strings. They give compile-time separation at zero runtime cost, because the representation is unchanged. Use them where a wrong value would be a silent bug, and not as a general wrapper habit.

Exercises 4

  1. Write one function with a required positional, an optional positional, a required named and a defaulted named parameter, and call it three ways.
  2. Create a closure counter and prove each call to counter() returns an independent one.
  3. Write the loop-variable closure test and confirm Dart prints 0, 1, 2. Then explain why JavaScript does not.
  4. Deliberately write map with an async callback and print the runtime types. Then fix it both ways.
  5. Write extensions for String and List, including a groupBy, and use them in real code.
  6. Define an extension type for a UserId and a NonEmptyString, then refactor two functions to use them.
  7. Replace a boolean parameter in an existing function with a named parameter and note how many call sites become clearer.

What an extension may add, and the three rules that keep it safe

An extension adds members to a type without modifying it — on any type, including one from another library. That is what makes it the right tool for adding a method to String or BuildContext that the core library does not have, and what makes it dangerous in exactly the ways extensions generally are: the added member competes with a real one for the same name, and it is resolved statically, so what you get depends on which import is in scope.

// the shape
extension StringX on String {
  bool get isEmail => contains('@') && split('@').length == 2;
  String truncate(int max) => length <= max ? this : substring(0, max - 1) + '...';
}
'ab@x.com'.isEmail;        // true
'long enough'.truncate(6); // 'long...'

// extensions work on ANY type, including generics with a bound
extension ListX<T extends Comparable<T>> on List<T> {
  T get maxOrNull => isEmpty ? (null as T) : reduce((a, b) => a > b ? a : b);
}
extension<T> on Iterable<T> {
  Iterable<T> whereNotNull([bool Function(T)? test]) =>
      where((e) => e != null);
}

// a static extension: no `on`, callable by name
extension Str on String {
  static String slug(String s) =>
      s.toLowerCase().replaceAll(RegExp('[^a-z0-9]+'), '-');
}
Str.slug('Hello World');    // 'hello-world'

// and an extension on a nullable type, which is where they earn the most
extension NullableString on String? {
  bool get isNullOrEmpty => this == null || this!.isEmpty;
  String orDefault(String d) => this ?? d;
}
String? maybe;
maybe.isNullOrEmpty;       // true - and no null check at the call site

Resolution is static and import-scoped, and that produces two failure modes worth knowing exactly. If a real member and an extension member have the same name, the real member always wins — an extension cannot override anything, so a name collision is resolved in favour of the type's own method and the extension becomes invisible rather than wrong. And if two extensions from different imports both provide the member and neither is more specific, the call is a compile-time error rather than a silent choice, so the ambiguity is caught rather than resolved arbitrarily.

// a real member always beats an extension member
extension StrX on String {
  int get length => 99;      // legal, and never called
}
'abc'.length;                  // 3 - String.length wins

// two extensions providing the same member: a compile error
// file a.dart
extension StrA on String { String get shout => toUpperCase(); }
// file b.dart
extension StrB on String { String get shout => toLowerCase(); }
// main.dart
import 'a.dart';
import 'b.dart';
void f() { print('x'.shout); }   // ERROR - ambiguous

// the fix: hide one, or qualify
import 'a.dart' show StrA;
import 'b.dart' hide StrB;

// and an extension on Object leaks into EVERYTHING - avoid
extension Anything on Object {
  String get describe => runtimeType.toString();
}
1.describe;      // legal, and a bad idea: `describe` is now a name that
                 // cannot be used for anything else in the file

// explicit application also works, and is the way to disambiguate
print(StrA('x').shout);          // the extension by name
print('x'.toUpperCase());        // the real thing

The third rule is the one about scope: an extension is only in scope where it is imported, and a member added by an extension is only callable when the extension is in scope. So a String method that works in one file and not another is not a mystery — the file that has the import is the only one where the method exists, and the compiler error names the method as undefined rather than mentioning the extension. This is the direct consequence of static resolution, and it is why an extension in a utility file is a dependency of every file that uses the method and a surprise in every file that does not.

// an extension is visible only where imported
// lib/format.dart
extension Fmt on String {
  String get initials => split(' ').map((w) => w[0]).join();
}
// lib/a.dart imports format.dart - works
// lib/b.dart does not            - "The method 'initials' isn't defined"

// so the design question: where do the extensions live?
// 1. next to the type they extend, in the same package  - a type's own
//    operations belong with the type, even if the library cannot add them
// 2. in a clearly named file, imported explicitly where wanted
// 3. NOT on Object, NOT on num/String/int unless the operation is
//    genuinely universal

// the extension-type alternative (Dart 3.3), for wrapping rather than adding
extension type UserId(int id) {
  int get value => id;
  // ...this creates a DISTINCT compile-time type with a representation of
  // int, so UserId and OrderId are no longer interchangeable, and the
  // conversion is free at run time
}
extension type const Celsius(double value) {
  Celsius operator +(Celsius other) => Celsius(value + other.value);
}
// which is the answer to the "typedef cannot create a type" limitation:
// no runtime class, no boxing, real compile-time distinctness.

// and the boundary that catches people: a nullable receiver
extension NullableInt on int? {
  int get doubled => (this ?? 0) * 2;
}
int? x;
x.doubled;          // 0 - because the receiver type is int?
// ...so the extension on `int?` and the one on `int` are different, and
// which one applies depends on the STATIC type of the receiver, not its value

4 · Classes, Constructors and Immutability

4.1 A class and its members4.2 The constructor forms4.3 Initializer lists and factories4.4 Const constructors4.5 Inheritance, abstract and interfaces4.6 Mixins, and extension on behaviour4.7 Immutability and copyWith4.8 Equality, hashing and toString

Dart's object model, with a strong default toward immutability that pays off in every later chapter.

4.1 A class and its members

Fields, visibility, getters and setters, and the static and instance members.

class Point {
  // fields: public by default, _prefixed for private
  final double x;
  final double y;

  // a private field with a public getter: read-only to callers,
  // writable inside the class
  int _cache = -1;

  // static: on the class, not the instance
  static const int dimensions = 2;
  static final List<String> registry = [];

  // a named constructor
  Point.origin()
      : x = 0,
        y = 0;

  // the unnamed (default) constructor
  Point(this.x, this.y);

  // an initialiser block, run before the body
  Point.polar(double angle, double radius)
      : x = radius * _cos(angle),
        y = radius * _sin(angle) {
    assert(radius >= 0);
  }

  double get magnitude => _sqrt(x * x + y * y);

  set magnitude(double v) { /* not possible with final fields */ }

  static double _cos(double a) => a;   // a stand-in for dart:math
  static double _sin(double a) => a;
  static double _sqrt(double v) => v;
}

print(Point.dimensions);   // 2, on the class
final p = Point(3, 4);
print(p.x);               // 3
print(p.magnitude);        // 5
// visibility: it is LIBRARY private, not class private
// a leading underscore means private to the FILE

class BankAccount {
  final String id;
  double _balance = 0;

  double get balance => _balance;        // read-only from outside

  void deposit(double amount) {
    if (amount <= 0) throw ArgumentError.value(amount, 'amount', 'must be > 0');
    _balance += amount;
  }
}

// _balance is invisible outside bank_account.dart, so the invariant
// (never negative) cannot be broken by a caller

Fields, getters, and the visibility that decides the design

A Dart class has fields, getters, methods and a constructor, and the language makes almost no distinction between a field and a getter — both are read with .. What it distinguishes sharply is visibility, and that single mechanism is what determines whether a class can be evolved without breaking its callers.

PrefixVisible toUse for
nameThe declaring libraryImplementation detail
_nameThe declaring library, not the classWhat the class hides from other classes in the file
name with no prefixEveryoneThe public API

The underscore is library-private, not class-private, which is the detail that catches people coming from Java. A class in the same file cannot see another class's _field, because a file is not a class; but every class in the same file can see a top-level function's underscore, and a part file shares the parent library's privacy entirely. The practical rule is that the underscore is about the file as the unit of compilation, and it is a convention the compiler enforces rather than a mechanism it provides.

class Account {
  final String id;
  final String _secret;        // hidden outside this library
  double _balance = 0;         // private, mutable

  Account(this.id, String secret) : _secret = secret;

  double get balance => _balance;
  set balance(double v) {
    if (v < 0) throw ArgumentError.value(v, 'v', 'balance cannot be negative');
    _balance = v;
  }
  // ...a setter that validates is how a field stops being a public attribute
  // and becomes an operation, and the getter/setter pair reads exactly like
  // a field to every caller

  void deposit(double amount) {
    if (amount <= 0) throw ArgumentError.value(amount);
    _balance += amount;
  }
}

// the rule: a private field with a validating public accessor
// this is the ONLY way Dart lets you change how a value is read or written,
// and it is why a field cannot be a field and a setter at once
class Bad {
  int value;
  set value(int v) {}          // ERROR: cannot have both a field and a setter
}

A field that is final is initialised once and cannot be assigned again — but that is a statement about the reference, not about the contents. A final List<int> is a list anyone can append to, which is why the standard library has UnmodifiableListView and why a const constructor is the mechanism for a deeply immutable object. Making a field final is the right first step and is usually where people stop, which is the most common reason a supposedly immutable class turns out not to be.

// final fixes the reference; it says nothing about the list
class Config1 {
  final List<String> tags;
  Config1(this.tags);
}
final c = Config1([]);
c.tags.add('x');          // legal - and now two holders share one list

// the three ways to be actually immutable, in increasing cost
class Config2 {
  final List<String> tags;
  Config2(List<String> t) : tags = List.unmodifiable(t);   // a copy
}

class Config3 {
  final List<String> tags;
  Config3(List<String> t) : tags = UnmodifiableListView(t); // a view
}

const CONFIG = Config4(['a']);   // canonical, and const all the way down

// ...so a defensive copy protects against later writes to the SOURCE,
// and a view protects against writes through the object but not through the
// source. Which you want depends on who owns the list.

// and the rule of thumb: a public final field of a mutable type is a leak
// with a type annotation on it

Getters and setters are not accessors in the Java sense — there is no separate backing-field mechanism, no getX/setX pairing, and no property metadata. A getter is a method named without parentheses, and a setter is a method named with one parameter and the set keyword. That means you can write a getter that computes, a setter that validates, or a getter that is deliberately expensive, and the call site cannot tell the difference — which is exactly the property you want, and also the reason an expensive getter must never be used in a hot loop by accident.

class Grid {
  final List<int> _cells;
  Grid(this._cells);

  // a COMPUTED getter: nothing is stored
  int get total => _cells.fold(0, (a, b) => a + b);
  bool get isEmpty => _cells.every((c) => c == 0);

  // a CACHED computed getter: the ??= idiom
  int? _total;
  int get totalCached => _total ??= _cells.fold(0, (a, b) => a + b);

  // a setter that is NOT a field assignment, which is the point
  set total(int v) {
    if (v < 0) throw RangeError.range(v, 0, null, 'total');
    _cells[0] = v;
  }
}

final g = Grid([1, 2, 3]);
g.total;         // 6 - computed each call
g.total = 10;    // writes into _cells[0], not into a `total` field
g.total;         // 13 - because the getter reads _cells

// ...which is why a getter/setter pair is only a field replacement when the
// backing field is the obvious thing. If the pair can differ from what a
// field would do, a method is clearer, and the caller reads better too

4.2 The constructor forms

The six forms and when each is the right one.

class Config {
  final String host;
  final int port;
  final bool debug;

  // 1. generative, with initialising formals
  Config(this.host, this.port, {this.debug = false});

  // 2. generative, redirecting to another
  Config.localhost() : this('127.0.0.1', 8080);

  // 3. named generative
  Config.production() : this('api.acme.com', 443, debug: false);

  // 4. redirecting factory: a different way to reach a constructor
  factory Config.fromEnv(Map<String, String> env) {
    return Config(
      env['HOST'] ?? 'localhost',
      int.tryParse(env['PORT'] ?? '') ?? 8080,
    );
  }

  // 5. factory that returns a cached instance
  static final Config _default = Config('localhost', 8080);
  factory Config.defaults() => _default;

  // 6. const generative
  const Config.raw(this.host, this.port) : debug = false;

  // 7. initialising formals with a different name and a default
  Config.withPort(int p, {this.host = 'localhost'}) : port = p, debug = false;
}
// initialising formals vs the initialiser list
class A {
  final int x;
  A(this.x);                     // concise: assigns x directly
}

class B {
  final int x;
  final int y;
  B(int value)
    : x = value,                 // explicit: can compute
      y = value * 2;             // initialisers can be expressions
}

class C {
  final int x;
  final int y;
  C(int value)
    : x = value,
      y = value * 2 {
    // the BODY runs after both initialisers
    print('constructed with x=$x y=$y');
  }
}

// a redirecting constructor uses ': this(...)' and has NO body
class D {
  final int x;
  D(int x) : this._internal(x);
  D._internal(this.x);
  // a redirecting constructor cannot have a body: the target runs it

Use this.field initialising formals when the parameter is just the field; use the initialiser list when you need to compute something. The rule of thumb: if the initialiser list line is x = x, you wanted this.x.

Named, unnamed, factory, redirecting, and const

Dart has five constructor forms and they are not interchangeable. The unnamed form is a function whose name is the class name; a named form carries a suffix and is called with a colon; a factory returns an instance without calling this; a redirecting factory delegates to another constructor; a const constructor is the only one that can be invoked in a const context.

FormWritesReturnsExtensible
Point(this.x)Initialiser listThe instanceNo
Point(this.x) { … }BothThe instanceNo
factory Point.x() => …NothingAnythingYes — a subclass
factory Point.x() : this.y()NothingDelegatesNo
const Point(this.x)Initialiser listCanonicalNo

The distinction that matters most is that a generative constructor — one that is not a factory — cannot run any code before its initialiser list and cannot return anything but the instance being constructed. That is what makes const possible, and it is why a constructor body cannot be used to compute a value the initialiser needs: the field must be available first. A factory has no such restriction, which is why every constructor that needs to do real work — parsing, validating, choosing a subclass — is a factory.

// the four shapes
class Point {
  final double x, y;

  // 1. generative, unnamed - the minimal form
  Point(this.x, this.y);

  // 2. generative, named - a second way to build the same thing
  Point.origin() : x = 0, y = 0;

  // 3. redirecting factory - a NAMED constructor with no body
  Point.polar(double r, double a)
      : this(r * cos(a), r * sin(a));
  // ...it has no body at all, so nothing in it must be constant, and it
  // returns a fully initialised instance. This is the elegant way to express
  // "one constructor is defined in terms of another".

  // 4. factory that returns something else
  factory Point.fromJson(Map<String, Object?> j) =>
      Point((j['x']! as num).toDouble(), (j['y']! as num).toDouble());
}

// the case a factory exists for: returning a SUBCLASS
abstract class Shape {
  factory Shape(String kind) {
    return switch (kind) {
      'circle' => Circle(1),
      'square' => Square(1),
      _ => throw ArgumentError.value(kind),
    };
  }
}
class Circle extends Shape { final double r; Circle(this.r); }
class Square extends Shape { final double s; Square(this.s); }

// a generative constructor CANNOT do this: it can only build `this`
Point bad(String kind) {          // not valid constructor syntax
  if (kind == 'a') return Point(0, 0);   // returning a different instance
  return Point(1, 1);             // ...from a generative constructor
}

Initialiser lists run before the constructor body, in the order written, and that order is the whole rule. A field initialised in the list is final from the moment the list finishes; a field assigned in the body is not final at all and cannot be, which is why every final field must appear in the initialiser list or an initialiser. The list is also where this.x differs from x — the former reads the parameter, the latter the field — a distinction that becomes unreadable with same-named parameters and is the reason many codebases use different names.

// initialiser list versus body, and what each can do
class Config {
  final String host;
  final int port;
  final String url;

  Config({required String host, int port = 8080})
      : host = host.trim(),                    // transform in the LIST
        port = port,
        url = 'http://$host:$port';            // DERIVED in the LIST
  // ...url is final and derives from the parameters, which is only possible
  // in the list, and which means it is computed exactly once

  // the version that cannot work
  Config.bad({required String host, int port = 8080}) {
    this.host = host.trim();   // ERROR: final field must be initialised
    this.url = 'http://$host:$port';   // ...and this cannot read this.host
  }                                        //     because the body runs later
}

// and the ordering within the list
class A {
  final int a, b, c;
  A() : a = 1, b = a + 1, c = b + 1;   // 1, 2, 3 - declaration order is
                                       // irrelevant, LIST order is what counts
}

// the super call, and its placement rules
class Child extends Parent {
  final int z;
  Child(int x) : z = x * 2, super(x);   // super() must be LAST
  Child.named() : super(0);
  // ...a super initialiser is an initialiser, so it is subject to the same
  // ordering, and it must come after every field initialiser. That is why
  // `super(...)` before `z = ...` is a compile error rather than a subtle bug.

// a const constructor, and the fields that stop it being legal
class Id {
  final int value;
  const Id(this.value);         // legal - value is a literal parameter
}
const a = Id(1);
const b = Id(1);
print(identical(a, b));         // TRUE - canonicalised, so one object

class NotConst {
  final DateTime now;
  NotConst() : now = DateTime.now();   // ERROR: a const constructor needs
                                        // a const-initialisable expression
}
