Initialiser assertions complete the picture, and they are the mechanism for a class to guarantee its own invariants at construction rather than leaving the check to the caller. assert in an initialiser list runs in debug builds and is stripped in release, so it is for programmer error rather than for input validation — an untrusted value needs a real throw. And because assertions in an initialiser list are evaluated before the object is usable, they can reference fields already initialised, which makes them a natural place for a check that one derived field is consistent with another.

// an assertion, and what it is for
class Range {
  final int lo, hi;
  Range(this.lo, this.hi) : assert(lo <= hi, 'lo must not exceed hi') {
    // ...runs in debug only, stripped in release, and throws AssertionError
  }
}
Range(0, 10);      // fine
Range(10, 0);      // AssertionError in debug; silent in release

// so an assertion is for a contract YOU control, not for input
class Account {
  final int id;
  Account(this.id) : assert(id > 0);
}
Account(-1);        // debug: AssertionError
                   // release: an account with id -1, and everything after
                   //           has to cope with it

// for untrusted input, throw - in the initialiser list or in a factory
class Account2 {
  final int id;
  Account2(int rawId) : id = _validate(rawId);
  static int _validate(int v) {
    if (v <= 0) throw ArgumentError.value(v, 'rawId');
    return v;
  }
}

// and the distinction that matters for release builds
// assert(...)        stripped in release, zero cost, debug-time only
// if (bad) throw     always present, always costs
// so: assertions for internal contracts, throws for anything from outside

4.3 Initializer lists and factories

What runs in what order, and when a factory is the right call.

// THE ORDER, which is fixed and worth knowing
class Order {
  final int a;
  final int b;
  int c = 0;

  Order(int v)
      : a = v,           // 1. initialiser list, in written order
        b = v * 2 {
    c = 99;             // 4. the body
  }

  // 2. super constructor
  // 3. instance field initialisers (the 'c = 0' above)
  // 4. the constructor body
  // 5. the object is usable
}

// FACTORY CONSTRUCTORS: they do not create the object themselves
// they return an instance, so they can return a subtype

abstract class Shape {
  const Shape();

  // a factory that picks the implementation
  factory Shape.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) {
    return switch (json['type']) {
      'circle' => Circle(json['r'] as double),
      'rect' => Rect.fromJson(json),
      _ => throw FormatException('unknown shape: ${json['type']}'),
    };
  }
}

class Circle extends Shape {
  final double r;
  const Circle(this.r);
}

class Rect extends Shape {
  final double w, h;
  const Rect(this.w, this.h);
  Rect.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> j) : w = j['w'] as double, h = j['h'] as double;
}

final shape = Shape.fromJson({'type': 'circle', 'r': 5.0});
print(shape is Circle);   // true
// a factory for validation: reject invalid input at construction
class Email {
  final String value;
  const Email._(this.value);

  factory Email(String input) {
    final trimmed = input.trim();
    if (!_pattern.hasMatch(trimmed)) {
      throw FormatException('not an email: $input');
    }
    return Email._(trimmed);
  }

  // the null case, handled at the type level
  factory Email.tryParse(String? input) {
    if (input == null) return null as Email;   // see the note below
    try {
      return Email(input);
    } on FormatException {
      return null as Email;
    }
  }

  static final _pattern = RegExp(r'^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$');
  @override
  String toString() => 'Email($value)';
}

// the idiomatic nullable variant
Email? tryEmail(String? input) {
  if (input == null) return null;
  try {
    return Email(input);
  } on FormatException {
    return null;
  }
}

return null as Email in the example above is a deliberate mistake, shown so you see the correct pattern. A factory on a non-nullable class cannot return null. When absence is possible, either make the return type Email? with a top-level function, or add a separate static method. Throwing from a factory is right for programmer error; returning null is right for user input.

Declaration order, field initialisers, and the trap in between

A class's field initialisers run in declaration order, before the initialiser list, before the constructor body, and — importantly — before any superclass constructor body. That ordering is the cause of a bug that reads as impossible: a field that references another field which has not been initialised yet, and gets null or a default instead of the value.

// field initialisers run in DECLARATION order, before the constructor body
class Config {
  final List<String> items = ['a', 'b'];
  final int count = items.length;      // 2 - items is declared first

  final int bad = missing.length;     // ERROR: missing is not initialised yet
  final List<String> missing = [];
}

// the reverse order silently gives 0, in a language where the reference is
// legal but the value is wrong
class Order {
  final int n = items.length;          // 0 - `items` is still null
  final List<String> items = [];
  // ...this compiles, and the mistake is invisible in review because both
  // lines look reasonable in isolation
}

// the fix: declare in dependency order, or compute in a constructor
class Fixed {
  final List<String> items;
  final int count;
  Fixed() : items = ['a'], count = items.length;   // 1 - the list is ready
}

// and the three-phase order, which is worth being able to state
// 1. field initialisers, in declaration order, for this class
// 2. the superclass constructor (initialiser list, then body)
// 3. this class's initialiser list, then its body
// ...wait - the actual order is:
// 1. this class's FIELD INITIALISERS, in declaration order
// 2. the superclass's initialiser list and field initialisers
// 3. the superclass's constructor BODY
// 4. this class's INITIALISER LIST
// 5. this class's constructor BODY
// so a derived field cannot use a base field in a field initialiser, and
// this is why `super` must be last in the list

The trap is worse with inheritance, because the superclass constructor body runs after the subclass's field initialisers. A pattern where a base class calls an overridable method from its constructor — the classic template-method mistake — therefore dispatches to the subclass implementation before the subclass's fields exist, and the override reads uninitialised state. Dart does not forbid it, and the failure appears as a null or a default rather than as an error, which is why it survives review.

// the template-method trap, in Dart
class Base {
  final String id;
  Base(this.id);

  init() {
    validate();          // DISPATCHES to Sub.validate
    setup();
  }
  void validate() {}
  void setup() {}
}

class Sub extends Base {
  final String? name;
  Sub(this.name) : super('s') {
    // ...and `name` is assigned by the super constructor call, so it is
    // available here - but NOT inside the super's init()
  }

  @override
  void validate() {
    if (name == null) throw StateError('name required');
  }
}

// the version that actually breaks
class Base2 {
  String label = '';              // a field initialiser, runs first
  Base2() {
    describe();                   // dispatches to the subclass
  }
  void describe() => print(label);
}
class Sub2 extends Base2 {
  final String extra;
  Sub2(this.extra) : super() {
    extra = 'set';                // ...too late - describe() already ran
  }
  @override
  void describe() => print('$label + $extra');   // prints " + null"

// so the rules
// - never call an overridable method from a constructor
// - never rely on a field of the subclass being set during a super call
// - use init() as a separate, explicitly called phase if a template method
//   is genuinely needed, and document the call order

Late field initialisers interact with all of this, and they are the fourth place a value can come from. A field declared late final x = compute(); is initialised on first read rather than at construction, which means it escapes the whole ordering scheme — and that is exactly why it is also the right answer for a value that genuinely cannot be computed during construction, such as one that depends on a service injected after the fact.

// late final FIELD initialiser: computed on first read
class Repo {
  final Database _db;
  Repo(this._db);

  late final List<User> all = _db.query('SELECT * FROM users');
  // ...the query runs when `all` is first read, not when Repo is built,
  // and the result is cached for the lifetime of the object

  int reads = 0;
  int get userCount { reads++; return all.length; }
}

// when that is right
// - the value needs something not available at construction
// - the computation is expensive and may never be needed
// - the object is created early and configured later (a widget, a controller)

// when it is wrong
// - the failure should surface at construction rather than at first use
// - the object may be shared across threads/isolates and the initialiser is
//   not safe to run twice (it will not be, but the reasoning is harder)
// - there is more than one way the object can be read, and the order of
//   initialisation matters

// the explicit alternative, which makes the phase visible
class Repo2 {
  final Database _db;
  List<User>? _all;
  Repo2(this._db);

  Future<void> load() async {
    _all = await _db.query('SELECT * FROM users');
  }
  List<User> get all {
    final v = _all;
    if (v == null) throw StateError('call load() first');
    return v;
  }
}
// ...same guarantee, but the error names the missing step instead of being a
// LateInitializationError from a different file

The last piece is that a field initialiser cannot reference constructor parameters, which forces a real decision about where computed state is computed. Either the computation moves into the initialiser list, where parameters are in scope and the field can be final; or the field is not final and is assigned in the body, losing the guarantee that it is set at all. For anything a reader would expect to be immutable, the first is the only defensible choice, and it is worth recognising a non-final field assigned in a constructor body as a signal that the class has a state-transition method rather than a constructor.

// a field initialiser cannot see parameters
class Bad1 {
  final double x;
  Bad1(double x) { this.x = x; }        // legal, but `final` is not set
                                            // until the body - which works
                                            // but loses the guarantee at
                                            // the point of initialisation
}

// the shape to prefer: everything in the initialiser list
class Good {
  final double x;
  final double y;
  final double magnitude;

  Good(double x, double y)
      : x = x,
        y = y,
        magnitude = sqrt(x * x + y * y);
  // ...all three are final and all three are computed at construction, in a
  // defined order, with no uninitialised window

// and the anti-pattern to recognise
class Stateful {
  String name = '';           // a default
  Stateful(this.name);        // ...then overwritten by the parameter
  // redundant, and the field's declaration now says two different things

// the case where the body IS right
class Mutable {
  List<int> data;
  Mutable(List<int> d) { data = [...d]; }   // a defensive copy
  void add(int v) => data.add(v);
}
// ...here the object is genuinely mutable after construction, so the field
// cannot be final, and the constructor's job is to establish a valid state
// rather than to be the only thing that ever changes it

4.4 Const constructors

Compile-time instances, and the rules that make them possible.

// a const constructor lets the compiler create the object at compile time
class Point {
  final double x, y;
  const Point(this.x, this.y);
}

const origin = Point(0, 0);          // a compile-time instance
const points = [Point(0, 0), Point(1, 1)];   // a const list too

// the rules:
//   1. all fields must be final
//   2. the class must have ONLY a const constructor
//   3. all field initialisers must be compile-time constants
//   4. no instance variables that are not final

class NotConst {
  final int x;
  int y = 0;          // ERROR: y is not final
  NotConst(this.x);
}

// a const constructor CAN compute, at compile time
class Color {
  final int r, g, b, a;
  const Color(this.r, this.g, this.b, {this.a = 255});

  const Color.black() : this(0, 0, 0);
  const Color.red() : this(255, 0, 0);

  Color get darker => Color((r * .7).round(), (g * .7).round(), (b * .7).round());
}
const black = Color.black();

// and const works in collection literals and switch cases
const flags = {'debug': true, 'verbose': false};
const defaultTimeout = Duration(seconds: 30);   // Duration has a const ctor

void configure({bool debug = flags['debug']!}) {}  // hmm, prefer a plain const

// how to tell if a class COULD be const
// run the analyzer: it says "The constructor can't be const because
// the field is not final" or similar. That is a compile error, so the
// fix is guided.

Compile-time constants, and the four rules that decide canonicity

A const value is computed by the compiler, embedded in the program, and canonicalised — so two const expressions that evaluate to the same value are the same object. That is a stronger guarantee than immutability, and it is why const collections are legal as default parameter values and map keys while a final list is not.

DeclarationRuntime objectIdentical across occurrencesUsable as a default
final x = 5YesNoNo
const x = 5NoYesYes
const []NoYesYes
final []YesNoNo
const Duration(s: 1)NoYesYes
Duration(seconds: 1)YesNoNo

Four conditions must all hold for a value to be a compile-time constant, and they are worth memorising because each produces a slightly different error. The expression must be a literal or a constant expression; every field the constructor touches must be final; every value passed must itself be constant; and the constructor must be declared const. Fail any one and the diagnostic names it, but the failure is often reported at the use site rather than the declaration, which makes it look like a problem with the default parameter instead of the class.

// a const class, in full
class Point {
  final double x, y;
  const Point(this.x, this.y);           // the constructor must be const
}
const origin = Point(0, 0);
const unit = Point(1, 1);
print(identical(origin, origin));        // true - trivially
print(origin == unit);                    // false - different values

// what breaks const, one rule at a time
class A { final int n; A(this.n); }              // not a const CONSTRUCTOR
const a = A(1);                                  // ERROR

class B { int n; B(this.n); }                    // field not final
const b = B(1);                                  // ERROR

class C { final int n; const C(this.n); }
const c = C(DateTime.now().millisecondsSinceEpoch);  // ERROR: not constant

class D { final int n; const D(this.n); }
void f({D d = const D(1)}) {}                     // legal - const in the default
void g({D d = D(1)}) {}                           // ERROR - and the message
                                                //   names `d`, not D

Canonicity is what makes const more than an optimisation. Because the compiler guarantees one instance per distinct value, a const collection can be used as a map key, compared with identical, or shared between two callers without either of them being able to affect the other. That is what makes a const configuration object or a const lookup table a legitimate thing to build: the shared-mutable-state bug cannot occur, because there is no mutable state and no second copy.

// canonicity, and what it makes safe
const routes = <String, String>{
  '/': '/home',
  '/about': '/about',
};
print(identical(routes, routes));         // true

// two separately-written but identical const objects are the SAME object
const listA = <int>[1, 2, 3];
const listB = <int>[1, 2, 3];
print(identical(listA, listB));           // TRUE - canonicalised by value

// so a const collection can be a map key, and a final one cannot
final k1 = ObjectKey(listA);
final k2 = ObjectKey(listA);
print(identical(k1, k2));                 // true - one canonical instance
// ...where a final list would give a different key every time

// and sharing is safe without copying
void render(List<int> data) {
  for (final v in data) print(v);          // cannot modify it
}
render(listA);                              // fine - nobody can mutate it

// the contrast, which is the reason const exists
final mutable = [1, 2, 3];
render(mutable);
mutable.add(4);                             // ...but this works

// and a const set as a memoisation key
const cacheKey = 'default-config';
final cache = <String, Config>{};
Config get(String k) => cache.putIfAbsent(k, () => build(k));

Const constructors can do real work at compile time, which is how some libraries generate lookup tables with no run-time cost at all. A static const field initialised by an expression the compiler can evaluate becomes part of the program image, so a table of a thousand entries built at compile time costs nothing to load. The limit is that the computation must be something the compiler's constant evaluator can run — arithmetic, string operations, collection literals, and switch expressions over constants — and anything involving I/O, dates or non-const object construction is out.

// a compile-time table, built by the compiler
class Units {
  static const Map<String, double> toMetres = {
    'mm': 0.001,
    'cm': 0.01,
    'm': 1.0,
    'km': 1000.0,
  };

  static const List<String> all = <String>['mm', 'cm', 'm', 'km'];

  static const double maxOf = 1000.0;
  static const List<int> primes = [2, 3, 5, 7, 11];
  // ...everything above is in the program image; nothing is computed at
  // startup, and each list is one canonical instance
}

// what the compiler can and cannot evaluate
const sum = 1 + 2 * 3;                       // 7 - yes
const joined = 'a' + 'b';                    // 'ab' - yes
const list = <int>[for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) i * i];   // [0,1,4] - yes
const now = DateTime.now();                  // ERROR - not constant
const parsed = int.parse('42');              // ERROR - not constant
const fromList = List.filled(3, 0);          // ERROR - not a const ctor

// and a const constructor that computes, which the compiler runs once
class Version {
  final int major, minor, patch;
  const Version(this.major, this.minor, this.patch);

  String get label => '$major.$minor.$patch';
  int get encoded => major * 10000 + minor * 100 + patch;
}
const v = Version(1, 2, 3);
const w = Version(1, 2, 3);
print(identical(v, w));                      // true - one object, shared
// ...so two identical version constants in two libraries are the same
// instance, and mutating one would be a disaster - which is exactly why
// const also means unmodifiable

The remaining trap is that const inside a const context is inferred. Inside a const collection literal or a const constructor's initialiser list, nested literals are automatically constant, so writing const again is redundant — and in a non-const context the same expression is a runtime allocation. This produces a class of bug where a "constant" declaration is actually allocating on every call because one word was missing, and it is invisible until someone measures.

// implicit const inside a const context
const defaults = <String, int>{
  'retries': 3,                 // implicit const
  'timeout': 30,
};

// the same, non-const, and now it allocates
final defaults2 = <String, int>{
  'retries': 3,                 // a NEW map every time the function runs
};

// so the check: is it inside a const context?
const table = <String, List<int>>{
  'a': [1, 2],                  // implicitly const
};
table['a']!.add(3);              // ERROR - UnmodifiableListException

// and the reverse mistake: writing const where it is not needed and costs
// nothing but noise
final x = const 5;               // legal, identical to `final x = 5`

// the case that actually bites: a default parameter
class Client {
  final Map<String, String> headers;
  // WRONG - allocates a new map per Client with no headers supplied
  Client({Map<String, String> headers = const {}});
  // ...which is correct! the default is const. The wrong version is
  // `= {}`, which is a compile error because a default must be constant
}

// so the rule: a default parameter value MUST be a const expression, and
// the compiler enforces it, which means the question is never "should this
// be const" but "which const expression" - and the answer for a collection
// is almost always `const []` or `const {}`

4.5 Inheritance, abstract and interfaces

Dart has single inheritance plus interfaces, and no abstract keyword needed.

// abstract: a class that cannot be instantiated
abstract class Animal {
  final String name;
  Animal(this.name);

  String speak();                       // no body: must be implemented

  void describe() => print('$name says ${speak()}');  // has a body
}

class Dog extends Animal {
  Dog(super.name);                      // super parameters, Dart 2.17+
  @override
  String speak() => 'Woof';
}

class Cat extends Animal {
  Cat(super.name);
  @override
  String speak() => 'Meow';

  // a class can override to ADD behaviour
  void purr() => print('$name purrs');
}

// an INTERFACE: any class, implicitly. There is no `implements`
// keyword requirement, but using it documents intent.
abstract class Serializable {
  Map<String, dynamic> toJson();
}

// a class can implement several
class User extends Animal implements Serializable {
  User(super.name);
  @override
  String speak() => '...';
  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> toJson() => {'name': name};
}

// implements requires re-implementing EVERYTHING, including inherited
// concrete members. extends inherits them. Choose deliberately.
// abstract class + implements: both must be considered
class Dog extends Animal with Logging implements Serializable { }

// extends Animal     - gets Animal's concrete methods (describe)
// with Logging       - mixes in behaviour
// implements Serializable - must provide toJson()

// when to use extends vs implements:
//   extends  - the subclass IS-A and can reuse the parent's behaviour
//   implements - you only need the SHAPE, and cannot inherit safely
//               (or the parent is third-party and you do not control it)
// @override is optional but should always be present:
// it makes the analyzer catch a typo in a method name, which would
// otherwise silently add a new method instead of overriding one.

class Dog extends Animal {
  @override
  String speek() => 'Woof';   // SPELLING ERROR
}
// with @override: ERROR - does not override anything
// without:          no error, and speak() still returns the parent's

The three ways to add behaviour, and the one to reach for first

Dart offers inheritance, mixins and composition, and the order of preference is the opposite of what a Java-trained reader expects: prefer composition, use a mixin for shared behaviour without a hierarchy, and use inheritance only when the subtype relation is genuine and total.

MechanismAddsIs-a chainUse for
CompositionNothing; holds a fieldNoThe default answer
mixinMembers to any classNoCross-cutting behaviour
extendsMembers to one subclassYesA genuine subtype
interface / implementsNothing; a contractYes, nominallyCapability, not taxonomy
withMembers to this classNoCapability on one class

The reason to prefer composition is not style but substitutability. Inheritance creates an is-a relationship that every caller can rely on, so a subclass must honour the parent's contract in all its details — including the parts it did not override and would rather not. Composition creates a has-a relationship with no such obligation, so the held object can be replaced, decorated, or a different implementation entirely without any caller being able to notice. A hierarchy is a claim you cannot cheaply take back.

// composition: no obligation, and substitutable at run time
class Logger {
  void log(String m) => print(m);
}
class Service {
  final Logger _log;              // has-a, not is-a
  Service(this._log);

  void run() {
    _log.log('starting');
    // ...and a caller can pass a different Logger with no type change:
    // Service(FileLogger()), Service(SilentLogger())
  }
}

// inheritance: a real subtype relation, and an obligation
abstract class Animal {
  String get sound;
  void speak() => print(sound);       // concrete, inherited by all
}
class Dog extends Animal {
  @override
  String get sound => 'woof';
}
class Cat extends Animal {
  @override
  String get sound => 'meow';
}

// a caller can rely on the relation
void makeItSpeak(Animal a) => a.speak();   // correct for any subtype
makeItSpeak(Dog());

// ...and that reliance is the cost: if Animal ever adds a method with a
// default that is wrong for Dog, every existing caller silently changes

// interfaces: capability, not taxonomy
abstract interface class Serializable {
  String serialize();
}
class Doc implements Serializable {
  @override
  String serialize() => '…';
}
class Cache implements Serializable {
  @override
  String serialize() => 'cached-data';
}
// a Doc is NOT "a serializable thing that happens to be a document" -
// it is a thing that can be serialized. The interface says what it can do,
// and nothing about what it is.

Method resolution follows a fixed order that is worth being able to state, because most "my override is not being called" reports are an ordering mistake rather than a mistake in the override itself. A class's own members win; then anything mixed into the class; then super, which searches the superclass chain; and a member declared in a mixin wins over the same member in the superclass. That last part is the one that surprises people — a mixin can shadow a superclass method without the superclass knowing.

// the resolution order, demonstrated
class Base {
  String who() => 'base';
}
mixin Loud {
  String who() => 'LOUD ' + super.who();   // calls the next in chain
}
mixin Quiet {
  String who() => 'quiet ' + super.who();
}
class Thing extends Base with Loud, Quiet {}

Thing().who();
// resolution: Thing (nothing) -> Loud -> Quiet -> Base
// Loud calls super, which is Quiet, which calls super, which is Base:
//   'LOUD quiet base'
// so the ORDER OF `with` IS the order of precedence, left to right, and
// `super` in a mixin means "the next thing in the linearised chain" - not
// the superclass specifically.

// explicit super call, for the cases where the chain should be skipped
class Direct extends Base {
  @override
  String who() => 'direct';              // Base.who is NOT called
}

// and calling it anyway
class Both extends Base {
  @override
  String who() => 'both: ' + super.who();  // 'both: base'
}

// the order that people confuse: superclass first or mixins first
class Ordered extends Base with Loud {}
// resolution is Ordered -> Loud -> Base
// ...so the mixin shadows the superclass, NOT the other way round

extends, with and implements also differ in what they force you to write, and that difference is what tells you which one you are looking at. extends inherits concrete members and requires only the abstract ones to be provided. with inherits the mixin's members and adds none. implements inherits nothing — every member of the interface must be implemented, even ones the class already has — which is why implementing an interface means re-declaring members that would have been inherited for free.

// implements requires re-declaring everything
abstract class Sized {
  int get size;                 // abstract
  void printSize() => print(size);   // CONCRETE
}
class Box implements Sized {
  final List<int> _items;
  Box(this._items);

  @override
  int get size => _items.length;

  @override
  void printSize() => print(size);    // HAD to be re-declared!
}

// versus with, which brings the concrete method along
mixin Printable {
  void printSize() => print(size);      // wait - needs a size
}

// the Dart 3 answer, which removes the whole distinction
// `abstract interface class` cannot be extended - only implemented
abstract interface class Sized {
  int get size;
  void printSize() => print(size);
}
class Box implements Sized { … }          // same obligation, clearer intent

// and `base`, which restricts who may extend
base class Shape {
  void describe() => print('a shape');
}
final class Square extends Shape {}        // OK
// class Circle extends Shape {}           // ERROR: Shape is `base`
// ...so `base` + `final` documents the hierarchy's edges at the type level,
// which is the only way to make "do not subclass this" enforceable

4.6 Mixins, and extension on behaviour

The tool for sharing behaviour without an inheritance relationship.

// a mixin: behaviour with no constructor, no fields
mixin Logging {
  void log(String message) => print('[$runtimeType] $message');
  String get logTag => runtimeType.toString();
}

// use it
class Service with Logging {
  void run() {
    log('starting');       // inherited behaviour
  }
}

class ApiClient with Logging { ... }

// a mixin ON a class, applied only where it makes sense
class Database with Logging, Caching { ... }

// CONSTRAINED mixins: require a member to be present
mixin RequiresName on Animal {
  String get shoutName => name.toUpperCase();
}

class Bird extends Animal with RequiresName {
  Bird(super.name);
  @override
  String speak() => 'Tweet';
}
print(Bird('tweety').shoutName);   // TWEETY

// a mixin that adds a member a class can override
mixin Persistence {
  String get tableName;              // an abstract member: the class must define it
  Future<void> save() async {
    await db.write(tableName, toMap());
  }
  Map<String, dynamic> toMap();
}

class Entry with Persistence {
  @override
  String get tableName => 'entries';
  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> toMap() => {'id': id};
}
// when a mixin is better than inheritance
//
// inheritance: "IS-A" and you want ALL the parent's behaviour
//            (Dog IS-A Animal)
//
// mixin:       "this behaviour applies here" and you want to compose
//             (Logging applies to Service, ApiClient, Database)
//
// the classic error: a deep hierarchy where "IS-A" becomes untrue
// three levels down. Mixins flatten that.

// THE HEAP SHOTGUN WARNING: a class with many mixins, where you
// cannot see which one provides a method, is a maintenance problem.
// if you need four mixins, consider a collaborator object instead.

What a mixin is, and the on clause that replaced a bug

A mixin is a reusable set of members applied to a class without requiring inheritance from anything. Before Dart 2.1 a mixin could only be applied to a class with no superclass, which meant any mixin usable on a real class had to be an abstract class with a mixin keyword — and that form had a defect: it could be applied to a class whose superclass did not satisfy its implicit requirements.

// the modern form: `mixin M on Constraint`
mixin Validatable on Entity {
  bool isValid() => validate().isEmpty;

  List<String> validate() {
    final errors = <String>[];
    if (id <= 0) errors.add('id must be positive');
    if (name.isEmpty) errors.add('name required');
    return errors;
  }
}

// the `on` clause is a REQUIREMENT, checked at the application site
class Entity { final int id; final String name; Entity(this.id, this.name); }
class User extends Entity with Validatable {}

class NotAnEntity {}
class Broken extends NotAnEntity with Validatable {}   // ERROR: Validatable
                                                          // requires Entity
// ...and this is the fix for the old defect: the requirement is declared,
// checked, and does not have to be re-derived from an awkward hierarchy

// `on` can name several types, and the mixin may then use members from any
mixin Tagged on Entity, Comparable<Entity> {
  String tag() => '$id-${compareTo(this)}';
}

// and a mixin with no `on` clause applies to anything
mixin Timestamped {
  final createdAt = DateTime.now();
  String stamp() => createdAt.toIso8601String();
}
class Doc extends Entity with Timested {}   // any class can use it

What a mixin may do is constrained in one important way: it cannot declare instance fields unless the on clause is a class in the same library — and even then the field must be final and there is a restriction on types. The reason is that a mixin's fields have nowhere to live in a multiple-inheritance layout, so Dart restricts them rather than inventing a layout. What a mixin can do freely is add methods, getters, operators and static members, which covers the large majority of what a mixin is for.

A mixin may declareConstraint
Methods, getters, settersNone
OperatorsNone
Static membersNone
final fieldsOnly with on, and the type must be safe to combine
ConstructorsNone — a mixin has no constructor
Mutable fieldsNot allowed on a class outside the library
// what a mixin can and cannot declare
mixin Good {
  void doThing() {}                 // fine
  int get value => 1;             // fine - a getter needs no storage
  static const int max = 10;       // fine
  static int counter = 0;           // fine
  int operator +(other) => value; // fine

  Good();                           // ERROR: a mixin has no constructor
  var state = 0;                    // ERROR: a mutable field
}

// the `on` clause buys field storage, with restrictions
mixin WithCache on Service {
  final Map<String, Object> _cache = {};   // a final field - allowed
  Object get(String k) => _cache.putIfAbsent(k, compute);
}

// the pattern for state a mixin genuinely needs
mixin Logged {
  final List<String> _entries = [];   // each class gets its OWN copy
  void record(String e) => _entries.add(e);
  List<String> get entries => List.unmodifiable(_entries);
}
class A with Logged {}
class B with Logged {}
final a = A(), b = B();
a.record('one');
print(b.entries);      // [] - not shared
// ...each mixin application is a separate copy of the field, which is what
// makes `final` on a mixin field safe

Two mixins that both define the same member do not conflict at the application site as long as they never coexist on the same class, but they do compose into a diamond where the member is required twice — and super in each is how a mixin joins a chain rather than replacing what came before it. The linearisation order is left to right in the with clause, and it applies across the whole chain including the superclass, which is worth writing down once because every mixin ordering bug is this rule misremembered.

// composition, and what super means in a mixin
class Logger {
  void log(String m) => print('LOG $m');
}
mixin Timestamped on Logger {
  void log(String m) {
    super.log('[$time] $m');       // the NEXT Logger in the chain
    send(m);                        // plus this mixin's own work
  }
  void send(String m) {}
}
mixin Retrying on Logger {
  void log(String m) {
    super.log(m);
    if (shouldRetry) retry();
  }
}

class Service with Timestamped, Retrying {}
// order: Service -> Timestamped -> Retrying -> Logger
// one log call: Timestamped.log -> Retrying.log -> Logger.log
// ...so the FIRST mixin in the list wraps the rest, and each `super.log`
// hands off rather than restarting

// a mixin requiring another mixin
mixin Cacheable on Service with Timestamped {
  void log(String m) {
    if (!seen.contains(m)) {
      seen.add(m);
      super.log(m);               // reaches Timestamped
    }
  }
}

// the diamond, and why super exists to resolve it
// A -> Mixin1 -> Mixin2 -> Base   and   A -> Mixin2 -> Base
// ...without `super`, Mixin1 would replace Mixin2 entirely. With it, each
// layer's super call reaches the next, so nothing is skipped.

// the conflict, which IS an error
mixin X { void f() => print('X'); }
mixin Y { void f() => print('Y'); }
class C with X, Y {}          // legal to DECLARE - and at runtime the
                              // order decides; `with Y, X` inverts it
// ...but if neither calls super and both are applied, one silently wins
// by position, which is the bug `on` and explicit super calls prevent

Whether a behaviour belongs in a mixin at all is a question about the shape of the callers, and the answer is usually yes when the behaviour needs the host's data and no when it needs its own. A mixin that reads three fields from its on type is a mixin that is really a set of extension methods with an implicit parameter; a mixin that adds methods using only its own state is a self-contained capability. The first is harder to read, to test and to reason about, so it is worth writing those as ordinary methods on the class and keeping the mixin for the genuinely shared, genuinely stateless-until-applied behaviour.

// a mixin that is really an extension, with three dependencies
mixin Auditable on Entity {
  void audit() {
    record('before: $id $name');
    if (id < 0) record('impossible');
    record('after');
  }
  void record(String s) {}      // NOT on Entity - the mixin invented it
}
// ...`record` is invented by the mixin, so this works. But if it needed
// three more Entity fields, it would be a class with a parameter.

// the same behaviour as a method, which is clearer
class Entity2 {
  final int id;
  final String name;
  final List<String> log = [];
  Entity2(this.id, this.name);

  void audit() {
    log.add('before: $id $name');
    if (id < 0) log.add('impossible');
    log.add('after');
  }
}

// the test that decides: does the mixin need the host's DATA?
// no  -> a mixin, or better an extension method
// one -> a mixin with an `on` clause
// many -> a base class, or composition, or ordinary methods
//
// and the other test: is the behaviour about the host or about a role?
// 'this entity can be validated'  -> mixin, capability
// 'this entity IS a validated thing' -> inheritance, taxonomy

4.7 Immutability and copyWith

The single most valuable habit in Dart, and the pattern that makes it cheap.

// an immutable value class: every field final
class Entry {
  final String id;
  final String title;
  final String body;
  final DateTime createdAt;
  final List<String> tags;
  final bool archived;

  const Entry({
    required this.id,
    required this.title,
    required this.body,
    required this.createdAt,
    this.tags = const [],
    this.archived = false,
  });

  // the pattern: a copy with some fields changed
  // write it by hand, or generate it (see below)
  Entry copyWith({
    String? title,
    String? body,
    List<String>? tags,
    bool? archived,
  }) {
    return Entry(
      id: id,
      title: title ?? this.title,
      body: body ?? this.body,
      createdAt: createdAt,
      tags: tags ?? this.tags,
      archived: archived ?? this.archived,
    );
  }
}

var e = Entry(id: '1', title: 'Draft', body: '', createdAt: DateTime.now());
e = e.copyWith(title: 'Final', tags: ['work']);   // a NEW object
// the old one is untouched: safe to share, safe to cache
// the deep-immutability problem: a final List is still mutable
final tags = ['a', 'b'];
final e = Entry(id: '1', title: 't', body: '', createdAt: now, tags: tags);
tags.add('c');          // the "immutable" Entry just changed
print(e.tags);          // ['a', 'b', 'c']

// fixes, in order of preference
// 1. UnmodifiableListView
class Entry2 {
  final List<String> tags;
  Entry2({required this.tags})
    : tags = List.unmodifiable(tags);      // deep-ish: the list cannot change
}

// 2. const default + never store the caller's list directly
// 3. an immutable collection: package:collection's UnmodifiableListView
//    or a private List with a public unmodifiable view

class Entry3 {
  final List<String> _tags;
  Entry3({List<String>? tags}) : _tags = List.of(tags ?? const []);
  List<String> get tags => UnmodifiableListView(_tags);   // the type says so
  Entry3 addTag(String t) => Entry3(tags: [..._tags, t]);   // returns a new one
}

// 4. generate the whole class: freezed, equatable, json_serializable
//    with @freezed, the immutability, ==, hashCode, copyWith and
//    toJson all come from one annotation
// freezed: the annotation does it all
// part 'entry.freezed.dart';
// @freezed
// class Entry with _$Entry {
//   const factory Entry({
//     required String id,
//     required String title,
//     @Default(<String>[]) List<String> tags,
//     @Default(false) bool archived,
//   }) = _Entry;
// }
//
// generated, automatically:
//   - const factory
//   - copyWith with correct nullable handling
//   - == and hashCode by value
//   - toString
//   - a union type if you declare variants
//
// run: dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs

Immutability is what makes const constructors, cheap structural sharing, safe caching, correct == and reliable copyWith possible. It also removes a whole category of "it was fine until two screens shared it" bugs. Start with final on every field and add mutation only where a measurement shows you need it.

Making immutability real, and the four leaks that defeat it

An immutable object is one whose observable state cannot change after construction. Dart gives you final fields and const constructors, and between them most of the job — but four leaks remain, and each has a specific fix that is worth knowing rather than discovering.

LeakSymptomFix
final mutable fieldA shared list changesCopy in, or wrap in a view
Mutable staticState depends on call orderConst, or inject
Lazy cache fieldIdentity changes over timeCompute eagerly
covariant fieldA subclass swaps the typeNever covariant on a field

The first leak is the one that appears in every codebase at least once: a final field holding a mutable object. The field cannot be reassigned, so the class looks immutable, and the list inside it can be appended to by anyone holding it. The fix is a defensive copy at construction — List.unmodifiable(t) or List.of(t) — and the choice between them is a decision about ownership: a copy protects against writes through the source, a view protects against writes through the object.

// the leak
class Report {
  final List<String> lines;
  Report(this.lines);
}
final src = ['a'];
final r = Report(src);
src.add('b');              // the supposedly immutable report changed
r.lines.add('c');          // and so did this

// fix 1: a copy - the source can no longer affect it
class Report1 {
  final List<String> lines;
  Report1(List<String> l) : lines = List.unmodifiable(l);
}
final r1 = Report1(src);
src.add('b');              // r1.lines is unaffected
// ...and the copy also means a later mutation of `src` does not leak in,
// which is the property that makes the class safe to cache

// fix 2: a view - no copy, but the source can still change it
class Report2 {
  final List<String> lines;
  Report2(List<String> l) : lines = UnmodifiableListView(l);
}
// ...cheaper, and correct when the host owns the list and promises not to
// change it. The trap is that the promise is invisible.

// fix 3: const, which solves it at compile time
class Report3 {
  final List<String> lines;
  const Report3(this.lines);
}
const r3 = Report3(['a']);   // the list is implicitly const - unmodifiable
// ...so a const constructor requires const arguments, which is precisely
// what forces the values to be immutable

The second leak is a mutable static, which produces behaviour that depends on initialisation order — the class of bug where a test passes alone and fails in the suite, because another test constructed an object first and left the static in a different state. The fix is either to make the static const, so it is genuinely fixed, or to stop having one and inject the value, so each instance has its own. A static cache is the usual offender and there is a real argument for it, so the honest answer is to make the cache keyed on something rather than a single slot, and to accept that a cached mutable value is not immutable.

// the order-dependent static
class Config {
  static String? url;              // mutable global state
  static Config? _instance;

  static Config get instance =>
      _instance ??= Config(url ?? 'default');
}
// Config.url = 'x'; then Config.instance -> url x
// Config.instance;    then Config.url = 'y'  -> instance still has x
// ...the second read is a cache hit, so the value is stale, and which
// happens depends on the order of unrelated code

// fix 1: inject
class Client {
  final Uri base;
  Client(this.base);
}
final prod = Client(Uri.parse('https://api.example.com'));

// fix 2: const where possible
class Endpoints {
  static const prod = Uri.parse('https://api.example.com');
}

// fix 3: key the cache, so a stale hit is impossible
class Pool {
  final Map<String, Client> _cache = {};

  Client forBase(String base) =>
      _cache.putIfAbsent(base, () => Client(Uri.parse(base)));
}
// ...now the key is the input, so a different input cannot read another's
// entry. This is the shape that makes a static safe.

// and the honest cost: a mutable cache means the object is not immutable,
// so if immutability is the point, do not cache

The third leak is subtler and is specific to Dart: a lazily computed field. A final field computed on first read has the same value every time but not the same identity — the object exists in two states, before and after the read — which breaks anything that compares by identity or uses the object as a map key. It also means a const object is impossible, because a const object is computed entirely at compile time. The fix is to compute eagerly in the constructor whenever the cost allows, and to accept a late final only when the cost genuinely does not.

// the lazy field, and the two-state problem
class Summary {
  final List<Row> rows;
  Summary(this.rows);

  late final double total = rows.fold(0.0, (a, r) => a + r.value);
  // value is stable, identity is not, and the object cannot be const
}

// so: compute eagerly unless it is genuinely expensive
class Summary2 {
  final List<Row> rows;
  final double total;
  Summary2(this.rows) : total = rows.fold(0.0, (a, r) => a + r.value);
}

// the third leak, which is Dart-specific: covariant fields
class Container {
  final Object value;               // fine
}
class StringContainer extends Container {
  @override
  final covariant String value;     // legal, and a lie
}
// ...the field is declared String but the superclass slot holds Object, so
// the runtime checks differ and a write through the superclass's reference
// can put a non-String in a String-typed field. It exists for generics
// interop; on a plain field it is a bug. Never write it by hand.

// so the recipe, in order
// 1. every field final
// 2. every field's TYPE immutable, or defensively copied in the constructor
// 3. no mutable statics - const, or keyed caches
// 4. no lazy fields unless the cost requires it
// 5. a const constructor if every field can be a const expression, because
//    that makes the compiler verify points 2 and 4 for you

The strongest form of immutability available is const, because it makes the compiler enforce rather than the author remember. A const class cannot hold a mutable field, cannot have a lazy field, cannot take a non-constant default, and cannot be constructed with a runtime value — every one of which is a leak closed by construction. The cost is that every construction site becomes a compile-time expression, so a const class cannot be built from a database row or a user input. The resolution is usually two classes: a const one for the cases that are genuinely compile-time, and a plain immutable one for the rest.

// two classes, and the boundary between them
enum Axis { x, y }                       // const by nature

class Measurement {
  final num value;
  final Axis axis;
  const Measurement(this.value, this.axis);
  // ...const, so every field must be a const expression. `num` is fine -
  // the VALUE is const, not the type.

  Measurement.fromReading(num v, String a)
      : value = v,
        axis = Axis.values.firstWhere((e) => e.name == a);
  // ...a named constructor that is NOT const, for the runtime case - and it
  // delegates: field initialisers run, so it produces the same immutable
  // shape, just not canonicalised.

  static const zero = Measurement(0, Axis.x);   // one shared instance
}

// so the pattern: the class is immutable, and SOME constructors are const
// ...which gives a canonical instance for the common cases and correctness
// for the rest, with no second class needed.

// and the test for whether const is achievable
// can every field's value be named as a literal or a const expression?
//   yes -> make the constructor const, and the compiler checks everything
//   no  -> make it final, and verify immutability in the constructor
// the middle case, where MOST constructors are const and one is not, is
// common and is fine

4.8 Equality, hashing and toString

The default is identity, and overriding it wrongly breaks collections.

// by default, == is IDENTITY
class Point {
  final int x, y;
  Point(this.x, this.y);
}

final a = Point(1, 2);
final b = Point(1, 2);
print(a == b);              // FALSE - different objects
print(identical(a, b));     // false
print(identical(a, a));     // true

final set = {a, b};
print(set.length);           // 2, because they are not equal

// override == AND hashCode, together, always
class Point2 {
  final int x, y;
  const Point2(this.x, this.y);

  @override
  bool operator ==(Object other) {
    if (identical(this, other)) return true;
    return other is Point2 && other.x == x && other.y == y;
  }

  @override
  int get hashCode => Object.hash(x, y);

  @override
  String toString() => 'Point2($x, $y)';
}

final c = Point2(1, 2);
final d = Point2(1, 2);
print(c == d);               // true
print({c, d}.length);        // 1  - the set deduplicated
print(c);                    // Point2(1, 2)
// the hashCode rules that are not negotiable
//
// 1. a == b MUST imply a.hashCode == b.hashCode
// 2. the hash must be stable for the object's lifetime
// 3. a MUTABLE field used in == or hashCode is a bug:
//      put it in a Set, mutate it, and the set is now corrupt
// 4. Object.hash(a, b, c) is the correct multi-field hash
// 5. do NOT use a random or time-based hash

// the third rule, demonstrated
class Counter {
  int value;
  Counter(this.value);
  @override
  bool operator ==(Object o) => o is Counter && o.value == value;
  @override
  int get hashCode => value.hashCode;
}

final set2 = {Counter(1)};
final counter = set2.first;
counter.value = 5;      // now its hash is 5, but it lives in a bucket for 1
set2.contains(Counter(5));   // FALSE, and the set can never find it again
// the performant override, when a field is expensive to compare
class Matrix {
  final List<List<double>> cells;
  Matrix(this.cells);

  @override
  bool operator ==(Object other) {
    if (identical(this, other)) return true;
    if (other is! Matrix) return false;
    if (other.cells.length != cells.length) return false;
    for (var i = 0; i < cells.length; i++) {
      if (!const ListEquality<double>().equals(cells[i], other.cells[i])) {
        return false;
      }
    }
    return true;
  }

  @override
  int get hashCode {
    var h = 0;
    for (final row in cells) {
      for (final v in row) {
        h = 0x1fffffff & (h + v.hashCode);
        h = 0x1fffffff & (h + ((0x0007ffff & h) << 10));
        h ^= h >>> 6;
      }
    }
    h = 0x1fffffff & (h + ((0x03ffffff & h) << 3));
    h ^= h >> 11;
    return 0x1fffffff & (h + ((0x00003fff & h) << 15));
  }
}

// for data classes, just use Equatable or freezed rather than
// writing this by hand

Overriding == without hashCode is a real bug, not a style issue: the object goes into a Map or Set using the inherited identity hash, then lookups by value fail. The analyzer lint hash_and_equals catches exactly this. Enable it.

Exercises 5

  1. Write a class with all six constructor forms and confirm each produces the right state.
  2. Write a factory that validates an email and throws on invalid input, then a nullable wrapper that returns null.
  3. Make a class const-constructible and create a const list of them. Then add a non-final field and read the error.
  4. Write a copyWith by hand, then discover the nullable-field problem: how do you set a field TO null? Solve it.
  5. Prove the deep-immutability bug with a final List, then fix it three different ways.
  6. Override == and hashCode, verify a Set deduplicates, then break the mutable-field rule and show the Set failing.
  7. Set up freezed, generate a model, and confirm you get copyWith, == and a const factory for free.

Value equality, hash codes, and the pairs that must agree

Every class inherits == and hashCode from Object, and both default to identity. Overriding == without overriding hashCode is the single most common collection bug in Dart, and it is silent: the object behaves correctly in == comparisons and disappears from every Set and Map that contains it.

RuleStatementConsequence if broken
Contract 1a == b implies a.hashCode == b.hashCodeEqual objects live in different buckets
Contract 2Equal objects must be equal by ==Symmetry breaks
Contract 3hashCode should be stable for the object's lifeMutation while in a Set corrupts it
ConvenienceIdentical objects must be equalAlways true if == is correct

The rule behind contract 1 is that Set and Map do not compare every element. They compute a hash, index into a bucket array, and compare only within a bucket — so a Set containing an object whose hashCode changed is in a bucket that no longer matches, and contains will report false even though the same instance is present. The same applies to removing from a Map: it computes the hash to find the bucket, and a changed hash means it looks in the wrong place.

// the bug, demonstrated
class Point {
  final double x, y;
  Point(this.x, this.y);
  // ...no == override, so identity

  // override == but forget hashCode
  @override
  bool operator ==(Object other) =>
      other is Point && other.x == x && other.y == y;
}

final set = <Point>{Point(1, 2)};
print(set.contains(Point(1, 2)));   // FALSE - hashCodes differ
// ...and `set.add(Point(1, 2))` ADDS it, so the set now has two "equal"
// elements, which is a contradiction the collection cannot represent

// the fix
class Point2 {
  final double x, y;
  const Point2(this.x, this.y);

  @override
  bool operator ==(Object other) =>
      identical(this, other) || (other is Point2 && other.x == x && other.y == y);

  @override
  int get hashCode => Object.hash(x, y);
  // ...Object.hash combines with a proper mix, so it is not the same as
  // x.hashCode ^ y.hashCode, which collides badly on structured data

  @override
  String toString() => 'Point2($x, $y)';
}

final set2 = <Point2>{const Point2(1, 2)};
print(set2.contains(const Point2(1, 2)));   // true

// and for a Map
final map = {const Point2(1, 2): 'origin'};
print(map[const Point2(1, 2)]);             // 'origin'

Object.hash and Object.hashAll exist because the obvious implementation is a bad one. hashCode ^ other.hashCode collides: (1, 2) and (2, 1) and (3, 3) can all produce the same combined value, and a collection with many collisions degrades to a linear scan. Object.hash applies the same mixing function each primitive hash uses, so combining its results produces a well-distributed value. It is not a cryptographic hash and does not need to be — it needs to be fast and well-distributed.

// the collision, and why XOR is the wrong combiner
(1 ^ 2) == (2 ^ 1);                 // true - order does not matter!
(1 ^ 2) == (3 ^ 3);                 // true - and these differ entirely

// Object.hash mixes properly
Object.hash(1, 2) == Object.hash(2, 1);    // false - order matters
Object.hash(1, 2) == Object.hash(3, 3);    // false

// a hash for a list-valued field, which is the case that catches people
class Row {
  final List<int> values;
  Row(this.values);

  @override
  bool operator ==(Object other) =>
      other is Row && _listEq(values, other.values);

  @override
  int get hashCode => Object.hashAll(values);
}
bool _listEq(List<int> a, List<int> b) {
  if (a.length != b.length) return false;
  for (var i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
    if (a[i] != b[i]) return false;
  }
  return true;
}
// ...`==` must compare by VALUE, so a list comparison has to be written
// out; `identical(values, other.values)` would be fast and wrong, because
// two equal-by-value lists are different objects

// and `identical` in the fast path, which is free and catches self-compare
@override
bool operator ==(Object other) =>
    identical(this, other) || _listEq(values, (other as Row).values);
// ...careful: `other as Row` throws for a wrong type, so check first unless
// you have already tested

A hash code must be stable for the object's lifetime, which is what rules out hashing a mutable field. An object in a HashSet whose hashed field changes is unreachable by lookup and cannot be removed — the collection holds an object it can no longer find, and it will only be released when the whole set is. This is why an object with value equality should have final fields, and it connects directly to the immutability section: value equality without immutability is not a style preference, it is a requirement of the collection's own invariants.

// mutating a hashed field corrupts the set
class Item {
  final int id;
  int priority;                     // MUTABLE
  Item(this.id, this.priority);

  @override
  int get hashCode => priority;   // ...hashed on a mutable field
}

final s = <Item>{};
final it = Item(1, 5);
s.add(it);
it.priority = 9;                    // legal
s.contains(Item(1, 9));            // true - found in the new bucket
s.remove(Item(1, 9));               // works
// but:
s.contains(Item(1, 5));             // false - the OLD bucket is not searched
s.remove(Item(1, 5));               // NO-OP - the object is still in the set
// ...so the set now permanently contains an item it cannot remove by value

// the rule: hash only over final fields
@override
int get hashCode => Object.hash(id, priority);
// ...no, that's the same bug if priority changes. Only:
// @override
int get hashCode => id.hashCode;

// and if the value must be mutable and hashable, the key must be a
// separate immutable projection
final byPriority = <int, Set<Item>>{};
void reindex(Item it) {
  byPriority.putIfAbsent(it.priority, () => <Item>{}).add(it);
  // ...and on a change, remove from the old bucket first - which is the
  // whole reason a HashMap of mutable keys is a data structure with rules

Equality is also about symmetry and transitivity, and both are broken in ordinary-looking code. Symmetry means a == b implies b == a, which fails when two classes each recognise only their own type and are compared against each other. Transitivity means a == b and b == c implies a == c, which fails when equality is defined by a field that is not itself transitively compared — such as a list compared with contains rather than element-wise. Both failures produce a collection that behaves inconsistently depending on which side the comparison starts from, and both are cheap to avoid by delegating to one canonical implementation.

// symmetry, broken by a cross-type comparison
class Money {
  final int cents;
  Money(this.cents);
  @override
  bool operator ==(Object o) => o is Money && o.cents == cents;
  @override
  int get hashCode => cents.hashCode;
}
class Zero {
  @override
  bool operator ==(Object o) => o is Money && o.cents == 0;
  // ...so Money(0) == Zero() is true and Zero() == Money(0) is false
}
print(Money(0) == Zero());    // true
print(Zero() == Money(0));    // false  - SYMMETRY BROKEN

// transitivity, broken by a shallow comparison
class Bag {
  final List<Object> items;
  Bag(this.items);
  @override
  bool operator ==(Object o) => o is Bag && items.contains(o.items);
  // ...Bag([1,2]) == Bag([2]) is true
  // Bag([1,2]) == Bag([2]) and Bag([2]) == Bag([1]) but
  // Bag([1,2]) != Bag([1])  - TRANSITIVITY BROKEN
}

// the fix for both: one canonical comparison, always
class Money2 {
  final int cents;
  const Money2(this.cents);
  @override
  bool operator ==(Object o) => o is Money2 && o.cents == cents;
  @override
  int get hashCode => cents.hashCode;
}
// ...`o is Money2` excludes every other type on both sides, so symmetry
// holds. Never write a cross-type == , and never use contains on a nested
// collection in an == - both are the two ways to break it accidentally

5 · Collections and Iterables

5.1 Iterable is lazy, and that matters5.2 List operations5.3 Set operations5.4 Map operations5.5 The full Iterable API5.6 Choosing a collection5.7 Allocation and performance

Dart's collections are richer than most languages'. Understanding laziness is the difference between a fast pipeline and a mysterious performance problem.

5.1 Iterable is lazy, and that matters

The single most important property of Dart's collection API.

// EAGER: the list literal evaluates everything immediately
final eager = [for (var i = 0; i < 1000000; i++) expensive(i)];
// 1,000,000 calls, all results in memory, right now

// LAZY: the collection-for in an Iterable context is lazy
final lazy = [for (var i = 0; i < 1000000; i++) expensive(i)].where(_keep);
// 0 calls so far

print(lazy.length);   // now it evaluates: 1,000,000 calls

// or with an Iterable.generate and a lazy iterable
final lazy2 = Iterable<int>.generate(1000000, expensive)
    .where(_keep)
    .map(_transform);
print(lazy2.take(5).toList());   // only the first 5 are computed
// where/map/expand are lazy; toList/toSet/fold are eager
final source = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];

final w = source.where((e) => e.isEven);
print('nothing computed yet');
print(w.length);      // NOW it iterates the source

// the practical consequence: an infinite lazy iterable is fine
final naturals = Iterable<int>.generate(0, (i) => i);
print(naturals.take(5).toList());   // [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]  - terminates

// but takeWhile needs a bounded source
final positives = [1, 2, -1, 3].takeWhile((e) => e > 0).toList();  // [1, 2]

// the trap: a lazy chain over a MUTABLE source
var data = [1, 2, 3];
final snapshot = data.where((e) => e > 1).map((e) => e * 2);
data.add(4);            // modifying while the lazy chain is pending
print(snapshot.toList());   // [4, 6, 8] - 4 got included!
// if you need a stable view, force it: .toList() when you create it

Laziness is why chain.first on a filtered list of a million items is instant, and why the same chain followed by .toList() is not. It is also why a lazy chain over data that is still loading gives surprising results. When in doubt, force the evaluation at the point you create it, and treat the eager result as the source of truth.

What Iterable actually is

Iterable is the interface every collection in dart:core implements, including the lazy ones. It declares almost nothing: length, a getter for the current element while iterating, and about twenty derived methods that are implemented in terms of those. That is unusual and it is the point — where, map, expand, fold, skip, take, firstWhere and join are all written once in the base class in terms of a single iterator method, so every collection gets all of them for free.

The second thing about Iterable is that it is not necessarily a collection at all. Iterable.generate, Iterable.empty and a Stream converted with asyncMap all produce an Iterable that has no backing storage and possibly no known length. That is why length on a lazy iterable can be O(n) or even impossible, and why code that reads length out of habit is a performance bug on a pipeline and a correctness question on a generator.

// the generators, and the fact that none of them allocates a list
Iterable<int> countFrom(int n) sync* {
  for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) yield i;
}
Iterable<int> countTo(int n) sync* {
  for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) yield n - i;
}

// infinite sources, which a List cannot express at all
Iterable<int> naturals() sync* {
  var i = 1;
  while (true) yield i++;
}
Iterable<int> primes() sync* {
  final seen = <int>{};
  for (var n = 2; ; n++) {
    if (seen.every((p) => n % p != 0)) {
      seen.add(n);
      yield n;
    }
  }
}
primes().take(5).toList();      // [2, 3, 5, 7, 11] - and it terminates

// the `async*` form, for a generator that awaits
Stream<int> fetchPages(String url) async* {
  var page = 1;
  while (true) {
    final res = await http.get(Uri.parse('$url?page=$page'));
    yield* parse(res.body);       // yields each element of a collection
    if (!hasMore(res)) break;
    page++;
  }
}
await for (final item in fetchPages(url)) { … }

// and the two rules: a sync* generator must not be async, and an async*
// generator must not be synchronous — hence the two keywords

Yield delegation and the cost of a generator

A sync* function compiles to a state machine: calling it allocates a controller, and every yield is a call into it. That is real overhead per element, which is invisible for a pipeline that does substantial work per element and dominant for one that does almost none. So a generator is the right tool when the per-element work is non-trivial or when the sequence is unbounded, and the wrong one when it is a thin wrapper over an existing list.

// delegating, which avoids re-writing the sequence
Iterable<int> evens(Iterable<int> src) sync* {
  for (final x in src) {
    if (x.isEven) yield x;
  }
}
Iterable<int> evens2(Iterable<int> src) sync* {
  yield* src.where((x) => x.isEven);
}
// ...yield* delegates to another iterable's iterator, so evens2 is one
// generator frame instead of a generator plus a where

// the three delegation forms, and what each costs
Iterable<T> a(Iterable<T> s) sync* { yield* s; }              // delegate
Iterable<T> b(Iterable<T> s) sync* { yield s.first; yield* s.skip(1); }  // partial
Iterable<T> c(Iterable<T> s) sync* { return s; }              // no generator at all!
Iterable<T> d(Iterable<int> s) sync* { yield s.length; }     // one value

// a generator over a collection that is only iterated once is often a
// function returning the collection
List<Row> activeRows(List<Row> rows) {
  if (rows.length < 1000) return rows.where((r) => r.active).toList();
  return activeRowsLazy(rows);       // a generator, for the large case
}

// and `return` in a sync* function ends the sequence without yielding more
Iterable<int> first5(Iterable<int> s) sync* {
  var n = 0;
  for (final x in s) {
    yield x;
    if (++n >= 5) return;          // ends it - equivalent to take(5)
  }
}

// the measurement that settles it
var sw = Stopwatch()..start();
final a1 = evens(naturals().take(1000000)).toList();
sw.stop(); print('generator  ${sw.elapsedMilliseconds}ms');
sw.reset();
final a2 = naturals().take(1000000).where((x) => x.isEven).toList();
sw.stop(); print('where      ${sw.elapsedMilliseconds}ms');
// ...the second is meaningfully faster, because `where` on a source that is
// already an Iterable is a view, not a generator

Finally, laziness has a hazard that a List never has: the source can change between the call and the iteration. A method that returns rows.where(...) without materialising it has promised nothing about what the caller will see, and a caller that mutates the list in between gets results that correspond to no point in time. The rule that resolves it is to return a List from a function whose job is to produce a value, and an Iterable only from a function whose job is to describe a computation — and to say which one in the return type.

5.2 List operations

The mutating and non-mutating methods, and the ones that surprise people.

final list = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6];

// NON-MUTATING: return a new list
list.reversed;                 // [6, 2, 9, 5, 1, 4, 1, 3]
list.sorted((a, b) => a.compareTo(b));   // [1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9]
list.where((e) => e > 3);       // [4, 5, 9, 6]
list.map((e) => e * 2);         // [6, 2, 8, 2, 10, 18, 4, 12]
list.take(3);                   // [3, 1, 4]
list.skip(3);                   // [1, 5, 9, 2, 6]
list.sublist(2, 5);             // [4, 1, 5]
list.toSet().toList();          // deduplicated
list.first;                     // 3      - throws if empty
list.last;                      // 6      - throws if empty
list.elementAt(2);              // 4      - throws if out of range
list.reduce((a, b) => a + b); // 31
list.fold<int>(0, (a, b) => a + b);  // 31
list.expand((e) => [e, e]);   // flatten one level
list.join(', ');                // a String
// MUTATING: change the list in place
final l = [3, 1, 2];
l.add(4);                   // [3, 1, 2, 4]
l.addAll([5, 6]);           // [3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6]
l.insert(0, 0);             // [0, 3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6]
l.insertAll(2, [9, 9]);     // [0, 3, 9, 9, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6]
l.remove(0);                // removes the VALUE 0: [3, 9, 9, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6]
l.removeAt(0);              // removes BY INDEX 0: [9, 9, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6]
l.removeLast();             // [9, 9, 1, 2, 4, 5]
l.removeWhere((e) => e > 4);  // [9, 9, 1, 2]
l.retainWhere((e) => e > 4);  // [9, 9]
l.clear();
l.sort();
l.shuffle(Random(42));
l.setRange(0, 2, [7, 8]);
l.fillRange(0, 2, 0);
l.length = 2;               // TRUNCATES or pads with nulls (typed list) - avoid
// the pair people get wrong
final list = [1, 2, 3, 2, 1];
list.remove(2);          // removes ONE occurrence: [1, 3, 2, 1]
list.removeWhere((e) => e == 2);   // removes ALL: [1, 3, 1]

// and the sorting trap: sort() is not stable in the general case,
// and the comparator must be consistent
final people = [
  Person('Ana', 30), Person('Bo', 30), Person('Cy', 25),
];
// a BAD comparator: <= is inconsistent
// people.sort((a, b) => a.age <= b.age ? -1 : 1);
// a GOOD comparator: use compareTo
people.sort((a, b) => a.age.compareTo(b.age));

// if you need stability, sort by (age, then name)
people.sort((a, b) {
  final c = a.age.compareTo(b.age);
  return c != 0 ? c : a.name.compareTo(b.name);
});
// fixed-length and unmodifiable lists
final fixed = List<int>.filled(5, 0);      // length 5, cannot add
final fromIter = List<int>.from([1, 2, 3]);
final unmod = List<int>.unmodifiable([1, 2, 3]);
// unmod.add(4);                            // UnsupportedError

// sublist returns a NEW list, so mutating it is safe
final sub = list.sublist(0, 3);
sub.add(99);                                 // list is unaffected

// but sort() on a fixed-length list throws
// fixed.sort();                             // UnsupportedError

Four list constructors, and what each costs

List in Dart is an interface with several implementations, and the choice is made by how the list is created rather than by its type. A growable list backed by an array, a fixed-length list, an unmodifiable view, and a list of a length known in advance behave identically through the interface and quite differently underneath.

ConstructorGrowableMutableBacking
[]YesYesArray, grows by doubling
List.filled(n, v)NoYesFixed array
List.generate(n, f)NoYesFixed array, values computed
List.of(other)YesYesA copy
List.unmodifiable(other)NoNoA copy, frozen
UnmodifiableListView(o)NoNoA view, no copy
List<T>.of(..., growable: false)NoYesA fixed copy
// growable: the default, and the one that reallocates
var a = <int>[];
for (var i = 0; i < 10000; i++) { a.add(i); }
// ...each growth copies the whole array. Dart over-allocates, so it is
// O(n) amortised, but the peak memory is well above the final size.

// fixed-length, when the size is known: no reallocation at all
final b = List<int>.filled(10000, 0);
for (var i = 0; i < 10000; i++) { b[i] = i; }
b.add(1);                      // ERROR: does not exist

// generated, which computes the values rather than copying
final c = List<int>.generate(10000, (i) => i * i);
// List.generate(3, () => 0)  - a full List, allocated eagerly

// the copies, and when each is right
final d = List.of(source);          // a mutable COPY - the source can change
final e = List.unmodifiable(source); // a frozen COPY
final f = UnmodifiableListView(source); // a frozen VIEW over the source

// ...the difference that matters
final src = [1, 2, 3];
final copy = List.unmodifiable(src);
final view = UnmodifiableListView(src);
src.add(4);
print(copy.length);   // 3 - unaffected
print(view.length);   // 4 - the source changed it
// so: copy when you are taking ownership; view when the host owns the data
// and promises stability. A view's guarantee depends on a promise made
// somewhere else, which is why copies are safer by default.

// set-length, the operation that only a growable list has
final g = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
g.length = 2;             // [1, 2] - the tail is discarded
g.length = 4;             // [1, 2, null, null] - and this is the trap
g.length;                 // 4 - and now it holds nulls in a List<int>

The list operations that are not about construction are the ones with real performance consequences, and three of them are quadratic or worse. insert and removeAt shift every following element, so building a list by inserting at index zero is O(n²) — the case that appears whenever a list is used as a stack or a queue. indexOf and contains are linear, so testing membership in a loop is O(n·m). And List.of inside a loop copies repeatedly, which is the same quadratic pattern with a different disguise.

// insert at zero, in a loop: O(n^2) and it looks innocent
var list = <int>[];
for (final x in items) {
  list.insert(0, x);          // every insert shifts the whole list
}

// the fix: append, then reverse once
var list2 = <int>[];
for (final x in items) { list2.add(x); }
list2 = list2.reversed.toList();   // one O(n) pass

// or collect and reverse in place
list2 = list2.reversed.toList();   // same

// membership in a loop: O(n*m)
final allowed = users.map((u) => u.id).toList();
final ok = messages.where((m) => allowed.contains(m.userId));

// the fix: a Set, built once
final allowed2 = users.map((u) => u.id).toSet();   // O(n)
final ok2 = messages.where((m) => allowed2.contains(m.userId));  // O(m)

// removeAt in a loop: O(n^2)
var copy = [...items];
for (var i = copy.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
  if (!wanted(copy[i])) copy.removeAt(i);      // backwards, so indices hold
}
// ...backwards is the whole trick: removing at i does not move the elements
// before it. Removing forwards shifts everything down and skips one.

// or, better, build only what you want
final kept = items.where(wanted).toList();

// and the operation that is not quadratic but is still worth knowing
list.sort((a, b) => a.n.compareTo(b.n));   // O(n log n), in place
list.indexOf(x, 1);                         // start index - avoids a prefix scan
list.lastIndexOf(x);                        // O(n) backwards

Two more list operations change what they mean on a sublist, and both are load-bearing for fixed-size views. setRange and fillRange mutate in place, so on an UnmodifiableListView they throw rather than silently copy — which is the correct behaviour and the reason a view is a genuine guarantee rather than a wrapper that quietly degrades. And sublist is a copy, not a view, so a.sublist(0, 3) allocates and subsequent changes to a do not affect it; the view equivalent is a.getRange with ListView, which is a common source of confusion because the names suggest they are alternatives.

// sublist copies
final a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
final b = a.sublist(0, 3);      // [1, 2, 3]
a[0] = 99;
print(b[0]);                    // 1 - a copy, unaffected

// a range view does not
final v = ListView<int>.filled(3, 0);   // hmm - filled is a copy
// the view constructors:
final window = ListView<int>.from(a, 0, 3);   // a VIEW of a[0..3)
a[0] = 99;
print(window[0]);               // 99 - it followed the change
// ...which is what a sliding window wants and what a snapshot does not

// setRange throws on a view rather than degrading
final frozen = UnmodifiableListView(a);
frozen[0] = 1;                   // ERROR: UnsupportedError
frozen.setRange(0, 2, [7, 8]);   // ERROR: UnsupportedError
frozen.fillRange(0, 2, 0);       // ERROR: UnsupportedError
// ...all three throw, so an unmodifiable list is a real guarantee

// but a copy is a different guarantee
final c = List.unmodifiable(a);
c[0] = 1;                       // ERROR - the same

// and where a copy is required because the type says so
List<int> asList(Iterable<int> src) => src.toList();     // a copy
List<int> asList2(Iterable<int> src) => List.of(src);    // also a copy
// ...`sublist` on a lazy iterable does not exist, which is the compiler
// telling you that a lazy source has no random access

5.3 Set operations

Membership, the set operations, and why LinkedHashSet preserves order.

final a = {1, 2, 3};
final b = {3, 4, 5};

a.union(b);        // {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
a.intersection(b); // {3}
a.difference(b);   // {1, 2}
a.symmetricDifference(b);   // {1, 2, 4, 5}

a.contains(2);     // true
a.containsAll([1, 2]);   // true
a.any((e) => e > 2);  // true
a.every((e) => e > 0); // true
a.map((e) => e.toString()).toSet();
a.expand((e) => [e, e]);   // Set<int>
a.toList();         // order is not guaranteed for a plain {} literal
a.join(',');
// the iteration order of a Set: READ THIS
const literal = {'b', 'a', 'c'};
print(literal);              // {b, a, c}  - literal preserves insertion order

const numeric = {3, 1, 2};
print(numeric);              // {3, 1, 2}  - NOT sorted, despite the intuition

// so: never rely on it. if you need order, use a List, or a
// LinkedHashSet explicitly:
final ordered = LinkedHashSet.of([3, 1, 2]);
print(ordered);              // {3, 1, 2}  - insertion order guaranteed

// SplayTreeSet for sorted iteration
final sorted = SplayTreeSet<int>([3, 1, 2]);
print(sorted);               // {1, 2, 3}

// and the practical use: deduplicate while preserving order
final seen = <String>{};
final unique = input.where(seen.add).toList();

// the other practical use: O(1) membership in a loop
final ids = userIds.toSet();     // build ONCE
for (final entry in entries) {
  if (ids.contains(entry.userId)) { ... }   // O(1), not O(n)
}
// a Set of objects: == and hashCode decide membership
final ids = <int>{1, 2, 3};
print(ids.contains(1));   // true

// with a class that overrides == by value, the Set deduplicates
class Id {
  final int v;
  const Id(this.v);
  @override bool operator ==(Object o) => o is Id && o.v == v;
  @override int get hashCode => v.hashCode;
}

final s = {const Id(1), const Id(1), const Id(2)};
print(s.length);          // 2

Set semantics, and the operations that follow from them

A Set is an unordered collection of unique elements, and Dart has four implementations with different performance characteristics and different iteration orders. The default {} literal is a LinkedHashSet, which preserves insertion order and is backed by a hash table; HashSet drops the order; LinkedHashSet is the ordered default; and SplayTreeSet keeps elements sorted and gives logarithmic lookup.

TypeOrderedLookupInsertUse for
HashSetNoO(1) expectedO(1)Membership only
LinkedHashSetInsertionO(1) expectedO(1)The default; needs stable order
SplayTreeSetSortedO(log n)O(log n)Range queries, sorted iteration
Set.of(x)InsertionO(1)O(1)Copying
{}.identityNoO(1)O(1)Identity, not equality

Which one you want follows from whether the order matters. The default literal is a LinkedHashSet, not a HashSet, and that is a deliberate choice: iteration order that is stable across runs is worth a small overhead for the majority of uses, and code that renders a set into a UI should not reshuffle between reloads.
