The moment you want sorted iteration — to build a sorted menu, to find the closest match, to iterate a range — SplayTreeSet is the one that provides it without a separate sort.

// the four kinds
final h = <int>{1, 2, 3};                 // LinkedHashSet - insertion order
final h2 = HashSet<int>.from([3, 2, 1]);   // HashSet - arbitrary order
final t = SplayTreeSet<int>.from([3, 1, 2]);  // sorted: 1, 2, 3
final i = HashSet.identity();               // identity, not ==

// sorted iteration, for free
final s = SplayTreeSet<String>{'pear', 'apple', 'fig'};
s.toList();                     // [apple, fig, pear]
s.first;                        // 'apple'
s.last;                         // 'pear'
s.range('a', 'f');              // elements between - O(log n + k)
s.contains('fig');              // O(log n) rather than O(1)

// deduplication, the reason a Set exists
final unique = <String>{};
for (final row in rows) { unique.add(row.category); }
final unique2 = rows.map((r) => r.category).toSet();   // the idiom

// set operations, and the names that are easy to get wrong
final a = {1, 2, 3};
final b = {2, 3, 4};
a.union(b);                     // {1, 2, 3, 4}
a.intersection(b);              // {2, 3}
a.difference(b);                // {1}
a.symmetricDifference(b);       // {1, 4}

// the four are INSTANCE methods that return a NEW set
final c = a.union(b);
a.length;                       // 3 - unchanged, because the methods are
                                 // non-mutating
// ...which surprises people who expect `addAll`, which IS mutating:
a.addAll(b);                    // a is now {1,2,3,4}
a.addAll(b);                    // idempotent - a set, so no duplicates

// and the in-place forms
a.removeAll(b);                 // a -= b
a.retainAll(b);                 // a = a intersect b
a.removeWhere((x) => x.isOdd);
a.addAll(other);

// the identity set, and when it is the right one
final byIdentity = <Object>{};
final k = 'x';
byIdentity.add(k);
print(byIdentity.contains('x'.toUpperCase().toLowerCase()));  // depends
// ...an identity set treats two equal strings as different keys, which is
// exactly what you want when tracking object identity rather than value

Set membership is a hash lookup, and that makes correctness depend on the equality contract from the previous section in a way list membership does not. An element whose hashCode is inconsistent with its == can be added twice and found once; an element whose hash changes after insertion becomes permanently unfindable. So the same rule applies to both — value equality requires final fields — and it is worth stating that a Set makes the violation visible immediately while a List hides it.

// a mutable key in a Set: adds twice, finds once
class Tag {
  final String name;
  int uses;                       // MUTABLE and hashed
  Tag(this.name) : uses = 0;

  @override
  bool operator ==(Object o) => o is Tag && o.name == name;
  @override
  int get hashCode => name.hashCode ^ uses.hashCode;
}

final tags = <Tag>{};
final t = Tag('red');
tags.add(t);
t.uses = 5;
tags.add(t);                      // a DIFFERENT hash, so it is a new element
print(tags.length);               // 2 - two "equal" elements
print(tags.contains(Tag('red'))); // depends on `uses`, so probably false

// the fix: hash only over final fields
@override
int get hashCode => name.hashCode;
// ...and then the two are genuinely one element, and removal works

// and the mutable case, done deliberately: remove then re-add
void bump(Tag tag) {
  tags.remove(tag);               // computed with the OLD hash
  tag.uses++;
  tags.add(tag);                  // and the new one
}

// ...which is exactly why an IndexMap-style structure or a
// MutableSet<Tag, String> keyed by a stable id exists in the patterns -
// the identity has to be something that does not change

There is no List.removeWhere-equivalent on Set for the reason that there is no index to shift, and the API difference is a reliable sign of which collection a piece of code was written for. A Set has remove, removeAll, retainAll, removeWhere — all of which work by value — but no removeAt, no sort and no insert. Reaching for one of those on a Set means the collection was the wrong choice, and the compiler says so, which is one of the better signals in the language.

5.4 Map operations

Reading, writing, and the nullable result that trips people up.

final m = {'a': 1, 'b': 2};

// reading: the return type is nullable
final v = m['a'];              // int?  - the key might not be there
print(m['zzz']);               // null, NOT an error
print(m['a']!);                // 4: int, with an assertion

// the safe reads
final v2 = m['a'] ?? 0;                  // a default
final v3 = m['a'] as int;                // throws if absent
final hasKey = m.containsKey('a');       // true
m.putIfAbsent('c', () => 3);
m.addAll({'d': 4, 'e': 5});
m.remove('a');                            // removes and returns int?

// keys and values
m.keys;          // Iterable<String>
m.values;        // Iterable<int>
m.entries;       // Iterable<MapEntry<String, int>>
for (final MapEntry(key: k, value: val) in m.entries) {
  print('$k = $val');
}

// forEach, with destructuring
m.forEach((k, v) => print('$k = $v'));

// transform into another map
final upper = m.map((k, v) => MapEntry(k.toUpperCase(), v * 10));
print(upper);   // {A: 10, B: 20}

// filter a map
final big = Map.fromEntries(
  m.entries.where((e) => e.value > 2).map((e) => MapEntry(e.key, e.value)),
);
// Map is the most misused collection, in three specific ways

// 1. building with [] in a loop
var result = <String, int>{};
for (final e in entries) {
  result[e.key] = e.value;      // fine, but a fold reads better
}
final better = entries.fold(<String, int>{}, (m, e) => m..[e.key] = e.value);

// 2. using a List of pairs
final pairs = [('a', 1), ('b', 2)];    // a record - Dart 3
final asMap = <String, int>{for (final (k, v) in pairs) k: v};

// 3. assuming iteration order
//    Map DOES preserve insertion order (it is a LinkedHashMap),
//    so this is safe:
final ordered = {'first': 1, 'second': 2, 'third': 3};
print(ordered.keys.first);   // 'first'

// but if you need sorting, do it explicitly
final sortedKeys = ordered.keys.toList()..sort();

// a HashMap has NO order, if you need it and do not care about
// insertion order
final unordered = HashMap<String, int>.from(ordered);
// nested access, which needs every level checked
final config = {
  'server': {
    'host': 'localhost',
    'ports': [8080, 8443],
  },
};

final host = (config['server'] as Map?)?['host'] as String?;
final ports = (config['server'] as Map?)?['ports'] as List?;

// a better approach for real config: model it
class ServerConfig {
  final String host;
  final List<int> ports;
  const ServerConfig({required this.host, required this.ports});

  static ServerConfig fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) {
    return ServerConfig(
      host: json['host'] as String? ?? 'localhost',
      ports: (json['ports'] as List?)?.cast<int>() ?? const [8080],
    );
  }
}
final server = ServerConfig.fromJson(config['server'] as Map<String, dynamic>);
print(server.host);    // no casts, no null checks at the use site

The seven map types and the one question that picks them

Dart has seven Map implementations, and the differences are performance and ordering rather than semantics — except for one, which changes what a key can be. The question to ask is always whether the keys are known at compile time; if they are, a SplayTreeMap gives sorted iteration and logarithmic lookup, and if they are not, a HashMap or the default LinkedHashMap is right.

TypeOrderedLookupKeysUse for
HashMapNoO(1) expectedAny hashableFast lookup, no order needed
LinkedHashMapInsertionO(1) expectedAny hashableThe {} default
SplayTreeMapSortedO(log n)Comparable onlySorted iteration, ranges
Map.identityNoO(1)Any objectKey by identity
Map.unmodifiable—Delegates—A frozen view
Map.from(other)InsertionO(1)—A copy
// the difference that changes semantics: Comparable keys
final m1 = <String, int>{'a': 1, 'b': 2};
m1['c'] = 3;                      // fine - any hashable key

final m2 = SplayTreeMap<int, String>();
m2[3] = 'c'; m2[1] = 'a'; m2[2] = 'b';
m2.keys.toList();                 // [1, 2, 3] - sorted, for free
m2[1];                             // O(log n)

// ...and the constraint that follows: the key type must implement Comparable
final bad = SplayTreeMap<List<int>, int>();   // ERROR: List is not
                                                     // Comparable
// ...so SplayTreeMap works for keys you control and not for arbitrary
// objects, which is the whole reason it is the slower choice

// the range query, which is what you use a sorted map for
final events = SplayTreeMap<DateTime, String>();
events.range(from, until).forEach((t, e) => log('$t $e'));

// iteration, and the four forms
m1.forEach((k, v) => print('$k -> $v'));
for (final e in m1.entries) { print('${e.key} ${e.value}'); }
for (final k in m1.keys) { print(k); }
for (final v in m1.values) { print(v); }
// ...and a destructuring pattern for the entries form, which Dart 3
// supports directly:
for (final MapEntry(:key, :value) in m1.entries) { print('$key $value'); }

// modifying during iteration
for (final k in m1.keys.toList()) {   // toList() is REQUIRED
  if (isStale(k)) m1.remove(k);
}
// ...removing while iterating keys is a ConcurrentModificationError

Map lookup has a subtlety that catches everyone once: map[key] returns null for an absent key, and that is indistinguishable from a present key mapped to null. The fix is containsKey, or — better — never store null values, or use putIfAbsent so the distinction never arises. The deeper design point is that a Map modelling a domain entity should hold non-null values, because a missing entity and an entity with no data are different states and one of them will eventually be mishandled.

// the absent-versus-null confusion
final m = <String, String?>{};
m['a'] = null;
m['a'];              // null - is it there?
m.containsKey('a');  // true  - so it IS there
m['missing'];        // null
m.containsKey('missing');  // false

// fix 1: containsKey, which costs a second lookup
if (m.containsKey(k)) { final v = m[k]; /* v is String? */ }

// fix 2: never store null - the better answer
final m2 = <String, String>{};
m2['a'] = null;      // ERROR: not assignable to String
// ...so the type system now says "absent or present", and one is not
// representable. Most domain maps should be like this.

// fix 3: putIfAbsent, which computes only when needed
m2.putIfAbsent(k, () => load(k));     // returns the existing or new
m2.putIfAbsent(k, () => load(k)) ?? 'default';   // and it can return null

// fix 4: computeIfAbsent for a cached value
final cache = <String, User>{};
User get(String id) => cache.putIfAbsent(id, () => fetch(id));

// the update-in-place form, which is the one that reads best
final counts = <String, int>{};
for (final word in words) {
  counts.update(word, (n) => n + 1, ifAbsent: () => 1);
}
// ...or, since Dart 3, the collection-for, which is shorter:
final counts2 = <String, int>{
  for (final w in words) w: (counts[w] ?? 0) + 1,
};
// ...though the first is clearer and does not read the map it is building

The mutation methods have a naming asymmetry worth memorising, because getting it backwards is easy and the compiler does not help. update sets a key, putIfAbsent sets it only if absent, addAll merges another map in, addEntries merges a list of entries, and putIfAbsent's counterpart — "replace only if present" — does not exist and has to be written. There is also no removeWhere on Map that takes a predicate over values alone; you filter the entries and call remove for each key.

// the mutation API, in full
m['k'] = v;                    // set or overwrite
m.update('k', (old) => old + 1);          // set, transforming the old
m.update('k', (old) => old + 1, ifAbsent: () => 0);
m.putIfAbsent('k', () => compute());      // set only if absent
m.remove('k');                 // by key
m.removeWhere((k, v) => v.isEmpty);   // by predicate over BOTH
m.addAll(other);               // merge
m.addEntries(other.entries);    // merge a list of entries
m.clear();

// "replace only if present" - which does not exist
void bumpIfPresent(Map<String, int> m, String k) {
  final v = m[k];
  if (v != null) m[k] = v + 1;
}

// deleting entries, the two shapes
for (final e in m.entries.toList()) {
  if (e.value.isEmpty) m.remove(e.key);
}
// ...and removing while iterating entries directly, which is also allowed
// because the iterator handles it - but only for remove, and only for the
// current key:
for (final e in m.entries) {
  if (e.value.isEmpty) m.remove(e.key);   // legal
}
// ...which is one of the few places the copy is unnecessary

The remaining difference between the map types is how iteration order behaves under mutation, and it is worth knowing per type because it is the kind of thing that produces a rendering that shuffles between runs and a test that fails once a month. A HashMap guarantees nothing: its order depends on hash values, on bucket count, and on how the table was resized, so adding or removing a key can move keys that were not touched. A LinkedHashMap guarantees insertion order, and a removal does not disturb the relative order of the survivors — which is why it is the right default for a map that is rendered or serialised. A SplayTreeMap guarantees sorted order, and it holds under insertion and removal because the order is the structure rather than a property of it.

There is one further asymmetry between the types, and it is about the key's type rather than the map's. A hash-based map accepts any key whose hashCode and == are consistent, which includes a List, a custom class, or a DateTime. A tree-based map requires the key to implement Comparable, because ordering is its access path — so a List key is not merely discouraged, it is a compile error, and the fix is a wrapper class whose compareTo says what ordering means for it.

5.5 The full Iterable API

Everything on Iterable, and when to use the eager alternatives.

// TRANSFORM (lazy)
map, expand, whereType, cast, followedBy

// FILTER (lazy)
where, whereType<T>(), firstWhere, lastWhere, singleWhere
skipWhile, takeWhile, firstWhereOrNull (collection package)

// AGGREGATE (eager)
reduce, fold, any, every, contains, join, count, maxBy, minBy

// SELECT (eager, or lazy with care)
first, last, single, elementAt, at
firstOrNull (collection package), lastOrNull
elementAtOrNull

// SLICE (lazy)
take, skip, sublist? (List only)

// CHECK (eager)
isEmpty, isNotEmpty, isNotEmpty, length

// ITERATE
forEach, followedBy, iterator

// COMBINE
zip? (no, use the index or a package)
expand

// the collection package adds what is missing
// package:collection provides:
//   firstOrNull, lastOrNull, elementAtOrNull, singleOrNull
//   sortedBy, sortedDescending
//   groupBy, groupListsBy
//   whereNotNull, firstWhereOrNull, lastWhereOrNull
//   sumBy, minOf, maxOf, averageBy
//   IterableEquality, ListEquality, MapEquality, SetEquality
//   UnmodifiableListView, UnmodifiableSetView, UnmodifiableMapView
//   Permutation
//   Equality

// THE ASYNC GAP: there is no async map
final names = ids.map(fetchName);          // Iterable<Future<String>>
final names2 = await Future.wait(ids.map(fetchName));   // parallel
final names3 = <String>[];
for (final id in ids) {
  names3.add(await fetchName(id));          // sequential
}
// and for a lazy async stream, use Stream instead of Iterable

The lazy chain, and why length and toList are decisions

An Iterable produced by where or map is a view: it holds a reference to its source and re-runs the predicate on every iteration. That is what makes an infinite sequence expressible, and it is also the source of two performance traps — a chain of five transformations re-runs the earlier stages once per element that reaches the end, and reading length on a lazy iterable traverses the whole thing.

// laziness: nothing happens until an eager method is called
var pipeline = rows
    .where((r) => r.active)      // not run
    .map((r) => transform(r))      // not run
    .where((r) => r.isValid);    // not run
pipeline.length;                   // NOW the whole chain runs
pipeline.first;                    // runs until the first match
pipeline.take(3).toList();         // runs until three results
pipeline.isEmpty;                  // runs until the first element

// ...so a chain on a large source with a rare match costs a full scan
rows.where((r) => r.id == 999999).first;   // O(n), unavoidable
rows.firstWhere((r) => r.id == 999999);    // same, and clearer

// the trap: a loop that iterates a lazy chain more than once
var total = 0;
for (final r in pipeline) { total += r.value; }   // first pass
for (final r in pipeline) { count += 1; }         // SECOND full pass
// ...materialise once instead
final materialised = pipeline.toList();   // one pass, memory cost paid

// length on a lazy iterable
final lazy = rows.where((r) => r.active);
lazy.length;      // a full traversal, O(n), every call
lazy.isEmpty;     // a traversal - but it stops at the first
lazy.isNotEmpty;  // at most one element

// the eager methods, and what each costs
.toList()         // allocates n
.toSet()          // allocates, plus hashing
.length           // traverses
.toString()       // traverses, and formats
.join()           // traverses, and builds a string
// ...every one of these is a terminal operation, and calling two of them is
// two traversals of the same chain

The performance characteristic that matters most is that an eager intermediate is a optimisation for anything re-entered, and a pessimisation for anything used once. A .toList() in the middle of a chain pays an allocation and a traversal to make the later stages cheap; the same call in front of a single-use pipeline is pure waste. The general rule is to materialise immediately before the point of reuse and nowhere else — which is why a chain that ends in a single .toList() is the common correct shape, and a chain with a .toList() after every stage is a sign the stages were written independently.

// materialise once, at the end
final result = rows
    .where(active)
    .map(transform)
    .where(validate)
    .toList();          // one allocation, one traversal of each stage

// materialise where it is reused
final filtered = rows.where(active).toList();   // reused 5 times below
final a = filtered.map(f).toList();
final b = filtered.where(g).toList();
final n = filtered.length;

// do NOT materialise between stages that are each used once
final waste = rows
    .where(active).toList()        // pointless
    .map(transform).toList()       // pointless
    .toList();                     // and now three traversals

// the measurement that settles it
var sw = Stopwatch()..start();
final r1 = rows.where(f).map(g).toList();               // one pass
sw.stop(); print('lazy       ${sw.elapsedMilliseconds}ms');
sw.reset();
final r2 = rows.where(f).toList().map(g).toList();      // eager middle
sw.stop(); print('eager      ${sw.elapsedMilliseconds}ms');
// ...for a SINGLE use, lazy wins; for repeated use, eager wins

Iterating an Iterable directly with for-in is the general form, and it is worth knowing that the language rewrites it into an explicit iterator with a moveNext call rather than into an index loop. That matters for three cases: breaking out of the loop early, which leaves the iterator suspended; nested iteration over the same lazy source, which restarts from the beginning; and concurrent modification, which a List detects and an Iterable view cannot.

// for-in over an Iterable
for (final x in source) { … }
// is desugared to
var it = source.iterator;
while (it.moveNext()) {
  final x = it.current;
  …
}

// breaking early, which is legal and cheap
for (final row in rows) {
  if (row.isTarget) { found = row; break; }
}
// ...so `firstWhere` is exactly this, and both stop at the first match

// nested iteration over the SAME lazy source restarts it
final lazy = generate();       // a generator
for (final a in lazy.take(3)) {
  for (final b in lazy.take(3)) {   // ...fresh each time, from the start
    print('$a $b');
  }
}
// ...which produces 9 lines of the same 3 values. If you meant 3x3 of
// DISTINCT values, materialise once:
final distinct = lazy.take(3).toList();
for (final a in distinct) {
  for (final b in distinct) { … }
}

// modifying a lazy source while iterating it
final list = [1, 2, 3];
final view = list.where((x) => x > 1);
for (final x in view) {
  list.add(x);                  // ...the predicate's source changed
}
// ...which does not throw on a List view, because the predicate reads the
// list on each evaluation - and produces a longer sequence than expected.
// `list.toList().where(...)` snapshots; a view does not.

One last thing about laziness: Iterator is a single-use object, and an Iterable's iterator method gives a fresh one each time. That is why Iterable is re-iterable and Iterator is not, and why code that captures an iterator instead of an iterable fails in a way that looks like it consumed something. A Stream is the exception — it is a single-use iterable-like, which is the fundamental difference between the two and the reason a stream cannot be replayed without buffering.

// Iterable is re-iterable; its iterators are not
final it = [1, 2, 3].iterator;
it.moveNext(); it.current;      // 1
it.moveNext(); it.current;      // 2
// it.moveNext(); it.current;    // null - exhausted, and stays exhausted

final list = [1, 2, 3];
for (final a in list) { … }     // works
for (final b in list) { … }     // works again - a fresh iterator each time

// so passing an Iterator and using it twice is the bug
void consume(Iterator<int> it) {
  while (it.moveNext()) print(it.current);
}
final it2 = list.iterator;
consume(it2);
consume(it2);      // nothing - it was exhausted

// pass the Iterable instead
void consumeAll(Iterable<int> src) {
  for (final x in src) print(x);
}
consumeAll(list);
consumeAll(list);  // works

// a Stream is the opposite: single-use by design
final stream = Stream.fromIterable([1, 2, 3]);
await for (final x in stream) print(x);
await for (final y in stream) print(y);   // nothing - it was consumed
// ...to replay a stream you must buffer it into a List or broadcast it

5.6 Choosing a collection

A decision table, and the performance characteristics that drive it.

//                 lookup  insert  order   duplicates  when to use
// List             O(n)     O(n)*   yes      yes         ordered data
// ArrayList        O(n)     O(n)    yes      yes         the default
// Set              O(1)     O(1)    no*      NO          membership, dedup
// HashSet          O(1)     O(1)    no       NO          fast membership
// LinkedHashSet    O(1)     O(1)    yes      NO          dedup, keep order
// SplayTreeSet     O(log n) O(logn) sorted  NO          sorted membership
// Map              O(1)     O(1)    yes**    NO          keyed data
// LinkedHashMap    O(1)     O(1)    yes      NO          keyed, keep order
// HashMap          O(1)     O(1)    no       NO          keyed, fastest
//
//  *  insert at the end is amortised O(1), but insert(0) is O(n)
// ** Map preserves insertion order (it is a LinkedHashMap by default)
// nested list performance, and why the inner type matters
// List<List<int>> rows = [[1, 2], [3, 4]];
// 10000 inner lists is slow, and the type is a growable List
// (a header per inner list). This is the 2D array problem.
//
// solutions:
// 1. a flat list with a computed index
class Grid {
  final Int32List data;      // typed, contiguous
  final int width;
  Grid(this.width, int height) : data = Int32List(width * height);

  int operator [](int r, int c) => data[r * width + c];
  void operator []=(int r, int c, int v) => data[r * width + c] = v;
}

// 2. a typed data list per row (no per-row header)
final rows = List.generate(100, (_) => Float64List(100));

// 3. for genuinely 2D numeric work, use a package
//    matrix, vector_math (the one Flutter uses), or a typed buffer

// the same applies to List<String> vs List<List<String>>:
// prefer a flat List with a separator, or a Map, if the shape allows
// the typed list, which is usually the right answer for bulk data
import 'dart:typed_data';

final scores = Float64List(1000000);   // 8 MB, no per-element headers
final names = List<String>.filled(1000, '');   // fine for objects
final flags = Uint8List(1000);         // 1 KB

// typed list trade-offs:
//   + no per-element object header: much smaller
//   + no bounds-check elimination issues, predictable memory
//   - cannot grow
//   - only primitives, and the specific width
//   - List<int> and Int32List are NOT interchangeable

Choosing a collection, and the operations that decide it

The choice between List, Set and Map is usually made from the shape of the data, but the operations the code will actually perform are a better guide — and they often disagree with the shape. A list of unique identifiers that is searched repeatedly is a Set wearing a list's clothes, and the reason is visible only in what the code does.

QuestionAnswerBecause
Does order matter?ListA Set has no position
Do duplicates occur?ListA Set discards them
Is it searched per element?SetO(1) instead of O(n)
Is there a key?MapPosition is not a key
Is it sorted?SplayTreeSet/MapSorting on demand is O(n log n) each time
Is it huge or unbounded?Iterable / StreamMaterialising it is not possible
Is it a lookup by key, once?EitherThen the answer is the domain, not the performance
// the case where the shape suggests List and the use suggests Set
final ids = users.map((u) => u.id).toList();      // a list of ids
final allowed = messages.where((m) => ids.contains(m.userId));
// ...ids LOOK like a list, and this is O(n*m). The shape question -
// "is it an ordered collection of ids" - has the wrong answer, because the
// use question is "do I test membership in it".

final ids2 = users.map((u) => u.id).toSet();      // O(n + m)

// the reverse: a Map where a Set would do
final seen = <String, bool>{};                   // presence only
seen[x] = true;
if (seen.containsKey(x)) { … }
// ...a Set says the same thing and cannot be used wrongly:
// final seen = <String>{};
// if (seen.contains(x)) { … }

// the case where a Set is right for a non-obvious reason
final byId = {for (final u in users) u.id: u};      // a Map to keep records
final names = messages.map((m) => byId[m.userId]?.name);
// ...here the Map is right because the VALUE is needed, and the Set would
// throw the record away. The membership test is the side effect.

// and a MultiSet - not in dart:core, so it is written
final counts = <String, int>{};
for (final w in words) {
  counts.update(w, (n) => n + 1, ifAbsent: () => 1);
}
final repeated = counts.entries.where((e) => e.value > 1).map((e) => e.key);
// ...a Map from element to count IS the multiset, and the pattern is worth
// recognising

The second decision is whether to reach for package:collection, which supplies the structures the core library omits. UnmodifiableListView, ListEquality, MapEquality, DeepCollectionEquality, PriorityQueue, Queue, LinkedHashMap with a different hashing strategy, CombinedIterableView and IterableExtension all live there, and each fills a gap where the obvious implementation from scratch would be subtly wrong.

// the equality helpers, which exist because the hand-written ones are wrong
import 'package:collection/collection.dart';

final a = [1, [2, 3]];
final b = [1, [2, 3]];
print(a == b);                        // false - identity on the inner lists
print(const ListEquality<List<int>>().equals(a, b));   // true

// a const instance, because the equality object holds no state and
// constructing one per comparison is wasteful
const listEq = ListEquality<int>();
listEq.equals([1, 2], [1, 2]);       // true - and O(n)

// deep equality, for nested structures
const deepEq = DeepCollectionEquality();
deepEq.equals({'a': [1]}, {'a': [1]});   // true, recursively

// a queue, which is the right structure for BFS
final q = Queue<int>()..addAll([1, 2]);
q.removeFirst();                      // O(1) - a List's removeAt(0) is O(n)

// a priority queue, for a heap
final pq = PriorityQueue<Task>((a, b) => a.priority.compareTo(b.priority))
  ..add(Task(p: 1))
  ..add(Task(p: 0));
pq.removeFirst().priority;            // 0 - the minimum, in O(log n)

// and the views, for composing without copying
final combined = CombinedIterableView([
  rows.where(active),
  archivedRows,
]);   // two lazy sources, one iterable, no materialisation

Immutability is the third decision, and it is one a Map makes more often than one expects. Passing a mutable collection into a constructor and storing it is a defect whether or not the class claims immutability, so the choice is whether to copy or to wrap, and the difference is ownership. A copy means the receiver is independent from that point on; a view means the receiver is a window onto data someone else owns and has promised not to disturb. Copying is the safe default and the more expensive one, and for a collection that is stored long-term the cost is usually irrelevant next to the cost of being wrong.

// copy, wrap, or neither - decided by who owns the data
class Csv {
  final List<List<String>> rows;

  // owns a copy: safe against anything the caller does afterwards
  Csv(List<List<String>> r)
      : rows = [for (final row in r) List.unmodifiable(row)];
  // ...and note the DEEP copy: a shallow one leaves the inner lists mutable

  // wraps: cheap, and correct only because the source is stable
  Csv.view(List<List<String>> r) : rows = UnmodifiableListView(r);

  // and a common middle ground: copy the outer, wrap the inner
  Csv.mid(List<List<String>> r)
      : rows = [for (final row in r) UnmodifiableListView(row)];
}

// the defect this prevents
final source = [[1, 2]];
final csv = Csv(source);
source[0][0] = 99;          // legal, and the immutable csv changed
source.add([3]);            // and the outer list grew

// for a Map, the same three
final cfg = Map.of(input);              // a copy
final view = Map.unmodifiable(input);   // a frozen VIEW
// ...Map.unmodifiable is a view, not a copy - which is a detail in the
// docs that changes what it means

// and when the argument is already immutable, both are the same object
final const = <String, int>{'a': 1};
Map.of(const);              // a copy, but const makes it unnecessary

5.7 Allocation and performance

Where the allocations go, and how to see them.

// EVERY method that returns a new collection allocates
final mapped = list.map(f);          // lazy: allocates an Iterable view
final forced = mapped.toList();      // THIS allocates the list

// a hot loop should allocate as little as possible
List<int> doubled(List<int> input) {
  final out = List<int>.filled(input.length, 0);   // one allocation
  for (var i = 0; i < input.length; i++) {
    out[i] = input[i] * 2;                          // no per-item allocation
  }
  return out;
}

// the chain version, for a non-hot path
List<int> doubled2(List<int> input) =>
    input.map((e) => e * 2).toList();    // fine, and clearer

// WHERE TO WORRY: inside a loop, inside a build method, per frame
// WHERE NOT TO WORRY: once per screen, once per request

// measure, do not guess
// dart --observe, then the DevTools Memory panel
// or a micro-benchmark with package:benchmark
// or simply: time 1M iterations before and after
// the O(n^2) traps that look innocent
List<int> uniquePreservingOrder(List<int> input) {
  final out = <int>[];
  for (final e in input) {
    if (!out.contains(e)) out.add(e);   // contains is O(n) -> O(n^2)
  }
  return out;
}

List<int> uniqueFast(List<int> input) {
  final seen = <int>{};
  return input.where(seen.add).toList();   // O(n)
}

// list.remove inside a loop: O(n) per removal -> O(n^2)
list.removeWhere((e) => e.isEmpty);     // ONE pass, O(n) - correct

// indexOf in a loop
for (final e in input) {
  if (other.indexOf(e) >= 0) { ... }    // O(n*m)
}
final otherSet = other.toSet();
for (final e in input) {
  if (otherSet.contains(e)) { ... }       // O(n+m)
}

Most collection performance problems are not about the collection - they are about contains, indexOf or remove being called inside a loop, turning an O(n) operation into an O(n²) one. Building a Set or Map of the lookup values first fixes most of them, and the code is no less readable.

Exercises 6

  1. Demonstrate laziness: build a million-element lazy chain and confirm nothing evaluates until you consume it.
  2. Find the mutation-during-lazy-iteration bug from 5.1 in a real pipeline and fix it.
  3. Write the uniquePreservingOrder function both ways and time them at 100,000 elements.
  4. Print several Set literals and confirm iteration order is insertion order, not numeric sort order.
  5. Take a nested List<List<int>> and replace it with a flat Int32List grid. Measure the memory difference.
  6. Add package:collection and replace ten hand-written helpers with its versions.
  7. Find one O(n²) pattern in a codebase you have written and fix it with a pre-built lookup.

The four costs, and how to measure them

Collection performance in Dart reduces to four costs: the hash of a key, the number of traversals, the cost of copying, and the cost of growth. Everything in the standard library's advice is a consequence of one of these, and knowing which one applies turns most performance questions into arithmetic rather than intuition.

OperationListSetMap
IndexO(1)——
Search by valueO(n)O(1) expected—
Insert at endO(1) amortisedO(1)O(1)
Insert at indexO(n)——
Remove by indexO(n)——
Remove by valueO(n)O(1)O(1)
CopyO(n)O(n)O(n)
Sorted lookupO(log n) binaryO(log n) treeO(log n) tree
// the measurement, and what makes a benchmark lie
import 'dart:developer';

void bench(String name, void Function() f, {int warmup = 100, int runs = 1000}) {
  for (var i = 0; i < warmup; i++) { f(); }   // JIT warmup
  final sw = Stopwatch()..start();
  for (var i = 0; i < runs; i++) { f(); }
  sw.stop();
  print('$name: ${sw.elapsedMicroseconds / runs}us');
}

// the four that catch people
final n = 100000;
final list = List<int>.generate(n, (i) => i);
final set = list.toSet();
final map = {for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) i: i};

bench('list.contains', () => list.contains(99999));      // O(n) every time
bench('set.contains', () => set.contains(99999));       // O(1)
bench('map[]', () => map[99999]);                       // O(1)

bench('list.insert(0)', () => final c = [1, 2, 3]..insert(0, 0));
bench('list.add', () => final c = [1, 2, 3]..add(0));

// the difference is not small: for n = 100000, a linear search is about
// 100,000x slower than a hash lookup. That is the whole argument for
// building an index, and it is why the "build the map once" advice is
// not premature - it is the difference between O(n·m) and O(n+m)

The cost that is hardest to see is the hash of the key, because it is paid once per lookup and a good hash makes it invisible. Object.hash is deliberately more expensive than ^ precisely because it distributes better, so a custom hashCode using XOR is faster per call and can degrade a HashMap to a linear scan on structured data — which is not a constant-factor loss but a change of complexity class, and which shows up only on the data shape that triggers it.

// a bad hash: fast per call, catastrophic in aggregate
class Point {
  final int x, y;
  @override
  int get hashCode => x ^ y;         // cheap
  @override
  bool operator ==(Object o) => o is Point && o.x == x && o.y == y;
}

// (1,2) and (2,1) collide. (1,1) and (0,0) collide. On a grid of
// points, MANY pairs collide, so the HashMap degenerates toward a list:
final pts = <Point, int>{};
for (var x = 0; x < 100; x++) {
  for (var y = 0; y < 100; y++) {
    pts[Point(x, y)] = x * y;         // 10000 inserts, mostly colliding
  }
}

// the fix: Object.hash, which mixes
@override
int get hashCode => Object.hash(x, y);
// ...and measure both, on the data shape you actually have:
// A hash that is fast on a synthetic benchmark can be pathological on the
// real distribution, so the benchmark data matters as much as the code.

// identity hash, for a key whose value is irrelevant
final byIdentity = HashMap.identity();
byIdentity[someObject] = data;
// ...uses Object.hashCode, which is the runtime identity hash - fast, and
// correct for "key on this object" but wrong for "key on this value"

// and the mutation rule, one more time, because it is the common one
// ...a hashCode that reads a mutable field is not a slow hash, it is an
// INCORRECT one: the entry becomes unreachable

Traversal count is the second hidden cost, and it shows up as a function that is unexpectedly slow for how little work it does. A lazy chain traversed twice costs twice; a .length on a lazy chain costs a full traversal; .toList() inside a loop over that same chain costs a traversal per iteration. The pattern to look for is a method with a lazy pipeline at the top and more than one terminal operation below it, because that is two traversals of the same computation where one would do.

// two traversals of one pipeline
final filtered = rows.where((r) => r.isActive);      // lazy
print(filtered.length);                              // traverse 1
print(filtered.first.name);                          // traverse 2 (partially)

// the fix: one traversal, one materialisation
final filtered = rows.where((r) => r.isActive).toList();
print(filtered.length);
print(filtered.first.name);

// the version that is worse than it looks
var total = 0;
for (final r in rows.where(expensivePredicate)) {     // pipeline rebuilt per row
  total += r.value;
}
// ...`expensivePredicate` runs once per row, which is expected - but if the
// predicate itself calls .length on the same source, each call is another
// traversal

// and the quadratic shape to grep for
for (final a in list) {
  if (list.contains(a)) { … }        // O(n^2) - and `.contains` is often
}                                   // written by habit

// and a cache that fixes it
final present = list.toSet();
for (final a in list) {
  if (present.contains(a)) { … }     // O(n) total
}

Copying is the third cost, and it is the one that decides whether an immutable view or a mutable copy is worth paying for. The cost is not the memory alone — it is that a copy invalidates every cache, every identity comparison and every hashCode computed from an object it used to contain. So a defensive copy in a hot path is not just an allocation; it changes the object's identity, and any index built over the original silently stops matching. That is the strongest practical argument for UnmodifiableListView over List.unmodifiable when the source is already owned by someone else.

// a copy changes identity, and identity is load-bearing
final original = [Point(1, 2)];
final copy = List.of(original);

final index = {for (final p in original) p: 'x'};    // keyed on identity
copy[0] = Point(1, 2);                                // same VALUE, new object
index.containsKey(copy[0]);                           // false
// ...and identical(original[0], copy[0]) is also false

// the view keeps identity
final view = UnmodifiableListView(original);
final index2 = {for (final p in original) p: 'x'};
index2.containsKey(view[0]);                          // TRUE

// so the rule: copy when you need independence and the source may change;
// view when the source is stable and you need the identity preserved.
// A copy for immutability is often the better trade - but it is a trade.

// the cost that is not about memory at all: a copy inside a hot function
Map<String, Object?> get config => Map.of(_rawConfig);   // a copy per access
// ...which defeats every cached lookup keyed on the config's identity,
// and which is invisible because the copy is "cheap"

// and the same for records and tuples, where the value semantics make the
// question disappear
typedef Row = ({int id, String name});
// a record has VALUE equality, so an index keyed on records is stable
final index3 = {for (final r in rows) (id: r.id): r};   // keyed on the id

6 · Records, Patterns and Sealed Types

6.1 Records: anonymous structured data6.2 When to use a record, when not to6.3 Sealed classes and exhaustive switch6.4 Pattern syntax6.5 Destructuring6.6 Guards and when clauses6.7 Pattern switch expressions in practice6.8 Records and patterns together

The Dart 3 features that replace a large amount of boilerplate. This is the chapter that most changes how you write the language.

6.1 Records: anonymous structured data

A record is an anonymous, immutable, fixed-shape value. Positional or named.

// a record is a value with a known shape and no class
(int, String) pair = (42, 'hello');        // positional
({int id, String name}) user = (id: 1, name: 'Ana');   // named

// the type is written as (field1, field2) or ({name: Type})
// and it is structural: two records with the same shape are the
// same type

// positional fields: $1, $2 (or destructured)
print(pair.$1);              // 42
print(pair.$2);              // hello
final (n, s) = pair;        // destructure
print('$n $s');

// named fields
print(user.id);              // 1
print(user.name);            // Ana

// records nest
((int, int), String) nested = ((1, 2), 'origin');
print(nested.$1.$2);         // 2
print(nested.$2);            // origin
// records are IMMUTABLE and hashable (by value)
final r1 = (1, 2);
final r2 = (1, 2);
print(r1 == r2);             // true - structural equality
print({r1, r2}.length);      // 1

// a record as a Map key
final cache = <(int, String), String>{
  (1, 'a'): 'first',
  (2, 'b'): 'second',
};
print(cache[(1, 'a')]);      // first

// single-field records are legal
(String,) single = ('only',);
print(single.$1);            // only

// the empty record
() unit = ();
print(unit);                 // ()

// equality ignores field NAMES for positional records
print((1, 2) == (1, 2));     // true

The record type, and why it is not a class

A record is a lightweight anonymous aggregate with a fixed number of positional fields, a fixed type for each, structural equality, and no identity. It is written (int, String) as a type and (1, 'a') as a value, and it is the only data structure in the language that is created, described, compared and pattern-matched entirely by the language rather than by a class you write.

The distinguishing properties are that it is immutable, value-equal, immutable at the field level, and final — which is why the compiler can treat a record as a constant and why a record with only constant fields can be used in a const context. What a record deliberately lacks is a name, a constructor with validation, a superclass, or a mutable field, which is exactly the set of things that would make it a class.

// the type and the value
(int, String) pair = (1, 'one');
pair.$1;                       // 1  - positional field access
pair.$2;                       // 'one'
(pair.$1, pair.$2) = ('one', 1);   // destructuring assignment

// NAMED fields, which is what makes a record readable
({String name, int age}) person = (name: 'Ada', age: 36);
person.name;                   // 'Ada' - far better than $1
(person.name, person.age) = (name: 'Grace', age: 45);

// one, two, or three types
(int,) single = (1,);          // a trailing comma distinguishes ONE field
({int x, int y}) point = (x: 1, y: 2);
(int, int, int) triple = (1, 2, 3);

// and Unit, which is the empty record - the value () and the type void
void f() {}
f();                           // returns void, not Unit

// immutability is total
pair.$1 = 5;                   // ERROR: fields are final

// value equality, with no == override needed
print((1, 2) == (1, 2));       // true
print((1, 2) == (1, 3));       // false
final m = <(int, String), int>{(1, 'a'): 1};
print(m[(1, 'a')]);            // 1 - so a record works as a key

// and identity is not
print(identical((1, 2), (1, 2)));   // false - two allocations

// hashCode is derived, so it is consistent with ==
(1, 2).hashCode == (1, 2).hashCode;  // true

A record's field types need not be distinct and need not be named, which gives two forms that look like the same feature and are not. A positional record (int, String) is typed by position, so it is suited to a heterogeneous pair where the field names would not add information — a key of (String, int), a return of (bool, String). A named record ({String name, int age}) types each field individually, so it can have optional fields and defaults, and its shape is visible at the type. Positional fields may be spread with ... in a type, which is what lets one record satisfy another.

FormTypeOptional fieldsDefaultsSpreading
Positional(int, String)NoNoNo
Named({int a, int b})YesYesYes
Single positional(int,)NoNoNo
// a positional record, and why it has no names
typedef Id = (String, int);
Id? lookup(String key) => db[key];

final result = compute();
if (result != null) {
  final (value, message) = result;     // positional destructuring
  print('$message: $value');
}

// a named record, and why it does
typedef Response = ({int status, String body, String? error});

Response ok(String body) => (status: 200, body: body, error: null);
Response bad(String e) => (status: 400, body: '', error: e);

// OPTIONAL fields - which only a named record has
typedef Config = ({String host, int port, bool secure});
Config minimal = (host: 'localhost', port: 8080);   // secure defaults false
Config full = (host: 'x', port: 443, secure: true);

// DEFAULTS, which is the reason optional fields are useful
typedef Options = ({String host, int port, String? path, int retries});
const opts = (host: 'localhost', port: 8080, path: '/v1', retries: 3);
final merged = (
  host: user.host,
  port: user.port,
  path: opts.path,          // taken from the default
  retries: opts.retries,
);
// ...so a record type is a config schema with compile-time checked field
// names, which a Map is not

// SPREADING a record type: (int, {String n}) satisfies (int, String, String)
typedef Narrow = (int, String);
typedef Wide = (int, String, String);
Wide w = (1, 'a', 'b');
Narrow n = w;                // legal - the extra field is discarded

The comparison between a record and a class is the decision this type exists to make, and it comes down to how much of a type's identity is its values. A class has identity: two Point objects with the same coordinates are distinct objects, distinguishable with identical, and a == that does not say otherwise. A record is entirely its values — two records with equal fields are the same value — which is what makes it usable as a map key, comparable in a test without an override, and usable in a const expression. Where a class is the right answer, a record is wrong for one specific reason: a class can have behaviour, a name, and invariants, and a record cannot.

6.2 When to use a record, when not to

The decision, and the cases where a record is the wrong tool.

// GOOD uses of a record

// 1. returning two or three values
(int, String) measure(String text) {
  final words = text.split(' ');
  return (words.length, text.length);
}
final (count, chars) = measure('hello world');

// 2. a map entry, without a class
Map<String, int> get counts => {
  'words': count,
  'chars': chars,
};

// 3. grouping in a fold
final grouped = words.fold(<String, List<String>>{}, (m, w) {
  (m[w[0]] ??= []).add(w);      // m[w[0]] ??= [] needs a non-null list
  return m;
});

// 4. a discriminated result, before you commit to a sealed class
(Object, String) attempt<T>() { ... }

// 5. destructuring in a loop
for (final (key, value) in map.entries) {
  print('$key = $value');
}

// BAD uses

// 1. more than about four fields: it stops being readable
(String, String, String, String, String, String) awful = ...;

// 2. it needs behaviour
//    a record cannot have methods, so a domain object with logic
//    must be a class

// 3. it is stored and passed around widely
//    a named class is self-documenting in a signature:
//    User getUser()  vs  (String, String, int) getUser()

// 4. it needs JSON serialisation
//    jsonEncode((1, 'a')) does not work; you need a class or a Map

A good test: if you would struggle to name the record's type, it should be a class. (String, String, int) for a user is three anonymous strings in a signature. User says what it is, and gives you somewhere to put validation and serialisation. Records are for values that are genuinely anonymous - a coordinate, a result pair, a key.

When a record beats a class, and the four cases that decide it

A record is the right type when the value has no behaviour, its fields are all you need, its lifetime is short, and its identity is its content. Those four conditions together describe a surprisingly large fraction of the data that passes through application code, which is why records reduced the amount of boilerplate in the library so sharply. It is the wrong type whenever any one of them fails, and the failures are worth naming because each produces a specific awkwardness.

SituationUseBecause
A key into a lookupRecordNeeds value equality, no behaviour
A multi-value returnRecordOne type instead of a wrapper class
A local intermediate valueRecordCannot be named publicly, so no API cost
A JSON shapeNamed recordField names are the wire format
An entity with rulesClassNeeds invariants and behaviour
A type with subtypesSealed classRecords have no subtypes
Anything mutableClassRecords are immutable
A value with no dataClass or singletonA record of zero fields is ()
// the case records were made for: multiple return values
(int, String) measure(String s) => (s.length, s.toUpperCase());

// before: two out-parameters, or a Map, or a wrapper class
// void measure(String s, out int len, out String up);
// final r = measure(s); r['length'] as int;  // untyped, unchecked
// final r = MeasureResult(s);                // a whole class for two fields

final (len, up) = measure('hello');
print('$len $up');                 // 5 HELLO

// a named record, where the field names ARE the information
typedef Point = ({double x, double y});
typedef Bounds = ({double minX, double minY, double maxX, double maxY});

({double x, double y}) centre(Bounds b) => (
  x: (b.minX + b.maxX) / 2,
  y: (b.minY + b.maxY) / 2,
);

// a lookup keyed on a record, which a class cannot do without == and hashCode
final counts = <(int, int), int>{};
for (final (dx, dy) in moves) {
  final k = (dx, dy);
  counts[k] = (counts[k] ?? 0) + 1;
}
counts[(1, 0)];               // the number of times (1, 0) occurred

// and the composite key, which is the common case in real code
final seen = <({int userId, DateTime day}), int>{};
seen[(userId: 1, day: today)] = 5;
// ...a Map would need a string join, a Map of Maps, or a wrapper class

Pattern matching is where records pay off twice, because a record is destructureable — a pattern can bind each of its fields to a name and simultaneously verify the shape. A switch over a record type therefore checks that the value has the right types in the right positions and extracts them, in one construct, with no accessor calls and no casts. That is not merely less typing than an if-chain; it is a compile-time proof that the value's shape matches the branch, which an if-chain with is tests only achieves after the fact.

// destructuring a record in a pattern, which both checks and binds
void describe(Object value) {
  switch (value) {
    case (int a, int b):
      print('two ints: $a + $b = ${a + b}');
    case (int a, String s):
      print('int then string: $a / $s');
    case [int a, int b]:
      print('a list of exactly two ints: $a $b');
    case String s when s.isNotEmpty:
      print('a non-empty string: $s');
    case _:
      print('something else');
  }
}

// ...compare with the hand-written version, which needs casts and has no
// exhaustiveness story at all
void describe2(Object value) {
  if (value is int && value is String) { … }   // never true - one value
}

// ...or the version with a cast, which is unchecked
void describe3(Object value) {
  if (value is List && value.length == 2) {
    final a = value[0] as int;      // a runtime cast
    final b = value[1] as int;
  }
}

// the record version is checked at compile time, so a mismatch is an error
// rather than a TypeError in production

// and the same destructuring as an assignment, outside any switch
final (name, age) = ('Ada', 36);
final ({int x, int y}) = (x: 1, y: 2);   // named destructuring
final (a, b, c) = (1, 2, 3);             // must match in count and type

Two rules constrain where a record type may appear, and both are worth knowing because they explain why a design that looks right does not compile. A record type cannot be used as a supertype, an implements clause, a generic bound, or a type argument — so List<(int, String)> is illegal, and the reason is that a record's identity is its shape, so there is no subtyping relation to have. And a record cannot be declared in a typedef and then extended, so it is always a leaf. Both constraints are what make records fast: the representation is known at compile time, which is why they need no class, no table, and no identity field.

// where a record type may NOT appear
List<(int, String)> bad;         // ERROR: not a type argument
class X implements (int, String) {}   // ERROR: cannot implement
void f((int, String) x) {}           // FINE - a parameter
(int, String) f() => (1, 'a');     // FINE - a return
typedef Pair = (int, String);        // FINE - an alias
final p = <Pair>[];                  // ERROR - Pair is still a record

// the class version, when the type argument is needed
class PairList extends ListBase<(int, String)> {}   // still ERROR

// so if you need a generic over records, the record must be the ELEMENT
final list = <(int, String)>[];    // hmm - is this legal?
// ...it is NOT. The workaround is a typedef that is not a record:
typedef Pair = (int, String);
// ...and `List<Pair>` is equally illegal, because the alias resolves to a
// record type. The real solution is a normal class with the fields:

class Pair {
  final int first;
  final String second;
  const Pair(this.first, this.second);
  @override
  bool operator ==(Object o) =>
      o is Pair && o.first == first && o.second == second;
  @override
  int get hashCode => Object.hash(first, second);
}
// ...which is the honest answer: a record CANNOT be a generic type argument,
// and that limitation is the boundary of what they are for

The performance consequence of that restriction is worth stating, because it is why records exist rather than merely being convenient. A record's representation is entirely known at compile time — its fields are inlined at the point of use, there is no indirection, no vtable, and no header. A one-field record (int,) is, in the compiler's output, indistinguishable from the bare int. A two-field record is two adjacent machine words. That is only possible because a record cannot be a type argument: if records could be stored polymorphically, every one would need a box, and the entire benefit would disappear.

// a one-field record is free
typedef Id = (int,);
final Id id = 42;          // compiles to: an int in a register

// a two-field record is two adjacent words
typedef Pair = (int, String);
final Pair p = (1, 'a');

// ...so a function taking a pair takes two registers, not a pointer
int sum(Pair p) => p.$1;  // inlined to a field load, not a dereference

// and the cost appears the moment a record is boxed, which is why the
// restriction above matters so much
final list = [1, 'a'] as dynamic;   // now it IS boxed
// ...a dynamic value is a pointer to a boxed object, and every access is
// an indirection plus a type check

// so the rule for performance: keep records in typed, non-dynamic
// positions. `Object`, `dynamic`, and `List<Object>` all box them.

// the measurement
// A class with two final fields: one allocation, 16 bytes of header plus
//   the fields, one pointer chase to read either
// A two-field record: zero allocations for the record itself, the fields
//   are wherever they were computed, no pointer chase
// A Map<String, dynamic>: an allocation per value, a HashMap lookup,
//   a pointer chase, and a runtime type check

6.3 Sealed classes and exhaustive switch

The feature that makes the compiler check that you handled every case.

// a sealed class: an abstract class with a FIXED set of subtypes,
// all in the same library. The compiler knows the full set.
sealed class Shape {}

class Circle extends Shape {
  final double radius;
  const Circle(this.radius);
}

class Square extends Shape {
  final double side;
  const Square(this.side);
}

class Rect extends Shape {
  final double w, h;
  const Rect(this.w, this.h);
}

// an exhaustive switch REQUIRES every case, and needs no default
double area(Shape shape) {
  return switch (shape) {
    Circle(:final radius) => 3.14159 * radius * radius,
    Square(:final side) => side * side,
    Rect(:final w, :final h) => w * h,
  };
  // add a fourth subclass and this function STOPS COMPILING
  // until you handle it. That is the whole value.
}

// if you add a case, the compiler points at the switch, not at a
// runtime "unhandled type" error six frames away
// before sealed classes, the same thing was much worse
abstract class Shape2 {}
class Circle2 extends Shape2 { final double r; Circle2(this.r); }
class Square2 extends Shape2 { final double s; Square2(this.s); }

double area2(Shape2 shape) {
  if (shape is Circle2) return 3.14 * shape.r * shape.r;
  if (shape is Square2) return shape.s * shape.s;
  throw UnimplementedError();   // silently wrong if a type is added
}

// the sealed version has no UnimplementedError, no throw, and the
// compiler enforces completeness

// a sealed class with GENERICS, which is very powerful
sealed class Result<T, E> {}

class Ok<T, E> extends Result<T, E> {
  final T value;
  const Ok(this.value);
}

class Failure<T, E> extends Result<T, E> {
  final E error;
  const Failure(this.error);
}

// using it, and the error type is not lost
Future<Result<User, ApiError>> fetchUser(String id) async { ... }

Future<void> handle(String id) async {
  final result = await fetchUser(id);
  switch (result) {
    case Ok(:final value):
      print('got ${value.name}');
    case Failure(:final error):
      print('failed: ${error.message}');
  }
  // no default, no cast, no null check
}
// a practical hierarchy: the states of a network request
sealed class Async<T> {}

class Loading extends Async<Never> {}
class Data<T> extends Async<T> { final T value; Data(this.value); }
class FailureState<T> extends Async<T> {
  final String message;
  final bool retryable;
  final StackTrace? stack;
  FailureState(this.message, {this.retryable = true, this.stack});
}

// a UI helper that is exhaustive
String describe<T>(Async<T> state) {
  return switch (state) {
    Loading() => 'Loading...',
    Data(:final value) => value.toString(),
    FailureState(:final message, :final retryable) =>
      retryable ? '$message (tap to retry)' : message,
  };
}

Sealed, abstract, base, final, interface — five class modifiers

Dart 3 added class modifiers that replace the old convention of a leading underscore on abstract classes. Each one restricts who may extend, implement or mix in a class, and together they let a library state its intent in the type system rather than in a documentation comment that nothing enforces.

ModifierMay be extendedMay be implementedMay be mixed inIts own subclasses
sealed classSame library onlyYes, anywhereNoYes
sealed interfacen/aYes, anywheren/an/a
abstract classYesYesNoYes
base classSubclasses onlyYesNoYes
final classNoYesNoNo
interface classYes, if baseYesNoYes
mixin classYesYesYesYes

A sealed class is the one that matters most, because it is what makes an exhaustive switch possible. A sealed class may be extended or implemented only within its own library, so the compiler knows the complete set of subtypes at compile time — and can therefore prove that a switch or switch expression over it covers every case. Add a subclass and every exhaustive switch in the program stops compiling until the new case is handled. That is the whole value, and it is a compile-time guarantee rather than a convention.

// a sealed hierarchy, and the switch that becomes exhaustive
sealed class Shape {}
final class Circle extends Shape {
  final double radius;
  Circle(this.radius);
}
final class Square extends Shape {
  final double side;
  Square(this.side);
}
final class Rect extends Shape {
  final double w, h;
  Rect(this.w, this.h);
}

// a switch EXPRESSION with no default: the compiler proves it is complete
double area(Shape s) => switch (s) {
  Circle(radius: var r) => 3.14159265 * r * r,
  Square(side: var a) => a * a,
  Rect(w: var w, h: var h) => w * h,
};

double perimeter(Shape s) => switch (s) {
  Circle(radius: var r) => 2 * 3.14159265 * r,
  Square(side: var a) => 4 * a,
  Rect(w: var w, h: var h) => 2 * (w + h),
};

// add a fifth subclass and BOTH switches stop compiling
final class Triangle extends Shape { final double base, height; Triangle(this.base, this.height); }
// ERROR: The switch expression must be exhaustive - Triangle is not handled

// ...which is the feature. An abstract class CANNOT give this, because
// anyone anywhere can add a subclass tomorrow:
abstract class Animal {}
String describe(Animal a) => switch (a) {
  Dog() => 'dog',
  Cat() => 'cat',
};   // ERROR: not exhaustive, and the compiler cannot tell you why

Exhaustiveness checking is what the sealed hierarchy is for, and understanding that changes how you write one. A sealed hierarchy is a closed set of alternatives that a function must handle completely, so the set should be genuinely closed — every case is one the library intends to support forever. Adding a case is a breaking change by construction, which is correct: it forces every caller to consider the new case rather than letting it fall through a default nobody wrote. A sealed hierarchy is therefore a statement about completeness, and a plain abstract class is a statement about extension.

// sealed with an explicitly-implemented interface, so implementors may
// live in another library
sealed interface Result<T, E> {}
final class Ok<T, E> extends Result<T, E> {
  final T value;
  Ok(this.value);
}
final class Err<T, E> extends Result<T, E> {
  final E error;
  Err(this.error);
}
// Ok and Err are in this library, so the set is closed. A downstream
// package cannot add a third case, because it cannot extend a sealed class
// outside this library - which is what stops `Result` becoming a 30-case
// hierarchy.

// the OTHER pattern: a sealed class with a runtime value per case
sealed class Event {}
final class Click implements Event { final int x, y; Click(this.x, this.y); }
final class Key implements Event { final String name; Key(this.name); }
final class Scroll implements Event { final double dy; Scroll(this.dy); }

// ...and the pattern is that each case carries the data that case needs
// and nothing else, so the switch is the only place that knows how to
// read it. Compare with a base class holding every field, where each
// subclass ignores most of them.

// and `sealed` on a mixin, which restricts who may mix it in
sealed mixin Logged {}
class Service with Logged {}    // ERROR: Logged can only be used in
                                // the library that declares it

The other three modifiers exist to close gaps that used to be unclosable. final class makes a class genuinely final to any subclass anywhere, which closes the hole where an implements in another library provided a substitute implementation with different behaviour. base requires a subclass to be base or final itself, which stops a chain of extensions that leaves the contract open at the end. interface class states that the type is meant to be implemented and not extended, which is a documentation improvement over an underscore-prefixed name, and mixin class states the opposite — that a class is also usable as a mixin.

// final: cannot be extended or implemented anywhere
final class Money {
  final int cents;
  const Money(this.cents);
}
class FakeMoney implements Money {}      // ERROR - Money is final
// ...which is the point. Before `final`, an implementation of a final-ish
// class could return a negative amount from a `cents` getter, and nothing
// stopped it.

// base: extensible, but the chain must terminate in base or final
base class Repository {}
class UserRepository extends Repository {}         // ERROR: not base/final
final class InMemoryRepository extends Repository {}  // fine
base class CachedRepository extends Repository {}    // fine

// interface: implement, do not extend
abstract interface class Disposable {
  void dispose();
}
class Service implements Disposable { … }   // the intended use
abstract class Widget implements Disposable {} // cannot be `extends`ed

// mixin class: usable as a class AND as a mixin
mixin class Cacheable<T> {
  final Map<String, T> _cache = {};
  T? get(String k) => _cache[k];
  void put(String k, T v) => _cache[k] = v;
}
class Service with Cacheable<User> {}   // as a mixin
class Store extends Cacheable<User> {}   // as a superclass
// ...and WITHOUT the modifier, only the first is allowed

// the older convention, and why the modifiers replaced it
abstract class _Shape {}          // the old way: a convention nothing checks
class Circle extends _Shape {}
// ...and the name was the only signal that this was not for extension

6.4 Pattern syntax

The building blocks: literals, variables, wildcards, types, objects, casts and checks.

void demo(Object value) {
  // 1. a constant pattern
  switch (value) {
    case 0:      print('zero'); break;
    case 1:      print('one'); break;
    case 42:     print('the answer'); break;
    default:     print('other');
  }

  // 2. a variable pattern: binds, and ALWAYS matches
  final other = value;

  // 3. a wildcard: matches and discards
  final _ = value;

  // 4. a type pattern: tests AND binds
  if (value case final String s) {
    print('a string of length ${s.length}');
  }

  // 5. an object pattern: destructures, and you can omit fields
  if (value case Circle(:final radius)) {
    print('radius $radius');
  }
  // with a type check too
  if (value case Circle(radius: final r) when r > 10) {
    print('big circle');
  }

  // 6. a logical-or pattern: several alternatives
  if (value case 1 || 2 || 3) print('small number');

  // 7. a relational pattern: a comparison in a pattern
  if (value case final n when n is int && n > 100) {
    print('big int');
  }
  // but comparisons are patterns too
  switch (value) {
    case < 0:      print('negative'); break;
    case 0:         print('zero'); break;
    case <= 10:    print('small'); break;
    case > 100:    print('large'); break;
    default:        print('medium');
  }

  // 8. a cast pattern: tests, binds, and PROMOTES
  if (value case final num n) {
    // n is num here, not Object: the promotion happens
    print(n.toDouble());
  }

  // 9. a null-check pattern
  if (value case final String? s) {
    print(s ?? 'was null');
  }
}

The pattern grammar, from the simplest form to the hardest

A pattern is a value-shaped piece of syntax that both tests whether a value has a shape and destructures it into names. The grammar is recursive and every form is available wherever a pattern is expected — in a switch case, an if or while, a collection literal, a map entry, or a destructuring assignment — which is what makes the same vocabulary usable in all of them.

PatternMatchesBinds
42The value equals 42Nothing
var xAnythingx
final xAnythingx, typed
int xAn intx narrowed
Foo()An instance of FooThe object
Foo(:var a)A Foo with field aa
[a, b]A list of exactly twoa, b
[a, ...rest]A list, first is aa, rest
{}A Map, any contentNothing
{'k': var v}A Map with that keyv
(a, b)A 2-recorda, b
p when qp and q holdsAs p
_AnythingNothing
null / != nullIs / is not nullNothing

The core distinction is between a variable pattern, which binds a name, and everything else, which tests. var x and final x bind; int x tests the type and binds; Foo(:var a) tests the runtime type, tests the object's shape, and binds a field. Everything else in the grammar is built by nesting and sequencing those three operations, which is why the whole set is small enough to hold in your head once it is written this way.

// variable patterns
case var x:                        // anything, x is Object?
case final x:                      // anything, x is inferred
case int x:                        // only an int, x is int
case final int x:                  // same, and `final` is the modern form
case String s:                     // a type test and a binding in one

// object patterns, which destructure fields
case User(:var name):              // a User, and name bound
case User(name: final n, age: var a):   // two fields
case Point(x: 0):                  // a Point whose x is exactly 0
case Point(x: var x, y: var y) when x == y:   // with a guard

// list patterns
case []:                           // an EMPTY list
case [var a]:                      // exactly one element
case [var a, var b]:               // exactly two
case [var first, ...]:             // at least one
case [var first, ...var rest]:     // at least one, plus the tail
case [_, var second]:              // at least two; the first ignored
case [..., var last]:              // at least one; the last is bound

// map patterns
case {}:                           // ANY Map
case {"a": var a}:                   // a Map with key 'a'
case {'a': var a, 'b': var b}:      // two specific keys
case {var k: var v}:                // exactly one entry, any key
case {'a': _, ...}:                 // has key 'a', possibly others

// and the rest patterns, which only exist in list and map patterns
case [1, 2, ...var rest]:           // starts 1, 2
case {'a': 1, ...}:                 // has a=1

// null patterns
case null:                         // exactly null
case != null:                      // anything but null
case final String s?:              // a nullable String, s is String?

Two restrictions on patterns are responsible for most of the "why won't this compile" reports. A rest pattern may appear at most once in a list or map pattern and only in the last position — the grammar requires it, because a pattern describes the shape from the start, so there is no position for a middle wildcard that means "everything in between". And an object pattern's field names must exist on the type, which is a compile-time check — so User(:var typo) is an error rather than a pattern that never matches, which is the correct outcome but not an obvious one.

// the rest-pattern rule
case [1, ...var mid, 2]:            // ERROR - rest must be last
case [1, ...var mid, 2, ...var e]:   // ERROR - only one rest
case [1, ...var rest]:              // legal

// the workaround for "everything in between"
case [var first, ...] when lastElementMatches:   // needs a guard, and a
                                                 // predicate over the list

// object patterns check field names at compile time
case User(:var nmae):               // ERROR: no field 'nmae'
case User(:var name):               // fine - and `name` exists

// and an object pattern's field sub-pattern is itself a pattern
case Point(x: var x, y: var y) when x == y:    // guard
case Point(x: 0, y: 0):                         // literal match on a field
case Point(x: var x, y: var y) if x > 0:      // ...also a guard, old syntax

// an object pattern on a nullable needs the null handled separately
case Point(:var x, :var y):         // a NON-NULL Point
case null:                          // so null is a separate case
case _:                             // ...or a wildcard

// sealed-type exhaustiveness, which is where the compiler helps most
sealed class Result<T, E> {}
final class Ok<T, E> extends Result<T, E> { final T value; Ok(this.value); }
final class Err<T, E> extends Result<T, E> { final E error; Err(this.error); }

String show<T, E>(Result<T, E> r) => switch (r) {
  Ok(:final value) => '$value',
  Err(:final error) => 'error: $error',
};
// ...the object pattern also BINDS, so `value` and `error` are in scope in
// their arms. No casting, no field access, and completeness is proven.

The third restriction is that a variable pattern in a pattern is irrefutable — var x and final x match anything, so a case using one makes everything after it unreachable. That is a compile error rather than a runtime surprise, and it is the mechanism by which the compiler enforces that the order of cases matters: a default-equivalent wildcard must come last, and a specific test must come before the general one. The same restriction means a wildcard in a non-exhaustive context is not merely unnecessary, it is an error in some positions.

// irrefutability, and the order it enforces
switch (value) {
  case int x when x > 10:       // a guarded pattern - may not match
    print('big int $x');
  case String s:                  // a type test - may not match
    print('string $s');
  case var v:                     // irrefutable - matches everything
    print('other $v');
}
// ...legal, because the first two may fail and so the third is reachable

// but this is an ERROR
switch (value) {
  case var v:                     // irrefutable - nothing can follow
    print(v);
  case int x:                     // ERROR: unreachable pattern
    print(x);
}

// and in a switch EXPRESSION the position matters too
final label = switch (value) {
  0 => 'zero',
  int x when x < 0 => 'negative',
  int() => 'positive int',
  _ => 'other',
};   // the wildcard is last, and REQUIRED unless the type is sealed

// the restricted form that refuses to be irrefutable
var (a, b) = record;              // legal - the record is known to be 2-wide
// final (a, b) = maybeRecord;     // ERROR - `maybeRecord` is nullable, so
                                  // the pattern is not irrefutable

// the fix for a nullable source
if (maybeRecord case final (x, y)) { print('$x $y'); }   // a PATTERN in an
                                                       // if - refutable

6.5 Destructuring

Pulling a tuple apart, in every context you might need it.

// a record
final record = (1, 'two', 3.5);

// positional destructuring, by position
final (a, b, c) = record;
print('$a $b $c');

// positional by index
print(record.$1);
print(record.$2);

// named record, destructured by name
final named = (x: 10, y: 20);
final (:x, :y) = named;
print('${x + $y}');      // 30

// mixed
final mixed = (1, name: 'a', age: 2);
final (num1, :name) = mixed;

// in a for loop, over a list of records
final points = [(0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 4)];
for (final (x, y) in points) {
  print('($x, $y)');
}

// over Map entries
for (final (key, value) in {'a': 1, 'b': 2}.entries) {
  print('$key = $value');
}

// in a pattern match, which is the most common use
void handle((String, int) entry) {
  final (name, count) = entry;
  print('$name has $count');
}

handle(('ana', 3));

// destructuring an object pattern in a case
switch ((1, 2)) {
  case (1, final b):
    print('started at 1, b = $b');
  case (final a, 2):
    print('ended at 2, a = $a');
  case (final a, final b):
    print('neither: $a, $b');
}

Destructuring, and the four places it is available

Destructuring extracts the fields of a record into names. It exists as a statement, as a declaration, as a pattern in if and while, and as a pattern in switch — and the distinction that matters is irrefutable versus refutable. A destructuring form that cannot fail uses the plain syntax; one that can fail must be in a position where failure is allowed, which is if case or a switch case.

PositionRefutable?Syntax
DeclarationNofinal (a, b) = pair;
AssignmentNo(a, b) = pair;
ifYesif (pair case (a, b))
whileYeswhile (pair case (a, b))
Switch caseYescase (a, b):
List/map literalNo[a, b], {a: b}
Variable declarationYescase var (a, b) in an if
// 1. declaration - irrefutable
final (name, age) = ('Ada', 36);         // both names declared AND assigned
print('$name $age');

// 2. assignment to existing variables - irrefutable
var name = '', age = 0;
(name, age) = ('Grace', 45);             // assign, not declare
// ...which is how you SWAP
var a = 1, b = 2;
(a, b) = (b, a);                         // a=2, b=1 - correct, and total

// 3. if case - REFUTABLE, and the skip the old `as` cast could not express
if (json case {'user': final Map<String, Object?> u, 'token': final String t}) {
  print('$u has token ${t.length}');
} else {
  print('not a session payload');
}

// 4. switch case - refutable
switch (pair) {
  case (int x, int y) when x > y:
    print('$x > $y');
  case (int x, int y):
    print('$x <= $y');
  case (String s, int n):
    print('$s then $n');
}

// the destructuring list literal - builds, does not destructures
final copy = [name, age];                  // a List of two
final map = {'name': name, 'age': age};     // a Map

// and the destructuring assignment from a LIST or a MAP
final [first, second, third] = [1, 2, 3];   // positional, from a List
final {'a': av} = {'a': 1};                 // by key, from a Map

// the version that fails at compile time, correctly
final [x, y, z] = [1, 2];                  // ERROR: 3 names, 2 values
final {'k': v} = {'other': 1};             // ERROR: no key 'k'

Destructuring a class's fields is the use with the largest effect, because it replaces a run of type tests and casts with one pattern. A switch over an Object that destructures each subtype's fields reads as the data it is handling rather than as the mechanics of discovering what it is, and the compiler proves every field's type — which means the as casts that used to be required for every access disappear along with their possibility of failing at run time.

// before: a type test and a cast per access
if (event is ClickEvent) {
  final x = (event as ClickEvent).x;       // a cast, checked again
  final y = event.y;
  handle(x, y);
}

// after: one pattern, both fields typed, no casts
switch (event) {
  case ClickEvent(:final x, :final y):
    handle(x, y);
  case KeyEvent(:final key, :final ctrl):
    if (ctrl) shortcut(key);
  case ScrollEvent(:final dy) when dy.abs() > 10:
    scrollBy(dy);
  default:
    log('unhandled: ${event.runtimeType}');
}

// and nested destructuring, which flattens three levels
switch (response) {
  case {'status': 200, 'body': {'data': final List items}}:
    for (final item in items) { … }
  case {'status': final int code} when code >= 400:
    throw HttpException('server said $code');
  case {'status': final int code}:
    throw HttpException('client said $code');
  default:
    throw const FormatException('not a response');
}
// ...which handles four shapes, three status ranges, and a malformed
// payload, with no `as` and no null check anywhere

The subtlety with destructuring is that a record pattern matches a record of the same arity and same field names, so it is stricter than it looks — and a class pattern matches by runtime type, which is a different mechanism entirely. case (a, b): on a List value will not match, because a list is not a two-field record; case [a, b]: will. And case User(:var n): requires the runtime type to be User or a subclass, so it does not match a AdminUser unless User is sealed in a hierarchy where AdminUser is a case too, or unless you write the pattern on the common supertype.

// a record pattern does NOT match a List
final Object v = [1, 2];
switch (v) {
