  case (int a, int b): print('record $a $b');   // NO match - [1,2] is a List
  case [int a, int b]: print('list $a $b');     // matches
  default: print('neither');
}

// an object pattern DOES match a subclass
class User { final String name; User(this.name); }
class Admin extends User { final List<String> perms; Admin(super.name, this.perms); }

void f(User u) {
  switch (u) {
    case Admin(:final perms): print('admin: $perms');   // matches Admin
    case User(:final name): print('user: $name');       // matches User only
  }
}
// ...and note the ORDER: Admin is listed first, because `case User(...)`
// would also match an Admin. Order is load-bearing with any subtype case.

// and the analogous subtlety with map patterns
final m = {'a': 1, 'b': 2};
switch (m) {
  case {'a': 1}: print('has a=1');          // matches - extras are ignored
  case {'a': 1, 'b': 2}: print('exactly');  // also matches - the first wins
  case {'a': var x, ...}: print('a=$x');    // matches, binds x
  case {}: print('any map');                // matches ANY map, even {}
}

There is one destructuring form that is not about records at all and is worth knowing because it changes how a loop is written. A for loop can destructure each element, so a list of pairs iterates as a list of pairs rather than as a list of opaque values needing an index. Combined with the record pattern in an if case, that gives a shape-safe iteration over a heterogeneous collection — and the failure mode is a skipped element rather than a crash, which is the better of the two.

// destructuring in a for loop - no index, no cast
final points = [(1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 6)];
for (final (x, y) in points) {
  print('($x, $y)');
}

// the safe version over a heterogeneous list, where elements that do not
// match are SKIPPED rather than crashing
final items = <Object>[(1, 2), 'text', (3, 4), 42];
for (final item in items) {
  if (item case (int x, int y)) {
    print('pair $x $y');         // runs twice
  }
}

// ...which is the shape-safe filter, with no exception, no cast, and no
// `is` test followed by an `as`

// the same in a nested loop, for a table
final table = [
  ['Name', 'Qty'],
  ['Widget', 3],
  ['Gadget', 5],
];
for (final [row, name, qty] in table) {
  print('$row: $name x$qty');
}

// and in an await for, over a Stream of records
await for (final (id, name) in fetchRows()) {
  print('$id: $name');
}

// ...and the destructuring happens per element, so it costs nothing extra
// and cannot be forgotten on one branch of a loop body

6.6 Guards and when clauses

Restricting a pattern with a condition, and the order the compiler evaluates things in.

// a `when` clause guards a pattern
void classify(Object value) {
  // a type pattern, then a guard
  if (value case final List<int> l when l.length > 10) {
    print('a big list of ints: ${l.length}');
    return;
  }
  if (value case final List<int> l) {
    print('a small list of ints');
    return;
  }
  if (value case final List l) {
    print('a list of something else');
    return;
  }
  print('not a list');
}

// the guard runs only if the pattern matched
// so order matters: put the cheap test first

// a realistic use: narrowing a union by value
sealed class Command {}
class SetName extends Command { final String name; SetName(this.name); }
class SetCount extends Command { final int count; SetCount(this.count); }

void run(Command cmd) {
  switch (cmd) {
    case SetName(name: final n) when n.isNotEmpty:
      print('renaming to $n');
    case SetName():
      print('ignoring an empty name');
    case SetCount(count: final c) when c > 0:
      print('count set to $c');
    case SetCount(count: final c):
      print('ignoring non-positive count $c');
  }
}

// a guard can reference anything in scope, including other bindings
switch (entry) {
  case (a, b) when a > b:
    print('descending');
  case (a, b) when a < b:
    print('ascending');
  case (a, _):
    print('equal');
}
// MULTIPLE GUARDS on one case, as alternatives
switch (value) {
  case int n when n < 0:
  case int n when n > 1000:
    print('out of range: $n');
    break;
  case int n:
    print('in range: $n');
    break;
}

// each `case` with the same variable name is a SEPARATE pattern
// that the compiler allows; a cleaner form:
switch (value) {
  case final int n when n < 0 || n > 1000:
    print('out of range');
  case final int n:
    print('in range');
}

// the gotcha: a case body cannot fall through
switch (value) {
  case 1:
  case 2:
    print('one or two');    // correct: shared body
    break;
  case 3:
    print('three');
    // no break needed in a switch EXPRESSION, but needed in a
    // switch STATEMENT in Dart unless the body ends in a jump
}

Guards, and why a guard is not the same as a nested condition

A when clause attaches a boolean condition to a pattern: the pattern must match and the condition must hold. That is the whole mechanism, and it is what makes a single switch able to express a partition of a type by a property of its values — a capability that in most languages requires either nested if inside a case, or duplicating the case with different bindings.

The important thing to understand is that a guard changes the pattern from a test into a test plus a test. A case with a guard may not match, so the cases after it are still reachable, and the compiler's exhaustiveness reasoning accounts for it. A case without a guard that is itself irrefutable makes everything after it unreachable, and the compiler rejects that. So when is what lets a general case be followed by a more specific one without the compiler complaining about order.

// a guard partitions a type by value
String classify(Object o) => switch (o) {
  int n when n < 0 => 'negative int',
  int() => 'non-negative int',
  double d when d.isNaN => 'not a number',
  double() => 'a number',
  String s when s.isEmpty => 'empty string',
  String s => '"$s"',
  _ => 'something else',
};
// ...`int n when n < 0` and `int()` together cover all ints, exhaustively,
// and both bind - but in different arms, with different types available

// the version WITHOUT a guard, which needs a nested if
String classify2(Object o) {
  if (o is int) {
    if (o < 0) return 'negative int';
    return 'non-negative int';
  }
  …
}
// ...which reads as nesting rather than as a partition, and each `if`
// re-tests a property of a value the switch has already sorted

// a guard on a FIELD, which is the most common form
final label = switch (user) {
  User(:final name, :final age) when age >= 18 => '$name (adult)',
  User(:final name) => '$name (minor)',
  Anonymous() => 'anonymous',
};

// and a guard combining destructuring with a computation
final bucket = switch (record) {
  (int a, int b) when a == b => 'equal',
  (int a, int b) when a > b => 'descending',
  (int a, _) => 'ascending',
  _ => 'not a pair',
};

There is an older syntax that is worth recognising because it still appears in older code and reads differently. if (x is! Type && condition) and the case x when ... if-clause form both exist, and both are implemented in terms of guards under the hood. The modern form is if (x case Type() when condition), which has one advantage that is easy to miss: it binds, so the guarded value's parts are in scope in the body without a second access, and the type is already promoted.

FormBindsPromotesModern?
if (x is! T) return; use(x)NoYes, after the early returnWorks, verbose
if (x case T v) use(v)YesInside onlyYes
if (x is T) use(x)NoInside onlyWorks
if (x case T() when c) use(x)NoInside onlyYes
if (x is T && c) use(x)NoInside onlyWorks
// the old guard syntax: a guard-clause after `case`
switch (value) {
  case int n if n > 10:      // OLD syntax: `if`, not `when`
    print('big');
}
// ...legal, and equivalent to `when`, and deprecated in style

// the modern form, and what it buys
if (json case {'user': final Map u} when u['active'] == true) {
  print('active user: $u');
} else {
  print('inactive or malformed');
}
// ...one expression, one test, and `u` is typed and in scope. The old form
// needed three statements and a re-lookup.

// and for the simple type case, `is` is still fine and shorter
if (value is int) print(value.isEven);

// where `case` wins is when the value has STRUCTURE
if (data case {'items': final List items} when items.isNotEmpty) {
  // ...`is` would need a cast and a separate length check
  for (final i in items) { … }
}

// a guard on a property that is expensive, and why that matters
switch (config) {
  case Config(:final cache) when cache.isWarm:   // checks, does not warm
    useFast();
  case Config(:final cache):
    warm(cache);
    useFast();
}
// ...so a guard is a PREDICATE, not an action. If the case needs to compute
// something and then use it, that belongs in the arm body

Guards interact with exhaustiveness in a specific way that is worth stating, because it is the reason a sealed hierarchy can be matched completely with guarded cases. The compiler treats a guarded case as potentially non-matching, so an exhaustive switch expression over a sealed type needs an unguarded case for each subtype, or a shared wildcard — but a set of guarded cases that logically covers a subtype is accepted when one of them has no guard. In practice the shape that works is: an unguarded case for the last variant of each type, with guarded cases above it for the refinements.

// exhaustiveness with guards, over a sealed type
sealed class Shape {}
final class Circle extends Shape { final double r; Circle(this.r); }
final class Square extends Shape { final double s; Square(this.s); }

// a wildcard is needed because both cases are guarded
String area(Shape s) => switch (s) {
  Circle(:final r) when r > 10 => 'large circle',
  Circle() => 'circle',                 // UNGUARDED - covers the rest
  Square(:final a) when a > 10 => 'large square',
  Square() => 'square',
};   // exhaustive: every sealed subtype has an unguarded case

// without the trailing unguarded cases, this does NOT compile
String areaBad(Shape s) => switch (s) {
  Circle(:final r) when r > 10 => 'large circle',
  Square(:final a) when a > 10 => 'large square',
};   // ERROR - a small Circle and a small Square match nothing

// and the wildcard does NOT make it exhaustive over a sealed type without
// saying why, which is the point of the error message:
String areaBad2(Shape s) => switch (s) {
  Circle(:final r) when r > 10 => 'large circle',
  Square(:final a) when a > 10 => 'large square',
  _ => 'small',                         // compiles, and is honest
};

// so the rule: a `_` over a sealed type is allowed but is a decision, and a
// set of unguarded cases is a proof. Prefer the proof.

/// and the guard that spans a destructured value
final size = switch (bounds) {
  (double w, double h) when w == h => 'square',
  (double w, double h) when w > h => 'landscape',
  (double _, double _) => 'portrait',   // unguarded, so exhaustive
};

Two costs of guards are worth naming so they are not used accidentally. A guard that calls a method, a property, or a function is re-evaluated on every attempt, so a guard with a side effect runs zero or one or many times depending on which cases were reached — which makes a guarded case a poor place for anything but a pure predicate. And a long guard is a nested condition in disguise, so when it needs three clauses it is usually better expressed as an early return inside the arm body, with the guard left carrying only the part that genuinely partitions the type.

// a guard with a side effect: how many times does it run?
var calls = 0;
final out = switch (value) {
  String s when expensiveCheck(s):     // called for every String that
    'yes',                             // reaches this arm
  String s => 'no',                  // ...and for none that do not
  _ => 'other',
};
// ...so `expensiveCheck` runs once per String value tested. Fine for a
// predicate; not fine for anything that mutates.

// the guard that should have been an early return
// BAD: a guard carrying the whole decision
final size = switch (bounds) {
  (double w, double h) when w > 100 && h > 100 && w == h => 'large square',
  (double w, double h) when w == h => 'square',
  (double w, _) => 'wide',
};

// BETTER: the guard partitions, the arm decides
final size = switch (bounds) {
  (double w, double h) when w == h => w > 100 ? 'large square' : 'square',
  (double w, _) => w > 100 ? 'large wide' : 'wide',
};
// ...the ternary is inside the arm, so it does not re-test the type on each
// clause, and the guard is one comparison

// the rule: a guard says "is this the case?"; anything longer than one
// clause is logic that belongs in the arm

6.7 Pattern switch expressions in practice

Where switch expressions replace long if-else chains, and the four forms that carry most of the value.

// 1. exhaustive over a sealed type - the compiler checks completeness
String render(State state) {
  return switch (state) {
    Loading() => spinner(),
    Ready(:final data) => list(data),
    Empty() => 'nothing here',
    Error(:final message, :final retryable) =>
      retryable ? '$message - retry?' : message,
  };
}

// 2. over a primitive, replacing a long if-else if
String grade(int score) {
  return switch (score) {
    >= 90 => 'A',
    >= 80 => 'B',
    >= 70 => 'C',
    >= 60 => 'D',
    < 60 => 'F',
  };
}

// 3. destructuring, which is unreadable without patterns
String describePair((int, String) pair) {
  return switch (pair) {
    (0, 'zero') => 'the origin',
    (var x, 'left') => 'left at $x',
    (var x, 'right') => 'right at $x',
    (var x, var dir) => '$dir at $x',
  };
}

// 4. a combination: type, then value, then guard
int price(Product p) {
  return switch (p) {
    Book(:final pages) when pages > 500 => 25,
    Book() => 15,
    DVD() => 20,
    Subscription(:final months) => months * 10,
  };
}

// and in a collection literal, a switch expression can transform
final labels = {
  for (final s in states) s.id: switch (s) {
        Loading() => 'loading',
        Ready() => 'ready',
        Error(:final message) => 'error: $message',
      },
};
// migrating an if-else chain, step by step

// BEFORE
String label(Shape s) {
  if (s is Circle) return 'circle';
  if (s is Square) return 'square';
  if (s is Rect) return 'rect';
  return 'unknown';
}

// AFTER: the same, and it cannot become wrong
String label2(Shape s) {
  return switch (s) {
    Circle() => 'circle',
    Square() => 'square',
    Rect() => 'rect',
  };
}

// and now the version that also uses the data, which is where the
// real reduction in code happens
String describe3(Shape s) {
  return switch (s) {
    Circle(:final radius) => 'a circle of radius $radius',
    Square(:final side) => 'a square of side $side',
    Rect(:final w, :final h) => 'a ${w}x$h rectangle',
  };
}

The switch expression, and the four things it removes

A switch expression is a switch with arms of the form pattern => value and no break, no case keyword, and no statement body. It must be exhaustive, its arms must all have the same type, and its result is a value. Those four constraints are what make it safe, and each one removes a mistake that the statement form permits.

ConstraintRemoves
Must be exhaustiveThe forgotten break, and the silent fall-through
Arms share a typeThe variable assigned in some branches only
Yields a valueThe uninitialised local, and the mutable accumulator
No case/breakThe nesting, and the accidental fall-through
// the statement form, and its three defects
String label(String status) {
  String result;                                  // uninitialised until assigned
  switch (status) {
    case 'draft':
      result = 'Draft';                           // ...and every case must
      break;                                      //    assign it, or the
    case 'published':                             //    compiler says "might
      result = 'Live';                            //    not be assigned"
      break;
    default:
      result = 'Unknown';
  }
  return result;
}
// ...four defects: a local that might not be assigned, four breaks that
// are optional by habit, fall-through if one is missed, and four
// statements where one expression belongs.

// the expression form: one expression, exhaustiveness checked, no breaks
String label2(String status) => switch (status) {
  'draft' => 'Draft',
  'published' => 'Live',
  _ => 'Unknown',
};
// ...and over a sealed type, even the wildcard is unnecessary:
String label3(Status s) => switch (s) {
  Status.draft => 'Draft',
  Status.published => 'Live',
  Status.archived => 'Archived',
};
// add a fourth Status and this STOPS COMPILING

// and it works anywhere an expression does
final descriptions = statuses.map((s) => switch (s) {
  Status.draft => 'a draft',
  Status.published => 'a live post',
  Status.archived => 'an archived post',
});

final httpCode = switch (method) {
  'GET' => 200,
  'POST' => 201,
  'PUT' => 200,
  'DELETE' => 204,
};

final total = items.fold(0, (sum, i) => sum + switch (i.kind) {
  Kind.book => 10,
  Kind.dvd => 15,
});

Every arm must have the same type, and that is a constraint with a purpose: it is what prevents a switch expression from being used to compute a value whose type is unclear, and it is why a common early draft fails to compile. The fix is not a cast — it is deciding what the result means. If the branches genuinely differ in type, the honest answer is a sealed Result as the expression's type, which says what happened rather than flattening it into Object.

// the arm-type constraint, and the two ways to satisfy it
// BAD: three different types
final x = switch (value) {
  int() => 1,
  String() => 'one',
  bool() => true,
};   // ERROR: the arms have types int, String and bool

// FIX 1: a sealed Result, which is the honest answer
sealed class Parsed<T> {}
final class Success<T> extends Parsed<T> { final T value; Success(this.value); }
final class Failure extends Parsed<Object?> { final String error; Failure(this.error); }

final Parsed<int> x2 = switch (raw) {
  '1' => Success(1),
  '2' => Success(2),
  final String s => Failure('not a number: $s'),
};
// ...the caller must handle both, and the failure carries its reason

// FIX 2: Object, when that is genuinely what you have
final Object x3 = switch (value) {
  int() => 1,
  String() => 'one',
  bool() => true,
};   // legal, and every caller must cast - which is worse than the Result

// FIX 3: widen explicitly, which is the version to reach for when the
// difference does not matter
final num x4 = switch (value) {
  int() => 1,
  double() => 2.5,
  _ => 0,
};
// ...a common supertype, stated once, and the compiler checks each arm

// the pattern that reads well: a sealed type whose branches differ
final render = switch (state) {
  Loading() => const Spinner(),
  Ready(:final data) => DataView(data),
  Error(:final message) => ErrorView(message),
};
// ...which is a switch EXPRESSION in a UI context, and it is the pattern
// that replaced most of the builder-and-null-check code in Flutter

Exhaustiveness has three sources in Dart, and they are worth distinguishing because only two of them are complete. A switch over a sealed type is checked. A switch over an enum is checked for a switch expression only, and a statement over an enum still needs a default — because an enum can gain a value and Dart does not treat it as sealed. A switch over anything else needs a wildcard, and the compiler will not prove it is complete. So "exhaustive" means one of three things depending on the subject, and knowing which is which prevents both an unnecessary wildcard and a false sense of safety.

// 1. sealed class - exhaustive with no wildcard, in BOTH forms
sealed class Shape {}
final class Circle extends Shape { … }
final class Square extends Shape { … }

double a1(Shape s) => switch (s) { Circle() => 1, Square() => 2 };  // OK
void a2(Shape s) { switch (s) { case Circle(): break; case Square(): break; } }  // OK

// 2. enum - exhaustive in an EXPRESSION, needs default in a STATEMENT
enum Colour { red, green, blue }

String b1(Colour c) => switch (c) {
  Colour.red => 'r', Colour.green => 'g', Colour.blue => 'b',
};   // OK - no default, and adding a 4th breaks it

String b2(Colour c) {
  switch (c) {
    case Colour.red: return 'r';
    case Colour.green: return 'g';
    // ...and now Colour.blue falls through to null
  }
  return '?';   // the statement form needs a default, and this is it
}

// 3. anything else - a wildcard, and no proof
String d(Object o) => switch (o) {
  int() => 'int',
  String() => 'string',
  _ => 'other',     // REQUIRED, and nothing proves it is the last case
};

// so the rule for a new type: if the set of cases is CLOSED, seal the class
// and get the proof; if it is OPEN, expect to add a case later and accept
// the wildcard - but put the wildcard LAST and give it a name

One behaviour to know before relying on a switch expression in a hot path is that an arm whose expression is a throw is not an expression, and is not allowed. That pushes failures into a separate case, and the alternative — returning a nullable or a Result — is a decision about whether the failure is part of the ordinary range of outcomes. It also means an arm cannot be a block of statements, so anything longer than one expression has to be extracted into a function, which is usually the better shape anyway.

// arms are expressions, so no blocks
final x = switch (v) {
  int() => { final s = v.toString(); return s.length; },   // ERROR
};

// the fix: extract
int lengthOf(Object v) {
  if (v is int) return v.toString().length;
  return 0;
}
final x2 = switch (v) { int() => lengthOf(v), _ => 0 };

// and `throw` is a statement, so it cannot be an arm either
final y = switch (v) {
  int() => 1,
  _ => throw ArgumentError('unexpected'),   // ERROR - not an expression
};

// ...so a fallible switch expression returns a Result
final Result<int> y2 = switch (v) {
  int() => Success(1),
  final String s => Failure('not a number: $s'),
  _ => Failure('unsupported type'),
};
// ...and the caller handles both, with no try/catch and no null check

// the arms must also agree on NULLABILITY
final List<int> z = switch (v) {
  null => [],
  final int i => [i],
  _ => [0, 0],
};   // all three arms are List<int> - legal

final w = switch (v) {
  null => null,
  final int i => i,
};   // ERROR - the arms are int? and int; the fix is a single `int?`

6.8 Records and patterns together

The combination that replaces most of the "wrapper class" code people write.

// a Result as a record, with a pattern match
typedef ParseResult = ({String? value, String? error});

ParseResult parse(String input) {
  if (input.isEmpty) return (value: null, error: 'empty');
  final n = int.tryParse(input);
  if (n == null) return (value: null, error: 'not a number: $input');
  return (value: input, error: null);
}

void use(String input) {
  final result = parse(input);

  // an object pattern destructures AND the guards make it exhaustive
  switch (result) {
    case (value: final v, error: null):
      print('ok: $v');
    case (value: null, error: final e):
      print('failed: $e');
    case (value: final v, error: final e):
      // both present: a bug, but the compiler makes you handle it
      print('impossible state: $v with $e');
  }
}

// the equivalent with a sealed class is longer, and this is the
// trade-off: a record is fine for a two-field result where neither
// field needs behaviour. Reach for a sealed class as soon as you
// need methods, or three or more fields, or a name in a signature.
// the record pattern that made async code much nicer
// (this is real code from a Flutter codebase)

// instead of:
Future<void> load() async {
  final data = await api.fetch();
  if (data.error != null) {
    setState(() => error = data.error);
    return;
  }
  setState(() => items = data.value);
}

// with records and a sealed class:
sealed class Loaded<T> {}
class Ok<T> extends Loaded<T> { final T value; Ok(this.value); }
class Err<T> extends Loaded<T> { final String message; Err(this.message); }

final loaded = await api.fetch();
setState(() {
  switch (loaded) {
    case Ok(:final value): items = value; error = null;
    case Err(:final message): error = message;
  }
});

// one place, exhaustive, and the compiler will not let a new error
// type slip through unnoticed

Records and patterns are syntactic, not semantic. A record has no name in a signature, so a reader has to look it up; a pattern match in a hot loop destructures into locals, which is usually free. Neither is a reason to avoid them. The genuine trade-off is documentation: if the type is part of a public API, name it.

Exercises 7

  1. Define a sealed hierarchy for a shape, a payment result and a network state, with exhaustive switches for each.
  2. Add a fourth variant to one hierarchy and confirm the compiler points at the switch that is now incomplete.
  3. Write a grade function as an if-else chain, then as a switch expression, and compare readability.
  4. Return a record from a function and use it in every destructuring form: positional, named, in a for loop, in a case.
  5. Build a ParseResult record and match all three states, including the impossible one.
  6. Find an if-else chain in a codebase and convert it to a switch expression. Note any that did not convert well, and understand why.
  7. Write a sealed generic Result<T, E> and use it to replace a nullable return in three functions.

Patterns with the rest of the language

Patterns are not a feature of switch. They appear in if, in while, in collection literals, in variable declarations, in for loops, in catch clauses, and in the right-hand side of an assignment — and the same pattern expression is valid in all of them. That uniformity is what makes destructuring a general technique rather than a switch feature.

PositionExampleRefutable
Switch casecase (a, b):Yes
Switch expression arm(a, b) => a + bYes
ifif (o case (int a, _))Yes
whilewhile (o case String s) { … }Yes
Destructuring declarationfinal (a, b) = pair;No
Destructuring assignment(a, b) = pair;No
List element[a, b] = pairNo
Map value{'k': (a, b)}No
Variable patterncase var (a, b)Yes
Rest element[first, ...tail]No
// if case - the filter-and-bind, and the alternative to a cast
void process(Object o) {
  if (o case (int a, int b) when a > b) {
    print('descending $a $b');
  } else if (o case (int a, int b)) {
    print('ascending $a $b');
  } else if (o case String s when s.isNotEmpty) {
    print('string of ${s.length}');
  } else {
    print('skip');
  }
}
// ...this is a chain of filters with no early return, no cast, and each
// binding is typed. It is the clearest form of a multi-way type dispatch.

// while case, for consuming a stream of mixed values
final queue = <Object>[1, 'two', (3, 4), 5.0];
while (queue case [final Object head, ...final rest]) {
  queue = rest;
  print(head);
}

// destructuring in a declaration, for a tuple
final (min, max) = computeRange(values);

// and an ASSIGNMENT, which is how you swap without a temporary
var a = 1, b = 2;
(a, b) = (b, a);
print('$a $b');          // 2 1

// collection literals: pattern-matching to CONSTRUCT
final [x, y] = point;                 // destructuring into a List
final {'x': px, 'y': py} = point;     // destructuring into a Map
final built = [x, y];                 // construction, not destructuring

// for loops
for (final (k, v) in entries) { … }
for (final [row, name, qty] in table) { … }

// and in a lambda, which is where it is most useful
rows.where((r) => r is Map).map((r) {
  final Map m = r;
  return m['id'] as int;
});
// ...which the record pattern makes safe:
rows.where((r) => r case {'id': final int _}).map((r) {
  final {'id': id} = r;
  return id;
});

Patterns compose with generics and with the type system in a way that changes what a function's signature must say. A function that takes Object and pattern-matches inside it is a function that can fail to produce a result, and the type system has no way to know that. A function that takes a sealed type and switches over it is total by construction, and that difference propagates: every caller of the sealed version is provably handled, while every caller of the Object version has a fallback that nothing verifies. The practical consequence is that the boundary of a sealed hierarchy is also the boundary of a proof, and extending it past that boundary loses the proof without gaining anything.

// a total function: the input says what is possible
sealed class Command {}
final class Load extends Command { final String path; Load(this.path); }
final class Save extends Command { final String path, body; Save(this.path, this.body); }
final class Quit extends Command {}

void execute(Command c) {
  switch (c) {
    case Load(:final path):
      print('loading $path');
    case Save(:final path, :final body):
      print('saving ${body.length} to $path');
    case Quit():
      exit(0);
  }
  // ...no default, no fallback, and adding a fourth Command BREAKS this -
  // which is exactly what a total function should do

// a partial function: the input says nothing
void execute2(Object c) {
  if (c is Load) { … }
  else if (c is Save) { … }
  else if (c is Quit) { exit(0); }
  // ...silently does nothing for anything else, and nothing says so
}

// so the design question for every dispatch: is the set of cases CLOSED?
// closed    -> a sealed type, a switch expression, a proof
// open      -> a type check, a fallback, and a documented default

// the case where it must be open, and how to make it safe anyway
void execute3(Object c) {
  switch (c) {
    case Load(:final path): print('loading $path');
    case Save(:final path, :final body): print('saving $body');
    case Quit(): exit(0);
    default:
      // ...and make the default LOUD rather than silent
      throw UnimplementedError('unknown command: $c');
  }
}

Records and patterns together give a way to express a tagged union with named accessors and no classes, and that is worth naming because it is the shape a great deal of application data actually has. A sealed class hierarchy plus object patterns gives it with a class per variant; a bare sealed interface plus a record field gives it with one type. The first is better when the variants need behaviour; the second is better when they are pure data and the whole point is to avoid writing a class per case.

// a tagged union with one class per variant: behaviour available
sealed class Shape {}
final class Circle extends Shape { final double r; Circle(this.r); double get area => 3.14 * r * r; }
final class Square extends Shape { final double s; Square(this.s); double get area => s * s; }
double total(List<Shape> shapes) => shapes.fold(0.0, (a, s) => a + s.area);
// ...each variant carries its own area, and the fold is one line

// a tagged union as a record: no classes at all
typedef Shape = ({double radius}) | ({double side}) | ({double width, double height});
// ^ union types over records - DART 3, and experimental

// the more common shape: a record with a tag field
typedef Event = ({String type, Object? payload});
final click = (type: 'click', payload: {'x': 1, 'y': 2});

String describe(Event e) => switch (e) {
  (type: 'click', payload: final Map p) => 'click at ${p['x']},${p['y']}',
  (type: 'key', payload: final String k) => 'key $k',
  (type: var t, payload: null) => '$t with no payload',
  (type: var t) => 'unhandled $t',
};
// ...one type, one field per concern, and the switch is exhaustive over
// the tag - and a Map would have needed `e['type'] as String` four times

// the tradeoff, plainly
// sealed classes: a class per variant, real methods, pattern-matched,
//              compiler-checked exhaustiveness
// records:      one type, no classes, `Object?` payloads so the fields
//              inside are NOT type-checked, exhaustiveness over the tag
//              only if the tag values are enumerated somewhere
// use records when the variants are pure data and short;
// use classes when there is behaviour, or when the field types matter

The final composition is the thing that makes pattern matching worth learning properly rather than as syntax: a pattern that combines a type test, a structural test, and a set of bindings in one expression, so that the code after it can be written as though every question has already been answered. The habit to build is to reach for if (x case …) instead of if (x is …) the moment the value has more than one field, and to use a switch expression instead of a chain of if assignments the moment there are three or more branches. Both are mechanical, both are checked at compile time, and both eliminate a class of run-time failure that is otherwise the most common one in code handling structured input.

7 · Errors, Exceptions and Assertions

7.1 The error hierarchy7.2 Throwing and catching7.3 finally, and the resource pattern7.4 Writing your own exceptions7.5 Errors in async code7.6 assert, and what it is for7.7 Error handling pitfalls7.8 Sealed results instead of exceptions

Dart's exceptions, the two kinds of error, and the discipline that keeps error handling from becoming noise.

7.1 The error hierarchy

Errors and exceptions are different types with different rules about who catches them.

Object
  +- Error                    - a programming bug. Do NOT catch.
  |    +- AssertionError      - an assert failed
  |    +- TypeError           - a wrong type at runtime
  |    |    +- CastError
  |    |    +- NullThrownError
  |    +- RangeError          - an index out of range
  |    |    +- IndexError
  |    |    +- RangeValueError
  |    +- ArgumentError       - a bad argument to a function
  |    |    +- RangeValueError
  |    +- StateError          - an operation invalid for the current state
  |    +- UnsupportedError    - an unimplemented or unsupported operation
  |    +- ConcurrentModificationError - mutating while iterating
  |    +- StackOverflowError
  |    +- OutOfMemoryError
  |    +- FormatException     - parsing
  |    +- FileSystemException
  |    +- SocketException
  |    +- HttpException
  |    +- TimeoutException
  |    +- NoSuchMethodError   - a missing method (rare, dynamic code)
  |    +- AssertionError (also on a failed assert)
  +- Exception                - an expected, recoverable condition. Catch it.
       +- FormatException
       +- ArgumentError
       +- StateError
       +- Exception             - the base you usually extend

// THE RULE:
//   Error    -> the program is wrong. Fix the code. Catching one
//               hides a bug.
//   Exception -> the environment is wrong (a file is missing, the
//               network is down, the user typed nonsense). Catch it
//               and handle it.
//   Note: many of the built-in types are BOTH, via
//   implements Exception, so the distinction is guidance, not a
//   compiler-enforced boundary.
// catching an Error is almost always wrong
try {
  final n = int.parse(input);
  print(n.toUpperCase());
} on TypeError catch (e) {
  // this has just hidden a compile-time error the analyser would
  // have caught, and made the code worse
}

try {
  list[100];
} on RangeError catch (e) {
  // same: the index was wrong, and now the bug is silent
}

// catching an Exception is often right
try {
  final config = await File('config.json').readAsString();
  final json = jsonDecode(config) as Map<String, dynamic>;
} on FileSystemException catch (e) {
  log('config unreadable: ${e.message}');
} on FormatException catch (e) {
  log('config is not valid JSON: ${e.message}');
  return Config.defaults();
}

Two roots, and the line between them

Dart has two root classes for anything that can be thrown: Error and Exception. Everything else extends one or the other, and the distinction is not arbitrary — it is a statement about whether the condition is a programming mistake or an expected operational condition. Nothing enforces the rule, but every catch site is easier to write once you know which one it is.

ClassMeansCatch it?
ErrorThe program is wrongNo — fix the code
ExceptionThe world is not what was expectedYes, where you can respond
TypeErrorA cast or access failedNo
RangeErrorAn index or value is out of rangeNo
ArgumentErrorA bad argumentSometimes — at a boundary
StateErrorAn operation invalid in this stateSometimes
UnsupportedErrorAn unimplemented operationNo
FormatExceptionParsing failedYes — it is expected
FileSystemExceptionFile or directory I/O failedYes
TimeoutExceptionAn operation exceeded its deadlineYes
OutOfMemoryErrorAllocation failedNo
StackOverflowErrorRecursion too deepNo

The convention that follows from this split is worth stating as a rule rather than a preference. An Exception is a thing your program is expected to handle, so it should be thrown deliberately, be part of your documented contract, and be caught somewhere that can do something useful. An Error is a bug, so it should be unhandled — caught at the top only to log and exit, so a programming mistake surfaces immediately in development rather than being papered over with a fallback. Code that catches Error locally is almost always hiding a defect, and code that throws Error for an ordinary condition is classifying it wrongly.

// the hierarchy, as it actually is
// Object
//  +- Error                     - a bug in the program
//  |    +- AssertionError
//  |    +- TypeError            - a failed cast or dynamic access
//  |    |    +- CastError
//  |    +- RangeError           - index out of bounds, or a bad value
//  |    |    +- IndexError
//  |    |    +- LengthError
//  |    +- StateError           - valid operation, wrong state
//  |    +- ArgumentError        - a bad argument
//  |    |    +- RangeError (via RangeValueError)
//  |    +- UnsupportedError
//  |    +- UnimplementedError
//  |    +- NoSuchMethodError
//  |    +- ConcurrentModificationError
//  |    +- OutOfMemoryError
//  |    +- StackOverflowError
//  +- Exception                 - an expected condition
//       +- FormatException
//       +- FileSystemException
//       +- HttpException (dart:io)
//       +- TimeoutException
//       +- SocketException
//       +- ProcessException
//       +- PlatformException   (flutter services)
//
// ...so `catch (e)` catches BOTH, and `on Error catch (e)` catches only
// bugs, and `on Exception catch (e)` only expected conditions.

// proving it, and using the type for something useful
try {
  json['count'] as int;
} on TypeError catch (e) {
  // a cast failed - so the shape is wrong, not the value
  throw FormatException('count is not an integer', json['count'].toString());
}

// `rethrow`, which preserves the original stack trace
try {
  process();
} on FormatException {
  rethrow;               // bare `rethrow` keeps the trace
} on Exception catch (e, st) {
  Error.throwWithStackTrace(FormatException('bad input'), st);
}

Two properties of the hierarchy are enforced rather than conventional. Error and Exception both extend Object, so anything can be thrown — throw 42; compiles and works, which is a real hazard and a reason to always declare a thrown type on a function that throws. And throw takes an instance, not a type: throw FormatException('...') constructs one and throws it, while throw FormatException — the class itself — throws a TypeError because a Type is not a valid thrown value in sound null safety.

WrittenWhat happens
throw FormatException('x')Correct — constructs and throws
throw FormatExceptionTypeError — you threw a class
throw ArgumentError.value(v, 'v')Correct — named factory, includes the value
throw 'string'Legal in legacy; discouraged — no type, no stack
throw e in a catchLegal — but loses the trace; use rethrow
Error.throwWithStackTrace(e, st)The correct way to rethrow with a new error

Choosing between ArgumentError, StateError and UnsupportedError is the decision that appears most often in well-written Dart, and the distinctions are sharp. ArgumentError says a value the caller supplied is wrong — so the call is wrong, and the message should name the parameter. StateError says the object's state makes this operation invalid — so the object is wrong, and the message should say what state was required. UnsupportedError says this operation does not exist here — so the object is of the wrong kind entirely, or the method is a deliberate stub. Three different subjects, three different fixes, and picking the wrong one sends a reader to the wrong file.

// ArgumentError - the CALL is wrong, and the message names the parameter
void setAge(int age) {
  if (age < 0 || age > 150) {
    throw ArgumentError.value(age, 'age', 'must be between 0 and 150');
  }
  _age = age;
}
// ArgumentError.value(value, name, message)   - the named factory to use
// ArgumentError.range(value, name, min, max)  - when there are bounds
// ArgumentError.notNull(name)                 - for a rejected null

// StateError - the OBJECT is in the wrong state, and the message says which
class Account {
  void withdraw(int amount) {
    if (_closed) {
      throw StateError('cannot withdraw from a closed account');
    }
    if (amount > _balance) {
      throw StateError('insufficient funds: $_balance available, $amount requested');
    }
    _balance -= amount;
  }
}

// UnsupportedError - the OPERATION does not exist for this object
class Csv {
  void save() {
    throw UnsupportedError('Csv is read-only; there is no save()');
  }
  void saveAs(String path) {
    throw UnimplementedError('saveAs() was never implemented for Csv');
  }
}
// ...UnsupportedError: this object type cannot do that at all.
//     UnimplementedError: somebody wrote a stub and left it.

// the four, with their subjects stated
// ArgumentError      -> the caller's value      -> fix the call
// StateError         -> the object's state      -> fix the sequence
// UnsupportedError   -> the object's kind       -> use a different type
// AssertionError     -> an internal invariant   -> fix the code

7.2 Throwing and catching

The five forms of catch clause, and how to choose.

// 1. a single type
try {
  risky();
} on FileSystemException catch (e) {
  print('file problem: ${e.message}');
}

// 2. a type, without the object
try {
  risky();
} on FileSystemException {
  print('a file problem, details not needed');
}

// 3. multiple types
try {
  risky();
} on FileSystemException catch (e) {
  print(e);
} on SocketException catch (e) {
  print(e);
}

// 4. a type with a STACK TRACE - always do this when rethrowing
//    or logging
try {
  risky();
} catch (e, stackTrace) {
  log('failed', error: e, stack: stackTrace);
  rethrow;          // rethrow preserves the original trace
}

// 5. catch everything - use sparingly
try {
  risky();
} catch (e) {
  print('something went wrong');
}

// 6. finally: always runs, even after a throw or a return
try {
  risky();
} finally {
  cleanup();          // even if risky() threw
}

// 7. a type parameter: catches only that type, rethrows others
Future<T> retry<T>(Future<T> Function() op, {int attempts = 3}) async {
  for (var i = 0; i < attempts; i++) {
    try {
      return await op();
    } on Exception {
      if (i == attempts - 1) rethrow;
      await Future.delayed(Duration(milliseconds: 100 * (i + 1)));
    }
  }
  throw StateError('unreachable');
}
// throw accepts any object, and a String is a bad idea
throw 'something failed';            // works, but terrible: no type
throw Exception('something failed'); // the type is useless
throw StateError('nothing loaded');  // descriptive: the state is wrong
throw ArgumentError.value(timeout, 'timeout', 'must be > 0');
throw FormatException('bad config', source, offset);   // with a location

// a helper for the common case
Never fail(String message, [Object? cause]) {
  throw StateError(message);
}

// and for a "cannot happen" that must be documented
Never unreachable(String what) {
  throw StateError('unreachable: $what');
}

// in a switch, an unreachable branch for the compiler
Never _unreachable() => throw StateError('unreachable');

The three forms of try, and what each is for

Dart has try/catch, try/finally, and try/catch/finally. The third is where the design decisions live, because finally runs on both paths and cannot change which path is taken — so anything in a finally that can itself throw will mask the original error, and anything in it that returns will silently discard the result.

// 1. bare try - legal, and does nothing except change scoping
// there is no reason to write it

// 2. try/catch, catching everything
try {
  risky();
} catch (e) {
  print('something failed: $e');
}
// ...catches Errors AND Exceptions, because `catch (e)` is Object

// 3. try/catch, typed - the form to write
try {
  risky();
} on FormatException catch (e, st) {
  print('bad format: ${e.message}');
  log(st);
} on FileSystemException catch (e) {
  print('io error on ${e.path}: ${e.osError?.message}');
} on Exception catch (e) {
  print('other: $e');
}
// ...typed clauses are tried IN ORDER, so put the specific ones first and
// the general ones last. An `on Exception` after three specifics catches
// only what they did not.

// 4. try/finally, no catch - for cleanup alone
var handle = open();
try {
  use(handle);
} finally {
  handle.close();      // runs on success AND on any throw
}

// 5. try/catch/finally - catch, then clean up
File? f;
try {
  f = File(path).openSync();
  process(f);
} on FileSystemException catch (e) {
  log(e);
} finally {
  f?.closeSync();      // the ?. is needed because f may be null if open threw
}

// the form to prefer when the resource is the whole problem
try {
  final content = File(path).readAsStringSync();
  parse(content);
} on FileSystemException {
  rethrow;             // not our problem - let the caller handle it
} on FormatException catch (e) {
  throw ConfigError('config at $path is invalid: ${e.message}');
}

Three properties of catch are worth being precise about. A catch clause that does not rethrow swallows the error, so the program continues in a state it was never designed to be in — which is the single most common source of "it failed but nothing happened" bugs. A catch clause is not entered for a type it does not name and the error is not rethrown automatically; it propagates to the enclosing handler. And the st variable in catch (e, st) is the stack trace at the point of the throw, which is not the same as the trace at the catch site — the difference is the frame or two the error travelled, and dropping it is why rethrown errors often point at the wrong file.

// swallowing, and why it is the default failure
try {
  save();
} catch (e) {
  log(e);              // logged, and the caller never learns
}
// save() returned as if it worked

// rethrowing with the trace preserved
try {
  save();
} catch (e, st) {
  log(e);
  rethrow;             // the BARE keyword - preserves e and st exactly
}
// ...`throw e;` instead would set a new trace point at the catch, so the
// reported location moves - which is how a stack trace ends up blaming the
// code that reported the problem

// converting, with the trace preserved
try {
  parse(raw);
} on FormatException catch (e, st) {
  Error.throwWithStackTrace(
    ConfigException('invalid config', cause: e),
    st,                  // ...the ORIGINAL trace, so the origin survives
  );
}

// the pattern with a cause chain
class ConfigException implements Exception {
  final String message;
  final Object? cause;
  const ConfigException(this.message, {this.cause});

  @override
  String toString() => 'ConfigException: $message${cause == null ? '' : ' (caused by $cause)'}';
}

// and the pattern that is almost always wrong
try {
  doEverything();
} catch (e) {
  // ...no rethrow, no return, no rethrow - and yet the function returns
  // normally, so every caller believes everything succeeded
}

The on clause and the catch parameter are independent, which is a source of confusion. on X alone names a type and gives you no variable; catch (e) alone names nothing and catches everything; on X catch (e) names both and the variable has the narrowed type; and catch (e, st) without on catches everything with a variable of static type Object. That last form means e has no useful members, so it must be cast or string-interpolated — which is why naming the type is nearly always better.

WrittenCatchese has type
on Foo { }Foo only—
catch (e) { }EverythingObject
on Foo catch (e) { }Foo onlyFoo
on Foo catch (e, st) { }Foo only, with traceFoo
catch (e, st) { }Everything, with traceObject
// the four forms, and the difference in `e`

try { a(); } on StateError { print('bad state'); }
// ...no variable - so you can only rethrow, or log the type

try { a(); } catch (e) { print('$e'); }
// ...e is Object, so `$e` calls Object.toString

try { a(); } on StateError catch (e) {
  print(e.message);     // e is StateError - e.message is checked
}
try { a(); } on StateError catch (e, st) {
  print('${e.message} at $st');   // and the trace
}

// using `on` alone, to handle a type without needing its data
try {
  await stream.listen(onError: (e, st) { … }).cancel();
} on ArgumentError {
  throw ArgumentError('bad subscription');    // re-raise a NEW one, no need
}                                            // to read the old one

// ...and the general principle: name the type so the variable is useful.
// `catch (e)` without `on` is the form to avoid, because it forces either
// a cast inside the block or string interpolation and nothing else.

// the exhaustive version, which is where the type names earn their keep
Future<void> fetch(String url) async {
  try {
    final res = await http.get(Uri.parse(url));
    if (res.statusCode != 200) {
      throw HttpException('${res.statusCode}', uri: Uri.parse(url));
    }
  } on SocketException catch (e, st) {
    throw NetworkUnavailable(e.osError?.message ?? 'socket', st);
  } on TimeoutException catch (e) {
    throw NetworkUnavailable('timeout after ${e.duration}');
  } on FormatException catch (e) {
    throw ConfigException('bad url: $url', cause: e);
  }
  // anything else propagates unchanged - which is correct, because it is
  // not this function's business
}

7.3 finally, and the resource pattern

Cleanup that runs whatever happens, and the several cases where a finally is still not enough.

// the basic pattern
File? file;
try {
  file = await File(path).open();
  await file.writeAsString(contents);
} on FileSystemException catch (e) {
  log(e.message);
} finally {
  await file?.close();     // runs on success, on throw, and on return
}

// better: a helper that makes the cleanup impossible to forget
Future<R> withFile<R>(
  String path,
  Future<R> Function(File file) body,
) async {
  final file = await File(path).open();
  try {
    return await body(file);
  } finally {
    await file.close();
  }
}

await withFile('log.txt', (file) async {
  await file.writeAsString('hello');
  return 42;
});

// the same idea for a lock, a transaction, a subscription, a timer
Future<T> withLock<T>(Lock lock, Future<T> Function() body) async {
  await lock.acquire();
  try {
    return await body();
  } finally {
    lock.release();
  }
}

Future<void> withSubscription(
  StreamSubscription sub,
  Future<void> Function() body,
) async {
  try {
    await body();
  } finally {
    await sub.cancel();
  }
}
// A finally BLOCK that can be bypassed: a return inside try
int getValue() {
  try {
    return compute();       // this FINALLY still runs. fine.
  } finally {
    log('done');
  }
}

// but a break or continue out of a loop skips it in some cases:
// in Dart, finally runs for break and continue too, but NOT for
// a process exit or a fatal error

// the real trap: an await inside finally after an error
try {
  await risky();
} finally {
  await cleanup();   // if risky() threw AND cleanup() also throws,
                     // the cleanup error replaces the original one
}

// the fix: never let cleanup throw
Future<void> safeCleanup() async {
  try {
    await cleanup();
  } catch (e, s) {
    log('cleanup failed', error: e, stack: s);   // swallow it
  }
}

A finally that throws discards the exception you were already handling. In practice, wrap the cleanup in its own try/catch that logs and swallows. This is the single most common subtle bug in resource management code, and it only shows up on the error path - which is exactly when you are already busy.

What finally guarantees, and the two ways to defeat it

A finally block runs when the try body exits, however it exits: normally, by a return, by a break or continue out of a loop, or by an exception. That is a stronger guarantee than most languages offer and it makes it the right place for resource release. The cost is that it is not an error handler — it cannot see the error, and it runs in addition to whatever catch clause matched, not instead of it.

// finally runs on every path, including return and break
void f(bool early) {
  try {
    acquire();
    if (early) return 'done';
    work();
    return 'complete';
  } finally {
    release();          // runs after EACH of those three returns
  }
}

// ...and it runs BEFORE the pending return value is delivered, so a
// mutation here is visible to the caller
class Cache {
  final Map<String, int> _m = {};
  int? get(String k, {int Function()? compute}) {
    _m[k] = 0;                     // a sentinel: "being computed"
    try {
      return _m[k];
    } finally {
      // ...cleanup runs, then the return value is delivered
    }
  }
}

// ordering, which is worth being able to state
void order() {
  try {
    print('body');
  } finally {
    print('finally');
  }
  print('after');
}
// body -> finally -> after

// with a catch, the catch runs BEFORE the finally
void order2() {
  try {
    throw Exception('x');
  } on Exception {
    print('catch');          // 1st
  } finally {
    print('finally');        // 2nd
  }
}

// and if the finally itself throws, the pending error is REPLACED
void order3() {
  try {
    throw StateError('the real problem');
  } finally {
    throw StateError('a different problem');
  }
}
// ...the caller sees 'a different problem', and 'the real problem' is lost
// entirely. This is the first way to defeat finally.

The two ways to defeat finally are worth memorising because both produce a symptom that looks like a leak in unrelated code. The first is a throw inside it, which discards the pending exception or return value — the code above shows it losing the original error, and it loses a return the same way. The second is System.exit or a process crash, which skips every finally in the process — so cleanup that matters has to be registered somewhere that the runtime itself will run, such as a ProcessSignal handler or an explicit flush before exit.

// defeat 1: a throw in finally, discarding a RETURN
int? result;
try {
  result = 42;
  return result;             // ...the pending value is 42
} finally {
  throw StateError('cleanup failed');
}
// the caller never receives 42 - and if this is a `return` from a setter
// or a state transition, the state has changed and the return did not happen

// the fix: catch inside the finally
int? result;
try {
  return 42;
} finally {
  try {
    cleanup();
  } catch (e, st) {
    log('cleanup failed', e, st);   // ...logged, and the 42 still returns
  }
}
// ...which is the correct shape for ANY cleanup that can itself fail

// defeat 2: the process exits, and no finally runs
void shutdown() {
  try {
    persist();
  } finally {
    cleanup();
  }
  exit(0);                  // fine - the finally already ran
}

void shutdownBad() {
  registerHandler(() {
    try {
      flush();
    } finally {
      cleanup();
    }
    exit(0);                // fine
  });
  // ...but a CRASH, a SIGKILL, or a Dart VM abort skips everything, so
  // anything that must survive has to be flushed eagerly rather than on exit

// and the async version, which has its own trap
Future<void> asyncFinally() async {
  final conn = await connect();
  try {
    await work();
  } finally {
    await conn.close();     // AWAIT is required - a bare call is not waited on
  }
}
// ...`finally` in an async function still allows `await`, which is one of
// its real advantages over a synchronous language's equivalent

// the common mistake: forgetting the await
} finally {
  conn.close();             // fires and forgets - the function returns
}                           // before the close completes

The best practical use of finally is to avoid it where a more specific construct exists. A Future's catchError runs a callback on failure without needing a try; a Stream's cancel is awaited rather than wrapped; a with-style scope manager in package:async handles acquisition and release as a pair; and Dart's cascade and pattern matching already removed much of the code that used to need a temporary variable and a finally. Where none of those fit, finally is the correct tool — but it is for releasing something you acquired, not for logic.

// without finally: acquire in one place, release in another
final conn = await connect();
await run(conn);
await conn.close();
// ...and every path between the two must release, which is a burden on
// every future edit. A `throw` in `run` leaks the connection.

// with finally: acquisition and release are adjacent
final conn = await connect();
try {
  await run(conn);
} finally {
  await conn.close();       // correct on every path, including the throw
}

// the package:async scope manager, which is this as a reusable object
import 'package:async/async.dart';

Future<T> withLock<T>(Lock lock, Future<T> Function() body) async {
  await lock.acquire();
  try {
    return await body();
  } finally {
    lock.release();         // the manager owns the pairing
  }
}

// a reusable Resource class, which is the general shape
class Resource implements AsyncCallback {
  final void Function() _close;
  bool _closed = false;
  Resource(this._close);

  @override
  Future<void> call() async => _close();
  @override
  String toString() => 'Resource(closed: $_closed)';
}

final code = await using((_) async { return compute(); });
// ...AsyncCallback makes the class work with `await using` (Dart 3.7), which
// guarantees release on BOTH paths and forbids forgetting it

// and the rule: `finally` is for symmetric acquisition. If the release is
// not the inverse of the acquisition, it belongs in a different construct.

7.4 Writing your own exceptions

The hierarchy, the fields worth carrying, and the message convention.

// a base for your domain
abstract class AppException implements Exception {
  final String message;
  final Object? cause;
  final StackTrace? stackTrace;

  AppException(this.message, {this.cause, this.stackTrace});

  @override
  String toString() => '$runtimeType: $message';
}

// specific ones
class NetworkException extends AppException {
  final int? statusCode;
  NetworkException(super.message, {this.statusCode, super.cause, super.stackTrace});
}

class ValidationException extends AppException {
  final Map<String, String> fieldErrors;
  ValidationException(super.message, this.fieldErrors) : super(cause: null, stackTrace: null);
}

class NotFoundException extends AppException {
  final String resource;
  NotFoundException(this.resource) : super('$resource not found');
}

class CacheException extends AppException {
  CacheException(String key, Object? cause)
      : super('cache miss for $key', cause: cause);
}

// a hierarchy, so a caller can catch broadly or precisely
sealed class AppException implements Exception { ... }
// or a normal abstract base if you want third parties to extend it
// using them
Future<User> loadUser(String id) async {
  try {
    final res = await _http.get(Uri.parse('/users/$id'));
    if (res.statusCode == 404) {
      throw NotFoundException('user $id');
    }
    if (res.statusCode != 200) {
      throw NetworkException('unexpected status', statusCode: res.statusCode);
    }
    return User.fromJson(jsonDecode(res.body) as Map<String, dynamic>);
  } on SocketException catch (e) {
    throw NetworkException('no connection', cause: e, stackTrace: s);
  }
}

// catching, precisely
try {
  final user = await loadUser('123');
  show(user);
} on NotFoundException catch (e) {
  showEmptyState();
} on NetworkException catch (e) when (e.statusCode == 503) {
  showTemporaryError();               // a retryable condition
} on NetworkException {
  showOfflineError();
} on AppException catch (e, s) {
  log(e.message, stack: s);
  showGenericError();
}

// and NOT catching Error
// on Error { rethrow; }   <- never do this; it is a no-op with a cost

Writing an exception class that a caller can act on

A custom exception should carry the data a caller needs in order to respond, and should carry nothing else. The test is whether a catch site can do something different for this exception than for a generic one — if it cannot, the class is a label with a constructor and has not earned its existence. In practice that means typed fields, a message, and a cause chain, and it means deciding deliberately whether the type extends Exception or Error.

// the minimum that is worth having
class ApiException implements Exception {
  final int statusCode;
  final String endpoint;
  final String message;
  final Object? cause;

  const ApiException(
    this.statusCode,
    this.endpoint, {
    this.message = '',
    this.cause,
  });

  @override
  String toString() =>
      'ApiException($statusCode from $endpoint): ${message.isEmpty ? cause : message}';
}

// ...implements Exception rather than extends it, because Exception has
// no members to inherit and `implements` states "quacks like an exception"

// the version that carries data a caller can use
sealed class DomainException implements Exception {
  final String message;
  final Object? cause;
  const DomainException(this.message, {this.cause});
}

// a sealed hierarchy of domain errors - and now they can be matched
final class NotFound extends DomainException {
  final String id;
  const NotFound(this.id, {super.cause})
      : super('no entity with id $id');
}
final class Unauthorized extends DomainException {
  final String? principal;
  const Unauthorized([this.principal, Object? cause])
      : super('not authorized', cause: cause);
}
final class Conflict extends DomainException {
  final String field;
  const Conflict(this.field, Object? reason)
      : super('conflict on $field: $reason');
}

// and a caller that can handle each DIFFERENTLY - which is the test
Future<void> update(User u) async {
  try {
    await repo.save(u);
  } on NotFound catch (e) {
    await repo.insert(u.copyWith(id: e.id));
  } on Unauthorized catch (e) {
    await promptLogin(principal: e.principal);
  } on Conflict catch (e) {
    showFieldError(e.field, e.message);
  }
}
// ...every catch does something specific. If two of them did the same,
// they would be one clause.

A well-designed exception carries the data that identifies the failure, not the data needed to fix it — and the distinction shows up in whether the exception knows how to recover. NotFound carrying the id is right, because the caller needs to know which entity was missing. NotFound carrying a retry() method is wrong, because recovery is a decision the caller makes with information the exception does not have. The exception is a description of what went wrong; the recovery is the caller's policy.

CarriesRightBecause
The identifier involvedYesThe caller needs it to act
A machine-readable codeYesCallers branch on it, not on the message
HTTP status, domain codeYesThe translation is the caller's
The underlying causeYesPreserves the diagnostic chain
A human messageYesLogs and UI
A retry methodNoRecovery is the caller's decision
A reconnection strategyNoSame
A callback to run on failureNoControl flow in a value
// the good shape: description, not policy
class RateLimited implements Exception {
  final int retryAfterSeconds;
  final String resource;
  const RateLimited(this.resource, this.retryAfterSeconds);
  @override
  String toString() => 'RateLimited($resource, retry in ${retryAfterSeconds}s)';
}

// the caller decides what to do about it
Future<Response> withBackoff(Future<Response> Function() f) async {
  var attempt = 0;
  while (true) {
    try {
      return await f();
    } on RateLimited catch (e) {
      if (++attempt >= 5) rethrow;
      await Future.delayed(Duration(seconds: e.retryAfterSeconds));
      // ...the POLICY - 5 attempts, exponential, give up - is here, not in
      // the exception, because it is this caller's business
    }
  }
}

// the BAD shape, which puts policy in the value
class RateLimitedBad implements Exception {
  final int retryAfterSeconds;
  void Function()? onRetry;         // a callback - control flow in a value
  int maxAttempts = 3;              // mutable state on an exception
  RateLimitedBad(this.retryAfterSeconds);
}
// ...now the exception is stateful, un-comparable, and its behaviour depends
// on who caught it and what they set. Two callers cannot differ.

// and the version that is almost as bad: the exception decides by itself
class RateLimitedWorse {
  Future<T> retry<T>(Future<T> Function() f) async { … }  // policy
  // ...`retry` is not an exception method, it is a helper function. Put it
  // beside the exception, not inside it.

Adding a code field is the thing that makes an exception branchable by data rather than by type. Matching on types requires a class per case and does not extend to a variable set of conditions; matching on a code requires one class and a switch. For an error set that is genuinely open — provider-specific failures, storage backends, third-party responses — a code is the only workable shape, and it is the same decision as using a Map rather than a sealed hierarchy.

// the code-based exception, for an OPEN error set
class StorageException implements Exception {
  final String code;              // 'quota', 'corrupt', 'unavailable', ...
  final String detail;
  const StorageException(this.code, this.detail);
  @override
  String toString() => 'StorageException($code): $detail';
}

Future<void> write(String key, String value) async {
  try {
    await box.put(key, value);
  } on StorageException catch (e) {
    switch (e.code) {
      case 'quota':
        await evictOldest();
        await write(key, value);          // retry, once
      case 'corrupt':
        await rebuildIndex();
      case 'unavailable':
        queueLocally(key, value);
      default:
        rethrow;                          // an unknown code is NOT swallowed
    }
  }
}
// ...so the caller branches on DATA, and an unrecognised code propagates -
// which is the property that makes an open set safe to extend

// the machine-readable form, which is the same idea made explicit
enum StorageCode { quota, corrupt, unavailable, unknown }

class StorageError implements Exception {
  final StorageCode code;
  final String detail;
  const StorageError(this.code, this.detail);
}
// ...and now the compiler knows the set is closed, and `switch (e.code)`
// with no default is exhaustive

// and the boundary translation, which is where domain errors come from
Future<void> load(String path) async {
  try {
    await rawRead(path);
  } on StorageException catch (e, st) {
    throw AppException(
      switch (e.code) {
        StorageCode.quota => AppError.diskFull,
        StorageCode.corrupt => AppError.dataCorrupt,
        _ => AppError.unknown,
      },
      detail: '${path}: ${e.detail}',
      cause: e,
      stackTrace: st,
    );
  }
}

Two details about custom exceptions are easy to get wrong and hard to debug. First, toString is what appears in logs and in an unhandled-error report, so it should carry the identity of the failure without a stack trace attached — the runtime adds that separately. Second, a class with mutable fields means two instances that "represent the same failure" are unequal, which breaks deduplication, comparison in tests, and any use as a map key. An exception value should be immutable, because it is a description of a past event rather than a live object.

// the mutable exception, and where it hurts
class Bad1 implements Exception {
  String message = '';
  int attempts = 0;
}
// ...these are two different objects, so a test asserting
// `expect(caught, Bad1()..message = 'x')` fails, a Set holds both, and
// `== ` is identity so nothing deduplicates

// the immutable version
class Bad2 implements Exception {
  final String message;
  final int attempts;
  const Bad2(this.message, {this.attempts = 0});

  @override
  bool operator ==(Object o) =>
      identical(this, o) || (o is Bad2 && o.message == message && o.attempts == attempts);
  @override
  int get hashCode => Object.hash(message, attempts);
}
// ...so a test can construct the expected value and compare

// toString: what it should and should not include
@override
String toString() => 'Bad2("$message", attempts: $attempts)';
// ...no stack trace, no cause chain unrolled, no newlines - because the
// runtime prints the trace itself, and a toString that includes one
// produces a doubled and unreadable report

// and the cause, done properly
class AppException implements Exception {
  final String message;
  final Object cause;
  final StackTrace stackTrace;
  final int errorCode;

  const AppException(this.message, {
    required this.cause,
    required this.stackTrace,
    this.errorCode = 0,
  });

  @override
  String toString() => 'AppException($errorCode): $message [caused by $cause]';
}
// ...which is what Error.throwWithStackTrace needs in order to preserve
// the original location while changing the type

7.5 Errors in async code

Where an exception in a Future goes, and the two that catch nothing.

// an uncaught error in a Future
Future<void> fetchData() async {
  throw Exception('boom');
}

void main() {
  fetchData();      // the exception is NOT thrown here
  print('continues');   // this runs
  // later, the error surfaces as an unhandled async error, and in
  // Flutter it hits FlutterError.onError
}

// so: always await, or attach a catchError
void main() async {
  try {
    await fetchData();
  } catch (e) {
    print('caught: $e');
  }
}

// a Future that is never awaited loses its error entirely
Future<void> fireAndForget() {
  unawaited(fetchData().catchError((e) => log('$e')));
}

// THE TWO THAT CATCH NOTHING
// 1. a callback-based API that throws synchronously
Timer.run(() {
  throw Exception('in a callback');   // goes to the zone, not to a catch
});

// 2. a Stream error, if you are not listening
final controller = StreamController<int>();
controller.addError(Exception('stream error'));
// if nobody listens, it is an unhandled error

// zone: the Dart 1 error-handling mechanism, still used for this
runZonedGuarded(() {
  Timer.run(() => throw Exception('caught by the zone'));
}, (error, stack) {
  print('zone caught: $error');
});

// modern Dart prefers Future.catchError and explicit try/catch;
// zones are for app-wide error reporting
// Stream error handling, which differs from Future
final stream = Stream<int>.multi((controller) {
  controller.add(1);
  controller.addError(Exception('bad value'));
  controller.add(2);
});

await for (final value in stream) {
  print(value);        // 1, then 2 - the error does NOT stop it
  // an error event is not a thrown exception
}

// to STOP on an error, listen for it
stream.listen(
  (value) => print(value),
  onError: (e) => print('error: $e'),
  onDone: () => print('done'),
  cancelOnError: true,      // stop after the first error
);

// and a stream's error is delivered to EVERY listener, not consumed

Errors crossing an async boundary

An error thrown inside an async function's body does not propagate synchronously — it completes the returned Future with an error. The consequence is that a try/catch around the call does not catch it unless the call is awaited, and an unawaited future's error becomes an unhandled asynchronous error that crashes the isolate at a later point than the code that caused it.

// the rule: await to catch
Future<void> f() async {
  try {
    await risky();          // ...the await is what makes it catchable
  } on StateError catch (e) {
    print('caught: $e');
  }
}

// WITHOUT await, the catch does not run
Future<void> g() async {
  try {
    risky();                // returns a Future; the error is in it
  } catch (e) {
    print('never printed');
  }
}
// ...`g()` completes normally, and the error surfaces later as an
// unhandled asynchronous error - which by default crashes the isolate.

// and `await` in a non-async function is not possible, so the alternative
Future<void> h() async {
  await risky().catchError((e, st) {
    Error.throwWithStackTrace(AppException('failed', cause: e, stackTrace: st), st);
  });
}

// Future.wait, where the errors aggregate differently
final results = await Future.wait([
  a(),       // throws
  b(),       // throws
  c(),       // succeeds
]);
// ...the FIRST error wins and the others become unhandled - so if all of
// them matter, wait for them individually:
final settled = await Future.wait([a(), b(), c()], eagerError: false);
// ...still throws on the first, but does not leave the others unhandled

// and the pattern that never leaks: await everything
final results2 = await Future.wait<Object>([
  a().then<Object>((v) => v).catchError((Object e) => e),
  b().then<Object>((v) => v).catchError((Object e) => e),
]);
// ...each future resolves to a value OR an error object, and the caller
// inspects - which is a Result type written with futures

The unhandled-error mechanism has one behaviour worth knowing precisely, because it surprises people in both directions. An error in a future with no listener is not swallowed — it is reported to the current zone, which rethrows it asynchronously and, if nothing handles it there, kills the isolate. That is a deliberate design: a fire-and-forget failure should be loud. The consequence is that every genuinely fire-and-forget operation needs an explicit catchError or a unawaited() wrapper, and the wrapper is what tells a reader the failure is handled elsewhere.

// unawaited, which makes the intent explicit
import 'dart:async';

void fireAndForget() {
  unawaited(sendAnalytics());      // the failure is logged, not fatal
}

// ...and with an explicit handler where it matters
unawaited(sendAnalytics().catchError((e, st) {
  log('analytics failed', e, st);
}));

// the older idiom, and why `unawaited` is better
void older() {
  sendAnalytics().then((_) {}, onError: (Object e, StackTrace st) {
    log('analytics failed', e, st);
  });
}

// Stream errors are separate from stream values
final stream = Stream.fromIterable([1, 2, 3])
    .map((x) {
      if (x == 2) throw StateError('bad $x');
      return x;
    });
await for (final v in stream) { print(v); }   // prints 1, then throws

// to handle an error mid-stream without ending it, use handleError or
// transform with a Result
final safe = Stream.fromIterable([1, 2, 3]).transform(
  StreamTransformer<int, Object>.fromHandlers(
    handleError: (e, st, sink) => sink.add(e),
  ),
);

// and `await for` in a try/catch DOES catch the stream's errors
try {
  await for (final v in stream) { … }
} on StateError catch (e, st) {
  print('stream failed at: $e');
}

Future.wait with eagerError: true is the default and it means "fail as soon as any fails" — which leaves the other futures running and their errors unhandled. Setting it to false waits for all of them and then throws the first error, which avoids the unhandled-error report at the cost of waiting for work whose result is being discarded. The choice is about whether the side effects of the other futures matter; if they do, false is the correct setting and the errors should be handled individually.

// eagerError: true - the default - and the leak it causes
Future<void> a() async { await sleep(1s); throw StateError('a'); }
Future<void> b() async { await sleep(2s); throw StateError('b'); }

await Future.wait([a(), b()]);
// throws StateError('a') after 1s
// ...then b() completes with an error at 2s, with no listener, and THAT
// is reported as an unhandled asynchronous error - a second crash, from
// code that appears unrelated

// eagerError: false - wait for all, throw the first
await Future.wait([a(), b()], eagerError: false);
// throws at 2s with StateError('a'), and b()'s error is... also unhandled,
// because only the first is reported

// the version that handles every one
final results = await Future.wait([
  a().then<Object>((v) => v).catchError((Object e, StackTrace s) {
    log('a failed', e, s);
    return e;
  }),
  b().then<Object>((v) => v).catchError((Object e, StackTrace s) {
    log('b failed', e, s);
    return e;
  }),
]);
// ...nothing is unhandled, and the caller inspects `results`

// or, if all-or-nothing is right, sequential - which is slower but makes
// the semantics obvious
final r1 = await a();
final r2 = await b();

Zones are the mechanism underneath all of this, and knowing one thing about them is enough for ordinary use: a zone captures the error handler that was registered when it was created, and any asynchronous work started inside it reports its errors there. That is how runZonedGuarded can catch an error thrown by code it did not call directly, and it is why an error's stack trace sometimes points at a Future rather than at the function that threw.

// a zone that catches everything started inside it
runZonedGuarded(() {
  unawaited(somethingThatMayFail());
  Timer.run(() => throw StateError('from a timer'));
}, (error, stack) {
  report(error, stack);       // ...one place, for all of it
});

// ...which is how a framework can install a global reporter without every
// call site adding a catchError

// what a zone does NOT do
runZonedGuarded(() {
  throw StateError('sync');     // the synchronous throw propagates OUT of
}, (e, st) { report(e, st); }); // the zone body normally - it is not caught
// ...the handler is for ASYNCHRONOUS errors. A synchronous throw inside the
// body has to be caught by a try/catch in the body.

// the modern replacement, which is usually what you want
await runZonedGuarded(() async {
  await work();
}, (e, st) => report(e, st));

// and the other thing a zone does: carry values
runZoned(() {
  Zone.current.fork(zoneValues: {#requestId: id}).run(() async {
    await work();
    final rid = Zone.current[#requestId];
  });
}, zoneSpecification: ZoneSpecification(
  print: (self, parent, zone, line) => log('$line [${zone[#requestId]}]'),
));
// ...which is request-scoped logging without threading a logger parameter
// through every function - the one thing zones are genuinely good for

7.6 assert, and what it is for

Debug-only checks, and the rule for what may go inside one.

// assert runs in DEBUG (JIT) and is REMOVED in release (AOT)
void check(int value) {
  assert(value >= 0, 'value must be non-negative');
  // this line does nothing in a release build
}

// what belongs in an assert:
//   1. internal invariants - "this should never be false"
//   2. arguments to a private function
//   3. conditions a caller was already told about in the docs
//
// what does NOT:
//   1. user input validation - it is stripped in release
//   2. anything with a side effect
//   3. anything the program depends on

// the correct pattern for user input
void setAge(int age) {
  if (age < 0 || age > 150) {
    throw ArgumentError.value(age, 'age', 'must be 0..150');
  }
  _age = age;
}

// the correct pattern for an invariant
class Stack {
  final List<int> _items = [];
  int get top {
    assert(_items.isNotEmpty, 'top of an empty stack');
    return _items.last;         // throws RangeError in release: still safe
  }
}

// an assert with a SIDE EFFECT is a real bug
