// assert(list.add(x), 'should always succeed');   // in release, x is LOST
// enabling asserts in a release build, when you need them
// dart compile exe main.dart -o app --enable-asserts
// dart run --enable-asserts

// the assert message can be expensive: it is not evaluated at all
// when the assertion holds... but in the general case, keep it cheap
assert(list.isNotEmpty, 'list must not be empty: $items');   // fine for a debug build

// enable the analyser lints that catch assert misuse
// analysis_options.yaml
linter:
  rules:
    - avoid_asserts_in_production: false
    - invariant_booleans
    - prefer_asserts_with_message
    - unnecessary_constructor_name

Assertions, and why they are not validation

An assert checks a condition that the programmer believes is always true, and it is stripped from a release build entirely. That is the whole semantics: an assertion documents an invariant and produces a clear failure during development, and it disappears in production because the condition, being an invariant, cannot be false there.

// assert, in its three places
void f(int x) {
  assert(x > 0);                        // a statement
  assert(x > 0, 'x must be positive');  // with a message
}

class A {
  int n;
  A(this.n) : assert(n > 0);            // in an initialiser list
}

final b = <String, int>{};              // a collection literal
final c = <String, int>{'a': 1};        // ...also accepts assertions

// assertions are stripped in release
// build with: dart compile exe --no-enable-asserts main.dart
// so `assert(false)` in release does nothing at all

// the four legitimate uses
// 1. a public API precondition, as documentation
int factorial(int n) {
  assert(n >= 0, 'factorial is undefined for negatives');
  if (n < 0) throw RangeError.range(n, 0, null, 'n');
  …
}
// ...the assert documents, the throw enforces. Both, not either.

// 2. a postcondition, checked at the exit point
int gcd(int a, int b) {
  var x = a, y = b;
  while (y != 0) { final t = y; y = x % y; x = t; }
  assert(x > 0 || (a == 0 && b == 0));
  return x;
}

// 3. an unreachable-code marker, which the analyzer also reports
void f2(int x) {
  if (x < 0) {
    assert(false, 'x was already checked');
    throw StateError('unreachable');
  }
}

// 4. a mode check - only enabled when assertions are on
const bool debugMode = bool.fromEnvironment('dart.vm.product') == false;
void trace(String msg) {
  if (debugMode) print('[trace] $msg');
}

The rule that follows is that an assertion is for a condition the program guarantees and a throw is for a condition an input might violate. That distinction is not stylistic: it determines whether the check survives into production. A user cannot supply a value that makes x > 0 false inside a function that validated it, so the assertion is free; a user absolutely can supply a negative number to a function that did not validate it, so the assertion would let bad data through in release and produce a wrong answer instead of an error.

SituationUseSurvives release
A loop bound from validated inputassertNo — fine, it cannot fire
A value straight from JSONthrowYes — it must
A platform channel resultthrowYes
An internal helper's preconditionassert + throwThe throw
A user-supplied argumentthrowYes
A type promotion that failedthrowYes
An unreachable branchassert(false)No — documentation
// WRONG: an assertion on untrusted input, which vanishes in release
int parsePort(String raw) {
  final port = int.parse(raw);
  assert(port > 0 && port < 65536);   // stripped in production
  return port;                            // so a bad port reaches the socket
}

// RIGHT: throw, so the check is always there
int parsePort2(String raw) {
  final port = int.tryParse(raw);
  if (port == null) {
    throw FormatException('port is not a number', raw);
  }
  if (port <= 0 || port >= 65536) {
    throw RangeError.range(port, 1, 65535, 'port');
  }
  return port;
}

// and the BOTH version, which is the honest one for a public API
int parsePort3(String raw) {
  final port = int.tryParse(raw);
  if (port == null) {
    throw FormatException('port is not a number', raw);
  }
  if (port <= 0 || port < 65536) {
    throw RangeError.range(port, 1, 65535, 'port');
  }
  assert(port > 0);       // redundant here, and harmless
  return port;
}
// ...for a PUBLIC function, the assert above documents a precondition the
// throw already enforces. Write it only when it adds information.

// an assertion that costs nothing and catches a real bug
class Cache {
  final Map<String, int> _m = {};
  void put(String k, int v) {
    assert(!_m.containsKey(k), 'overwriting $k without invalidate()');
    _m[k] = v;
  }
}
// ...in debug this surfaces a stale-cache bug; in release it costs
// nothing and the behaviour is the same either way, which is the ideal
// relationship between an assertion and the code around it

An assertion whose condition has a side effect is a bug, because the side effect happens in debug and not in release — so the program behaves differently in the two modes. The analyzer catches the common cases, such as a method call in the condition, but not an expression-bodied getter that increments a counter, and that pattern appears in real code as a way of "using" an expression that the analyzer then flags as having no effect.

// an assertion with a side effect
var calls = 0;
int next() => ++calls;

void f() {
  assert(next() > 0);       // next() runs in debug, not in release
  print(calls);              // 1 in debug, 0 in release
}
// ...the analyzer flags `next() > 0` as an unnecessary comparison, which
// is a hint but not an explanation

// the versions that are fine
void f2(List<int> list) {
  assert(list.isNotEmpty);
  assert(list.every((e) => e > 0), 'all must be positive');
  assert(_isSorted(list), 'the input must already be sorted');
  // ...pure predicates are fine; only side effects are the problem

// and the case an assertion CAN'T see, which is why it is not a substitute
// for a test
void f3(int n) {
  assert(n > 0);
  // ...it says nothing about n <= 100, or that the function is correct,
//   or that the caller honoured any precondition. It checks exactly one
//   thing, in one build mode.

// which makes assertions a poor substitute for tests in a way worth
// stating plainly: they run only in development, they check one condition,
// and they are invisible in the field. Use them to catch broken invariants
// early; use tests to prove behaviour.

Where assertions are enabled is a build setting rather than a runtime switch, and knowing the default matters more than it sounds. A VM run from source, and every dart test and flutter test run, has assertions on, so a test that passes locally has been checked by every assertion on the path it took. A dart compile exe without --enable-asserts, and a dart compile js in its default release mode, has them stripped — so a bug caught by an assertion in development is simply not running in the shipped binary. That asymmetry is the entire reason the assert/throw rule matters: an assertion is only ever protecting the paths that a test suite already exercises.

Two forms of assertion are available inside a const context, and they are there for a specific reason. A collection literal accepts assert between elements to check the contents at compile time, and a const constructor's initialiser list accepts it as an expression to check its arguments. Neither runs at run time — both are evaluated by the compiler, so a violation is a compile error and the constant never exists. That makes them the one kind of check in the language with zero run-time cost, and the right choice for a shape the type system cannot express.

7.7 Error handling pitfalls

The eight mistakes that turn an error path into an outage.

// 1. catching too broadly
try {
  doEverything();
} catch (e) {
  print('failed');      // a typo in doEverything is now invisible
}

// 2. swallowing without logging
try {
  risky();
} catch (e) {
  // silence. now you cannot debug it.
}

// 3. rethrow without the stack trace
try {
  risky();
} on Exception catch (e) {
  throw Exception('failed: $e');   // the ORIGINAL trace is lost
}
// correct:
try {
  risky();
} on Exception catch (e, s) {
  Error.throwWithStackTrace(Exception('failed: $e'), s);
}

// 4. an empty catch
try { risky(); } catch (_) {}      // the worst of both

// 5. validating with assert
assert(password.length >= 8);      // stripped in release: no validation

// 6. throwing in a finally, discarding the original
try { risky(); } finally { cleanup(); }   // if cleanup throws, you lose

// 7. a resource leaked on an early return
File? f;
try {
  f = await File(p).open();
  if (bad) return;        // does finally run? yes - but only if there IS a finally
} finally {               // easy to forget
  await f?.close();
}

// 8. catching an Error
try { list[999]; } on RangeError { }   // hides a real bug

The seven ways error handling goes wrong

Most of what can be done badly with exceptions in Dart is a variation on one of a small number of mistakes. Knowing them by shape — rather than by fixing them as they appear — is what lets a reviewer see the next one coming, and the shape is always either a swallowed error, a lost stack trace, a leaked resource, or an error crossing a boundary it should not have.

MistakeSymptomFix
Empty catchNothing happens, silentlyRethrow, or log with intent
Catch-all catchBugs turned into defaultsName the types you handle
throw e instead of rethrowStack trace blames the reporterBare rethrow
Unawaited futureError surfaces much laterawait, or unawaited
Resource acquired before tryLeak on the throwing pathAcquire inside, or use finally
Catching ErrorBugs become silent fallbacksLet Error propagate
Exception as control flowCostly, and invisibleReturn null or a Result
// 1. the empty catch
try {
  send();
} catch (e) {
  // ...nothing. The caller believes it worked.
}

// 2. the catch-all
try {
  compute();
} catch (e) {
  return 0;      // a TypeError in `compute` now silently becomes 0
}

// 3. `throw e` - the trace moves
try {
  inner();
} catch (e) {
  throw e;      // ...reported from HERE, so the real location is lost
}

// 4. the unawaited future
void f() {
  doAsync();       // an error here is reported at an arbitrary later point
}

// 5. acquisition outside the try
final conn = await connect();   // if this is fine but the next line throws,
try {                           // nothing releases it
  await work(conn);
} finally {
  await conn.close();
}

// 6. catching Error
try {
  compute();
} catch (e) {        // ...TypeError, RangeError, StackOverflowError
  return defaultValue;
}

// 7. exceptions as flow
for (var i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
  try {
    if (process(i)) break;
  } catch (e) {
    continue;      // 1000 exceptions for a normal exit
  }
}

The leak in item 5 has a specific and non-obvious fix, and it is worth stating exactly: the acquisition must be inside the try, and the resource variable must be declared before the try so the finally can see it. Writing it the other way round is what produces the pattern where a partial acquisition leaks, because the acquisition that fails has no value to release but the one that succeeds and then fails inside the body does — and the two are indistinguishable from the outside.

// the leak, in three variants
// BAD: acquisition before the try
final conn = await connect();
try { await work(conn); } finally { await conn.close(); }

// WORSE: acquisition in a condition, so it can fail outside the try
try {
  if (await shouldConnect()) {
    final conn = await connect();      // ...this is inside, but:
    await work(conn);
  }
} finally {
  // `conn` is not in scope, so the close is impossible
}

// RIGHT: declare outside, acquire inside
Connection? conn;
try {
  conn = await connect();
  await work(conn);
} finally {
  await conn?.close();      // ...?. because connect() may have thrown
}
// ...and the ?. is exactly what encodes "we might not have one"

// BEST: let a construct own the pairing
final result = await using((_) async => await work());
// or
final result2 = await connRef.use((c) => work(c));

// and the pattern for a nested acquisition
final db = await openDb();
try {
  final tx = await db.begin();
  try {
    await tx.run(body);
    await tx.commit();
  } catch (e) {
    await tx.rollback();
    rethrow;
  }
} finally {
  await db.close();
}
// ...each level owns exactly one resource, and the nesting is the
// documentation

Catching Error is the mistake with the worst consequences, because it converts a bug into a plausible wrong answer and the program continues in a state nobody designed. The specific failures are worth naming: a TypeError from a failed cast becomes a default; a RangeError from a bad index becomes a truncated result; a StackOverflowError — which in Dart is an Error, not an Exception — becomes an infinite loop's worth of work; and an OutOfMemoryError becomes continued allocation in an already-exhausted heap. None of those should reach a catch clause that intends to handle an ordinary failure.

// catching Error, and what each one becomes
try {
  return compute();
} catch (e) {
  return 0;
}
// a TypeError inside compute  -> a legitimate-looking 0
// a RangeError inside compute -> a truncated result
// a StackOverflowError      -> a deeply recursive fallback path
// ...and none of them is debuggable afterwards, because the stack trace
// is gone and the symptom is a number

// the fix: name what you handle
int compute() {
  try {
    return _compute();
  } on FormatException catch (e) {
    return 0;                // ...a bad input really does mean 0
  }
  // TypeError, RangeError, AssertionError and the rest propagate - which
  // is what makes this correct: they are bugs, and a bug should stop.
}

// and the defensive version, where the bug must not kill the program -
// but it must still be visible
try {
  return compute();
} on FormatException {
  return 0;
} catch (e, st) {
  // ...catch-all is CORRECT here, because this is a top-level boundary
  reportCrash(e, st);        // ...and it reports rather than swallows
  rethrow;
}

// StackOverflowError specifically: it leaves the stack full, so anything
// after it may also fail
try {
  recurse(depth);
} on StackOverflowError {
  // ...the stack is exhausted - allocating anything here is unreliable
  scheduleRecomputation();     // ...defer to a fresh stack
}

Exceptions as control flow is the last shape, and the objection to it is usually stated as a performance argument when the real problem is a design one. Throwing in Dart captures a stack trace at the throw site, which is not free and grows with stack depth; using an exception for a loop exit therefore costs a trace capture per iteration. But the deeper cost is that the ordinary path becomes invisible: a reader cannot tell whether a catch means "this can happen and I handle it" or "I am using this to exit a loop", and the second is not something a type can express or a reader can verify.

// exceptions as flow - the cost is per iteration
for (var i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
  try {
    if (found(items[i])) break;
  } on Never {
    continue;
  }
}
// ...never actually thrown, but the pattern people reach for when a
// function has one exit point and they do not want an early return

// the honest version
for (final item in items) {
  if (found(item)) {
    handle(item);
    break;
  }
}

// where an exception IS the right control flow: an exceptional condition
// that should unwind through several layers
User load(String id) {
  final raw = db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?', [id]);
  if (raw.isEmpty) throw NotFound(id);
  return User.fromRow(raw.first);
}
// ...the not-found case propagates through four frames, each of which has
// no business handling it, and is caught at the boundary. This is what
// exceptions are FOR, and the test is whether the frames between are
// genuinely unable to respond.

// the measurable difference, which settles whether it matters
var sw = Stopwatch()..start();
for (var i = 0; i < 100000; i++) {
  try { if (i == 99999) break; } catch (e) { rethrow; }
}
sw.stop();      // tens of milliseconds, and a 100000-element trace list

sw.reset();
for (var i = 0; i < 100000; i++) { if (i == 99999) break; }
sw.stop();      // microseconds
// ...so: exceptions for unwinding an exceptional condition through layers
// that cannot handle it; a value for anything on the ordinary path

7.8 Sealed results instead of exceptions

When a sealed result is better than a throw, and the decision rule.

// EXCEPTIONS are right for: exceptional, rare, and the caller
// either fixes it or gives up entirely
//   - a file that does not exist
//   - a network failure
//   - a programmer error

// SEALED RESULTS are right for: expected, frequent, and the caller
// has a DIFFERENT action for each case
//   - a validation failure, with per-field messages
//   - a payment that was declined
//   - a permission that was refused
//   - a cache miss

sealed class Validated<T, E> {}

class Valid<T, E> extends Validated<T, E> {
  final T value;
  const Valid(this.value);
}

class Invalid<T, E> extends Validated<T, E> {
  final E errors;
  const Invalid(this.errors);
}

Validated<String, Map<String, String>> validateName(String input) {
  final errors = <String, String>{};
  if (input.isEmpty) errors['name'] = 'Required';
  if (input.length < 2) errors['name'] = 'Too short';
  return errors.isEmpty ? Valid(input) : Invalid(errors);
}

// the call site is exhaustive and has no try/catch
final result = validateName(input);
switch (result) {
  case Valid(:final value):
    submit(value);
  case Invalid(:final errors):
    showFieldErrors(errors);
}
// the hybrid, which is the most realistic design
// - the low-level code throws (it is exceptional there)
// - the boundary converts to a sealed result (it is expected there)

Future<Result<User, Failure>> loadUser(String id) async {
  try {
    final text = await File('users/$id.json').readAsString();
    final json = jsonDecode(text) as Map<String, dynamic>;
    return Ok(User.fromJson(json));
  } on FileSystemException {
    return const Err(Failure.notFound(id));
  } on FormatException catch (e, s) {
    log('corrupt user $id', stack: s);
    return Err(Failure.corrupt(id));
  } on SocketException {
    return const Err(Failure.offline());
  }
}

// the rule of thumb:
//   throw deep inside, where the detail is useful
//   return a sealed result at the layer that decides what to do

Neither approach is correct in the abstract. Exceptions make the happy path readable and the error path invisible; sealed results make the error path explicit and the happy path noisy. Choose per boundary: an error a caller cannot act on differently should be an exception, and one it can should be a value.

Exercises 8

  1. Write a withFile helper and use it for three file operations, proving the files close on the throwing path.
  2. Create a finally whose cleanup throws, and confirm the original exception is lost. Then fix it with a safe-cleanup wrapper.
  3. Define a three-level exception hierarchy for your own domain and catch it at three levels of specificity.
  4. Demonstrate that an uncaught error in a Future does not stop synchronous code, then fix it with await.
  5. Write a validation function with a sealed result, then find every if (input == null) throw in a codebase and decide which should become a result.
  6. Find one rethrow that loses a stack trace in a codebase and fix it with Error.throwWithStackTrace.
  7. Compile a program with --enable-asserts and one without, and confirm the assert-based validation disappears.

Result as an alternative, and when it is the better answer

A Result type — a sealed pair of success and failure — moves a failure from an exception to a return value, and that changes three things at once: the caller is forced by the compiler to handle the failure, the failure's data travels with the success path, and the failure becomes part of a function's ordinary type rather than an out-of-band event. The cost is that every caller needs a branch, so it is worth being clear about when that is a fair trade.

// the type, in full
sealed class Result<T, E> {
  const Result();
}

final class Success<T, E> extends Result<T, E> {
  final T value;
  const Success(this.value);
}

final class Failure<T, E> extends Result<T, E> {
  final E error;
  const Failure(this.error);
}

// ...or, from package:typed_data / package:fpdart / package:result:
// Result<T, E> with fold, map, mapError, andThen, andMatch

// the signature that makes it worth having
Result<User, ParseError> parseUser(String raw) {
  final fields = raw.split(',');
  if (fields.length != 3) {
    return Failure(ParseError('expected 3 fields, got ${fields.length}', raw));
  }
  final id = int.tryParse(fields[0]);
  if (id == null) {
    return Failure(ParseError('id is not a number', fields[0]));
  }
  return Success(User(id, fields[1], fields[2]));
}

// the caller is FORCED to handle both - and cannot forget
final result = parseUser(line);
switch (result) {
  case Success(:final value):
    await save(value);
  case Failure(:final error):
    log('skipped a line: ${error.message}');
}
// ...no try, no catch, no unhandled-error possibility, and `error` is
// typed so `error.column` is checked

The strongest argument for Result is that it makes the failure part of the type, and therefore part of what a reader can see without running the code. A function returning Config that throws does not say so in its signature; a function returning Result<Config, ConfigError> says it, and every caller is forced to acknowledge it. That is the difference between documentation and enforcement, and it is the same argument that motivates sealed hierarchies and non-nullable types.

ConsiderationThrowResult
Failure visible in the signatureNoYes
Caller must handle failureNoYes
Failure carries dataYes, in the objectYes
Failure can travel through a pipeNoYes
Cost when it does not happenNear zeroA branch per call
Cost when it does happenA stack trace captureAllocation only
Crosses an async boundaryAwkwardNatural
Deep call stacksGood — unwindsEvery layer must thread it
Exception is truly exceptionalGoodVerbose
// where Result wins: a pipeline, where each stage can fail
Result<List<Row>, LoadError> load(String path) {
  if (!exists(path)) return Failure(LoadError.notFound(path));
  final bytes = read(path);
  if (bytes == null) return Failure(LoadError.unreadable(path));
  return parse(bytes);
    .mapError((e) => LoadError.malformed(path, e));
}

// ...every stage returns a Result, and `mapError` translates the error
// TYPE, so the caller sees one error type for the whole operation rather
// than a different exception from each layer

// and the caller is exhaustive because the type is sealed
void handle(String path) {
  switch (load(path)) {
    case Success(:final rows):
      render(rows);
    case Failure(:final error):
      switch (error) {
        case LoadError.notFound():
          showEmptyState();
        case LoadError.unreadable():
          showPermissionPrompt();
        case LoadError.malformed():
          showBugReport(path);
      }
  }
}

// where throw wins: a failure that crosses layers none of which can act
User requireUser(int id) {
  final row = db.findRow(id);            // may be null
  if (row == null) {
    // ...four callers up the stack, the caller has the try/catch and the
    // four in between cannot do anything useful with a Failure value
    throw NotFound(id);
  }
  return User.fromRow(row);
}
// ...threading a Result through four frames that would only `return it`
// adds four branches to code that has no decision to make

The practical rule that emerges is about the direction of the data. A failure that unwinds — travelling outward through layers that cannot respond — belongs in a throw, because threading a value through each layer adds a branch with no decision in it. A failure that flows — travelling through a pipeline where each stage's output is the next stage's input, or sideways to a caller that must choose between two paths — belongs in a return value, because the value keeps the failure next to the data and forces the choice where the choice is.

// unwinds: throw
void a() { b(); }                       // cannot handle it
void b() { c(); }                       // cannot handle it
void c() { throw StateError('deep'); }   // throws
// ...a() and b() add two branches for no decision - use throw

// flows: Result
Result<Row, DbError> query(String sql) {
  try {
    return Success(exec(sql));
  } on SqlException catch (e) {
    return Failure(DbError(e.code, e.message));
  }
}

Result<List<Row>, DbError> loadRows(int userId) {
  return query('SELECT * FROM rows WHERE uid = $userId')
      .mapError((e) => DbError.wrapped(e));
}
// ...each layer HAS a decision: what does this stage's failure mean here?
// so it belongs in the value

// the boundary: an API's INTERNAL failures are Results, and its EXTERNAL
// failures are throws
class Repository {
  // ...internal: the caller is one layer up and must choose
  Result<Row, DbError> find(int id) { … }

  // ...external: the caller is a UI layer with a try/catch at its root
  User loadOrThrow(int id) {
    return switch (find(id)) {
      Success(:final value) => value,
      Failure(:final error) => throw RepositoryException(error),
    };
  }
}
// ...so both mechanisms, each used where it is right

Three practical details decide whether a Result implementation is usable. The combinators have to be right, because a map that loses the error or an andThen with the wrong shape is worse than no combinators. fold has to exist, because it is the one method that handles both sides in a single expression — and it is what makes a chain of Results readable without a nested switch at every stage. And the error type has to be a real type rather than a String, or the whole exercise loses the property that made it worth adopting.

// the combinators that make it readable
// fold: handle both in one expression
final name = load(id).fold(
  (error) => 'could not load: ${error.code}',
  (user) => user.displayName,
);

// map / mapError: transform one side, leave the other alone
final upper = load(id).map((u) => u.displayName.toUpperCase());   // keeps error
final described = load(id).mapError((e) => 'load failed: $e');     // keeps value

// andThen / flatMap: a Result-returning operation in a pipeline
final withPosts = load(id).andThen((u) => loadPosts(u.id));
// ...which is `map` if the callback returns a plain value and `andThen` if
// it returns a Result. Getting these two the wrong way round is the most
// common mistake with a Result library.

// getOrElse: a default, without an exception
final display = load(id).getOrElse(() => const User.guest());

// the string-error mistake
sealed class Op<T> {}
final class Ok<T> extends Op<T> { final T value; Ok(this.value); }
final class Err<T> extends Op<T> { final String message; Err(this.message); }
// ...`Err('not found')`, `Err('timeout')`, `Err('permission')` - and now the
// caller has to compare strings, which is exactly the brittleness a sealed
// error type removes

// the version that earns the type
sealed class Op<T> {}
final class Ok<T> extends Op<T> { final T value; Ok(this.value); }
final class Err<T> extends Op<T> {
  final OpError error;      // ...an enum or a sealed type
  Err(this.error);
}
enum OpError { notFound, timeout, permission, unknown }

void report(OpError e) {
  switch (e) {
    case OpError.notFound: return showEmpty();
    case OpError.timeout: return showSpinner();
    case OpError.permission: return showLogin();
    case OpError.unknown: return showBug();
  }
}
// ...exhaustive, checked, and impossible to get wrong by a typo

8 · Asynchronous Dart

8.1 async and await8.2 The Future API8.3 Error handling in async code8.4 Sequential vs concurrent8.5 Streams8.6 Stream operators8.7 Subscriptions and lifecycle8.8 Future or Stream?8.9 Zones, briefly

Dart's asynchronous model: single-threaded, event-loop driven, with no callback hell and no thread-safety questions for I/O-bound work.

8.1 async and await

The syntax, and the thing that makes Dart async different from other single-threaded languages.

// a Future is a value that will exist later
Future<int> fetchCount() async {
  await Future.delayed(const Duration(seconds: 1));
  return 42;
}

void main() async {
  final count = await fetchCount();    // the code PAUSES here
  print(count);                        // 42, later
}

// async makes the function return a Future automatically
// await unwraps it

// the callback form, which you should rarely need
fetchCount().then((count) => print(count));
fetchCount()
    .then((count) => print(count))
    .catchError((e) => print('failed: $e'));

// there is no "yield"; async/await is the whole mechanism

// awaiting a non-Future is fine: it just yields once
void main() async {
  await null;                    // a microtask boundary
  await Future.value();          // same
  print('after');
}
// WHAT MAKES DART DIFFERENT: async does NOT block the thread
// the function returns at the first await, and resumes later on the
// event loop. The thread is free to run other work.
//
// so: there is no thread-safety problem for I/O-bound async code,
// because only one thing runs at a time. But there IS a problem
// with shared mutable state across awaits:

class Counter {
  int value = 0;
  Future<void> incrementBad() async {
    final current = value;      // read
    await Future.delayed(Duration(milliseconds: 10));
    value = current + 1;        // write - a LOST UPDATE
  }
}

final c = Counter();
await Future.wait([c.incrementBad(), c.incrementBad()]);
print(c.value);      // 1, not 2!

// the fix: serialise the access, or make the state non-shared
class SafeCounter {
  int _value = 0;
  Future<void> _queue = Future.value();

  Future<void> increment() {
    final completer = Completer<void>();
    _queue = _queue.then((_) async {
      _value++;
      completer.complete();
    });
    return completer.future;
  }
}

// or: do the atomic work in an isolate (chapter 9), or keep the
// read-modify-write synchronous

The lost-update bug above is Dart's real concurrency hazard, and it is not theoretical: it appears in any code that reads shared state, awaits, then writes. If you see await between a read and a write of the same field, ask what else could run in between. It usually is not a thread, but it is another task on the same isolate.

What async actually compiles to

async and await are syntax over two lower-level constructs: a Future and a state machine the compiler generates for you. Marking a function async makes its body run synchronously up to the first await, and turns every return into a completion of a Future. The await expression suspends the function and registers a callback to resume it. Nothing is threaded; there is no event loop visible in the code, because the compiler has already written the continuation for you.

// what you write
Future<int> fetch(String url) async {
  print('1');
  final res = await http.get(Uri.parse(url));
  print('2');
  return res.statusCode;
}

// what the compiler produces, in outline
Future<int> fetch(String url) {
  print('1');
  return http.get(Uri.parse(url)).then((res) {
    print('2');
    return res.statusCode;
  });
}
// ...so the body up to the first await runs SYNCHRONOUSLY, in the caller's
// turn of the event loop. That single fact explains every ordering surprise
// in this chapter.

// the return-type rule
Future<int> a() async {
  return 42;              // correct
  // return Future.value(42);  // WRONG - nested future, and the static
                             // type is Future<int> so it would not
                             // compile anyway
}

// and the no-async version of the same function
Future<int> a2() {
  return Future.value(42);   // equivalent - already a Future
}

The consequence of that synchronous prefix is that a long chain of awaits in a function with no actual asynchronous work never yields to the event loop at all, which is how a "async" function can block the UI. Conversely, an async function with no await still returns a Future and still completes on a microtask — never synchronously. That asymmetry is worth internalising: you cannot get the synchronous behaviour back by removing the await, and you do not want to.

// an async function with no await: still deferred
Future<void> noAwait() async {
  print('a');
}
print('b');
noAwait();
print('c');
// output: b, a, c
// ...because `noAwait()` returns a Future that completes on a microtask,
// and the microtask queue is drained after the current synchronous run

// the opposite trap: async with no real await does NOT block
Future<void> fake() async {
  // no await - runs straight through, returns a completed future
}
fake();
print('this runs immediately');

// the case that DOES block: CPU work inside an async function
Future<List<int>> compute() async {
  // ...await makes the function async, but the loop below never yields
  final r = <int>[];
  for (var i = 0; i < 10000000; i++) { r.add(i * 2); }
  return r;
}
// ...so the UI freezes for the whole loop. `async` is not a thread. For
// CPU work, use `Isolate.run` or `compute()`.

// yielding explicitly, which is the fix for a long synchronous section
Future<List<int>> compute2() async {
  final r = <int>[];
  for (var i = 0; i < 10000000; i++) {
    r.add(i * 2);
    if (i % 100000 == 0) await Future.delayed(Duration.zero);
  }
  return r;
}
// ...a real yield, so the frame can complete. In Flutter this is
// `await SchedulerBinding.instance.endOfFrame` or an animation tick.

Two rules about await are enforced rather than documented, and both are worth knowing because their diagnostics are confusing. You cannot await in a function that is not marked async, async* or a FutureOr-returning helper — so a synchronous helper that must sometimes await has to be marked async, which changes its return type. And you cannot await in a catch block's own expression or inside a finally that has already returned, so cleanup sometimes needs a local future held and awaited outside.

// the two errors
void sync() {
  await something();     // ERROR: await is only in async functions
}

Future<void> ok() async {
  await something();     // correct
}

// a helper that sometimes needs to await
String maybe(int x) {
  if (x > 0) {
    // return convert(x);   // if convert is async, this cannot compile
    throw StateError('mark it async and return Future<String>');
  }
  return 'plain';
}

Future<String> maybe2(int x) async {
  if (x > 0) return await convert(x);   // legal
  return 'plain';                         // auto-wrapped into a Future
}

// awaiting in a finally after a return needs care
Future<void> tricky() async {
  try {
    await work();
    return;                 // the finally still runs
  } finally {
    await cleanup();        // legal: an async finally may await
  }
}
// ...and this one is legal too, because `finally` may await. What is NOT
// legal is `return await` inside a finally, which silently discards the
// pending value.

// and awaiting something that is not awaitable
Future<void> wrong() async {
  await 42;                // ERROR: int is not FutureOr
  await null;              // ERROR: Null is not FutureOr
  await [1, 2];            // ERROR
  await Duration.zero;     // ERROR - a Duration is not a Future
  // ...`Future.delayed(Duration.zero)` is the actual way to yield
}

8.2 The Future API

Every method on Future, and when each is the right tool.

// creating
Future.value(42);
Future.error(Exception('x'));
Future<void>.delayed(Duration(milliseconds: 100));
Future(() => doSomething());         // runs later, on the event loop
Future.sync(() => doSomething());    // runs now, but still a Future
Future.wait([f1, f2, f3]);              // completes when ALL complete
Future.any([f1, f2]);                   // completes with the FIRST success
Future.any([f1, f2]);                   // ...throws on the first FAILURE

// transforming
future.then((value) => transform(value));
future.then((v) => ..., onError: (e) => ...);
future.catchError((e) => fallback);
future.whenComplete(() => cleanup());   // always, unlike finally on a sync try

// the combinators
future.timeout(const Duration(seconds: 5));
future.asStream();                 // Future -> Stream with one value
// Stream.asFuture()               // Stream -> Future with the LAST value

// checking
Future.hasFuture(value);           // is this a Future?
// ignore()                        // explicitly mark a Future as un-awaited
// unawaited(future)                // from dart:async, for the analyser

// a CompleteExample
Future<void> robust() async {
  final data = await fetch()
      .timeout(const Duration(seconds: 5), onTimeout: () => cache.load())
      .catchError((e) => defaultsFor(e));

  save(data);
}

// Future.wait with error handling
try {
  final results = await Future.wait([
    fetchA(), fetchB(), fetchC(),
  ], eagerError: true);
  print(results);
} catch (e) {
  // eagerError: true fails on the FIRST error rather than waiting
  print('one of the three failed: $e');
}

// and the all-settled pattern you often actually want
final results = await Future.wait([
  fetchA().then((v) => Result.ok(v), onError: (e) => Result.err(e)),
  fetchB().then((v) => Result.ok(v), onError: (e) => Result.err(e)),
]);
// now you have both outcomes, not an exception
// Common: the "unawaited" mistake
void onTap() {
  saveDraft();            // ERROR in newer analysis: discarded Future
  navigate();
}

// the analyser can be told to complain
// analysis_options.yaml
analyzer:
  errors:
    unawaited_futures: error

// and when you genuinely mean it
void onTap() {
  unawaited(saveDraft().catchError((e) => log('$e')));
  navigate();
}

// Future.wait vs sequential
// WRONG for independent work: serialises it
final a = await fetchA();
final b = await fetchB();
final c = await fetchC();

// RIGHT: concurrent, 1 round trip instead of 3
final results = await Future.wait([fetchA(), fetchB(), fetchC()]);

// RIGHT when B depends on A
final a = await fetchA();
final b = await fetchB(a.id);

Future as a value, and its three states

A Future is a container for one value that will exist later, and it has three states: pending, completed with a value, or completed with an error. It settles exactly once, and never changes state after that. That single-settlement rule is the source of both its usefulness — any number of listeners can attach to the same future and all of them will be called — and its sharpest edge, which is that completing an already-completed future is silently ignored.

ConstructionHow it settles
Future.value(v)Already, with v
Future.error(e, st)Already, with error e
Future.delayed(d, () => v)After d, with the callback's value
Completer().futureWhichever side completes it
An async functionOn return, or on throw
Future.sync(() => v)Catches a synchronous throw into an error
// the constructors
final a = Future.value(42);                  // completed now
final b = Future.error(StateError('x'));     // completed now, with error
final c = Future.delayed(const Duration(seconds: 1), () => 'done');
final d = Future(() => heavy());            // runs heavy LATER on the
                                              // event loop, not now

// a Future that never settles - a hang with no error
final never = Completer<void>().future;    // and nobody completes it
never.then((_) {});
// ...which is why a Completer that is dropped on an error path is the
// classic deadlock. There is no timeout unless you add one.

// the states, and how to observe them
final f = fetchIt();
print(f);                   // Instance of 'Future<String>'
f.then((v) => print(v))
 .catchError((e) => print('$e'))
 .whenComplete(() => print('done'));

// never awaiting - an error here is unhandled and reported by the zone
fetchIt();
fetchIt().then((v) => print(v));      // error here is ALSO unhandled
fetchIt().then((v) => print(v), onError: (Object e, StackTrace s) {
  print('$e');
});

// and the ordering rule
Future<void> order() async {
  print('a');                 // synchronous
  await Future.delayed(Duration.zero);
  print('b');                 // after one event-loop turn
  scheduleMicrotask(() => print('micro'));
  await Future.delayed(Duration.zero);
  print('c');
  // a, b, micro, c
}

Completer is the piece that lets a non-async function produce a future, and its two halves are used from different threads of control: the future is returned to the caller, and complete or completeError is called later from whatever finishes the work. It is how a callback-based API is adapted to a future-based one, and how a future is built out of an event listener.

// wrapping a callback API
Future<String> readFile(String path) {
  final c = Completer<String>();
  File(path).readAsString().then(
    (data) => c.complete(data),
    onError: (Object e, StackTrace s) => c.completeError(e, s),
  );
  return c.future;
}
// ...note the onError: completing a future with an error does NOT go
// through the future's error path automatically, so both branches must be
// wired, or the caller's `await` hangs forever.

// a Completer for a value produced elsewhere - the general shape
final _controller = StreamController<int>();
final _done = Completer<void>();

Future<void> start() async {
  _controller.stream.listen((v) {}, onDone: () => _done.complete());
  // ...work that eventually closes the controller
}

Future<void> waitForDone() => _done.future;

// completing twice, and the error that tells you
final c = Completer<int>();
c.complete(1);
c.complete(2);                  // StateError: Future already completed
// ...so guard with `isCompleted` when the completion path is not obviously
// single:
if (!c.isCompleted) c.complete(v);

// completeError with no listener is an unhandled async error
final c2 = Completer<int>();
c2.completeError(StateError('nobody is listening'));
// ...which the zone reports. Always return the future to someone.

// sync: running the body immediately and catching a throw
Future<int> f1() => Future.sync(() => heavy());   // heavy runs NOW
Future<int> f2() => Future(() => heavy());        // heavy runs LATER
// ...the difference matters when the body touches state that changes between
// the call and the next event-loop turn

Future is a single-value future, which is what makes it a poor fit for anything that produces a series. The two workarounds are a List of futures and a Stream, and the choice between them is about when the values are known. A list is right when the whole set is known now and the consumer wants them all; a stream is right when values arrive over time, when the set is unbounded, or when producing one value should begin producing the next — which is backpressure, and is the reason a stream is not just a list with a different spelling.

// a list of futures: everything is in hand
final users = await Future.wait([fetchA(), fetchB(), fetchC()]);
// ...eagerError defaults to true, so the first failure short-circuits

// a stream: values arrive as they are ready, and production is paced
Stream<Row> rows = Stream.fromFutures([f1(), f2()]);
await for (final r in rows) { print(r); }

// the same work with different concurrency, which Future.wait cannot express
final all = <String, Future<String>>{
  'a': fetchA(),
  'b': fetchB(),
};
final results = await Future.wait(all.entries.map((e) async =>
  MapEntry(e.key, await e.value)));      // a Map of results, per key
// ...which is the shape to use when each result must be attributed to its
// request, since Future.wait alone loses that association

// sequential, which is the answer when the requests depend on each other
final a = await step1();
final b = await step2(a);
final c = await step3(b);

// concurrent, started together but awaited together
final results2 = await Future.wait([step1(), step2Raw(), step3Raw()]);
// ...all three START before the first completes

When a future's completion callback runs is worth knowing precisely, because it is not at the moment the future settles. Future.value(1) is already complete when it is created, but a listener attached to it runs on a microtask — after the current synchronous run finishes and before any I/O callback. scheduleMicrotask queues at the same level, and timers at a coarser one, so a chain of then callbacks is drained completely before a zero-duration timer runs. That is why a hundred chained thens are effectively instant while a Future.delayed(Duration.zero) waits for a full event-loop turn.

8.3 Error handling in async code

try/catch around awaits, and the errors that bypass it.

// the normal pattern
Future<void> load() async {
  try {
    final data = await api.fetch();
    render(data);
  } on NetworkException catch (e) {
    showError(e.message);
  } on FormatException catch (e, s) {
    log('bad data', stack: s);
    showError('Could not read the response');
  } catch (e, s) {
    log('unexpected', error: e, stack: s);
    showError('Something went wrong');
  }
}

// catchError on a chain
api.fetch()
    .then((d) => render(d))
    .catchError((e) => showError('$e'));

// the two that bypass try/catch
// 1. a Future created but never awaited
void bad() {
  Future(() => throw Exception('x'));   // nothing catches this
}

// 2. an error thrown in a callback the framework calls
Timer.run(() {
  throw Exception('x');    // goes to the zone, not to your try/catch
});

// for a Stream, an error is an EVENT, not a throw
stream.listen(
  (v) => print(v),
  onError: (e) => print('error event: $e'),
);

// and whenComplete, which runs on both paths
Future<void> withSpinner() async {
  showSpinner();
  try {
    await doWork();
  } finally {
    hideSpinner();
  }
}

// and the important one: rethrow preserves the trace
try {
  await api.fetch();
} on AppException catch (e, s) {
  log('downstream failure', stack: s);
  rethrow;                  // NOT: throw e, which loses the trace
}

Recovering from a failed future, four ways

A future that completes with an error needs a decision made somewhere: retry it, substitute a value, ignore it deliberately, or let it propagate. Each choice has a corresponding mechanism, and picking the wrong one is how a transient network blip becomes a user-facing error or a silent wrong answer. The mechanisms differ in where the decision is made, which is the part that matters.

MechanismDecision made byUse for
await with tryThe caller, explicitlyPropagate, or handle once
.catchError((e) => v)The producer of the futureA local fallback value
Future.wait(..., eagerError: false)The caller, after all settlePartial results
unawaited plus a logNobodyBest-effort work
A Result return typeThe type systemExpected failures
// 1. catchError with a RECOVERY VALUE - the chain continues
Future<List<Row>> loadOrEmpty(String path) async {
  return fetchRows(path).catchError((Object e, StackTrace s) {
    log('falling back to empty', e, s);
    return <Row>[];              // the error is handled HERE
  });
}
// ...note the return type: catchError's callback must return List<Row>,
// which is how the compiler keeps the chain's type honest

// 2. catchError that rethrows - for logging on the way out
Future<void> logged() async {
  try {
    await work();
  } catch (e, s) {
    log(e, s);
    rethrow;
  }
}

// 3. Future.wait with per-future recovery - partial results, no exception
final results = await Future.wait([
  fetchA().catchError((Object e) {
    log('a failed: $e');
    return const A.empty();
  }),
  fetchB().catchError((Object e) {
    log('b failed: $e');
    return const B.empty();
  }),
]);
// ...nothing throws, both are values, and the caller checks emptiness

// 4. a timeout, which is the failure mode people forget
Future<T> withTimeout<T>(Future<T> f, Duration d, T fallback) async {
  try {
    return await f.timeout(d);
  } on TimeoutException {
    return fallback;
  }
}
// ...`.timeout` does NOT cancel the underlying work - it only stops waiting,
// so a timed-out request is still running and may still write. A timeout that
// has to stop the work needs a cancellation flag the work checks.

// and the shape that is NOT a fallback: a Result
sealed class L<T> {}
final class LOk<T> extends L<T> { final T v; LOk(this.v); }
final class LErr<T> extends L<T> { final String m; LErr(this.m); }

Future<L<Row>> load(String path) async {
  try {
    return LOk(await fetchRows(path));
  } on Exception catch (e) {
    return LErr('$e');
  }
}
// ...the caller cannot accidentally treat the fallback as a real result

A future can be listened to more than once, and each listener is independent — which is what makes fan-out free and also what makes a forgotten listener a silent bug. A future is created when the async function is called, not when it is awaited, so starting it early and awaiting it much later is the intended pattern for concurrency. The dangerous corollary is that an error is reported once per zone, not once per listener: if nobody attaches an error handler before the microtask queue drains, the error is reported as unhandled even if a listener attaches later.

// starting early, awaiting late - the concurrency idiom
Future<Config> _cfgFuture;
Future<Config> loadConfig() => _cfgFuture ??= _loadConfig();

Future<void> main() async {
  final a = loadConfig();      // starts the work NOW
  final b = loadConfig();      // the same future - deduplicated
  final c = doSomethingElse(); // runs concurrently with the config load

  await c;
  await a;                     // and now it is awaited
}
// ...the memoisation is the point: a, b and every later call share one
// future, so the config is fetched once even under concurrent demand.

// listeners are independent
final f = fetchIt();
f.then((v) => log('one: $v'));
f.then((v) => log('two: $v'));      // both run
// ...but the ERROR path is not: an unhandled error is reported once, to the
// zone, and attaching a second handler later does not undo the report

// the ordering that causes the report
final f2 = fetchIt();      // may fail
await somethingElse();     // ...time passes; the microtask queue drains here
f2.catchError(log);        // too late - the error was already reported

// so attach the handler in the same expression
final f3 = fetchIt().catchError(log);
await somethingElse();
f3;                          // ...now nothing is unhandled

Timeouts, retries and backoff compose, and each has one rule that is easy to get wrong. A retry must only cover failures where the operation is idempotent or where a duplicate is harmless — retrying a POST can create two orders. Backoff must be jittered, because an uncoordinated retry storm from many clients is what turns a small outage into a sustained one. And a retry budget must be finite, because a retry loop with no limit is a denial of service against your own dependency.

// a retry that is actually correct
Future<T> retry<T>(
  Future<T> Function() f, {
  int attempts = 3,
  Duration base = const Duration(milliseconds: 200),
  bool Function(Object)? isRetryable = _isTransient,
}) async {
  Object? last;
  for (var i = 0; i < attempts; i++) {
    try {
      return await f();
    } catch (e) {
      // ...only transient failures are retried
      if (isRetryable != null && !isRetryable(e)) rethrow;
      last = e;
      // ...and the delay grows, with jitter so clients do not synchronise
      final jitter = base * (1 + (i * 37 % 11) / 10);
      await Future.delayed(jitter);
    }
  }
  throw last!;
}

bool _isTransient(Object e) =>
    e is SocketException || e is TimeoutException || e is HttpException;

// the version that is a bug
Future<T> retryBad<T>(Future<T> Function() f) async {
  while (true) {
    try { return await f(); } catch (e) { await Future.delayed(1s); }
  }
}
// ...infinite, un-jittered, retries permanent failures, and retries a POST

// the version that retries the wrong thing
Future<T> retryAll<T>(Future<T> Function() f) async {
  for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try { return await f(); } catch (e) { /* anything */ }
  }
}
// ...a 400 Bad Request is retried three times, and so is a null dereference

One more failure mode is specific to concurrency: a future that never settles because something it was waiting on will not settle. There is no error, no log and no stack — the caller simply stops progressing, which in an application looks like a spinner that never stops and in a test looks like a timeout with no diagnostic. The defences are structural: every Completer is completed on every path including the error path, every await of external work has a .timeout, and a test framework's own timeout is treated as a real signal rather than as flakiness to be retried.

// the hang, and its two causes
Future<void> hang1() async {
  final c = Completer<void>();
  if (shouldFail()) {
    c.completeError(StateError('x'));
    return;
  }
  if (await other()) {
    c.complete();              // ...completed only on the happy path
  }
  // ...every other path leaves c pending forever
}

Future<void> hang2() async {
  await somethingWithNoTimeout();   // the socket never answers
}

// the defence: a timeout is not optional on external work
Future<Row> load(String id) async {
  return await fetchRow(id).timeout(const Duration(seconds: 5));
}

// and the diagnostic that finds the rest
// In tests: an `AsyncTimeout` from the test framework is a real defect.
// At runtime: log every future that is created and not settled after N
// seconds, with the call site captured at creation:
//
//   final origin = StackTrace.current;
//   timer(const Duration(seconds: 30), () {
//     log('future from $origin never settled');
//   });
//
// ...which is worth having in a service, because the alternative is a
// goroutine- or isolate-count leak that shows up as memory growth

8.4 Sequential vs concurrent

Choosing between the three patterns, and the fourth that surprises people.

// 1. SEQUENTIAL: each depends on the previous
Future<User> full() async {
  final token = await login();
  final profile = await fetchProfile(token);
  final prefs = await fetchPreferences(token);
  return User(token, profile, prefs);
}

// 2. CONCURRENT: independent, all at once
Future<Dashboard> dashboard() async {
  final results = await Future.wait([
    fetchProfile(),
    fetchNotifications(),
    fetchRecentActivity(),
  ]);
  return Dashboard(results[0] as Profile, results[1] as Notifications, results[2] as Activity);
}

// 3. GATHERED: independent, but you want partial results
Future<Dashboard> dashboard2() async {
  final profile = await fetchProfile().then(Ok.new).onError(Err.new);
  final notifications = await fetchNotifications().then(Ok.new).onError(Err.new);

  // a partial dashboard, with placeholders for what failed
  return Dashboard(
    profile: profile.valueOrNull,
    notifications: notifications.valueOrNull,
  );
}

// 4. LAZY: independent, but you do not want them all
//    a stream, so each is consumed as it arrives
Stream<Widget> dashboardStream() async* {
  yield loading();
  final profile = await fetchProfile();
  yield profileLoaded(profile);
  final activity = await fetchRecentActivity();
  yield activityLoaded(activity);
}

// the timing, concretely: 3 x 500ms calls
// sequential: 1500ms
// Future.wait: 500ms
// stream:      first result at 500ms, all by 500ms, consumed as they land
// the pattern for N independent calls where you want progress
Future<List<T>> fetchAll<T>(
  List<Future<T>> futures, {
  void Function(int completed, int total)? onProgress,
}) async {
  var completed = 0;
  final tracked = futures.map((f) async {
    try {
      return await f;
    } finally {
      onProgress?.call(++completed, futures.length);
    }
  });
  return Future.wait(tracked);
}

// with a concurrency cap, so you do not open 500 sockets
Future<List<T>> fetchAllLimited<T>(
  List<Future<T> Function()> tasks, {
  int limit = 4,
}) async {
  final results = List<T?>.filled(tasks.length, null);
  var next = 0;

  Future<void> worker() async {
    while (next < tasks.length) {
      final i = next++;
      results[i] = await tasks[i]();
    }
  }

  await Future.wait([
    for (var i = 0; i < limit; i++) worker(),
  ]);
  return results.cast<T>();
}

Concurrency, and the three shapes that mean different things

Three forms of "run several things" look similar and are genuinely different: concurrent work is in flight at the same time but interleaves on one thread, parallel work runs simultaneously on more than one, and sequential work does not overlap at all. In Dart an async function that awaits I/O is concurrent, not parallel — the isolate is blocked while waiting. True parallelism needs an isolate, and that is a different tool with different costs.

ShapeSyntaxOverheadUse for
Sequentialawait a(); await b();NoneDependent steps
ConcurrentFuture.wait([a(), b()])Tasks/futuresIndependent I/O
Concurrent, boundedA pool with a limitTasksMany independent I/O
ParallelIsolate.runIsolate, copyCPU work
Stream-drivenasyncMapSubscriptionsPaced pipelines
// SEQUENTIAL: each starts after the previous settles
final a = await step1();
final b = await step2(a);       // needs a's result
final c = await step3(b);
// ...total time is the SUM, and b could not have started earlier anyway

// CONCURRENT: all start immediately
final t0 = DateTime.now();
final results = await Future.wait([fetchA(), fetchB(), fetchC()]);
// ...total time is the MAX, not the sum

// the mistake that makes them look sequential
final a = await step1();
final b = await step2();
final c = await step3();
// ...this is three sequential calls written as if concurrent. To start them
// all first and await after:
final fa = step1();
final fb = step2();
final fc = step3();
final all = await Future.wait([fa, fb, fc]);

// CONCURRENT WITH BOUNDING - the real-world answer
// 1000 requests to an API that allows 5 at a time
Future<List<T>> bounded<T>(
  List<Future<T> Function()> tasks, {
  int limit = 5,
}) async {
  final results = <T?>[];
  var index = 0;
  Future<void> worker() async {
    while (index < tasks.length) {
      final i = index++;
      results[i] = await tasks[i]();
    }
  }
  await Future.wait(List.generate(limit, (_) => worker()));
  return results.cast<T>();
}
// ...`index++` before the await is what makes this safe: no two workers take
// the same task, because there is no await between the read and the write

// PARALLEL, for CPU work
final result = await Isolate.run(() => heavyComputation(rows));
// ...a real second isolate. The closure and its captured data are copied, and
// the result is copied back - so the data must be sendable and the transfer
// cost must be smaller than the computation.

Choosing between Future.wait and a bounded pool is the decision that matters at scale, and it has a sharp edge: the futures passed to Future.wait all start immediately, so a list of a thousand of them opens a thousand connections. A bounded pool starts a fixed number and pulls from the queue as each finishes, which is the only correct answer for an unbounded or large list. The cost of a pool is a mutable shared index, and the one rule that makes it correct is that the increment must happen before any await.

// the WRONG bounded pool - two workers take the same task
Future<void> worker() async {
  while (index < tasks.length) {
    final i = index;          // read
    await something();        // ...and the other worker runs here
    results[i] = await tasks[i]();   // index has moved
  }
}

// the RIGHT one: claim before awaiting
Future<void> worker() async {
  while (true) {
    final i = index++;         // atomic with respect to the event loop
    if (i >= tasks.length) return;
    results[i] = await tasks[i]();
  }
}

// ...which is why `index++` must be the FIRST statement, and why a pool over
// thousands of tasks needs no lock: Dart's event loop is single-threaded, so
// there is no interleaving between two synchronous statements.

// the error variant, which is the harder one
Future<List<T>> boundedAll<T>(List<Future<T> Function()> tasks,
    {int limit = 5}) async {
  final results = <Result<T>>[];
  var index = 0;
  Future<void> worker() async {
    while (true) {
      final i = index++;
      if (i >= tasks.length) return;
      try {
        results[i] = Ok(await tasks[i]());
      } catch (e) {
        results[i] = Err('$e');       // ...one failure does not stop the pool
      }
    }
  }
  await Future.wait(List.generate(limit, (_) => worker()));
  return results;
}
// ...a Result per task, indexed by position, so the caller can attribute
// every outcome. A pool that stops at the first error leaves the rest
// unfinished, which is a different and usually unwanted semantic.

// and the version that is genuinely serialised, for a resource that allows
// exactly one user at a time
final lock = _Mutex();
await lock.run(() => touchExclusiveResource());
// ...package:async's Mutex, which is a queue over a single-user resource

Concurrency inside a single isolate has one limit that shapes a lot of design: there is one thread of execution, so a loop that does not await cannot be interrupted, and a loop that awaits too often does no work. Every await is a suspension point that costs a microtask turn, so a loop of a million iterations with an await in the body is dominated by the awaits rather than by the work. The exceptions are the operations that are genuinely asynchronous — file and socket I/O, timers, channel messages — because those release the isolate while they wait.

// await cost: a real measurement, not a guess
var sw = Stopwatch()..start();
for (var i = 0; i < 1000000; i++) {
  await Future.value(i);            // ~ a microtask per iteration
}
print(sw.elapsedMilliseconds);       // hundreds of ms, for NO work

sw.reset();
for (var i = 0; i < 1000000; i++) {
  sum += i;                         // free
}
print(sw.elapsedMilliseconds);       // a few ms

// so: batch the awaits
final batched = <int>[];
for (var i = 0; i < 1000000; i++) {
  batched.add(i);
  if (batched.length == 1000) {
    await processBatch(batched);
    batched.clear();
  }
}

// I/O does not pay this cost, because it actually waits
sw.reset();
for (final f in files) {
  await File(f).readAsString();      // real waiting, and the isolate is free
}
print(sw.elapsedMilliseconds);
// ...which is why "await everything" is correct for I/O and wrong for
// arithmetic.

// and the one thing that genuinely cannot be made concurrent here
final total = <int>[];
for (var i = 0; i < 10000000; i++) {
  total.add(expensive(i));           // no await: 10M synchronous iterations
}
// ...the isolate is blocked for the whole duration. `async` did not make it
// concurrent. Only an isolate or a `compute()` call does.

8.5 Streams

A sequence of events over time, and how to create one.

// a Stream is an asynchronous sequence, like a Future but many
Stream<int> countTo(int n) async* {
  for (var i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
    await Future.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 100));
    yield i;              // emit a value
  }
}

await for (final i in countTo(3)) {
  print(i);              // 1, 2, 3
}

// other ways to build one
Stream<int> fromList() => Stream.fromIterable([1, 2, 3]);
Stream<int> periodic() => Stream.periodic(const Duration(seconds: 1), (i) => i);
Stream<int> empty() => Stream<int>.empty();
Stream<int> error() => Stream<int>.error(Exception('x'));

// a broadcast stream: many listeners, no buffering, events are LOST
final controller = StreamController<int>.broadcast();
controller.add(1);
controller.add(2);       // if nobody is listening, these are dropped

// a single-subscription stream: one listener, events are BUFFERED
final c2 = StreamController<int>();
c2.add(1);              // buffered until someone listens
c2.add(2);

// and a Stream.fromIterable is a single-subscription stream
await for (final v in [1, 2, 3].stream) print(v);
// listening, with all the options
final subscription = stream.listen(
  (value) => print('data: $value'),
  onError: (Object e, StackTrace s) => print('error: $e'),
  onDone: () => print('done'),
  cancelOnError: false,
  pause: someCondition,          // start paused
);

subscription.resume();            // start flowing
subscription.pause();
subscription.cancel();            // MUST be cancelled: see 8.7

// transform a single-subscription stream into a broadcast one
final broadcast = stream.asBroadcastStream();

// convert between Stream and Future
final firstValue = await stream.first;             // completes on the first
final lastValue = await stream.last;               // on the last
final firstThree = await stream.take(3).toList();
final asFuture = await stream.reduce((a, b) => a + b);

// and the reverse
final oneValue = await Future.value(1);   // a Future
oneValue.asStream().listen(print);         // a Stream with one element

Stream, and what it adds over a list of futures

A stream is a sequence of events delivered over time, produced by one side and consumed by the other, with three properties no list of futures has: the sequence may be unbounded, the producer can react to how fast the consumer is reading, and a failure partway through is an ordinary event rather than the end of the world. That third property is what makes streams the right abstraction for sockets, file reads, log tails and UI events, and it is also what makes them more complex than futures.

FutureStream
ValuesExactly oneZero to unbounded
When producedOne momentOver time
ListenersMany, all get the valueOne, by default
Re-listenableYesSingle-subscription only
BackpressureNone neededBuilt in
Cancel by listenerNoYes, with a cancel
Error terminatesAlwaysOnly in some operators
// the sources
Stream<int> a = Stream.value(1);                    // one value, done
Stream<int> b = Stream.fromIterable([1, 2, 3]);
Stream<int> c = Stream.fromFuture(fetchIt());       // one, when it lands
Stream<int> d = Stream.periodic(                    // unbounded
  const Duration(seconds: 1), (i) => i);
Stream<int> e = Stream.empty();
Stream<void> f = Stream.fromFutures([f1(), f2()]);  // each as it arrives

// consuming, in the four ways
await for (final v in stream) { print(v); }         // the usual
final list = await stream.toList();                 // drain it
final first = await stream.first;                   // stop at the first
await stream.forEach(print);                        // note: awaits internally

// with error handling over the whole sequence
try {
  await for (final v in stream) { print(v); }
} on FormatException catch (e, s) {
  print('bad item: $e');
}

// cancelling a subscription
final sub = stream.listen(print);
await Future.delayed(const Duration(seconds: 1));
await sub.cancel();          // ...stops the producer. Without this, a
                             // periodic stream runs forever

// and a stream that is never listened to produces nothing at all
final lazy = Stream.fromFuture(fetchIt());
// ...no listener, no future created. A stream is lazy in a way a Future is
// not: the Future was already running.

Single-subscription versus broadcast is a distinction that must be chosen deliberately and cannot be changed later. A single-subscription stream has one listener and delivers events to it, which is what allows it to pause, buffer and resume the producer — that is where backpressure comes from. A broadcast stream has many listeners and delivers to all of them, and because it cannot know what one of them is doing, it has to drop events or buffer unboundedly. So a broadcast stream silently loses data under backpressure, and the choice is not a style decision.

// single-subscription: the default, and backpressure-capable
final controller = StreamController<int>();
final sub = controller.stream.listen(print);
// ...the producer can pause: the controller's onListen/onPause and the
// subscription's pause() signal a consumer that is not keeping up

// BROADCAST: multiple listeners, no backpressure
final b = StreamController<int>.broadcast();
b.stream.listen(print);
b.stream.listen(print);
b.add(1);                        // both receive it

// the cost: a slow listener drops events
final slow = StreamController<int>.broadcast(
  onListen: (s) => s.pause(),
);
slow.stream.listen((v) async {
  await Future.delayed(const Duration(seconds: 1));
  print(v);                       // ...a slow consumer
});
slow.add(1);
slow.add(2);                      // 2 may be delivered before 1 finishes

// so the rule
// single-subscription: a pipeline, a file, a socket, anything consumed once
// broadcast:            an event bus, a UI state notifier, anything with
//                       several independent consumers

// and a broadcast stream cannot be awaited twice
final bs = StreamController<int>.broadcast();
bs.stream.listen(print);
bs.stream.listen(print);
bs.close();
await bs.stream.toList();         // ERROR or empty - already delivered

Controlling the producer is what makes a stream a real abstraction rather than a callback with nicer syntax. A StreamController exposes onListen, onPause and onResume, so the producer can start work when someone starts listening and suspend it when the consumer falls behind. That is what makes reading a large file or consuming a socket without dropping data possible, and it is the reason a hand-rolled producer loop that ignores these callbacks will buffer without limit.

// a controller that respects backpressure
class PagedSource extends Stream<Row> {
  final String path;
  PagedSource(this.path);

  @override
  StreamSubscription<Row> listen(void Function(Row)? onData,
      {Function? onError, void Function()? onDone, bool? cancelOnError}) {
    late StreamSubscription<Row> sub;
    var offset = 0;
    var reading = false;

    Future<void> pump() async {
      if (reading) return;      // one read in flight at a time
      reading = true;
      try {
        while (true) {
          if (sub.isPaused) return;      // ...stop; onResume restarts us
          final page = await readPage(path, offset);
          if (page.isEmpty) break;
          offset += page.length;
          sub.add(page.first);
        }
      } finally {
        reading = false;
      }
    }

    sub = Stream<Row>.multi((c) {
      c.onPause = () => sub.pause();
      c.onResume = () => pump();
      pump();
    }).listen(onData, onError: onError, onDone: onDone);

    return sub;
  }
}
// ...the essential shape is `if (sub.isPaused) return;` plus a resume hook -
// everything else is bookkeeping.

// the simpler version, when the producer is a Future per page
Stream<Row> paged(String path) async* {
  var offset = 0;
  while (true) {
    final page = await readPage(path, offset);
    if (page.isEmpty) return;
    offset += page.length;
    yield* page;                  // ...one yield per row, and the consumer's
                                  // pacing suspends this generator
  }
}
// ...which gets backpressure FOR FREE, because a suspended async* generator
// is not resumed until the consumer asks for more. This is the shape to
// prefer over a hand-written controller.

8.6 Stream operators

The transformation pipeline, and where it differs from an Iterable one.

final numbers = Stream.fromIterable([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);

// transform
numbers.map((e) => e * 2);
numbers.expand((e) => [e, e]);
numbers.cast<int>();
numbers.followedBy(Stream.value(6));

// filter
numbers.where((e) => e.isEven);
numbers.take(2);
numbers.skip(3);
numbers.takeWhile((e) => e < 4);
numbers.skipWhile((e) => e < 3);
numbers.distinct();

// aggregate (terminal - these close the stream)
await numbers.reduce((a, b) => a + b);
await numbers.fold<int>(0, (a, b) => a + b);
await numbers.toList();
await numbers.toSet();
await numbers.length;
await numbers.every((e) => e > 0);
await numbers.contains(3);
await numbers.first;
await numbers.last;
await numbers.single;

// combine streams
Stream<int> a = Stream.value(1);
Stream<int> b = Stream.value(2);

final zipped = a.asyncMap((v) async => v * 10);   // async transform
await a.toList(); await b.toList();

// merge: events interleaved as they arrive
Stream<int> merged() async* {
  yield* Stream.fromIterable([1, 2]);
  yield* Stream.fromIterable([3, 4]);
}

// concatenate: strictly sequential
Stream<int> sequential() async* {
  yield* Stream.fromIterable([1, 2]);
  await Future.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 100));
  yield* Stream.fromIterable([3, 4]);
}

// the important difference from Iterable: map with an async callback
// needs asyncMap, because Stream preserves order
final delayed = numbers.asyncMap((e) async {
  await Future.delayed(Duration(milliseconds: 100 * e));
  return e * 2;
});
// unlike Iterable.map, which would give you Futures

The operators, and which ones change termination

Streams have a large operator set, and the ones that matter are the transformations and the ones that decide what an error or a closed subscription does to the sequence. The transformation operators — map, where, expand, asyncMap, take, skip, distinct, fold — are lazy and composable. The termination operators are the ones to be careful with, because await for cancels on an error while listen does not unless told to.

OperatorShapeNotes
map1 → 1Sync; an exception propagates
asyncMap1 → 1Awaited, in order
where1 → 0/1The filter
expand1 → nFlattens an iterable
asyncExpand1 → streamFlattens a future stream
take / skipnTerminates the stream
takeWhile0..nTerminates on the first false
distinct1 → 0/1Uses ==
fold / reducen → 1Closes the stream
toListn → 1Materialises; loses laziness
handleError—Swallows or rethrows errors
transform—A custom operator
// the transformations, composed
final names = raw
    .where((r) => r.active)
    .map((r) => r.name.trim())
    .where((n) => n.isNotEmpty)
    .distinct()                     // consecutive duplicates
    .toList();

// asyncMap: sequential by default, which is usually what you want
final enriched = raw.asyncMap((r) async => await enrich(r));
// ...each element is awaited before the next starts, so order is preserved
// and there is never more than one request in flight

// the concurrent variant - unbounded, and usually a mistake
final all = await Future.wait(raw.map(enrich).toList());

// a bounded concurrent map, which is the shape that scales
Stream<R> mapConcurrent<T, R>(
  Stream<T> src,
  Future<R> Function(T) f, {
  int concurrency = 5,
}) async* {
  final inFlight = <Future<void>>[];
  await for (final item in src) {
    inFlight.add(f(item).then((r) => sinkAdd(r)));
    if (inFlight.length >= concurrency) {
      await Future.wait(inFlight);
      inFlight.clear();
    }
  }
  await Future.wait(inFlight);
}
// ...(simplified; the real one needs a sink) - the shape is: keep at most N
// futures, await the batch, repeat

// expand versus flatMap over an iterable
final ids = orders.expand((o) => o.itemIds).toList();

// takeWhile, which terminates rather than filters - an important difference
Stream<int> uptoZero(List<int> xs) async* {
  for (final x in xs) {
    if (x == 0) return;            // STOPS
    yield x;
  }
}
final stopped = source.takeWhile((x) => x != 0).toList();
// ...where(cond) with the same predicate would filter to empty

// handleError: swallow, log, or replace
final safe = source.handleError((e, s) {
  log('item failed', e, s);          // swallow: the stream CONTINUES
});
final loud = source.handleError((e, s) => throw e);   // rethrow: it ends

Whether an error terminates a stream depends on the operator and on how it was consumed, and the difference is the single most common source of "my loop stopped halfway". await for cancels the subscription on an error — the error propagates out of the loop and the stream is done. listen without cancelOnError: true keeps going. handleError without rethrowing keeps going. And a source that is a Stream.fromIterable wrapped in a failing operator terminates at the failure. So the same source behaves differently depending on the consumer, which is the thing to check first when a sequence truncates.

// three consumers, three behaviours
final src = Stream.fromIterable([1, 2, 3, 4]).map((x) {
  if (x == 3) throw StateError('bad $x');
  return x;
});

// 1. await for - the error propagates and the stream is cancelled
try {
  await for (final v in src) { print(v); }
} on StateError catch (e) {
  print('$e');                 // prints 1, 2, then this
}

// 2. listen - continues past the error
src.listen(
  print,
  onError: (Object e, StackTrace s) => print('err: $e'),
  onDone: () => print('done'),
);
// prints 1, 2, err: bad 3, done
// ...so the elements AFTER the failure are still delivered

// 3. handleError - converts the error into a value, and continues
src.handleError((e, s) => print('skipped')).listen(print);
// prints 1, 2, skipped

// 4. transform into a Result stream, which is the honest shape
src.transform(StreamTransformer<int, Object>.fromHandlers(
  handleError: (e, s, sink) => sink.add(e),
)).listen((Object v) {
  if (v is int) { … } else { log('failed: $v'); }
});
// ...nothing terminates, and every element is either a value or a failure

// the combination that is correct for a data pipeline
await for (final outcome in src.transform(_toOutcome)) {
  switch (outcome) {
    case Ok(:final value): apply(value);
    case Err(:final error): log('skipping', error);
  }
}

A stream operator is a StreamTransformer, and writing one is the general way to add behaviour without a manual subscription. A transformer has a bind method that takes the source and returns a new stream, and helpers like fromHandlers cover the common cases — mapping, adding a sink callback, or intercepting errors. Knowing this is what makes the ecosystem's operators readable rather than mysterious, and it is how you write one that is specific to your domain.

// a custom transformer, the explicit form
class _Debounce<T> extends StreamTransformerBase<T, T> {
  final Duration duration;
  _Debounce(this.duration);

  @override
  Stream<T> bind(Stream<T> source) {
    Timer? timer;
    T? pending;
    var hasPending = false;
    late StreamController<T> controller;

    controller = StreamController<T>(
      onListen: () {
        source.listen(
          (v) {
            pending = v;
            hasPending = true;
            timer?.cancel();
            timer = Timer(duration, () {
              controller.add(pending as T);
              hasPending = false;
            });
          },
          onError: controller.addError,
          onDone: () {
            timer?.cancel();
            if (hasPending) controller.add(pending as T);
            controller.close();
          },
        );
      },
      onPause: () => timer?.cancel(),
      onResume: () {
        if (hasPending) {
          timer = Timer(duration, () {
            controller.add(pending as T);
            hasPending = false;
          });
        }
      },
    );
    return controller.stream;
  }
}

final debounced = source.transform(_Debounce(const Duration(milliseconds: 300)));

// the short form, for the common cases
final mapped = source.transform(StreamTransformer.fromHandlers(
  handleData: (v, sink) => sink.add(process(v)),
  handleError: (e, s, sink) => sink.addError(e, s),
));

// and package:async's versions, which handle the lifecycle correctly
final d2 = source.debounce(const Duration(milliseconds: 300));
final t2 = source.timeout(const Duration(seconds: 5));
final w = source.takeUntil(cancelSignal);

8.7 Subscriptions and lifecycle

The leak every Dart developer hits once, and the patterns that prevent it.

// THE PROBLEM
void onMount() {
  stream.listen(print);
  Timer.periodic(const Duration(seconds: 1), tick);
}
// nothing cancels either, and both keep the object alive forever
