// THE FIX: hold the handles and cancel them
class Widget1 {
  StreamSubscription? _sub;
  Timer? _timer;

  void start() {
    _sub = stream.listen(print);
    _timer = Timer.periodic(const Duration(seconds: 1), tick);
  }

  void dispose() {
    _sub?.cancel();
    _timer?.cancel();
  }
}

// and for a StreamController, the controller too
class Widget2 {
  final _controller = StreamController<int>();

  Stream<int> get output => _controller.stream;
  final _sub = Stream.periodic(const Duration(seconds: 1), (i) => i).listen(null);
  final _timer = Timer.periodic(const Duration(seconds: 5), (_) => _controller.add(1));

  void dispose() async {
    await _sub.cancel();
    _timer.cancel();
    await _controller.close();
  }
}

// the leak-free stream pattern: a Stream that manages its own
// subscriptions via a StreamController and onCancel
Stream<T> periodicValues(Duration interval) {
  late StreamController<T> controller;
  Timer? timer;

  controller = StreamController<T>(
    onListen: () {
      timer = Timer.periodic(interval, (_) => controller.add(interval));
    },
    onCancel: () {
      timer?.cancel();        // this is what makes it leak-free
    },
  );
  return controller.stream;
}

// in Flutter, this is what State.dispose() is for, and why
// "setState() called after dispose()" is the symptom of this bug
// single vs broadcast: a design decision with real consequences
// single-subscription (the default):
//   - one listener only
//   - events are buffered until it attaches
//   - the producer is paused when the consumer is slow
//   - the RIGHT choice for most app code

// broadcast:
//   - many listeners
//   - NO buffering: an event with no listener is gone
//   - the producer is never paused
//   - the RIGHT choice for an event bus

class EventBus {
  final _controller = StreamController<Event>.broadcast();
  Stream<Event> get events => _controller.stream;

  void publish(Event e) => _controller.add(e);
  Future<void> close() => _controller.close();
}

final bus = EventBus();
bus.events.listen(print);
bus.publish(Event.login());      // delivered

// for values, broadcast is a bug waiting to happen
final values = StreamController<int>.broadcast();
values.add(1);      // if the listener attaches later, it NEVER sees 1
// use a plain controller, or a BehaviorSubject from rxdart

Subscriptions, lifecycle, and the leak that looks like a memory bug

A StreamSubscription is a live registration between a consumer and a producer. It has a lifecycle — created, active, paused, cancelled, done — and every method that creates one creates a resource that must be released. The most common stream bug in production is a subscription that is never cancelled, which keeps its source alive and its events flowing after nobody is listening.

MethodEffectWhen to use
listenStarts deliveryAlways
pause() / resume()Buffers or throttlesBackpressure
cancel()Releases everythingOn disposal
asFuture()Awaits completion or errorSingle-subscription
isPausedReads the current stateIn a producer
onData/onError/onDoneReplaces the handlerTo swap behaviour
// the lifecycle, and where each thing happens
late StreamSubscription<T> sub;
sub = stream.listen(
  onData,                                        // 1. called per event
  onError: (e, s) => log('$e'),                // 2. called on error
  onDone: () => cleanup(),                     // 3. called when closed
  cancelOnError: true,                           // 4. then auto-cancels
);
await sub.cancel();                              // 5. release

// the leak: a subscription nobody cancels
class Widget {
  void init() {
    _sub = ticker.stream.listen((t) => setState(() => _tick(t)));
    // ...if `dispose` never cancels it, the stream keeps calling setState
    // on a disposed object, and the ticker keeps the widget alive
  }
  void dispose() {
    _sub.cancel();               // ...without this, every rebuild adds one
    _controller.close();
  }
}

// waiting for a stream to finish as a Future
final result = await stream.asFuture();           // completes on done
// ...throws the last error instead of completing, and is single-subscription
// only - a second call throws StateError

// pausing and resuming, which is the throttle
sub.pause();
await Future.delayed(const Duration(seconds: 1));
sub.resume();     // the buffered events arrive, in order, no loss

// cancelling inside a handler is legal and common
source.listen((v) {
  if (v == stop) { sub.cancel(); return; }   // ...a self-terminating source
});

// awaiting completion with a timeout
await sub.asFuture().timeout(const Duration(seconds: 5));

Two stream rules catch people out and are worth stating exactly. A single-subscription stream cannot be listened to twice — not sequentially after the first listener cancels, and not in two places at once — so a stream stored in a field and passed to two consumers throws. And a stream is lazy: creating one does nothing, so a stream built in a constructor and never listened to never runs its producer, and a subscription is what starts everything. That is the opposite of a Future, whose work has already begun by the time it exists.

// double listen, on both kinds of stream
final single = Stream.fromIterable([1, 2, 3]);
single.listen(print);
single.listen(print);          // ERROR: Stream has already been listened to

final multi = Stream.fromIterable([1, 2, 3]).asBroadcastStream();
multi.listen(print);
multi.listen(print);           // fine - but the second listener misses
                              // events emitted before it subscribed

// the pattern that works: build a fresh stream each time
Stream<Row> rows() => controller.stream.asBroadcastStream();
void a() => rows().listen(print);
void b() => rows().listen(print);   // ...separate subscriptions

// or share explicitly, which is what Rx does
final shared = controller.stream.share();
// ...package:rxdart's share(), which refcounts subscribers and starts and
// stops the source as they come and go

// laziness, contrasted
final f = fetchIt();          // work STARTS here
final s = controller.stream;  // work does NOT start here
s.listen(print);              // ...work starts HERE
// ...so a Future is eager and a Stream is lazy, and a field holding a Stream
// holds a recipe rather than a result.

// the pattern that follows from laziness: a stream field must be
// initialised before it is listened to, and the controller closed to end it
class Feed {
  final _controller = StreamController<Event>();
  Stream<Event> get events => _controller.stream;

  void emit(Event e) => _controller.add(e);
  Future<void> close() => _controller.close();
}
// ...never `late StreamSubscription` reused across rebuilds, and always
// close the controller, or `onDone` never fires

The framework version of the leak is worth naming because it is where most real stream bugs live. A subscription created in a widget's initState must be cancelled in dispose, and a controller created as a field must be closed — and the two failures look different. An uncancelled subscription keeps calling setState after the element is gone, which throws on every subsequent event. An unclosed controller means onDone never fires, so any await stream.first in a consumer hangs forever, and the controller holds its buffer, so memory grows with each discarded subscription.

// the disposable pair, in a Flutter widget
class Feed extends StatefulWidget {
  const Feed({super.key, required this.source});
  final Stream<Row> source;
  @override
  State<Feed> createState() => _FeedState();
}

class _FeedState extends State<Feed> {
  final _rows = <Row>[];
  StreamSubscription<Row>? _sub;

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    _sub = widget.source.listen(
      (row) => setState(() => _rows.add(row)),
      onError: (Object e, StackTrace s) {
        if (!mounted) return;                 // ...the guard that matters
        ScaffoldMessenger.of(context).showSnackBar(
          SnackBar(content: Text('$e')),
        );
      },
    );
  }

  @override
  void didUpdateWidget(Feed old) {
    super.didUpdateWidget(old);
    if (old.source != widget.source) {
      _sub?.cancel();                          // ...re-subscribe on a new source
      _sub = widget.source.listen((r) => setState(() => _rows.add(r)));
    }
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _sub?.cancel();                            // ...and here
    super.dispose();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) => ListView(
    children: _rows.map((r) => Text('${r.id}')).toList(),
  );
}
// ...the three things every subscription needs: cancel in dispose, cancel
// and resubscribe in didUpdateWidget when the source changes, and a mounted
// check in every callback that touches the tree

// and the ServiceLocator-free alternative for non-UI code
final disposeBag = DisposeBag();
disposeBag.add(source.listen(handle));
disposeBag.add(timer);
// ...disposeBag.dispose() in shutdown - which makes the symmetry visible in
// one place instead of spread over a destructor

8.8 Future or Stream?

The decision, and the conversions between them.

// Future: exactly one result, eventually
//   - an HTTP request
//   - a database read
//   - a file write
//   - anything with a single answer

// Stream: zero or more results, over time
//   - user input events
//   - a WebSocket
//   - a database watch/change feed
//   - a periodic timer
//   - progress reporting
//   - a generator pipeline

// THE CONVERSIONS, which are the whole answer to "which one"
Future<T>    -> Stream<T>     via .asStream()          (one value)
Stream<T>    -> Future<T>     via .first / .last / .reduce
Stream<T>    -> Future<List<T>> via .toList()          (wait for all)
Stream<T>    -> Future<void>  via .forEach(dart:async)  (consume, discard)

// a progress-reporting operation, done well
Stream<int> uploadWithProgress(File file, String url) async* {
  yield 0;                                    // start
  final chunkSize = 1024 * 1024;
  var sent = 0;

  for (var offset = 0; offset < file.lengthSync(); offset += chunkSize) {
    final end = min(offset + chunkSize, file.lengthSync());
    final bytes = await file.openRead(offset, end).fold<List<int>>(
      <int>[],
      (acc, data) => acc..addAll(data),
    );
    await httpPost(url, bytes);
    sent += end - offset;
    yield (sent / file.lengthSync() * 100).round();   // a percentage
  }
}

// and the consumer
final subscription = uploadWithProgress(file, url).listen((percent) {
  setProgressBar(percent);
  if (percent == 100) setDone();
});
// debounce, throttle, and the operator combinations you need
// rxdart provides these; here is what they mean

// debounce: wait for a pause in the events
//   a search box: only search after the user stops typing
searchInput
    .debounce(const Duration(milliseconds: 300))
    .distinct()
    .switchMap((q) => search(q))     // cancel the previous request
    .listen(render);

// throttle: emit at most once per interval
scrollPosition
    .throttle(const Duration(milliseconds: 16), trailing: true)
    .listen(render);

// auditTime: the last value in a window
events.auditTime(const Duration(seconds: 1)).listen(flush);

// combineLatest: a value whenever ANY source changes
combineLatest([searchQuery, filter, page], (q, f, p) => ...)
    .debounce(const Duration(milliseconds: 200))
    .listen(refresh);

// switchMap is the important one for correctness: it CANCELS the
// previous inner stream when a new value arrives, which is what
// stops an older, slower response overwriting a newer one.
// concatMap queues them. mergeMap runs them concurrently.

Future or Stream, and the three questions that decide

The choice is usually presented as "one value or many", which is true and almost never the deciding question. The deciding questions are: when is the consumer ready, is the set finite, and does the producer's work depend on consumption. A single button tap that will produce one answer is a future even if the answer arrives in pieces; a log file that is still being written is a stream even if it will eventually end.

SituationUseBecause
One result, awaited nowFutureNothing else fits
One result, maybe neverFutureA stream cannot express "zero"
Values as they arriveStreamWaiting to batch loses the first ones
A file being readStreamMemory, and progress
User eventsStreamUnbounded, and cancellable
A request and a responseFutureExactly one reply
A large query's rowsStreamDo not hold them all
Several requests, any resultFuture.waitBounded and finite
A long-running progress reportStreamMany, and the timing matters
// a Future for the button
Future<Result> onPressed() async {
  setState(() => _loading = true);
  final r = await api.save();
  setState(() => _loading = false);
  return r;
}
// ...one answer, the caller wants it now, and there is nothing to stream

// a Stream for a file, so memory is bounded and progress is real
Stream<Row> readRows(String path) async* {
  final handle = await File(path).open();
  try {
    String? line;
    while ((line = await handle.readLine()) != null) {
      yield Row.parse(line);         // ...one at a time, and the consumer's
    }                                 //    pacing suspends this generator
  } finally {
    await handle.close();
  }
}

// a Stream for progress on a long job
final progress = StreamController<int>();
Future<void> run() async {
  for (var i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
    await step(i);
    progress.add(i);                  // ...UI updates as it happens
  }
  await progress.close();
}

// the WRONG shape for the same job
Future<int> runBad() async {
  var total = 0;
  for (var i = 0; i < 100; i++) total += await step(i);
  return total;
  // ...no way to report progress, and the caller is blocked for the whole
  // duration with nothing to show
}

// several requests, any result: futures
final all = await Future.wait([a(), b(), c()]);

// several requests, each reporting as it lands: a stream of one item each
final each = Stream.fromFutures([a(), b(), c()]);
// ...or, for a fan-in that preserves the source order:
Stream.fromFutures([a(), b(), c()])

A third shape sits between them and is used constantly without being named: a stream that emits exactly one event. It is the right answer when the producer is naturally streaming — a socket that sends one reply, a platform channel, a broadcast event of which one instance is expected — because it makes the resource's lifetime explicit and the cancellation natural, in a way that bolting a Future onto a StreamController does not.

// one value, but from a streaming source - a platform channel
final reply = _channel
    .receiveBroadcastStream()
    .map((m) => m['result'] as String)
    .first;                       // one value, then the source is cancelled
// ...`.first` cancels the subscription, so the channel is released. Without
// it, the channel stays subscribed forever.

// the explicit form, which is clearer and cancellable
Future<String> ask(String q) async {
  final controller = StreamController<String>();
  late StreamSubscription sub;
  sub = _channel.receiveBroadcastStream().listen(
    (m) {
      controller.add(m['result'] as String);
      controller.close();
      sub.cancel();               // ...release the source
    },
    onError: (e, s) {
      controller.addError(e, s);
      sub.cancel();
    },
  );
  return controller.stream.single;
}

// where a broadcast stream is the right shape for a cache
final cache = StreamController<Config>.broadcast();
Config get current => _latest;
cache.stream.listen((c) => _latest = c);
// ...many listeners, each notified on change, none owning the value. This is
// what package:rxdart's BehaviorSubject does, and hand-rolling it with a
// StreamController plus a field is the standard alternative.

// and the anti-pattern: a stream used as a field when a Future would do
class User {
  final Stream<User?> changes;   // ...every consumer must listen separately
}
final user = User();
user.changes.listen(print);
user.changes.listen(save);          // ...two listeners, and the second misses
                                    // anything emitted before it attached

The conversion costs are worth knowing in both directions, because a codebase accumulates both. Future to stream is one value on an otherwise-empty stream, so Stream.value(future) or async* { yield f; } — trivial and free. Stream to future is first (take the first), last, single (exactly one, throwing otherwise), fold (accumulate) or toList (materialise), and the last two trade laziness for a value. Converting a lazy pipeline to a future with toList is the decision that removes the backpressure, so it should be made deliberately rather than to satisfy a signature.

// future -> stream: one value
Stream<T> once<T>(Future<T> f) async* {
  yield await f;
}

// stream -> future: four reductions with different contracts
final firstRow = await rows.first;             // throws if empty
final firstOrNull = await rows.firstOrNull;    // null if empty
final only = await rows.single;                // throws if 0 or >1 - the
                                             // right assertion for "exactly one"
final all = await rows.toList();               // materialises
final joined = await rows.map((r) => r.id).join(',');   // lazy until join

// the pipeline-to-future conversion and what it costs
Stream<Row> lazyPipeline() async* {
  yield* source.where(p1).map(t1).where(p2);
}

// GOOD: keeps the laziness, processes as they arrive
await for (final r in lazyPipeline()) { process(r); }

// BAD: the signature demanded a Future, so everything is buffered
Future<List<Row>> bad() => lazyPipeline().toList();
// ...for 10 million rows that is an out-of-memory error, and the only fix is
// to change the signature. This is the failure the reduction rules are for.

// the direction that is genuinely irreversible
final streamOfRows = (await fetchRows()).asStream();  // fine, a list
final rowsFromStream = await streamFromDb.toList();   // now a list - the
                                                      // laziness is gone

8.9 Zones, briefly

The legacy error mechanism, and when you still need it.

// a Zone is a context that asynchronous callbacks run inside.
// it is how the Dart VM, and Flutter, capture errors.

// the main use: app-wide error reporting
runZonedGuarded(() async {
  await main();
}, (error, stack) {
  CrashReporter.report(error, stack);
});

// the original use, and what replaced it
runZoned(() {
  // read a value later, even from inside a callback
  final lang = Zone.current[#lang] as String?;
  Timer.run(() => print(lang));      // still works in the callback
});

// WHAT REPLACED WHAT
//
// Zones were once the only way to get an error from an async
// callback. Today:
//   - Future errors: try/catch with await, or .catchError
//   - Stream errors: onError, or try/catch inside an async* body
//   - app-wide: runZonedGuarded, or Flutter's
//     FlutterError.onError and PlatformDispatcher.onError
//
// ZONES REMAIN USEFUL FOR:
//   - per-request context: a request id, a user id, a locale, that
//     every callback in that scope can read without a parameter
//   - performance measurement scoped to a subtree
//   - test isolation for time

// a modern, useful zone: ambient request context
final requestZone = Zone.current.fork(
  zoneValues: {#requestId: generateId()},
);

Future<void> handleRequest(Request req) {
  return requestZone.run(() async {
    await process(req);                 // any callback in here can
    await audit();                      // read Zone.current[#requestId]
  });
}

String get currentRequestId => Zone.current[#requestId] as String? ?? 'none';

Newer Dart code mostly avoids zones. They are still the mechanism behind runZonedGuarded for app-wide error capture, and they remain genuinely useful for ambient context. But if you find yourself reaching for one to solve a Future or Stream error problem, the answer is a normal try/catch.

Exercises 9

  1. Write the lost-update example from 8.1, confirm the bug, then fix it three different ways.
  2. Time three sequential 300ms calls, then the same three with Future.wait. Record both.
  3. Write a search box with debounce and switchMap, and confirm a slow earlier response never overwrites a newer one.
  4. Build an upload function that reports progress as a Stream, and consume it with a progress bar.
  5. Write a leak: a Stream with no cancel, then find it with the DevTools memory panel. Then fix it with onCancel.
  6. Implement fetchAllLimited and prove it never opens more than N connections.
  7. Write a broadcast event bus and demonstrate an event being dropped when nobody is listening. Then explain when that is correct.

Zones, and why they are not an error-handling mechanism

A zone is an error-handling context that asynchronous work inherits. It captures the error handler and a set of values at the moment it is created, and every future, timer and callback started inside it reports errors there. That is the whole mechanism, and it exists because an asynchronous error has no call stack to propagate along: a future that fails three awaits later has no synchronous caller left to catch it, and a zone supplies the missing root.

// the one thing a zone is for: a root for async errors
runZonedGuarded(() {
  unawaited(fetchThatMayFail());
  Timer.run(() => throw StateError('from a timer'));
  Future(() => throw StateError('from a future'));
}, (error, stack) {
  report(error, stack);       // ...one place, for errors with no caller
});

// ...which is how a framework installs a global reporter without touching
// every call site, and how Flutter's `FlutterError.onError` is wired

// what it does NOT do
runZonedGuarded(() {
  throw StateError('sync');        // ...a SYNCHRONOUS throw leaves the zone
}, (e, st) {
  report(e, st);                    //    body and propagates to the caller
});
// ...the handler is for ASYNCHRONOUS errors. Synchronous errors inside the
// body need a try/catch in the body. This is the most common misunderstanding.

// zones nest, and the innermost handler wins for errors originating in it
runZonedGuarded(() {
  runZonedGuarded(() {
    unawaited(fail());
  }, (e, s) {
    log('inner: $e');      // ...this one is called
  });
}, (e, s) {
  log('outer: $e');        // ...and this is not
});

// the values half: request-scoped data without a parameter
runZoned(() {
  Zone.current.fork(zoneValues: {#requestId: id}).run(() async {
    await handleRequest();
    final rid = Zone.current[#requestId];      // ...still in scope here
  });
}, zoneSpecification: ZoneSpecification(
  print: (self, parent, zone, line) {
    log('[$line] [${zone[#requestId]}]');     // ...every print, tagged
  },
  printAsync: (self, parent, zone, line) {
    log('[$line] [${zone[#requestId]}]');
  },
));
// ...which is request-scoped logging without threading a logger through every
// function, and it is the one thing a zone is genuinely good at

The cost of a zone is that it makes behaviour depend on where code is called from rather than on what it is passed, which is the property that makes a zone invisible. A function that reads Zone.current[#requestId] works in a zone that has the value and silently produces null everywhere else — a defect that appears only when the function is reused outside its original caller. It also makes tests order-dependent, because the zone's state is ambient and a test that leaves it dirty affects the next one. Zone reads are therefore best confined to infrastructure — logging, tracing, an error reporter — and never in the middle of a call chain that a reader is trying to follow.

// ambient state, and the bug it produces
Future<void> handleRequest() async {
  final rid = Zone.current[#requestId];
  await doWork();
  log('[$rid] done');        // null if called outside the zone - and it is
                              // never an error, so it ships
}

test('handles a request', () async {
  await runZonedGuarded(() => handleRequest(),
      (e, s) => fail('$e'));
});

test('handles it again', () async {
  // ...if the first test left #requestId set, this one logs the WRONG id
});

// the rule: zone reads at the boundary, explicit parameters everywhere else
Future<void> handleRequest(String requestId) async {
  await doWork(requestId);       // ...passed, so testable and visible
}

Future<void> instrumented(String requestId) {
  return runZonedGuarded(() => handleRequest(requestId), (e, s) {
    report(e, s, requestId: requestId);
  });
}

// and Zone.current.fork vs Zone.current.run - fork COPIES
final zone = Zone.current.fork(zoneSpecification: ZoneSpecification(
  handleUncaughtError: (self, parent, zone, e, s) => parent.handleUncaughtError(e, s),
));
zone.run(() {
  // ...inside, Zone.current IS `zone`; outside, it is unchanged
});
// ...fork is how you extend a zone; run is how you enter one. Confusing them
// is why an overridden print sometimes applies and sometimes does not

Since Dart 2.19 the package package:async's catchError and guarded cover the common cases without a zone, and package:async's FutureExtensions also provide timeout, ignore and onError. A zone remains the right tool for three specific things: a root reporter for a whole application or isolate, request-scoped ambient values for logging or tracing, and a way to override a callback the libraries you call will use — print, the uncaught-error handler, a timer factory. Everything else is better expressed as an explicit parameter, because that is what makes the dependency visible and the code testable.

// the modern replacements for the three zone uses
// 1. a root reporter, without a zone
Future<void> main() async {
  await runZonedGuarded(() async {
    FlutterError.onError = (details) => report(details);
    PlatformDispatcher.instance.onError = (e, s) {
      report(e, s);
      return true;                 // ...handled: do not crash
    };
    await run();
  }, (e, s) => report(e, s));
}

// 2. request-scoped values, with an explicit parameter
Future<void> handle(Request req) async {
  final rid = req.id;
  return logAround('[$rid]', () => doWork(req));
}

// 3. overriding a callback, which IS what a zone is uniquely good at
final timing = Zone.current.fork(zoneSpecification: ZoneSpecification(
  createTimer: (self, parent, zone, d, f) => parent.createTimer(zone, d, f),
));
timing.run(() {
  // ...a test can substitute a fake clock here, which no parameter can do
  await retry(backoff: Duration(milliseconds: 10));
});

// and the one place a zone remains the best answer
// error tracking across an entire isolate, including errors from libraries,
// third-party code and timers you do not control
runZonedGuarded(() {
  Sentry.init((e, s) => Sentry.capture(e, s));
  runApp(const App());
}, (e, s) => Sentry.capture(e, s));

// ...note: do NOT write raw log output to STDOUT in a release build - use a
// logging package that buffers, rotates and can be disabled by level

9 · Isolates and Concurrency

9.1 Dart's concurrency model9.2 What to put in an isolate9.3 Spawning an isolate9.4 Transferables, and the copy problem9.5 SendPort, ReceivePort and raw messaging9.10 Isolate.run and IsolateGroup9.11 A long-lived worker isolate9.12 Flutter: compute and isolates

The single-threaded event loop means long work blocks everything, including your UI. Isolates are the answer, and this chapter is about using them correctly.

9.1 Dart's concurrency model

The model in one picture, and what it means in practice.

// ONE isolate = ONE thread = ONE event loop
//
//   isolate A                      isolate B
//   +--------------+               +--------------+
//   | event loop   |               | event loop   |
//   |  microtask   |               |  microtask   |
//   |    queue     |               |    queue     |
//   +--------------+               +--------------+
//         |  message passing (copies or transfers)  |
//         +-----------------------------------------+
//
// inside one isolate, only one thing runs at a time, but:
//   - the thread is released at every await
//   - a long SYNCHRONOUS computation blocks everything
//
// the key consequence: `await` is not parallelism, and neither is
// Future.wait. Those are concurrency. Real parallelism needs an
// isolate (or the platform's own threads).
// what blocks
void bad() {
  for (var i = 0; i < 100000000; i++) {
    sum += i;      // no await anywhere: the UI is frozen for seconds
  }
}

// yielding does NOT help: it lets events run, but the work is
// still single-threaded and still slow
void stillBad() async {
  for (var i = 0; i < 100000000; i++) {
    sum += i;
    if (i % 10000 == 0) await Future.delayed(Duration.zero);
  }
}

// the fix: a separate isolate
double heavyWork() => 0;   // lives in the worker isolate

Future<double> compute() async {
  return Isolate.run(heavyWork);
}

Three kinds of concurrency, and Dart has two of them

Asynchronous Dart (chapter 8) is concurrency: several things are in flight at once, interleaved on one thread. It is not parallelism, and the distinction is not academic — it determines whether the work you put inside an async function can overlap with anything. An isolate is parallelism: real threads, each with its own heap, genuinely executing at the same time.

So there are two mechanisms and a common confusion about which does what. async lets your program interleave waiting without blocking, and it runs everything on one thread. An isolate runs code on another thread, in its own memory space, and communicates only by message passing. Most code that needs "not blocking the UI" needs only the first.

Propertyasync / awaitIsolate
ThreadsOneOne per isolate
Shared memoryTotalNone
Cost to startZero — it is a language featureMilliseconds
Suitable forWaiting on I/OComputation
Overhead per messageN/AMicroseconds to milliseconds
Can it block?Yes, and that blocks everythingYes, harmlessly

The row that decides most cases is the last one. An async function can contain synchronous work, and that work blocks the single thread — so a async function that parses a 40 MB JSON file without an await before the parse blocks exactly as long as a synchronous function would. async does not make anything parallel, and the label "async" invites the belief that it does.

// the misunderstanding, in one function
Future<List<Row>> load(String path) async {
  final text = await File(path).readAsString();   // ...the await suspends here:
                                                   //    the event loop is free
  final rows = parse(text);                        // ...and NOT here. There is
  return rows;                                     //    no await in this line,
}                                                  //    so it runs to completion
                                                   //    on the same thread and
// ...the event loop stays blocked for its entire duration. `async` gave the
// caller a Future to await; it gave the CPU nothing.

// and the check, which is one question
//   does this function SPEND TIME WAITING, or SPEND TIME COMPUTING?
//   waiting (a network read, a database query, a file read) -> await it.
//     I/O releases the thread, so the event loop does other work meanwhile.
//   computing (parsing, encrypting, image work, a tight loop) -> an isolate.
//     The thread is busy, and no amount of awaiting helps.
Future<List<Row>> heavy(String text) async {
  // ...this is the only correct use of an isolate: the parse is CPU-bound and
  // there is no await that could release the thread.
  return Isolate.run(() => parse(text));
}
// ...and note the cost it pays to get that right: the input is COPIED to the new
// isolate and the output is COPIED back. Chapter 9.4 is entirely about when that
// copy is worth paying.

Why no shared memory, and what that buys

Dart isolates do not share a heap, and there is no mechanism by which they could: no shared int variable, no shared List, no atomic increment. The only channel between two isolates is a message delivered through a port, and the only data that crosses is what the receiving isolate can reach from its own heap — which means every message is deep-copied, except for the one case chapter 9.4 covers.

This is a real constraint and it is also the property that makes isolates correct rather than merely different. A race condition needs two accesses to the same location, and there is no same location. Two isolates cannot deadlock each other through shared state, cannot see a torn read, and cannot race on a collection's internal length. In exchange you give up atomics, synchronized blocks, and any algorithm whose cost is dominated by fine-grained shared-memory access.

// what that rules out, and what it buys
// RULED OUT: a counter incremented from several workers
final results = await Future.wait([for (final chunk in chunks) Isolate.run(() =>
  countWords(chunk),   // ...each isolate counts independently - correct, and it
)]);                    //    scales. A shared counter would be a race AND
//                      //    would serialise, so it would be both wrong and
//                      //    slower.

// RULED OUT: passing a large structure and mutating it in place
final bigList = List.generate(1_000_000, (i) => i);
final copy = await Isolate.run(() => bigList.length);  // ...the list was
print(copy);                                               //    COPIED to reach
// ...`.length` on it. A megabyte of integers copied to answer a question that
// a plain function call would answer. So: pass primitives, pass small records,
// and compute inside the isolate rather than shipping data into it.

// BUYED: reasoning about the program
// Because there is no shared state, an isolate's behaviour depends only on
// the messages it receives. That makes three things possible which would be
// impossible with threads:
//   1. the isolate is a SEPARATE PROGRAM, and can be tested by sending it
//      messages - no mocking, no locks, no memory barriers to reason about
//   2. it CANNOT corrupt the caller, whatever it does. A worker that throws,
//      loops forever, or writes to a collection it was sent is contained.
//   3. the caller is not blocked by it. An isolate that spins on one core
//      leaves the main isolate running normally.
//
// and the price, stated once so it is not a surprise in 9.4
//   every message COPIES its payload, deeply, except typed data sent
//   specially. There is no zero-copy for a List of objects, and the copy is
//   not free: it is proportional to the size of the graph you send.

9.2 What to put in an isolate

The decision, and the cases where an isolate is the wrong answer.

// USE AN ISOLATE for:
//   - CPU-heavy computation: image processing, parsing a huge file,
//     encryption, compression, statistics
//   - blocking a call that cannot be made async
//   - a background service that must keep running

// DO NOT USE AN ISOLATE for:
//   - I/O. an await releases the thread; there is no need.
//   - small work. the spawn cost is milliseconds; a 2ms
//     computation is faster inline
//   - anything that needs to share live objects (see 9.4)
//   - state that changes constantly. the copy cost dominates

// a realistic set
//   GOOD: decode a 50MB JSON, resize an image, compute a checksum
//   GOOD: run a long-running loop for a background sync
//   GOOD: a pure-Dart crypto or compression implementation
//   BAD: fetch ten HTTP requests      (use Future.wait)
//   BAD: query a database             (await it)
//   BAD: update a widget              (the UI thread is where that goes)
// the cost of an isolate, so you can decide
//
// spawn + teardown:    ~0.1 - 1ms (Dart 3's Isolate.run is fast)
// copying a small data:  ~microseconds
// copying 1MB:          ~1ms
// copying 10MB:         ~10ms  - now it matters
//
// MEASURE before optimising. Isolate.run on a 50MB parse is a huge
// win. Isolate.run on a list of 100 ints is a net loss.

The decision, and the threshold

The question "should this go in an isolate" has a rough quantitative answer, and while the exact number depends on hardware and payload, the order of magnitude is stable enough to be worth memorising because it converts a judgement call into arithmetic. Spawning an isolate costs on the order of a millisecond and copying a payload costs on the order of microseconds per kilobyte. So an isolate pays for itself only when the work it moves is comfortably larger than both.

The practical rule: below about one millisecond of pure computation, do not use an isolate — the spawn cost is a significant fraction of the work itself. Above roughly five milliseconds, use one without hesitating, because you are now competing with the UI's 16 ms frame budget rather than with a spinner. In between, measure, and the measurement is the reason the rest of this section exists.

Work per itemOverheadVerdict
< 100 µsSpawn dominatesKeep it inline
100 µs – 1 msComparableMeasure; batch instead
1 – 5 ms20–50% overheadWorth it if it is per item
> 5 msNegligibleIsolate, and do not think again
Per item, many itemsAmortisedBatching beats isolates

The last row is the one most often missed. If you have 10,000 items averaging 200 microseconds, spawning 10,000 isolates is a catastrophically wrong answer — but so is 10,000 individual isolates' worth of work inline, because 10,000 × 200 µs is two seconds of blocked UI. The right answer is neither: send a batch to a small number of long-lived isolates, so spawn cost is paid once and the UI is freed. Batching is nearly always the better first move, because it is cheaper and it does not require the isolation decision at all.

// three shapes, in increasing order of cost to introduce

// 1. BATCH FIRST. Usually the whole answer.
Future<List<Row>> loadAll(List<File> files) async {
  const batchSize = 64;
  final rows = <Row>[];
  for (var i = 0; i < files.length; i += batchSize) {
    final batch = files.sublist(i, (i + batchSize).clamp(0, files.length));
    rows.addAll(await parseBatch(batch));   // ...one call, one event loop turn,
  }                                          //    one copy of the file list
  return rows;
}
// ...cost: nothing. You moved the boundary from "one item per await" to "one
// batch per await", which is a two-line change and often a 100x improvement.

// 2. ISOLATE FOR THE BATCH. Now the parse of 64 files is one chunk of work.
Future<List<Row>> parseBatch(List<File> batch) {
  return Isolate.run(() {
    final out = <Row>[];
    for (final f in batch) {
      out.addAll(parseSync(f.readAsStringSync()));   // ...sync inside the
    }                                                //    isolate is correct
    return out;                                      //    and often faster
  });
}
// ...note `readAsStringSync`. Inside an isolate there is no reason to be async:
// the thread belongs to this job alone. Using `await` per file here would add a
// suspension per file and copy the result per file, for nothing.

// 3. A POOL OF LONG-LIVED ISOLATES. Only when the batches themselves are large
//    enough that spawn cost matters across thousands of them.
// ...that is chapter 9.11, and it is a genuine complexity increase. The rule is
//    to reach for 3 only after 1 and 2 have been measured and found
//    insufficient.

// and what NOT to put in an isolate
// - anything under about 1 ms: the spawn cost exceeds the saving
// - a single already-fast operation, measured: if the whole function takes
//   300 µs, an isolate cannot make the program faster than 300 µs plus spawn
// - work that is already I/O bound, which `await` handles at no cost
// - a function that needs the caller's object graph: an isolate cannot reach
//   it, so you must serialise everything it touches, which is usually more
//   expensive than the computation you moved
// ...and the last one is the real reason to stop: isolates pay for themselves
// only in code that is self-contained. Work that needs ten fields of the
// caller's state is not worth isolating, because sending those ten fields is
// the cost you were trying to avoid.

9.3 Spawning an isolate

The simple form, and when to reach past it.

import 'dart:isolate';

Future<T> runInBackground<T>(
  T Function() computation, {
  T? fallback,
}) async {
  return Isolate.run(() => computation());
}

// the constraint, stated plainly: the function and its arguments
// must be sendable, which means they must be a primitive, a String,
// a List/Map of sendable things, a TransferableTypedData, or a
// closure that captures only sendable values

// a worked example: parsing a large JSON document
Future<List<Entry>> parseEntries(String jsonText) {
  return Isolate.run(() {
    final decoded = jsonDecode(jsonText) as List<dynamic>;
    return decoded
        .map((e) => Entry.fromJson(e as Map<String, dynamic>))
        .toList(growable: false);
  });
}

// the constraint bites here
// BAD: the closure captures a non-sendable object
//   return Isolate.run(() => process(myRepository));
// GOOD: pass the data in, return the result
Future<int> countWords(String text) {
  return Isolate.run(() => text.split(' ').length);
}
// a full example: an image pipeline
import 'dart:isolate';
import 'dart:typed_data';

class ImageJob {
  final Uint8List bytes;
  final int width, height;
  final int quality;
  const ImageJob(this.bytes, this.width, this.height, this.quality);
}

Future<Uint8List> processImage(ImageJob job) async {
  // the work
  final processed = await Isolate.run(() async {
    final pixels = _decode(job.bytes);
    final grey = _toGreyscale(pixels, job.width, job.height);
    final resized = _resize(grey, job.width, job.height);
    return _encode(resized, job.quality);
  });
  return processed;
}

Future<Uint8List> _decode(Uint8List b) async => b;
Future<Uint8List> _toGreyscale(Uint8List b, int w, int h) async => b;
Future<Uint8List> _resize(Uint8List b, int w, int h) async => b;
Future<Uint8List> _encode(Uint8List b, int q) async => b;

The API, and the three constraints that shape it

Isolate.spawn has a signature that looks fussy and is actually three decisions expressed together: what runs, what it receives, and what happens to the result. Read those three and the fussy parts are obvious.

// the full signature, then each argument justified
Future<T?> computeInBackground<T, R>(
  T input,
  String entryPointName,        // 1. WHAT RUNS - by NAME, not as a closure
  R Function(T) entryPoint,      //    and the function must be top-level or
  {                             //    static
  String? debugName,            // 2. WHAT IT RECEIVES - exactly one value,
  bool paused = false,          //    sent as the first argument to entryPoint
  SendPort? onExit,             // 3. WHAT HAPPENS NEXT - a port notified when
  SendPort? onError,            //    the isolate exits, and a port that
  SendPort? errorsAreFatal,     //    receives uncaught errors
}) {
  final exit = ReceivePort();
  final error = ReceivePort();
  final result = ReceivePort();
  try {
    await Isolate.spawn(
      entryPoint,                       // ...the function to run
      [result.sendPort, input],          // ...arguments: the result port FIRST,
                                         //    then your value
      debugName: debugName ?? entryPointName,
      onExit: onExit ?? exit.sendPort,
      onError: onError ?? error.sendPort,
      errorsAreFatal: errorsAreFatal ?? exit.sendPort,
      paused: paused,
    );
    return await result.first as T?;
  } finally {
    exit.close();
    error.close();
    result.close();
  }
}
// ...and the three constraints that this shape exists to satisfy:

// CONSTRAINT 1: the entry point is named, not passed. A closure capturing
// variables cannot be sent, because a closure IS a heap object and the new
// isolate has a different heap. So the function must be reachable by name, and
// it must be a top-level function or a static method. `() => heavy(work)` does
// not compile; `() => heavy(work)` where heavy is top-level and work is passed
// as the message does.
Future<int> one() => Isolate.run(() => heavy(_work));  // WRONG: `_work`
//                                                       // is a captured field

// CONSTRAINT 2: exactly one message carries the input. You send a LIST of
// arguments and the first element must be a SendPort. So the shape is
// [sendPort, yourPayload] and there is no way to send zero, two, or a
// different arrangement.

// CONSTRAINT 3: the result comes back through a port, so it must be
// SENDABLE - which is chapter 9.4's list, and is the constraint people hit
// last because it fails as a runtime error, not a compile error.

onExit, onError, and the port that must be closed

The three optional ports are how a spawned isolate reports its fate, and getting them wrong produces a failure that is genuinely hard to diagnose — typically a process that exits silently or a Future that never completes. Both are port lifecycle mistakes rather than compute mistakes.

// the three ports, and what each reports
final isolate = await Isolate.spawn(worker, [port.sendPort, input],
  onExit: exitPort.sendPort,      // ...fires when the isolate TERMINATES, for
                                  //    ANY reason: normal return, uncaught
                                  //    error, or process shutdown. The message
                                  //    is the exit code (int), and it is the
                                  //    ONLY way to learn that a worker died
                                  //    after returning its result.
  onError: errorPort.sendPort,    // ...fires for an UNCAUGHT error, twice: the
                                  //    error object, then the stack trace as a
                                  //    List. Receive BOTH or the next error is
                                  //    misread as a stack trace.
  errorsAreFatal: exitPort.sendPort,  // ...when true, the isolate is KILLED on
                                  //    the first uncaught error instead of
                                  //    continuing. Almost always what you want:
                                  //    a worker in an unknown state is worse
                                  //    than a dead worker.
);

// the two-failure pattern in onError, and why the count matters
errorPort.listen((message) {
  if (message is List) {
    // ...a stack trace: a List<String>. Note it is a LIST, not a String, which
    //    is why a handler that assumes String gets a type error here and hides
    //    the original problem.
    stderr.writeln(message.join('\n'));
  } else {
    stderr.writeln('uncaught: $message');
  }
});
// ...the reason you must handle both is that if you only handle the first and
// return, the second message is delivered to no listener, and the port's
// subscription is left dangling.

// and the port that must be closed, which is the failure nobody diagnoses
final result = ReceivePort();
try {
  await Isolate.spawn(worker, [result.sendPort, input], onExit: exit.sendPort);
  final value = await result.first;      // ...`first` cancels its subscription
  return value;
} finally {
  result.close();
  exit.close();
}
// ...a ReceivePort that is never closed keeps its subscription alive for the
// lifetime of the enclosing zone. Three ports left open per request, ten
// thousand requests, and the process holds 30,000 live subscriptions. The
// symptom is not an error: it is memory growth over hours, which is why it is
// found by chapter 15's allocation tooling and not by the test suite.
//
// and why `result.first` rather than `result.listen`
// `.first` completes on the first message AND cancels the subscription. A
// `listen` with no cancellation leaks. So for a one-shot result, `.first` is
// both shorter and correct, and the explicit `close()` in the finally covers
// the port itself rather than the subscription.

// and the error that is not an error
Future<int> f() async {
  final r = ReceivePort();
  await Isolate.spawn(workerThatThrows, [r.sendPort]);  // ...no errorsAreFatal,
  return await r.first as int;                           //    no onError
}
// ...the isolate throws, the error goes to the ROOT zone's uncaught handler
// (or is printed), the result port never receives anything, and `r.first`
// never completes. The Future returned by f() hangs forever, and the
// application does not crash - it just stops making progress. Adding
// errorsAreFatal does not fix it; only completing the result port on error
// does, which means wrapping the entry point:
//   void worker(SendPort p, int x) {
//     try { p.send(compute(x)); } catch (e, s) { p.send(WorkerError(e, s)); }
//   }

Debugging an isolate, and the three questions that always come up

Isolates are hard to debug for three reasons, and each has a specific answer. A stack trace from inside a worker names no location. A worker's failure arrives in a different isolate than the one that owns the state. And an isolate that hangs looks exactly like an isolate that is slow. Knowing which of the three you have is most of the work.

// 1. THE UNNAMED ISOLATE. The default debugName is "Isolate", so every worker
//    appears identically and a trace cannot say which one failed.
await Isolate.spawn(worker, [port.sendPort, input], debugName: 'thumbnail-$id');
// ...and for Isolate.run the name is derived from the enclosing function, which
// is better than nothing and still not useful when the same function is used
// for three different jobs. Wrap the callback so the name says which:
//   return Isolate.run(() => _resize(path, kind: 'thumb'));
// ...that appears in DevTools' isolate list and in any error the isolate logs.

// 2. THE TRACE THAT DOES NOT NAME A FILE. A stack trace crossing a port has
//    the frames of the code that was SENDING, because the frames at the point
//    of the throw are in a different isolate and cannot be serialised into a
//    trace that is travelling to another one.
void entry(SendPort reply, String path) {
  try {
    reply.send(Ok(_resize(path)));
  } catch (e, s) {
    // ...`s` here is a real StackTrace, and it DOES contain the worker's
    // frames, because it was captured inside the worker. That is the whole
    // answer: capture the trace where the throw happened and send it as a
    // value, rather than letting the error travel uncaught.
    reply.send(WorkerFailed(e, s));
  }
}
// ...and this is why `errorsAreFatal: false` produces worse diagnostics than a
// try/catch. The uncaught path sends the error object and then the trace to
// onError, but the trace arrives as a bare List<String> with no association
// to the error, so a handler that logs them together has to guess. The
// try/catch keeps them paired because it constructs the pair.

// 3. THE HANG THAT IS NOT A HANG. Four distinct causes produce a worker that
//    never answers, and they need different diagnostics.
Future<T> spawnWithWatchdog<T>(String name, FutureOr<T> Function() body,
    {Duration limit = const Duration(seconds: 5)}) async {
  final result = ReceivePort();
  await Isolate.spawn(() {
    final r = ReceivePort();
    try {
      r.send(Ok(body()));
    } catch (e, s) {
      r.send(Failed(e, s));
    }
    result.sendPort;   // ...held open so the isolate cannot exit early
  }, [result.sendPort], debugName: name);

  return (await result.first.timeout(limit, onTimeout: () {
    throw TimeoutException('$name did not answer in $limit', limit);
  })) as T;
}
// ...a timeout converts all four into one named failure, which is not a fix but
// is a huge improvement: "thumbnail-3 did not answer in 5s" tells you which
// worker and that it was a hang, where a bare timeout tells you neither.
//
//   and the four causes, so the timeout can be turned into a diagnosis
//   a) the callback never returns - a Future that never completes. Add
//      `.timeout()` on every await INSIDE the worker.
//   b) the callback returns an unsendable value - a runtime error, so the
//      result port never receives it. The error goes to onError.
//   c) an exception escaped before the try block - the entry point's own code.
//   d) the isolate was killed - `Isolate.kill`, an OOM, or a crash. The onExit
//      port fires, and that is the only way to distinguish it from (a).

// and the DevTools question, because DevTools can attach to worker isolates
$ dart run --observe=8181/127.0.0.1 bin/app.dart
// ...open DevTools, and the isolate list shows every isolate including workers,
// with names. Selecting one gives you its own timeline, allocation profile and
// heap snapshot. So a worker that leaks is diagnosable exactly like the main
// isolate: record an allocation profile in the worker and read its dominator
// tree. This is the practical answer to "how do I see what the worker is
// doing" and it needs no instrumentation.

// and what you CANNOT see, which bounds the debugging story
//   - nothing about the worker's OWN event loop timing appears on the UI
//     isolate's timeline. Two traces, not one.
//   - `print` from a worker goes to the same stdout, interleaved with the
//     main isolate's output, with no indication of which isolate produced it.
//     Prefix worker logs with the worker's debugName or they are unreadable.
//   - the wall-clock relationship between the two isolates is not observable.
//     A worker that finishes in 1 ms and a message that takes 100 ms to be
//     delivered look identical from the caller's timeline.

What the signature does not tell you

Having read the signature and the ports, the remaining gap is not the API but the set of things that are true of every call and are stated in none of them. These are the properties that determine whether a given call site is correct, and a reader who does not know them will write something that compiles, works in a test, and fails under load.

The first is that spawning is not cheap. It allocates a thread, a heap, and the runtime structures that go with them, and it costs on the order of a millisecond. Every figure quoted for an isolate's performance is dwarfed by that number if the isolate is short-lived, which is why chapter 9.2's batching rule and chapter 9.11's pool are not micro-optimisations but the difference between a mechanism that helps and one that hurts. If you take one thing from this section: count the spawns.

The second is that the input is snapshotted. The value you send is deep-copied at the moment you send it. If you then mutate the original, the worker sees the state as of the send, not as of its processing. This is a feature — it removes a whole category of data race — but it means a pattern like "send the list, then append the next batch while it works" is a logic error rather than an optimisation, and it fails intermittently in a way that depends on timing.

The third is that completion is not the end of the isolate's life. An isolate that has sent its result is no longer doing your work, but it is still holding its heap, its thread, and its subscriptions until something explicitly ends it. Isolate.run handles this; a hand-rolled spawn does not, and the leak is one isolate per call — which is the failure mode that makes a naive isolate-per-request implementation look catastrophic after an hour.

The fourth is that error handling is opt-in and lossy. The default for an uncaught error in a worker is to route it to the current zone's uncaught-error handler, which in a service usually means a log line with no association to the request that caused it. And the default for the caller is to wait forever. So the two behaviours you must opt into — a try/catch that completes the result port, and a timeout on the caller's side — are both absent by default, and their absence looks like a hang rather than like a mistake.

The four ways a call site gets it wrong

// 1. SPAWNING PER ITEM. The most common, and the most expensive mistake:
//    each call pays a spawn and two copies for one item of work.
for (final item in items) {
  results.add(await Isolate.run(() => heavySync(item)));   // ...N spawns
}
// ...the fix is one spawn for the batch, and it is the same amount of code:
final results = await Isolate.run(() => [for (final i in items) heavySync(i)]);

// 2. AN ENTRY POINT THAT CAN CAPTURE. The closure compiles if the captured
//    variables are all sendable, and fails at runtime when they are not. So it
//    works in development with simple inputs and fails with a real object.
Future<int> ok(int n) => Isolate.run(() => compute(n));
Future<int> broken(Ctx ctx) => Isolate.run(() => ctx.compute());
// ...fix: pass `ctx` as the argument and call a top-level function on it.

// 3. NO ERROR PATH, so a worker exception hangs the caller.
Future<int> hangs() {
  final r = ReceivePort();
  Isolate.spawn(() => throw StateError('boom'), [r.sendPort]);  // ...nothing
  return r.first as int;                                          //    sent back
}
// ...fix: a try/catch in the entry point that sends a failure value, plus a
// timeout on the caller's side so a bug in that try/catch is still bounded.

// 4. FORGETTING THE CLOSE, which is invisible and cumulative.
Future<int> perRequest(String p) async {
  final r = ReceivePort();
  try {
    await Isolate.spawn(worker, [r.sendPort, p]);
    return await r.first as int;
  } finally {
    r.close();          // ...this line is the difference between a service and
  }                     //    a slow leak. It costs one line and is missed
}                       //    because nothing fails when it is absent.

Of the four, the first and the last account for nearly all the real incidents. The second is found in the first development run, because real code captures something unsendable almost immediately. The third is found whenever a worker throws, which — if the worker has an untested error path — is sooner rather than later.

That leaves the pattern to actually follow, and it is not exciting: one isolate for a batch of work, a top-level entry point that takes exactly one argument and cannot fail without saying so, a result port closed in a finally, and a timeout on the caller's side. Everything else in this chapter is an optimisation of that, and the optimisation is only worth making once the base version is correct and measured.

9.4 Transferables, and the copy problem

Why passing 50MB to an isolate is slow, and how to make it free.

// the problem: isolate messages are COPIED
//   isolate A                  isolate B
//   50MB in RAM      COPY      50MB in RAM
//   time: ~10-50ms            now 100MB total
//
// two solutions, depending on the direction

// 1. TransferableTypedData: MOVE the memory, do not copy
//    the sending isolate's copy becomes invalid
final data = await file.readAsBytes();
final transferable = TransferableTypedData.fromList([data]);

final result = await Isolate.run(() {
  // the bytes arrive here, with no copy
  final received = transferable.materialize().asUint8List();
  return _process(received);
});

Uint8List _process(Uint8List b) => b;

// you can only do this ONCE per TransferableTypedData: the
// underlying buffer is detached after materialise()
// 2. SharedArrayBuffer: a buffer BOTH isolates can read and write
import 'dart:typed_data';
import 'dart:isolate';

Future<List<int>> heavyWithShared(List<int> input) async {
  final buffer = SharedArrayBuffer.fromList(input);

  await Isolate.run(() {
    final view = Int32List.from(buffer);    // no copy
    for (var i = 0; i < view.length; i++) {
      view[i] = view[i] * 2;
    }
  });

  return buffer.toList(growable: false);   // a copy ONCE, at the end
}

// or return the buffer itself
Future<SharedArrayBuffer> heavyReturningBuffer(List<int> input) {
  final buffer = SharedArrayBuffer.fromList(input);
  return Isolate.run(() {
    final view = Int32List.from(buffer);
    for (var i = 0; i < view.length; i++) {
      view[i] *= 2;
    }
    return buffer;                          // zero copies, both ways
  });
}

// the caveat: with a shared buffer, the two isolates are genuinely
// concurrent, so you need a barrier. A Future returned by Isolate.run
// IS the barrier: the isolate does not complete until its work is done.
// what is sendable?
//
//   YES  null, bool, int, double, String
//   YES  List, Map, Set of sendable values
//   YES  TransferableTypedData
//   YES  SharedArrayBuffer
//   YES  SendPort, Capability
//   YES  a closure whose captured variables are all sendable
//        (Isolate.run checks this and throws a clear error)
//
//   NO   a Socket, HttpClient, File handle
//   NO   a Timer, a StreamController, a StreamSubscription
//   NO   a Database connection
//   NO   any object with a native resource behind it
//   NO   a closure that captures a widget, a controller, or `this`
//        from a State
//
// the error is clear when you get it wrong:
//   "Illegal argument in isolate message: object is unsendable -
//    Library:dart:async Zone" or a similar message naming the type

Passing a File, a database connection or an HttpClient to an isolate is the most common isolate mistake, and it fails immediately with a clear error. The fix is to pass the path and open the file inside the isolate. That also means the worker owns its own resources and cleans them up in the isolate, not in the caller.

What can cross, and what it costs to copy

An isolate's heap is not reachable from another isolate's heap, so every value in a message is deep-copied on the way out, and every value in a reply is deep-copied on the way back. There is one mechanism that avoids this for large binary data, and understanding the shape of the copy is what tells you when to use it.

The list of sendable types is short and worth memorising, because the compile-time checking is asymmetric: sending an unsendable value is a runtime error with a message that names the type, so it is found in development rather than in review.

SendableCopiedNotes
num, bool, StringBy valueCheap, except large strings
null, SendPort, CapabilityBy valueThe port is the mechanism itself
List, Map, SetDeep, recursiveEverything inside must also be sendable
Custom class instancesDeep, recursiveLegal; there is no type identity check
TypedDataCopied, or transferredThe one case with a zero-copy path
ReceivePort, DynamicLibrary, closures, socketsNot sendableRuntime error naming the type
// the copy, and why its cost is not what you expect
final data = List.generate(1_000_000, (i) => i);       // 8 MB of ints
final n = await Isolate.run(() => data.length);
// ...`data` is deep-copied to the new isolate. 8 MB of memory allocated,
// 1,000,000 elements walked, and the answer is 1. Measured cost: 8-15 ms on a
// laptop. So `Isolate.run(() => data.length)` is about 100x SLOWER than the
// expression it wrapped, and it is a shape people write.

// a List of maps is far worse than 8 MB, because the copy is per-object
final rows = List.generate(1000, (i) => {'id': i, 'name': 'n$i', 'tags': []});
await Isolate.run(() => rows.length);
// ...1,000 maps, each with a nested list. The copy is not 8 MB of integers, it
// is 4,000 separately allocated objects with 4,000 hash insertions. This is
// usually where "isolate spawn is slow" actually comes from.

// the zero-copy path, and its two rules
final bytes = await File(path).readAsBytes();            // a Uint8List
final result = await Isolate.run(() {
  // ...TransferableTypedData MOVES the buffer rather than copying it. Two
  // rules make it work:
  //   1. the transferable must be the ONLY argument to Isolate.run
  //   2. the receiving side must Materialise it, and the original becomes
  //      detached - using it afterwards throws
  final ttd = TransferableTypedData.fromList([bytes]);
  return ttd;
});
final copy = result.materialize().asUint8List();         // ...now a real buffer
// ...so the pattern is: build the TransferableTypedData OUTSIDE, send it as the
// single argument, materialise INSIDE. Written the other way round, the copy has
// already happened by the time you get to the transfer.

// and the rule of thumb for choosing
//   under about 64 KB     : just send it. The copy is microseconds.
//   64 KB - 4 MB         : measure. The copy is milliseconds and may exceed
//                          the work you moved.
//   over 4 MB            : TransferableTypedData, or do not send data at all -
//                          have the isolate READ the file. `Isolate.run` has no
//                          filesystem access by default, so pass the PATH, which
//                          is a string, and let the isolate open the file. That
//                          is almost always the right answer for large data: a
//                          path costs 40 bytes.

Deep copy means cycles and identity are the interesting cases

A deep copy is a graph walk, and graph walks have two well-known behaviours that catch people out: cycles terminate and identity is not preserved. Both follow from the implementation, and both are worth stating explicitly because the failure is silent — the copy succeeds and produces a different graph than you sent.

// a cycle survives the copy, because the walk tracks visited objects
class Node {
  Node? next;
  String label = '';
}
final a = Node()..label = 'a';
final b = Node()..label = 'b';
a.next = b;
b.next = a;                        // ...a two-node cycle

final copy = await Isolate.run(() => [a]) as List;
// ...this WORKS and terminates. So there is no "cannot copy a cyclic graph"
// error to look for, which means a cyclic graph is silently copied as a cyclic
// graph, and a caller that relied on the copy having a fixed depth will not
// notice anything is wrong. Traverse with a visited set, always.

// identity is NOT preserved across the copy
final original = Node()..label = 'x';
final sent = [original, original];        // the SAME object twice
final copy = await Isolate.run(() => sent) as List;
print(copy[0] == copy[1]);       // true - structural equality, so this looks
                                // fine
print(identical(copy[0], copy[1]));   // ...and this depends on whether your
                                     //    == is identity or structural
// ...the practical consequence: a graph where identity matters — a cache keyed on
// object, a cycle-detection scheme using a visited LIST rather than a set, a
// graph node with a parent pointer — behaves differently on the other side. The
// copy has its own object graph with its own identity relationships, so the
// only thing guaranteed to survive is STRUCTURE.

// and the case that produces a runtime error with no compile-time hint
final controller = StreamController<int>();
await Isolate.run(() => [controller]);      // Invalid argument(s): Illegal
                                            // argument in isolate message:
//                                            // object is unsendable - Library:
//                                            // dart:async _SyncStreamController<int>
// ...and note how late the message arrives: the type is named, but only at the
// point of sending, at runtime, in development. So the practical rule is to
// send PRIMITIVES and small records rather than live objects, and to treat any
// unsendable error as a signal that a domain object has crept into a boundary
// that should have been a plain value.

// and what DOES survive reliably, and is usually what you want
// send a record of primitives:
final (String, int, bool) request = ('/users', 42, true);
final reply = await Isolate.run(() => handle(request)) as (String, int);
// ...records are copied structurally, so the types work out on both sides, the
// payload is tiny, and there is no object graph to reason about. Most isolate
// boundaries should look like this: a record of primitives in, a record of
// primitives out. Anything richer is a sign the work does not belong in an
// isolate.

Measuring the copy, because the intuition about it is wrong

The intuition says the copy is "fast because it's just memory". That is wrong in a way that matters, and the reason is that a deep copy of a collection of objects is not a memory copy at all — it is a graph traversal that allocates every node again. A List<int> of a million elements is one buffer and one loop. A List<Map> of a thousand rows with four keys each is four thousand allocations and four thousand hash operations, and it is a completely ordinary shape of data.

The practical consequence is that copy cost tracks the number of objects, not the number of bytes. So the question to ask about a payload is never "how big is it" but "how many objects is it", and a small payload of objects can be far more expensive to send than a large payload of primitives.

// the measurement, which takes a minute and settles the question
Future<void> measureCopy() async {
  for (final payload in [
    () => List<int>.filled(1_000_000, 0),                 // 1 object graph node
    () => List<int>.filled(1_000, 0),                    // 1,000
    () => List.generate(1000, (i) => [i, i]),             // 1,001
    () => List.generate(1000, (i) => {'id': i, 'a': i, 'b': i, 'c': i}),
    () => List.generate(1000, (i) => {'id': i, 'tags': [i, i, i, i]}),
  ]) {
    final data = payload();
    final sw = Stopwatch()..start();
    // ...Isolate.run with a trivial body: what is measured is the round trip,
    // i.e. copy out, copy back, plus the spawn. Run it WITHOUT the isolate too
    // so the spawn cost can be separated from the copy cost.
    final out = await Isolate.run(() => data.length);
    final roundTrip = sw.elapsedMicroseconds;

    sw.reset();
    final direct = _lengthOf(data);
    final local = sw.elapsedMicroseconds;

    print('nodes ${_count(data).padLeft(7)}  '
        'local ${local}us  roundTrip ${roundTrip}us  '
        'delta ${roundTrip - local}us  n=$out');
  }
}
// ...the expected shape of that output, and it is the point:
//   nodes       1  local      2us  roundTrip   14500us   <- spawn dominates
//   nodes    1000  local      3us  roundTrip   14100us
//   nodes    2001  local     30us  roundTrip   14300us
//   nodes    5001  local    210us  roundTrip   16200us   <- the copy appears
//   nodes    9001  local    480us  roundTrip   18100us
// ...spawn is about 14 ms of every row. The copy is visible from the fourth row
// and is a few milliseconds for 9,000 objects. So for realistic application
// payloads the SPAWN dominates unless the payload is large, and for a large
// payload the copy is a linear function of object count that would take
// hundreds of milliseconds to matter.

// and the two ways to avoid the copy, in order of preference
// 1. DO NOT SEND THE DATA. Send a path, an id, or a key, and let the worker
//    fetch or rebuild it.
Future<List<Row>> best(String dbPath, List<int> ids) {
  // ...a String and a List<int>: 1,001 nodes, and the worker opens the
  //    database itself. Nothing large crosses the boundary at all.
  return Isolate.run(() {
    final db = SqliteDb(dbPath);
    return [for (final id in ids) db.row(id)];
  });
}
// ...this is almost always available and almost always the right answer. An
// isolate that must RECEIVE a large dataset is usually a design that has
// confused "compute" with "transfer".

// 2. TRANSFER THE BUFFER, for genuine binary data you already hold in memory.
Future<Uint8List> process(TransferableTypedData ttd) {
  return Isolate.run(() {
    final bytes = ttd.materialize().asUint8List();
    final out = _transform(bytes);
    // ...and transfer the OUTPUT back the same way, or you have solved half the
    //    problem:
    return TransferableTypedData.fromList([out]);
  });
}
// ...this is the only zero-copy path Dart has, and it applies only to
// TypedData. If your data is a list of records, it does not apply.

// and the measurement that tells you which problem you have
//   delta large, roundTrip large   -> the COPY. Fix with a path or a transfer.
//   delta small, roundTrip large   -> the SPAWN. Fix with a pool, or batch.
//   both large                     -> both, and the pool is the bigger win
//   both small                     -> you do not need an isolate
// ...and these are four genuinely different problems that all present as "the
// isolate is slow", which is why measuring before choosing the fix is not
// optional. Guessing correctly here means batching; guessing wrong means
// spending a day making a copy cheaper when the copy was never the cost.

9.5 SendPort, ReceivePort and raw messaging

The underlying mechanism, and why you usually do not need it.

// Isolate.run is a wrapper over this. Know the mechanism to read
// the documentation, and to write a long-lived worker.

final receivePort = ReceivePort();
final sendPort = receivePort.sendPort;

await Isolate.spawn(_worker, sendPort);

final firstReply = await receivePort.first as SendPort;
print('worker ready');

// keep the port open
receivePort.listen((message) {
  if (message is List && message.length == 2) {
    final (id, result) = (message[0] as int, message[1]);
    print('job $id -> $result');
  }
});

sendPort.send([1, 6 * 7]);
sendPort.send([2, _expensiveSum()]);

receivePort.close();   // the isolate dies when its port closes

// the worker
void _worker(SendPort initialPort) {
  final commandPort = ReceivePort();
  initialPort.send(commandPort.sendPort);

  commandPort.listen((message) {
    final (id, job) = (message[0] as int, message[1] as int);
    final result = _sum(job);
    commandPort.sendPort.send([id, result]);
  });
}

int _sum(int n) {
  var total = 0;
  for (var i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
    total += i;
  }
  return total;
}

int _expensiveSum() => _sum(1000000000);
// a request/response wrapper, which is what Isolate.run does
class IsolatePool {
  final List<SendPort> _ports;
  final ReceivePort _replyPort;
  int _next = 0;
  final Map<int, Completer<Object?>> _pending = {};
  int _jobId = 0;

  IsolatePool._(this._ports, this._replyPort) {
    _replyPort.listen((message) {
      final (id, result, error) = (message[0] as int, message[1], message[2] as String?);
      final completer = _pending.remove(id);
      if (completer == null) return;
      if (error != null) {
        completer.completeError(StateError(error));
      } else {
        completer.complete(result);
      }
    });
  }

  static Future<IsolatePool> spawn(int size) async {
    final ready = ReceivePort();
    final ports = <SendPort>[];
    for (var i = 0; i < size; i++) {
      ports.add(await Isolate.spawn(_pooledWorker, ready.sendPort));
    }
    ready.close();
    return IsolatePool._(ports, ReceivePort());
  }

  Future<T> submit<T>(FutureOr<T> Function() job) {
    final id = _jobId++;
    final completer = Completer<T>();
    _pending[id] = completer;
    _ports[_next++ % _ports.length].send([id, null, null]);
    return completer.future;
  }

  void dispose() {
    _replyPort.close();
  }
}

// A POOL, not a spawn-per-job: spawning for every 5ms job is
// slower than doing it inline

Ports as values, and what that enables

A port is the only sendable value that references something on the other side, which is the property the whole isolate model rests on. Because a SendPort can be sent inside a message, two isolates can be introduced to each other and then talk directly, and neither needs to relay through the third. That is what makes a worker pool possible rather than a single worker.

The mechanics: ReceivePort is a mailbox with a subscription. port.send(x) copies x into the receiver's heap and schedules a delivery. SendPort is the writable half — the ability to deliver — and it is a sendable value, so it travels inside messages.

// introducing two isolates so they can talk directly
final aToB = ReceivePort();      // ...A receives; this port is given to B
final bToA = ReceivePort();      // ...B receives; this port is given to A

final aPort = SendPort(aToB.sendPort);   // ...A's writable handle
final bPort = SendPort(bToA.sendPort);

// spawn each with the OTHER's port in its initial message
await Isolate.spawn(() => worker(bPort), [aPort, 'job-1']);   // ...A gets
await Isolate.spawn(() => worker(aPort), [bPort, 'job-2']);   //    bPort
// ...so A now holds a SendPort that writes into B's mailbox, and vice versa.
// Neither goes through main again.

// the pattern that needs this: a pool
final pool = <SendPort>[];
final ready = ReceivePort();
for (var i = 0; i < workerCount; i++) {
  final inbox = ReceivePort();                       // ...each worker gets its
  pool.add(SendPort(inbox.sendPort));                //    OWN inbox port
  inbox.listen((msg) { ... });                       //    and a listener
  await Isolate.spawn(() => worker(SendPort(inbox.sendPort)), [pool[i]]);
}
// ...and a worker that needs to talk to another worker receives that worker's
// SendPort as a normal message. Routing then needs no central coordinator:
//   worker: pool.send(someOtherWorkersPort);
// ...which is either a nice decoupling or an emergent distributed system,
// depending on how it goes.

// RawReceivePort, and why it exists
final raw = RawReceivePort(handler);
raw.sendPort;    // ...a SendPort that talks directly to `handler`
// ...`handler` is a plain function, invoked for every message, with NO
// subscription object and no event-loop scheduling in between. That makes it
// meaningfully faster per message and it makes the handler unable to be
// asynchronous. Use it for a hot protocol with many small messages — which a
// worker pool with thousands of jobs is exactly — and use ReceivePort for
// everything else, because RawReceivePort cannot await, cannot yield, and
// a long handler blocks the receiving isolate's event loop entirely.

// and the ordering guarantee, which is the one thing you can rely on
raw.handler = (dynamic message) {
  // ...messages from ONE SendPort arrive in the order they were sent.
  // Messages from DIFFERENT SendPorts have no relative order at all.
};
// ...so a protocol on one port is a simple sequence; a protocol across several
// ports is a distributed system with all the ordering problems that implies,
// and it should be designed as one — with sequence numbers if correctness
// depends on order, or by making the operations independent if it does not.

// and the trap: a port is not a queue you can inspect
final r = ReceivePort();
r.sendPort.send(1);
r.sendPort.send(2);
print(r.length);      // COMPILE ERROR - there is no `length` on ReceivePort
// ...there is no API to ask how many messages are pending, no way to peek, and no
// way to drain selectively. Messages arrive when delivered. So back-pressure
// cannot be implemented by counting: it has to be implemented by the protocol,
// which is why the pool pattern sends an ack.

Designing the protocol, and the four questions

Because a port's API is send-only, every real design decision lives in the messages rather than in the mechanism, and a worker protocol that has not answered four questions will fail in a way that is hard to trace. These are the four, and they are not specific to isolates — they are the questions any message-passing interface needs.

// Q1: how does the caller know a result arrived, and did it succeed?
// The result port carrying a bare value cannot distinguish success from failure.
sealed class Reply {}
class Ok extends Reply { final int value; Ok(this.value); }
class Failed extends Reply { final Object error; final StackTrace? stack;
  Failed(this.error, this.stack); }
class TimedOut extends Reply { final Duration after; TimedOut(this.after); }

// and the discipline that goes with it: the entry point NEVER lets an exception
// escape, because an escaped exception sends nothing and the caller waits forever
void entry(SendPort reply, Job job) {
  try {
    reply.send(Ok(run(job)));
  } catch (e, s) {
