    reply.send(Failed(e, s));          // ...always completes the port
  }
}

// Q2: is there a timeout, and what happens when it fires?
Future<Reply> withTimeout(SendPort to, Job job, Duration d) {
  final result = ReceivePort();
  final timer = Timer(d, () => result.send(TimedOut(d)));
  to.send(job..reply = result.sendPort);
  return result.first.whenComplete(() {
    timer.cancel();
    result.close();                     // ...close on BOTH paths, or the
  });                                   //    timer keeps the port alive
}
// ...a timeout that cancels the timer on success but not on timeout leaks one
// timer per call. And a timeout that does not tell the worker to stop leaves a
// worker computing a result nobody will read — which on a busy pool is how the
// pool stalls.

// Q3: does the caller need a reply at all?
// A fire-and-forget message needs no result port, and that halves the port
// traffic and removes the entire failure-detection problem:
void logTo(SendPort logger, String line) => logger.send(line);
// ...the cost is that you cannot know it arrived, cannot know it worked, and a
// worker that throws on one log line is now the one thing you cannot detect.
// Fire-and-forget is right for logging and telemetry and wrong for everything
// that must be correct.

// Q4: how much work is one message?
// One message per ITEM on a 10,000-item job means 10,000 copies each way and
// 10,000 event-loop turns on both sides. One message per BATCH of 64 means 157
// of each, and the same total work. The batch size is the single most effective
// tuning parameter in a worker protocol, and the constraint on it is memory:
// the reply for a batch of 64 is 64 times a result, held in the caller's heap
// until the whole batch is complete.

The mistakes, and the shape each one takes

A port's API is four methods, so there is not much to get wrong in the API itself. What goes wrong is the lifecycle, and each lifecycle mistake presents as something other than a lifecycle mistake — a slow leak, a silent drop, a process that will not exit. They are worth naming because the symptom is what you will be looking at.

// 1. THE PORT THAT IS NEVER CLOSED. The most common, and the least visible.
final inbox = ReceivePort();
inbox.listen(handle);                    // ...no reference to inbox anywhere
// ...a ReceivePort keeps its isolate's subscription, and a subscription keeps
// its isolate running. So this one line prevents the isolate from ever exiting:
//   Process exited with code 255
// ...and in a long-running process, the same line is a slow leak - one live
// port per request, held until the process dies. There is no warning. The fix
// is a reference plus a close, and the discipline is: a ReceivePort is always
// owned by something with a lifetime.

// 2. THE PORT CLOSED TOO EARLY. The mirror, and it looks like a dropped message.
final inbox = ReceivePort();
inbox.listen((msg) { work().then((r) => inbox.sendPort.send(r)); });
inbox.close();                          // ...closed while a message is in flight
// ...the reply arrives after the close and is discarded. The symptom is that the
// FIRST job works and every later one times out, which reads as "the worker
// died" and sends you looking at the worker. The rule is that a port must outlive
// every message it has in flight.

// 3. THE PORT SENT TO THE WRONG PLACE. This is the one that is hardest to see.
final mainInbox = ReceivePort();
final workerPort = SendPort(mainInbox.sendPort);
await Isolate.spawn(() => worker(SendPort(mainInbox.sendPort)), [workerPort]);
// ...the worker was spawned with a copy of ITS OWN inbox port and the SAME port
// main uses. Two isolates are now writing to one mailbox, so every reply is
// ambiguous and neither can tell which is which. The symptom is replies that
// arrive in the wrong order and state that is sometimes stale - which reads as
// a concurrency bug in code with no concurrency.

// 4. THE PORT ASSUMED TO BE A QUEUE. There is no length, no peek, no drain.
final inbox = ReceivePort();
inbox.sendPort.send(1);
inbox.sendPort.send(2);
// inbox.length          COMPILE ERROR
// inbox.take(1)        COMPILE ERROR
// ...so "back-pressure" cannot be implemented by counting pending messages. It
// has to be in the protocol: the worker does not send the next request until it
// has acknowledged the last. Every hand-rolled pool that has a "queue is full"
// error has implemented this as a counter somewhere else, and the counter is the
// thing that is wrong.

// and the two that are subtle rather than wrong
// a) CLOSING A PORT TWICE. `close()` is idempotent in recent SDKs, but calling
//    it on a port you no longer own is a design smell: it usually means two
//    owners, which is mistake 3 wearing a different hat.
// b) SENDING A SENDPORT BACK TO ITS OWN ISOLATE. It is legal - a port can be
//    sent anywhere, including back - and it works. It also means a message the
//    receiver did not expect, because the protocol now has a loop. If a worker
//    appears to receive its own replies, this is why.

// and the fix for all of them, which is structural rather than careful
// Wrap each channel in an object with one owner and a close method, so there is
// exactly one place that can forget.
class Channel<T> {
  Channel(this._handler) {
    _port.listen((dynamic m) => _handler(m as T));
  }
  final _port = ReceivePort();
  final void Function(T) _handler;
  SendPort get sendPort => _port.sendPort;

  Future<void> close() async {
    await _port.close();       // ...`close` returns a Future in recent SDKs,
  }                            //    and it is NOT synchronous, so a
}                              //    fire-and-forget close can race the close
// ...that is the sixth mistake, and it is the reason the close is awaited here
// rather than called. The pattern is unremarkable in itself; the value is that
// it makes "who closes this" answerable by reading one class.

9.10 Isolate.run and IsolateGroup

The modern API, and the shared-code problem it creates.

// Isolate.run: the simple case, introduced in Dart 2.19
Future<T> runInIsolate<T>(T Function() body) => Isolate.run(body);

// it handles spawn, message, reply, cleanup and error propagation
Future<int> sumAsync(int n) => Isolate.run(() => _sum(n));

// THE CAVEAT: Isolate.run uses Isolate.exit, which shares the
// PROGRAM. You can send any object that is in the same isolate
// GROUP, so passing a non-sendable value can SILENTLY succeed on
// the VM and fail on the web, or behave differently in AOT.

// the older API used Isolate.spawn, which does NOT share code and
// enforces sendability strictly. That is why some packages still
// use it, and why some bugs only appear in release mode.

Future<T> runStrict<T>(T Function() body) {
  final receivePort = ReceivePort();
  Isolate.spawn(
    _entry,
    [_IsolateEntry(body, receivePort.sendPort)],
    debugName: 'strict',
  );
  return receivePort.first as Future<T>;
}

class _IsolateEntry {
  final Object Function() body;
  final SendPort replyTo;
  _IsolateEntry(this.body, this.replyTo);
}

void _entry(List<Object?> args) async {
  final entry = args[0] as _IsolateEntry;
  try {
    final result = await (entry.body as dynamic)();
    entry.replyTo.send(result);
  } catch (e, s) {
    entry.replyTo.send(e);
  }
}

// the practical advice: prefer Isolate.run, and test in RELEASE
// mode, because AOT changes what is legal
// why "test in release mode" matters
//
// in JIT (dart run):
//   - an unsendable object is copied by reference in some cases
//   - you see a clear error
// in AOT (dart compile exe, and every Flutter release build):
//   - the constraints are enforced differently
//   - a violation may crash at the boundary instead of throwing
//
// so: any isolate code path must be exercised in a release build
// before you ship it. This catches more than the isolates - the
// whole tree-shaking and const evaluation changes too.

Isolate.run, and why it is almost always the right API

Isolate.run is a one-shot worker: it spawns an isolate, runs a callback, sends back the return value, and terminates. It exists because the five lines it replaces are easy to get subtly wrong — ports that are not closed, errors that never complete the result port, entry points that cannot be named — and because it was written to be used instead of Isolate.spawn wherever the lifetime is one job.

Its constraints are the same ones Isolate.spawn has, plus one that is easy to forget: the callback runs in a different isolate, so it cannot capture anything. That makes the common mistake — a closure over local state — a runtime error rather than a compile error, and the error message names the unsendable object rather than the mistake.

// Isolate.run, and the constraint people hit
Future<int> fine(List<int> input) {
  return Isolate.run(() => input.fold(0, (a, b) => a + b));
}

// BROKEN: the callback captures `rows` from the enclosing scope
Future<int> broken(List<int> rows) {
  final factor = 3;
  return Isolate.run(() => rows.fold(0, (a, b) => a + b) * factor);
}
// ...`factor` is a captured variable. Because the callback is a closure and a
// closure is a heap object, sending it requires the object graph it captures.
// An `int` is sendable, so `factor` is fine. Change it to a `List` of
// non-sendable things and this fails at runtime with "object is unsendable".
// The rule that avoids the whole class: the callback should capture NOTHING.
// Put everything it needs in the argument.

// the three things it handles for you that spawn does not
// 1. errors become a completed Future with an error - no hanging result port
Future<int> throws() => Isolate.run(() => throw StateError('x'));
// ...the future completes with StateError. A hand-rolled spawn whose entry point
// throws sends nothing and hangs. This is the single most valuable difference.

// 2. the return value must be sendable, and the error names the type
await Isolate.run(() => <StreamController<int>>());
// ...Invalid argument: object is unsendable - _SyncStreamController<int>
//    found by SendPort.send

// 3. the isolate is terminated when the result is delivered
// ...so there is no cleanup to do and no pool to manage. The cost is that the
// spawn happens per call, which is why the next section exists.

// and the restriction that surprises people
await Isolate.run(() {
  return Completer<int>().future;    // ...completes only if something else
});                                     //    completes it - and nothing in this
// ...isolate can, so this HANGS. Isolate.run waits for the callback's future,
// and the future is pending, and the isolate has nothing to do and does not
// exit. It is a deadlock with no diagnostic.

// and a return type that is checked on the way back
Future<List<Row>> parseAll(String text) {
  return Isolate.run(() => parseSync(text));   // inferred as Future<List<Row>>
}
// ...the generic is inferred from the callback, and if the callback returns
// something unsendable the error is at the send, not at the declaration. So the
// type system does not check this - only the runtime does.

IsolateGroup, and the problem it solves

An IsolateGroup is a set of isolates that share one heap's static state. It exists for a narrow problem, and the problem is this: by default each isolate has its own copy of every top-level variable and every static field, so a configuration value parsed once in the main isolate is absent from every worker, and each worker must parse it again.

Joining a group makes those shared, so a worker sees the same static values the main isolate initialised. That is genuinely useful for configuration and for anything expensive at initialisation, and it is a sharp tool: the shared state is shared concurrently, so a group turns the "no shared memory" guarantee off for exactly the variables it covers.

// the group, and what it shares
static late final Config config = Config.load();   // ...parsed ONCE

Future<int> withoutGroup(String path) {
  // ...this worker has its OWN `config`, uninitialised. `config.host` throws
  // LateInitializationError inside the isolate, and the error message names a
  // variable the reader believes is shared:
  return Isolate.run(() => fetch(config.host, path));
}

Future<int> withGroup(String path) {
  final group = IsolateGroup();
  try {
    return Isolate.run(() => fetch(config.host, path), onGroups: {group});
    // ...now `config` was initialised in the MAIN isolate before the group was
    //    created, so this worker sees the same object. Saving one Config.parse
    //    per worker, and more importantly making the configuration consistent.
  } finally {
    group.shutdown();     // ...close the group when the work is done
  }
}
// ...the rule is that the group must be SHUT DOWN. A group holds its isolates
// alive past their own completion, and an un-shutdown group is a leak whose
// symptom is memory that never returns.

// the tool that makes this correct rather than lucky
class WorkerGroup {
  final _group = IsolateGroup();
  final _pending = <Isolate>[];

  Future<T> submit<T>(Future<T> Function() body) async {
    final iso = await Isolate.spawn(
      null,                              // ...no entry point
      null,
      onGroups: {_group},                // ...joined to the group
      onExit: _pending.remove,           // ...tracked so shutdown can wait
    );
    return Isolate.exit(iso, body);      // ...run `body` HERE and exit
  }

  Future<void> dispose() async {
    _group.shutdown();                    // ...kill every isolate in the group
    await Future.wait(_pending.map(Isolate.getExitCode));
  }
}
// ...`Isolate.exit(port, value)` is the piece that makes this ergonomic: it
// returns a value from the spawned isolate without an entry point function,
// so the isolate can be spawned for its GROUP MEMBERSHIP and then told what to
// do. Without it, group-based pools need an entry point per job, which defeats
// the purpose.

// and the honest warning
// Group-shared statics are read-write shared state. The compiler will not
// complain, there is no lock, and two workers incrementing a group-shared
// counter produce a lost update. Use it for:
//   - configuration, initialised before any isolate is created, read-only after
//   - expensive tables that would otherwise be rebuilt per isolate
// Do NOT use it for:
//   - a mutable counter, a cache that is written, or anything two workers touch
//     where a lost update would matter
// ...and note that this reintroduces exactly the class of bug the isolate model
// exists to prevent, so it should be a decision you make deliberately and
// comment, not one you arrive at by trying IsolateGroup and seeing it work.

9.11 A long-lived worker isolate

The pattern for a background service, and the lifecycle that makes it safe.

// a worker that lives for the app's lifetime
class Worker {
  final ReceivePort _commands;
  final SendPort _toMain;
  final Isolate _isolate;
  bool _disposed = false;

  Worker._(this._commands, this._toMain, this._isolate);

  static Future<Worker> spawn() async {
    final commands = ReceivePort();
    final toMain = ReceivePort();
    await Isolate.spawn(
      _backgroundLoop,
      _Bootstrap(commands.sendPort, toMain.sendPort),
      debugName: 'sync-worker',
    );
    // the worker sends back when it is ready
    await toMain.first;
    return Worker._(commands, toMain.sendPort, await _isolateOf(commands));
  }

  SendPort get port => _commands.sendPort;

  void dispose() {
    if (_disposed) return;
    _disposed = true;
    _commands.close();          // the loop ends, the isolate exits
  }
}

// the isolate entry point
class _Bootstrap {
  final SendPort toMain;
  final SendPort toWorker;
  _Bootstrap(this.toWorker, this.toMain);
}

Future<void> _backgroundLoop(_Bootstrap boot) async {
  // a dedicated receive port for commands
  final commands = ReceivePort();
  boot.toWorker.send(commands.sendPort);
  boot.toMain.send('ready');

  // the worker's own state, living in the isolate
  final queue = <Job>[];
  Timer? ticker;

  commands.listen((message) {
    switch (message) {
      case ['enqueue', Job job]:
        queue.add(job);
        if (ticker == null) {
          ticker = Timer.periodic(const Duration(seconds: 2), (_) {
            final batch = List<Job>.from(queue)..sort(_byPriority);
            queue.clear();
            for (final job in batch) {
              final result = _process(job);
              boot.toMain.send(['done', job.id, result]);
            }
          });
        }
      case ['cancel']:
        queue.clear();
        ticker?.cancel();
        ticker = null;
      case ['shutdown']:
        ticker?.cancel();
        commands.close();      // this ends the isolate
    }
  });
}

int _byPriority(Job a, Job b) => a.priority.compareTo(b.priority);
Object? _process(Job job) => job.payload;
// the resource rule for a worker isolate:
// EVERY resource it opens, it closes, in the same isolate.
// Nothing crosses the boundary except plain data.

void _syncLoop(_Bootstrap boot) async {
  // opened here...
  final db = await _openDatabase();
  final http = HttpClient();

  // ...and closed here, on the same side
  try {
    boot.toMain.send(['ready', db.id]);
    await for (final command in _commands) {
      // ...
    }
  } finally {
    db.close();
    http.close(force: true);
  }
}

// and a test for the lifecycle, because leaks here are invisible
test('the worker releases its resources on dispose', () async {
  final worker = await Worker.spawn();
  worker.port.send(['enqueue', Job(payload: 1)]);
  worker.dispose();

  // the port is closed
  expect(worker.port, isNotNull);       // still referenced, but:
  // no more messages are processed
  await Future.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 100));
  expect(isProcessing, isFalse);        // your own flag
});

The shape, and why it is worth the complexity

A long-lived worker isolate is the right structure when three conditions hold together: individual jobs are too small to justify a spawn, there are many more jobs than workers, and the workers can be kept warm. Failing the first, use Isolate.run. Failing the second, a pool adds bookkeeping for nothing.

When all three hold, the pool is a large win, because spawn cost is paid once rather than per job and the workers can hold state between jobs — a parsed schema, a warm connection, an index. That retained state is the other reason to do it, and it is also the reason it is dangerous: a worker that leaks memory across jobs is a leak that only appears under sustained load.

// the complete shape: acquire, use, release
class IsolatePool {
  IsolatePool(this.size) {
    for (var i = 0; i < size; i++) {
      final inbox = ReceivePort();
      final done = ReceivePort();
      _idle.add(SendPort(inbox.sendPort));
      inbox.listen((msg) async {
        final job = msg as Job;
        try {
          final r = await _run(job);
          done.send(WorkerOk(r));
        } catch (e, s) {
          done.send(WorkerFailed(e, s));
        } finally {
          // ...CRITICAL: return the worker to the idle set even on failure.
          // A worker that is never returned is a leak in the pool, and the
          // pool silently shrinks until it is exhausted.
          _idle.add(SendPort(inbox.sendPort));
        }
      });
      Isolate.spawn(() => _entry(SendPort(inbox.sendPort)), done.sendPort,
          debugName: 'pool-$i', onExit: _onExit);
    }
  }

  final int size;
  final _idle = Queue<SendPort>();
  var _live = 0;

  void _onExit(int code) => _live--;     // ...so exhaustion is detectable

  Future<R> submit<R>(Job job) async {
    if (_idle.isEmpty) {
      if (_live < size) {
        await Future<void>.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 5));
        return submit(job);                 // ...wait for a return, do not grow
      }
      throw StateError('pool exhausted');  // ...and say so rather than hanging
    }
    final port = _idle.removeFirst();
    _live++;
    final reply = ReceivePort();
    port.send(job..reply = reply.sendPort);
    return (await reply.first as R) as R;
  }
}

// the entry point, and the part that is easy to forget: the FIRST argument
// must be the worker's OWN reply port, so it can address itself later
void _entry(SendPort self) {
  final state = WorkerState();     // ...retained across every job this worker
  self.send(WorkerReady(state.schema));   //    runs. This is the reason a pool
}                                       //    beats Isolate.run: `state` is
                                        //    paid for once.

The four failure modes, all of which look the same from outside

A pool has a distinctive pathology: it does not crash, it stops making progress. Every one of its failure modes presents as a hang or as a slow drain rather than as an error, which is why each needs an explicit detection mechanism. These four account for essentially all of them.

// 1. THE WORKER DIED. The port is in _idle forever, holding a
//    SendPort whose isolate no longer exists. Every job sent there is dropped
//    and never answered, so submit() hangs.
final _deadPorts = <SendPort>{};

void _onExit(int code, SendPort port) {
  _idle.remove(port);                  // ...remove it from the idle set
  _deadPorts.add(port);                // ...and never hand it out again
  _live--;
  if (code != 0) log.warning('worker exited $code');
}
// ...the alternative, which many implementations use, is to RESPAWN on exit:
//   if (_live < size) _spawnReplacement();
// ...that converts a fatal worker error into a silent performance
// degradation: one worker dies every few minutes, the pool stays at size, and
// throughput drops by 10%. Logging is the better first move; respawning is the
// better second.

// 2. THE WORKER IS BUSY AND NEVER REPORTS. A job that awaits something that
//    never completes leaves the worker out of _idle forever.
Future<R> submitWithDeadline<R>(Job job, Duration d) async {
  final r = submit<R>(job);
  return r.timeout(d, onTimeout: () {
    // ...the TIMEOUT fires but the worker stays busy, so it is never returned.
    // The pool leaks one worker per timeout, and after `size` timeouts the
    // pool is permanently empty. The fix is a task INSIDE the worker:
    _run(job).timeout(d);   // ...the inner timeout releases the worker even
                            //    though the outer one has already given up
  });
}

// 3. A JOB HOLDS STATE THE WORKER NEVER RELEASES. The pool works fine under a
//    test and leaks under load.
class WorkerState {
  final _cache = <String, CompiledSchema>{};    // ...unbounded
  final _open = <Socket>[];                      // ...never closed
  void onJobEnd(Job j) {
    _cache.remove(j.schemaHash);                    // ...the discipline: an
    if (!j.needsSocket) _open.removeLast();         //    explicit teardown at
  }                                                  //    the end of every job,
}                                                   //    not at the end of the
// ...worker's life. Without it, memory grows with JOBS, which is invisible in
// a benchmark of 100 and obvious in production after a day.

// 4. AN EXCEPTION IN THE LISTENER. `_inbox.listen(...)` swallows a
//    synchronous throw in the handler by routing it to the zone, so the worker
//    is neither dead nor returned, and no log line names the problem.
_inbox.listen((msg) {
  try {
    _handle(msg);
  } catch (e, s) {
    log.severe('worker handler failed', e, s);   // ...or it appears as an
    _returned = false;                            //    unhandled async error
  }
});
// ...this one presents as "some errors are silently lost", which is the hardest
// symptom in the list to trace because there is no symptom at all.

// and the observability that makes all four diagnosable, which is four numbers
final _stats = {
  'pool.live': _live,                       // ...must equal size; if it drifts,
  'pool.idle': _idle.length,                //    workers are being lost
  'pool.jobs.completed': _completed,        // ...if it is flat, nothing is
  'pool.jobs.failed': _failed,              //    completing - a hang, not a loss
};
// ...`live + idle == size` is the invariant, and checking it in a periodic
// health check turns "the service is slow" into "the pool leaked 3 workers",
// which is actionable. It is four lines and it is the difference between a
// two-day investigation and a two-minute one.

Shutdown, which is where pools usually go wrong

A pool that starts correctly and stops badly is worse than no pool, because a stopped pool takes down the process. Shutdown is the part that is almost always deferred until something breaks, and it has three requirements that pull in different directions: stop accepting work, finish the work already accepted, and reclaim the workers. Doing them in the wrong order loses jobs; not doing the third leaks memory; not doing the first means new work arrives after you started tearing down.

// the three phases, and the order is the whole design
class IsolatePool {
  var _state = _State.open;      // open -> draining -> closed

  Future<void> shutdown({Duration grace = const Duration(seconds: 10)}) async {
    // PHASE 1: stop accepting. Submit() now refuses rather than queueing, and
    // a caller that gets an error knows to retry elsewhere instead of hanging
    // until the process exits.
    _state = _State.draining;

    // PHASE 2: let in-flight work finish, with a bound.
    final deadline = DateTime.now().add(grace);
    while (_inFlight > 0 && DateTime.now().isBefore(deadline)) {
      await Future<void>.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 20));
    }
    // ...a Bounded grace is essential. Without it, one worker stuck on a
    // network read means the process never exits, which in a container means a
    // SIGKILL after the grace period, which means the in-flight jobs are lost
    // anyway - just less visibly.

    // PHASE 3: kill the rest and reclaim.
    _state = _State.closed;
    _group.shutdown();                 // ...this is what actually reclaims
    await Future.wait(_live.map(Isolate.getExitCode));
    _ports.clear();                    // ...and this drops the port references,
    _inboxPorts.clear();               //    without which the ReceivePorts
  }                                    //    keep their subscriptions and the
}                                      //    isolates never exit. Both, not
                                       //    either.

// and the worker side: the worker must not send a reply after shutdown, or the
// result port has already been closed and the send throws
void entry(SendPort self, SendPort commands) {
  commands.listen((msg) {
    if (msg is Shutdown) return;         // ...stop consuming, and
    if (msg is Job) self.send(handle(msg));
  });
}
// ...note the exit condition. The worker does not exit when it is told to; it
// exits when its command ReceivePort is closed, because that removes the last
// subscription keeping it alive. So closing the COMMAND port is the shutdown
// signal, and _group.shutdown() is the backstop for a worker that has already
// stopped reading commands. Both are needed: either alone leaves a live isolate.

// and what a job accepted during phase 2 must do. This is the requirement that
// is most often missed and it is a correctness one, not a tidiness one:
Future<T> submit<T>(Job job) async {
  if (_state != _State.open) {
    throw PoolClosedException();       // ...the caller decides what to do
  }
  _inFlight++;
  try {
    return await _dispatch(job);
  } finally {
    _inFlight--;                       // ...and the counter must be decremented
  }                                    //    on BOTH paths, or a failed job
}                                      //    permanently inflates the count
// ...and the counter must be checked before the dispatch, not after, because a
// job dispatched after phase 2 has started may never complete - the worker is
// being told to stop - and then _inFlight never returns to zero and phase 2
// waits for its full grace on every shutdown even though nothing is running.

// the one-line check that makes shutdown observable, which is worth more than
// the rest of it: after shutdown, assert every port is closed and every isolate
// has exited. If a pool survives that check, it leaks; if it does not survive,
// the assertion names which one.

Testing a pool, without depending on timing

A pool is the hardest thing in this chapter to test, because it is concurrent, it is timing-dependent, and its bugs are leaks rather than wrong values. The tests that fail reliably are the ones that assert on invariants rather than on outcomes — the invariants are countable after the fact, so the test does not need to observe anything while it happens.

// 1. THE NO-WORK-LOST TEST. Every submitted job gets a reply.
test('every submitted job is answered exactly once', () async {
  final pool = IsolatePool(4);
  final replies = await Future.wait(
    [for (var i = 0; i < 500; i++) pool.submit(Job(i))],
  );
  expect(replies.toSet(), [for (var i = 0; i < 500; i++) i]);
  expect(replies.length, 500);
  await pool.shutdown();
});
// ...this catches mistake 1 (a worker taken out of the idle set and never
// returned) and mistake 2 (a port closed while a message is in flight), because
// both leave a job unanswered and both make this test TIME OUT rather than fail.
// Which is why it needs an explicit per-job timeout: a hang is not a failure the
// test framework reports usefully.

// 2. THE COUNT-BALANCE TEST, run after the fact and requiring no observation.
test('workers are neither lost nor duplicated', () async {
  final pool = IsolatePool(4);
  await Future.wait([for (var i = 0; i < 200; i++) pool.submit(Job(i))]);
  expect(pool.liveWorkerCount, 4);      // ...not 3: a job crashed a worker
  expect(pool.idleWorkerCount, 4);       // ...not 5: a worker returned twice
  await pool.shutdown();
});
// ...`idleWorkerCount == 5` is the duplicate-return bug, and it is invisible in
// every other test: two workers processing the queue is faster, not wrong, until
// the same job runs on two workers and a counter is incremented twice. This
// assertion is what makes that a caught failure.

// 3. THE EXHAUSTION TEST, which is the one nobody writes and the one that
//    finds the leak.
test('a pool recovers from a failing job', () async {
  final pool = IsolatePool(2);
  await pool.submit(ThrowingJob());          // ...this worker is now poisoned
  final results = await Future.wait([
    for (var i = 0; i < 20; i++)
      pool.submit(Job(i)).timeout(const Duration(seconds: 2)),
  ]);
  expect(results.length, 20);                // ...all 20 answered, so the pool
  expect(pool.liveWorkerCount, 2);           //    did not shrink permanently
});
// ...this is the test that distinguishes a pool that leaks one worker per
// failure from one that does not. With 2 workers, two failures and no recovery
// means the pool is permanently empty and jobs 3 through 20 time out. It is a
// four-line test and it is the highest-value one in the list, because worker
// death under partial failure is the normal case rather than the exceptional
// one.

// 4. THE SHUTDOWN TEST, because shutdown is where the bugs are.
test('shutdown refuses new work and drains in-flight work', () async {
  final pool = IsolatePool(2);
  final inFlight = pool.submit(SlowJob(const Duration(milliseconds: 200)));
  await pool.shutdown(grace: const Duration(seconds: 5));
  expect(inFlight, completes);                    // ...phase 2: it finished
  expect(() => pool.submit(Job(1)), throwsA(isA<PoolClosedException>()));
  expect(pool.liveWorkerCount, 0);                 // ...phase 3: reclaimed
});
// ...the middle assertion is the one that is easy to get wrong and expensive to
// discover: if submit does not refuse, a job dispatched during shutdown is
// accepted and then never completed, and the caller's future hangs forever.

// and the three anti-patterns in testing a pool
//   - sleeping: `await Future.delayed(const Duration(seconds: 1))` and hoping.
//     It is slow when it passes and it hides every race, because the sleep gives
//     the bug time to not happen.
//   - asserting on timing: "100 jobs took under 500 ms". This fails on a loaded CI
//     machine and passes on a real failure that merely made it slower.
//   - one big test: a single 500-job test reports one failure. Twenty-five tests
//     of twenty jobs each report which twenty failed.
// ...and the rule that follows: assert on state that can be counted after the
// fact (live workers, idle workers, replies received, jobs answered), because
// state you must sample during the run is state you will sample at the wrong
// moment.

9.12 Flutter: compute and isolates

The Flutter-specific APIs, and how they map to what you have learned.

// the modern Flutter APIs, all wrappers over Isolate.run
// which is why the Dart 3 story applies directly

// 1. compute: the simple case
final result = await compute(parseJson, jsonText);
T compute<T>(ParseCallback<T> callback, T message) =>
    Isolate.run(() => callback(message));

typedef ParseCallback<T> = T Function(String message);

// 2. the O(n) rule, which is the important heuristic
// Flutter has a 16ms frame budget. Spawning an isolate costs
// roughly 0.1-1ms, plus the data copy.
//
// below ~16ms of work:  do it inline
// above ~16ms:        use an isolate
//
// which means an isolate is worth it for work that would drop
// frames, not for work that is merely "big"

// 3. long-lived workers in Flutter: the same pattern as 9.11,
//    spawned in main() and disposed when the app shuts down
Future<void> main() async {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  await Database.open();                  // on the main isolate: cheap
  runApp(const MyApp());
}

// 4. the web has NO isolates
//    on the web, Isolate.run is unavailable and compute throws.
//    so: web code must be structured so the expensive path is
//    either absent, or a Web Worker you talk to with
//    package:web. Chapter 13 covers this.
// the architecture that works on all platforms
//   put the expensive work behind an interface
//   provide an isolate implementation for native
//   provide a Web Worker (or an inline) implementation for web

abstract class HeavyWorker {
  Future<List<Entry>> parse(String text);
  Future<Uint8List> transform(Uint8List bytes, int quality);
  void dispose();
}

// native
class IsolateWorker implements HeavyWorker {
  // Isolate.run based
}

// web
class WebWorker implements HeavyWorker {
  // package:web Worker based
}

// a trivial implementation for small inputs, which avoids the
// spawn cost entirely
class InlineWorker implements HeavyWorker {
  // just calls the functions directly
}

// and pick one at startup
HeavyWorker createWorker() {
  if (kIsWeb) return WebWorker();
  return IsolateWorker();
}

The most valuable thing isolates give you is not speed, it is responsiveness. Moving a 300ms computation off the UI thread turns a frozen interface into a slightly slower one, and that is a completely different product. That is the argument to make when someone asks whether the complexity is worth it.

Exercises 10

  1. Write a program that sums a billion numbers inline, time it, then move it to an isolate and time it again. Record both.
  2. Demonstrate the copy cost: pass a 50MB Uint8List to an isolate, then repeat with TransferableTypedData. Compare.
  3. Try to pass a File to an isolate, read the exact error, then fix it by passing the path.
  4. Build an IsolatePool of size four and prove it never runs more than four jobs at once.
  5. Write a long-lived worker isolate with a command queue, and verify it releases its resources on dispose.
  6. Compile a program with isolates in both JIT and AOT mode, and confirm the behaviour is identical.
  7. Implement the HeavyWorker interface with both an isolate and a Web Worker backend, and pick correctly per platform.

compute, and why it is not the same as Isolate.run

compute() is Flutter's wrapper: it spawns an isolate, runs the callback, and returns its future to the caller. The API is compute rather than Isolate.run because of one thing it does that Isolate.run does not — it is safe to call during a build, which means it can be used from a widget and not only from a lifecycle method.

That is the whole difference, and it is worth knowing precisely because the name suggests more. It shares the two important constraints: the callback is sendable, so it cannot capture anything, and its argument and return value must both be sendable. Everything in the previous sections about copying and closure capture applies unchanged.

// the two APIs, side by side
Future<Uint8List> a(String path) => compute(_resize, path);
Future<Uint8List> b(String path) => Isolate.run(() => _resize(path));

// the difference, and it is about WHERE you may call it
@override
Widget build(BuildContext context) {
  // ...SAFE: compute() schedules the work after the current build, so calling
  //    it during build does not block the frame or trip the "setState during
  //    build" assertion:
  final future = compute(_resize, path);

  return FutureBuilder<Uint8List>(
    future: future,
    builder: (context, snap) {
      // ...this is why compute() exists: an isolate CANNOT be spawned from a
      //    build method in a widget subtree, because Isolate.run is not allowed
      //    to be called during a build - the platform rejects it to protect
      //    against exactly the kind of work that would jank the frame.
      if (!snap.hasData) return const CircularProgressIndicator();
      return Image.memory(snap.data!);
    },
  );
}

// the constraint, in both APIs
Uint8List _resize(String path) { ... }   // ...TOP-LEVEL or static. A closure
// ...cannot cross, so `(path) => _resize(path)` fails at runtime in both.

// and where the callback's result must be sendable
Future<Uint8List> c(String path) {
  return compute((String p) async {
    final codec = await ui.instantiateImageCodec(await File(p).readAsBytes());
    final frame = await codec.getNextFrame();
    return frame.image.toByteData();   // ...a ByteData is sendable
  }, path);
}
// ...`ui.Image` is NOT sendable, which is the constraint people hit: the
// image has to be converted to bytes inside the isolate, because an image
// belongs to the engine's handle table and there is no way to reconstruct one
// in another isolate.

What isolates do and do not fix in a Flutter app

The value of an isolate in a Flutter app is specific, and it is not "the app is faster". It is that work which would otherwise occupy the UI thread moves off it, so frames continue to be produced at the display's refresh rate while the work happens. The consequence is narrower than it sounds: the animation and input stay smooth, while the work itself takes exactly as long as it did.

That distinction matters for expectations. An isolate does not make a janky scroll become instant; it makes a janky scroll continue to accept input and animate. And it only works for work that is genuinely off-threadable, which in Flutter means computation over data rather than anything touching the widget tree, the engine, or platform channels.

WorkIsolate helps?Why
Image decode and resizeYesPure computation over bytes
JSON parsing of a large payloadYesPure computation
Encryption, hashing, compressionYesPure computation
Sorting or filtering a large listYesPure computation
Database queryNoAlready off-thread; the channel is the cost
HTTP requestNoAlready async
A slow build methodNoIt must run on the UI thread
Custom paintingNoRasterisation is on the raster thread
A platform channel callNoChannels are main-isolate only
Reading a file into memoryNoAlready off-thread via the async API
// the frame budget, and the arithmetic that decides it
// Flutter renders at the display rate: 60 Hz is 16.7 ms, 120 Hz is 8.3 ms.
// A frame that overruns is dropped, and a dropped frame is visible as stutter.
//
// A frame is: BUILD -> LAYOUT -> PAINT, in the UI thread, plus RASTERISE
// on the raster thread. So the budget splits:
const frameBudgetUs = 8333;              // 120 Hz
const uiThreadBudgetUs = 6000;           // ...UI thread: build + layout + paint
const rasterBudgetUs = 2000;             // ...raster thread, off the UI thread

// ...so the diagnostic is: if the UI thread is over budget, the fix is either to
// reduce the build/layout/paint work or to move something off it. Isolates are
// for the second. They cannot reduce build cost, because build runs on the UI
// thread by definition.

// and the measuring, in the order that works
// 1. the frame timeline in DevTools, with Track frames on. A red band is a
//    frame that overran; the coloured phases say which one.
// 2. `debugRepaintRainbowEnabled = true` for repaint problems, which are a
//    paint-phase problem and not an isolate problem at all.
// 3. Timeline widgets around the work that might be moved:
    import 'package:flutter/scheduler.dart' show Timeline;
//    ...
//    Timeline.startSync('decode image', handler: () {
      final result = compute(_resize, path);
      // ...note: Timeline spans the SPAWN, not the work, because the work
      //    happens on another thread with its own timeline. To measure the
      //    work itself, put a Timeline.startSync inside the isolate callback.
// 4. and for the isolate itself:
//    Isolate.current.debugName        // ...null in a normal isolate; set it
//    //                                  with the debugName parameter and it
//    //                                  appears in DevTools and in any stack
//    //                                  trace from inside the worker
// ...which is the single most useful thing to know here: an unnamed isolate
// appears in a stack trace as "Isolate: <unnamed>" with no location, so naming
// workers turns a useless trace into a usable one.

// and the anti-pattern, which is common enough to name
Future<void> onTap() async {
  setState(() => loading = true);
  for (var i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
    final rows = await compute(_parseOne, items[i]);   // ...10,000 spawns
  }
  setState(() => loading = false);
}
// ...each compute() spawns an isolate, sends one item, receives one result, and
// terminates. The spawn cost dominates by two orders of magnitude, the frame
// budget is consumed by message delivery rather than by work, and this is
// SLOWER than doing it inline. The fix is one line: send the whole list, do the
// loop inside. `compute(_parseAll, items)` is faster than the loop above by a
// factor of hundreds, and is the same amount of code.
// ...which is the general shape of the mistake: an isolate per ITEM rather than
// per BATCH. Chapter 9.2's batching rule applies here with no exceptions.

10 · Libraries, Packages and pub

10.1 Package layout and the pubspec10.2 Every pubspec field that matters10.3 Dependencies and version constraints10.4 The pub commands you will use10.5 Monorepos and path dependencies10.6 Publishing a package10.7 Designing a package API10.8 Code generation10.9 Assets and platform channels

How Dart code is organised, shared, versioned and published. The pub tool is the whole story here.

10.1 Package layout and the pubspec

The standard directory structure, and what each part is for.

my_package/
├── pubspec.yaml          the manifest: the most important file
├── analysis_options.yaml the lints and the analyser configuration
├── README.md
├── CHANGELOG.md
├── LICENSE
├── lib/
│   ├── my_package.dart   the public API: what others import
│   └── src/              the implementation: conventionally private
│       ├── models/
│       ├── data/
│       └── platform/
├── bin/
│   └── my_package.dart   the executable entry point
├── test/
│   ├── my_package_test.dart
│   └── data/repo_test.dart
├── test_driver/          integration tests (dart test -p vm)
├── example/              a runnable example, and CI tests it
├── tool/                 build scripts, generators, migrations
├── assets/               images, fonts, templates
└── build/                generated code (git-ignored)
// the two rules that make a package pleasant to use
//
// 1. lib/my_package.dart is a THIN barrel file
//    it exports the public API and nothing else.
//    everything under lib/src/ is conventionally private, so you can
//    change it without a major version bump.
//
// lib/my_package.dart
export 'src/models/entry.dart';
export 'src/data/repository.dart';
export 'src/data/local_db.dart';
export 'src/platform/storage.dart' show Storage, MemoryStorage;
export 'src/result.dart';

// 2. example/ must compile
//    it is the documentation, it is what pub.dev renders, and CI
//    runs it so it cannot rot.

// the .g.dart convention
// a generated file sits next to its source with a .g.dart suffix,
// and is excluded from analysis: it is not written by a human
// lib/src/models/entry.dart
// lib/src/models/entry.g.dart    <- generated, never edited
// analysis_options.yaml:
//   analyzer:
//     exclude:
//       - "**/*.g.dart"

The directory layout pub expects

A Dart package is a directory with a pubspec.yaml in it, and the convention is that the package name matches the directory name. Everything pub does — resolution, caching, publishing, importing — keys off that file, so a package without one is just a folder. The layout below is the shape every package on pub.dev follows, and each directory has a rule attached rather than being a convention for its own sake.

PathPurposeRule
lib/Public APIOnly this is importable by others
bin/ExecutablesOne file per command
test/TestsNever shipped to users
example/Runnable examplesEach may have its own pubspec
tool/Dev scriptsNot importable, not shipped
lib/src/Private implementationDocumented as unstable
assets/Bundled filesDeclared in the pubspec

The rule that catches people is the one about lib/src. Dart has no access modifiers, so privacy is by path convention: importing package:foo/src/bar.dart directly works, the compiler permits it, and nothing warns you. What the convention buys is a promise the author makes — anything under src may change in any release, so a consumer who imports it has opted out of semver. Analysis options can enforce it, and the standard linter configuration does.

// the import path says what is public
import 'package:my_pkg/models/user.dart';      // public API - stable
import 'package:my_pkg/src/internal.dart';     // NOT stable - your choice

// lib/
//   my_pkg.dart              <-- the barrel: exports everything public
//   models/
//     user.dart              <-- public
//     post.dart              <-- public
//   src/
//     _database.dart         <-- private
//     _codec.dart            <-- private
// bin/
//   my_pkg.dart              <-- the executable
// test/
//   user_test.dart
// example/
//   my_pkg_example.dart      <-- has its own pubspec with a path dep
// tool/
//   generate.dart            <-- build_runner and friends

// the barrel, which is a deliberate API surface
// lib/my_pkg.dart
library;

export 'src/database.dart' show Database, DatabaseException;
export 'src/codec.dart' show Codec;
// ...`show` is the important part: exporting the whole file also exports its
// private helpers, which then become part of your public API by accident

// enforcing the convention
// analysis_options.yaml
linter:
  rules:
    - implementation_imports     # flags package:foo/src/... from outside
    - depend_on_referenced_packages

Three file naming rules complete the picture and each prevents a specific problem. Public files are named in snake_case and match what they declare, so an import reads as package:foo/user_repository.dart rather than package:foo/UserRepository.dart. Private files start with an underscore, which the implementation_imports lint and every reviewer recognise. And one public concept lives in one file, so a documentation page, a coverage report and an API diff all refer to the same path — which is what makes the generated docs coherent.

// one concept, one file, named for the concept
// lib/user_repository.dart
class UserRepository { … }
// lib/src/_postgres_user_repository.dart
class PostgresUserRepository implements UserRepository { … }

// the same rule for extensions on the public type
// lib/user_repository.dart  - the extension lives with the class, not in
extension UserRepositoryX on UserRepository {   // its own file
  Future<User?> byEmail(String email) => …;
}

// and for tests: the test file name mirrors the file it tests
// test/user_repository_test.dart   tests lib/user_repository.dart
// test/src/postgres_user_repository_test.dart   tests the private one

// the layout that does not scale, and why
// lib/models.dart       <-- one file, forty classes
// lib/utils.dart        <-- one file, everything else
// ...both become the file everyone opens, both are imported everywhere, and
// a change to one forces a rebuild of everything. Split by concept, and
// accept the directory.

Whether a package is an application or a library changes almost nothing about the layout and everything about the pubspec. An application has a bin/ or lib/main.dart and is never published, so it can depend on anything and its dependency section is expected to be large. A library has a public API under lib, may be published, and its dependency section is a declaration about what a consumer inherits — which is why a library's dependency constraints are usually looser than its own resolution, and why a library should depend on as few things as possible.

// an application
name: my_app
publish_to: none          <-- explicitly NOT published
version: 1.0.0+1
dependencies:
  flutter:
    sdk: flutter
  http: ^1.2.0
dev_dependencies:
  flutter_test:
    sdk: flutter
// ...`publish_to: none` is the explicit form, and it makes `dart pub publish`
// refuse rather than publishing by accident

// a library
name: my_pkg
version: 1.0.0
description: Does one thing, so it can be depended on.
repository: https://github.com/org/my_pkg
topics: [parsing, text]
environment:
  sdk: ^3.5.0

dependencies:
  collection: ^1.18.0        # ...ONE dependency, and it is justified
dev_dependencies:
  test: ^1.25.0
  lints: ^5.0.0

// the difference that matters
// application: dependencies are yours, pinned as tightly as you like
// library:      dependencies are your consumers' problem, so constraints
//               must be loose enough that a consumer's other packages can
//               coexist with them

// the version to bump when you change what
// 1.0.0  -> 1.0.1  a fix, no API change
// 1.0.1  -> 1.1.0  a new feature, backward compatible
// 1.1.0  -> 2.0.0  a breaking change

10.2 Every pubspec field that matters

A complete pubspec, annotated.

name: my_package
description: >-
  A one-line summary that appears in search results. Must be 60-180
  characters, and must not be "A Dart package." - say what it does.
version: 1.4.0
repository: https://github.com/you/my_package
issue_tracker: https://github.com/you/my_package/issues
documentation: https://pub.dev/documentation/my_package/latest

# SEMVER, because your users depend on it
environment:
  sdk: ">=3.0.0 <4.0.0"

# RUNTIME dependencies: your package will not work without them
dependencies:
  http: ^1.2.0
  meta: ^1.12.0

# DEV dependencies: tests, lints, generators. Not shipped.
dev_dependencies:
  test: ^1.25.0
  lints: ^4.0.0
  build_runner: ^2.4.0
  json_serializable: ^6.8.0

# a code-generation section, read by the generator
build:
  builder: json_serializable:serializable
  options:
    explicit_to_json: true

# for packages with native code, asset bundles, or executables
executables:
  my_tool: my_tool

flutter:
  plugin:
    platforms:
      android:
        package: com.you.my_package
        pluginClass: MyPackagePlugin
      ios:
        pluginClass: MyPackagePlugin
    assets:
      - assets/templates/
// the fields most people get wrong

// version: SEMVER, and it must be a NUMBER, not a date
//   1.0.0   first stable release
//   0.1.0   pre-release; pub warns if you publish 0.x to production
//   1.0.0+1 build metadata: pub.dev shows it, pub does not use it

// environment.sdk: this is a COMPATIBILITY range for the Dart SDK,
// NOT a version of your package. Getting it wrong means either
// users with a valid SDK cannot use you, or you are silently
// running on a Dart version that does not support your code.

// description: pub.dev search ranks on it. "A Flutter package for
// doing things." is worth nothing. "Parse and validate JWT tokens
// with expiry and audience validation." is what someone searches for.

// repository: without it, pub.dev gives a warning and your package
// is much harder to trust.

// homepage / documentation: optional but they drive the pub.dev UI.

Every field, and the ones people get wrong

A pubspec.yaml is small enough to read in full and every field in it has a consequence. The ones that cause trouble are the ones a tool fills in for you — version, environment, resolution — because pub will write them without explaining what they commit you to.

FieldRequiredWhat it commits you to
nameYesThe published identity; lowercase, underscores
versionYesSemver, and pub enforces it on publish
environmentYes in practiceThe SDK range your code needs
descriptionTo publish60–180 characters, checked by pub
repositoryTo publishWhere the source lives
dependenciesYesWhat a consumer inherits
dev_dependenciesNoNot inherited; tests and tooling only
publish_toNonone makes it unpublishable
resolutionNoPackage import resolution mode
topicsTo publishAt most five; how people find you
executablesNoThe names dart pub global activate installs
name: my_pkg
version: 1.2.3
description: >-
  A one-sentence description of what this does, written for someone deciding
  whether to depend on it. Pub scores it, and a truncated first line looks bad.
repository: https://github.com/org/my_pkg
issue_tracker: https://github.com/org/my_pkg/issues

environment:
  sdk: ^3.5.0
# ...a CARET on a 3.x SDK means >=3.5.0 <4.0.0. It is the single most
# important line in the file, because it is what stops your package installing
# on a Dart too old to understand your syntax.

dependencies:
  collection: ^1.18.0

dev_dependencies:
  test: ^1.25.0
  lints: ^5.0.0

# analysis_options.yaml is a separate file, referenced by name
lints:
  rules:
    - avoid_print

environment.sdk is a promise about your code's syntax, and it is easy to understate it. If you use records or patterns, you need ^3.0.0; if you use class modifiers with base or sealed you need ^3.3.0; if you use await using you need ^3.7.0. Getting this wrong does not fail on your machine — it fails in someone else's, with a parse error in your library, which is the least pleasant possible failure mode. Declaring an upper bound is what lets the language evolve: without <4.0.0, a Dart 4 that changes a syntax detail would break every package that never declared it.

// the constraint forms, and what each means
sdk: '>=3.5.0 <4.0.0'   # the explicit form of ^3.5.0
sdk: ^3.5.0             # identical - caret is shorthand for the same range
sdk: '>=3.5.0 <4.2.0'   # a tighter upper bound, if you tested up to 4.2
sdk: '>=3.0.0 <4.0.0'   # broad, and safe for a library

// what the constraint must match
// - the minimum SDK whose parser can read every file in lib/
// - an upper bound, always, so a major release is not silently adopted
// - NOT the SDK you happen to be running (too narrow, excludes consumers)
// - NOT the SDK you hope people have (too broad, breaks on older ones)

// and the Flutter equivalent
environment:
  sdk: ^3.5.0
  flutter: '>=3.24.0'      # ...a plugin also constrains Flutter
dependencies:
  flutter:
    sdk: flutter

// what pub does when a consumer's SDK is out of range
// $ dart pub get
// Because my_pkg requires SDK version >=3.5.0 <4.0.0, version solving failed.
// ...and it names YOUR package, in THEIR build output. This is why the
// constraint is worth getting right.

Two fields are machine-facing rather than human-facing and are worth recognising. resolution selects how package:-prefixed imports inside your package are resolved — workspace-relative or package-relative — and it exists because a monorepo and a published package need different behaviour. And flutter as a top-level plugin declaration, which lists the plugin platforms a Flutter plugin supports; it is not a dependency but it lives beside them.

// resolution: workspace package import resolution
name: my_pkg
resolution: workspace
// ...so `package:my_pkg/foo.dart` inside your own package resolves to
// ../my_pkg/foo.dart rather than through the package graph. This makes
// intra-package imports work identically in a monorepo and in the published
// tarball, which is exactly the bug it fixes.

// the Flutter plugin fields
name: my_plugin
flutter:
  plugin:
    platforms:
      android:
        package: org.example.my_plugin
        pluginClass: MyPlugin
      ios:
        pluginClass: MyPlugin
      web:
        pluginClass: MyPluginWeb
      # ...each platform's entry point is declared here, and a missing one
      # means the plugin silently does not exist on that platform
    platforms: <no web entry>
    dartPluginClass: MyPluginDart

// what pub validates at publish time, and fails on
// - name format: lowercase, underscores, no dots, not a reserved word
// - version: a valid semver, and NOT already taken
// - description: 60-180 characters, and not a copy of another package's
// - homepage/repository: a URL that resolves
// - topics: 1-5, lowercase, from a fixed vocabulary

Beyond the required fields there are optional ones that change behaviour rather than metadata. executables renames what dart pub global activate installs, so a package with several entry points in bin/ can expose several commands under names of your choosing rather than under file names. funding and issue_tracker are surfaced on the package page, and screenshots in the form of image URLs appears in the gallery — all three affect the scoring, none is validated, and each is a place where an unmaintained package visibly looks abandoned.

name: my_tool
version: 2.1.0

executables:
  mytool: my_tool          # installs the command `mytool`
  mytool-admin: my_tool_admin
# ...bin/my_tool.dart and bin/my_tool_admin.dart, and both become runnable
# commands after `dart pub global activate my_tool`

funding:
  - https://github.com/sponsors/org
issue_tracker: https://github.com/org/my_pkg/issues
# ...and for a Flutter package's gallery, on pub.dev's own page
screenshots:
  - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/org/my_pkg/main/doc/shot1.png

One more field of a sort is not in the pubspec at all: the generated .dart_tool/package_config.json, which is how the analyzer and the runtime actually find packages. It is derived from the pubspec and the lockfile, it must never be committed, and every "the import works in the IDE but not on the command line" report is a stale copy of it. That is why dart pub get is the first step of any fresh checkout and the first thing to try when an import behaves inconsistently between environments.

10.3 Dependencies and version constraints

The constraint syntax, the two kinds of dependency, and resolving conflicts.

// the constraint syntax
dependencies:
  exact: 1.2.3        // exactly this version
  caret: ^1.2.3       // >=1.2.3 <2.0.0   - the DEFAULT, and usually right
  caret_minor: ^1.2.3 // same thing; ^1.2.3 means >=1.2.3 <2.0.0
  tilde: ~1.2.3       // >=1.2.3 <1.3.0   - more conservative
  any: any            // >=0.0.0 - almost always wrong
  none: ">=1.0.0 <2.0.0"   // an explicit range

// WHY ^ IS THE DEFAULT
//   ^1.2.3 allows 1.9.0: a minor bump, which SEMVER says is
//   backward compatible. It does NOT allow 2.0.0, which is not.
//   This means your users get bug fixes automatically, and a
//   breaking change requires an explicit action from you.

// transitive dependencies: you get them for free
// if `a` depends on `b`, and you depend on `a`, you can import `b`
// without listing it. But DO NOT: if `a` drops `b`, your code breaks.
//   the lint: depend_on_referenced_packages

// the conflict you will hit
//   you need package ^1.0.0
//   package A needs ^2.0.0 of the same
//   -> the solver cannot find a solution
//
// the fix, in order of preference:
//   1. upgrade A (it may have widened its constraint)
//   2. downgrade yourself
//   3. use a dependency_overrides, and understand the risk
//   4. fork

dependency_overrides:
  http: ^2.0.0     # forces a version; the risk is a broken A

// understanding the lockfile
// pubspec.lock   - the RESOLVED versions, committed for apps,
//                   git-ignored for packages
// it is what makes a build reproducible
// the difference between an application and a package
//
// APPLICATION (a thing people run):
//   commit pubspec.lock    -> everyone gets the same versions
//   do not put anything in dev_dependencies you need at runtime
//   care about the whole transitive tree
//
// LIBRARY (a thing people import):
//   git-ignore pubspec.lock  -> your users resolve their own
//   keep dev_dependencies minimal so your users install less
//   be conservative: your constraint is a promise

// a library should declare the NARROWEST range it can support
dependencies:
  collection: ">=1.17.0 <2.0.0"   // if you only use what has been
                                  // stable since 1.17, say so
// every constraint you widen is a compatibility promise you make
// to every user, forever

Version constraints, and what each one costs

A constraint is a range, and pub solves for the best version in every range simultaneously. The caret is the default and the right answer almost always: ^1.2.3 means >=1.2.3 <2.0.0, which takes patch and minor updates but refuses a major one — and a major is where breaking changes live, so this is the range that stops your build from breaking under you.

ConstraintRangeTakesRisk
^1.2.3>=1.2.3 <2.0.0Patches, minorsLow
^0.2.3>=0.2.3 <0.3.0Patches onlyLow
^0.0.3>=0.0.3 <0.0.4NothingPinned
1.2.3Exactly thatNothingHighest
>=1.2.3 <2.0.0ExplicitSame as caretLow
anyNo limitEverythingHigh
^1.0.0 + sdkRange plus SDK——

The 0.x row is the one that surprises people, and it is deliberate. Under semver, a 0.y.z release is not a stable API — the caret on a zero-major stops at the next minor for exactly that reason. So a package that wants to make breaking changes freely while it stabilises uses 0.x, and its consumers get an automatic signal when a release could break them. A package that publishes 1.0.0 has made the opposite promise, and the caret now means what everyone expects.

// the same package under different constraints
dependencies:
  a: ^1.2.3        # >=1.2.3 <2.0.0   - patches and minors
  b: ^0.2.3        # >=0.2.3 <0.3.0   - patches only, because 0.x
  c: 1.2.3         # exactly 1.2.3         - pinned, fragile
  d: any           # whatever pub likes     - never

// a constraint can be a union, which is occasionally necessary
e: '>=2.0.0 <3.0.0 || >=4.0.0 <5.0.0'

// a git dependency, and its three problems
f:
  git:
    url: https://github.com/org/repo.git
    ref: main              # a BRANCH - not reproducible
    # path: packages/f     # a subdirectory, for a monorepo
# ...`ref: main` means the build depends on what a remote branch looks like
# today. Use a tag or a commit SHA for anything that must reproduce, and
# remember that a published package may not have git dependencies at all.

// a hosted dependency with a private source
g:
  hosted: https://internal.example.com/api/packages/mycompany
  version: ^2.1.0
# ...so an internal package resolves from your own registry

// and an SDK dependency, which is not a version at all
flutter:
  sdk: flutter
dart:
  sdk: '>=3.5.0 <4.0.0'
test:
  sdk: flutter_test        # an SDK package, so no version constraint

dev_dependencies versus dependencies is a distinction with a real cost, and the rule is simply whether a consumer needs it at run time. Anything your lib/ code imports is a real dependency; anything only your tests, examples or build scripts import is a dev dependency. Getting it wrong in one direction means your consumer's build fails with an unresolved import; getting it wrong in the other means every consumer downloads your test framework and never uses it. The analyzer's depend_on_referenced_packages lint catches the first automatically.

// the classification, by where the import appears
// lib/src/parser.dart  imports  package:collection/collection.dart
//   -> dependencies: because lib/ is shipped and it is imported there

// test/parser_test.dart  imports  package:test/test.dart
//   -> dev_dependencies: never shipped to a consumer

// example/demo.dart  imports  package:my_pkg/my_pkg.dart
//   -> no entry needed: the example's own pubspec has the path dep

// the lints that enforce it
// analysis_options.yaml
linter:
  rules:
    - depend_on_referenced_packages   # a lib/ file importing a dev dep
    - implementation_imports          # importing package:foo/src/...
    - directives_ordering             # imports sorted: dart, package, relative
    - always_declare_return_types
    - avoid_relative_lib_imports      # use package:foo/... not ../lib/...

// and the command that shows you
// $ dart pub deps --style=compact
// my_pkg 1.2.3
// |- collection 1.18.0
// |- test 1.25.0 (dev)

A path dependency is the escape hatch for local work, and it is the one dependency kind that cannot be published. It points at a directory on disk, so it works on your machine and nowhere else; pub refuses to publish a package that has one. That refusal is why the pattern has a required extra step, and getting it wrong is a common way to discover that someone committed a local path into a shared repository.

// a path dependency, for local development
dependencies:
  my_core:
    path: ../my_core
# ...resolved from disk, never fetched. Works. Unpublishable.

// what pub says if you try
// $ dart pub publish
// my_app has a path dependency on my_core.
// Packages with path dependencies cannot be published.

// the correct pattern: develop against the path, publish against the version
// 1. add the path dependency, develop, test
// 2. before publishing:
//      path: ../my_core        ->     ^1.4.0
// 3. dart pub publish
// 4. keep the path in a separate branch or a local override

// the clean modern answer: a pubspec_overrides.yaml, which is NOT committed
// dependencies:
  my_core: ^1.4.0
# pubspec_overrides.yaml (git-ignored)
dependency_overrides:
  my_core:
    path: ../my_core
# ...so the pubspec stays publishable and every developer on the team gets
# their own local version. This is the shape to use.

# and for a monorepo where the packages genuinely move together,
// Dart 3.6's `dart pub workspace` is better still - see ch9b-workspaces

10.4 The pub commands you will use

The full set, with the ones worth memorising marked.

// THE DAILY SIX
dart pub get             fetch and resolve        (npm install)
dart pub add http        add a dependency        (npm install http)
dart pub remove http     remove it
dart pub deps            the dependency tree
dart pub outdated        what could be upgraded
dart pub upgrade         upgrade everything, rewriting the lockfile

// THE ONES YOU WILL NEED
dart pub run build_runner build       run code generators
dart pub run build_runner watch       ...continuously, while you work
dart pub publish --dry-run            check a package before publishing
dart pub global activate <tool>       install a CLI tool
dart pub cache repair                 if something is corrupted
dart pub cache clean                  free disk space

// THE FLUTTER EQUIVALENTS
flutter pub get
flutter pub add
flutter pub deps
flutter pub outdated
flutter pub upgrade
flutter pub publish --dry-run

// the flag that matters
dart pub outdated --mode=null-safety
// shows which packages have not been migrated to null safety
// diagnosing a dependency problem
// 1. the tree
dart pub deps --style=compact
// look for: the SAME package at two versions, or a package with a
// very old constraint

// 2. why is this version
dart pub deps --json | python -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(d['packages'])"
// or just read pubspec.lock

// 3. the "resolution failed" message is verbose but precise.
// read the LAST part: it names the conflicting constraints.

// 4. the nuclear options, in increasing severity
dart pub cache repair          # corrupted download cache
rm -rf .dart_tool pubspec.lock # start resolution over
rm -rf ~/.pub-cache            # the whole cache - slow, rarely needed

// 5. why a package will not upgrade
//    its constraint is too narrow, or it depends on something that
//    conflicts. Read its pubspec on pub.dev; the constraints are
//    right there.

The commands, grouped by what you are trying to do

Pub has a small command set and they are worth learning as a set rather than by looking them up. Four of them you will run daily, get, add, remove and upgrade; a handful more handle publishing, linking and caching; and one, deps, is the diagnostic you reach for when a resolution surprises you.

CommandWhat it doesWhen
getResolve, write the lockfileAfter editing the pubspec
addAdd a dep and resolveAdding one dependency
removeDrop a dep and resolveDropping one
upgradeRe-resolve, moving everything allowedA new version is out
upgrade pkgMove one dependency onlyThe common case
depsPrint the resolved treeDiagnosing a version
outdatedCompare resolved against latestBefore a release
publishValidate and uploadReleasing
publish --dry-runValidate onlyAlways first
global activateInstall a CLI toolInstalling a tool
cache repairRe-download the cacheCorrupt cache
runRun an executable from a depRunning a tool

dart pub upgrade and dart pub get differ in what they are allowed to move, and the distinction matters more than it sounds. get honours the lockfile: if a resolved version still satisfies the constraints, it stays. upgrade ignores the lockfile's versions and re-solves from the constraints, so it moves every dependency as far as its range allows — which on a project with forty dependencies is a large diff and a probable source of a new bug. When you want a single new version, the answer is upgrade <name>, which touches one line.

// the daily four
dart pub get                       # after any pubspec edit
dart pub add collection            # adds the constraint AND resolves
dart pub remove collection         # ...and it also cleans unused imports? No -
                                  //    it does not; run `dart fix` after
dart pub upgrade --major-versions  # a big, deliberate jump

// the one you actually want
dart pub upgrade collection
// ...moves collection as far as its constraint allows, leaves the rest of the
// lockfile alone. A one-line diff.

// seeing what moved
dart pub outdated
# package  current  resolvable  latest
# http     1.1.0    1.2.0       1.2.0
# path     1.8.0    1.8.3       1.9.0    (latest is outside your constraint)

// the diagnostic when resolution surprises you
dart pub deps --style=tree
# my_app 1.0.0
# |- args 2.5.0
# |  - meta 1.9.0
# |- http 1.2.0
# |  |- async 2.11.0
# |  |  - collection 1.18.0    <-- ONE version, shared

dart pub deps --json | jq '.packages[] | select(.kind=="direct")'
# ...to check which constraints are actually yours

dart pub deps --dev                              # include dev deps
dart pub deps --no-dev

The lockfile is the mechanism that makes builds reproducible, and its role is narrower than most people assume. pubspec.lock pins exact versions for applications and is committed. For published libraries it is deliberately not committed, because a library should resolve against whatever its consumer's other packages need — committing it would make every consumer of that library get your exact resolution. This is why an application repository has a lockfile and a library repository does not, and it is a rule pub enforces rather than suggests.

// pubspec.lock for an APPLICATION - commit it
// packages:
//   collection:
//     dependency: "direct main"
//     source: hosted
//     version: "1.18.0"
// sdks:
//   dart: ">=3.4.0 <4.0.0"
// ...every entry has a `source`, which is how pub knows whether a package
// came from pub.dev, git, or a path - and it refuses to mix sources for one
// package name.

// for a LIBRARY - do not commit it
// .gitignore
pubspec.lock
# ...and pub warns on publish if it is present:
// "Your pubspec.lock is not being committed, which is correct for a
//  library, but note that consumers will resolve their own versions."

// the CI shape for an application
// .github/workflows/ci.yml
- run: dart pub get
- run: dart analyze
- run: dart test
# ...`pub get` on a committed lockfile is deterministic. Never `upgrade`
// in CI: it turns a passing build into a coin flip.

// and the Docker/CLI case
COPY pubspec.yaml pubspec.lock ./
RUN dart pub get --offline        # ...restore from the cache with no network
COPY . .
RUN dart pub get --enforce-lockfile
RUN dart pub run test

Three commands handle tooling rather than the current package, and their shared property is that they install into a separate activated snapshot rather than into the project. global activate installs a CLI, dart run runs an executable from a dependency without installing anything, and dart pub global run runs an activated one. Choosing between them is a question of whether the tool should be pinned to a project or available everywhere.

// three ways to run a CLI tool

// 1. dart run - the RIGHT way for project tools
//    a dev_dependency pins the version, and everyone gets the same one
dev_dependencies:
  build_runner: ^2.4.0
  json_serializable: ^6.8.0
// $ dart run build_runner build

// 2. global activate - for a tool you want everywhere
dart pub global activate dart_style
dart pub global activate cli_tools 1.2.3   # ...pin it, or you get surprises
// $ dart pub global run dart_style:format .
// the PATH needs ~/.pub-cache/bin on it, which is a common setup failure

// 3. dart pub exec - a one-off, without activating
dart pub global activate --source path .
// ...rarely what you want

// the Flutter equivalents, which are not pub commands at all
flutter pub get
flutter pub add http
flutter pub upgrade --major-versions
flutter pub run build_runner build
// ...`flutter pub` is a wrapper that also resolves the Flutter SDK version
// and keeps the flutter constraint consistent. Use it in a Flutter project.

// what to put in CI
- run: dart pub get
- run: dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
- run: dart test
// ...`--delete-conflicting-outputs` is required when generated files are
// committed and the generator's output would differ from them

10.5 Monorepos and path dependencies

Sharing code across several packages in one repository.

// the simple approach: path dependencies
// packages/app/pubspec.yaml
dependencies:
  core:
    path: ../core
  data:
    path: ../data

// works immediately, no publishing. but:
//   - the path is absolute-ish: it works on YOUR machine only
//   - it does not work for anyone who installs your app
//   - so this is for development, not for release

// the better approach: pub workspaces (Dart 3.6+)
// a single pubspec at the root
// my_monorepo/pubspec.yaml
name: my_monorepo
publish_to: none
environment:
  sdk: "^3.6.0"
workspace:
  - packages/core
  - packages/data
  - packages/app

// and each member is a normal package
// packages/core/pubspec.yaml
name: core
environment:
  sdk: "^3.6.0"
dependencies:
  meta: ^1.12.0

// then from anywhere in the workspace:
dart pub get
dart run packages/app/bin/main.dart
dart test packages/core/test/

// one pubspec.lock for the whole workspace
// one .dart_tool/package_config.json
// the members can depend on each other by name, as if published
// a monorepo layout that works
my_monorepo/
├── pubspec.yaml              the workspace root
├── packages/
│   ├── core/                 no Flutter, no platform code
│   │   ├── lib/core.dart
│   │   ├── lib/src/
│   │   └── test/
│   ├── data/                 repositories, DTOs, local storage
│   │   └── lib/data.dart
│   ├── ui/                   widgets, theme, design system
│   │   └── lib/ui.dart
│   └── app/                  the app itself: main, wiring, platform
│       ├── lib/app.dart
│       └── bin/main.dart
├── tool/                     scripts
└── analysis_options.yaml     shared lints, one config

// the dependency direction, enforced by review and by imports:
//   app -> ui, data, core
//   data -> core
//   ui   -> core
//   core -> nothing internal
//
// core has no dependencies on its siblings, which means it cannot
// create a cycle, and it is trivially testable.

Monorepos: path dependencies versus a pub workspace

A monorepo with several Dart packages needs one decision made consistently: how a package in the repository depends on its sibling. Two mechanisms exist — path dependencies with a pubspec_overrides.yaml, and Dart 3.6's native dart pub workspace — and they differ in what a member's lockfile contains, which determines whether a release of one package can break another.

Path deps + overridesPub workspace
Declared inEach member's overrides fileThe root pubspec
LockfileOne per memberOne for the whole repo
ResolutionPer memberShared across all members
PublishableYes, with a version swapYes, overrides are ignored
Conflicting versionsPossible between membersImpossible
Added inAny versionDart 3.6

The defining difference is that a workspace has one resolution for the whole repository. If two members need incompatible versions of a package, a workspace fails to resolve and the conflict must be fixed; with independent path dependencies, each member resolves separately and both work. That is a feature rather than a limitation for a repository whose packages are meant to be used together, and it is also why a workspace is a poor fit for a set of unrelated packages that happen to share a git remote.

// a workspace, in full
// repo/
//   pubspec.yaml
//   analysis_options.yaml
//   packages/
//     core/
//       pubspec.yaml
//       lib/core.dart
//     ui/
//       pubspec.yaml
//       lib/ui.dart
//     app/
//       pubspec.yaml
//       lib/main.dart
//   pubspec.lock                <-- ONE lockfile for all three

// repo/pubspec.yaml
name: my_monorepo
publish_to: none
environment:
  sdk: ^3.6.0
workspace:
  - packages/core
  - packages/ui
  - packages/app
dev_dependencies:
  lints: ^5.0.0
  test: ^1.25.0

// packages/ui/pubspec.yaml
name: my_ui
version: 0.1.0
environment:
  sdk: ^3.6.0
dependencies:
  my_core:
    path: ../core        # <-- a path dep, but resolved by the workspace

// what you can no longer do
// - a member may not have its own pubspec.lock
// - pubspec_overrides.yaml is ignored in a workspace
// - `dart pub get` must be run from the ROOT, not from a member
// - every member must agree on its SDK constraint, or resolution fails

// the command form
dart pub workspace add packages/new_thing
dart pub workspace list

Publishing from a monorepo is where the two approaches diverge most, and it is worth being precise about the sequence because getting it wrong publishes a broken dependency. A member's path dependency must not be present at the moment dart pub publish runs, and neither the workspace nor the overrides file is used to resolve it — the published version must be in the member's own dependencies. So the release is a three-step dance in which the version has to be correct before publication rather than swapped in afterwards.

// the publish sequence, per package, in dependency order
// 1. publish the leaf with no internal deps
