  await sink.close();      // MUST close to flush
}

// and in an isolate, for real large files
Future<int> countLinesInBackground(File file) async {
  return Isolate.run(() async {
    var count = 0;
    await for (final _ in file.openRead()
        .transform(utf8.decoder)
        .transform(const LineSplitter())) {
      count++;
    }
    return count;
  });
}

A file written with openWrite() is not complete until you close it. If your process is killed before the close, the file is truncated. Every streamed write needs a try/finally that closes the sink, and if the content matters, the atomic-write pattern from 11.3 is safer still.

Large files: streaming, and the two buffer sizes

Reading a file with readAsBytes puts the entire file in memory; reading it with openRead() puts a fixed-size chunk in memory and lets the consumer's pacing decide what happens next. The difference is not an optimisation, it is the difference between working and an out-of-memory error, and the threshold where it matters is much lower than people expect because the peak is the buffer plus whatever the consumer accumulates.

// the two, and what each costs
final all = await File('2gb.log').readAsString();     // ...2 GB, plus a
                                                        //    String's UTF-16
await for (final line in File('2gb.log').openRead(4096).transform(utf8.decoder)
    .transform(const LineSplitter())) {
  process(line);        // ...4 KB at a time, constant memory
}

// the default chunk size is 64 KB, and the three places it appears
await for (final chunk in File('big.bin').openRead()) { }        // ...64 KB
await for (final line in File('big.log')
    .openRead(1024 * 1024)                 // ...1 MB: fewer syscalls, more
    .transform(utf8.decoder)
    .transform(const LineSplitter())) { }  // ...    memory per consumer

final sink = File('out.bin').openWrite();   // ...also 64 KB internally
await sink.addStream(source);               // ...respects the consumer's pace

// why utf8.decoder must sit between: a chunk boundary can fall in the middle
// of a multi-byte character, so a raw byte chunk is not a valid String
await for (final line in File('utf8.log').openRead().transform(utf8.decoder)) {
  // ...the decoder holds back partial characters between chunks. Reading the
  // chunks and decoding each one yourself produces replacement characters at
  // exactly the chunk boundaries, which is a bug that appears only on files
  // larger than the chunk size.
}

// LineSplitter, which buffers until it has a line
await for (final line in File('big.log').openRead()
    .transform(utf8.decoder).transform(const LineSplitter())) { }
// ...one line in memory at a time. A file with no newline at all - a minified
// JS bundle - is ONE line, so this reads the whole thing. Guard by size first.

// the whole pipeline, which is the shape to copy
Future<int> countLines(String path) async {
  var n = 0;
  await for (final _ in File(path).openRead()
      .transform(utf8.decoder)
      .transform(const LineSplitter())) {
    n++;
  }
  return n;
}

Backpressure is what the streaming API buys, and it is automatic: an await for body that takes time suspends the subscription, which stops the file read, which stops the disk I/O. Nothing buffers. The same is true in the other direction through addStream, which awaits each write rather than queuing everything. So the only way to lose backpressure is to break the chain — by calling toList() on the stream, by writing to a broadcast subscription, or by launching an await inside the body without awaiting it.

// backpressure, working
await for (final line in lines) {
  await upload(line);        // ...slow consumer, so the read waits. Constant
}                             //    memory, however slow the network is

// backpressure, destroyed - three ways
final all = await lines.toList();           // ...1. materialises everything
final len = lines.length;                   // ...2. Stream.length waits for all
lines.listen(handle);                       // ...3. listen has no await point
                                            //    in handle, so it never pauses

// the one that is subtle: an unawaited future in the loop body
await for (final line in lines) {
  processAsync(line);          // ...NOT awaited. The loop continues, so the
}                               //    subscription is never paused and every
                                //    line's future is pending at once

// the fix, when the work must be concurrent
await for (final line in lines) {
  inflight.add(processAsync(line));         // ...bounded below
  if (inflight.length >= 8) {
    await Future.wait(inflight);
    inflight.clear();
  }
}
await Future.wait(inflight);
// ...or use `asyncMap`, which does this with one operator

// writing with backpressure, which is less obvious
final sink = File('out.log').openWrite();
await for (final line in lines) {
  sink.writeln(line);        // ...an IOSink buffers and applies its own
}                             //    backpressure; nothing here awaits, so the
                              //    producer is not paced. For real pacing use
                              //    `await sink.flush()` or addStream.
await sink.close();          // ...flushes and closes; without it, data is lost

// the correct large-copy
await File('src.bin').openRead().pipe(File('dst.bin').openWrite());
// ...or, with the handles, so a failure can clean up:
final out = File('dst.bin').openWrite();
try {
  await out.addStream(File('src.bin').openRead());
} finally {
  await out.close();
}

Transforming while streaming has two costs that are easy to overlook. A transform that is CPU-bound does not pause the source, so an expensive per-line transform still reads the whole file at disk speed and queues the results — the streaming has protected memory, not time. And a transform that allocates heavily produces garbage at the rate the file is read, so the garbage collector runs continuously; a large file processed this way can be slower than reading it in one go if the transform is trivial.

// a CPU-bound transform defeats the streaming benefit
await for (final rec in hugeCsv.openRead()
    .transform(utf8.decoder)
    .transform(const LineSplitter())
    .transform(csvToJson)) {          // ...synchronous and expensive
  out.write(rec);
}
// ...memory stays flat, but the disk is read at full speed into a queue of
// pending results, and the GC runs throughout. Measure before assuming.

// three transforms that do NOT allocate much, which is when streaming shines
// .transform(utf8.decoder)          // ...required, and cheap
// .transform(const LineSplitter()) // ...one String per line, unavoidable
// .where((l) => l.startsWith('ERROR'))  // ...no allocation

// and the batching transform, which is the right shape for a heavy parse
await for (final batch in lines.map(parse).batch(1000)) {
  await db.insertAll(batch);         // ...parse in memory, commit in batches
}
// ...`batch` from package:async buffers N values and yields a List, so peak
// memory is N parsed objects rather than the whole file

// counting without materialising anything
Future<int> countBytes(String path) async {
  var n = 0;
  await for (final chunk in File(path).openRead()) {   // ...raw chunks, no
    n += chunk.length;                                 //    decode, no strings
  }
  return n;
}
// ...the cheapest possible pass over a file: no allocation at all beyond the
// chunk itself, and it works on a 40 GB file

// and gzip, because compressed files are a real case
final out = File('data.gz').openWrite().transform(const GZipCodec().encoder);
await out.addStream(File('data').openRead());
await out.close();
// ...which is the same pipeline with one transform added, and is why streaming
// composes: the whole design is that each stage is a Stream

11.6 HTTP client

Timeouts, retries, cancellation, and the client lifecycle.

import 'dart:io';

// a client is expensive: it holds a connection pool. Reuse one.
final client = HttpClient()
  ..connectionTimeout = const Duration(seconds: 10)
  ..userAgent = 'MyApp/1.0';

// a GET
final request = await client.getUrl(Uri.parse('https://api.acme.com/entries'));
final response = await request.close();
if (response.statusCode == 200) {
  final body = await response.transform(utf8.decoder).join();
  final data = jsonDecode(body) as Map<String, dynamic>;
}

// with headers, a body, and a timeout
final request = await client.postUrl(Uri.parse('https://api.acme.com/entries'));
request.headers.contentType = ContentType.json;
request.headers.set('Authorization', 'Bearer $token');
request.write(jsonEncode({'title': 'New', 'body': 'Text'}));
final response = await request.close().timeout(const Duration(seconds: 15));
final created = await response.transform(utf8.decoder).join();

// errors
if (response.statusCode >= 400) {
  final error = await response.transform(utf8.decoder).join();
  throw HttpException('HTTP ${response.statusCode}: $error', uri: request.uri);
}

// the client must be closed, or the sockets leak
client.close(force: true);

// in practice, a wrapper that manages the lifecycle
class ApiClient {
  final HttpClient _client = HttpClient();
  final String baseUrl;
  final String? token;

  ApiClient({required this.baseUrl, this.token}) {
    _client.connectionTimeout = const Duration(seconds: 10);
  }

  Future<dynamic> get(String path) async {
    final uri = Uri.parse('$baseUrl$path');
    final request = await _client.getUrl(uri);
    if (token != null) request.headers.set('Authorization', 'Bearer $token');
    final response = await request.close().timeout(const Duration(seconds: 15));

    if (response.statusCode != 200) {
      throw ApiException(response.statusCode, await _body(response));
    }
    final text = await _body(response);
    return text.isEmpty ? null : jsonDecode(text);
  }

  void dispose() => _client.close(force: true);
}
// CANCELLATION: a long request the user navigated away from
final controller = AbortController();   // from package:http, or manual
// with package:http:
final request = http.Request('GET', uri);
final streamed = await client.send(request);
// and on a cancellable operation, close the subscription

// with dart:io, the trick is to not await, and to keep the request
final future = request.close();
try {
  final response = await future.timeout(Duration(seconds: 10));
  // ...
} on TimeoutException {
  // the request is still open; force it closed
  request.abort();          // HttpClientRequest has no abort();
  // so in practice, use a timeout and accept the socket is closed
  // when the client is closed
}

// RETRIES, only for transient failures
Future<T> withRetry<T>(
  Future<T> Function() op, {
  int attempts = 3,
  Duration Function(int)? backoff,
}) async {
  for (var i = 0; i < attempts; i++) {
    try {
      return await op();
    } on SocketException {
      if (i == attempts - 1) rethrow;
      final delay = backoff?.call(i) ??
          Duration(milliseconds: 200 * (1 << i));
      await Future.delayed(delay);
    } on HttpException catch (e) {
      // only retry 5xx and 429, never 4xx
      if (e.message.contains('40') || i == attempts - 1) rethrow;
      await Future.delayed(Duration(milliseconds: 500 * (i + 1)));
    }
  }
  throw StateError('unreachable');
}

// for real HTTP, use package:http: it has interceptors, proper
// cancellation, and a testing story. dart:io's HttpClient is the
// low-level tool underneath it.

The HTTP client, and the six defaults to change

HttpClient is the built-in client, it is a Stream<Uint8List> underneath, and it does not throw on an HTTP error status — a 404 is a successful response whose status says otherwise. That single design decision accounts for most of the bugs in code using it, because a naive await response.close() with no status check treats a 500 as a valid body.

import 'dart:io';

Future<void> main() async {
  final client = HttpClient();
  try {
    final req = await client.getUrl(Uri.parse('https://api.example.com/users'));
    final res = await req.close();
    // ...note what is NOT here: no exception for a 404. `res.statusCode` is 404
    // and `res` is a perfectly good response object.

    if (res.statusCode != 200) {
      await res.drain<void>();          // ...drain, or the connection stalls
      throw HttpException('HTTP ${res.statusCode}', uri: req.uri);
    }
    final body = await res.transform(utf8.decoder).join();
    print(body);
  } finally {
    client.close(force: true);
  }
}

// the one-line shape, and its four omissions
final body = await (await client.getUrl(uri).then((r) => r.close()))
    .transform(utf8.decoder).join();
// ...omits: the status check, the timeout, the redirect policy, and the client
// close. Each is a real defect in a long-running process.

The defaults that need changing are the same in every project and each has a consequence. There is no timeout, so a request to an unresponsive server hangs forever and the connection is never released. Redirects are followed automatically, so a redirect to another host sends the Authorization header with it. There is no cap on the response body, so a hostile or broken server can stream gigabytes into memory. And connections are kept alive, so a HttpClient that is created per request leaks sockets rather than reusing them.

SettingDefaultChange to
connectionTimeoutnone5–30 s
Request timeoutnonefuture.timeout(d)
Max redirects5, automatic0–3, or handle manually
Body sizeunboundedCount while reading
Client lifetimeper-request if you are carelessOne per app
User-AgentDart/xYours
// the client, configured once
final client = HttpClient()
  ..connectionTimeout = const Duration(seconds: 10)
  ..maxConnections = 8
  ..idleTimeout = const Duration(seconds: 30)
  ..userAgent = 'myapp/1.0';

Future<HttpClientResponse> fetch(Uri uri, {Map<String,String>? headers}) async {
  final req = await client.getUrl(uri);
  headers?.forEach(req.headers.set);
  final res = await req.close().timeout(const Duration(seconds: 30));
  if (res.statusCode < 200 || res.statusCode >= 300) {
    await res.drain<void>();        // ...NEVER skip this on an error path
    throw HttpException('HTTP ${res.statusCode}', uri: uri);
  }
  return res;
}

// bounding the body, which almost no example code does
Future<String> fetchText(Uri uri, {int maxBytes = 4 * 1024 * 1024}) async {
  final res = await fetch(uri);
  var total = 0;
  final buffer = StringBuffer();
  await for (final chunk in res.transform(utf8.decoder)) {
    total += chunk.length;
    if (total > maxBytes) {
      throw StateError('response over $maxBytes bytes');
    }
    buffer.write(chunk);
  }
  return buffer.toString();
}

// redirects: turn them off so a 301 cannot silently move your auth header
final strict = HttpClient()..autoUncompress = true;
final res = await strict.getUrl(uri).then((r) => r.close());
if (res.redirects.length > 3) throw StateError('too many redirects');
for (final r in res.redirects) {
  if (r.location.host != uri.host) {
    throw StateError('cross-host redirect to ${r.location.host}');
  }
}
// ...and to refuse entirely: HttpClient()..followRedirects = false, then handle
// the 301 yourself

// why drain matters
final res2 = await client.getUrl(uri).then((r) => r.close());
if (res2.statusCode != 200) {
  throw HttpException('bad');       // ...WITHOUT drain: the response body is
}                                   //    never read, the connection cannot be
                                    //    reused, and after a few hundred such
                                    //    failures the socket pool is exhausted
                                    //    and every request hangs

Request bodies, methods and headers have their own set of rules, and two of them are error-prone. A request body must be written by adding to the request's sink and closing it, and forgetting the close means the request is never sent. And headers cannot be set after the request is closed — attempting to set one throws, which is the correct behaviour but produces a confusing diagnostic when the header is being set in a loop.

// a POST with a JSON body
Future<void> postJson(Uri uri, Map<String, dynamic> body) async {
  final req = await client.postUrl(uri);
  req.headers
    ..contentType = ContentType.json
    ..set('Accept', 'application/json');
  req.write(jsonEncode(body));
  await req.close();               // ...this sends it. Without it, nothing.
  final res = await req.response;
  if (res.statusCode != 200) {
    await res.drain<void>();
    throw HttpException('HTTP ${res.statusCode}', uri: uri);
  }
}

// streaming a body, for uploads larger than memory
Future<void> upload(Uri uri, File file) async {
  final req = await client.putUrl(uri);
  req.headers.contentType = ContentType.binary;
  await req.addStream(file.openRead());   // ...backpressure-aware
  final res = await req.close();
  await res.drain<void>();
}

// headers: set before close, and ContentType has its own setter
req.headers.set(HttpHeaders.authorizationHeader, 'Bearer $token');
req.headers.contentType = ContentType('application', 'vnd.api+json', charset: 'utf-8');
req.headers.set('X-Request-Id', id);
// ...headers.set('Accept', ...) vs the convenience setters: use the constants
// for the standard ones and set() for everything else

// and the content-length trap
// HttpClient does NOT add Content-Length automatically for a stream body, so
// the server may see chunked encoding. Set it when you know it:
req.headers.contentLength = await file.length();

// and gzip, which is usually worth it and is one line
final client = HttpClient()
  ..autoUncompress = true       // ...transparent: the caller sees plain bytes
                                //    even if the server sent gzip
  ..autoUncompress = false;     // ...set false if you want to forward bytes

There is a second HTTP client in the SDK — HttpClient from package:http — and the choice between them is worth stating because both are correct and they suit different situations. The dart:io client is the lower-level one: it exposes the connection pool, the redirect list, the uncaught-error handler on sockets and the idle timeout, and it streams. The package:http client is a thin, ergonomic wrapper whose most-used implementation is IOClient, wrapping the same thing, and it composes far better because a client is a plain object that can be passed and faked.

// package:http - the ergonomic shape
import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;

final client = http.Client();          // ...reusable; close it when done

Future<http.Response> get(String url) async {
  final res = await client.get(Uri.parse(url), headers: {
    'Accept': 'application/json',
  }).timeout(const Duration(seconds: 15));
  if (res.statusCode != 200) {
    throw HttpException('HTTP ${res.statusCode}', uri: Uri.parse(url));
  }
  return res;
}

// a POST, which is one line here and five in dart:io
final res = await client.post(uri,
    headers: {'Content-Type': 'application/json'},
    body: jsonEncode(payload));

// streaming, via the send() form
final req = http.Request('POST', uri);
req.bodyBytes = bigBytes;              // ...or:
final streamed = await client.send(req);
await streamed.stream.pipe(file.openWrite());

// the trade, stated
// dart:io HttpClient:
//   + connection pool, idleTimeout, maxConnections, per-host limits
//   + access to res.redirects, req.followRedirects
//   + sockets exposed, for a proxy or a custom TLS config
//   - more ceremony; every call is three lines
//
// package:http:
//   + one line for the common case; a Client is a value you can inject
//   + BaseClient subclass = a test double in four lines
//   + the same underlying client, so the performance is identical
//   - a few advanced knobs are not exposed and need IOClient directly

// the test double, which is why the wrapper is worth having
class FakeClient extends http.BaseClient {
  final Map<Uri, http.Response> responses = {};
  @override
  Future<http.StreamedResponse> send(http.BaseRequest req) async {
    final res = responses[req.url];
    if (res == null) throw StateError('no fixture for ${req.url}');
    return http.StreamedResponse(
      Stream.value(res.bodyBytes), res.statusCode,
      headers: res.headers, request: req,
    );
  }
}

11.7 Sockets and servers

TCP, UDP, WebSockets, and a minimal server.

// a TCP client
final socket = await Socket.connect('example.com', 80);
socket.write('GET / HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n');
await socket.flush();
await for (final data in socket) {
  print(String.fromCharCodes(data));
}
await socket.close();
await socket.done;      // wait for the close to complete

// a TCP server
final server = await ServerSocket.bind('0.0.0.0', 8080);
print('listening on ${server.port}');
await for (final client in server) {
  client.write('HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\n\r\nhi');
  await client.flush();
  await client.close();
}
await server.close();     // required, or the process will not exit

// UDP
final server = await RawDatagramSocket.bind('0.0.0.0', 9000);
server.listen((event) {
  if (event != RawSocketEvent.read) return;
  final dg = server.receive();
  if (dg != null) print('from ${dg.address}: ${utf8.decode(dg.data)}');
});

// WebSocket
import 'dart:io';
final ws = await WebSocket.connect('wss://api.acme.com/ws');
ws.listen((message) => print('received: $message'));
ws.add('hello');
await ws.close();

// a WebSocket SERVER
final server = await HttpServer.bind('0.0.0.0', 8080);
await for (final request in server) {
  if (WebSocketTransformer.isUpgradeRequest(request)) {
    final ws = await WebSocketTransformer.upgrade(request);
    ws.listen((m) => ws.add('echo: $m'));
  } else {
    request.response.write('expected a websocket');
    await request.response.close();
  }
}

// for anything beyond a demo, use package:web_socket_channel
// the resources that leak, and the pattern that does not
class TcpServer {
  final ServerSocket _server;
  final List<Socket> _clients = [];

  TcpServer._(this._server);

  static Future<TcpServer> start(int port) async {
    final server = await ServerSocket.bind('0.0.0.0', port);
    final instance = TcpServer._(server);
    unawaited(instance._acceptLoop());
    return instance;
  }

  Future<void> _acceptLoop() async {
    await for (final socket in _server) {
      _clients.add(socket);
      socket.listen(
        (data) { /* handle */ },
        onError: (e) { /* log */ },
        onDone: () => _clients.remove(socket),
        cancelOnError: true,
      );
    }
  }

  Future<void> dispose() async {
    for (final socket in _clients) {
      await socket.close();
    }
    _clients.clear();
    await _server.close();
  }
}

// the three things every server needs:
//   1. a way to stop accepting
//   2. a way to close every open connection
//   3. an onDone handler per connection, so the list stays accurate

Sockets, servers, and the framing problem

ServerSocket.bind is a five-line echo server, and everything beyond that is about framing: a TCP stream is a byte stream with no message boundaries, so the two ends must agree on how a message ends. The three framings in common use are a length prefix, a delimiter and a terminator, and each has a failure mode that the other two do not.

// the smallest useful server
Future<void> serve(int port) async {
  final server = await ServerSocket.bind('0.0.0.0', port);
  print('listening on ${server.port}');
  await for (final socket in server) {          // ...one subscription,
    socket.listen(                                  //    one handler each
      (data) => socket.add(data),                   // ...echo
      onError: (e) => socket.destroy(),
      onDone: () => socket.destroy(),
      cancelOnError: true,
    );
  }
}

// an echo server is 8 lines; a PROTOCOL server is where the work is
// ...because a TCP connection has no message boundaries at all. `data` is an
// arbitrary chunk: two messages, or half of one, or eleven messages at once.

// the three framings
// 1. length prefix - 4-byte big-endian length, then that many bytes
//    binary, exact, and requires both ends to agree before either speaks
final buf = BytesBuilder();
await for (final chunk in socket) {
  buf.add(chunk);
  while (buf.length >= 4) {
    final b = buf.toBytes();
    final len = ByteData.sublistView(b, 0, 4).getUint32(0, Endian.big);
    if (b.length < 4 + len) break;            // ...wait for more
    final message = b.sublist(4, 4 + len);
    handle(message);
    // ...and then drop the consumed bytes - BytesBuilder has no offset, so
    // the real implementation keeps a list of chunks and a consumed count
  }
}

// 2. delimiter - one message per newline, for text protocols
var pending = '';
await for (final chunk in socket) {
  pending += utf8.decode(chunk, allowMalformed: true);
  var i;
  while ((i = pending.indexOf('\n')) >= 0) {
    handle(pending.substring(0, i));
    pending = pending.substring(i + 1);
  }
}
// ...one line at a time, no length prefix, but: a message containing a newline
// cannot be sent, and `pending` grows without bound if the peer never sends a
// delimiter. Both are why JSON-lines caps the line length.

// 3. terminator - the delimiter case with a fixed end, for a fixed record
//    and HTTP/1.1's header terminator is this: \r\n\r\n

// 4. TLS, which is one line and should never be optional
final server = await SecureServerSocket.bind('0.0.0.0', 8443, ctx);

Connecting out has the same framing responsibility and one extra hazard: timeouts. A Socket.connect with no timeout waits on a firewalled host for the operating system's own retry schedule, which is minutes, and a loop doing that looks like a hang. And a socket's destroy() is the only reliable way to abandon a connection that is not going to produce more data, because a half-closed socket with no destroy holds its file descriptor until the process ends.

// connecting, with the timeout that is not optional
Future<Socket> connect(String host, int port) async {
  return Socket.connect(host, port,
      timeout: const Duration(seconds: 5));
}

// the client side of a line protocol
final socket = await Socket.connect(host, port,
    timeout: const Duration(seconds: 5));
socket
    .transform(utf8.decoder)
    .transform(const LineSplitter())
    .listen(handleLine,
        onError: (e) => print('err $e'),
        onDone: () => print('server closed'));

// sending
socket.write('PING\n');
await socket.flush();          // ...without a flush, small writes may sit in
                                //    the buffer indefinitely

// and the failure that leaks descriptors
Future<void> handle(Socket s) async {
  s.listen(onData);
  final result = await doWork();
  // ...if this throws, `s` is never destroyed and the connection leaks. Every
  // exit path must destroy.
}
// ...`StreamSocket.destroy()` is immediate; `close()` is a graceful FIN and
// waits for the peer's data to drain. For a protocol you control, close() then
// destroy() on completion.

// the production shape: per-connection state in one object
class Connection {
  final Socket socket;
  final StringBuffer line = StringBuffer();
  int failures = 0;

  Connection(this.socket) {
    socket.listen(_onData,
        onError: (Object e) { failures++; _teardown(); },
        onDone: _teardown,
        cancelOnError: true);
  }

  void _onData(List<int> data) {
    line.write(utf8.decode(data, allowMalformed: true));
    var i;
    while ((i = line.toString().indexOf('\n')) >= 0) {
      final s = line.toString();
      handleLine(s.substring(0, i));
      line = StringBuffer(s.substring(i + 1));
      if (++failures > 5) { socket.destroy(); return; }   // ...a peer that
      // ...will not behave is disconnected rather than allowed to consume
    }
  }

  void _teardown() { socket.destroy(); }
}

// and the server that must bound its own resource use
final server = await ServerSocket.bind(addr, port);
await for (final socket in server) {
  if (active >= maxClients) {          // ...before reading a single byte
    socket.write('BUSY\n');
    socket.destroy();
    continue;
  }
  Connection(socket);
}

Three socket options are easy to set and easy to get wrong, and each has a consequence that appears under load rather than immediately. Socket.setOption for SO_REUSEADDR matters because without it a restart fails with "address already in use" while the previous process's socket is in TIME_WAIT — which lasts minutes and is the reason a server that restarts in a loop refuses to rebind. The tcpNoDelay option disables Nagle's algorithm, which matters for a chatty request/response protocol where a small message waits up to 40 ms for company that is never coming.

// binding, with the options a server needs
final server = await ServerSocket.bind(
  InternetAddress.anyIPv4, 8080,
  shared: false,
);
// ...`shared: false` (the default on most platforms) means SO_REUSEADDR is off,
// which on Linux lets another process bind the same port and silently steal
// traffic. If two instances are supposed to coexist deliberately, set it
// explicitly - and understand what it means.

// setting options on an accepted socket
socket.setOption(SocketOption.tcpNoDelay, true);     // ...Nagle off: send
                                                       //    immediately
socket.setOption(SocketOption.reuseAddr, true);
// ...and on ServerSocket, before bind, via the option constructor

// the two symptoms, and their causes
// "Address already in use" on restart
//   cause: TIME_WAIT from the previous run. Either SO_REUSEADDR, or wait 60s.
//   This is why every server restart script needs the reuse option.
//
// requests arriving in bursts, 40 ms apart, with tiny payloads
//   cause: Nagle's algorithm delaying small writes. tcpNoDelay fixes it.
//   Symptoms: it works locally, and is intermittently slow over a real network.

// and shutdown, which a server that restarts needs
Future<void> shutdown(ServerSocket server) async {
  await server.close();            // ...stop accepting
  for (final c in active) {
    c.socket.write('SHUTTING DOWN\n');
    await c.socket.flush();
    c.socket.destroy();
  }
  // ...`server.close()` alone leaves existing connections running, so a
  // graceful stop that only closes the listener looks like a hang.

// WebSocket, which is the case where the framing is already solved
final ws = await WebSocket.connect('wss://echo.example.com');
ws.listen((m) { if (m is String) ws.add(m); });
await ws.close();                  // ...1009, 'normal', or a code + reason

There are two more transports worth knowing, and both are shorter than TCP. Process runs a child program and gives its stdout and stderr as streams, which is how a Dart program drives git or ffmpeg — and the reason to use start rather than runSync is the same backpressure argument as for files. RawDatagramSocket is UDP: connectionless, unordered, unreliable, and cheap, which makes it right for telemetry and wrong for anything where losing a packet is unacceptable.

// running a child process, with both streams drained
Future<int> run(List<String> args) async {
  final process = await Process.start(args.first, args.sublist(1));
  // ...drain BOTH, or the child blocks writing to a full pipe buffer and
  // deadlocks. This is the single most common Process bug.
  final out = process.stdout.transform(utf8.decoder).join();
  final err = process.stderr.transform(utf8.decoder).join();
  final code = await process.exitCode;
  final stdoutText = await out;
  final stderrText = await err;
  if (code != 0) throw ProcessException(args.first, args, stderrText);
  return code;
}

// streaming a child's output, which is what you actually want for ffmpeg
final process = await Process.start('ffmpeg', args);
process.stdout
    .transform(utf8.decoder)
    .transform(const LineSplitter())
    .where((l) => l.contains('frame='))      // ...progress lines only
    .listen((l) => updateProgress(l));
await process.exitCode;

// a simpler alternative for small commands
final res = await Process.run('git', ['rev-parse', 'HEAD']);
res.exitCode;    // ...0
res.stdout;      // ...a String
res.stderr;
// ...this buffers everything in memory - fine for `git rev-parse`, wrong for
// anything that produces gigabytes

// UDP, where the whole point is that delivery is not guaranteed
final socket = await RawDatagramSocket.bind(InternetAddress.anyIPv4, 0);
socket.send(
  utf8.encode('metric value 42'),
  InternetAddress('127.0.0.1', type: InternetAddressType.IPv4),
  9999,
);
// ...no connection, no ordering, no retry, and a size cap around 65 KB per
// datagram. If you need reliability, use TCP; if a lost datagram is fine, UDP
// is dramatically cheaper - which is why metrics and DNS use it.

11.8 Serialization: JSON and beyond

The dart:convert API, the traps, and when to use something else.

import 'dart:convert';

// encode / decode
final text = jsonEncode({'name': 'Ana', 'age': 31});
final data = jsonDecode(text);            // dynamic: ALWAYS validate

// the pretty variant, for a file a human will read
final pretty = const JsonEncoder.withIndent('  ').convert(data);

// decoding options
final lenient = jsonDecode(text, reviver: (key, value) => value);   // nothing special

// base64, for binary in a JSON payload
final b64 = base64Encode(bytes);
final back = base64Decode(b64);
final urlSafeB64 = base64Url.encode(bytes);   // for a URL
final u = utf8.encode('hello');
final s = utf8.decode(u);

// a typed decode, so the result is not dynamic
T decodeTyped<T>(String text, T Function(Map<String, dynamic>) build) {
  final decoded = jsonDecode(text);
  if (decoded is! Map<String, dynamic>) {
    throw const FormatException('expected an object');
  }
  return build(decoded);
}

final entry = decodeTyped(
  text,
  (json) => Entry(
    id: json['id'] as String,
    title: json['title'] as String,
    tags: (json['tags'] as List?)?.cast<String>() ?? const [],
  ),
);
// THE TRAPS
// 1. jsonDecode returns dynamic. Every use is untyped.
final map = jsonDecode(text) as Map<String, dynamic>;   // better, but a cast

// 2. an int that is large becomes a double
jsonDecode('{"id": 12345678901234567890}');
// -> {id: 1.2345678901234567e+19}
// fix: send large integers as strings, and parse them yourself

// 3. a DateTime is silently stringified in a non-obvious format
jsonEncode({'at': DateTime.now()});
// -> {"at":"2026-03-14 10:22:31.123456"}   NOT ISO 8601

// 4. NaN and Infinity are invalid JSON
jsonEncode({'v': double.nan});    // throws JsonUnsupportedObjectError

// 5. a Map with non-string keys
jsonEncode({1: 'a'});             // {"1":"a"} - it converts, silently
// the robust approach: model classes with a generated codec
@JsonSerializable()
class Entry {
  const Entry({required this.id, required this.title, this.createdAt});

  factory Entry.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) =>
      _$EntryFromJson(json);
  Map<String, dynamic> toJson() => _$EntryToJson(this);

  final String id;
  final String title;
  final DateTime? createdAt;
}

// and a strict parser that REJECTS unknown fields, so a server
// change is a loud error rather than a silent data loss
Entry parseEntry(String text) {
  final map = jsonDecode(text) as Map<String, dynamic>;
  final unknown = map.keys.toSet()
    ..removeAll({'id', 'title', 'createdAt'});
  if (unknown.isNotEmpty) {
    throw FormatException('unknown fields: $unknown');
  }
  return Entry.fromJson(map);
}

// WHEN TO USE SOMETHING ELSE
//   JSON      - the default; universal, debuggable, slow to parse
//   MessagePack/Protobuf - smaller and faster, needs a schema
//   CBOR      - compact binary JSON, good for constrained devices
//   SQLite    - not a serialization format, but the right tool for
//               relational data you need to QUERY
//
// a rule of thumb: if it crosses a network boundary and you do not
// control both ends, JSON. If you control both ends and size matters,
// MessagePack. If you need to query it, it belongs in a database.

Exercises 12

  1. Build a path helper that rejects any input escaping a base directory, and prove it stops a traversal attempt.
  2. Implement an atomic write and kill the process mid-write to prove the original survives.
  3. Count the lines in a 1GB file by streaming, and confirm memory use stays flat in DevTools.
  4. Write a file with openWrite, terminate before closing, and observe the truncation. Then fix it.
  5. Build an HTTP client with a connection pool, a timeout, and retries only for 5xx. Verify the 4xx path does not retry.
  6. Write a TCP server that tracks its connections and closes all of them on dispose.
  7. Demonstrate the large-int JSON problem and the DateTime format problem, then fix both with a typed codec.

Serialization: JSON, and the traps in dart:convert

dart:convert gives you jsonEncode, jsonDecode, a streaming JsonEncoder and JsonDecoder, plus utf8 and base64. The API is small, and its traps are all about what happens to a type that has no JSON representation — which is most of them, because a Dart DateTime becomes a string and comes back a string.

import 'dart:convert';

// the two calls
final text = jsonEncode({'a': 1, 'b': [2, 3]});
final data = jsonDecode(text) as Map<String, dynamic>;
// ...`as Map<String, dynamic>` is a CAST, not a check: jsonDecode returns
// dynamic, and a List decodes to a List, so the cast throws at runtime.

// what each Dart type becomes
jsonEncode({
  'i': 42,                  // ...42
  'd': 3.14,                // ...3.14
  's': 'x',                 // ..."x"
  'b': true,                // ...true
  'n': null,                // ...null
  'l': [1, 2],              // ...[1,2]
  'm': {'k': 'v'},          // ...{"k":"v"}
  'set': {1, 2},            // ...ERROR: Set is not JSON-encodable
  'dt': DateTime.now(),     // ...ERROR: DateTime is not encodable
  'du': Duration(minutes: 1),   // ...ERROR
  'uri': Uri.parse('x'),    // ...ERROR
  'bytes': [1, 2],          // ...[1,2] - fine, but it is a List not bytes
  'nan': double.nan,        // ...ERROR: NaN is not valid JSON
  'inf': double.infinity,   // ...ERROR
});
// ...so `toJson()` on a class with a DateTime throws, and the fix is a manual
// conversion - or a code generator that writes it for you

// the manual conversion, which is the only honest way
class Row {
  final int id;
  final DateTime at;
  const Row(this.id, this.at);

  Map<String, dynamic> toJson() => {'id': id, 'at': at.toIso8601String()};
  factory Row.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> j) =>
      Row(j['id'] as int, DateTime.parse(j['at'] as String));
}
// ...and the inverse failure: fromJson receives no type information at all, so
// `j['id']` is dynamic and every field needs a cast. A wrong shape throws
// with no indication of which field.

// the versioned form, which is what you should do on day one
Map<String, dynamic> toJson() =>
    {'v': 1, 'id': id, 'at': at.toIso8601String()};
// ...because adding a field later, or renaming one, and re-reading an old file
// is otherwise an unrecoverable data problem

Streaming JSON matters for the same reason streaming files do, and the encoder's output shape is configurable in ways that affect both size and correctness. The default jsonEncode has no whitespace; the streaming encoder by default writes indented output, which is right for a human and wrong for a machine. And a large array built through JsonEncoder.convert holds the whole string in memory, whereas the streaming form can write each element as it is produced.

// writing a large array incrementally, with no trailing comma
final out = StringBuffer();
out.write('[');
var first = true;
for (final row in rowsFromDatabase()) {
  if (!first) out.write(',');
  first = false;
  out.write(jsonEncode(row.toJson()));
}
out.write(']');
await File('out.json').writeAsString(out.toString());
// ...StringBuffer grows, so this is not streaming either - it is just
// predictable. For a file larger than memory, use the encoder.

// the streaming encoder, and the two options that matter
final pretty = const JsonEncoder.withIndent('  ');
final compact = JsonEncoder();                  // ...no whitespace

// a Stream<List<int>> that yields a JSON array element by element
Stream<List<int>> encodeRows(Stream<Row> rows) async* {
  yield '[\n';
  var first = true;
  await for (final r in rows) {
    if (!first) yield ',\n';
    first = false;
    yield '  ${jsonEncode(r.toJson())}';
  }
  yield '\n]\n';
}

await File('big.json').openWrite()
    .addStream(encodeRows(rows))
    .catchError((e) => throw e);
// ...the real form, with the close on every path:
final sink = File('big.json').openWrite();
try { await sink.addStream(encodeRows(rows)); } finally { await sink.close(); }

// decoding incrementally, which jsonDecode cannot do
final decoder = const JsonDecoder();
final sink = StringBuffer();
await for (final chunk in File('big.json').openRead()) {
  sink.write(utf8.decode(chunk));
}
// ...`JsonDecoder` decodes ONE complete JSON value and throws if the input has
// trailing content, so it is not an incremental parser. For a huge file that
// is one array of objects, split on the framing yourself, or use a package.

// and the number trap
jsonDecode('{"a": 1.0}');        // ...double 1.0
jsonDecode('{"a": 1}');          // ...int 1
jsonDecode('{"a": 1e400}');      // ...Infinity - and JSON forbids it
jsonDecode('{"a": 9007199254740993}');  // ...precision loss: it is a double
// ...so an int64 identifier above 2^53 becomes silently wrong through JSON.
/// Use a String, or a BigInt-aware encoder.

Two other formats come from dart:convert and each has one specific use. base64 is for embedding binary in text — data URIs, HTTP basic auth, JSON fields carrying bytes — and utf8 is the encoder/decoder pair that everything textual passes through. There is also ascii, whose encode throws on a non-ASCII character rather than replacing it, which makes it the right choice when a silent substitution would be worse than an error.

// base64, and the padding/URL variants
base64Encode([1, 2, 3]);                    // ...'AQID'
base64Decode('AQID');                       // ...[1, 2, 3]
base64Url.encode(bytes);                    // ...URL-safe alphabet: - and _
// ...`base64Url` is what a JWT uses, and mixing the two alphabets is why a
// hand-rolled JWT decoder fails on a token with - or _ in it

// a data URI, which is base64 with a header
'data:image/png;base64,${base64Encode(pngBytes)}';
// ...33% larger than the bytes, and unreadable - so it is a last resort for
// embedding an image in a CSS file or an HTML attribute

// UTF-8, and the strictness that matters
utf8.encode('café');                        // ...[99,97,102,195,169]
utf8.decode(bytes);                         // ...allowMalformed defaults to false
utf8.decode(bytes, allowMalformed: true);   // ...U+FFFD instead of a throw
utf8.encode('café');                  // ...2-byte é: not valid UTF-8
// ...so if you build a string from bytes whose encoding you do not know,
// `allowMalformed: true` silently corrupts rather than failing

// ascii, which fails loudly - the right default for a wire protocol
ascii.encode('café');                       // ...THROWS: non-ASCII character
// ...use it for a protocol that must be 7-bit, so a client that sends a
// smart quote gets an error rather than a mangled command

// line/word wrapping, for terminal output
const LineSplitter();                       // ...splitting
// package:convert has a LineSplitter with a configurable length

// hex and CRC, which dart:convert does NOT have
// package:convert provides: hex, crc32, asn1, utf16/utf32
// These are in a separate package because the core library stays small.

For anything more than plain data — a protocol, a strongly typed tree, a file format with a header — the question is whether to take a dependency or to hand-roll a binary format. The case for a dependency is strong because binary formats are where correctness bugs live: endianness, alignment, length prefixes, and version negotiation are four separate ways to be wrong, and each produces a file that is subtly corrupt rather than obviously broken. The case for hand-rolling is a format you fully control where the alternative is a dependency with its own version constraints.

// a binary format, done carefully - the four things that matter
class Frame {
  final int type;
  final Uint8List payload;

  Uint8List encode() {
    final out = BytesBuilder();
    // 1. a magic number, so a wrong file is detected immediately
    out.add([0x4D, 0x53, 0x47, 0x31]);        // 'MSG1'
    // 2. an explicit version, so the format can change
    out.addByte(1);
    // 3. the length, in a fixed width and a stated endianness
    final len = ByteData(4)..setUint32(0, payload.length, Endian.big);
    out.add(len.buffer.asUint8List());
    // 4. the payload
    out.add(payload);
    return out.toBytes();
  }

  static Frame? tryDecode(Uint8List bytes) {
    if (bytes.length < 9) return null;
    if (bytes[0] != 0x4D || bytes[4] != 1) {
      throw FormatException('not a v1 MSG frame');
    }
    final len = ByteData.sublistView(bytes, 5, 9)
        .getUint32(0, Endian.big);
    if (bytes.length < 9 + len) return null;   // ...incomplete: return null,
    return Frame(bytes[3], bytes.sublist(9, 9 + len));   //    do not throw
  }
}
// ...four rules, each of which exists because its absence is a bug that only
// shows up when a file from another machine is read: magic, version, explicit
// endianness, and a length that lets a partial read be detected

// the alternatives, and when each is right
// package:protobuf  - cross-language, schema-driven, wire-compatible
// package:msgpack   - same, compact, JSON-ish, much faster to write
// freezed + json_serializable - Dart-only, removes the hand-written mapping
// dart:convert      - the two functions, and nothing else

// the check that catches format bugs: a round-trip test on every case
test('every field survives a round trip', () {
  final f = Frame(7, Uint8List.fromList([0, 255, 128]));
  final back = Frame.tryDecode(f.encode())!;
  expect(back.type, 7);
  expect(back.payload, [0, 255, 128]);
});
// ...including 0xFF and 0x80, which catch a signed/unsigned mistake that a
// test with [1, 2, 3] would pass

12 · Native Interop and FFI

12.1 When and why to leave Dart12.2 The C ABI, and why it exists12.3 dart:ffi, the low-level API12.4 package:ffi, the usable API12.5 Structs, unions and arrays12.6 Callbacks from native into Dart12.7 Memory management12.8 Platform channels, from Dart12.9 When NOT to use FFI

Calling C and C++ from Dart without a plugin. Powerful, fast, and the source of the most segfaults in the Dart ecosystem.

12.1 When and why to leave Dart

The four legitimate reasons, and the many illegitimate ones.

// LEGITIMATE reasons to use FFI
//  1. a library you must use, that has no Dart equivalent
//     - a proprietary SDK: a barcode scanner, a crypto library
//     - an existing C/C++ codebase you do not want to rewrite
//     - a system library: sqlite3, zlib, openssl, libjpeg
//  2. performance, for a specific hot function
//     - image resizing, video encoding, a physics kernel
//     - usually better achieved with an isolate first (chapter 9)
//  3. a platform API with no plugin
//     - a vendor SDK, a niche hardware API
//  4. embedding, for a tool
//     - calling into a game engine, a database engine

// ILLEGITIMATE reasons, which are most attempts
//  1. "Dart is not fast enough"
//     measured? an isolate handles CPU work; only a genuinely hot
//     inner loop justifies FFI
//  2. "I know C better"
//     the porting cost is high and the maintenance cost is forever
//  3. "the plugin is not maintained"
//     a fork is usually less work than an FFI binding
//  4. avoiding a dependency
//     an FFI binding is a dependency on a NATIVE library, which is
//     harder to ship than a pub package

The four reasons to call native code, and their costs

Crossing into native code is not free and not reversible in one direction: once a Dart program hands a pointer to C, it has committed to the C memory model's rules about ownership, thread affinity and error reporting, and none of them are enforced by the Dart compiler. There are four legitimate reasons to do it, and three illegitimate ones, and telling them apart is most of the judgement involved.

ReasonExampleCost
No Dart equivalent existsA proprietary codec, an SDKAll of FFI's costs
Performance on hot CPU workImage resampling, codecAll of FFI's costs
A C library you already havelibcurl, libpq, zlibPortability, ABI
Access to a platform APIWin32, Core FoundationTwo platform paths
Isolate insteadCPU work, blocking I/ONone
AOT-compiled Dart insteadHot pathsNone

The first thing to check is whether an isolate solves it. A Dart isolate is a second thread of execution with its own heap and its own copy of static state, and Isolate.run hands work to one and brings the result back. It gives real parallelism for CPU-bound work, it enforces message-passing rather than shared memory, and it needs no native library, no build step and no cross-platform configuration. The cost is that the arguments and the result must be sendable, which means a copy in and a copy out. So for a computation over a large data set, an isolate loses on the copies and FFI wins; for a small hot function called a million times, an isolate loses on overhead and FFI wins.

// an isolate first: no native code, no build, real parallelism
final result = await Isolate.run(() => heavyComputation(rows));
// ...cost: rows and result are copied in and out. For 100 MB that is two
// copies of 100 MB, which can exceed the cost of the computation itself.

// making the copy cheap: transfer ownership of typed data
final transfer = TransferableTypedData.fromList([bigList]);
final result = await Isolate.run(() => transfer.materialize().asUint8List());
// ...the send MOVES the buffer rather than copying it, so a large list costs
// one allocation, not two copies. `Isolate.spawn` with a SendPort does the same.

// FFI instead, when the copies are the problem or the code already exists
final sum = nativeSum(ptr, count);      // ...no copy at all: a pointer
// ...and every cost below.

// the decision, stated as a rule
// - the operation is CPU-bound AND dominated by data movement &rarr; isolate
// - the operation is CPU-bound AND dominated by computation &rarr; FFI
// - the operation is a C library you cannot replace      &rarr; FFI
// - the operation blocks (a sync syscall, a legacy API)  &rarr; isolate
// - you are unsure                                            &rarr; isolate

// and the two reasons that are not reasons
// "native is faster"  - AOT Dart is within a small factor of C for most
//                       numeric work, and an isolate gives real parallelism.
//                       Measure before assuming.
// "it is already written in C" - a binding still has to be written, tested and
//                       kept working across three platforms. Writing it twice
//                       is often cheaper than maintaining FFI forever.

Cost-wise, FFI carries four burdens that a pure Dart program does not, and it is worth being explicit about all four before starting. There is a build system: a C compiler, a set of platform-specific build rules, and binaries that must be produced for every target. There is an ABI: a library compiled for one architecture is not loadable on another, so macOS arm64 and x64 are separate artifacts. There is no type safety at the boundary: a signature mismatch produces memory corruption rather than a compile error. And there is no safety net: a bad pointer is a segfault, and the Dart runtime cannot catch it, so the whole process dies.

// 1. the build system, per platform
// macOS, universal binary for arm64 and x64:
clang -dynamiclib -arch arm64 -arch x86_64 -o libnative.dylib native.c
// Linux, shared object:
gcc -shared -fPIC -o libnative.so native.c
// Windows, a DLL:
cl /LD native.c /Fe:native.dll

// 2. the ABI: separate artifacts
// build/
//   macos_arm64/libnative.dylib
//   macos_x64/libnative.dylib
//   linux_x64/libnative.so
//   linux_arm64/libnative.so
//   windows_x64/native.dll
// ...one per (OS, architecture, ABI) pair. Dart FFI cannot load a .so on
// macOS or a .dylib on Linux - the extension is a hard requirement.

// 3. no type safety
final wrong = nativeCall(123);      // ...a Dart int where a pointer was
                                     //    expected. On a 64-bit machine an int
                                     //    IS a pointer-sized value, so it
                                    //    COMPILES and then corrupts memory.

// 4. no safety net
final p = malloc<Uint8>(16);
final q = p + 40;            // ...out of bounds. Reads whatever is there.
final r = p + 0;             // ...free of the start pointer. Segfault.
final s = malloc<Uint8>(1 << 62);   // ...huge. OOM-killed or abort.

There is a fourth reason that has no costs at all and is underused: accessing a platform API that has no Dart binding, where the alternative is implementing the API's behaviour in Dart. A Windows service control call, a macOS keychain read, a system-specific GPU driver call — these are thin wrappers around a C surface that the vendor only publishes natively. That is the cleanest FFI use case, because the native side is stable, small and does not need to be written or maintained by you.

// a platform API, where the native side is not yours to maintain
import 'dart:ffi';
import 'dart:io';

// a Win32 call, guarded by platform
bool isServiceRunning(String name) {
  if (!Platform.isWindows) return false;
  final advapi = DynamicLibrary.open('advapi32.dll');
  final openService = advapi.lookupFunction<IntPtr Function(IntPtr, UintPtr, Uint32),
      IntPtr Function(int, int, int)>('OpenServiceA');
  final query = advapi.lookupFunction<IntPtr Function(IntPtr, Int32, IntPtr, UintPtr, Uint32),
      int Function(int, int, int, int, int)>('QueryServiceStatusExA');
  // ...note every parameter: a pointer for a handle, an int for a flag, an
  // out-pointer for the result. There is no type system here to help.
  return false;
}

// and the same call through a maintained binding, which is better
// package:win32 already has every Win32 declaration, correctly typed
// final h = OpenSCManager(0, null, SC_MANAGER_CONNECT);
// final s = OpenService(h, name, SERVICE_QUERY_STATUS);
// final status = malloc<SERVICE_STATUS>(sizeOf<SERVICE_STATUS>());
// QueryServiceStatusEx(s, SC_STATUS_PROCESS_INFO, status,
//     sizeOf<SERVICE_STATUS>(), null);

// the rule this encodes: reach for FFI at the boundary, not past it. Every
// function you call should be one you cannot avoid, and everything above it
// should be ordinary Dart.

12.2 The C ABI, and why it exists

The stable boundary, and the two ways to cross it.

// Every platform has ONE binary interface that is guaranteed
// stable forever: the C calling convention.
//
//   method channel  (a message, JSON or a standard codec)
//     - simple, safe, portable
//     - a serialise/serialise cost per call: microseconds
//     - fine for anything that is not in a hot loop
//
//   FFI              (a direct function call)
//     - fast: a call is nanoseconds, no serialisation
//     - unsafe: a wrong signature is a segfault
//     - platform-specific: you write it per architecture
//
// the choice, in one line: FFI if it is called in a loop, a method
// channel if it is called a few times per user action.

// FFI is native only: dart:ffi does not exist on the web.
// so any FFI-using code is behind a conditional import.
// a C library you might bind
// src/native/greet.h
#ifndef GREET_H
#define GREET_H
#include <stdint.h>

typedef struct {
    const char* name;
    int32_t     length;
} GreetName;

int32_t greet_length(const char* text);
char*   greet_duplicate(const char* text);
void    greet_free(char* ptr);
#endif

The C ABI, and what it promises you

The C ABI is the smallest common denominator on which two independently compiled pieces of code can agree to call each other. It is small on purpose: a name, an argument list, a calling convention, and a set of conventions about who owns memory. Everything Dart FFI does is a consequence of that ABI being all there is, and understanding the ABI directly explains most FFI errors.

ConceptWhat it fixesWhat goes wrong
Name manglingA name means one functionOverloading is impossible
Calling conventionWho puts an argument in which registerWindows x64 vs SysV differ
Type sizesint is 32 bitslong is 8 on LP64, 4 on Windows
Struct layoutField order and paddingPacking, alignment
OwnershipWho calls freeTwo owners, or none
ErrorsAn integer return codeNo exception crosses the boundary
StringsNothing — a char pointerEncoding, lifetime

The portability traps in that table are the ones that cost real time, and two of them are absolute: long and size_t. In C, long is 32 bits on Windows and 64 bits on 64-bit Linux and macOS — the LLP64 model versus LP64. So a function declared long f(void) must be bound as Int32 Function() on Windows and Int64 Function() everywhere else, and binding it wrong compiles and misbehaves. size_t has the same problem plus platform-dependent width, which is why a C API that wants a size should prefer int or take a fixed-width type.

// the sizes, and why the C signature must be copied exactly
// type        Windows x64   Linux/macOS x64
// char              1             1
// short             2             2
// int               4             4
// long              4             8      <-- the trap
// long long         8             8
// float             4             4
// double            8             8
// void *           8             8
// size_t            8             8      (4 on 32-bit)
// char *           8             8

// so one C declaration needs a conditional binding
typedef _version_t = IntPtr;
final version = Platform.isWindows
    ? lib.lookupFunction<Int32 Function(), int Function()>('version')
    : lib.lookupFunction<Int64 Function(), int Function()>('version');
// ...because `long` is 32-bit on Windows. Bind it as Int64 and you read
// garbage; bind it as Int32 and the upper half of the register is ignored,
// which happens to work. Bind it wrong on a struct field and you corrupt.

// the fixed-width types, which is the correct answer in new C code
// int32_t, uint64_t, int_least32_t - and Dart's Int32, Uint64
// ...so a header that uses them needs no conditional binding at all. This is
// why modern C libraries are ffi-friendly and older ones are a chore.

// struct alignment, which is the other invisible one
// struct S { char c; int i; };      sizeof is 8, not 5
// ...the compiler inserts 3 bytes of padding after `c`. Dart's Struct layout
// must declare it the same way, or every field after the first is wrong.

// and the calling convention, which differs by platform
// System V x64: rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9 - then the stack
// Windows x64:   rcx, rdx, r8, r9      - then the stack
// ...same argument ORDER to the caller, different registers, and a floating
// point argument goes in xmm0 rather than an integer register. Dart's
// lookupFunction handles this per platform, which is why you must declare
// `Function` and `NativeFunction` types rather than hand-assemble anything.

Two more conventions are worth stating explicitly because they are what every binding must decide: how a C function reports failure, and who owns returned memory. Neither is standardised. A C function reports failure by returning a sentinel — NULL, -1, errno, or a status struct filled through an out-parameter — and a binding has to pick one and check it. Ownership is worse: a function returning a buffer it allocated expects the caller to free it, one returning a pointer into its own static data expects the caller to do nothing, and one taking a buffer expects the caller to allocate it. There is no way to tell which from the signature, so it must come from the documentation.

// the three failure conventions, each needing a different binding
// 1. sentinel return
typedef _get_n = IntPtr Function(IntPtr);
final getName = lib.lookupFunction<_get_n, int Function(int)>('get_name');
final p = getName(handle);
if (p == 0) throw StateError('get_name failed: errno=${errnoGetter()}');
// ...check the sentinel BEFORE using the value, because a NULL deref inside C
// is a segfault and Dart cannot catch it.

// 2. errno, set by the call
// the sentinel is -1 and the reason is in errno. Reading errno needs a second
// lookupFunction, and it is only valid immediately after the failing call -
// any Dart code in between may have reset it.

// 3. an out-parameter status struct
typedef _open_f = Int32 Function(IntPtr, UintPtr, IntPtr, Uint32, Int32);
final openFile = lib.lookupFunction<_open_f, int Function(int, int, int, int, int)>('open');
final status = calloc<Int32>(1);          // ...1 int, zeroed
final rc = openFile(path, 0, status, 0, 0);
if (rc != 0) {
  throw StateError('open failed: code=${status.value}');
}
calloc.free(status);                       // ...and it must be freed on
                                            //    EVERY path, including throws

// the ownership table every binding needs, from the C documentation
//   returns a malloc'd buffer   -> caller frees with free()
//   returns a static pointer   -> caller frees nothing
//   returns a pointer to owned  -> caller frees with the library's free fn
//     library memory
//   takes a buffer               -> caller allocates AND frees
//   takes a string              -> caller allocates; C may or may not free it
// ...guessing wrong is a double free (crash) or a leak (grows quietly).

Strings across the boundary are the single most common source of real bugs, and there are three encodings to get wrong. A char * in C is bytes terminated by NUL, with no encoding attached; Dart strings are UTF-16 code units, so every conversion is a transcode, not a copy. And strlen on a string containing an interior NUL returns the length up to that NUL, which silently truncates. The two APIs package:ffi provides for this — toNativeUtf8 and toNativeUtf8Function — get the allocation right, and using them by hand almost always does not.

// the three ways, and the one to use
import 'package:ffi/ffi.dart';

// 1. by hand - what not to do, and why each version is wrong
final bytes = codeUnits.map((c) => c.toString()).join();   // ...abandoned
final p = malloc<Uint8>(bytes.length + 1);
for (var i = 0; i < bytes.length; i++) {
  p[i] = bytes.codeUnitAt(i);                 // ...WRONG above 127: a code
}                                              //    unit above 255 is
p[bytes.length] = 0;                          //    truncated to 8 bits
final s = p.cast<Utf8>.toDartString();      // ...so 'é' becomes garbage
// ...and the malloc is never freed, and `s` is a Uint8 typed as String.

// 2. toNativeUtf8 - allocates, and you own the pointer
final namePtr = 'hello'.toNativeUtf8();
try {
  nativeGreet(namePtr);
} finally {
  calloc.free(namePtr);          // ...NOT optional: this is a malloc
}
// ...handles the encoding and the terminator correctly. You must free it.

// 3. toNativeUtf8Function - allocates and frees on every call, for a
//    parameter that is the same shape every time
typedef _GreetNative = Void Function(Pointer<Utf8>);
typedef _GreetDart = void Function(Pointer<Utf8>);
final greet = lib.lookupFunction<_GreetNative, _GreetDart>('greet');
final greeting = greetingFunction(lib, 'greet');   // ...from package:ffi
greeting('hello');           // ...allocates, calls, frees. No try/finally.

// when you MUST hold the pointer longer
final p2 = json.toNativeUtf8();
try {
  final handle = open(p2);
  addTearDown(() {                        // ...Dart has no destructors;
    close(handle);                         //    scope the lifetime to the
    calloc.free(p2);                       //    function that owns it
  });
} catch (e) {
  calloc.free(p2);
  rethrow;
}

// the interior-NUL trap, which is a silent truncation
final weird = 'a\u0000b'.toNativeUtf8();
nativeLen(weird);      // ...returns 1, not 3. strlen stops at the NUL.
calloc.free(weird);
// ...which is why passing a Dart string containing NUL is a data-corruption
// bug rather than an error. Check for it, or use a length parameter instead.

12.3 dart:ffi, the low-level API

The primitives, so the higher-level API makes sense.

import 'dart:ffi';

// the fundamental types
typedef _GreetLengthNative = Int32 Function(Pointer<Utf8>);
typedef _GreetLengthDart = int Function(Pointer<Utf8>);

// a lookup: the library, and a symbol from it
final DynamicLibrary lib = () {
  if (Platform.isWindows) {
    return DynamicLibrary.open('greet.dll');
  }
  if (Platform.isMacOS) {
    return DynamicLibrary.open('libgreet.dylib');
  }
  return DynamicLibrary.open('libgreet.so');
}();

final greetLength =
    lib.lookupFunction<_GreetLengthNative, _GreetLengthDart>('greet_length');

// converting between Dart Strings and C strings
final text = 'hello';
final ptr = text.toNativeUtf8();     // allocates in the C heap
try {
  final length = greetLength(ptr);
  print(length);
} finally {
  malloc.free(ptr);                  // ALWAYS free
}

// or use a scope, which frees automatically
void withCString(String s, void Function(Pointer<Utf8>) body) {
  final ptr = s.toNativeUtf8();
  try {
    body(ptr);
  } finally {
    malloc.free(ptr);
  }
}

withCString('hello', (ptr) {
  print(greetLength(ptr));
});
// the whole type mapping, which you will need
//   C                  Dart
//   void                void
//   int8_t   int16_t    Int8   Int16
//   int32_t             Int32
//   int64_t             Int64
//   uint8_t  ...        Uint8  Uint16 Uint32 Uint64
//   float               Float
//   double              Double
//   Bool                Int    (C _Bool is 1 byte, use Int)
//   char*               Pointer<Uint8>   or Pointer<Utf8>
//   void*               Pointer<Void>
//   int (*)(int)        Pointer<NativeFunction<Int32 Function(Int32)>>

// A FUNCTION TYPE is written in the NATIVE style
typedef _AddNative = Int64 Function(Int64 a, Int64 b);
typedef _AddDart = int Function(int a, int b);   // Dart types, not C

// note: the native signature uses the same names but the types must
// match what the C compiler would produce. Getting one wrong is
// undefined behaviour, not a compile error.

dart:ffi: looking up and calling

The dart:ffi API has three concepts. A DynamicLibrary is a loaded shared library. lookupFunction takes that library plus a C function's name and returns a Dart callable. And the signature is written twice — once as a NativeFunction type describing the C side, once as a Dart function type describing the Dart side. Writing both correctly is the whole skill, and the compiler checks that they agree.

import 'dart:ffi';

// three ways to get a library
final lib = DynamicLibrary.open('./libnative.so');   // ...absolute path
final lib2 = DynamicLibrary.process();               // ...the current process -
                                                     //    for a plugin loaded
                                                     //    into this executable
final lib3 = Platform.isWindows
    ? DynamicLibrary.open('native.dll')             // ...searched in PATH on
    : DynamicLibrary.open('libnative.so');          //    Windows, in the
                                                     //    system paths on
                                                     //    Linux and macOS

// the two signature types, and what each half is for
typedef _AddNative = Int32 Function(Int32 a, Int32 b);   // the C side: the
                                                           //   ABI, raw
typedef _AddDart = int Function(int a, int b);           // the Dart side: the
                                                           //   types you use

final add = lib.lookupFunction<_AddNative, _AddDart>('add');
print(add(2, 3));                    // ...5

// the mapping, which is mechanical
// C              NativeType        Dart type
// void           Void              void
// int            Int32             int
// unsigned int   Uint32            int
// long long      Int64             int
// float          Float             double
// double         Double            double
// char *         Pointer<Uint8>     String via Utf8
// void *         Pointer<Void>      Pointer<T>
// const char *   Pointer<Uint8>     same - const is not in the ABI

// the four that bite
typedef _SizeNative = UintPtr Function();               // size_t: pointer-width
typedef _SizeDart = int Function();                      // ...an int, NOT void
typedef _StrlenNative = UintPtr Function(Pointer<Utf8>);
typedef _StrlenDart = int Function(Pointer<Utf8>);      // ...returns int, and
                                                         //    can exceed 2^53 -
                                                         //    impossible for a
                                                         //    real string

// and the one that cannot be expressed
typedef _VarargsNative = Int32 Function();     // ...varargs exist in C
                                               //    and CANNOT be bound. The
                                               //    signature must be
                                               //    hard-coded per call site.

// lookupFunction, and the three failure modes
final missing = () {
  try {
    return lib.lookupFunction<_AddNative, _AddDart>('no_such_symbol');
  } on ArgumentError {
    throw StateError('not in this library - check the name and the library');
  }
}();      // ...throws at CALL time, not at load time, so a missing symbol in a
           // rarely-taken path is a runtime failure in production

A Dart function type and its NativeFunction counterpart must agree, and the compiler enforces the agreement only on the types — not on the meaning. The two most consequential checks are that the argument count matches and that each position has a compatible width, and a mismatch in width on a 64-bit machine is the case that compiles and then misbehaves. The pattern that avoids almost all of it is a single typedef pair per native function, declared once and reused, so a signature change is a one-line edit rather than a search.

// the pair, declared once per function
typedef _HashInit = Void Function(Pointer<Uint8> out);
typedef _HashUpdate = Void Function(
    Pointer<Void> ctx, Pointer<Uint8> data, UintPtr len);
typedef _HashFinal = Uint8 Function(Pointer<Void> ctx, Pointer<Uint8> out);

class Sha256 {
  final _Pointer _lib;
  late final _HashInit _init = _lib.lookupFunction<_HashInit, void Function(Pointer<Uint8>)>('sha256_init');
  late final _HashUpdate _update = _lib.lookupFunction<_HashUpdate, void Function(Pointer<Void>, Pointer<Uint8>, int)>('sha256_update');
  late final _HashFinal _final = _lib.lookupFunction<_HashFinal, int Function(Pointer<Void>, Pointer<Uint8>)>('sha256_final');

  Sha256(this._lib);

  Uint8List digest(List<int> data) {
    final ctx = calloc<Uint8>(32);          // ...32 bytes: read the header
    final out = calloc<Uint8>(32);
    final buf = data.isEmpty ? Uint8List(0) : data;
    try {
      _init(out);
      if (data.isNotEmpty) {
        _update(ctx, buf.toNativeUtf8() == null ? nullptr : nullptr, 0);
      }
      _final(ctx, out);
      return out.asTypedList(32);
    } finally {
      calloc.free(ctx);                      // ...every allocation, every path
      calloc.free(out);
    }
  }
}

// and the length type, which must be pointer-width on both sides
typedef _MemcpyNative = Pointer<Void> Function(Pointer<Void>, Pointer<Void>, UintPtr);
typedef _MemcpyDart = Pointer<Void> Function(Pointer<Void>, Pointer<Void>, int);
// ...`UintPtr`/`int` here. Using Int32 for a size_t on a 64-bit library
// truncates every allocation over 2 GB and every offset over 4 GB.

// a lookup that checks the name, which is worth doing once
T lookup<T extends Function>(DynamicLibrary lib, String name) {
  try {
    return lib.lookupFunction<T, T>(name);
  } on ArgumentError {
    throw StateError('symbol $name not found in ${lib}');
  }
}

Calling into C is synchronous and blocking, and there is no way to make a foreign function call yield. Three things follow, and each has a established answer. A long-running native call freezes the isolate, so it belongs on an isolate or in a worker. A native call that re-enters Dart through a callback requires a NativeCallable, which requires an isolate. And a native function that blocks on something the Dart event loop must service — a synchronous read on a socket another Dart code owns — deadlocks, because the isolate cannot make progress.

// a foreign call is blocking, with no way to yield
final res = nativeExpensive(arg);      // ...the isolate is unusable for the
                                       //    duration. No await can help.

// so it goes on an isolate
final r = await Isolate.run(() => nativeExpensive(arg));
// ...but then the arguments are COPIED, so a large buffer must be a
// pointer into shared memory, or use Isolate.run's own copying carefully.

// the deadlock, precisely
final socket = await ServerSocket.bind('0.0.0.0', 0);
final pending = socket.first;             // ...a future for the next connection
final data = nativeBlockingRead(socketfd); // ...blocks the isolate
await pending;                            // ...which can never complete: the
                                         //    isolate is blocked in native
                                         //    code and nothing else runs
// ...the lesson: a native function that waits for another Dart-held resource
// must not be called from the isolate that owns it.

// and the reverse: native code calling back into Dart needs an isolate that
// can be synchronously entered
// (covered in ch11-callback)

// the three cheap answers before you reach FFI
// - cache the result and compute it once
// - move the loop to the other side: pass a whole buffer, get one answer back
// - batch: one foreign call for 10,000 items, not 10,000 calls

12.4 package:ffi, the usable API

The same thing with generics, extensions, and much less boilerplate.

import 'package:ffi/ffi.dart';

// the dynamic library, with a fallback path for macOS frameworks
final DynamicLibrary openLib() {
  if (Platform.isMacOS) {
    return DynamicLibrary.open('libgreet.dylib');
  }
  if (Platform.isWindows) return DynamicLibrary.open('greet.dll');
  return DynamicLibrary.open('libgreet.so');
}

// a generated binding, from the annotation
@Native<Int32 Function(Int32)>(symbol: 'pow_int')
external int powInt(int base, int exponent);

@Native<Int32 Function(Pointer<Utf8>)>(symbol: 'greet_length')
external int greetLength(Pointer<Utf8> text);

// the extension-based form, which you would write by hand or
// generate
extension GreetFfi on String {
  int get length {
    final ptr = toNativeUtf8();
    try {
      return greetLength(ptr);
    } finally {
      malloc.free(ptr);
    }
  }
}

// with allocation helpers, so a String round-trip is one line
String greetDuplicate(String input) {
  return input.toNativeUtf8().cast<Utf8>().toDartStringFree();
}

// toDartString() does NOT free: you must free yourself
// toDartStringFree() calls the native free function: much safer
// use toDartStringFree() unless you know the native side allocated
// it with a different allocator
// a helper that removes the manual-free pattern
T withNativeString<T>(
  String input,
  T Function(Pointer<Utf8> ptr) body,
) {
  final ptr = input.toNativeUtf8();
  try {
    return body(ptr);
  } finally {
    malloc.free(ptr);
  }
}

// usage
final length = withNativeString('hello', greetLength);

// and for lists of strings
T withNativeStrings<T>(
  List<String> inputs,
  T Function(List<Pointer<Utf8>> ptrs) body,
) {
  final ptrs = inputs.map((s) => s.toNativeUtf8()).toList();
  try {
    return body(ptrs);
  } finally {
    for (final p in ptrs) {
      malloc.free(p);
    }
  }
}

package:ffi: the layer that makes bindings writable

dart:ffi gives you malloc, calloc, lookupFunction and the type mapping. package:ffi adds allocation helpers, a SizedNativeFunction for types that vary by platform, asFunction for turning a bare Pointer into a callable, and — most usefully — generated bindings. Almost every hand-written binding in Dart uses this package under the hood.

import 'package:ffi/ffi.dart';

// allocation, with the three that matter
final p = malloc<Uint8>(1024);      // ...uninitialised: garbage contents
final c = calloc<Uint8>(1024);      // ...zeroed: slower, predictable
final n = nullptr;                       // ...a NULL Pointer, for optional args
calloc.free(p);                          // ...free either with calloc.free

// a struct, allocated on the C heap and filled through a pointer
final s = calloc<MyStruct>();
s.ref.field = 42;                       // ...`ref` - assign a whole struct
s.ref.nested.name = 'abc';              // ...nested by reference
calloc.free(s);

// a typed view over a pointer - no copy, no free
final ints = ptr.cast<Int32>().asTypedList(100);
// ...writes through it land in C's memory. `sublist` copies; `asTypedList`
// aliases. Getting this backwards is either a silent data loss or a
// use-after-free.

// SizedNativeFunction, for the types whose size varies
// size_t is 8 bytes on 64-bit and 4 on 32-bit; long is 8 on LP64 and 4 on
// Windows. A binding for either must declare the signature twice.
typedef _MallocNative = Pointer<Void> Function(UintPtr n);
typedef _MallocDart = Pointer<Void> Function(int n);

Pointer<Void> cMalloc(int n) {
  final f = _lib.lookupFunction<_MallocNative, _MallocDart>('malloc');
  return f(n);
}
// ...and `package:ffi`'s SizedNativeFunction does it from one declaration on
// platforms that support it, so a 32-bit build does not need a second file.

// asFunction: turning a pointer into a callable
// a struct whose FIRST field is a function pointer is itself callable - this
// is how a C callback table looks from Dart
typedef _OpsNative = Void Function();
typedef _OpsDart = void Function();

final ops = _lib.lookup<Pointer<Void>>('get_ops');
final call = ops.cast<_OpsNative>().asFunction<_OpsDart>();
call();
// ...note `lookup` (pointer only) versus `lookupFunction` (callable). You use
// lookup when the symbol is a data symbol, or when you want to pass the
// function's address to C.

// the calloc vs malloc choice, and why it is not cosmetic
final fromC = malloc<Uint8>(16);
print(fromC[0]);       // ...whatever was there before. Often 0, often not.
final fromZero = calloc<Uint8>(16);
print(fromZero[0]);    // ...guaranteed 0
// ...a buffer of a password or a key read without initialising it is an
// information leak out of another allocation.

Bindings are generated by ffigen, which parses a C header and emits Dart, and the decision of whether to use it is worth stating plainly because the answer is usually yes. A header declares types, functions, structs and constants; ffigen turns that into Dart declarations that are correct by construction rather than by careful transcription. The hand-written alternative wins in exactly two cases — a handful of functions where the generated API is noisier than a direct binding, and a header ffigen cannot parse.

// the generation step, which is a build target, not a script
// pubspec.yaml
dev_dependencies:
  ffigen: ^14.0.0

// ffigen.yaml
name: NativeBindings
description: Bindings for libnative
output: 'lib/src/native_bindings.dart'
headers:
  entry-points:
    - 'native/native.h'
  include-directives:
    - '**native.h'
comments:
  style: any
  length: full

// the invocation
dart run ffigen

// what it produces, and why it is better than hand-writing it
