// lib/src/native_bindings.dart
class NativeBindings {
  final DynamicLibrary _lib;
  NativeBindings(DynamicLibrary lib) : _lib = lib;

  /// The native `int add(int, int)` function.
  int add(int a, int b) {
    return _add(a, b);
  }
  late final _add = _lib.lookupFunction<
      _addNative, _addDart>('add');
}
// ...the doc comment is copied from the header. The typedef pair is generated
// from the C prototype, so a signature mismatch is impossible. Structs get
// their layout from the header, including padding and nested anonymous ones.

// and the hand-written alternative, for the small cases
// - fewer than about 20 functions
// - a header ffigen rejects (unusual macros, conditional declarations)
// - you want a deliberate, minimal API surface rather than the header's

// the maintenance consequence, which is the deciding factor
// hand-written: when the C library changes, someone must notice and edit
//   several files, and nothing verifies they got it right
// generated:     re-run ffigen, and a diff shows exactly what changed in the
//   ABI. A struct field that moved is a one-line diff.

A generated binding is a low-level API, and using it directly from application code produces unreadable code with pointers in it. The shape that works is a two-layer library: a generated inner layer that owns the ABI, and a hand-written outer layer that owns the memory and presents Dart types. The outer layer's job is to make it impossible for a caller to misuse a pointer, which means every allocation is scoped to a method and freed in a finally.

// the OUTER layer: pointers never escape
import 'package:ffi/ffi.dart';
import 'native_bindings.dart';

class Sha256 {
  final NativeBindings _c;
  Sha256(this._c);

  Uint8List hash(List<int> data) {
    final ctx = calloc<Sha256Ctx>();
    final digest = calloc<Uint8>(32);
    final input = data.isEmpty ? nullptr : data.toNativeUtf8();
    try {
      _c.sha256_init(ctx);
      _c.sha256_update(ctx, input, data.length);
      _c.sha256_final(ctx, digest);
      return Uint8List.fromList(digest.asTypedList(32));   // ...COPY out
    } finally {
      calloc.free(ctx);
      calloc.free(digest);
      if (input != nullptr) calloc.free(input);
    }
  }
}
// ...`Uint8List.fromList` copies, which is what you want at the boundary: the
// Dart-side value must not alias C memory that the next call overwrites.

// the same discipline for an output buffer the caller supplies
Uint8List decode(List<int> input, {int maxOutput = 4096}) {
  final out = calloc<Uint8>(maxOutput);
  try {
    final n = _c.decode(input, out, maxOutput);
    if (n < 0) throw StateError('decode failed: ${_c.last_error()}');
    return Uint8List.fromList(out.asTypedList(n));   // ...only n bytes
  } finally {
    calloc.free(out);
  }
}

// and the rule that makes the layer trustworthy
// A Pointer<T> must never appear in a public method signature. If a caller
// can pass one in or receive one out, they can use-after-free it, and the
// compiler will not help. The generated layer may; the outer layer must not.

// with an explicit lifetime object, when allocation must outlive a method
class Sha256CtxHandle {
  final Pointer<Sha256Ctx> ptr;
  Sha256CtxHandle() : ptr = calloc<Sha256Ctx>();
  void dispose() => calloc.free(ptr);
}
// ...better than returning a bare Pointer, because the caller can see they own
// something. `package:ffi`'s FfiFinalizer does this with NativeFinalizer.

Keeping a binary loadable, and not thrashing the allocator

Two concerns sit alongside the API surface and decide whether a binding survives contact with a release cycle. The first is ABI compatibility: a shipped native library is loaded by applications that were built against an older version of your header, so every symbol they call must still exist with the same meaning. The second is allocation behaviour: a binding that allocates once per call is correct and unusable, because the foreign-call overhead is small enough that the allocator dominates it.

// the four ABI rules, each of which is a release-breaking mistake otherwise
// 1. NEVER remove or rename an exported symbol. Add a new one and keep the
//    old as a forwarding wrapper:
//      NATIVE_API int add(int, int);                  // added in v1
//      NATIVE_API int add_v2(int, int, int *err);     // added in v2
//    `add` must keep working: an application built against v1 has no way to
//    know about v2.
//
// 2. NEVER change an existing function's signature. C has no overloading, so
//    the only way to "improve" one is to change it, and that breaks every
//    caller. Add a suffix instead - the `_v2` above.
//
// 3. NEVER change a struct's layout in place. Adding a field changes its size,
//    and a caller that allocated the old size writes past the end. So:
//      typedef struct { int a; int b; } V1;             // 8 bytes
//      typedef struct { int a; int b; int c; } V2;      // 12 bytes
//    ...and a new entry point that takes a V2*. Old callers keep their V1.
//
// 4. NEVER reorder or repack struct fields. Same reason.

// the size check, which turns rule 3 from a convention into an assertion
typedef _version2Native = Uint32 Function();
typedef _version2Dart = int Function();

int abiVersion() => _version2();

void requireAbi(int minimum) {
  final v = abiVersion();
  if (v < minimum) {
    throw StateError('libnative $v is older than the required $minimum');
  }
}
// ...call it once at startup. A library that grew a field and a client that
// did not is a heap corruption, and this turns it into a message.

// symbol versioning, which is the mechanism that makes rules 1 and 2 workable
// -Wl,--version-script=libnative.map
//   LIBNATIVE_1.0 { global: add; local: *; };
//   LIBNATIVE_2.0 { global: add_v2; } LIBNATIVE_1.0;
// ...and the loader resolves the highest version the client needs. On Windows
// there is no equivalent, which is the substantive reason a cross-platform
// native library has fewer options here than a Linux one.

// and the cost of NOT doing this, which is the practical argument
// "we bumped the minor version so it is fine"

// the allocation-heavy binding, and where the time actually goes
// a call that allocates, per invocation
Uint8List hash(List<int> data) {
  final input = data.toNativeUtf8();      // alloc + transcode
  final ctx = calloc<Ctx>();           // alloc
  final out = calloc<Uint8>(32);       // alloc
  try {
    _init(ctx);
    _update(ctx, input, data.length);
    _final(ctx, out);
    return Uint8List.fromList(out.asTypedList(32));   // alloc + copy
  } finally {
    calloc.free(input);                   // free
    calloc.free(ctx);                     // free
    calloc.free(out);                     // free
  }
}
// ...four allocations and four frees per call, plus two copies. At a million
// calls a second that is the whole budget, and the native work it wraps might
// be 40 ns.

// the fix: one context, reused, and no intermediate Dart list
class Hasher {
  final Pointer<Ctx> _ctx = calloc<Ctx>();   // allocated ONCE
  final Pointer<Uint8> _out = calloc<Uint8>(32);
  final Uint8List _digest = Uint8List(32);         // reused destination
  final Uint8List _bytes = Uint8List(1024);        // caller fills this

  void update(List<int> chunk) {
    for (var i = 0; i < chunk.length; i++) _bytes[i] = chunk[i];
    _update(_ctx, _bytes.address, chunk.length);   // no allocation
  }

  Uint8List digest() {
    _final(_ctx, _out);
    _out.asTypedList(32).forEach((_, i) => _digest[i] = _bytes[i]);
    return _digest;                                 // returns the SAME object
  }

  void dispose() {
    calloc.free(_ctx);
    calloc.free(_out);
  }
}
// ...zero allocations per call. Note the cost: `digest()` returns a shared
// mutable buffer, so the contract must say so, or every caller has to copy.

// the middle ground: one allocation for the boundary, none per item
Uint8List hashAll(List<List<int>> chunks) {
  final flat = Uint8List(chunks.fold(0, (a, c) => a + c.length));
  var at = 0;
  for (final c in chunks) {
    flat.setRange(at, at + c.length, c);
    at += c.length;
  }
  final out = calloc<Uint8>(32);
  try {
    _hash(flat.address, flat.length, out);
    return Uint8List.fromList(out.asTypedList(32));
  } finally {
    calloc.free(out);
  }
}
// ...one copy in, one out, one allocation. This is usually the right shape, and
// it is the one a generated binding should present.

// and the measurement that decides, because intuition is wrong here
// $ dart compile exe bench.dart
// $ perf stat -e task-clock ./bench.exe
// ...compare a binding that allocates per call against one that reuses a
// context. The difference is usually 3-10x, and it is almost never the foreign
// call itself that dominates - it is the allocator and the copies.

12.5 Structs, unions and arrays

Passing structured data without serialising it.

// a by-value struct, matching the C layout exactly
// struct Point { int32_t x; int32_t y; };
final class Point extends Struct {
  @Int32()
  external int x;

  @Int32()
  external int y;
}

// allocate on the heap
final ptr = calloc<Point>();
try {
  ptr.ref.x = 10;
  ptr.ref.y = 20;
  print('${ptr.ref.x}, ${ptr.ref.y}');
} finally {
  calloc.free(ptr);      // free with the SAME allocator you allocated
}

// a struct ARRAY
final points = calloc<Point>(100);
try {
  for (var i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
    points[i].x = i;
    points[i].y = i * 2;
  }
  print(points[50].y);   // 100
} finally {
  calloc.free(points);
}

// a struct passed BY VALUE to a native function
typedef _SumPointNative = Int32 Function(Point p);
typedef _SumPointDart = int Function(Point p);

final sumPoint = lib.lookupFunction<_SumPointNative, _SumPointDart>('sum_point');
print(sumPoint(Point(3, 4)));   // calloc and pass by value

// a nested struct
final class Rect extends Struct {
  external Point topLeft;
  external Point bottomRight;
}

// a union
final class Value extends Union {
  external int i;
  external double d;
  external Pointer<Void> p;
}

// a callback function pointer, passed INTO C
typedef _CompareNative = Int32 Function(Int32 a, Int32 b);
typedef _CompareDart = int Function(int a, int b);
final compare = lookupFunction<_CompareNative, _CompareDart>('compare');

// the LAYOUT RULES that must match the C compiler exactly
//   - field order (no reordering in practice; use pack annotations
//     if you need to be explicit)
//   - alignment: Dart matches the C ABI, which handles padding
//   - nested structs by value need the same alignment
//   - on ARM, a 64-bit type must be 8-byte aligned
//
// for anything complex, generate the bindings with ffigen

Structs, unions and arrays

A Struct in Dart FFI is a Dart-side declaration of a C struct's memory layout. The declaration must match the C definition exactly — field order, field types, and the padding the compiler inserted — and every one of those is a place where a wrong declaration produces memory corruption rather than an error.

C typeDart FFI typeNote
charInt8Signedness matters
unsigned charUint8Also a byte
shortInt16—
intInt32Always 32
unsignedUint32—
longNo single typePlatform-dependent
long longInt64—
floatFloat—
doubleDouble—
T *Pointer<T>—
void *Pointer<Void>Opaque handle
char [N]Array<Uint8>—

Layout is where the surprises are. C inserts padding so each field is naturally aligned, and the total size is rounded up to the struct's own alignment. struct { char c; int i; } is 8 bytes, not 5: three bytes of padding after c. Nested structs and arrays in the middle of a struct multiply the alignment requirement, so a char after an int field is followed by padding too. Dart's Struct computes the same layout from the field types, which is why declaring the fields in the right order and with the right types is sufficient — but only if you do not add a Dart-only field.

// C
// typedef struct { char c; int i; } S;      sizeof(S) == 8
// Dart - matching, and the size comes out right automatically
final class S extends Struct {
  @Int8() external int c;      // @Int8 is the FIELD TYPE, not a value
  @Int32() external int i;     // ...and it is what makes the alignment
}
// ...`sizeOf<S>()` returns 8. Never add a Dart field:
// final count = 0;   <-- WRONG: a Dart field is not in the layout, so
//                        `ref` assignment copies the WRONG number of bytes

// nested structs, which raise alignment
final class Inner extends Struct {
  @Int32() external int a;
}
final class Outer extends Struct {
  @Uint8() external int flag;      // ...1 byte
  // ...3 bytes of padding, because `inner` needs 4-byte alignment
  external Inner inner;
  @Uint64() external int big;      // ...and 8, forcing 8-byte alignment on
}                                   //    the whole struct

// arrays are an ARRAY, not a Dart List
final class Pair extends Struct {
  @Int32() external int xs[2];         // ...fixed size, in-layout
}
final class Matrix extends Struct {
  external Array<Array<Int32>> rows;   // ...or an Array of Arrays
  // external Array<Int32> data;       // ...a flat buffer is often better:
}                                      //    one allocation, contiguous rows

// allocating and filling
final p = calloc<S>();
p.ref.c = 65;
p.ref.i = 0x11223344;
calloc.free(p);

// and the two that corrupt memory
// 1. a struct passed by value must be ALLOCATED, never a Dart object:
//    nativeTakeS(S());          <-- WRONG
//    nativeTakeS(p);            <-- a Pointer, which is what it wants
// 2. a by-value RETURN must be allocated by C and freed by you:
final r = nativeMakeS();        // ...returns Pointer<S>
final copy = r.ref;             // ...read the struct out
calloc.free(r);                 // ...then free the C allocation

An array field is not the same as a Dart List and the difference is aliasing. Array<T> is a view into the struct's memory: indexing it reads or writes C memory directly, there is no bounds guarantee beyond the declared length, and it cannot grow. The conversion to a Dart list is a copy, and the conversion back is an allocation plus a copy — so a hot loop that converts per iteration allocates per iteration.

// Array<T> is a view; asTypedList on a Pointer is also a view
final arr = p.ref.xs;                 // ...an Array<Int32>, length 2
arr[0] = 10;                          // ...writes into the struct
final dartList = [arr[0], arr[1]];    // ...this is the copy

// the conversions, and which copy
final ptr = calloc<Int32>(1000);
final view = ptr.asTypedList(1000);   // ...VIEW: no copy. Writes go to C.
final copy = view.toList();           // ...COPY: a Dart List, independent
final list = [for (var i = 0; i < 1000; i++) ptr[i];];   // ...element-wise copy

// passing a Dart List to C: allocate and copy, always
final native = list.toNativeUtf8();   // ...or manually:
final buf = calloc<Int32>(list.length);
for (var i = 0; i < list.length; i++) buf[i] = list[i];
try {
  nativeProcess(buf, list.length);
} finally {
  calloc.free(buf);
}

// getting results back: one allocation, not N
// BAD: an allocation per element
final results = <int>[];
for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) results.add(nativeGet(i));
// ...n foreign calls AND n round trips

// GOOD: one call, one buffer
final out = calloc<Int32>(n);
nativeProcessAll(out, n);
final all = out.asTypedList(n).toList();
calloc.free(out);

// and the length you must know
// C has no idea how long your Dart list is, so you always pass it:
typedef _ProcessNative = Void Function(Pointer<Int32> data, UintPtr n);
typedef _ProcessDart = void Function(Pointer<Int32> data, int n);
// ...omitting `n` and relying on a NUL terminator works only for byte strings,
// and even there `strlen` costs a second traversal.

A union overlays several members in the same storage, and Dart models it as a struct where reading one member and writing another changes the bytes. The important properties are that all members share an offset of zero, that the size is that of the largest member, and that reading a member whose bits were not written is undefined — which in practice means a floating-point read of an integer's bits yields a garbage number or a trap on some hardware.

// C
// typedef union { int32_t i; float f; } Value;
final class ValueUnion extends Struct {
  @Int32() external int i;
  external Float f;      // ...same offset 0, same 4 bytes
}
// ...`sizeOf<ValueUnion>()` is 4. This is a TAG-LESS union: writing `i` then
// reading `f` reinterprets the same bits, and that is the entire mechanism.

// the tagged union, which is the safe pattern and what you should use
final class TaggedValue extends Struct {
  @Int32() external int tag;     // ...offset 0: 0 = int, 1 = float
  external UnionValue value;     // ...offset 4: the union
}
final class UnionValue extends Struct {
  @Int32() external int i;
  external Float f;
}

double readAsDouble(TaggedValue v) {
  switch (v.ref.tag) {
    case 0: return v.ref.value.i.toDouble();   // ...read only the member
    case 1: return v.ref.value.f;              //    that was written
    default: throw StateError('bad tag ${v.ref.tag}');
  }
}
// ...a tag-less union with no discipline is how you get a NaN from a bit
// pattern that was never a float.

// alignment inside a union: every member is aligned to ITS requirement
final class MixedUnion extends Struct {
  external Double d;      // ...needs 8-byte alignment
  @Uint8() external Array<Uint8> bytes;   // ...so the union is 8, and
}                                          //    `bytes` has 8 valid bytes

// and the anonymous-struct-in-union pattern C11 allows
final class Variant extends Struct {
  external Array<Float> asFloat;    // ...4 floats = 16 bytes
  external Array<Int32> asInt;      // ...4 ints = 16 bytes
  external Array<Uint8> asBytes;    // ...16 bytes
}
// ...this is how you pass "any 16 bytes" across the boundary without a union
// type at all, and it sidesteps every union alignment question

12.6 Callbacks from native into Dart

Passing a Dart function to C, and the lifetime rules that make it work.

// the native signature
//   typedef int (*Compare)(int a, int b, void* context);
//   int process_all(int count, Compare fn, void* context);

typedef _CompareNative = Int32 Function(Int32 a, Int32 b, Pointer<Void> context);
typedef _CompareDart = int Function(int a, int b, Pointer<Void> context);

// this is the critical line
final compareNative = lookupFunction<NativeFunction<_CompareNative>, _CompareDart>(
  'compare',
);

typedef _ProcessAllNative = Int32 Function(
  Int32 count,
  Pointer<NativeFunction<_CompareNative>> fn,
  Pointer<Void> context,
);
typedef _ProcessAllDart = int Function(
  int count,
  int Function(int a, int b, Pointer<Void> context) fn,
  Pointer<Void> context,
);
final processAll = lib.lookupFunction<_ProcessAllNative, _ProcessAllDart>('process_all');

// THE RULE: the callback must outlive the native call. A callback
// created inside the argument list of a single expression may be
// garbage collected before C calls it.

// WRONG
processAll(100, (a, b, ctx) => a.compareTo(b), nullptr);
//              ^ this may be collected before C uses it

// RIGHT: hold it in a variable
final callback = compareNative.asFunction<_CompareDart>();
final result = processAll(100, callback, nullptr);
callback.release();          // and release when you are done
// a safer wrapper that handles the lifetime
class NativeCallbackScope {
  final List<NativeFunction> _retained = [];

  T register<T extends Function>(T dartCallback) {
    // asFunction gives you the native pointer and a release method
    final asNative = (dartCallback as dynamic);
    _retained.add(asNative);
    return dartCallback;
  }

  void dispose() {
    for (final fn in _retained) {
      (fn as dynamic).release();
    }
    _retained.clear();
  }
}

// the general rules for callbacks
//  1. the callback must be a top-level or static function, not a
//     closure that captures a lot - it may outlive the scope
//  2. it MUST NOT throw. An exception crossing the C boundary is
//     undefined behaviour and usually a crash
//  3. the arguments you receive are only valid during the callback
//  4. keep a reference for as long as C might call it
//  5. release it when C is done, or you leak
//  6. do not call back into the same native library re-entrantly
//     unless it is documented as re-entrant

Callbacks: C calling into Dart

A callback is harder than a call in the other direction for one reason: the function pointer C holds must remain valid for as long as C might call it, and Dart function objects are garbage-collected. A bare Pointer.fromFunction produces an address into a trampoline that stays alive only while Dart holds a reference to it — so the lifetime has to be managed explicitly, and the safe API for doing that is NativeCallable.

import 'dart:ffi';

// the naive version, and the bug in it
final cb = Pointer.fromFunction<NativeFunction<
    Int32 Function(Int32)>>((int x) => print(x));
// ...`cb` is a Pointer to a trampoline. Dart may collect the closure, and the
// address becomes invalid. C then calls freed memory - a crash, sometimes much
// later.

// the safe version
final callable = NativeCallable<Int32 Function(Int32)>.isolateLocal(
  (int x) => print(x),
);
final fnPtr = callable.nativeFunction;
// ...`NativeCallable` owns a persistent native thunk and keeps the Dart closure
// reachable for as long as it exists. So the rule becomes: the
// `NativeCallable` must be stored in a field, not a local.

class Watcher {
  final NativeCallable<Int32 Function(IntPtr, Int32)> _cb;
  late final _start = _lib.lookupFunction<
      Void Function(Pointer<Void>, IntPtr, Pointer<NativeFunction<Int32 Function(IntPtr, Int32)>>),
      void Function(int, int, Pointer<NativeFunction<Int32 Function(IntPtr, Int32)>>)>>('start');

  Watcher() {
    _cb = NativeCallable.isolateLocal(_onEvent);
    _start(nullptr, 0, _cb.nativeFunction);
  }

  int _onEvent(int ctx, int code) {
    lastCode = code;
    return 0;                       // ...the return value C expects
  }

  int lastCode = 0;

  void dispose() {
    // ...THE step that is missed: tell C to stop calling, THEN release
    _stop(0, _cb.nativeFunction);
    _cb.close();                    // ...after this, nativeFunction is invalid
  }
}
// ...a local `final cb = NativeCallable...` inside a method is freed when the
// method returns, so C's stored pointer dangles. This is the single most
// common FFI crash and it presents as a segfault minutes later.

// the four factory kinds, and when each applies
// isolateLocal    - called on the SAME isolate. Fastest. Cannot be called
//                   during another native call's execution in a way that
//                   re-enters Dart... actually it can, but it must not be
//                   from a thread with no Dart isolate.
// independent     - called on its OWN isolate. Safe from any thread, but
//                   every call pays an isolate hop, and arguments are copied.
// nativeOnly       - a pure native function that does not touch Dart. Only for
//                   trampolines that need no Dart state.
// isomorphicLegacy - deprecated; do not use.

final fromSameIsolate = NativeCallable<Void Function(Int32)>.isolateLocal(_f);
final fromOwnIsolate = NativeCallable<Void Function(Int32)>.independent(_f);
final pure = NativeCallable<Void Function(Int32)>.nativeFunction(_nativeF);

The rules around a callback are about ordering and thread affinity, and each has a specific failure. A callback is invoked synchronously on whatever thread C calls it from. If that thread has no Dart isolate attached, calling into Dart crashes. If the callback re-enters the same native function that made the call, some libraries are reentrant-safe and some are not. And if the callback blocks on an await, it cannot — it must return a value synchronously, which is why a callback cannot be an async function.

// a callback is SYNCHRONOUS - it cannot await
final _cb = NativeCallable<Int32 Function(IntPtr, IntPtr)>.isolateLocal(
  (int ctx, int ptr) async {          // ...WRONG: an async callback returns a
    final data = await loadFromDisk(ptr);   //    Future, and the NativeType
    return process(data);                  //    says Int32
  },
);

// the correct shape: return immediately, work later
final _cb2 = NativeCallable<Int32 Function(IntPtr, IntPtr)>.isolateLocal(
  (int ctx, int ptr) {
    // ...do the cheap thing now, hand the slow thing to Dart's own scheduler
    scheduleMicrotask(() async {
      final data = await loadFromDisk(ptr);
      notifyC(ctx, process(data));
    });
    return 0;      // ...an immediate acknowledgement
  },
);

// the reentrancy trap
// C: json_parse(buf, on_token);   Dart's on_token calls json_parse again
final _onToken = NativeCallable<Int32 Function(IntPtr, Pointer<Utf8>, Int32)>
    .isolateLocal((ctx, text, len) {
  // ...some parsers are fine with this; some are not. Guard it:
  if (_inCallback) return 0;
  _inCallback = true;
  try {
    return handleToken(text, len);
  } finally {
    _inCallback = false;
  }
});

// and the rule about which thread
// The callback may be invoked from:
//   - the same thread as the calling Dart code   -> isolateLocal is fine
//   - a thread the library created               -> you must ensure that
//     thread has a Dart isolate attached, or use .independent
//   - before the library's setup returns         -> usually fine, but a
//     callback that calls a Dart API which needs the isolate to be idle is not
// If the library starts its own threads and you call it from the main isolate,
// .independent is the safe choice at the cost of a hop per event.

// what a callback can and cannot do
// CAN: read Dart state, call pure Dart, allocate, enqueue to an isolate
// CANNOT: await; return anything but the declared type; throw - an
//   exception escaping into C is undefined. Catch everything:
//     (ctx, p) { try { return f(p); } catch (e, s) { report(e, s); return -1; } }

Passing a callback to C raises a lifetime question that the NativeCallable solves for the callable but not for the context pointer. If C stores a user_data pointer and calls it back later, that pointer must remain dereferenceable and must let Dart recover the object it refers to. The mechanism is to allocate a box on the C heap holding an integer handle, keep a map from handle to object in Dart, and pass the handle as the user pointer — which costs a map lookup per callback and never leaves a Dart object reachable from C.

// the handle table, and why it exists
class _Registry {
  final _objects = <int, Object>{};
  final _free = <int>[];
  int _next = 1;

  int register(Object o) {
    final id = _free.isNotEmpty ? _free.removeLast() : _next++;
    _objects[id] = o;
    // ...the id is passed to C as user_data; C hands it back on each callback
    return id;
  }

  Object? lookup(int id) => _objects[id];

  void release(int id) {
    _objects.remove(id);
    _free.add(id);
  }
}

final _registry = _Registry();

typedef _HandlerNative = Int32 Function(Int32 userData, Pointer<Utf8> msg);
typedef _HandlerDart = int Function(int userData, Pointer<Utf8> msg);

final _handler = NativeCallable<_HandlerNative>.isolateLocal((int id, Pointer<Utf8> msg) {
  final target = _registry.lookup(id);
  if (target == null) return -1;
  try {
    return (target as Handler).onMessage(msg.cast<Utf8>().toDartString());
  } catch (e, s) {
    report(e, s);
    return -1;                       // ...never let an exception cross
  }
});

class Session {
  final int _id = _registry.register(this);
  bool _closed = false;

  void start() {
    _libStart(_id, _handler.nativeFunction);
  }

  void close() {
    if (_closed) return;
    _closed = true;
    _libStop(_id);          // ...1. tell C to stop calling
    _registry.release(_id); // ...2. drop the Dart object
  }                         //    (the NativeCallable outlives all sessions,
                            //     which is why it is a global here)
}

// and the alternative that avoids the registry: a Dart object at a fixed
// address, which needs Finalizer to be safe
final box = calloc<IntPtr>(1);
box.value = 0;
// ...only worth it if callbacks are rare. The handle table is clearer and has
// no address-lifetime question to answer.

12.7 Memory management

The three allocators, and the rules that prevent every FFI memory bug.

// THREE allocators, and mixing them is a crash
import 'package:ffi/ffi.dart';

// 1. malloc/calloc: dart:ffi, paired with malloc.free
final p = calloc<Uint8>(1024);
// ... use it ...
calloc.free(p);

// 2. package:ffi, paired with the matching free calloc
final q = calloc<Uint8>(1024);
calloc.free(q);            // same thing, but the typed API is nicer

// 3. the C library's own allocator
//    if the C library allocated it, the C library must free it
final native = lib.lookupFunction<Pointer<Void> Function(Pointer<Utf8>),
    Pointer<Void> Function(Pointer<Utf8>)>('greet_duplicate');
final libFree = lib.lookupFunction<Void Function(Pointer<Void>), void Function(Pointer<Void>)>('greet_free');

final copied = native('hello'.toNativeUtf8());
final dartString = copied.cast<Utf8>().toDartString();
libFree(copied);           // freed by the LIBRARY's free, not calloc

// THE RULES
//  1. every allocation has exactly one matching free
//  2. free with the SAME allocator that allocated
//  3. free exactly once: a double free is a crash
//  4. do not free memory C still holds a pointer to
//  5. free in a finally, so an exception does not leak

// the leak that is hard to find
void process() {
  final p = toNativeUtf8();
  mightThrow();             // if this throws, p leaks
  malloc.free(p);
}

// the correct version
void process() {
  final p = toNativeUtf8();
  try {
    mightThrow();
  } finally {
    malloc.free(p);
  }
}
// a finalizer, for the cases a try/finally cannot cover
class NativeBuffer {
  final Pointer<Uint8> _ptr;
  final int _length;

  NativeBuffer(this._length) : _ptr = calloc<Uint8>(_length);

  Pointer<Uint8> get pointer => _ptr;
  int get length => _length;

  void release() {
    if (_ptr != nullptr) {
      calloc.free(_ptr);
    }
  }
}

// for a Dart-owned object that wraps native memory:
// this is what NativeFinalizer is for
final finalizer = NativeFinalizer(calloc.nativeFree.cast());

class NativeOwned {
  final Pointer<Uint8> ptr;
  NativeOwned(this.ptr);
}

// or a plain Finalizer, which Dart 3 supports for this
class Buffer {
  Buffer(int size) : _ptr = calloc<Uint8>(size);
  final Pointer<Uint8> _ptr;

  static final _cleaner = Finalizer<Pointer<Uint8>>((p) => calloc.free(p));

  void dispose() {
    _cleaner.detach(this);
    calloc.free(_ptr);
  }
}
// attach in the constructor, detach in dispose
// NOTE: a finalizer runs at an UNPREDICTABLE time. it prevents
// leaks; it does not replace a deterministic free.

// a leak test
test('every allocation is released', () {
  final before = _allocatedBytes();
  for (var i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    final p = calloc<Uint8>(1024 * 1024);   // 1MB
    calloc.free(p);
  }
  expect(_allocatedBytes(), closeTo(before, 1024));   // 1MB of slack
});

Memory: who allocates, who frees, and who gives up

FFI memory is not garbage collected. Every malloc from dart:ffi and every calloc from package:ffi must be matched with a free, and a missing one is a leak while a doubled one is a crash. Dart has no destructors, so ownership has to be expressed structurally — by scoping the allocation to the function that owns it, and by wrapping anything that outlives a call in an object with a dispose.

// the three allocation APIs, and their cost
import 'dart:ffi';
import 'package:ffi/ffi.dart';

final a = malloc<Uint8>(n);      // ...fast: bump allocator, NOT zeroed
final b = calloc<Uint8>(n);      // ...zeroed: a full pass over memory
final c = malloc<Uint8>(n);      // ...same as a
// ...`calloc` on a large allocation is not free: it touches every page, which
// for 100 MB is a real cost. Use it when the content matters, malloc otherwise.

// the rule: one owner, and the owner frees
Uint8List process(List<int> input) {
  final buf = calloc<Uint8>(input.length);
  try {
    for (var i = 0; i < input.length; i++) buf[i] = input[i];
    final out = nativeProcess(buf, input.length);
    return Uint8List.fromList(out.asTypedList(out.length));
  } finally {
    calloc.free(buf);      // ...runs on the throw path too, which is the point
  }
}

// the object form, for anything that outlives a call
class Buffer {
  final Pointer<Uint8> ptr;
  final int length;
  bool _disposed = false;

  Buffer(this.length)
      : ptr = calloc<Uint8>(length),
        length = length;      // ...throw here leaks: the field initialisers
                              //    have already run. Allocate in the body:
                              // Buffer(int n) : ptr = calloc(n), length = n {
                              //      if (n <= 0) { calloc.free(ptr); ... }
                              //    }

  Uint8List toList() {
    _assertLive();
    return ptr.asTypedList(length).toList();   // ...COPY out
  }

  void dispose() {
    if (_disposed) return;
    _disposed = true;
    calloc.free(ptr);
  }

  void _assertLive() {
    if (_disposed) throw StateError('use after dispose');
  }
}

// and the ownership rules, stated so they can be checked
// 1. memory from malloc/calloc is freed by whoever allocated it
// 2. memory C allocates for you is freed by YOU with C's free function
// 3. memory you pass in is freed by YOU unless C documents taking ownership
// 4. memory Dart holds in a Uint8List is freed by the GC - never free it
// 5. a Pointer stored in a Dart field keeps the memory alive only while that
//    field exists; the memory itself does NOT outlive dispose()

Three memory errors account for nearly all FFI crashes, and each has a distinctive symptom. A use-after-free reads or writes memory that has been returned to the allocator, so it usually corrupts something else and surfaces as a crash far from the cause. A buffer overflow writes past the end of an allocation, which often hits the allocator's own metadata and aborts on the next free. And a double free is detected by most allocators immediately, with a message naming the allocator.

// 1. use-after-free - the quiet one
final p = calloc<Uint8>(16);
calloc.free(p);
print(p[0]);            // ...reads freed memory. Often still readable, which
                        //    is why the crash comes later, elsewhere.

// the realistic version: a disposed buffer captured by a closure
final buf = Buffer(64)..dispose();
scheduleMicrotask(() => buf.toList());   // ...runs after dispose
// ...StateError from _assertLive, which is the point of having it

// 2. overflow - writing one past the end
final p2 = calloc<Uint8>(8);
for (var i = 0; i <= 8; i++) {           // ...<= is one too many
  p2[i] = i;
}
// ...the 9th byte is the allocator's bookkeeping. Symptom: an abort inside
// free(), or a heap corruption warning under a sanitizer.

// 3. double free - caught immediately
final p3 = calloc<Uint8>(8);
calloc.free(p3);
calloc.free(p3);      // ...glibc: "double free or corruption". Immediate.

// the allocation-size mistake, which is the most common of the four
final data = Uint8List.fromList(bytes);
final p4 = calloc<Uint8>(data.length);
// ...but the C function writes a NUL terminator, so it needs length + 1 and
// overflows by one. READ THE HEADER about whether it writes.

// and the size_t trap in one line
calloc<Uint8>(data.length);      // ...`length` is a Dart int (64-bit);
                                    //    the parameter is size_t (also 64-bit
                                    //    here) - but on a 32-bit build this
                                    //    call silently truncates

There are two ways to stop leaking memory without auditing every allocation by hand. NativeFinalizer attaches a finalizer to a Dart object and frees the native memory when that object becomes unreachable, which is the correct solution for memory whose lifetime should follow a Dart object's. And Finalizer itself can run a Dart callback, which covers a native library whose free function is not a plain free. Both have one sharp edge worth stating: the finalizer runs at an unspecified time, so a pointer to that memory must never be used after the Dart object has become unreachable — which means the Dart object has to hold the pointer's owner, not just be nearby it.

// NativeFinalizer: native memory tied to a Dart object's lifetime
final _finalizer = NativeFinalizer(
  callocPointer.cast(),       // ...the library's free function as a pointer
  (void ptr) {
    callocPointerFunction(ptr);
  },
);

// the Dart wrapper is the thing that gets collected
final class NativeBuffer {
  final Pointer<Uint8> ptr;
  final int length;

  NativeBuffer(this.length) : ptr = calloc<Uint8>(length), length = length {
    // ...the association the finalizer needs: WITHOUT this second argument
    // the buffer is freed while this object is still alive
    _finalizer.attach(this, ptr.cast(), detach: this);
  }

  void detach() => _finalizer.detach(this);

  Uint8List toList() => ptr.asTypedList(length).toList();
}
// ...`attach(obj, token)` - when `obj` is unreachable, `token` is freed. The
// detach token is any object; passing `this` is the standard way to be able to
// cancel.

// the leak this does NOT solve
class Cache {
  final _buffers = <int, NativeBuffer>{};
  void put(int k, List<int> v) {
    _buffers[k]?.detach();          // ...the old one will NOT be freed by the
    _buffers[k] = NativeBuffer(v.length);   //    finalizer once detached, so
  }                                     //    it must be freed explicitly
}
// ...a bounded cache is the real fix; a finalizer cannot free a buffer that is
// still in a map, and evicting one without freeing it is the classic FFI leak.

// the arithmetic that finds a leak, in a long-running process
// - RSS grows while resident set should be flat
// - a simple test: allocate 10 million 8-byte buffers in a loop, freeing each
//   in the loop. If RSS is flat, free works. If it grows 80 MB, something is
//   wrong, and the cause is almost always a pointer kept in a Dart field that
//   nothing clears.

Two C-side memory behaviours leak into Dart code even when the Dart side is correct, and both come from the library's own design. A library with an explicit free function per object needs that function bound and called, which is a per-object obligation the Dart type system cannot enforce — the Finalizer pattern handles it, but the finalize method must be bound correctly. And a library that manages a pool internally needs its own teardown function, which a binding that omits it will never call, so the process leaks the pool at exit and looks like a leak in every long test run.

// binding the library's own free, per object type
typedef _HandleFreeNative = Void Function(IntPtr h);
typedef _HandleFreeDart = void Function(int h);
final _handleFree = _lib.lookupFunction<_HandleFreeNative, _HandleFreeDart>('handle_free');

final _ctxFree = _lib.lookupFunction<
    Void Function(Pointer<Void>),
    void Function(Pointer<Void>)>('context_free');

// so a library object is two Dart objects: a handle wrapper and a finalizer
class Handle {
  final int _h;
  bool _closed = false;

  Handle(this._h);

  void close() {
    if (_closed) return;
    _closed = true;
    _handleFree(_h);
  }
}
// ...and the Finalizer, for the paths where close() is forgotten:
final _handleFinalizer = Finalizer<Pointer<Void>>((p) {
  // ...p is the Dart object we associated, not a raw pointer
});
// in practice: store an int id in a registry and finalise by id, as in the
// callback registry in ch11-callback.

// and the library-wide teardown, which must happen exactly once
typedef _ShutdownNative = Void Function();
typedef _ShutdownDart = void Function();
final _shutdown = _lib.lookupFunction<_ShutdownNative, _ShutdownDart>('shutdown');

// in main(), on every exit path including SIGINT:
void main() {
  try {
    run();
  } finally {
    _shutdown();
  }
}
// ...omitting this makes every process that uses the library leak its internal
// allocations, which shows up as a leak in a test suite and as slow growth in
// a service that restarts the library rather than the process.

// what not to rely on
// - that the GC will run, or run soon. It will not run because you leaked.
// - that exit frees anything. Dart's exit does not call your dispose methods.
// - that the OS reclaims memory promptly. It does at process exit, which is why
//   a leak in a short-lived process is invisible and a leak in a daemon is not.

12.8 Platform channels, from Dart

The alternative to FFI, and when to choose it.

import 'package:flutter/services.dart';

// method channel: request/response
class NativeStorage {
  static const _channel = MethodChannel('acme.com/storage');

  static Future<String?> read(String key) async {
    return _channel.invokeMethod<String>('read', {'key': key});
  }

  static Future<void> write(String key, String value) async {
    await _channel.invokeMethod('write', {'key': key, 'value': value});
  }
}

// event channel: a native-to-Dart stream
class Battery {
  static const _events = EventChannel('acme.com/battery_events');

  static Stream<int> onLevelChanged() {
    return _events
        .receiveBroadcastStream()
        .map((event) => (event as Map<String, dynamic>)['level'] as int);
  }
}

// WHEN A METHOD CHANNEL IS ENOUGH
//   - you call it a few times per user action
//   - the argument is small (a string, a number, a map)
//   - the result is small
//   - the per-call overhead does not matter
//
// the cost, measured: a method channel round trip is roughly
// 10-100 microseconds. For a tap handler, irrelevant. For a 60fps
// animation loop, 100x too slow.

// the decision
//   FFI:                     method channel:
//   called 1000s of times     called occasionally
//   large data, per frame    small data
//   tight latency            100us is fine
//   you control the library   a plugin already exists
//   willing to debug segfaults  just want it to work

Platform differences that break a binding

A binding that works on one platform and not another is almost always failing on one of a short list of ABI facts. The differences are not numerous, they are all knowable in advance, and each has a conditional that is cheap to write once — which is why a binding without conditionals should be treated as unfinished rather than as working.

DifferenceWindowsLinux / macOS
Library extension.dll.so / .dylib
long32-bit64-bit
Call conventionrcx, rdx, r8, r9rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx
Path separator/
Symbol visibilityExplicit exportsAll exported by default
Char signednessSigned by defaultSigned; ARM differs
Library searchPATHSystem paths only
Static linkAllowedDiscouraged

The symbol-visibility row causes the most confusing failures, because on Linux and macOS every non-static function is exported by default, so a library builds and every symbol resolves. On Windows nothing is exported unless the __declspec(dllexport) is applied or a .def file lists it, so the same library exports an empty table and lookupFunction throws ArgumentError for every call. The C side needs an export macro, and it is a one-line change that only manifests on one platform.

/* native.h - the export macro that makes it work on both */
#ifdef _WIN32
#  ifdef NATIVE_BUILD
#    define NATIVE_API __declspec(dllexport)
#  else
#    define NATIVE_API __declspec(dllimport)
#  endif
#else
#  define NATIVE_API __attribute__((visibility("default")))
#endif

NATIVE_API int add(int a, int b);
NATIVE_API const char* name(void);
// ...WITHOUT this: Linux and macOS work (default visibility), Windows exports
// nothing and every lookupFunction throws ArgumentError. It builds fine.

// and the symbol-name mangling difference, which ffigen handles
// C++  name mangling: _Z3addii
// C    no mangling: add
// ...so a library written in C++ and compiled as C++ has mangled names.
// ffigen reads the header and produces the mangled name, so it works; a
// hand-written binding with the source name fails on Linux and macOS and
// works on MSVC (which mangles differently). One of the strongest reasons to
// use ffigen.

// hiding non-API symbols
#ifdef __GNUC__
#  define NATIVE_HIDDEN __attribute__((visibility("hidden")))
#else
#  define NATIVE_HIDDEN
#endif
NATIVE_HIDDEN int internal_helper(void);
// ...so your internal functions are not part of your ABI by accident

// calling convention
#ifdef _WIN32
#  define NATIVE_CALL __cdecl        // or __stdcall, matching the header
#else
#  define NATIVE_CALL
#endif

Library loading is the second area where the platforms diverge, and the divergence is about where a bare name is searched rather than whether it is found. A bare DynamicLibrary.open('libz.so') on Linux searches the system paths, not the current directory, so a library built next to the executable is not found. On Windows a bare native.dll is searched in the current directory and then in PATH, which usually works by accident. On macOS there are three library formats with different names and extensions for the same file.

// resolving the library portably, which is never one line
import 'dart:io';
import 'dart:ffi';

DynamicLibrary openNative(String baseName) {
  if (Platform.isWindows) {
    return DynamicLibrary.open('$baseName.dll');
  }
  if (Platform.isMacOS) {
    // .dylib for a normal shared library; .framework for a bundle
    return DynamicLibrary.open('lib$baseName.dylib');
  }
  // Linux and every other POSIX: libNAME.so, and in a search path
  return DynamicLibrary.open('lib$baseName.so');
}

// and the three ways to make a bare name work, which you should prefer
// 1. ship the library next to the executable and give a path
final exeDir = File(Platform.resolvedExecutable).parent;
final lib = DynamicLibrary.open(p.join(exeDir.path, 'libnative.so'));

// 2. on Linux, set the search path before the process starts
//    LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/opt/myapp/lib
//    (Windows: the DLL beside the .exe, or on PATH)

// 3. macOS: @loader_path and @executable_path in the install name
//    clang -dynamiclib -install_name @loader_path/libnative.dylib ...

// and bundling, which is a packaging decision not an FFI one
// macOS: codesign the dylib too, or the app will not launch
//   codesign --force --sign "Developer ID" libnative.dylib
// Linux: set RPATH so the loader finds it
//   gcc -shared -fPIC -Wl,-rpath,'$ORIGIN' -o libnative.so native.c
// Windows: the DLL must be in the same directory as the .exe, or on PATH

// and macOS's arch problem
// an Apple Silicon Mac runs arm64. A binary built only for x64 needs Rosetta,
// which may not be installed. Building a universal binary is one flag:
//   clang -arch arm64 -arch x86_64 -o libnative.dylib native.c
//   dart compile exe main.dart -- -arch arm64 -arch x86_64

The last platform difference worth planning for is the direction of the trap: a binding developed on the developer's platform will be correct there and fail in production, and the failure is a load error or a wrong value rather than a compile error. The defences are unglamorous and effective — resolve the library path through one function used by every binding, assert sizeOf for every struct against the C header in a test, and run the test suite on all three platforms in CI. The struct assertion is the one that catches the silent failures.

// the test that catches a layout mistake, and it is cheap
// C asserts, in a test-only function:
//   assert(sizeof(S) == 8);
//   assert(offsetof(S, i) == 4);

import 'package:ffi/ffi.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  test('S matches the C layout', () {
    expect(sizeOf<S>(), 8);
    // ...and the offset of a nested field, which a size check alone misses:
    final p = calloc<S>();
    final base = p.address;
    // C's offsetof(T, field) == ((char*)&((T*)0)->field) - (char*)0
    expect(p.ref.i.address - base, 4);
    calloc.free(p);
  });

  test('every required symbol resolves', () {
    for (final name in ['add', 'mul', 'name', 'version']) {
      expect(() => _lib.lookupFunction<Void Function(), void Function()>(name),
          returnsNormally, reason: 'missing symbol $name');
    }
  });

  test('long is the right width on this platform', () {
    expect(sizeOf<Int32>(), 4);
    if (Platform.isWindows) {
      expect(sizeOf<Int64>(), 8);      // ...Dart's Int64 is always 8; the
    }                                    //    question is which one the C
  });                                   //    `long` was bound as

  test('a round trip produces the same bytes', () {
    final data = Uint8List.fromList(List.generate(256, (i) => i));
    expect(decode(encode(data)), data);   // ...catches every signedness bug
  });
}

// and what belongs in CI
// - build the native library for the runner's platform in the job
// - run the round-trip test on ubuntu, macos and windows
// - a job that builds a FAT macOS binary (arm64 + x64) and runs the tests on
//   both architectures, which is the only way to catch an arch-specific
//   size or long assumption

12.9 When NOT to use FFI

The cases where FFI is the wrong answer, and what to use instead.

// 1. a maintained package already does it
//    FFI is not free: you are writing and testing a binding layer
//    that someone has already written. Check pub.dev first.

// 2. the work is CPU-bound but not hot
//    an isolate (chapter 9) is safer, debuggable, and portable to
//    the web. Only reach for FFI when profiling shows the isolate
//    is the bottleneck AND the loop is genuinely tight.

// 3. you need structured data at volume
//    FFI is fastest, but you are now managing raw buffers. For
//    image or video, a plugin that handles the format is almost
//    always better than raw FFI.

// 4. you need to target the web
//    dart:ffi does not exist on the web. Any FFI code is native-only
//    and needs a second implementation. If web is a target, that
//    doubles the work.

// 5. you are not prepared to debug a segfault
//    A wrong signature, a double free, or a dangling pointer does not
//    throw a Dart exception. It crashes the process, with a stack
//    trace in a language you may not know. Budget real time for it.

// 6. the library is a C++ one
//    C++ has name mangling, exceptions, constructors and destructors,
//    none of which are in the C ABI. A C++ library must expose a
//    extern "C" wrapper, which is extra work, and exceptions
//    crossing the boundary are undefined behaviour. If you must bind
//    C++, use a wrapper library rather than binding directly.
// the practical path, if FFI is right
// 1. write the extern "C" wrapper yourself, so the boundary is
//    simple and C++-free
// extern "C" {
//   typedef struct GreetContext GreetContext;
//   GreetContext* greet_create(const char* config);
//   int32_t      greet_run(GreetContext* ctx, const uint8_t* in,
//                          int32_t len, uint8_t* out, int32_t outCap);
//   void         greet_free(uint8_t* ptr);
//   void         greet_destroy(GreetContext* ctx);
// }
//
// 2. generate the Dart bindings with ffigen
//    dart run ffigen
//
// 3. wrap the raw FFI in a Dart class that owns the memory
//    and exposes a Dart-shaped API
//    class Greeter {
//      Greeter(String config) : _ctx = _create(config.toNativeUtf8());
//      Uint8List run(Uint8List input) { ... }
//      void dispose() { _destroy(_ctx); }
//    }
//
// 4. test the Dart wrapper with a MOCK native implementation,
//    so most of your tests do not need the library present
//
// 5. test the real thing on a real device, in a release build
//    (AOT changes what is legal, and a segfault only shows up there)

Every FFI rule in this chapter exists because violating it does not produce an error message. A wrong signature, freeing with the wrong allocator, or letting a callback be collected are all silent until the process crashes. That is why the try/finally discipline and the "free with the same allocator" rule are non-negotiable rather than stylistic.

Exercises 13

  1. Write a C library with three functions, compile it for Windows, macOS and Linux, and load it with a DynamicLibrary lookup per platform.
  2. Bind a function that takes and returns a string, with a try/finally around every allocation. Verify no leak with a repeated-call test.
  3. Pass a struct by value, and an array of structs, and verify the memory layout matches what the C side reads.
  4. Pass a Dart callback into C, then deliberately drop the reference to show the crash. Then fix it with a retained reference.
  5. Build a leak detector: allocate, track, free, and assert the balance is zero over ten thousand iterations.
  6. Write a method channel and an FFI binding for the same operation, and measure the round-trip cost of each.
  7. Deliberately free memory with the wrong allocator and observe what happens. Read the crash report and find the double-free.

When not to use FFI, and the alternatives in order

The decision to use FFI is worth making explicitly rather than by default, because FFI has costs that are invisible in a small prototype and dominant in a product. In order of preference, the alternatives are: do it in Dart; do it on another isolate; do it in JavaScript with dart:js_interop; do it by calling a service; and only then reach for FFI.

AlternativeWhen it winsIts own cost
Pure Dart, AOTAlmost always worth trying firstDevelopment time
An isolateCPU work; blocking callsCopying at the boundary
WASMCross-platform, sandboxed native-ishBridge cost, size
A subprocessCrash isolation; existing toolingProcess management, IPC
A network callThe capability exists remotelyLatency, failure modes
A process pluginPlatform APIs needing channelsPlatform code in another language
FFIThe library is native and localAll of ch11

An isolate is the alternative people skip, because it is available in pure Dart and requires no extra toolchain. Isolate.run gives real parallelism for CPU-bound work with no native code at all, and the only cost is copying arguments and results. That cost is often smaller than it sounds, because TransferableTypedData moves a buffer rather than copying it — and because a computation over ten megabytes of data takes long enough that the copy is a rounding error.

// the isolate version, which needs no native toolchain at all
Future<Result> analyze(Uint8List data) async {
  final transfer = TransferableTypedData.fromList([data]);
  return Isolate.run(() {
    final input = transfer.materialize().asUint8List();
    return heavyParse(input);            // ...in another thread, for real
  });
}
// ...`Isolate.run` returns a Future, so this is fully async. Cost: one
// allocation to move the buffer, one to materialise it.

// when an isolate is genuinely wrong
// - the argument is a pointer into memory the other side already owns (FFFI)
// - the function is called in a tight loop, where the isolate hop dominates
// - you need the answer synchronously
// - the work is a few microseconds and you call it a million times

// a process plugin, which is the right tool for platform APIs
// pubspec.yaml
flutter:
  plugins:
    platforms:
      windows:
        ffiPlugin: true
// ...and Dart calls it through Dart's normal plugin interface, not FFI
// directly. The plugin's own implementation may use C++ and FFI internally;
// the Dart side sees a normal MethodChannel.

// WebAssembly, for a native library that must be portable
// dart compile wasm main.dart
// ...and a WASM module compiled from Rust or C can be called from it. This is
// the emerging answer for "native performance, many platforms, no toolchain":
// it is sandboxed, memory-safe, and the build is a single artifact.

// a subprocess, for crash isolation and existing tools
final p = await Process.start('ffprobe', args);
final result = await p.exitCode;
p.stdout.transform(utf8.decoder).transform(const LineSplitter()).listen(...);
// ...slower than FFI and far more robust: a segfault in ffmpeg does not take
// down your service. Worth it whenever the native work is not in the hot path.

// a network call, which sounds wrong and is often right
// ...if the capability is a remote API (a geocoder, an OCR service, a
// recommendation engine), calling it costs latency and adds a dependency.
// For non-interactive work it is the right answer, and it removes FFI's
// entire cost surface from the build.

There is also a case where FFI is the wrong tool for a reason unrelated to performance: the capability you need is not a function but a framework, and frameworks have state, threads, event loops and lifecycles that a function-pointer binding cannot express. Binding half of such a library — enough to initialise it and call one entry point, and no more — produces code that deadlocks or crashes under load in ways that are very hard to diagnose. The honest options there are a maintained binding package, a subprocess, or a service.

// the framework case, and why it is worse than it looks
// C library: a runtime with its own heap, thread pool and event loop.
// A binding that exposes init() and run() cannot express:
//   - which thread the callbacks arrive on
//   - when the runtime must be shut down
//   - what to do with an error on a runtime thread
// Result: crashes that only appear under load, and only on one platform.

// the three honest options
// 1. a maintained binding package, if one exists
//    $ dart pub search native_sdk
//    ...check its last-published date and issue count first. An unmaintained
//    binding for a moving native library is worse than none.

// 2. a subprocess, when the native tool is a command-line program anyway
final result = await Process.run('ffmpeg', ['-i', input, '-f', 'null', '-']);
if (result.exitCode != 0) throw StateError(result.stderr);
// ...and this is usually what you want: no build for the native side at all,
// because the tool is already installed.

// 3. a service, when the native thing is heavy enough to be shared
// ...one long-lived native worker process, driven over a pipe or a socket,
// shared by every isolate in your program. Startup cost is paid once and the
// crash isolation is real.

// and the case that is simply FFI, stated for contrast
// - a numeric kernel over a buffer you already have
// - a codec with a clean C API
// - a hashing or compression library with one well-known entry point
// - a vendored C library with no Dart equivalent whatsoever
// ...all of these are functions, not frameworks, and FFI is exactly right

Whichever way the decision goes, the cost should be recognised up front because it is recurring. FFI adds a build system that must work on three platforms and two architectures, an ABI that must be tracked against the native library's version, and a memory model the compiler cannot check. A project that adopts FFI for one convenience feature has adopted all three permanently, and the realistic question is not "can I use FFI here" but "can this project carry FFI at all".

// the checklist, and the honest answers
//
// Does a pure Dart implementation exist or is one achievable?
//   YES -> do that. It is a day of work versus a permanent build dependency.
//
// Can the work move to an isolate?
//   YES -> do that. Zero native code, real parallelism.
//
// Does a maintained binding package exist and is it current?
//   YES -> depend on it. You inherit someone else's ABI maintenance.
//
// Is the capability a command-line tool?
//   YES -> Process.run. No build for the native side at all.
//
// Is the native library a framework rather than a function library?
//   YES -> subprocess or service. NOT a hand-written binding.
//
// Is it a hot numeric kernel with a clean C API?
//   YES -> FFI is the correct answer. Budget for the build, the CI matrix,
//     and the size_of tests.
//
// If you reach here, the questions that follow are:
//   - how many platforms must this build on? (three is the honest answer)
//   - who updates the binding when the native library changes?
//   - what is the plan when the native library's ABI changes without notice?
//   - can the program still start if the library is missing? (a useful
//     property: degrade to a Dart implementation, so a missing .so is a
//     slow path rather than a crash)

13 · Platform Compilation

13.1 JIT, AOT and the two runtimes13.2 The compile commands13.3 Native: executable, AOT snapshot, cross-compilation13.4 Compiling for Android13.5 Compiling for iOS13.6 The web: dart2js and dart2wasm13.7 The web without dart:io13.8 The platform abstraction pattern13.9 Conditional imports13.10 Shipping checklist per platform

What each compilation target actually does, and the constraints each one imposes on your code.

13.1 JIT, AOT and the two runtimes

Two compilation strategies and two runtimes, and which combination each platform uses.

//            compilation        runtime           used by
//
// dart run    JIT                Dart VM           development only
// debug       (just-in-time)     (with the VM
//                                service, so you
//                                can attach a
//                                debugger)
//
// dart        AOT                Dart AOT runtime   release native apps,
// compile exe (ahead-of-time)                       CLI tools, servers
//             into machine code
//
// dart        AOT snapshot        Dart AOT runtime   Flutter release
// compile                               (a snapshot,  mobile and desktop
// aot-snapshot                        loaded at      Flutter apps
//                                     startup)
//
// dart        AOT -> JavaScript  a browser         web
// compile js
//
// dart        AOT ->             a browser         web, with better
// compile wasm    WebAssembly                       performance and
//                                                     smaller code
//
// THE KEY DIFFERENCE: the JIT has a VM with a garbage collector and
// a runtime data structure. The AOT runtime has only the collector
// and a much smaller surface. Anything that relies on VM
// introspection - dynamic loading, mirrors, some proxies - does not
// work in AOT.
// WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOUR CODE
//
// 1. no dart:mirrors in a release build. Use code generation
//    (build_runner) instead: it runs at BUILD time, not run time.
//
// 2. `dart run` behaviour is not the same as release behaviour
//    test in release before shipping.
//
// 3. AOT startup is faster, but there is no JIT fallback, so a
//    dynamically-typed hot path is slower and uses more memory.
//
// 4. reflection-like behaviour via mirrors is unavailable, which
//    is why json_serializable, freezed and injectable GENERATE code
//    rather than using reflection at runtime.
//
// 5. const evaluation happens at compile time, so a const
//    constructor that is valid in JIT is valid in AOT, but a
//    non-const value that happens to be constant in JIT is not.

The most common release-only bug in Dart is a dart:mirrors import. It works perfectly in dart run and crashes or fails to compile in a release build. If you need runtime type information, use code generation. This is why the whole build_runner ecosystem exists, and it is not an accident of design.

JIT, AOT, and what each one costs

Dart ships two compilers that differ in when they run and what they emit, and almost every performance or deployment question reduces to which one produced the artefact. The JIT compiler optimises at runtime, on the machine that will actually execute the code, using the real types as they arrive. The AOT compiler runs once, before execution, and must decide everything from static analysis alone. That single difference explains the whole table below.

PropertyJITAOT
RunsAt runtime, on first execution of each functionAt build time
Sees real typesYes — after the first call or twoNo — only declared types
StartupSlow first run, fast afterwardsFast, no compile step
Peak throughputHighest, because of type feedbackVery close for typed code
OutputKernel snapshot + machine code in memoryA native binary or snapshot
DeoptimisationSupportedNot applicable
Used bydart run, Flutter debugRelease builds, production

The consequence that surprises people is that AOT is worse than JIT in exactly one situation, and it is a common one: a generic function called with several types. List.copy is a fine name in a library, but in a given program it is called with List<int> in one place and List<String> in another. JIT compiles both separately and both at full speed. AOT compiles one version and, in the most recent runtimes, inserts a dispatch check; if it cannot prove a single type, it uses the unoptimised version. So generic-heavy code is where the two compilers' performance diverges most, and it is also where profiling finds it.

// the code that reveals the difference
import 'dart:math';

List<T> shuffled<T>(List<T> input, Random rng) {
  final out = List<T>.of(input);
  for (var i = out.length - 1; i > 0; i--) {
    final j = rng.nextInt(i + 1);
    final tmp = out[i];
    out[i] = out[j];
    out[j] = tmp;
  }
  return out;
}

void main() {
  // ...called with two concrete types, so JIT makes two optimised versions
  shuffled([1, 2, 3], Random());
  shuffled(['a', 'b'], Random());
}
// ...JIT: fast after the first few thousand iterations. AOT: one shared,
// less-specialised version. The gap is real but usually small - measure it.

// the fix, when it does matter: monomorphise at the call site
final nums = shuffled<int>([1, 2, 3], Random());     // explicit type arg
// ...or duplicate the function per type in generated code, which is what a
// code generator does

// the same effect with dart2js, and much larger there
// dart2js's type feedback is coarser and its optimiser is less mature than the
// VM's, so a polymorphic call site in a hot loop can be 3-5x slower than the
// equivalent AOT build. On the web, this is a first-order design constraint
// rather than a footnote.

There is a third mode worth naming, and it is what Flutter's release builds use: AOT for the main isolate's hot code, plus a JIT snapshot for the same code so that debugging and hot reload remain available. On the dart CLI there is no such hybrid, so the choice is simply dart run for development and dart compile for production — and the honest reason to keep using JIT in production is not speed but a diagnostic: a JIT build can print a stack trace with resolved names and let you attach a debugger, and an AOT binary can only do the former.

// telling which runtime you are on, and why a guard is needed
import 'dart:io' show Platform;

bool get isJit {
  // ...Platform.script differs: the SOURCE file under `dart run`, the snapshot
  // under a compiled executable. That is not a documented API.
  // The supported test is whether the kernel can be found:
  return Platform.script.toString().endsWith('.dart');
}
// ...fragile and rarely worth it. The honest approaches:
//   - assert in a helper: bool get debugMode => !bool.fromEnvironment('dart.vm.product');
//   - a build-time define, set by the build system:
//       dart compile exe -DVERBOSE=true app.dart
//   - or simply: do not branch on the runtime. Behaviour should not depend
//     on it, and if it does, that is the bug.

// the one thing you may legitimately vary by runtime
// ...time. Never behaviour. A `--enable-asserts` build that behaves differently
// from a production build is a test that tests the wrong thing, because the
// failing path is never the one that ships.

// and the flag that people leave on by accident
// $ dart run --enable-asserts app.dart        // asserts ON
// $ dart run app.dart                        // asserts OFF - the default
// ...asserts are compiled out entirely in release, so an assert that was doing
// real work is a no-op in production and a crash in development. Never put a
// side effect inside one.

13.2 The compile commands

Every compilation command, with the flags that matter.

// a native executable
dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o app
dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o app --obfuscate     // harder to reverse
dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o app --no-source-maps
dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o app -DPROD=true     // a define
dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o app --enable-asserts // keep asserts
dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o app --verbosity=all

// an AOT snapshot (a library, loadable at runtime)
dart compile aot-snapshot lib/mylib.dart -o mylib.aot

// a JIT kernel snapshot
dart compile kernel bin/main.dart -o app.dill

// JavaScript
dart compile js bin/main.dart -o app.js
dart compile js bin/main.dart -o app.js -O2           // 0..4, default 2
dart compile js bin/main.dart -o app.js --minify
dart compile js bin/main.dart -o app.js -DNO_MINIFY=false

// WebAssembly
dart compile wasm bin/main.dart -o app.wasm
dart compile wasm bin/main.dart -o app.wasm -O2

// a Dart library as a kernel file, for a host to load
dart compile kernel lib/thing.dart -o thing.dill
// the defines, which are the compile-time configuration
// dart define is available in 3.x and is the modern way
dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o app -DAPI_URL=https://api.acme.com -DLOGGING=false

// read them in the code
const apiUrl = String.fromEnvironment('API_URL',
    defaultValue: 'http://localhost:8080');
const logging = bool.fromEnvironment('LOGGING', defaultValue: false);

if (logging) print('debug mode');

// IMPORTANT: a const fromEnvironment is a COMPILE-TIME constant.
// it is inlined, so changing it requires a rebuild.
// for a value that changes at runtime, read a file or an env var
// (on native) instead.

// the trade-offs of a compile-time define
//   + zero runtime cost, tree-shakeable
//   - cannot change without a rebuild
//   - a Web app cannot have environment-specific builds easily:
//     you must recompile per environment, or fetch config at runtime

The compile commands, and which one you want

dart compile has four subcommands and they are not variations on one output: exe produces a self-contained native executable, aot-snapshot produces a Dart-runtime-independent snapshot for a bundled runtime, js produces JavaScript, and wasm produces WebAssembly. Choosing between the first two is the decision most projects need to make, and it comes down to whether the runtime is bundled.

CommandOutputRuntimeFor
dart compile exeOne native binaryBundledCLI tools, services, anything shipped alone
dart compile aot-snapshot.aot fileSeparateEmbedded in a Flutter app; a controlled environment
dart compile js.js + .js.mapdart.jsWeb, with the lowest barrier
dart compile wasm.wasm + .jsdart.jsWeb, with real AOT performance

Every compile command takes the same five options that matter in practice, and three of them are worth understanding rather than copying. -O0 through -O4 select optimisation level; -O4 is the default and is almost always right. --define injects a compile-time constant, which is how you build a debug and a release variant of one source tree. And --no-sound-null-safety removes the runtime null checks — which should never be done, and is worth writing down as a rule because it is tempting and measurably faster.

// the four commands, with what each needs
// $ dart compile exe   bin/server.dart -o server
// $ dart compile exe   bin/cli.dart   -o cli --define=VERBOSE=true
// $ dart compile aot-snapshot bin/server.dart -o server.aot
// $ dart compile js    web/main.dart -o web/main.js -O2
// $ dart compile wasm  web/main.dart -o web/main.wasm

// the -D flag is a compile-time constant, so `const` propagation removes it
// entirely from release output
const bool kVerbose = bool.fromEnvironment('VERBOSE');
const String kApiBase = String.fromEnvironment('API_BASE',
    defaultValue: 'https://api.example.com');

void main() {
  if (kVerbose) {
    // ...this branch does not exist in a build without the define. The
    // surrounding code is tree-shaken away, so a verbose logging helper
    // included under -DVERBOSE costs nothing when it is off - provided its
    // arguments are also const or side-effect free.
    log('starting');
  }
  serve(kApiBase);
}
// ...so the pattern for a build variant is a const from the environment, not an
// `if (debugMode)` sprinkled through the code.

// what the compiler needs to know beyond your source
// $ dart compile exe bin/server.dart -o server //     --packages=.dart_tool/package_config.json
// ...it reads the package config from the script's directory upward, so this is
// only needed when building from a different working directory.

/* what each flag actually does, measured:
//   -O0  no optimisation        ~4x slower, useful only for a debug build
//   -O1  minimal               ~1.5x slower, fastest to compile
//   -O2  some inlining         the historical default
//   -O3  aggressive            sometimes larger and slower than -O4
//   -O4  default               best for release; what you want
// ...the -O3 anomaly is real: the more aggressive transforms can duplicate
// code. Benchmark rather than assuming monotonic improvement. */

// and the flags that are NOT there for a reason
// --no-sound-null-safety   removes null checks AND soundness. A nullability
//                          error becomes memory corruption instead of an
//                          exception. Faster by 5-15%. Almost never worth it.

Two details of the output decide whether it will start on a machine other than the one that built it, and both are silent failures. dart compile exe by default produces a binary that depends on the Dart runtime being present only as itself — it is self-contained, so it works — but the target triple it is built for is the host's, so an x64 binary will not run on arm64. And the compiled binary embeds the absolute paths of your source files for stack traces, which is harmless and occasionally useful, but -DSTRIP and obfuscation change what a trace looks like.

// what you get
$ dart compile exe bin/server.dart -o build/server
// build/server is a self-contained native executable. `ldd build/server` on
// Linux shows libpthread/libdl/libc and nothing else — no Dart runtime files.

// checking what you actually produced
$ file build/server
build/server: ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64, dynamically linked
// ...`x86-64` is the answer to "will this run on the deploy box".

// size, and where it goes
$ ls -lh build/server
-rwxr-xr-x 1 user staff 8.4M
// ...a hello world is ~8 MB, because the AOT runtime is compiled in. Removing
// the unused libraries shrinks it; there is no --gc-sections equivalent, so
// the practical lever is not importing what you do not use.

// stack traces: what a user sees, and the three levels of detail
// 1. unstripped, symbols present
//    #0      Server.serve (package:myapp/server.dart:42:7)
//    #1      _rootRunUnary (dart:async/zone.dart:1399:13)
// ...full names, package: URIs, line numbers. This is what you want in a
// staging environment.
//
// 2. stripped
//    #0      Server.serve (dart:core:0:0)
// ...the frame exists but the symbol is gone. Faster to ship, useless to debug.
//
// 3. obfuscated, for a client application
//    #0      _k9Qd2Lm (dart:core:0:0)
// ...names are replaced. The app runs identically; a stack trace is unreadable
// unless you kept the mapping file that the same build produced. Keep it.

// and the decision for a container
// ...prefer a distroless or scratch base and copy in the single binary, but
// note that `dart compile exe` still links libc dynamically, so `scratch` does
// not work. Use `distroless/base` or a static build from the musl SDK.

13.3 Native: executable, AOT snapshot, cross-compilation

Where cross-compilation works, and the traps.

// CROSS-COMPILATION: Dart can target another platform from your
// machine, for the AOT runtime.

// Linux to Windows
dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o app.exe
// Linux to macOS
dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o app
// macOS to Linux
dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o app
// any to arm64
dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o app --target-os=macos --target-arch=arm64

// the available targets
dart compile exe --help
// --target-os   linux | macos | windows | android | ios
// --target-arch arm | arm64 | ia32 | x64 | riscv32 | riscv64
// --target-abi  e.g. android-arm64, macos-arm64-x64

// THE TRAPS
// 1. you can cross-COMPILE the Dart code, but you cannot run it.
//    And if it needs a native library, you need one for the
//    target, built for the target.
//
// 2. the target must be a platform the Dart AOT runtime supports.
//    Android and iOS are special: see the next two sections.
//
// 3. a snapshot built for one architecture is not portable to
//    another. You need one artefact per architecture, or a
//    universal binary.
//
// 4. glibc version matters on Linux. A binary built on a new
//    distro will not run on an old one. Static linking avoids it:
dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o app --extra-compiler-flag=-static-linked

Cross-compilation, and building for a target you do not own

You can only produce a Dart artefact for the architecture of the machine doing the compiling, unless you use a cross-compilation SDK. The three mechanisms are: the Flutter SDK, which ships cross-compilation support for every target it supports; the Dart SDK, which supports a small set of explicit targets; and a third-party toolchain for the rest. The first is what most projects should use, and the important part of understanding it is knowing which parts are provided and which are not.

TargetHowToolchain comes from
Linux x64 / arm64dart compile exeYour Dart SDK
macOS x64 / arm64dart compile exeYour Dart SDK
Windows x64dart compile exeYour Dart SDK
Androidflutter build apkFlutter SDK + Android NDK
iOSflutter build iosFlutter SDK + Xcode
Linux from WindowsDocker or a CI runnerYou provide the image
Embedded (bare metal)dart compile exe + custom SDKA board-specific SDK

The rule that resolves almost every cross-compilation question is that the Dart SDK's own compile exe produces a binary for the host triple, and nothing else. So a build that must run on arm64 Linux and is being produced on x64 macOS needs either an arm64 machine, or a Docker image, or the Flutter SDK's target matrix. Docker is usually the answer for a server, because it also pins the libc version, which is the other portability problem and the one people forget.

// the three approaches, and when each is right

// 1. build natively. Simplest, and correct when CI has runners per platform.
$ dart compile exe bin/server.dart -o build/server
// ...GitHub Actions has macos-latest, windows-latest and ubuntu-latest, so
// "build on a runner per platform" needs no extra tooling.

// 2. cross-compile with the Dart SDK's explicit target flags, where they exist
$ dart compile exe bin/server.dart -o server-arm64     --target-os linux --target-arch arm64
// ...supported for linux/macos/windows x64 and arm64. It uses the host's
// toolchain, so on Windows targeting Linux you get a PE file, not an ELF one -
// check the result rather than trusting the flag.

// 3. Docker. The one that also solves the libc problem.
# Dockerfile
FROM dart:stable AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY pubspec.* ./
RUN dart pub get
COPY . .
RUN dart compile exe bin/server.dart -o /server

FROM gcr.io/distroless/base
COPY --from=build /server /server
ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]
// ...builds the binary ON Linux for Linux, so the target triple is right, and
// the runtime image is the same base the binary was linked against. `distroless`
// rather than `scratch` because `dart compile exe` links libc dynamically.

// the cross-compile trap: architecture is not the whole target
$ file build/server-linux-arm64
// ...x86-64 or aarch64, fine. But:
// - glibc version:  built on Ubuntu 22.04, deployed on 20.04 -> "GLIBC_2.34
