//   not found" at startup, with no useful message
// - musl vs glibc:  a musl target cannot use glibc-only libraries
// - CPU features:   compiling on a machine with AVX-512 produces a binary that
//                   faults with SIGILL on one without it. Pass
//                   --target-cpu to pin the baseline.
// ...so pinning the base image in a Dockerfile is not ceremony, it is the fix.

/* the CPU baseline, which is worth setting explicitly for anything server-side
   $ dart compile exe bin/server.dart -o server --target-cpu=generic
   ...or arm
   ...generic is the conservative choice and costs perhaps 10%. Omitting it means
   the binary is tuned for the build machine, which is the single most common
   cause of "works in CI, crashes in production on the other node type". */

A bare-metal target is the fourth case and it has its own constraint: there is no Dart VM, so the SDK is a custom build of the runtime plus a platform definition that names the memory layout, the entry point and the interrupt handlers. The Dart SDK supports dart compile exe --target-os=baremetal against a board-support package, and the result runs on a microcontroller with tens of kilobytes of RAM. It is a real and supported configuration, and it is also the point at which the abstraction starts to cost: no reflection, no dart:mirrors, a restricted core library, and no JIT.

// the shape of a bare-metal build
// 1. a board support package that describes the hardware
//    - memory map and linker script
//    - the reset handler and the vector table
//    - clock, timers, GPIO, UART
// 2. a main that never returns
import 'dart:async';
import 'package:board/board.dart';

void main() {
  board.init();
  Timer.periodic(const Duration(seconds: 1), (_) {
    board.uart.write('tick
');
  });
  // ...never returns, and never should: on bare metal there is nothing to
  // return to. The runtime's main() never returns either.
}

// what you lose, explicitly
// - dart:io entirely: no files, no sockets, no processes
// - dart:mirrors: no runtime reflection, so no json_serializable's reflection
//   fallback and no dynamic invocation
// - most of package:* — anything pulling in dart:io or dart:ffi will not link
// - the GC is still there, but the heap is a fixed region you declared
// ...so the practical constraint is dependency selection: check whether a
// package imports dart:io before you add it, because on this target that is a
// link error at build time rather than a runtime surprise.

// and the honest size comparison, because "tiny" needs a number
// ...a Dart CLI tool compiled with `dart compile exe`: ~8 MB, runs anywhere
// ...a Dart bare-metal binary: ~30-80 KB including the runtime, runs on a
//    microcontroller
// ...hand-written C: ~1 KB, and you wrote the runtime yourself

13.4 Compiling for Android

The AOT snapshot model, and why Flutter does not work the same way.

// ANDROID: a plain Dart app (no Flutter)
// build an AOT snapshot per ABI, and the snapshot goes into the APK

dart compile aot-snapshot bin/main.dart -o app.android-arm64.aot \
  --target-os=android --target-arch=arm64
dart compile aot-snapshot bin/main.dart -o app.android-armx.aot \
  --target-os=android --target-arch=arm
dart compile aot-snapshot bin/main.dart -o app.android-x64.aot \
  --target-os=android --target-arch=x64

// place them where the runtime expects them:
//   android/app/src/main/assets/flutter_assets/  (Flutter)
//   assets/dart/                                 (plain Dart apps)
// and reference them from build.gradle, with the ABI split

// the alternative: a JIT-based app with a bundled kernel
// dart compile kernel bin/main.dart -o libapp.so
// the app can then run on any device, and attach a debugger

// the ABI split, which controls what you ship
// android {
//   splits {
//     abi {
//       enable true
//       reset()
//       include 'arm64-v8a'   // 99% of devices in 2026
//       // include 'armeabi-v7a'  // old 32-bit devices
//       // include 'x86_64'      // emulators only
//     }
//   }
// }
// the Google Play bundle (AAB) does this split automatically
// FLUTTER FOR ANDROID: not dart compile, but gradle
flutter build appbundle --release
flutter build apk --release --split-per-abi
flutter build apk --release --target-platform android-arm64

// what the build produces
//   build/app/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab

// the size story
//   an AAB is uploaded, and Play generates per-device APKs
//   containing only that device's native libraries
//   so one native plugin does not mean every user downloads
//   every architecture

// the R8/ProGuard step
//   Flutter runs R8 on the Java/Kotlin side
//   your Dart code is AOT compiled, so it is already obfuscated
//   if you use reflection in the Kotlin layer, keep rules:
android {
    buildTypes {
        release {
            proguardFiles getDefaultProguardFile('proguard-android-optimize.txt'),
                        'proguard-rules.pro'
        }
    }
}

Compiling for Android

Android is the target with the most moving parts that are not yours: four ABIs, several API levels, a build system with its own language, and a packaging format that has changed twice. Flutter hides most of it behind flutter build apk, and the value of understanding the details is almost entirely in knowing what to do when that command does not do what you want.

ABIArchitectureDevicesKeep?
armeabi-v7aARM 32-bitOld, still significant in some marketsUsually
arm64-v8aARM 64-bitEvery current deviceAlways
x86_64Intel/AMD 64-bitEmulators, ChromebooksEmulator builds

Two commands cover everything: flutter build apk produces a single fat archive containing every requested ABI, and flutter build appbundle produces an .aab for Play, which is mandatory now and which lets Play deliver only the ABI the device needs. The difference in size is substantial — often 2× — because the fat APK ships all three. Neither command is a Dart compile; they are Gradle invocations that end up invoking one dart compile per ABI.

// the commands that matter
$ flutter build apk --release                 # one fat APK, all ABIs
$ flutter build appbundle --release           # the format Play requires
$ flutter build apk --release --split-per-abi # three APKs, pick per device
$ flutter build appbundle --release     --target-platform android-arm64,android-arm,android-x64

// what is inside, and why it is large
$ unzip -l build/app/outputs/flutter-apk/app-release.apk | grep lib
  lib/arm64-v8a/libapp.so       12.1 MB     <- YOUR Dart AOT code
  lib/arm64-v8a/libflutter.so    8.4 MB     <- the Flutter engine
  lib/armeabi-v7a/libapp.so     11.7 MB
  lib/armeabi-v7a/libflutter.so  7.9 MB
// ...so a release APK is ~40 MB mostly because three copies of the engine are
// present. `--split-per-abi` makes each ~14 MB and the delivered one ~20 MB.

// and the AOT snapshot is the other big item, in assets
$ unzip -l app-release.apk | grep flutter_assets
  assets/flutter_assets/kernel_blob.bin   0    <- ZERO in release
  assets/flutter_assets/isolate_snapshot_data  9.8 MB
  assets/flutter_assets/vm_snapshot_data      11.6 MB
// ...`kernel_blob.bin` being 0 bytes is the visible sign of an AOT build: no
// Dart source is shipped, which is both a size win and a licensing one.

// the API level, which is set per-app not per-build
// android/app/build.gradle.kts
android {
    defaultConfig {
        minSdk = 21        // Android 5.0
        targetSdk = 35
        compileSdk = 35
    }
}
// ...minSdk 21 is Dart's floor for Flutter. Raising targetSdk is what Android
// requires for an update, and it brings new runtime behaviours you must handle.

// a native library, which is the case that needs per-ABI work
// android/app/build.gradle.kts
android {
    defaultConfig {
        ndk {
            // ...abiFilters must list every ABI you actually ship a .so for,
            // or Gradle packages the Flutter engine's libs for all of them and
            // the APK grows without your library ever being used
            abiFilters += listOf("arm64-v8a", "armeabi-v7a")
        }
    }
}
// ...and the library itself needs one build per ABI:
//   android { buildTypes { release { ndk { abiFilters "arm64-v8a" } } } }

// the thing that fails most often, and what it means
// * What went wrong: Execution failed for task :app:mergeReleaseNativeLibs
//   > A problem occurred starting process 'command line'
// ...this is a Java/Gradle version mismatch, not a Dart problem. Check
// ./gradlew --version and the JDK required by your AGP version.

// and the release-signing step, without which the APK will not install
$ keytool -genkey -v -keystore ~/upload.jks -keyalg RSA     -keysize 2048 -validity 10000 -alias upload
$ flutter build appbundle --release     --key-store ~/upload.jks --key-alias upload     --key-password-file=~/ks-pass.txt
// ...`--obfuscate` and `--split-debug-info` are the release-hardening flags, and
// both write files you must archive: the symbol map is the only way to read a
// stack trace from a crashed release build.

The Flutter-specific Android knowledge that matters is smaller than it looks, and it is three things. Platform.isAndroid is not how you ask what you need; you ask about capabilities. Android version gating goes through the API level, not through a Dart constant. And permission requests are a plugin, not an API — the permission_handler package is the interface, and its Android implementation is where the manifest merging and the runtime prompt live.

// the three that matter

// 1. gate on capability, not on platform
// WRONG
if (Platform.isAndroid) { useAndroidSpecificThing(); }
// RIGHT
if (await hasBluetooth()) { await scan(); }
// ...the second also works on iOS and web, and does not need a rebuild when a
// new platform is added.

// 2. version checks come from the platform, and are cheap
if (Platform.isAndroid && (await deviceInfo.androidVersion) >= 30) {
  // ...scoped storage, and the file APIs changed behaviour here
}

// 3. permissions are asynchronous and can be denied permanently
import 'package:permission_handler/permission_handler.dart';

Future<bool> ensureCamera() async {
  final status = await Permission.camera.request();
  if (status.isGranted) return true;
  if (status.isPermanentlyDenied) {
    // ...the user chose "don't ask again". There is NO prompt available; the
    // only route is to open the settings screen:
    await openAppSettings();
    return false;
  }
  return false;   // ...denied once - the prompt will appear again
}
// ...the permanently-denied state is the one that produces "the app cannot
// access the camera and I cannot fix it in code" bug reports. Handle it.

// and the manifest, which is merged from every plugin
// android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET" />
<uses-feature android:name="android.hardware.camera" android:required="false" />
// ...`required="false"` matters: with it true, your app is hidden from devices
// without a camera. That is often wrong and is invisible until you check.
// Merge conflicts in the manifest are the standard Android build failure; the
// merged result is at build/app/intermediates/merged_manifests/.

Profiling an Android build, and the two costs that are not Dart's

An Android release build is the case where measurement matters most, because three separate costs stack on top of each other and only one of them is visible in a Dart profile: the APK's size, the install's size, and the process's memory. They have different causes and different fixes, and conflating them produces work that does not help.

CostMeasured byDominant cause
APK sizeunzip -l on the artefactOne copy of the engine per ABI
Download sizePlay Console's size reportWhatever the APK contains, compressed
Install sizeadb shell du on deviceNative code, not assets
Baseline RSSDumpsys meminfoThe Dart heap's initial size
Growth over timeThe same, after N minutesA retained cache or a listener leak

The Dart heap's initial size is the one that surprises people, because it is set by a flag rather than by allocation. A Flutter app's heap starts at whatever the engine requests — often a few megabytes — and grows in pages, and it does not shrink eagerly. So an app that once processed a 40 MB image keeps that memory for the rest of the session, and "the app uses 200 MB" is often a true observation about a moment ten minutes in rather than about the steady state. Measuring the baseline and the peak separately is the only way to tell a large initial reservation from a leak.

// the measurement that distinguishes the two
$ adb shell dumpsys meminfo com.example.app | head -8
  App Summary
                       Pss(KB)                        Rss(KB)
                    ------                        ------
           Java Heap:    18392                        32768
         Native Heap:    21440                        24576    <-- Dart heap
              Dalvik:     8236                        10432
 TOTAL PSS:   108304                       TOTAL RSS:  142336
// ...Native Heap is where the Dart heap and Skia's buffers live. A steady
// 21 MB is fine. 21 MB at startup growing to 400 MB after five minutes is a
// retention bug, and the two are indistinguishable from one screenshot.

// how to find a retention bug rather than guess at one
// 1. reproduce the flow, then wait for a GC to settle
$ adb shell am send-trim-memory com.example.app RUNNING_LOW
// ...forces the system to ask the app to trim, which the Dart VM answers by
// collecting. The number after the trim is the retained set.
//
// 2. take a heap snapshot and look at what survives
$ adb shell am dumpheap com.example.app /data/local/tmp/heap.hprof
$ adb pull /data/local/tmp/heap.hprof
// ...in Android Studio: open the .hprof, switch to the "Dart" tab if the
// build has the Dart VM service symbols, and the dominator tree shows what is
// still reachable. In practice the answer is almost always one of:
//   - an image cache with no size bound
//   - a Stream subscription never cancelled, so its closure holds a controller
//   - a static Map used as a cache, which is never collected at all
//   - a controller with no dispose(), still holding its listeners

// 3. for a Dart-only leak, the allocation profiler is more direct
$ flutter run --profile
// DevTools > Memory > Track allocations, then the flame chart shows every
// allocation that has not been freed, attributed to its call site

// and the three fixes that cover most of it
// a cache that is bounded and evicts:
class LruCache<K, V> {
  final _map = <K, V>{};
  final int _max;
  LruCache(this._max);
  void put(K k, V v) {
    _map.remove(k);
    _map[k] = v;
    if (_map.length > _max) _map.remove(_map.keys.first);
  }
}
// a subscription that is cancelled:
late final StreamSubscription _sub;
void init() {
  _sub = stream.listen(handle);
}
void dispose() {
  _sub.cancel();      // ...without this, `handle` and everything it
}                     //    closes over stays reachable for the app's life
// and a controller that is disposed:
class MyWidget extends StatefulWidget { ... }
// its State must override dispose() and call controller.dispose()

Size has its own discipline, and the useful measurement is a diff against a known baseline rather than an absolute number. Flutter provides the tool for this — flutter build appbundle prints a per-ABI breakdown and the analyzer can diff two builds — and the practice that makes it useful is failing the build on a size regression rather than reporting it, because a report that nobody has to act on is a report nobody reads.

// what the toolchain gives you
$ flutter build appbundle --release --analyze-size
Running Gradle task...
app-release.aab  (18.2 MB)
  assets/                             1.1 MB
  lib/arm64-v8a/libapp.so              9.8 MB
  lib/arm64-v8a/libflutter.so          6.1 MB
  lib/armeabi-v7a/libapp.so            9.1 MB
  lib/armeabi-v7a/libflutter.so        5.4 MB
// ...libapp.so is YOUR compiled Dart. 9.8 MB for a typical app is high, and the
// causes are almost always: reflection-reachable code that tree shaking cannot
// remove, a large generated file, or a dependency pulling in a whole SDK.

// tree shaking, and the flag that governs it
// dart compile exe -O4 --no-source-maps
$ dart compile exe bin/app.dart -o app --extra-gen-snapshot=unused.json
// ...and inspect unused.json, which lists every declaration dart2js/AOT proved
// unreachable. It is the only direct evidence you get, and it is produced only
// when you ask for it.

// the three dependencies that defeat tree shaking
// - dart:mirrors: reflection makes every type potentially reachable
// - a large generated table: a const List of 50,000 records is code, and it is
//   in the binary whether or not the user needs it. Move it to an asset file.
// - registering a class by name in a string: 'MyWidget' by string is invisible
//   to the analyser, so its code and everything it reaches is retained
// ...the third is the one that surprises, because the string looks harmless.

// and the size decisions that are not about code
// images:  a 2000x2000 PNG is 400 KB and often 80 KB as WebP; a Flutter asset
//   image is decoded to a texture at full resolution, so the decoded size is
//   2000*2000*4 = 16 MB of GPU memory regardless of the file size
// fonts:   a family with four weights in two scripts is 2-4 MB; subset to the
//   characters you render
// audio:   an MP3 for a 3-second sound is larger than the code that plays it

13.5 Compiling for iOS

The most constrained target, and what it requires.

// iOS REQUIRES macOS. There is no cross-compilation to iOS from
// Linux or Windows: the SDK, the linker and the codesign tool only
// exist on macOS, and Apple's licence requires it.
//
// for a plain Dart app:
// 1. build the AOT snapshot for iOS
dart compile aot-snapshot bin/main.dart -o app.ios.aot \
  --target-os=ios --target-arch=arm64
// (iOS is arm64 only: no 32-bit, no x86 in the App Store)

// 2. add it to the Xcode project as a resource
// 3. build with xcodebuild
xcodebuild -workspace Runner.xcworkspace -scheme Runner \
  -configuration Release -sdk iphoneos \
  -archivePath build/Runner.xcarchive archive

// FLUTTER FOR iOS
flutter build ipa
flutter build ipa --release --build-number=42 --build-name=1.4.0
flutter build appbundle   # for the Play Store, from a Mac
flutter build ios --simulator   // for the simulator

// THE iOS CONSTRAINTS
// - arm64 only
// - bitcode is required for some App Store submissions
//   (Xcode 14+ removed the bitcode requirement)
// - all code must be signed, including any native library
// - the App Store rejects an app that is a repackaged website
//   (guideline 4.2 minimum functionality) - which is what a
//   Flutter app that is only a WebView would be

Compiling for iOS

iOS is the target where the build system is not optional and the constraints are not negotiable, and where the practical answer is to delegate everything to flutter build ipa or Xcode. What is worth understanding is the set of constraints that produced those rules, because each one has a consequence you will meet.

ConstraintRuleConsequence
Code signingEvery binary signed with a certificate from AppleNeeds an Apple account and a provisioning profile
Bitcode / architecturearm64 only; no 32-bitSimulator and device builds differ
FilesystemNo arbitrary paths; sandboxed containersPaths are getApplicationDocumentsDirectory and friends
Dynamic codeNo eval, no downloaded native codeA JIT cannot run; AOT is required, always
Store reviewAny API use is reviewedPrivate API use is a rejection

The constraint with the most reach is the ban on downloaded or generated native code, which is why the AOT snapshot is not an optimisation on iOS but a requirement, and why Flutter's release builds are AOT while its debug builds use a JIT over the VM service — a local debugging protocol, not downloaded code. For a pure Dart CLI that matters less, but for anything shipping to a device it is the reason dart run has no iOS story.

// the commands, in increasing order of ceremony
$ flutter run -d <simulator-id>            # debug on a simulator
$ flutter build ios --debug                # a debug build as an Xcode project
$ flutter build ios --release              # a release build
$ flutter build ipa --release              # an .ipa for distribution
$ flutter build appbundle --release        # an .aab for the App Store

// what each needs
// flutter run / build ios
//   - Xcode with the iOS SDK
//   - CocoaPods (installed via `pod install`, run automatically)
//   - a simulator for the device-less path
// flutter build ipa
//   + an Apple Developer account
//   + a signing certificate (.p12)
//   + a provisioning profile (.mobileprovision)
// ...and the certificate must be in your keychain. The common failure is
// "No signing certificate iOS Development found", which means pod install
// succeeded and signing did not.

// the two builds, and why they are not interchangeable
//   simulator:  x86_64 or arm64 on macOS silicon, runs on the Mac
//   device:     arm64, signed, runs on the phone
// ...`flutter build ios --simulator` produces something that cannot be
// installed on a phone, and the error message when you try is not helpful.

// the architecture detail that confuses everyone on Apple silicon
// An M-series Mac has arm64. iPhones have arm64. The simulator runs arm64
// binaries ON macOS, which works, but Xcode still supports x86_64 simulators
// for older tooling. So a build that "works on my M1" may be arm64-simulator
// and still fail on a CI runner that is Intel.

// signing, concretely
// 1. an Apple ID, enrolled in the developer program
// 2. a certificate:  Xcode > Manage Certificates > + Apple Development
//    or: openssl + a .csr submitted to Apple
// 3. a profile: an App ID (a reverse-DNS identifier) plus a device list
//    Automatic signing generates this; manual signing lets you pin it
// ...Automatic signing is right until you need a device UDID added, at which
// point the profile must be regenerated and the build re-signed.

// and the export step, which is a separate tool
$ xcodebuild -exportArchive -archive build/ios/archive/Runner.xcarchive     -exportOptionsPlist ExportOptions.plist -exportPath build/ipa
// ...ExportOptions.plist selects the method:
//   method: app-store-connect   (App Store, no ad-hoc)
//   method: ad-hoc              (a fixed list of devices)
//   method: development         (a development profile)
//   method: enterprise          (in-house distribution)

Two iOS-specific behaviours in Dart code are worth knowing because they produce bugs that only appear on that platform: the filesystem is a sandbox with no paths you choose, and the keyboard and text input have their own rules. The first is mostly handled by path_provider; the second is not, and is the reason a text field's behaviour differs from Android in ways a user notices.

// paths, which is the sandbox
import 'package:path_provider/path_provider.dart';

Future<Directory> writableDir() async {
  if (Platform.isIOS) {
    // ...Documents: backed up to iCloud, visible in Files.app if
    // UIFileSharingEnabled. Persistent, user-visible, backed up.
    return getApplicationDocumentsDirectory();
  }
  // Android's equivalent is getExternalStorageDirectory(), but note that on
  // Android 10+ that path is scoped storage and a hard failure for other apps.
  return getApplicationDocumentsDirectory();
}

// the three iOS directories that are NOT interchangeable
//   Documents        persists, backed up to iCloud, user-visible
//   Library          persists, backed up, NOT user-visible - use for caches you
//                    cannot lose and do not want backed up
//   tmp              may be purged by the system at any time
// ...and Caches is: may be purged, not backed up. Putting a database in
// Documents means it is backed up, which is right for user data and wrong for
// a cache, and putting a database in Caches means iOS can delete it.

// and the text input rules, which are the ones that look like bugs
// - the on-screen keyboard covers the bottom half of the screen, so a focused
//   field can be behind it. Use MediaQuery.viewInsetsOf(context).bottom
// - autocorrect and predictive text replace what the user typed; read
//   TextEditingController.text, not the raw key events
// - a numeric keyboard has no decimal separator on some locales, so parse
//   defensively
// - there is no "select all" gesture on a long-press; it is a double tap or a
//   three-finger gesture, which is why a custom select-all is worth having

Debugging on a device, and the release-only failures

iOS debugging is constrained in a way that has nothing to do with the language: you cannot attach an arbitrary debugger to a shipped app, and the debugging protocol that does exist is opt-in. That produces one class of failure that only ever happens in production — a crash on a device you do not own, with no symbol and no reproduction — and the defences for it are the same on every platform but more necessary here.

FailureOnly onWhy
Missing capability checkA specific modelA model without the hardware your code assumed
Memory ceilingOlder devicesiOS jetsam is stricter and non-obvious
Thermal throttlingProlonged loadCPU frequency drops; timing-sensitive code fails
Locale formattingA specific regionA locale where the separator is not a dot
Bitcode / arm64 onlyAll devicesA 32-bit assumption fails to launch
App Store reviewSubmissionPrivate API use is rejected

The memory ceiling is the one that produces the most reports and the least obvious symptoms, because iOS does not crash the app the way an out-of-memory condition does elsewhere: the system kills it, and the user sees it return to the home screen with no error dialog. The fix is to know the limit and to release memory under pressure rather than hoping. The signal arrives as a memory warning, and the correct response is to discard caches and drop references to anything reconstructible.

// the jetsam limit, and why it is not a number you can hard-code
// An app's memory ceiling is a FRACTION OF THE DEVICE'S, chosen by the system
// based on foreground state, memory pressure and what else is running. There
// is no API that returns it, and no documented constant.
// ...so the design rule is: hold less than the smallest device's comfortable
// share, and respond to pressure rather than predicting it.

// the correct response to a memory warning
import 'dart:async';

class Cache {
  final _entries = <String, Uint8List>{};
  final _maxBytes = 32 << 20;

  void add(String key, Uint8List value) {
    _entries[key] = value;
    _trim();
  }

  void handlePressure() {
    // ...discard everything reconstructible. This is the one safe action:
    // a decoded image, a parsed response, a computed index - all of it can be
    // produced again, and discarding costs latency rather than correctness.
    _entries.clear();
  }

  void _trim() {
    var total = _entries.values.fold<int>(0, (a, b) => a + b.length);
    while (total > _maxBytes && _entries.isNotEmpty) {
      final oldest = _entries.keys.first;
      total -= _entries.remove(oldest)!.length;
    }
  }
}

// subscribing to the warning - Flutter's WidgetsBindingObserver, or on a
// pure-Dart platform layer, a platform channel to UIApplication's
// didReceiveMemoryWarning notification
class MyApp extends StatefulWidget { ... }

class _MyAppState extends State<MyApp> with WidgetsBindingObserver {
  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    WidgetsBinding.instance.addObserver(this);
    cache.handlePressure.bindTo(this);   // your own wiring
  }

  @override
  void didHaveMemoryPressure() {
    cache.handlePressure();
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    WidgetsBinding.instance.removeObserver(this);
    super.dispose();
  }
}
// ...`addObserver` without a matching `removeObserver` is itself a leak: the
// binding holds the State, and the State holds the whole widget tree.

// the other release-only failure: the launch crash
// An app that is killed in the background and relaunched restores state. If
// that restoration path assumed a fresh start, the app crashes on resume -
// and only on resume, so it looks like a random crash to users.
// ...so every piece of cached state must be reconstructible, and a restore
// handler must tolerate it being absent, stale or the wrong shape.
//   - a saved scroll position for a list that has been refetched and is now
//     shorter: out of range
//   - a deep link to content the user's session no longer grants: 403
//   - a cached object decoded from an older schema: missing fields

Two platform behaviours are specific enough to cause real bugs and specific enough to test for. The keyboard is the first: iOS sizes its suggestion bar differently by keyboard type, so a form built in a simulator with the default keyboard can be hidden behind the real keyboard on a device. And the back gesture is the second — an interactive swipe from the left edge must be allowed to pop a route, and an app that intercepts horizontal drags breaks it in a way that only a device reveals.

// 1. the keyboard, and why the simulator lies
// WidgetsApp has a `resizeToAvoidBottomInset` flag, and it defaults to true,
// which is right. The problem is different: iOS's keyboard height varies by
// TYPE, so a numeric field's keyboard is shorter than a text field's.
// ...and a `TextFormField` with keyboardType: TextInputType.number does not
// show a decimal separator on some locales, so `double.parse(value)` throws
// on 3,14 in a locale that formats with a comma.

double parseDecimal(String input) {
  // ...normalise rather than assume
  final normalised = input
      .replaceAll(RegExp(r'[^0-9eE+\-.,]'), '')
      .replaceFirst(',', '.');      // ...first comma only: 1,234.56 -> 1.234.56
  return double.tryParse(normalised) ?? 0;
}
// ...and a locale-aware formatter for the other direction:
import 'package:intl/intl.dart';
final fmt = NumberFormat.decimalPattern(localeName);
// ...NumberFormat('en_US') gives 1,234.56 and NumberFormat('de_DE') gives
// 1.234,56, so building the display string and the parse in one place removes
// the class of bug entirely.

// 2. the interactive back gesture
// WidgetsApp handles it via a BackButtonDispatcher, and PopScope/WillPopScope
// are what an app overrides. The failure is an app that wraps the content in a
// horizontal-drag gesture recognizer:
//   HorizontalDragGestureRecognizer
// ...that wins the arena against the system's edge-swipe on the first few
// pixels of movement, so the swipe does nothing. Fix: do not claim the left
// edge; if a horizontal gesture is needed, exclude the edge region, or put the
// custom gesture on a child view that is not full-width.

// 3. and the two that are about signing rather than behaviour
//   "ApplicationVerificationFailed"  the profile's bundle id does not match
//                                    Info.plist's CFBundleIdentifier
//   "Application is not installed"    fine on the simulator, never on a
//                                    device - means the build was made for
//                                    the simulator SDK (arm64 vs x86_64)

13.6 The web: dart2js and dart2wasm

The two web targets, their trade-offs, and the constraints of the browser.

// DART2JS: Dart -> JavaScript -> browser
//   the default. broad support. slower, larger output.
dart compile js bin/main.dart -o app.js -O2 --minify

// DART2WASM: Dart -> WebAssembly
//   newer. faster, smaller, but requires a browser with WasmGC.
dart compile wasm bin/main.dart -o app.wasm -O2

// the optimisation levels
//   -O0  fastest to compile, largest, fastest to run
//   -O1
//   -O2  the default
//   -O3
//   -O4  slowest to compile, smallest and fastest
// use -O4 for production if you can wait for the build

// the output, for dart2js
//   app.js         the compiled code
//   app.js.map     the source map, for debugging
//   app.js.deps
//   app.js.symbols

// dart2wasm output
//   app.wasm       the module
//   app.mjs        the JS loader/reflector
//   app.wasm.map
// the sizes, roughly, for a medium application
//   dart2js -O2 minified:  ~600KB - 1.2MB
//   dart2wasm -O2:         ~300KB - 800KB
//   Flutter web:           ~1.5MB - 3MB (it includes CanvasKit)

// dart2js vs dart2wasm
//   dart2js:
//     + works in every browser
//     + no cross-origin isolation headers required
//     - the output is large, and it is interpreted by the JS engine
//
//   dart2wasm:
//     + smaller and faster, including startup
//     + no JavaScript compilation step
//     - needs WasmGC: Chrome 119+, Safari 18+, Firefox 120+
//     - needs COOP/COEP headers for best performance:
//       Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
//       Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp
//     - shared memory (threads) needs those headers too
//
// the practical advice: dart2js unless you have measured a problem

The web: dart2js and dart2wasm

Both web compilers produce the same three-part output: a JavaScript file that loads the runtime, a compiled artefact, and a source map. The two differ in what the artefact is and how it runs, and the difference is now large enough that the choice is not "wasm is new so avoid it".

Propertydart2jsdart2wasm
OutputJavaScriptWebAssembly + JS glue
RunsThe JS engine directlyIn the Wasm engine
StartupLower — one fewer fetch and compile stepHigher — the glue plus the module
Peak throughputGood, but behind a JS engine's own JITClose to native for typed code
Compilation timeFastNoticeably slower
InteropAny JS library, directlyJS through the glue; no direct DOM
Browser floorAny with ES5Modern: WasmGC required

The performance story is the interesting one. A JavaScript engine optimises JavaScript at runtime using type feedback, so dart2js output competes with hand-written JavaScript on equal terms — and loses slightly, because the DDC-generated code is more polymorphic than code a person wrote. WebAssembly has no such feedback, but it is compiled once, ahead of time, to machine code with proper types throughout, so a hot loop runs at a speed JavaScript's JIT can approach but not reliably exceed. The crossover is compute: below roughly 100 ms of work, startup dominates and dart2js wins; above it, throughput dominates and dart2wasm wins.

// both outputs, and the three files
$ dart compile js web/main.dart -o build/web/main.js
  build/web/main.js       1.8 MB   // your code + the runtime
  build/web/main.js.map   4.1 MB   // source map; never ship to production

$ dart compile wasm web/main.dart -o build/web/main.wasm
  build/web/main.wasm     2.6 MB   // the compiled module
  build/web/main.mjs      12 KB    // the loader/glue
  build/web/main.wasm.map 4.1 MB   // source map
// ...`.mjs` not `.js`: the glue is an ES module, so it cannot be served from
// a classic script tag. Your HTML must use type="module".

// the three things that dominate size, and only one is your code
// - the runtime:  ~1.1 MB minified for dart2js, ~350 KB for dart2wasm's core
// - tree shaking: dart2js removes unreachable code; dart2wasm removes less,
//   so an app that uses one small feature still ships most of dart:core
// - source maps: not counted in the load, but present in the artefact unless
//   you exclude them
// ...so a hello-world Dart web app is ~1.8 MB, which is larger than most
// hand-written JS bundles and much larger than a compiled language like
// Rust/Wasm. The argument for Dart on the web is team productivity, not
// payload size.

// the html, which differs between the two
<!-- dart2js -->
<script defer src="main.js"></script>

<!-- dart2wasm -->
<script type="module">
  import instantiate from './main.mjs';
  const { instance } = await instantiateStreaming(fetch('main.wasm'));
  // ...and the Dart entry point must be exported with @JSExport for it to be
  // callable from here
</script>

// and what the wasm target cannot do, stated plainly
// - no dart:html or dart:js_interop DOM access; everything crosses the glue
// - no dart:io, obviously
// - no synchronous XHR-style blocking of any kind
// - no dynamic `dart:mirrors`
// ...which in practice means a dart2wasm app is written with
// `package:web` + `dart:js_interop` for all DOM access, and that is a
// different code style from a dart2js app using dart:html.

Serving the output has one requirement that is easy to get wrong and produces a blank page with no console error: the MIME type. A .wasm file served as application/octet-stream cannot be compiled with instantiateStreaming, so the fetch succeeds and the compile step fails silently in some browsers. The other requirement is compression: .wasm compresses to roughly a quarter of its size with gzip and about a fifth with brotli, and shipping it uncompressed is the most common self-inflicted web performance problem in this stack.

// nginx, and the two lines that decide whether it works at all
location ~* \.wasm$ {
    types { } default application/wasm;   # NOT octet-stream
    gzip on;
    gzip_types application/wasm;         # and compress it
}
location ~* \.mjs$ {
    types { } default text/javascript;    # so the module loads
}
# ...`.wasm` must be brotli-encoded for `instantiateStreaming` to get the
# biggest win; with gzip only, use `await WebAssembly.compile(await r.arrayBuffer())`

// a robust loader that works either way, which is worth having in a library
Future<WebAssembly.Instance> loadWasm(String url) async {
  final res = await fetch(url);
  if (!res.ok) throw StateError('wasm fetch failed: ${res.status}');
  // ...try the streaming path, which lets the browser compile while downloading
  if (res.headers.get('content-type')?.contains('application/wasm') ?? false) {
    try {
      return await WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming(res, imports);
    } catch (_) {
      // ...falls through: some CDNs strip or rewrite the header
    }
  }
  // ...the fallback, which buffers the whole module
  final bytes = await res.arrayBuffer();
  final result = await WebAssembly.instantiate(bytes, imports);
  return result.instance;
}

// and the numbers that justify the compression requirement
// main.wasm          2,600,000 bytes raw
// with gzip          780,000     30%
// with brotli        520,000     20%
// ...against a 100 ms budget on a 4G connection, that is the difference
// between loading and not loading.

// the caching headers, which matter more than the compression
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
// ...with a content-hashed filename, which is what `dart compile wasm -o
// main.<hash>.wasm` or a bundler plugin gives you. Without the hash the
// immutable header is a bug: users keep a stale build for a year.

13.7 The web without dart:io

The API substitutions a web build forces on you.

// dart:io DOES NOT EXIST ON THE WEB. This is not a compatibility
// layer; the whole library is simply absent. Importing it is a
// COMPILE ERROR for the web target.

// the substitutions
//   dart:io                package:web (or dart:html, deprecated)
//   File read/write        the File System Access API, or IndexedDB
//   Directory              none: the browser has no directories
//   HttpClient             fetch(), or package:http
//   Socket / ServerSocket  WebSocket
//   Platform.isX           a conditional import, or navigator.userAgent
//   Random.secure()        crypto.getRandomValues
//   Process                none
//   stdout / stderr        console.log
//   Directory.systemTemp   in-memory, or a Blob URL
//
// the practical consequence: your data layer needs an interface
// with two implementations. Chapter 13.8 is that pattern.
// storage on the web: IndexedDB, via a small wrapper
import 'package:web/web.dart' as web;

class WebStorage {
  web.IDBDatabase? _db;
  final String _name = 'myapp';
  final int _version = 1;

  Future<void> open() async {
    _db = await web.IDBFactory.instance!.open(_name, _version, web.IDBOpenDBOptions(
      upgrade: (db, oldVersion, newVersion) {
        if (!db.objectStoreNames.contains('kv')) {
          db.createObjectStore('kv', web.IDBStringKeyPathOptions(keyPath: 'key'));
        }
      },
    ));
  }

  Future<Object?> get(String key) async {
    final db = _db!;
    final tx = db.transaction('kv', 'readonly');
    final store = tx.objectStore('kv');
    return (await store.get(key) as web.IDBRequest).result;
  }

  Future<void> put(String key, Object value) async {
    final db = _db!;
    final tx = db.transaction('kv', 'readwrite');
    await (tx.objectStore('kv') as web.IDBObjectStore)
        .put({'key': key, 'value': value});
  }
}

// or, if you only need key-value, use a package:
//   localstorage, js, or hive (which has a web backend)
// and for HTTP, package:http works identically on both platforms,
// which is the main reason to prefer it over dart:io's HttpClient

Running without dart:io

The constraint that defines web Dart is not dart:io being different — it is dart:io being absent, and the compile-time error that says so. A program that imports dart:io does not compile for the web at all, which means the browser build fails as a whole rather than at a call site. That design choice is what forces the shape of portable code, and understanding it explains every pattern below.

// the failure, which is a compile error and not a runtime one
// import 'dart:io';
// void main() { print(File('x').existsSync()); }
// $ dart compile js main.dart -o out.js
// Error: Dart library 'dart:io' is not available on this platform.
// ...the whole build fails. There is no way to stub it, no partial support,
// and no runtime flag. This is why the abstract-base-class pattern is not a
// stylistic preference: it is the only way one source tree can build for both.

// what IS available
// dart:core          yes
// dart:async         yes  (Streams, Futures, zones)
// dart:convert       yes  (json, utf8, base64)
// dart:collection    yes
// dart:math          yes
// dart:typed_data    yes  (Uint8List, ByteData)
// dart:developer     yes  (mostly)
// dart:html          DEPRECATED - use package:web
// dart:js, dart:js_util   legacy, for dart2js only
// dart:isolate       NO on the web - no threads in a browser
// dart:io            NO
// dart:ffi           NO
// dart:mirrors       NO
// dart:ffi / native  NO

// and the one that surprises: dart:isolate is unavailable, so
// Isolate.run - the answer to every CPU-bound problem in chapter 11 - does not
// work on the web. A Web Worker is the substitute, and it requires message
// passing with structured clone, so only simple values cross.

// the replacement for each dart:io capability
// file read/write   -> fetch() for reads, an <input> or XHR for uploads,
//                     IndexedDB or OPFS for persistence
// sockets           -> WebSocket, or fetch for request/response
// process           -> none. There is no subprocess on the web.
// environment       -> dart:js_interop for window, navigator, location
// paths             -> URLs, and package:path for the parts that still apply
// stdin/stdout      -> print() goes to the console; stdout has no equivalent
// Platform.isX     -> not needed; ask what the browser can do

The Web API is reached through package:web and dart:js_interop, both of which are null-safe and typed, and neither of which is the old dart:html. The pattern is a set of top-level extension getters and functions rather than document.querySelector chains, and the difference is that the types are real Dart types rather than dynamic. What that buys is that a typo in an element property is a compile error.

// package:web - typed, and that is the whole point
import 'package:web/web.dart' as web;

void main() {
  final root = web.document.querySelector('#root')!;
  final button = web.document.querySelector('button')! as web.HTMLButtonElement;
  button.textContent = 'Clicked';
  button.disabled = true;            // typed: this is real, not dynamic

  button.addEventListener('click', (web.Event e) {
    final input = web.document.querySelector('#name')! as web.HTMLInputElement;
    final name = input.value;         // typed: value, not getAttribute('value')
    print('hello $name');
  });

  // ...and the APIs Dart has no syntax for
  web.window.localStorage['theme'] = 'dark';
  web.window.history.replaceState(null, '', '/home');
  web.navigator.clipboard.writeText('copied');
  final canvas = web.document.querySelector('canvas')! as web.HTMLCanvasElement;
  final ctx = canvas.getContext('2d') as web.CanvasRenderingContext2D;
  ctx.fillRect(0, 0, 100, 100);
}
// ...without package:web every one of these is a dynamic call and every
// property name is unchecked.

// the older API, still in every tutorial
// import 'dart:html';
// document.querySelector('#root')!.innerHtml = 'x';
// ...`dart:html` is deprecated, is not null-safe, and returns dynamic
// everywhere. It is not removed, so old code compiles; do not write new code
// with it.

// and how it looks for a Flutter web app, which is the common case
// ...there is no `dart:html` at all. Flutter renders to a canvas and the
// browser surface is: `dart:ui_web`, the `kIsWeb` conditional, and platform
// channels to a small JS host. So the "web without dart:io" problem is mostly
// solved by a framework, and the platform-abstraction pattern below is what
// you write when you are not using one.

Testing web code has one genuine constraint and one common surprise. The constraint is that there are no threads, so anything you would have backgrounded is now serial with the UI, and a synchronous XHR is both deprecated and absent. The surprise is that package:test runs in a headless browser for web-targeted tests, which means the test runner needs a browser installed and the suite is meaningfully slower than on the VM — which is why the convention is to keep platform-specific tests small and put the bulk of the suite on the VM.

// the compile-time platform split, which is the point of the whole section
// lib/platform.dart
export 'platform_stub.dart'
    if (dart.library.js_interop) 'platform_web.dart'
    if (dart.library.io) 'platform_io.dart';
// ...read this right-to-left: `dart.library.js_interop` is true only when
// compiling for the web, and `dart.library.io` is true for the VM and AOT but
// NOT for the web. So the web build picks platform_web.dart and everything else
// picks platform_io.dart.

// each file declares the SAME abstract class
// lib/platform_stub.dart
abstract class Platform {
  String get name;
  Future<String> read(String path);
}
// ...and neither implementation imports the other's dart:io, because the web
// build would then fail to compile. That is the whole mechanism.

// the third condition worth knowing, for a Flutter app
export 'stub.dart'
    if (dart.library.io) 'mobile.dart'
    if (dart.library.js_interop) 'web.dart';
// ...Flutter web also defines dart.library.js_interop, so a mobile app with a
// web target needs this three-way split and nothing less.

// the test side
$ dart test                      # VM: fast, the bulk of the suite
$ dart test -p chrome            # headless Chrome: the DOM tests
$ dart test -p chrome -t 'web '   # a name prefix, so one suite is separable
// ...`dart test -p chrome` needs Chrome on PATH and downloads nothing. On CI,
// use an image with it, or `apt-get install -y chromium`.

// and the worker substitute for Isolate.run
import 'package:web/web.dart' as web;

Future<List<int>> computeInWorker(String url) async {
  final worker = web.Worker('worker.js');
  worker.postMessage(url);
  final result = await web.window.onMessage.first;
  worker.terminate();
  return result.data as List<int>;
}
// ...a real second thread, but only transferable data crosses: primitives,
// Lists, Maps, and ArrayBuffers with transfer. A Dart object with a method
// cannot. So the worker is a separate entry point, not an isolate.

What the compiler cannot help you with

The browser imposes three limits that no Dart construct addresses, and code that hits them fails in ways that look like Dart bugs: there is one thread, so Isolate.run does not exist and a synchronous operation blocks everything; the event loop is not yours, so a tight for loop starves it; and the main thread can be terminated without warning, so nothing in memory survives. Each has a standard answer, and all three involve moving work off the main thread or yielding to it.

// 1. no threads, so no isolates: the substitute is a Worker
import 'package:web/web.dart' as web;

/// Runs [fn] in a Worker. The function must be a top-level entry point and its
/// arguments must survive structured clone - so primitives, Lists, Maps, and
/// transferable ArrayBuffers. A closure capturing state cannot cross.
web.Worker spawnCompute(String functionName, Object message) {
  final worker = web.Worker(functionName);
  worker.postMessage(message);
  return worker;
}

Future<Object?> oneRoundTrip(web.Worker w) {
  final done = Completer<Object?>();
  w.onMessage.listen((e) => done.complete(e.data));
  w.onError.listen((e) => done.completeError(StateError('$e')));
  return done.future;
}
// ...and the worker side is a SEPARATE Dart program, not a class:
//   // compute.dart
//   import 'dart:js_interop';
//   @JSExport() external void initialise();
// ...with dart2js, `dart compile js compute.dart -o compute.js`. Each worker is
// another network fetch and another runtime instance, which is why one worker
// handling a queue beats four workers each handling a quarter.

// 2. the event loop is not yours
// THE defect this prevents: a synchronous loop that runs for 300 ms freezes
// the page, and the user sees a white screen and cannot even tap Cancel.
void processAll(List<Row> rows) {
  for (final r in rows) {          // ...100,000 rows: 400 ms of frozen UI
    handle(r);
  }
}

// the fix, and the rule: yield every N items, and make N small enough
Future<void> processAllYielding(List<Row> rows) async {
  var sinceYield = 0;
  for (final r in rows) {
    handle(r);
    if (++sinceYield >= 50) {
      sinceYield = 0;
      await Future<void>.delayed(Duration.zero);   // ...a macrotask, so
      //    the browser can paint, respond to input, and run timers
    }
  }
}

// a scheduler, which is the reusable form
class FrameBudget {
  final Duration _budget;
  DateTime _frameStart = DateTime.now();
  void reset() => _frameStart = DateTime.now();
  bool get expired =>
      DateTime.now().difference(_frameStart) > _budget;
}

// and the measurement that sets N
// DevTools > Performance, record a run, look at the longest frame.
// ...16.7 ms is one frame at 60 Hz. A script task longer than about 50 ms is
// visible as a dropped frame; over 200 ms is an unresponsive page. Yield every
// 50 items if each takes 1 ms; the number is measured, not guessed.

// 3. memory does not survive, so nothing may rely on it
// A tab can be discarded and restored, or discarded and not restored. On
// restore, your app starts again. So:
//   - persist anything the user would miss, on every meaningful change
//   - keep an unsubscribe path that works even if the page was frozen
//   - never assume a WebSocket survived: reconnect on load, and on every
//     visibilitychange, because a backgrounded tab's socket is closed
// ...the visibility rule, which is the one that is easy to get wrong:
web.document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', (web.Event _) {
  if (web.document.visibilityState == 'visible') reconnectEverything();
  else pausePolling();       // ...a background tab's timers are throttled to
                              //    once a minute, so a polling loop wastes
                              //    nothing but also achieves nothing
});

13.8 The platform abstraction pattern

The one pattern that makes a cross-platform codebase maintainable.

// the rule: ONE interface per capability, TWO implementations,
// and the choice made once at startup.

// 1. the interface, in lib/src/, with no platform imports
abstract class KeyValueStore {
  Future<String?> get(String key);
  Future<void> set(String key, String value);
  Future<void> remove(String key);
  Future<void> clear();
}

// 2. the native implementation
// lib/src/store_native.dart
import 'dart:io';
import 'store.dart';

class NativeStore implements KeyValueStore {
  final Map<String, String> _cache = {};

  @override
  Future<String?> get(String key) async {
    if (_cache.containsKey(key)) return _cache[key];
    final file = File('${Directory.systemTemp.path}/$key.json');
    if (!await file.exists()) return null;
    final text = await file.readAsString();
    return _cache[key] = jsonDecode(text) as String?;
  }

  @override
  Future<void> set(String key, String value) async {
    _cache[key] = value;
    final file = File('${Directory.systemTemp.path}/$key.json');
    await file.writeAsString(jsonEncode(value));
  }

  @override
  Future<void> remove(String key) async {
    _cache.remove(key);
    final file = File('${Directory.systemTemp.path}/$key.json');
    if (await file.exists()) await file.delete();
  }

  @override
  Future<void> clear() async {
    _cache.clear();
    final dir = Directory(Directory.systemTemp.path);
    for (final e in await dir.list()) {
      if (e is File && e.path.endsWith('.json')) await e.delete();
    }
  }
}
// 3. the web implementation
// lib/src/store_web.dart
import 'store.dart';
import 'package:web/web.dart' as web;

class WebStore implements KeyValueStore {
  // localStorage for small values; IndexedDB for large ones.
  // this implementation uses localStorage for simplicity.
  @override
  Future<String?> get(String key) async => web.window.localStorage.getItem(key);

  @override
  Future<void> set(String key, String value) async {
    web.window.localStorage.setItem(key, value);
  }

  @override
  Future<void> remove(String key) async {
    web.window.localStorage.removeItem(key);
  }

  @override
  Future<void> clear() async {
    web.window.localStorage.clear();
  }
}

// 4. the in-memory implementation, for tests: a third
// lib/src/store_memory.dart
class MemoryStore implements KeyValueStore {
  final Map<String, String> _data = {};
  @override
  Future<String?> get(String key) async => _data[key];
  @override
  Future<void> set(String key, String value) async => _data[key] = value;
  @override
  Future<void> remove(String key) async => _data.remove(key);
  @override
  Future<void> clear() async => _data.clear();
}
// 5. the factory, which is the only place that knows the platform
// lib/src/store_factory.dart
import 'store.dart';
import 'dart:io' show Platform;

KeyValueStore createStore() {
  if (Platform.isAndroid || Platform.isIOS || Platform.isLinux ||
      Platform.isMacOS || Platform.isWindows) {
    return NativeStore();
  }
  return WebStore();
}

// and a test store, for tests
KeyValueStore createTestStore() => MemoryStore();

The platform abstraction pattern

The pattern is: define an abstract interface in pure Dart, provide one implementation per platform, and select between them with a conditional import. It is the only mechanism Dart offers for this, and it has three properties that are worth stating because they determine whether it works. Selection happens at compile time. Each implementation file must be independently compilable. And nothing in the interface may mention a platform-specific type.

// the four files, and the rule each one obeys

// 1. lib/platform.dart - the selector. No implementation, no dart:io.
export 'platform_stub.dart'
    if (dart.library.js_interop) 'platform_web.dart'
    if (dart.library.io) 'platform_io.dart';

// 2. lib/platform_stub.dart - the interface. NO dart:io, ever: a web build
//    compiles this file too, and one import of dart:io fails the whole build.
import 'dart:async';

abstract class Platform {
  String get name;
  bool get isMobile;
  Future<String> readText(String path);
  Future<void> writeText(String path, String contents);
  Future<DirectoryInfo> stat(String path);
  Stream<String> readLines(String path);
}

class DirectoryInfo {
  final int size;
  final DateTime modified;
  const DirectoryInfo(this.size, this.modified);
}

// 3. lib/platform_io.dart - the VM/AOT implementation
import 'dart:io';
import 'platform_stub.dart' as api;

class IoPlatform implements api.Platform {
  @override
  String get name => Platform.operatingSystem;
  @override
  bool get isMobile => Platform.isAndroid || Platform.isIOS;

  @override
  Future<String> readText(String path) => File(path).readAsString();

  @override
  Future<void> writeText(String path, String c) =>
      File(path).writeAsString(c, flush: true);

  @override
  Future<api.DirectoryInfo> stat(String path) async {
    final s = await File(path).stat();
    return api.DirectoryInfo(s.size, s.modified);
  }

  @override
  Stream<String> readLines(String path) =>
      File(path).openRead().transform(utf8.decoder)
          .transform(const LineSplitter());
}

// 4. lib/platform_web.dart - the web implementation, using storage only
import 'package:web/web.dart' as web;
import 'platform_stub.dart' as api;

class WebPlatform implements api.Platform {
  final _store = web.window.localStorage;   // strings, ~5 MB, synchronous

  @override
  String get name => web.window.navigator.userAgent;
  @override
  bool get isMobile =>
      web.window.matchMedia('(pointer: coarse)').matches;

  @override
  Future<String> readText(String path) async =>
      _store[path] ?? '';

  @override
  Future<void> writeText(String path, String c) async =>
      _store[path] = c;

  @override
  Future<api.DirectoryInfo> stat(String path) async {
    final raw = _store[path];
    if (raw == null) throw StateError('no such entry: $path');
    return api.DirectoryInfo(raw.length * 2,
        DateTime.fromMillisecondsSinceEpoch(0));
  }

  @override
  Stream<String> readLines(String path) async* {
    final raw = _store[path];
    if (raw == null) throw StateError('no such entry: $path');
    for (final line in raw.split('\n')) yield line;
  }
}
// ...note what WebPlatform does NOT do: pretend to be a filesystem. It stores
// whole strings under string keys, which is the honest mapping. A caller that
// assumed `writeText` then `readLines` streamed would be surprised — and the
// fix belongs in the interface, which is what the next section is about.

The failure mode of this pattern is interface erosion, and it is worth naming because it happens gradually. Somebody needs one method that dart:io has and the web does not, and adds it to the interface. Then somebody else needs another. Each addition is reasonable in isolation and each narrows what the pattern can honestly express, until the interface has a method whose web implementation throws UnimplementedError — which is a lie at every call site, because the type says the capability exists.

// the erosion, and the three ways to stop it

// 1. Refuse platform types in the signature. This is the rule that does the
//    work: if the interface cannot mention File, Stream<List<int>>, or
//    int (a socket descriptor), then it cannot leak a platform capability.
//    ...Which is why every method above takes a String and returns String.

// 2. Make the interface a union of what ALL platforms can do, and put
//    platform-only things on a SEPARATE interface that only the native code
//    ever sees.
abstract class Platform {
  String get name;
  Future<String> readText(String path);
}

// ...and, in platform_io.dart only:
abstract class NativePlatform extends Platform {
  Future<int> openSocket(String host, int port);
  Future<Process> startProcess(String exe, List<String> args);
}
// ...callers that need a socket take a NativePlatform, which the web build
// simply cannot produce. The type system enforces the platform check.

// 3. Test the interface, not the implementation
abstract class PlatformContract {
  Platform create();
  // ...every test in a shared file, run against every implementation
}

void main() {
  group('platform contract', () {
    test('round-trips text', () async {
      final p = IoPlatform();
      await p.writeText('/tmp/contract.txt', 'a\nb');
      expect(await p.readText('/tmp/contract.txt'), 'a\nb');
    });

    test('absent path throws rather than returning empty', () async {
      // ...this is the assertion that catches an interface shaped around
      // whichever implementation was written first
      expect(() => IoPlatform().readText('/tmp/nope'), throwsA(anything));
    });
  });
}
// ...the second test is the one that would have caught the WebPlatform above
// returning '' for a missing key. An interface whose error semantics differ
// between implementations is a bug that only appears on one platform.

// and the cost of the pattern, stated so it is not adopted reflexively
// - an indirection on every call
// - one file per platform per concern
// - a capability that exists natively is unavailable until you model it
// - no runtime override: a test cannot substitute a fake by changing an
//   import, it must take a Platform parameter
// ...which is the right trade when the code genuinely must run on both, and
// the wrong one for a CLI tool that will never ship to a browser.

Choosing where the seam goes, and the four shapes it takes

The conditional-import pattern answers a narrow question — which implementation of one interface — and real code needs seams in four other places. Knowing which shape applies is most of the design, because three of the four do not use conditional imports at all, and picking the wrong one produces either a build failure or an untestable design.

SeamMechanismSelected
Compile-time capabilityConditional importBuild time
Runtime choice, injectedA parameterCall time
Runtime choice, globalA service locatorStartup
Build-time valuefromEnvironmentCompile time

The parameter is the right answer far more often than the conditional import, and the reason is testability: a seam that is a parameter can be passed a fake with no build step, no second source file and no CI matrix. Conditional imports are for capabilities that differ structurally — where the web has a genuinely different mechanism and no reasonable common denominator. "Which file system API" qualifies. "Which clock" does not, because both platforms have DateTime.now().

// the parameter seam, and why it is usually the right one
abstract class Clock {
  DateTime now();
}

class SystemClock implements Clock {
  @override
  DateTime now() => DateTime.now();
}

class FakeClock implements Clock {
  DateTime _now;
  FakeClock(this._now);
  @override
  DateTime now() => _now;
  void advance(Duration d) => _now = _now.add(d);
}

// ...and now the retry logic is testable with no build step and no CI matrix:
Future<T> retry<T>(Clock clock, Future<T> Function() op) async {
  for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    try {
      return await op();
    } catch (e) {
      await Future.delayed(Duration(milliseconds: 100 * (1 << i)));
    }
  }
  throw StateError('gave up at ${clock.now()}');
}

test('retries three times then succeeds', () async {
  final clock = FakeClock(DateTime(2026, 1, 1));
  var calls = 0;
  final r = await retry(clock, () async {
    if (++calls < 4) throw Exception('not yet');
    return 'ok';
  });
  expect(r, 'ok');
  expect(calls, 4);
});
// ...which is a test that runs in 400 ms on the VM. The conditional-import
// version of the same seam would need this test in a file that only compiles
// on one platform, run in a second CI job, with the other implementation
// untested.

// the seam for a VALUE, which needs no interface at all
const apiBase = String.fromEnvironment('API_BASE',
    defaultValue: 'https://staging.example.com');
const verbose = bool.fromEnvironment('VERBOSE');
// ...compile-time, tree-shakeable, and therefore free at runtime. The cost is
// that it cannot change without a rebuild, so it is wrong for anything a user
// can adjust and right for build identity: API endpoints, feature flags that
// must be consistent across a fleet, and version strings.

// the seam for a SERVICE, where a global registry is the pragmatic choice
class Services {
  static final _log = <LogSink>[];
  static LogSink get log => _log.isEmpty ? const ConsoleLogSink() : _log.first;
  static void install(LogSink s) => _log.insert(0, s);
  static void reset() => _log.clear();   // ...a test must be able to put
}                                         //    it back, or it leaks into the
                                          //    next test in the same process

// when a service locator is acceptable: a Flutter app, where the widget tree
// already IS a locator through InheritedWidget, and a CLI, where there is one
// composition root. Never in a library - a library takes its dependencies as
// constructor parameters, and a library with a static registry cannot be used
// twice in one process with different configurations.

/* the anti-pattern this section exists to prevent, from a real codebase:
   abstract class HttpClient {}
   // file: http_io.dart, imported everywhere, which means EVERY platform needs
   // dart:io to compile, so the web build fails on an import in a module that
   // has nothing to do with the web.
   ...the fix is that the interface belongs to the CALLER, not to the
   implementation module. The caller declares what it needs; the platform layer
   supplies it. */

13.9 Conditional imports

The mechanism that makes a single file contain both implementations.

// CONDITIONAL IMPORT: the compiler picks the file at build time.
// this is how a single import path gives a platform-specific
// implementation.

// lib/src/store.dart
export 'store_stub.dart'
    if (dart.library.io) 'store_io.dart'
    if (dart.library.js_interop) 'store_web.dart';

// read it backwards: "use store_stub, EXCEPT if dart:io is
// available, in which case use store_io; and if JS interop is
// available, use store_web."

// then anyone just imports 'store.dart' and gets the right one
import 'store.dart';
final store = createStore();

// each of the three files exports the same symbols
// store_stub.dart - throws, for platforms you did not plan for
import 'store_interface.dart';
Store createStore() => throw UnsupportedError('no store for this platform');

// store_io.dart - the native version
// store_web.dart - the web version

// WHY THIS IS BETTER THAN A RUNTIME CHECK
//   a runtime check means dart:io is compiled in, and it is not
//   available on the web at all, so it does not compile
//   a conditional import removes the unreachable file entirely
// the same thing for a whole library
// lib/my_app.dart
export 'src/app_stub.dart'
    if (dart.library.io) 'src/app_native.dart'
    if (dart.library.js_interop) 'src/app_web.dart';

// and the conditions you can test
//   dart.library.io          dart:io is available
//   dart.library.js_interop package:js / package:web is available
//   dart.library.html       the old dart:html (deprecated)
//   dart.library.js         the old dart:js (deprecated)
//
// the STUB matters: it is what a platform you did not anticipate
// gets, and it should fail loudly rather than silently misbehave.

// the common mistake
// lib/foo.dart
import 'dart:io';   // <- this makes foo.dart native-only,
//                      even with a conditional export below
// the fix: no dart:io anywhere in the shared file

Conditional imports in full

The selector syntax has more conditions than most code uses, and each covers a case that comes up. The general form is a default export followed by zero or more if clauses, and the conditions are evaluated in order with the first match winning — so the most specific must come first, and a broad condition placed early silently shadows a narrow one after it.

// the general form
export 'src/stub.dart'
    if (dart.library.io) 'src/impl_io.dart'
    if (dart.library.js_interop) 'src/impl_web.dart'
    if (dart.library.nativewrappers) 'src/impl_native.dart';

// the conditions the SDK defines
// dart.library.io              true on the VM and in AOT; FALSE on the web
// dart.library.js_interop      true when compiling to JS or Wasm
// dart.library.js_util         the legacy dart:js_util
// dart.library.html            the legacy dart:html
// dart.library.nativewrappers  true in native AOT builds (FFI available)
// dart.library.ffi             FFI is available at runtime
// dart.library.async           always true on every platform
// dart.library.collection      always true
// dart.library.mirrors         true on the VM, FALSE on web and on AOT
// dart.library.isolate         true on the VM, FALSE on the web

// what each combination selects
//            io    js_interop  nativewrappers  ->  impl_io.dart (first match)
//   web      no    yes         no              ->  impl_web.dart
//   native   yes   no          yes             ->  impl_io.dart (same file)

// the ordering trap, which is silent
export 'stub.dart'
    if (dart.library.io) 'generic.dart'        // ...matches the VM
    if (dart.library.js_interop) 'web.dart';   // ...NEVER reached on the VM,
//                                                  and on the web the first
//                                                  condition is false, so
//                                                  this DOES match - which is
//                                                  correct but only by luck
// ...and this version is genuinely broken:
// export 'stub.dart'
//     if (dart.library.async) 'everything.dart';   // async is ALWAYS true
// ...so `everything.dart` is selected on every platform and the two conditions
// below it are dead. Nothing warns. The whole file wins, and the stub is
// unreachable, so a build that should have used the web implementation uses a
// dart:io one and fails.

// and the import-if form, which is for TYPES not values
import 'dart:io'
    if (dart.library.js_interop) 'dart:io' as io;
// ...rarely needed. `export ... if` is the form you want, because the
// implementations are libraries, not single symbols.

// and the two things the selector does NOT do
// 1. It is not runtime. There is no `if (isWeb)` at runtime that picks a file -
//    the selection happened at compile time and both alternatives may not even
//    be in the build.
// 2. It does not tree-shake the unused implementations out of a JS build by
//    itself. dart2js does, but only for code it can prove unreachable, and a
//    conditional export is one of the cases it handles.

Testing code that uses conditional imports needs one specific arrangement, because the selection is fixed at compile time and a single test file can only ever exercise one branch. The standard solution is a test per target, and it is a real cost that should be budgeted for: the interface needs tests, and each implementation needs its own file.

// test/platform_io_test.dart
import 'package:myapp/platform_io.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  // ...tests the implementation directly, so dart:io is fine here
  test('reads a file it wrote', () async {
    final p = IoPlatform();
    await p.writeText('/tmp/t.txt', 'hello');
    expect(await p.readText('/tmp/t.txt'), 'hello');
  });
}

// test/platform_web_test.dart
@TestOn('browser')
library;

import 'package:myapp/platform_web.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  // ...@TestOn('browser') means this file only runs under `dart test -p chrome`.
  // Without it, `dart test` tries to compile it on the VM, where
  // platform_web.dart's package:web import still works but
  // window.localStorage does not exist, and it fails at runtime.
  test('round-trips through localStorage', () async {
    final p = WebPlatform();
    await p.writeText('k', 'v');
    expect(await p.readText('k'), 'v');
  });
}

// and the shared contract tests, which is the valuable part
// test/platform_contract_test.dart
// ...run this against EACH implementation, from each implementation's own test
// file, so the interface's promises are verified on both platforms:
Future<void> runContract(api.Platform p) async {
  test('name is non-empty', () => expect(p.name, isNotEmpty));
  test('round-trips text', () async {
    await p.writeText('contract', 'a\nb');
    expect(await p.readText('contract'), 'a\nb');
  });
  test('reads lines in order', () async {
    await p.writeText('lines', 'a\nb\nc');
    expect(await p.readLines('lines').toList(), ['a', 'b', 'c']);
  });
  test('missing path throws', () async {
    expect(p.readText('no-such-key'), throwsA(isA<Exception>()));
  });
}

// the CI matrix, which is the cost made explicit
//   $ dart test                    # VM:  the io tests
//   $ dart test -p chrome          # web: the web tests
// ...two commands in CI. Not one. The failure mode when only the first runs is
// a web build that compiles and then throws UnimplementedError at the first
// platform call, discovered by a user.

// and the third target, which is easy to forget
//   $ flutter test                  # Flutter's own runner, if the app is one
// ...`flutter test` uses a different runner than `dart test`, so a pure-Dart
// package tested with flutter test is being tested by a tool built for another
// framework. Use `dart test` for the package and `flutter test` for the app.

How the conditional import actually resolves, and the debugging

When a conditional import does not do what you expect, the useful move is to ask the compiler which file it chose. Three separate mechanisms report that, and between them they answer every version of the question — which file was selected, why, and whether the other one is even in the output.

// 1. does the selector itself resolve? `dart analyze` on the selector file
$ dart analyze lib/platform.dart
  info - Unnecessary import: 'src/platform_stub.dart' - lib/platform.dart:1:8
// ...this message appears when BOTH the default and a condition resolve to the
// same file, which is a configuration mistake worth knowing about.

// 2. what does the condition evaluate to, on this target?
// The condition is a compile-time const, so the cheapest probe is to assert it
// where the decision is made:
const bool _isWeb = identical(0, 0.0) && !_hasDartIo();  // no

// ...the honest way, which is to print it from each target's own build:
lib/platform.dart
  export 'src/platform_stub.dart'
      if (dart.library.js_interop) 'src/platform_web.dart'
      if (dart.library.io) 'src/platform_io.dart';

lib/platform_debug.dart (added temporarily, never shipped)
  import 'platform.dart';
  void platformProbe() {
    print('io=${_constOf("dart.library.io")} '
          'js=${_constOf("dart.library.js_interop")} '
          'native=${_constOf("dart.library.nativewrappers")}');
  }
const bool _constOf(String name) {
  switch (name) {
    case 'dart.library.io': return bool.fromEnvironment('dart.library.io');
    // ...and so on - the environment constants are readable, which is what
    // makes this possible
    default: return false;
  }
}
// ...and $ dart compile js lib/main_probe.dart, then run it in a browser with
// the console open. This is slow but it is definitive.

// 3. is the unused implementation still in the OUTPUT? (the size question)
$ dart compile js main.dart -o out.js --extra-gen-snapshot=unused.json
$ python -c "import json;d=json.load(open('unused.json'));print(len(d['unusedElements']))"
// ...a large number means tree shaking did not reach the platform code. Two
// common reasons: dart:mirrors anywhere in the dependency graph, or a class
// referenced by a string rather than by a symbol.

// 4. the failure modes and what each one looks like
// "Dart library 'dart:io' is not available on this platform"
//   ...an import of dart:io somewhere the web build compiles. The message names
//   the FILE, and the fix is to move that code behind a conditional import or
//   to stop importing it.
// "Error: Dart library 'dart:ui' is not available on this platform"
//   ...a Flutter import reached pure Dart. The fix is never to conditionalise
//   it: Flutter code does not belong in a package that also targets the web.
// "UnimplementedError" at runtime
//   ...the web implementation's method throws. The interface was eroded, or the
//   feature is genuinely unavailable. Chapter 12.8's contract tests catch it.
// a page that works locally and fails on a server
//   ...not the selector: it is the MIME type or a caching header. Check the
//   network panel, not the Dart build.

Two structural mistakes are worth naming because they pass every check and still ship wrong code. The first is putting the conditional import in the wrong direction: exporting from a file that itself imports dart:io defeats the purpose, because the web build compiles the selector's imports too. The second is a conditional import inside a package that is not compiled for the web at all, which means both conditions are dead and the file is noise.

// mistake 1: the selector imports something platform-specific
// WRONG - lib/platform.dart
import 'dart:io';                       // ...this makes the WEB BUILD FAIL,
                                         //     because the selector is compiled
                                         //     for every target
export 'platform_io.dart' if (dart.library.js_interop) 'platform_web.dart';

// RIGHT - lib/platform.dart
export 'platform_stub.dart'
    if (dart.library.js_interop) 'platform_web.dart'
    if (dart.library.io) 'platform_io.dart';
// ...the selector contains nothing but export directives. That is the whole
// rule, and it is the rule most often broken by adding one convenient import.

// mistake 2: a conditional import that never fires
// package:my_server is a server-only package. It has:
//   import 'storage_io.dart' if (dart.library.js_interop) 'storage_web.dart';
// ...`dart.library.js_interop` is never true for it, `dart.library.io` is always
// true, and `storage_web.dart` is dead code that will rot without anyone
// noticing. Detect it:
//   $ dart compile js bin/main.dart -o /dev/null
// ...if it succeeds for a server package, the conditional import is pointless.

// and the pattern for a package that IS cross-platform, which needs the
// dependency declared honestly so a web-only consumer does not pull dart:io
// name: my_cross_platform
// dependencies:
//   path: ^1.9.0
//   http: ^1.2.0
// dev_dependencies:
//   test: ^1.25.0
// ...a package with NO dart:io dependency in pubspec.yaml that imports dart:io
// transitively through one of its dependencies cannot build for the web, and
// the failure names the dependency, not your file. Check with:
//   $ dart pub deps --style=compact | grep -i io
// ...or, better, build the web target in CI even for a package you believe is
// native-only. It costs one job and catches this permanently.

13.10 Shipping checklist per platform

What to verify before each target, and the checks people skip.

// COMMON, for every target
dart analyze                       // zero errors, zero warnings
dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed .
dart test
dart pub publish --dry-run         // if it is a package
// verify the example still builds
cd example && dart pub get && dart run
// NATIVE EXECUTABLE
dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o app
./app
// check: does it run on a MACHINE WITHOUT the Dart SDK? (it should)
// check: does it run on an older distro? (glibc)
// check: what is the binary size? (a Dart hello world is ~6MB)
// check: does it handle a SIGINT cleanly?

// ANDROID
flutter build appbundle --release
// or, for a plain Dart app, per-ABI AOT snapshots
// check: the ABI split, so you are not shipping 4 architectures
// check: R8 did not strip something reflection needs
// check: the INTERNET permission is declared
// check: run on a physical device, not just an emulator

// iOS  (macOS only)
flutter build ipa --release
// check: arm64 only
