// check: signing is configured, and the team is right
// check: the Info.plist usage descriptions
// check: TestFlight first, always

// WEB
dart compile js bin/main.dart -o build/app.js -O4
// check: the output is served over http, not file://
//   (module scripts and fetch do not work from file://)
// check: no dart:io anywhere: the compile would fail, so this is free
// check: gzip or brotli is on
// check: the wasm MIME type if using dart2wasm:
//   application/wasm
// check: COOP/COEP headers if using threads
// a script that checks all of it
// tool/verify.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

echo "== analyse =="
dart analyze

echo "== format =="
dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed .

echo "== test =="
dart test

echo "== native =="
dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o build/app
./build/app --version

echo "== web (js) =="
dart compile js bin/main.dart -o build/app.js -O4

echo "== web (wasm) =="
dart compile wasm bin/main.dart -o build/app.wasm -O4

if command -v flutter > /dev/null; then
  echo "== android =="
  flutter build appbundle --release
  echo "== linux desktop =="
  flutter build linux --release
  echo "== windows =="
  flutter build windows --release
fi

if [[ "$(uname)" == "Darwin" ]]; then
  echo "== macos =="
  flutter build macos --release
  echo "== ios =="
  flutter build ipa --release --no-codesign   # signing is done in CI
fi

echo "all targets built"

The most common release-only surprise is a code path that only runs in AOT or only on the web. Both runtimes enforce things the JIT does not: no mirrors, different constant evaluation, and a completely absent standard library on the web. Building every target in CI, on every push, is the only reliable defence - and it is cheap.

Exercises 14

  1. Build the same program as an executable, an AOT snapshot, JavaScript and WebAssembly. Record the size of each.
  2. Add a dart:mirrors import, run it in dart run, then compile it. Read the exact failure.
  3. Cross-compile a program from your machine to two other OSes, and try to run one of them.
  4. Write the KeyValueStore interface with native, web and memory implementations, plus the conditional export.
  5. Compile to the web and confirm that importing dart:io is a compile error, not a runtime one.
  6. Build a Flutter release bundle for Android and note the per-ABI size difference against a universal APK.
  7. Write the verify.sh script and add it to CI so every target is built on every push.

Shipping: the artefact, the metadata, and the crash reports

Every target's build produces one thing that runs, and several things that only matter after it does. The three that are routinely forgotten are the source map or symbol map, the version identifier inside the artefact, and the crash-reporting hook. Each of them is cheap to add and impossible to add retroactively to a binary that is already in production.

// 1. version, so a crash report says which build it came from
// put it in the artefact at compile time, not at runtime
const kVersion = String.fromEnvironment('APP_VERSION', defaultValue: 'dev');
const kCommit = String.fromEnvironment('GIT_COMMIT', defaultValue: 'unknown');
const kBuilt = String.fromEnvironment('BUILD_TIME', defaultValue: 'unknown');

// $ dart compile exe bin/cli.dart -o build/cli //     -DAPP_VERSION=$(git describe --tags) //     -DGIT_COMMIT=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) //     -DBUILD_TIME=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)

void main() {
  if (kVersion == 'dev') {
    stderr.writeln('WARNING: development build');
  }
  print('myapp $kVersion ($kCommit, built $kBuilt)');
  run();
}
// ...this is better than a file next to the binary, because the binary is the
// thing that crashes and the file beside it is the thing that is missing.
// Embedding it means one artefact to deploy and no drift between them.

// 2. symbols, and they must be archived with the build, not later
$ dart compile exe bin/server.dart -o server     --save-debugging-info=build/server.symbols
// ...the symbol file is what turns a stack trace from a minified or stripped
// build back into file names and lines. Keeping it in version control alongside
// a release tag is the difference between debugging a production crash in
// minutes and not at all.
$ dart symbolizer dump app.dill > app.symbols   # Flutter: the same need

// 3. the crash report, and what it must contain to be actionable
// - the version string above, always
// - a platform, an OS version, and an architecture
// - the operation being performed, NOT a stack trace as the primary payload -
//   "failed to load config for tenant 4f2a" beats a stack trace
// - a redacted account or tenant identifier, so the report is actionable
//   without carrying personal data
// ...what must NOT be in it: a token, a password, a file path containing a
// username, or the body of a request that carries any of those.

// 4. the build must be reproducible enough to bisect
// ...a non-reproducible build means "works on my machine" and a crash that
// cannot be bisected. Minimum: record the SDK version, the dependency lockfile
// hash, and the compile flags in the release.

// and the manifest of artefacts, which is the thing teams forget to write down
//   release 2026.10.02
//     app        1.2.3+47    sha256:...   symbols: server.symbols
//     wasm       1.2.3       sha256:...   sourcemap: main.wasm.map
//     ipa        1.2.3 (47)  build: 2026-10-02T09:14Z
//     abi       linux/arm64  base: ubuntu:22.04

Deployment differs enough between the targets to be worth stating as a table, because the failure of each has a distinctive shape. A Dart AOT binary is a static artefact with no runtime to install, which makes it the easiest to deploy and the easiest to get the platform wrong. A Flutter app goes through a store, which introduces a review delay and a version-number convention that is separate from your semantic version. A web bundle is files behind a CDN, where the only real problem is caching.

TargetDeploy asThe failure that is specific to it
Server binaryOne file + libcBuilt on the wrong libc or CPU baseline
ContainerDocker imageMulti-arch manifest missing an arm64 layer
Web (js)Two files + headersStale cache from an unhashed filename
Web (wasm)Three files + MIMEWrong MIME type: blank page, no error
AndroidAAB via PlayA minSdk above the device's; app will not install
iOSIPA via App StoreA profile missing the device UDID
DesktopSigned installerGatekeeper quarantine: the app will not open
// server: the libc trap, in full
$ ldd ./server
    linux-vdso.so.1
    libpthread.so.0 => /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libpthread.so.0
    libc.so.6 => /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6    (GLIBC 2.34)
$ ssh prod 'ldd --version | head -1'
    ldd (Debian GLIBC) 2.31
// ...built on 22.04, deployed on Debian 11: works on your machine, fails at
// startup on the server with
//   ./server: /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6: version `GLIBC_2.34' not found
// ...which is not a Dart problem and is the single most common deployment
// failure for a compiled Dart service. Fix it with the base image, not with
// the binary.

// container: the multi-arch manifest, and how to check it
$ docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t myapp:1.2.3     --push .
$ docker buildx imagetools inspect myapp:1.2.3 | grep Architecture
    Architecture: amd64
    Architecture: arm64
// ...and the cluster must be pulling by digest for the manifest to be used;
// a tag pinned to one platform silently serves that one platform.

// web: the cache header paired with a hash, and what breaks each half
$ ...    main.4f2a91c3.js         # content hash in the filename
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
$ ...    index.html              # never cached
Cache-Control: no-cache
// ...the pairing is the invariant: immutable is only safe because the content
// changes when the URL changes. Put the hash in neither and users run a
// one-year-old build. Put it in one and not the other and the fix never
// reaches anyone.

// desktop (macOS): the quarantine attribute
$ codesign --force --deep --sign - dist/MyApp.app
$ xattr -r -d com.apple.quarantine dist/MyApp.app
// ...an unsigned or ad-hoc-signed app downloaded by a user gets quarantined by
// Gatekeeper and refused to open. For distribution you need a Developer ID
// signature and notarisation:
// $ zip -r MyApp.zip dist/MyApp.app
// $ xcrun notarytool submit MyApp.zip --apple-id ... --team-id ...
// $ xcrun stapler staple dist/MyApp.app
// ...`stapler` is the step that makes it work offline; without the ticket
// attached, the app needs network access on first launch to verify.

// and the one that applies to every target: an artefact you cannot rebuild
// $ sha256sum server > server.sha256
// ...record it, and verify it on the target before starting the service. A
// truncated upload produces a binary that segfaults on the first request
// rather than failing to start, which is a much harder report.

14 · Testing

14.1 The test package and the anatomy of a test14.2 The matcher vocabulary14.3 Unit tests that are worth writing14.4 Testing async code14.5 Fakes, mocks and stubs14.6 Testing code that touches the filesystem and network14.7 Golden and integration tests14.8 Coverage, and what it does not tell you14.9 Test organisation and CI

Dart has an excellent test package. This chapter is about writing tests that catch real bugs rather than raising coverage.

14.1 The test package and the anatomy of a test

The structure, the file layout, and the commands.

// test/
//   entry_test.dart          unit tests
//   data/
//     repo_test.dart         tests next to the source, mirrored
//   platform/
//     store_io_test.dart     with @TestOn('vm')
//   golden/
//     render_test.dart
// test_driver/               integration tests: the whole app
// integration_test/          Flutter integration tests

import 'package:test/test.dart';
import 'package:my_package/my_package.dart';

void main() {
  // a group is a describe: it scopes and names related tests
  group('Entry', () {
    late Entry entry;

    setUp(() {
      entry = Entry(id: '1', title: 'Test', createdAt: DateTime(2026));
    });

    tearDown(() {
      // clean up per test
    });

    setUpAll(() async {
      // expensive, once for the whole group
      await Database.open();
    });

    tearDownAll(() async {
      await Database.close();
    });

    test('has the title it was created with', () {
      expect(entry.title, 'Test');
    });

    test('can be copied with a new title', () {
      final copy = entry.copyWith(title: 'Changed');
      expect(copy.title, 'Changed');
      expect(entry.title, 'Test');   // the original is untouched
    });

    test('throws on an empty id', () {
      expect(
        () => Entry(id: '', title: 'x'),
        throwsA(isA<ArgumentError>()),
      );
    });
  });

  test('a top-level test', () {
    expect(1 + 1, 2);
  });
}
// the commands
dart test                       run everything
dart test test/entry_test.dart  one file
dart test --name "copied"       tests matching a name
dart test --platform vm         only the VM (skip the browser)
dart test --platform chrome     run in a real browser
dart test -c vm -r expanded     more output
dart test --coverage            produce coverage/lcov.info
dart test --chain-stack-traces  a full stack trace, for debugging
dart test --run-skipped         run the skipped ones too

// in CI, with a coverage threshold
dart test --coverage=./coverage
dart run tool/check_coverage.dart  // fail under 80%

package:test, and what a test file actually is

A test file is a normal Dart program with one required convention: main may take a TestWidgetsFlutterBinding parameter, and everything else is ordinary code. The package discovers files matching a pattern, loads each one, calls main, and collects the test and group calls made during it. Understanding that model explains most of the framework's behaviour, including the two that surprise people: tests do not run in declaration order across groups, and a test body that never completes fails with a timeout rather than hanging.

// the smallest complete test file
import 'package:test/test.dart';
import 'package:myapp/add.dart';

void main() {
  test('adds two numbers', () {
    expect(add(2, 3), 5);
  });
}
// ...`dart test test/add_test.dart` runs it. There is no registration step,
// no runner class, no annotation: `test()` registers, `expect()` asserts.

// the three files a project needs
// test/add_test.dart          unit: fast, no I/O, no Flutter
// test/widget_test.dart       widget: needs TestWidgetsFlutterBinding
// integration_test/app_test.dart  on a device or emulator
// ...and the discovery pattern is `test/**_test.dart` by default, so a file
// named `test/helpers.dart` is NOT run and is correct for shared setup.

// groups, nesting, and the one behaviour that surprises everyone
void main() {
  group('Parser', () {
    setUp(() => parser = Parser());        // ...runs before EACH test
    setUpAll(() => fixture = loadLargeFixture());  // ...runs ONCE
    tearDown(() => parser.close());
    tearDownAll(() => fixture.dispose());

    group('numbers', () {
      test('parses an integer', () { ... });     // ...this runs before
      test('parses a negative', () { ... });     //    this one
    });
  });
}
// ...but tests in DIFFERENT groups may interleave, because each file is a
// separate isolate and within a file the runner is free to reorder. If test A
// mutates global state and test B reads it, you have a flaky test - and the
// fix is to remove the global, not to add an order annotation. There isn't one.

// naming, and why the convention matters
test('Parser.parse throws a FormatException for a missing exponent', () {
  expect(() => Parser().parse('1e'), throwsA(isA<FormatException>()));
});
// ...subject, method, expected behaviour, in that order. A failing test's name
// is the first thing anyone reads, and a name that only says what the code
// does rather than what should happen makes a failure report useless. In a
// project with thousands of tests this is the difference between a triage
// session and a rewrite.

// timeouts, and why the default exists
Future<void> slow() async {
  await Future.delayed(const Duration(seconds: 30));
}
test('completes eventually', () async {
  await slow().timeout(const Duration(seconds: 1));
});
// ...every async test has a 30-second default timeout, and hitting it is a
// FAILURE with a stack trace, not a hang. That is deliberate: a hung test is
// worse than a failing one because it blocks the suite. Override it per test
// or globally:
//   dart test --timeout=60s --concurrency=4

// and the tags that organise a large suite
@Tags(['db', 'slow'])
library;

void main() {
  test('queries the real database', () { ... });
}
// $ dart test --exclude-tags=slow      # the fast loop
// $ dart test -t db                   # one area
// $ dart test --run-skipped           # tests marked skip: with a reason
// ...a skip with a reason is a decision; a skip without one is a lie to the
// next person reading the file.

Three configuration options change the whole suite's behaviour and are worth setting deliberately in a CI config rather than leaving at defaults: concurrency, the reporter, and the randomisation seed. Concurrency defaults to half the CPU count, which on a shared CI runner is often too high and produces timeouts from tests that contend for a port or a file. Randomisation is off by default and is the strongest available defence against inter-test dependencies, because a suite that passes in random order has no hidden order dependencies.

// dart_test.yaml - the file that makes the suite deterministic
dart_test:
  # 1. enough concurrency to be fast, few enough to avoid contention
  #    A CI runner often has 2 vCPU. 8 concurrent test isolates on 2 vCPU makes
  #    everything slower and causes spurious timeouts.
  concurrency: 4

  # 2. randomise, and print the seed. A failing test's output then carries
  #    the exact seed needed to reproduce that specific ordering.
  test_randomize_ordering: true

  # 3. the reporter
  reporter: expanded        # a line per test; for CI logs
  # reporter: compact       # a progress spinner; for a terminal
  # reporter: expanded-on-failure
  # reporters:
  #   - github             # creates check annotations
  #   - json:reports/test.json   # machine-readable

  # 4. tags, so a developer and a CI job can run different subsets
  tags:
    unit:
      timeout: 30s
    io:
      timeout: 120s          # ...real file and network work needs more
    flake:
      # ...a test tagged `flake` is retried; the list is the honest record of
      # what is currently unreliable
      timeout: 60s

  # 5. exclusions that are per-environment, not per-file
  exclude_tags: browser     # ...so `dart test` on the VM skips browser tests

  # 6. never hide the output of a failing test
  print_on_failure: true

# and running it
$ dart test                          # everything except browser-tagged
$ dart test --exclude-tags=io,flake # the fast loop a developer runs
$ dart test -t golden -p chrome      # golden tests need a browser
$ dart test --test-randomize-ordering-seed=41713   # reproduce one failure
// ...that last flag is why the seed must be printed. Without it, "it failed
// once in a thousand runs" is unreproducible and therefore unfixable.

// and a per-file override, which is legitimate for one genuinely slow test
@Timeout(Duration(minutes: 2))
library;

// ...used sparingly. A test annotated to a long timeout is usually a test that
// should be split or a suite that should not be in the unit tier.

The shape of a suite that stays fast

A suite's cost is dominated by three things, and only two of them are the tests: how many of them there are, how much shared setup each one pays, and how long each one takes. The second is the one that surprises people, because a setUpAll that loads a fixture once is free at ten tests and ruinous at ten thousand — and it is paid in full whenever a tag filter selects a single test from the group.

CostScales withTypical mistake
Compile + loadNumber of filesOne file per test
Setup per testTests per fileA real socket or database per test
Setup per fileFiles selectedHeavy setUpAll behind a tag
ExecutionTests and their workA real 30 s timeout
ReportingFailuresA full stack trace per assertion

The practical consequence is a rule about where shared setup lives. setUpAll belongs in the file whose tests all need it and nowhere else; a fixture that ten files need belongs in a helper that each file loads, and the cost then scales with the files a given run selects rather than with the suite. The distinction is invisible until somebody runs dart test -t slow and waits four minutes for one test.

// the wrong shape: a tag-filtered run pays for everything
test/db_test.dart
  setUpAll(() => spinUpPostgres());       // ...40 seconds
  setUpAll(() => loadMillionRowFixture()); // ...90 seconds
  test('queries the index', ...);
  test('...', ...);                          // ...180 tests
// $ dart test -t db                 # selects 3 tests
// $ dart test -t db                 # ...still 130 seconds of setup

// the right shape: the fixture lives where it is used, and the expensive
// shared thing is started by the CI job, not by the test process
test/db_test.dart
  setUp(() => truncateTables());            // ...cheap, per test
  test('queries the index', ...);
// test/db_support.dart
  Future<Database> openTestDatabase() => Database.connect(
    Platform.environment['TEST_DATABASE_URL'] ?? 'postgres://localhost/test',
  );
// ...and CI starts Postgres ONCE as a service container, so the per-run cost is
// a connection, not a server boot. The suite becomes: fast locally against a
// dev database, and identical in CI.

// the shape that actually keeps a large suite fast
test/
  unit/          2,400 tests   no I/O at all          ~20 s
  integration/     180 tests   one container, reused   ~3 min
  e2e/              12 tests   real deploy, real UI    ~40 min, nightly only
// ...and the tags mirror the directories, so:
$ dart test test/unit                       # the loop a developer runs
$ dart test -t integration                 # a PR gate
$ dart test -t e2e                         # nightly
// ...which means the fast loop is fast BECAUSE it is nameable, not because
// anyone was disciplined about it.

// and the measurement that tells you which of the three is hurting
$ dart test --reporter=json > report.json
// ...then group the durations by group name. The output is a list of
// {"test":{"name":"...","group":["..."]},"result":..,"time":{"total_ms":N}}
// records, so summing `time` per group is a few lines of script and names the
// offending group instead of leaving you to guess. Do this monthly; the answer
// changes as the suite grows.

Two suite-level behaviours are worth knowing because they change what a green run means. Retries, if configured, turn a failure into a pass on the second attempt — which means a green build no longer proves the test is reliable, only that it passed twice out of two. And concurrency means tests in different files run concurrently in separate isolates, which is what makes a suite fast and also what makes shared mutable state across files a real hazard rather than a theoretical one.

// retries: what a green build then means
// dart_test.yaml
dart_test:
  retries: 2
// ...a test that fails once and passes twice is GREEN. So:
//   - never enable retries on the PR gate; enable it on the nightly, where the
//     report lists what needed a retry
//   - and record it: a suite with retries on reports a higher pass rate while
//     its defect-discovery rate is unchanged, which is the most expensive kind
//     of green to have
// ...the right response to a flaky test is to fix or delete it, and a nightly
// job that lists retried tests is what makes that queue visible.

// concurrency, and the two hazards it creates
dart_test:
  concurrency: 8
// 1. FILES run in separate isolates, so a `static` variable is per-file, not
//    global. This surprises people who used a static as a test fixture and then
//    found two tests in DIFFERENT files not sharing it.
// 2. within a file, tests run in declaration order unless randomised. So the
//    intra-file order is deterministic and the inter-file parallelism is not -
//    which is why a suite can be flaky only under CI's higher concurrency.
// ...the fix for a contention fault is to make the resource unique per test,
// never to lower concurrency, because lowering it only hides the bug until the
// suite grows past the new limit.

// and what a test suite should report that it usually does not
//   duration per group          so the slow group is named
//   retry count                 so flakiness is visible
//   randomisation seed          so a failure is reproducible
//   the count of tests SKIPPED  so a `skip:` never hides in a green build
// ...a suite with all four reports is one where "it passed" means something.
// A suite with none of them is one where "it passed" means the process exited
// zero, which is a weaker claim than it looks.

14.2 The matcher vocabulary

Every matcher you will use, grouped by what it is for.

// EQUALITY
expect(actual, 42);
expect(actual, equals(42));
expect(list, [1, 2, 3]);
expect(map, {'a': 1});
expect(set, {1, 2});                    // set equality, order-independent
expect(complex, isNot(42));
expect(complex, isNot(same(42)));       // identity, not equality
expect(a, b);                          // the two are equal

// NUMBERS
expect(value, greaterThan(10));
expect(value, greaterThanOrEqualTo(10));
expect(value, lessThan(10));
expect(value, inInclusiveRange(1, 10));
expect(value, closeTo(3.14, 0.01));     // for doubles
expect(double.infinity, isNaN.isFalse);

// STRINGS
expect(s, startsWith('hello'));
expect(s, endsWith('world'));
expect(s, contains('lo wo'));
expect(s, matches(RegExp(r'^\d{3}$')));
expect(s, isEmpty);
expect(s, isNotEmpty);
expect(s.trim(), 'x');
expect(s, predicate((v) => v.length < 10, 'shorter than 10'));

// COLLECTIONS
expect(list, isEmpty);
expect(list, isNotEmpty);
expect(list, hasLength(3));
expect(list, contains(2));
expect(list, containsAll([1, 2]));
expect(list, containsAllInOrder([1, 2, 3]));
expect(list, hasPairwiseOrder);         // the pairs match
expect(list, unorderedEquals([3, 1, 2]));
expect(list, everyElement(isPositive));
expect(list, anyElement(isEven));
expect(list.first, 1);
expect(list.last, 3);
expect(list, isNot(contains(99)));     // careful: contains is ambiguous here
// THROWING
expect(() => risky(), throwsA(isA<FormatException>()));
expect(() => risky(), throwsFormatException);
expect(() => risky(), throwsRangeError);
expect(() => risky(), throwsArgumentError);
expect(() => risky(), throwsStateError);
expect(() => risky(), throwsUnsupportedError);
expect(() => risky(), throwsException);         // any Exception
expect(() => risky(), throwsA(isA<AppError>()
    .having((e) => e.code, 'code', 42)));        // and check the fields
expect(() => risky(), throwsUnsupportedError);
expect(() => risky(), returnsNormally);
expect(risky(), completion(42));                  // an async function
expect(future, throwsA(isA<HttpException>()));

// THE ASYNC-SYNC MISTAKE
// WRONG: this passes even if the function throws, because the
// closure is never called
expect(risky(), throwsA(isA<FormatException>()));

// RIGHT: wrap the call in a closure
expect(() => risky(), throwsA(isA<FormatException>()));

// ASYNC
test('awaits a future', () async {
  final result = await fetch();
  expect(result, 42);
});

test('handles a rejected future', () async {
  await expectLater(fetchBad(), throwsA(isA<HttpException>()));
  // or
  try {
    await fetchBad();
    fail('should have thrown');
  } on HttpException catch (e) {
    expect(e.statusCode, 404);
  }
});
// TYPES
expect(value, isA<String>());
expect(value, isA<int>());
expect(value, isNot(isA<String>()));
expect(value, isA<List<int>>());
expect(value, predicate((v) => v is String && v.isNotEmpty));

// OBJECTS
expect(obj, same(otherObj));            // identical
expect(obj, isNot(same(otherObj)));
expect(obj.property, value);            // and its fields

// CUSTOM MATCHERS, for a domain concept
class IsValidEmail extends Matcher {
  @override
  bool matches(Object? item, Map matchState) {
    if (item is! String) return false;
    return RegExp(r'^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$').hasMatch(item);
  }

  @override
  Description describe(Description description) {
    return description.add('a valid email');
  }
}

expect('ana@acme.com', isAValidEmail());
expect('not-an-email', isNot(isAValidEmail()));

// timing, for async
expect(future, completion(42));
await expectLater(future, completion(42));
expect(slowFuture(), completes);

The matcher vocabulary

expect takes an actual value and a matcher, and the matcher is where the expressive power is. A test written entirely with equals on primitives tests almost nothing, because it only reports a difference when the whole value differs — so a test whose subject is a ten-field object reports "expected: <Instance>, actual: <Instance>" and tells you nothing. The matchers that report which part differ are the ones worth learning.

MatcherUseReports
equalsDeep equality on any valueDeep diff
isA<T>()Type checkActual type
hasLengthSized collectionsExpected vs actual length
containsMembershipThe element it did not find
containsPairMap entriesThe missing key
hasPropertyFields on an objectThe field value
completionAsync resultsThe whole failure
throwsAExceptionsActual vs expected type
isNaN, inInclusiveRangeNumbersPrecise

The composition rules are the part that is genuinely hard, and they come down to three word-like matchers — isNot, anyOf and allOf — plus the Matcher base class for anything else. isNot negates, anyOf passes if one does, and allOf requires all. Everything else is either a specialised form or built from these.

// the three, and where each is right
expect(value, isNotNull);
expect(value, isNotEmpty);                     // ...collections and strings
expect(value, isNot(equals(0)));
expect(list, isNot(contains('forbidden')));
expect(map, isNot(containsPair('k', 'v')));

expect(status, anyOf(equals(200), equals(204)));   // ...one of
expect(result, allOf(                                       // ...all of,
    isA<List<int>>(),                          //    and the diff names
    hasLength(3),                                    //    WHICH failed
    everyElement(greaterThan(0)),
));

// deep equality, and what it compares
expect(
  User('a', 30, [1, 2]),
  equals(User('a', 30, [1, 2])),
);   // ...deep, and List is deep-compared element by element
// ...so a test with `equals` on an object graph IS checking every field. What
// it does NOT do is tell you WHICH field differed, because equals produces one
// boolean. That is the whole motivation for the matchers below.

// hasProperty, and why it is the most useful one
expect(
  response,
  allOf(
    hasProperty('statusCode', equals(200)),
    hasProperty('body', contains('"id":42')),
    hasProperty('headers', containsPair('content-type', contains('json'))),
  ),
);
// ...on failure it says which property of which object was wrong. With
// `equals(response)` on a five-field object, it says nothing.

// and the two that catch a whole class of mistake
expect(double.parse(result), closeTo(3.14, 0.001));   // ...floats
expect(elapsed.inMilliseconds, lessThan(200));
expect(expensive(), completion(equals(expected)));    // ...async, chapter 13.4

// custom matchers, for a rule that recurs
Matcher isValidUser() => isA<User>()
    .having((u) => u.id, 'id', greaterThan(0))
    .having((u) => u.name, 'name', isNotEmpty)
    .having((u) => u.email, 'email', contains('@'));

// ...`having` is the general form and it is worth learning, because it turns
// "three separate expects" into one assertion with three named sub-conditions,
// and the failure message names the condition.
expect(user, isValidUser());
// FAIL: Expected: <User> with id: greater than 0
//   Actual: <User(id:0, name:'Ana', email:'a@b.c')>
//   Which: id 0
// ...which is the difference between a two-minute fix and an afternoon of
// print statements.

// and the vocabulary that reads as English, which is the design
// expect(list, isEmpty);
expect(list, contains(42));
expect(list, containsAll([1, 2, 3]));
expect(list, containsAllInOrder([1, 2, 3]));
expect(list, hasLength(3));
expect(map, containsPair('k', 'v'));
expect(set, containsAll(['a', 'b']));
expect(obj, isNot(same(nested)));       // identity, not equality
expect(x, sameInstanceAs(y));            // ...the readable form
expect(n, isPositive);
expect(n, isZero);
expect(n, isNaN);
expect(n, inInclusiveRange(1, 10));
expect(n, inExclusiveRange(1, 10));
expect(s, startsWith('a'));
expect(s, endsWith('z'));
expect(s, matches(RegExp(r'^d+$')));   // ...RegExp, not a string
expect(f, returnsNormally);
expect(f, throwsA(isA<StateError>()));
expect(f, throwsArgumentError);          // ...a shorthand for one type
expect(f, throwsUnsupportedError);
expect(f, throwsFormatException);
expect(f, throwsStateError);
expect(f, throwsException);              // ...the broadest: any Exception
expect(f, throwsA(anything));            // ...broadest of all, incl. Error
// ...note throwsA(isA<X>()) rather than throwsX: `throwsStateError` is a
// shorthand, and the explicit form composes with anyOtherMatcher.

Two matchers deserve special care because using them the obvious way produces a test that cannot fail. throwsA takes a closure, and if you pass the function under test's result rather than a closure calling it, the assertion passes before the function runs. And anything is a matcher that always passes, so throwsA(anything) asserts only that something was thrown — which is occasionally what you want and frequently a test that passes on any exception at all.

// the closure trap: three ways to write it, two wrong
void test1() {
  expect(thrower(), throwsStateError);   // WRONG: thrower() runs FIRST and
}                                       // throws out of the test body, so the
                                        // expectation is never evaluated.
// ...the failure is an unhandled error in the test, which looks like a crash
// rather than an assertion failure, so it is easy to misread as "the code
// under test crashed" when in fact the test was wrong.

void test2() {
  expect(() => thrower(), throwsStateError);   // RIGHT
}

void test3() {
  expect(() async => thrower(), throwsStateError);  // WRONG
}                                                 // ...`() async =>` makes an
//    async closure whose RESULT is the return of thrower(); the throw happens
//    inside an un-awaited future. The matcher sees a closure that returns
//    immediately and successfully, so it fails with "expected throws, actual
//    returns normally" - a confusing message for a test that is in fact
//    testing the right thing with the wrong wrapper.
// ...the async forms are in the next section.

// and the assertion that cannot fail
void test4() {
  expect(() => thrower(), throwsA(anything));
}   // ...passes for ANY error, including the ones you did not anticipate. It is
//     the right assertion for "this input must be rejected" and the wrong one
//     for "this must be rejected for this specific reason".
// ...prefer the narrowest matcher that expresses the requirement:
//    throwsA(isA<FormatException>()
//        .having((e) => e.message, 'message', contains('exponent')))
// ...which asserts the type AND the reason, and reports both when it fails.

// and the third trap, which is subtler: a matcher that always passes because
// of what it was given
void test5() {
  expect(List<int>.empty, isEmpty);          // ...fine
  expect([1, 2, 3], everyElement(greaterThan(0)));  // ...fine
  expect([0, 1, 2], everyElement(greaterThan(0)));  // FAILS, and correctly:
}                                                   // ...everyElement on a
//    collection with one non-matching element reports it. But
//    expect([], everyElement(greaterThan(0)));   // PASSES on an empty list,
}                                                //    which is vacuously true -
//    a test that asserts nothing. If emptiness is not acceptable, assert
//    isNotEmpty FIRST.

The failure message is the actual output

An assertion's purpose is not to pass. It is to fail, and the quality of its failure is what determines how long the bug takes to find. Most matchers report that a difference exists; the ones worth reaching for report where and how big. That is the whole argument for hasProperty over equals on an object, and for having over three bare expect calls.

// the failure nobody can act on
test('parses the header', () {
  final h = Parser().parse(input);
  expect(h, equals(Header('id', 2, ['a', 'b'])));
});
// FAIL: Expected: <Instance of 'Header'>
//   Actual: <Instance of 'Header'>
// ...three fields, all wrong, and the message says nothing at all. This is the
// signature of a class with no toString(). Fix the class and the whole suite
// becomes readable, which is why toString() on a value type is a testing
// investment and not decoration.

// the same assertion, reported usefully
test('parses the header', () {
  expect(
    Parser().parse(input),
    isA<Header>()
      .having((h) => h.id, 'id', 'id')
      .having((h) => h.version, 'version', 2)
      .having((h) => h.flags, 'flags', ['a', 'b']),
  );
});
// FAIL: Expected: <Header>
//   with id: "id"
//   with version: 2
//   with flags: ["a", "b"
//   Actual: <Header(id:"id", version:1, flags:["a"])>
//        ^ which: version 1
// ...and that last line - WHICH: - is the difference between a two-minute fix
// and reading the source. `having` is the matcher that produces it.

// and for collections, where equals gives a diff but not a shape
expect(rows, equals([
  {'id': 1, 'name': 'a'},
  {'id': 2, 'name': 'b'},
]));
// FAIL: Expected: [ {id: 1, name: "a"}, {id: 2, name: "b"} ]
//   Actual: [ {id: 1, name: "a"}, {id: 2, name: "c"} ]
// ...readable, and for a ten-element list it is still readable. `equals` on a
// list is fine; `equals` on a class instance is the failure above.

// and the shape of a good name, which is 80% of the value
test('rejects a header whose version is below the minimum', ...);   // good
test('test header 3', ...);                                        // useless
test('Header', ...);                                               // worse
// ...the name should let a person decide whether the failure matters WITHOUT
// opening the file. "rejects a version below the minimum" does that; "test
// header 3" requires reading the body, and the body is the thing that is
// suspected of being wrong.

// and the reason: field, which is the other half
expect(actual, expected,
  reason: 'the API returns ISO-8601 with a Z, and the fixture has no zone');
// ...`reason` is printed above the diff. Use it for the requirement the
// assertion is expressing, not for a restatement of the matcher - "expected 2
// actual 3" is noise, while the sentence above explains WHY 2 is the number.
// ...and prefer it to a comment, because a comment is not in the failure output.

// the four matchers whose messages are weakest, and what to do instead
//   equals on a class instance   -> isA<T>().having(...), plus toString()
//   equals on a large object    -> hasProperty per field that matters
//   equals on a Map             -> containsPair for the entries under test
//   anything / isNotNull        -> name the property and its expected shape
// ...and the one whose message is strongest, worth knowing for the reverse
// reason: `throwsA` reports the actual exception's type AND its message, which
// is why asserting on a message substring is better than asserting on a type
// alone. `throwsA(isA<StateError>())` passes for every StateError ever
// thrown; `throwsA(isA<StateError>().having((e) => e.message, 'message',
// contains('not configured')))` passes only for the one you meant.

// and one trap: an assertion inside a loop reports only the FIRST failure
for (final c in cases) {
  expect(check(c), isValid());     // ...stops at the first bad case
}
// ...so a table-driven test over 40 cases reports one failure and you re-run 40
// times. The fix is to collect the failures and assert once:
final failures = cases.where((c) => !isValid(c)).toList();
expect(failures, isEmpty,
    reason: failures.map(describe).join('
'));
// ...now one run names every bad case. `reason` is the mechanism, and using it
// to carry a LIST is the single highest-leverage change to a table-driven
// suite's diagnostic quality.

14.3 Unit tests that are worth writing

Where the value is, and the tests that are usually a waste of time.

// HIGH VALUE, always worth it
//  1. the logic with branches: merge, conflict resolution, validation
//  2. the boundary of a bug you have already fixed (a regression test)
//  3. anything where a mistake is silent and expensive
//  4. the null-safety and type edge cases: empty, huge, unicode
//  5. serialisation round-trips

group('mergeEntry', () {
  final base = ServerEntry(id: '1', title: 'A', body: 'x',
                           updatedAt: 1000, serverVersion: 7);

  test('takes the local edit when only the local side changed', () {
    final result = mergeEntry(base, LocalEdit(
      id: '1', changedFields: {'body': 'y'}, basedOnVersion: 7,
    ));
    expect(result.body, 'y');
    expect(result.conflicted, isFalse);
  });

  test('takes the server value when only the server changed', () {
    final result = mergeEntry({...base, body: 'server'},
        LocalEdit(id: '1', changedFields: {}, basedOnVersion: 7));
    expect(result.body, 'server');
  });

  test('merges non-overlapping changes', () {
    final result = mergeEntry({...base, body: 'server'},
        LocalEdit(id: '1', changedFields: {'title': 'B'}, basedOnVersion: 7));
    expect(result.body, 'server');
    expect(result.title, 'B');
  });

  test('flags an overlapping change as a conflict', () {
    final result = mergeEntry({...base, body: 'server'},
        LocalEdit(id: '1', changedFields: {'body': 'mine'}, basedOnVersion: 7));
    expect(result.conflicted, isTrue);
    expect(result.conflictFields, ['body']);
  });

  test('handles an empty changedFields', () { ... });
  test('handles null in a changed field', () { ... });
});

// LOW VALUE, usually a waste
//  1. a getter that returns a field
//  2. a setter that assigns a field
//  3. a constructor that assigns its arguments
//  4. "it does not throw" with no assertion about the result
//  5. testing the framework: that List.add adds, that jsonDecode works

test('getter returns the title', () {
  final e = Entry(title: 'x');
  expect(e.title, 'x');     // this tests the compiler, not your logic
});
// the regression test, which is the highest-value test there is
// a bug is found, fixed, and the test locks the fix in place
test('regression: does not crash on an empty file', () async {
  final file = File(p.join(tempDir.path, 'empty.json'));
  await file.writeAsString('');            // the input that broke it

  final result = await Repository(file.parent).read(file.path);
  // it should return empty, not throw
  expect(result, isEmpty);
});

// the edge cases that actually break
group('Entry edge cases', () {
  test('handles an empty title', () { ... });
  test('handles a very long title', () { ... });
  test('handles emoji in the title', () {
    final e = Entry(title: '🎉 party 🎉');
    expect(e.title.runes.length, greaterThan(5));
    expect(e.copyWith().title, e.title);
  });
  test('handles a null createdAt', () { ... });
  test('handles a timestamp at the epoch', () { ... });
});

Which tests are worth writing

The worth of a test is not what it covers but what failure it would catch, and that ratio is very uneven. Four categories are worth almost always: behaviour with a specification (a parser, a calculation, a state machine), edge cases and boundaries, error paths, and anything where the same input has historically produced more than one answer. Three categories are usually not: getters and setters over a field, one-line delegations, and anything whose only assertion is that it did not throw.

CategoryWorthWhy
Pure logic, spec'dHighEdges are enumerable and easy to get wrong
State machinesHighThe transitions are the bug surface
Error pathsHighUntested, and the ones users hit
Serialisation round tripsHighField-order and precision bugs
Boundary valuesHighOff-by-one is universal
Getters / simple delegationLowTests the compiler
Trivial wrappersLowRetests a dependency you trust
Private implementation detailNegativeFails on a refactor, catches nothing

The most valuable pattern in testing is table-driven: one test body, many inputs, each case named. It is more valuable than it looks because the case names become the specification, and a reviewer reading the table can tell whether a case is missing without reading the implementation. The cost is that a failure report names the case rather than the value, so the value belongs in the name.

// table-driven, which is the pattern worth copying
void main() {
  group('Levenshtein', () {
    // the signature: (inputs..., expected, why it matters)
    final cases = <List<Object>>[
      ['', '', 0, 'empty against empty'],
      ['a', '', 1, 'one insertion'],
      ['', 'a', 1, 'one deletion'],
      ['a', 'a', 0, 'identical'],
      ['kitten', 'sitting', 3, 'the textbook example'],
      ['', 'abc', 3, 'empty source, 3 insertions'],
      ['abc', '', 3, 'empty target, 3 deletions'],
      ['aaa', 'aab', 1, 'transposition costs 1 in true Damerau'],
      ['abcdef', 'fbcdea', 2, 'block move'],
      ['', '', 0, 'repeated - proves no state leaks between cases'],
    ];

    for (final c in cases) {
      final a = c[0] as String;
      final b = c[1] as String;
      final expected = c[2] as int;
      final why = c[3] as String;

      test('$a -> $b is $expected  [$why]', () {
        expect(levenshtein(a, b), expected);
      });
    }
  });
}
// ...and the properties of this shape:
// - every case is named, so a failure reports WHICH behaviour broke
// - the third column is a comment that survives review
// - adding a case is a one-line change, so the table is easy to extend when a
//   bug report arrives
// - the last case catches order-dependence, which is why it is there

// and the test for something with no specification at all: a property.
// The specification is the law, not the value.
void main() {
  test('levenshtein is symmetric', () {
    final words = ['kitten', 'sitting', '', 'a', 'abcdefghij'];
    for (final w in words) {
      expect(levenshtein(w, ''), w.length, reason: 'distance to empty');
    }
  });

  test('levenshtein(a,b) + levenshtein(b,a) is not necessarily equal, but
        distance to self is 0 and distance to empty is length', () {
    for (final w in ['abc', '', 'xyzzy']) {
      expect(levenshtein(w, w), 0);
      expect(levenshtein(w, ''), w.length);
    }
  });

  test('concatenating never costs more than the sum', () {
    final parts = ['foo', 'bar', 'baz'];
    final total = levenshtein('', parts.join(''));
    final viaEmpty = levenshtein('', parts.first) +
        levenshtein('', parts.skip(1).join(''));
    expect(total, lessThanOrEqualTo(viaEmpty + 1));
  });
}
// ...property-based testing generalises this: generate inputs, assert the law
// holds for all of them. `package:check` and `package:quiver`'s property tests
// both exist, and the technique is disproportionately good at finding
// edge cases nobody thought of - because the generator reaches cases a person
// would not write down.

// and the three assertions that find real bugs most often, in order
// 1. boundary values: 0, 1, minimum, minimum-1, maximum, maximum+1
// 2. empty input to anything that takes a collection
// 3. round trips: encode then decode equals the original
void main() {
  test('round trip', () {
    for (final v in [0, -1, 1, 255, 65535, 2147483647]) {
      final bytes = encode(v);
      expect(decode(bytes), v, reason: 'round trip failed for $v');
    }
  });
}
// ...the round-trip test catches every field-order bug, every precision bug,
// and every signedness bug in a serialiser, and it is a single loop. Include
// the boundary values explicitly: a round-trip test over random values alone
// will never hit 0 or the maximum.

There is one category of test that is not a unit test and not an integration test and that catches a genuinely different class of defect: the test that asserts a non-functional property. A parser that returns the right answer in quadratic time is functionally correct and unusable on real input, and no functional test catches it. These tests are awkward to write — they need a threshold and a stable machine — and the correct response is to make them coarse and to put them in a separate tier that runs on dedicated hardware, not to make them precise and flaky.

// a scalability test, which is the non-functional unit test
@TestOn('vm')
library;

import 'package:test/test.dart';
import 'package:myapp/parser.dart';

void main() {
  // The claim is not "18 ms is correct" but "doubling the input does not more
  // than triple the time", which is a claim about complexity and survives a
  // slow CI runner.
  test('parsing is better than quadratic', () {
    final small = makeSource(1000);
    final large = makeSource(2000);

    final t1 = _time(() => Parser.parse(small));
    final t2 = _time(() => Parser.parse(large));

    // ...2x input. Linear costs ~2x, quadratic costs ~4x. 3x separates them.
    expect(t2, lessThan(t1 * 3),
        reason: 'doubling input took ${(t2 / t1).toStringAsFixed(1)}x - '
                'that is worse than linear');
  });

  test('a 10 MB file does not exhaust memory', () {
    // ...the threshold is a ceiling, not a measurement, so it is stable
    final before = ProcessInfo.currentRss;
    Parser.parse(makeSource(2_000_000));
    final growth = ProcessInfo.currentRss - before;
    expect(growth, lessThan(512 << 20), reason: 'grew ${growth >> 20} MB');
  });
}

int _time(void Function() f) {
  // ...run twice and take the second: the first pays for JIT warm-up, and a
  // benchmark that measures warm-up is measuring the wrong thing
  f();
  final sw = Stopwatch()..start();
  f();
  return sw.elapsedMicroseconds;
}

// and what to do when it fails
// A scalability test that fails on CI is usually one of three things:
// 1. a shared runner with 1/4 the CPU of a laptop - which is why the threshold
//    is a RATIO and not a duration
// 2. a genuine regression - which is the case the test exists for
// 3. first-call JIT, which _time() above already handles
// ...and the one thing never to do is raise the threshold until it passes.

14.4 Testing async code

FakeAsync, and the three ways to make time pass in a test.

import 'package:fake_async/fake_async.dart';

test('retries three times before failing', () {
  fakeAsync((async) {
    var attempts = 0;
    final future = retry(() async {
      attempts++;
      if (attempts < 3) throw Exception('not yet');
      return 'ok';
    }, attempts: 5);

    // 1. nothing has happened yet
    expect(attempts, 0);

    // 2. move time forward, flushing the microtask queue
    async.elapse(const Duration(milliseconds: 300));
    expect(attempts, 3);

    // 3. check the result
    expect(future, completion('ok'));
    async.flushMicrotasks();
  });
});

test('a timeout fires after the duration', () {
  fakeAsync((async) {
    final result = slow().timeout(const Duration(seconds: 5));
    async.elapse(const Duration(seconds: 6));
    expect(result, throwsA(isA<TimeoutException>()));
  });
});

test('a periodic timer ticks five times', () {
  fakeAsync((async) {
    var ticks = 0;
    Timer.periodic(const Duration(milliseconds: 100), (_) => ticks++);
    async.elapse(const Duration(milliseconds: 500));
    expect(ticks, 5);
  });
});

// the three ways to handle time
//  1. fakeAsync: for timers, debounce, polling
//  2. a real delay: await Future.delayed. Slow, but real.
//  3. inject a Clock: the most testable, and the most code

// 3. the injection approach, for anything important
abstract class Clock {
  DateTime now();
}

class SystemClock implements Clock {
  @override
  DateTime now() => DateTime.now();
}

class FixedClock implements Clock {
  FixedClock(this._now);
  DateTime _now;

  set now(DateTime value) => _now = value;
  @override
  DateTime now() => _now;
}

// then a class that depends on it
class TokenService {
  TokenService(this._clock);
  final Clock _clock;

  bool isExpired(Token t) => _clock.now().isAfter(t.expiresAt);
}

// the test is now instant and deterministic
test('a token expires exactly at its expiry time', () {
  final clock = FixedClock(DateTime(2026, 1, 1));
  final service = TokenService(clock);
  final token = Token(expiresAt: DateTime(2026, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1));

  expect(service.isExpired(token), isFalse);
  clock.now = DateTime(2026, 1, 1, 0, 0, 2);
  expect(service.isExpired(token), isTrue);
});

Testing async code

Async tests fail in ways that have nothing to do with the code under test, and every one of them has a specific cause. A test that does not complete fails with a timeout. A test that completes before the operation finishes passes vacuously. And a test that leaves a pending timer fails in a later test, at a point where the cause is invisible. The four matchers and helpers below exist for these four problems.

NeedUseNot
Assert an async resultcompletion(m)await in a sync test
Assert an async errorthrowsA(m) on an async calltry/catch in the test
Assert completion, not a valuecompletesisTrue on a flag
Assert several async thingsexpectLater([...])Several bare expects
Order-dependent async stepsexpectLater(f, completion(...))Bare expect

The single most important rule is that an assertion about an asynchronous result must be registered with expect or expectLater, never awaited before the expect. A bare expect(future, matcher) registers a matcher against a future value and passes immediately if the matcher accepts it — and it does not, so the real answer is that a bare expect on a Future is meaningless. completion is what bridges the two.

// the four forms, and what each actually asserts
Future<int> load() async => 42;

test('the result equals 42', () {
  expect(load(), completion(equals(42)));
});
// ...`completion` registers an asynchronous assertion: expect() returns, the
// test waits for the future, and the matcher is applied to its value. This is
// the correct form for a sync test body.

test('the result equals 42', () async {
  expect(await load(), 42);
});
// ...equally correct, and clearer when there is post-assertion work. Use THIS
// form by default; the completion form is for when you cannot make the body
// async.

test('the future completes at all', () {
  expect(load(), completes);          // ...asserts only that it finished -
}                                      //    no value, no error. Useful when a
                                       //    later test checks the value.

test('a failure surfaces as the right type', () {
  expect(Future.error(StateError('x')), throwsA(isA<StateError>()));
});
// ...IMPORTANT: this is a SYNC test with a sync closure-free argument. The
// failure is registered before the error can become unhandled, so the runner
// sees it. Passing `() => failingCall()` would be wrong - see 13.2.

// several assertions, all of which must hold
test('all four fields are right', () async {
  final u = await loadUser();
  expectLater([
    expectLater(u.id, greaterThan(0)),
    expectLater(u.name, isNotEmpty),
    expectLater(u.email, contains('@')),
    expectLater(u.created.isBefore(DateTime.now()), isTrue),
  ], completes);
});
// ...This is the ONLY correct way to assert several independent futures. The
// `expect` calls must be created INSIDE the argument list, because passing
// four bare `expect(future, ...)` calls asserts nothing.

// and the async error forms, which are where most people get it wrong
Future<void> doWork() async {
  await Future.delayed(Duration.zero);
  throw StateError('boom');
}

test('throws', () async {
  await expectLater(doWork(), throwsA(isA<StateError>()));
});

test('throws with a message', () async {
  await expectLater(
    doWork(),
    throwsA(isA<StateError>().having((e) => e.message, 'message', 'boom')),
  );
});

test('throws, with an async body', () {
  // ...the closure form that people expect, and the one that does not work
  // expect(() async => doWork(), throwsStateError);      // WRONG
  expect(doWork, throwsStateError);                       // WRONG
  expect(doWork(), throwsStateError);                     // RIGHT
});

Fake asynchronous time, because a test that really waits is a test that is slow, flaky, and occasionally takes an hour. fakeAsync from package:fake_async gives a virtual clock whose time advances only when the test says so, so a timer of one hour is tested instantly and deterministically. It is the answer for anything involving Timer, Future.delayed, debounce, retry, timeout and polling — which is most of the code that goes wrong in production.

import 'package:fake_async/fake_async.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

// a debounced search: the case where fakeAsync is the only practical answer
class SearchBox {
  final _controller = StreamController<String>();
  Timer? _debounce;
  final results = <String>[];

  void onInput(String text) {
    _debounce?.cancel();
    _debounce = Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 300), () {
      _controller.add(text);
    });
  }
  Future<void> close() => _controller.close();
  Stream<String> get resultsStream => _controller.stream;
}

void main() {
  test('debounces rapid input into one query', () {
    fakeAsync((async) {
      final box = SearchBox();
      final seen = <String>[];
      box.resultsStream.listen(seen.add);

      box.onInput('a');
      box.onInput('ab');
      box.onInput('abc');
      async.elapse(const Duration(milliseconds: 100));
      expect(seen, isEmpty, reason: 'nothing fires before the window closes');

      async.elapse(const Duration(milliseconds: 250));
      expect(seen, equals(['abc']),
          reason: 'only the LAST input fires - the previous two were cancelled');

      box.close();
    });
  });

  test('a retry gives up after the configured attempts', () {
    fakeAsync((async) {
      var attempts = 0;
      void retry() {
        attempts++;
        if (attempts < 5) {
          Timer(const Duration(seconds: 1), retry);
        }
      }
      retry();
      expect(attempts, 1);

      async.elapse(const Duration(seconds: 4));
      expect(attempts, 4, reason: 'one attempt per second, not yet giving up');

      async.elapse(const Duration(seconds: 1));
      expect(attempts, 5, reason: 'the fifth attempt is the last');

      async.elapse(const Duration(hours: 1));
      expect(attempts, 5, reason: 'and it stops');
    });
  });
}
// ...`async.elapse` advances the virtual clock AND flushes the microtask queue,
// which is why a Future chain resolves inside it without anything else having
// to yield. Forgetting that is the cause of "fakeAsync sees nothing happen".

// and the same technique for a timeout, where the real wait is the whole point
test('the request times out after 30 seconds', () {
  fakeAsync((async) {
    var timedOut = false;
    final slow = () async {
      await Future.delayed(const Duration(seconds: 60));
      return 'late';
    };
    slow().timeout(const Duration(seconds: 30))
      .then((_) {}, onError: (Object e) => timedOut = true);

    async.elapse(const Duration(seconds: 29));
    expect(timedOut, isFalse);

    async.elapse(const Duration(seconds: 2));
    expect(timedOut, isTrue);
  });
});
// ...a real test of this waits 30 seconds, occasionally times out on a loaded
// CI runner, and cannot test the boundary. This one is instant and exact.

// what fakeAsync cannot do: it only fakes the clock, not the event loop's
// real I/O. A `Future` that completes from a socket does not complete inside
// `fakeAsync`, so awaiting real I/O inside one hangs. For that, use
// `fakeAsync().flushMicrotasks()` only where no real I/O is involved, and
// otherwise inject the clock as the parameter seam from chapter 12.8.

Two failure modes produce tests that fail intermittently and consume more time than the feature they test. The first is a leaked subscription: a test that starts a Stream subscription and never cancels it leaves a pending timer, which the runner reports as an error in whichever test runs next. The second is shared mutable state at module scope, which is the same defect as inter-test ordering dependence and has the same fix — make the state local to the test.

// the leak, and the runner's report
var shared = ApiClient();          // ...module scope: state survives every
                                   //    test in this FILE

void main() {
  test('a', () async {
    await shared.fetch();          // ...starts a retry Timer. Never cancelled,
  });                              //    because nothing holds a subscription.
  test('b', () async {
    // ...b passes; then, AFTER b finishes, the runner sees a pending timer and
    //    reports: "a test is still running / a Timer is still pending"
  });
}

// the fix: everything inside, and every subscription cancelled
void main() {
  late ApiClient client;
  var subscriptions = <StreamSubscription>[];

  setUp(() {
    client = ApiClient();
  });

  tearDown(() async {
    // ...the whole point: drain the subscriptions so no timer survives
    for (final s in subscriptions) {
      await s.cancel();
    }
    subscriptions.clear();
    await client.close();
  });

  test('a', () async {
    subscriptions.add(shared.fetch().listen((_) {}));
    await client.ready();
  });
}

// and the runner flag that makes this diagnosable rather than mysterious
$ dart test --reporter expanded
  00:01 +3: loading /path/to/test.dart
  00:02 +3: test b [E]
    Expected: <0>  Actual: <1>
  00:02 +4: some other tests passed
  00:02 +4: test a [E]
    Timer is still pending even after the widget tree was disposed.
  00:02 +5: All tests passed!
// ...note "All tests passed" alongside two errors. The runner reports the
// leaked timer against test A even though it was detected during test B, and
// the suite's exit code is still non-zero - so CI catches it, but the message
// points at the wrong test. Fixing the leak removes both problems.

// the three ways a test can be accidentally slow, each with a specific fix
// 1. a real network call      -> inject an HttpClient, or use a local server
// 2. a real sleep             -> fakeAsync, or a Clock parameter
// 3. a real disk write        -> a temp directory, removed in tearDown
// ...and one that is often missed:
// 4. setUpAll that does expensive work every time ANY test in the file is
//    selected by a tag filter. `dart test -t slow` pays the full fixture cost
//    even for one test. Split the fixture into the file that needs it.

14.5 Fakes, mocks and stubs

The three kinds of test double, and when each is right.

// STUB: returns a canned value, ignores the input
class StubUserService implements UserService {
  @override
  Future<User?> byId(String id) async => const User(id: '1', name: 'Stub');

// MOCK: records the calls, so you assert on them
class MockUserService implements UserService {
  final calls = <String, Object?>{};

  @override
  Future<User?> byId(String id) async {
    calls['byId'] = id;
    return const User(id: id, name: 'Mock');
  }

  @override
  Future<void> save(User user) async {
    calls['save'] = user;
  }
}

test('saves the user when the form is submitted', () async {
  final mock = MockUserService();
  final form = ProfileForm(mock);

  await form.submit(name: 'Ana');

  expect(mock.calls['save'], isA<User>().having((u) => u.name, 'name', 'Ana'));
});

// FAKE: a working implementation with a simplified contract.
// the most useful kind, and the hardest to write
class InMemoryUserService implements UserService {
  final Map<String, User> _users = {};
  var failNextCall = false;

  @override
  Future<User?> byId(String id) async {
    if (failNextCall) throw Exception('network down');
    return _users[id];
  }

  @override
  Future<User> save(User user) async {
    if (failNextCall) throw Exception('network down');
    _users[user.id] = user;
    return user;
  }

  @override
  Future<void> delete(String id) async => _users.remove(id);
}

// a fake lets you test a whole flow, including the error path
test('shows an error when the network fails', () async {
  final service = InMemoryUserService()..failNextCall = true;
  final controller = ProfileController(service);

  await controller.load('1');

  expect(controller.state, ProfileState.error);
  expect(controller.errorMessage, contains('network'));
});
// the package that makes this easy
// package:mockito
import 'package:mockito/mockito.dart';

class MockUserService extends Mock implements UserService {}

// verify the interaction
verify(mock.save(any)).called(1);
verify(mock.save(captureAny)).captured;
verifyNever(mock.delete(any));
verify(mock.save(any)).called(0);
verifyInOrder([mock.byId('1'), mock.save(any)]);
// too many times
verify(mock.load()).called(1);

// stub a return value
when(mock.byId('1')).thenAnswer((_) async => const User(id: '1'));
when(mock.fetch()).thenThrow(Exception('x'));
when(mock.compute(any)).thenAnswer((invocation) {
  final n = invocation.positionalArguments[0] as int;
  return n * 2;
});
// a sequence of answers
when(mock.fetch()).thenAnswer((_) async => 'a')
    .thenAnswer((_) async => 'b');

// annotation-driven, with build_runner
@GenerateNiceMocks([MockSpec<UserService>()])
class Mocks extends Mock {}

test('...', () {
  when(() => mock.fetch()).thenAnswer((_) async => 'x');
});

Fakes, stubs and mocks, and why you rarely need a mocking library

Three words are used interchangeably and mean three different things. A fake is a working implementation with a simpler backend — an in-memory repository instead of a real database. A stub returns canned values. A mock records what it was called with and lets the test assert on that. The practical consequence is that only the third requires a library, and that a hand-written fake is usually better because it is a real object that keeps working when the interface changes.

KindHasAsserts onHand-write it?
FakeA working, simpler implementationBehaviour of the callerYes, usually
StubCanned return valuesNothing, by itselfYes
MockCall recordingThe calls madeOnly if not trivial
SpyCall recording, delegatesThe calls madeRarely

The argument for hand-writing is stronger than it looks. A mock generated from an interface re-implements that interface, so when the interface gains a method the mock is stale and the test stops compiling — which is noise, not safety. A fake is a real class implementing the same interface, so it has the same problem, but you can also give it real behaviour, which means tests written against it keep passing as the code grows. The exception is mocking a third-party class whose methods are final or whose construction is expensive, where a generated mock is the only option.

// the interface under test
abstract class UserRepository {
  Future<User?> findByEmail(String email);
  Future<User> save(User user);
  Future<void> deleteById(String id);
  Stream<User> watch();
}

// a FAKE: real behaviour, simpler backend. This is the one to write.
class InMemoryUserRepository implements UserRepository {
  final _byId = <String, User>{};
  final _byEmail = <String, String>{};
  final _controller = StreamController<User>.broadcast();

  /// Test hook: makes the next [findByEmail] fail, to exercise the error path.
  Object? failWith;
  int findCallCount = 0;

  @override
  Future<User?> findByEmail(String email) async {
    findCallCount++;
    if (failWith != null) throw failWith!;    // ...and this is why a fake
    final id = _byEmail[email];               //    beats a stub: you can make
    return id == null ? null : _byId[id];      //    it fail, which a canned
  }                                            //    return value cannot

  @override
  Future<User> save(User user) async {
    _byId[user.id] = user;
    _byEmail[user.email] = user.id;
    _controller.add(user);
    return user;
  }

  @override
  Future<void> deleteById(String id) async {
    final u = _byId.remove(id);
    if (u != null) _byEmail.remove(u.email);
  }

  @override
  Stream<User> watch() => _controller.stream;

  Future<void> close() => _controller.close();
}

// and the tests, which read as behaviour rather than as plumbing
void main() {
  late InMemoryUserRepository repo;
  late UserService service;

  setUp(() {
    repo = InMemoryUserRepository();
    service = UserService(repo);
  });

  tearDown(() => repo.close());

  test('registers a new user', () async {
    final u = await service.register('ana@example.com', 'Ana');
    expect(u.id, isNotEmpty);
    expect(await repo.findByEmail('ana@example.com'), isNotNull);
  });

  test('rejects a duplicate email', () async {
    await service.register('ana@example.com', 'Ana');
    expect(
      () => service.register('ana@example.com', 'Ana again'),
      throwsA(isA<DuplicateEmailException>()),
    );
  });

  test('surfaces a repository failure rather than swallowing it', () async {
    repo.failWith = const SocketException('db down');
    await expectLater(
      service.register('ana@example.com', 'Ana'),
      throwsA(isA<SocketException>()),
    );
  });
}
// ...`repo.findCallCount` and `repo.failWith` are what a mock would give you,
// written by hand and available on any platform with no dependency.

When a mocking library is genuinely the right answer — verifying that which methods were called, and in what order, without caring what they returned — mockito is the standard, and its generated mocks work well for interfaces with many methods. The two things to know are that the codegen step is required, and that an unstubbed method on a strict mock returns null and fails at the use site rather than at the call, which is why a mock-heavy test fails with a TypeError rather than with a helpful message.

// build_runner codegen, which is the step people miss
// dev_dependencies:
//   mockito: ^5.4.0
//   build_runner: ^2.4.0
// $ dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs

// the annotated interface
@GenerateNiceMocks([MockSpec<PaymentGateway>])
abstract class MockPaymentGateway extends Mock implements PaymentGateway {}

// the test
void main() {
  late MockPaymentGateway gateway;
  late Checkout checkout;

  setUp(() {
    gateway = MockPaymentGateway();
    // ...`NiceMocks` auto-stubs void methods to do nothing, so only the ones
    // this test cares about need an explicit when:
    when(() => gateway.charge(any(), any()))
        .thenAnswer((_) async => Receipt(id: 'r1'));
    checkout = Checkout(gateway);
  });

  test('charges the card and records the receipt', () async {
    final r = await checkout.complete(card, amount: 100);
    expect(r.id, 'r1');
    // ...this is the mock's purpose: verifying the OUTCOME plus the CALL
    verify(() => gateway.charge('card-123', 100)).called(1);
  });

  test('does not charge when the cart is empty', () async {
    await expectLater(checkout.complete(card, cart: []),
        throwsA(isA<StateError>()));
    verifyNever(() => gateway.charge(any(), any()));
    // ...`verifyNever` is the assertion that a stub cannot express: "this
    // interaction must not have happened".
  });

  test('propagates a declined card', () async {
    when(() => gateway.charge(any(), any()))
        .thenThrow(DeclinedException(code: '51'));
    await expectLater(checkout.complete(card, amount: 100),
        throwsA(isA<DeclinedException>().having((e) => e.code, 'code', '51')));
    // ...a real thrown exception, so the error path is genuinely exercised
    // rather than asserted about.
  });
}

// the pattern worth naming: a fake with a recorded call list, which covers the
// common case without a dependency
class RecordingGateway implements PaymentGateway {
  final calls = <String>[];
  @override
  Future<Receipt> charge(String card, int amount) async {
    calls.add('charge($card,$amount)');
    return Receipt(id: 'r${calls.length}');
  }
  @override
  Future<void> refund(String id) async => calls.add('refund($id)');
}

test('records the calls in order', () async {
  final g = RecordingGateway();
  await Checkout(g).complete(card, amount: 100);
  expect(g.calls, ['charge(card-123,100)']);
  // ...and if the interface grows a method, `implements` fails to compile until
  // you handle it, which is the correct pressure. A generated mock would also
  // fail - but it would fail with "the generated file is stale", which is a
  // worse message.

14.6 Testing code that touches the filesystem and network

Temporary directories, an in-memory store, and a real or fake server.

import 'dart:io';
import 'package:path/path.dart' as p;

// FILESYSTEM: a real temp directory, cleaned up
late Directory tempDir;
late Repository repo;

setUp(() async {
  tempDir = await Directory.systemTemp.createTemp('test_');
  repo = await Repository.open(tempDir);
});

tearDown(() async {
  await repo.close();
  await tempDir.delete(recursive: true);
});

test('writes and reads an entry', () async {
  await repo.save(const Entry(id: '1', title: 'A'));
  final loaded = await repo.byId('1');
  expect(loaded?.title, 'A');
});

test('returns null for a missing entry', () async {
  expect(await repo.byId('nope'), isNull);
});

// why a real directory rather than a mock of File:
//   - it tests the actual IO code
//   - it catches path bugs
//   - it is fast enough (a few ms)

// for code that must not touch the disk at all, inject a
// KeyValueStore (chapter 13) and use the in-memory implementation
import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;
import 'package:http/testing.dart';

// NETWORK 1: MockClient, from package:http. The right answer.
test('fetches and parses the profile', () async {
  final client = MockClient((request) async {
    // assert on the request: this is where a bug in your URL
    // or headers shows up
    expect(request.url.path, '/users/1');
    expect(request.headers['authorization'], 'Bearer token');

    return http.Response(
      jsonEncode({'id': '1', 'name': 'Ana'}),
      200,
      headers: {'content-type': 'application/json'},
    );
  });

  final api = ApiClient(baseUrl: 'https://api.test', httpClient: client);
  final user = await api.profile();

  expect(user.name, 'Ana');
});

test('maps a 404 to a NotFoundException', () async {
  final client = MockClient((_) async => http.Response('{}', 404));
  final api = ApiClient(baseUrl: 'https://api.test', httpClient: client);

  await expectLater(
    api.profile(),
    throwsA(isA<NotFoundException>()),
  );
});

test('retries a 500 but not a 400', () async {
  var calls = 0;
  final client = MockClient((_) async {
    calls++;
    return http.Response('{}', 500);
  });
  final api = ApiClient(baseUrl: 'https://api.test', httpClient: client);

  await expectLater(api.profile(), throwsA(anything));
  expect(calls, 3);      // 1 + 2 retries
});

// NETWORK 2: a real server, for an end-to-end test
test('serves and consumes against a real socket', () async {
  final server = await HttpServer.bind('127.0.0.1', 0);
  addTearDown(() => server.close(force: true));

  server.listen((request) async {
    request.response
      ..headers.contentType = ContentType.json
      ..write(jsonEncode({'id': '1', 'name': 'Ana'}));
    await request.response.close();
  });

  final api = ApiClient(baseUrl: 'http://127.0.0.1:${server.port}');
  expect((await api.profile()).name, 'Ana');
});

Testing code that touches the file system

File-system tests have a bad reputation for flakiness, and the reason is almost always one thing: the tests share a directory. A test that writes to a fixed path fails when two tests run concurrently, and it fails on a developer's machine with leftover state from yesterday's run. Three rules eliminate essentially all of it, and none require a library.

import 'dart:io';
import 'package:path/path.dart' as p;
import 'package:test/test.dart';

/// A directory that exists only for the duration of one test.
class TempDir {
  final Directory dir;
  TempDir._(this.dir);
  static Future<TempDir> create() async {
    // ...createTemp gives a UNIQUE name with restrictive permissions, so two
    // concurrent runs cannot collide and another user cannot pre-create it
    final d = await Directory.systemTemp.createTemp('test_');
    return TempDir._(d);
  }
  String path(String name) => p.join(dir.path, name);
  Future<void> dispose() => dir.delete(recursive: true);
}

void main() {
  late TempDir temp;

  setUp(() => temp = await TempDir.create());
  // ...note: setUp can be async. It is awaited before each test.

  tearDown(() => temp.dispose());

  test('writes and reads back', () async {
    await File(temp.path('a.txt')).writeAsString('hello');
    expect(await File(temp.path('a.txt')).readAsString(), 'hello');
  });

  test('creates a missing directory on demand', () async {
    final target = Directory(temp.path('deep/nested/out'));
    expect(target.existsSync(), isFalse);
    await Config.load(temp.path('deep/nested/out/config.yaml'));
    expect(target.existsSync(), isTrue);
  });
}

// ...rule 1: a fresh directory per test, created and removed by the framework.
// ...rule 2: never a path outside the temp directory. A test that writes to
//    './out.txt' leaves the file, so the NEXT run finds it and the test's
//    precondition ("the file does not exist") is false before it starts.
// ...rule 3: no test depends on another having run. If they must share
//    fixtures, that is a setUpAll with an explicit reset.

Two file-system behaviours are worth testing explicitly because they are the ones that differ between platforms and between test runs: file locking and case-insensitivity. A test that asserts a path's case is preserved passes on Linux and fails on macOS and Windows, and a test that writes a lock file leaves it behind on a failed run, so the next run's existsSync assertion fails for a reason that has nothing to do with the code.

// the case-sensitivity trap, which is platform-dependent
test('paths are case sensitive', () async {
  await File(temp.path('Report.csv')).writeAsString('x');
  expect(File(temp.path('report.csv')).existsSync(), isFalse);
});
// ...PASSES on Linux. FAILS on macOS (case-insensitive by default) and on
// Windows. So:
// ...either skip it off Linux:
//   test('...', onPlatform: 'linux');
// ...or, better, assert the property that is actually portable:
//   test('two paths differing only in case are the same file on Windows', () {
//     if (Platform.isWindows) {
//       expect(File(temp.path('A.csv')).resolveSymbolicLinksSync(),
//           File(temp.path('a.csv')).resolveSymbolicLinksSync());
//     }
//   });

// and the leftover-lock trap
test('acquires the lock', () async {
  final lock = LockFile(temp.path('db.lock'));
  expect(await lock.tryAcquire(), isTrue);
  expect(await lock.tryAcquire(), isFalse, reason: 'second acquire fails');
});
// ...if this test fails BEFORE the release, the lock file stays. The next run
// reads it and `tryAcquire` returns false, so the FIRST assertion fails - and
// the error points at the wrong thing entirely.
// ...the fix is to make release unconditional, in tearDown rather than at the
// end of the test body:
tearDown(() async {
  if (await File(temp.path('db.lock')).exists()) {
    await File(temp.path('db.lock')).delete();
  }
  await temp.dispose();
});
// ...and that is a genuine difference from production code: in a test, the
// cleanup belongs in the framework, because the test may not reach its own
// cleanup path.

// and the third: a file left behind by the previous run of a DIFFERENT file
$ dart test
// 00:01 +12: creates the config [E]
//     Expected: true  Actual: false
// ...the previous run wrote the file and the test asserted it was absent, or
// wrote it and the second write found it present. The only durable fix is a
// per-test directory, which is what TempDir above is for.

// and what NOT to do
// $ dart test --concurrency=8 test/db_test.dart
// ...with a shared './test.db' and 8 concurrent tests. This is the standard way
// to produce a suite that passes alone and fails in CI, and no amount of
// retrying fixes it.

HTTP is the same problem with one extra layer, and there are two approaches with different trade-offs. A real local server gives the most faithful test and the most flakiness, because it involves a socket, a port and a scheduler. An injected client interface gives a fast deterministic test and misses the whole point of the HTTP layer. The pragmatic answer is to use the injected interface for the majority of tests and one real-server test for the parts the interface cannot represent — the parts where the server's actual behaviour is what is being tested.

// the seam: an interface, not an HttpClient
abstract class HttpPort {
  Future<HttpResponse> get(String url, {Map<String, String>? headers});
}

class RealHttp implements HttpPort {
  RealHttp() : _client = HttpClient();
  final HttpClient _client;
  @override
  Future<HttpResponse> get(String url, {Map<String, String>? headers}) async {
    final req = await _client.getUrl(Uri.parse(url));
    headers?.forEach(req.headers.set);
    final res = await req.close();
    // ...the status check that the seam FORCES into existence, because a fake
    // returns an HttpResponse and a real one must build it honestly
