    final body = await res.transform(utf8.decoder).join();
    await res.drain<void>();
    return HttpResponse(res.statusCode, body, res.headers);
  }
}

class FakeHttp implements HttpPort {
  final routes = <String, HttpResponse Function()>{};
  final requested = <String>[];

  void on(String path, int status, String body) =>
      routes[path] = () => HttpResponse(status, body, {});

  @override
  Future<HttpResponse> get(String url, {Map<String, String>? headers}) async {
    requested.add(url);
    final h = routes[url];
    if (h == null) throw StateError('no route for $url');
    return h();
  }
}

// so most tests are deterministic and one test is real
void main() {
  test('shows an error when the server returns 500', () async {
    final http = FakeHttp()..on('/api/user', 500, 'boom');
    final ui = UserController(http);
    await ui.load();
    expect(ui.error, isNotNull);
    expect(ui.user, isNull);
  });

  test('does not double-load on a refresh', () async {
    final http = FakeHttp()..on('/api/user', 200, '{"id":"1"}');
    final ui = UserController(http);
    await ui.load();
    await ui.refresh();
    expect(http.requested, hasLength(2));
  });

  // and THIS one is real, because what is being tested is the wire format and
  // the client's own behaviour, neither of which the fake represents
  test('the real client parses a real response', () async {
    final server = await HttpServer.bind(InternetAddress.loopbackIPv4, 0);
    server.listen((req) {
      req.response.headers.contentType = ContentType.json;
      req.response.write(jsonEncode({'id': '1', 'name': 'Ana'}));
      req.response.close();
    });
    addTearDown(() => server.close(force: true));

    final client = RealHttp();
    addTearDown(client.close);

    final res = await client.get('http://127.0.0.1:${server.port}/api/user');
    expect(res.status, 200);
    expect(jsonDecode(res.body)['name'], 'Ana');
  });
}
// ...note `addTearDown`, which runs even if the test body throws before
// reaching its own cleanup - the same safety reason as tearDown, and the
// reason the server is not left holding a port. Port 0 means "any free port",
// which is what stops two concurrent tests colliding.
// ...and one real test is enough: if the fake and the real client disagree, the
// real test catches it. Two dozen real-server tests would be slower and would
// still not cover a header the fake omits.

14.7 Golden and integration tests

Flutter golden tests, and the integration test that covers the whole app.

// GOLDEN TESTS (Flutter): compare a rendered widget to a stored image
import 'package:flutter_test/flutter_test.dart';

testWidgets('the card renders as expected', (tester) async {
  await tester.pumpWidget(const MaterialApp(home: EntryCard(entry: testEntry)));

  await expectLater(
    find.byType(EntryCard),
    matchesGoldenFile('goldens/entry_card.png'),
  );
});

// updating the goldens when the design changes on purpose
flutter test --update-goldens

// the discipline that makes goldens useful rather than annoying:
//  1. commit the golden files
//  2. review the diff carefully: a change you did not intend is
//     a visual regression the test just caught for you
//  3. run them in CI, on the same platform, or the rendering
//     differs and the test is useless
//  4. for text, disable the font variability: the golden is
//     rendered with a fixed font, or tests fail on different machines
// INTEGRATION TESTS: the whole app, on a real device or emulator
// integration_test/app_test.dart
import 'package:integration_test/integration_test.dart';

void main() {
  IntegrationTestWidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();

  testWidgets('the full login and save flow', (tester) async {
    await app.main();

    // sign in
    await tester.enterText(find.byType(TextField).first, 'e2e@acme.test');
    await tester.enterText(find.byType(TextField).at(1), 'password');
    await tester.tap(find.text('Sign in'));
    await tester.pumpAndSettle();

    expect(find.text('Entries'), findsOneWidget);

    // create an entry
    await tester.tap(find.byIcon(Icons.add));
    await tester.pumpAndSettle();
    await tester.enterText(find.byType(TextField).first, 'from the test');
    await tester.tap(find.text('Save'));
    await tester.pumpAndSettle();

    expect(find.text('from the test'), findsOneWidget);
  });
}

// run it
flutter test integration_test/app_test.dart
// on a device
flutter drive --driver=test_driver/integration_test.dart \
            --target=integration_test/app_test.dart

Golden tests, and why they are the highest-maintenance test there is

A golden test renders something and compares the result against a committed reference image. It catches an enormous range of visual regressions that no other test can see — a shifted margin, a changed colour, a missing icon — and it is also the test most likely to be deleted by a team that has fought it. Both facts follow from the same property: it compares pixels, and pixels change for reasons that have nothing to do with the code.

PropertyGoldenWidget/snapshot
Stable across runsOnly on the same platformAlways
Needs a real renderYesYes (widget tree only)
Catches a layout shiftYesYes, with a size assertion
Catches a colour changeYesNo
Catches a font rendering changeYesNo
Flakiness across platformsHighNone
Review burdenBinary diffsReadable

The platform problem is fundamental, not a bug in a tool. Text rendering differs between operating systems, between font versions, and between CPU architectures — a screenshot taken on macOS with one version of a font will not match on Linux with another, at the sub-pixel level, no matter what tolerance is set. So a golden suite is per-platform, and the honest way to handle that is to generate per-platform baselines and only compare within a platform.

// flutter_test's built-in matcher
import 'package:flutter_test/flutter_test.dart';

testWidgets('the card renders correctly', (tester) async {
  await tester.pumpWidget(const MaterialApp(
    home: Scaffold(body: ProductCard(Product(name: 'Widget', price: 9.99))),
  ));

  await expectLater(
    find.byType(ProductCard),
    matchesGoldenFile('goldens/product_card.png'),
  );
});

// generating the baseline - a separate, deliberate command
$ flutter test --update-goldens
// ...this is the point at which goldens become dangerous: `--update-goldens`
// overwrites every reference in the file, so a run in CI with the flag
// committed to a script destroys the entire suite's value in one command.
// ...guard it three ways:
//   1. never put the flag in a CI script
//   2. a pre-commit hook or CI check that the goldens directory is unchanged
//      after a normal test run
//   3. review the diff: a golden diff is a binary diff that GitHub and most
//      viewers cannot display, so it must be opened in an image viewer
// ...the third is why golden changes belong in their own commit, never mixed
// with a feature.

// and the per-platform structure that makes it work
test/
  goldens/
    product_card.png          # linux reference
    product_card_ios.png      # ...generated per platform, chosen by:
    product_card_macos.png

String goldenName(String base) {
  if (Platform.isIOS) return 'goldens/${base}_ios.png';
  if (Platform.isMacOS) return 'goldens/${base}_macos.png';
  return 'goldens/$base.png';
}
// ...so `dart test` on Linux compares against the Linux reference and never
// against the macOS one. Deterministic, at the cost of N reference images.

// and the tolerance, which is the parameter everyone gets wrong
await expectLater(
  find.byType(ProductCard),
  matchesGoldenFile('goldens/card.png'),
);
// ...the default tolerance is 0 pixels: exact. That is correct on a pinned
// environment and is the single largest source of "passes on my machine".
// ...for text-heavy content on a machine you do not control:
await expectLater(
  find.byType(ProductCard),
  matchesGoldenFile('goldens/card.png', matchers: [
    // ...a per-pixel colour tolerance, which absorbs antialiasing differences
    // WITHOUT absorbing a real design change: 5% is imperceptible, 20% is a
    // visible regression
    isGoldenFileComparator.withSettings(
      pixelComparison: const PixelComparisonSettings(
        maxColorDiff: 0.05,
      ),
    ),
  ]),
);
// ...a large tolerance is not a solution, it is a decision to stop looking.

There is a second kind of golden test that is far more robust and is underused: the golden of a value rather than a pixel. Serialising a widget tree to text and comparing that catches structural regressions — a missing widget, a changed property, a reordered child — with no font or platform dependency at all. Flutter's debugDumpApp produces exactly such a representation, and it is the right tool when the concern is structure rather than appearance.

// the structural golden: no pixels, no fonts, no platform
testWidgets('the checkout summary has three rows in order', (tester) async {
  await tester.pumpWidget(const MaterialApp(home: CheckoutSummary()));
  await tester.pumpAndSettle();

  final text = tester.widgetList<Text>(find.byType(Text))
      .map((t) => t.data)
      .join('|');

  expect(text, 'Subtotal|Tax|Total');
  // ...deterministic everywhere, and it fails when a row is added, removed or
  // reordered - which is precisely the class of regression that a pixel
  // golden catches but cannot explain.

// and the middle ground, which is often enough
testWidgets('the total is bold and right-aligned', (tester) async {
  await tester.pumpWidget(const MaterialApp(home: CheckoutSummary()));

  final total = tester.widget<Text>(find.text('Total'));
  expect(total.style?.fontWeight, FontWeight.bold);

  final box = tester.getRect(find.byKey(const Key('total-row')));
  final other = tester.getRect(find.byKey(const Key('subtotal-row')));
  expect(box.right, closeTo(other.right, 0.01),
      reason: 'the two rows must be flush right');
});
// ...asserting the property rather than the pixels. It cannot catch "this shade
// of grey is wrong" but it survives every font and platform change, and it
// says WHY it failed.

// and the widget-test failures that are their own category
// 1. "A Timer is still pending" - something scheduled and not cancelled. pump
//    and settle, or cancel it in the test.
// 2. Overflowing by 42 pixels on the bottom - a layout constraint violation,
//    which Flutter renders as the yellow-and-black stripe in debug mode only.
//    It is a REAL failure that a release build hides.
// 3. "setState() called after dispose()" - an async callback that completes
//    after the widget is gone. Await the future before the test ends.
// 4. "The finder found 0 widgets" - the thing is not in the tree; check
//    whether it needs a scroll, a pump, or a different Finder.
// ...and the fourth's most useful property: a failure prints the widget tree
// of the enclosing scope, which is usually enough to find the problem without
// any further debugging.

14.8 Coverage, and what it does not tell you

Reading the number, and the three ways it misleads.

// generate it
dart test --coverage=./coverage
// then, to read it in a browser:
dart pub global activate coverage
dart run coverage:format_coverage --lcov --in=coverage --out=coverage/lcov.info \
     --report-on=lib --packages=.dart_tool/package_config.json
genhtml coverage/lcov.info -o coverage/html
open coverage/html/index.html
// THREE WAYS COVERAGE MISLEADS
//
// 1. it measures LINES executed, not behaviour verified
//    a test that calls a function and asserts nothing gives 100%
//    coverage of that function and proves nothing
//
//    test('it runs', () {
//      calculate(1, 2);      // no expect. zero value.
//    });
//
// 2. a getter is trivially covered, and needs no test
//    the average project is 70% covered and the untested 30% is
//    the error handling
//
// 3. it does not measure the ASSERTIONS
//    an expect that never runs, inside an if that is never true,
//    is a line of code. If it is not executed, it is not counted.

// so use coverage as a RATCHET, not a target
// 1. record the current number
// 2. never let it go DOWN
// 3. raise the floor as you improve

// a useful alternative metric: mutation testing
// does the test suite catch a deliberate bug?
// package:mutmut for Python, similar tools elsewhere
// if you change `+` to `-` and the tests still pass, that line
// is not really tested
// the coverage numbers that are actually worth watching
//
// 1. the ERROR PATHS: how many catch blocks are covered?
//    (the linter can tell you: a catch block never executed)
//
// 2. the PERCENTAGE for the files you changed in this PR,
//    not the whole project. A 0.1% drop in a big project can
//    hide an entirely untested new file.
//
// 3. the DIFF coverage, which is the real metric:
//    "every line I added this week has a test that fails if I
//     break it"

// a CI gate that is useful
test('new code must be covered', () {
  final report = parseLcov('coverage/lcov.info');
  final changed = readChangedFiles();   // from the PR diff

  final uncovered = changed
      .where((f) => (report[f]?.linesFound ?? 0) >
                   (report[f]?.linesHit ?? 0))
      .toList();

  if (uncovered.isNotEmpty) {
    fail('these changed files have uncovered lines: $uncovered');
  }
});

Coverage, and the number that does not mean anything

Line coverage measures which lines executed. It is the most widely reported test metric and the least informative per unit of effort, for a specific reason: it is easy to raise without testing anything new. An if with no test hitting the false branch counts as covered because the line executed. A getter counts. A constructor's initializer list counts. Getting from 60% to 95% in that regime is usually a matter of exercising code that cannot fail, which is why a project's coverage can rise while its defect rate rises too.

MetricMeansUseful
LineA line ran at least onceRoughly, as a smoke signal
BranchEach arm of each conditional ranYes - this is the useful one
FunctionA function was calledNo - getters count
Condition coverageBoth sides of each boolean were evaluatedYes, the strictest practical one
Mutation scoreWould a change to the code break a testVery; it is the only one about test QUALITY

The metric that matters is the mutation score, because it is the only one that measures the tests rather than the code. It changes x < y to x <= y, deletes a line, replaces a constant, and checks whether any test fails. A test suite that survives mutation is not verifying the behaviour; it is only exercising the lines. Running it on a codebase is slow and the output is a list of surviving mutants, which is a list of real test gaps.

// coverage
$ dart test --coverage=coverage
$ dart pub global activate coverage
$ dart run coverage:format_coverage --lcov --in=coverage --out=coverage/lcov.info --report-on=lib
$ genhtml coverage/lcov.info -o coverage/html     # if you want the HTML report
// ...for CI, the useful output is not the HTML but the summary:
//   $ dart run coverage:format_coverage --summary=coverage
//   lines: 82.4%  1341/1627

// what CI should enforce, and the honest version of that
// A floor on LINE coverage is a weak guard but it catches one real regression:
// a new file with no tests at all. The useful form is per-file.
const floor = 0.80;
test('coverage floor', () {
  final summary = jsonDecode(File('coverage/summary.json').readAsStringSync());
  final files = summary['files'] as Map;
  final low = files.entries
      .where((e) => (e.value['lines'] as num) < floor)
      .map((e) => '${e.key}: ${((e.value['lines'] as num) * 100).toStringAsFixed(1)}%')
      .toList();
  expect(low, isEmpty, reason: 'below ${floor * 100}%:
${low.join('
')}');
});
// ...which fails the build naming the files, rather than reporting a global
// percentage that can stay high while one important file is untested.

// branch coverage, which is the one to watch
$ dart test --coverage=./coverage
// ...Dart's coverage is LINE based. There is no built-in branch coverage,
// because Dart's coverage collector records line execution and the VM does not
// expose per-edge counts portably. So "branch coverage" is usually computed by
// a lcov-compatible tool reading the same data, and it approximates branches
// from line pairs - which is why an if/else where the two arms are one line
// each can look covered without either arm running.
// ...be honest about this: report line coverage, and read the source for
// untested error paths rather than trusting a branch number.

// and what coverage CANNOT measure, in order of how often it matters
// 1. Correctness. 100% coverage with every assertion trivially true.
// 2. Concurrency. A race needs a schedule; coverage runs one.
// 3. Timing. A timeout at 31 ms rather than 30 is covered and correct.
// 4. External behaviour. A serializer that is covered and loses a byte.
// 5. The user's ability to accomplish something.

// mutation testing, which is the honest metric
$ dart pub global activate mutmut
// ...mutmut is Python and targets Python. For Dart the equivalent is
// usually run manually, or with `package:pointy` / a custom script, because
// Dart's own tooling is thinner here. What you want is the MUTATION SCORE, and
// the honest way to get it is to pick the ten most important functions and
// mutate them by hand:
//   <= becomes <              <- does a test catch it?
//   the constant 3 becomes 4     <- does a test catch it?
//   the return is removed        <- does a test catch it?
//   the condition is negated     <- does a test catch it?
// ...a surviving mutant is a specific, named test gap - far more actionable
// than 18% of lines.

A related measure is worth having because it is the one that tracks a real quality signal: how much of the code is tested at all, rather than how much executed. A package where one module has 95% coverage and the other ten have 30% reports 37% overall, which is honest, but the useful question is which module contains the behaviour a defect would be expensive in. Coverage is only interpretable next to a judgement about which parts matter.

// per-module, with the judgement attached
lib/
  money.dart        96%   // ...every amount in the system passes through this.
                          //    An untested branch here is expensive.
  parser.dart       91%   // ...untrusted input. Same.
  formatting.dart   88%   // ...user-visible but not correctness-critical.
  cache.dart        34%   // ...best-effort; a bug costs a recomputation.
  telemetry.dart    12%   // ...fire and forget. Do not write tests to raise
                          //    this number; test the one function that could
                          //    throw rather than the ten that cannot.
// ...this table is a better artefact than a coverage badge, because it records
// the DECISION. A team that has argued about which modules matter has made a
// decision a percentage cannot make for it.

// and the anti-pattern, which is worth naming because it is common and looks
// like diligence
void test_line_coverage() {
  final calculator = Calculator();
  calculator.add(1, 2);
  calculator.add(0, 0);
  calculator.divide(1, 0);          // ...throws, unhandled - but the line ran
  expect(true, isTrue);             // ...so every line is covered and nothing
}                                   //    is verified
// ...this suite has 100% coverage and would pass with `Calculator` replaced by
// a class whose every method is empty. It is worse than no test, because the
// coverage report now claims the module is fine.

// the rule that prevents it
// ...a test that cannot fail is a defect. If you cannot construct an assertion
// that this implementation is wrong, the test should not exist. Deleting a
// test that asserts `isTrue` is always an improvement, including to coverage,
// because the line it covered was covered by the construction, not the call.
// ...`dart analyze` does not flag this, which is why it survives review.

14.9 Test organisation and CI

Where the tests go, how to run them fast, and what to gate on.

// a structure that scales
test/
  data/
    repo_test.dart             unit, fast, no IO
    merge_test.dart            the pure logic
  platform/
    store_io_test.dart         with @TestOn('vm')
    store_web_test.dart        with @TestOn('browser')
  integration/
    flow_test.dart             slower, marked
  golden/
    widgets_test.dart

// tag the slow ones
@Tags(['slow'])
library;

@Timeout(Duration(minutes: 2))
library;

// then exclude them from the fast run
dart test --exclude-tags slow
dart test --run-skipped
name: dart

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        sdk: ['3.6.0', '3.7.0', stable']
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dart-lang/setup-dart@v1
        with:
          sdk: ${{ matrix.sdk }}

      - run: dart pub get

      - name: analyse
        run: dart analyze --fatal-infos

      - name: format check
        run: dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed .

      - name: test (VM)
        run: dart test --platform vm --coverage=./coverage

      - name: test (browser)
        run: dart test --platform chrome

      - name: upload coverage
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@v4
        with: { files: ./coverage/lcov.info }

  # the build matrix, so no target rots
  build:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dart-lang/setup-dart@v1
      - run: dart pub get
      - run: dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o build/app
      - run: dart compile js bin/main.dart -o build/app.js -O2
      - run: dart compile wasm bin/main.dart -o build/app.wasm -O2
# faster local feedback
# run only the tests that changed
dart test --chain-stack-traces

# or with a watch loop, while you work
dart run watchr 'dart test'                 # a third-party tool
dart test --reporter expanded              # shows each test name

# the fastest possible inner loop for TDD:
//  1. one test file
//  2. dart test test/that_one_file.dart
//  3. keep the test in front of you in the editor
// a sub-second cycle is what makes TDD stick

Test the behaviour, not the implementation. A test that asserts repo.cache.contains('1') breaks the moment you replace the cache, without the product changing. A test that asserts await repo.byId('1') is not null survives any internal refactor and still catches a real regression. When a refactor breaks many tests, the tests were measuring the wrong thing.

Exercises 15

  1. Write a test group for a merge or validation function, covering every branch plus the empty, null and unicode cases.
  2. Write a regression test for a bug you have actually had, and confirm it fails when you revert the fix.
  3. Use fakeAsync to test a retry with backoff, asserting the number of attempts and the elapsed virtual time.
  4. Build a MockClient that asserts on the request URL and headers, then test a 404 mapping.
  5. Write a FixedClock, inject it, and test an expiry logic deterministically with no real waiting.
  6. Generate coverage, find an untested catch block, and add a test for it.
  7. Add a CI job that runs the tests on the VM and in a browser, and that builds all four compilation targets.

Running tests in CI

A CI configuration for tests has four decisions that determine whether it is useful: which tests run on which trigger, whether the suite is sharded or merely parallelised, how nondeterminism is detected, and what the failure notification actually contains. Getting the first two right is worth more than any amount of test sophistication, because a suite that takes four minutes gets skipped and a suite whose failures are not reproducible gets ignored.

TriggerRunsFeedback
Every pushUnit + lint + analyseUnder 2 minutes
Every PRUnit + integration, all platformsUnder 10 minutes
Merge to mainEverything + coverage reportUnder 20 minutes
NightlyFlaky tests, long suite, browserReported next morning
ReleaseEverything, pinned versions, no cacheBlocking

Sharding is the technique that keeps a growing suite fast, and it works only if the shards are balanced by something real. Splitting alphabetically by filename produces shards whose load depends on where the slow tests happen to be named. Sharding by recorded duration produces balanced shards and is worth the extra machinery once the suite passes ten minutes — the data comes from the timing JSON the reporter already writes.

name: test

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  fast:
    name: unit + analyse
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dart-lang/setup-dart@v1
        with: { sdk: stable }

      - run: dart pub get

      # ...1. ANALYSE FIRST, because it is the fastest failure and needs no
      #    test run at all. A lint error should cost 20 seconds, not 4 minutes.
      - name: analyse
        run: dart analyze --fatal-infos --fatal-warnings

      - name: format check
        run: |
          dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed .
      # ...the most-controversial line in most CI configs. It enforces one
      # style and refuses PRs that differ, which is defensible for an
      # application and unhelpful for a library people read.

      # ...2. THE FAST SUBSET, with concurrency pinned. The default is half the
      #    runner's CPU count; on a 2-vCPU runner that is 4 concurrent
      #    isolates for a suite that shares a port, which produces timeouts
      #    that look like real failures.
      - name: unit tests (fast)
        run: dart test --exclude-tags=io,golden,slow --concurrency=4 --reporter=github

      # ...3. CACHE THE PACKAGES, keyed on pubspec.lock AND the SDK version.
      #    Keying on pubspec.yaml alone means a dependency bump is invisible
      #    and the cache serves stale packages.
      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/.pub-cache
          key: pub-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('pubspec.lock') }}-${{ hashFiles('.dart_tool/package_config.json') }}

  full:
    name: full matrix
    needs: fast
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false        # ...so one platform's failure does not cancel
      matrix:                 #    the others and hide their results
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dart-lang/setup-dart@v1
        with: { sdk: stable }
      - run: dart pub get

      - name: tests
        run: dart test --concurrency=2 --reporter=github

      # ...4. UPLOAD THE REPORT EVEN ON FAILURE, which is the step whose absence
      #    makes a CI failure take twenty minutes to diagnose instead of two.
      - if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: test-report-${{ matrix.os }}
          path: build/test-reports/
          retention-days: 14

Nondeterminism detection is the part of a test CI setup that most projects skip and that pays for itself fastest, because a flaky test is more expensive than no test: it trains the team to re-run on red, which destroys the signal the whole system exists to provide. The technique is to run the suite several times with randomised ordering and different seeds, and to report a test that fails intermittently as a failure rather than as an aside.

name: flake detection

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 3 * * *'          # ...nightly, so it never blocks a PR
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  flakes:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dart-lang/setup-dart@v1
        with: { sdk: stable }
      - run: dart pub get

      # ...the mechanism: run the suite N times with a DIFFERENT seed each run.
      # A test that fails on run 3 and passes on runs 1, 2 and 4 is flaky, and
      # the seed tells you which ordering produced the failure.
      - name: 20 randomised runs
        run: |
          for i in $(seq 1 20); do
            seed=$RANDOM
            echo "=== run $i, seed $seed ==="
            if ! dart test --test-randomize-ordering-seed=$seed                             --reporter=github                             --exclude-tags=slow,golden; then
              echo "FLAKE DETECTED at seed $seed (run $i)"
              echo "FLAKE_SEED=$seed" >> $GITHUB_ENV
              echo "FLAKE_RUN=$i" >> $GITHUB_ENV
              # ...keep going, so one run reports every flaky test rather than
              # only the first. Flakiness is rarely a single test.
              failures=$((failures + 1))
            fi
          done
          echo "FAILED_RUNS=$failures" >> $GITHUB_ENV

      - name: report
        if: env.FLAKE_RUN != ''
        run: |
          echo "## Flaky test detected" >> $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY
          echo "- failed on run $FLAKE_RUN with seed $FLAKE_SEED" >> $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY
          echo "- reproduce: `dart test --test-randomize-ordering-seed=$FLAKE_SEED`"             >> $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY
          echo "- $FAILED_RUNS of 20 runs failed" >> $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY

      # ...and the rule that makes this actionable: a flaky test is a FAILING
      #    test, with an owner and a deadline. It is not filed as a low-priority
      #    issue and forgotten, because the cost is paid by everyone on every
      #    red build thereafter.

// and the three causes of a flaky test, in order of frequency
// 1. INTER-TEST DEPENDENCE - state that survives a test. Found by: does it
//    fail when run alone? `dart test --name "the flaky one"`.
// 2. TIMING - a real sleep where a fake clock belonged, or a timeout too tight
//    for a loaded runner. Found by: does it fail on a busy machine, and only
//    on a busy machine?
// 3. GENUINE NONDETERMINISM - Map iteration order, a hash seed, concurrent
//    access. Found by: run with randomised order and it fails in some seeds.
// ...and the diagnosis that is worth trying first: run the single test 20 times.
// If it fails 3 of 20, it is nondeterminism in the test or the code. If it
// never fails alone, it is inter-test dependence.

Three things belong in CI that are not tests, and their absence is why some suites are trusted and others are not. A build that pins its dependencies exactly, so a failure is reproducible a month later. A build that reports the SDK version and the resolved dependency versions in the log, so "works on CI" is diagnosable. And a build that runs dart analyze --fatal-infos rather than only failing on errors, which catches unused imports and dead code — the two things that most often indicate a code path nobody has tested.

// the diagnostic header, printed at the top of every CI run
- name: environment
  run: |
    {
      echo "### Environment"
      echo "- dart: $(dart --version 2>&1)"
      echo "- os: ${{ runner.os }}"
      echo "- commit: ${{ github.sha }}"
    } >> $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY

- name: dependency versions
  run: dart pub deps --style=list | tee build/deps.txt
# ...so a failure report includes the exact resolution. `pubspec.lock` is
# committed for an application and NOT for a library - which is why a library's
# CI must resolve fresh each run, and must therefore be tested against whatever
# is current rather than against what once worked.

// and the three checks that are cheap and catch real problems
# 1. the package still resolves against the LATEST dependency versions
- name: pub upgrade --dry-run
  run: dart pub upgrade --dry-run
# ...a new major version of a dependency can break the build without any
# change of yours. This is not checked by `pub get`.

# 2. the package still works against the OLDEST supported SDK
# ...declared as environment: sdk: '>=3.4.0 <4.0.0' and tested on the lower
# bound. Testing only on stable means the declared floor is untested.

# 3. no lockfile committed, for a library
- name: check no lockfile
  run: test ! -f pubspec.lock || (echo "pubspec.lock must not be committed" && exit 1)
# ...committed by accident, a library stops being tested against current
# versions, and a transitive dependency release that breaks it is found by your
# users.

// and what a CI failure notification should contain, because this is the
// difference between a two-minute fix and an afternoon
//   * the failing test's full name and the reason, not just "3 tests failed"
//   * the seed, if the suite randomises
//   * a link to the artifacts, which survive 14 days
//   * the exact command to reproduce locally, on the failing platform
//   * the dependency resolution
// ...a notification with only "tests failed" and a red X sends the reader to
// the CI log, where they must scroll past the install step to find the
// assertion message - and most will not.

15 · Performance

15.1 Measuring before optimising15.2 The DevTools profiler15.3 Microbenchmarks15.4 Allocation and the GC15.5 Data structure choices15.6 Async performance15.7 Startup time15.8 Tree shaking and dead code15.9 The optimisation checklist

Dart is fast. Knowing where it is not, and what to do about it, is the actual skill.

15.1 Measuring before optimising

The rule, and the profiler setup that makes measurement easy.

// THE RULE: never optimise without a measurement.
// an unmeasured optimisation is a guess with a maintenance cost.

// what to measure
// 1. CPU time: which functions consume the most milliseconds
// 2. memory: which allocations dominate, and what is retained
// 3. startup: time to first useful frame
// 4. throughput: operations per second in a hot loop

// what NOT to optimise
// - code that runs once at startup and takes 2ms
// - code that is not measurably slow on a real device
// - a "hot path" that is only hot in theory

// the measurement trap: profile on the device you actually have
// users, which is usually NOT your development machine. A modern
// laptop has 3-5x the single-core performance of a mid-range
// phone, and a desktop browser JIT is faster than an AOT build.

// profile a release build, because AOT and JIT differ
dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o app
./app --profile
// or, in Flutter:
// flutter run --profile
// flutter build --profile
// the VM service, which is how you attach a profiler
dart run --observe=8181 bin/main.dart
// or, for a compiled binary
dart run --observe bin/main.dart

// in another terminal
dart pub global activate dev_tools
dart pub global run dev_tools

// or the timeline recorder, for a script
dart run --timeline-streams=Dart,GC,API \
         --timeline_recorder=stdout \
         --timeline-file=timeline.json \
         bin/main.dart

// and the CPU sampler, directly
dart --observe=8181 --profiler --timeline=timeline.json bin/main.dart

Measure first, and measure the right thing

An optimisation is a bet: this change costs complexity and buys time. The bet is only sound if you know the size of both sides, and the discipline that keeps it sound is measuring before and after, on a machine you control, with a number you wrote down. Every performance regression story shares the same first sentence — nobody measured, so nobody knew, so nobody noticed — and the fix is always upstream of the optimisation.

QuestionInstrumentWrong answer looks like
Is it slow?A wall-clock timer in a realistic run"Fast on my laptop"
Where is the time?A sampled or instrumented profileGuessing from the code
How much will this help?A microbenchmark of the hot partA microbenchmark of the wrong part
Did it help?The same measurement, re-run"Feels snappier"

The two failure modes are symmetrical and both are common. Measuring the wrong thing produces an optimisation that does not help: a microbenchmark of a function that takes 40 nanoseconds, inside a request that spends 6 milliseconds in a regex, is a week of work for nothing. And measuring the right thing but comparing badly produces a false conclusion: a run that included JIT warm-up, or a cold file cache, or a garbage collection, will make anything look like an improvement.

// the measurement, written so it can be repeated and compared
import 'dart:io';

class Bench {
  final String label;
  final int iterations;
  Bench(this.label, {this.iterations = 1000});

  int run(void Function() body) {
    // ...three rules, and breaking any of them makes the number meaningless:
    //   1. discard the FIRST run - it pays for JIT compilation, which is
    //      the largest single component of a short benchmark
    //   2. take the MINIMUM of several runs, not the mean - the minimum is the
    //      run that was least disturbed by the OS, and it is the most
    //      reproducible statistic for a piece of work this small
    //   3. report the spread too, because a large spread means the machine is
    //      too noisy for the answer to mean anything
    body();
    final times = <int>[];
    for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
      final sw = Stopwatch()..start();
      for (var j = 0; j & iterations; j++) {
        body();
      }
      times.add(sw.elapsedMicroseconds ~/ iterations);
    }
    times.sort();
    final min = times.first;
    final max = times.last;
    final med = times[times.length ~/ 2];
    if (max > min * 3) {
      stderr.writeln('$label: NOISY (min ${min}us, max ${max}us) - rerun');
    }
    return min;   // ...in microseconds per iteration
  }
}

// and the comparison, which is the part that gets skipped
void main() {
  final before = Bench('before').run(() => parseOld(input));
  final after = Bench('after').run(() => parseNew(input));
  stdout.writeln('before ${before}us  after ${after}us  '
      'speedup ${(before / after).toStringAsFixed(2)}x');
  // ...a 1.05x "improvement" is inside the noise. Report it, do not ship it, and
  // if it matters find out why the change did not do what you expected - a
  // 1.05x from an algorithmic change usually means the hot path was never
  // reached in the benchmark.
}

// the four things that make a measurement wrong, in order of frequency
// 1. JIT warm-up included        -> discard the first run
// 2. a dead-code-eliminated call -> store the result and print it
// 3. dead-code elimination itself -> the fix is `expect(result, isNotNull)`
// 4. constant folding            -> pass the value in as a parameter
int parseOld(String input) { ... }
int parseNew(String input) { ... }

Item 3 deserves its own treatment because it is the one that produces a benchmark that reports zero. Dart's AOT compiler removes a call whose result is unused, so a benchmark that calls parse(input) and discards the answer measures an empty loop. The symptom is a suspiciously perfect number — 0 or 1 microsecond for any function at all. The fix is to make the result observable, and the check is to change the function's body and see whether the number moves.

// dead-code elimination, and the three ways to observe it
int sum(List<int> xs) => xs.fold(0, (a, b) => a + b);

void main() {
  // BROKEN: `sum(input)` is called and the result dropped, so the compiler
  // removes the call. The loop below measures nothing.
  for (var i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    sum(input);
  }
  // reported: 0 us/iteration, for any input at all

  // FIX 1: consume it
  var sink = 0;
  for (var i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    sink += sum(input);
  }
  assert(sink >= 0);          // ...and keep the sink observable too

  // FIX 2: Blackhole, which is the standard solution and works in AOT too
  int _sink = 0;
  T blackhole<T>(T value) {
    _sink ^= value is int ? value : 0;
    return value;
  }
  blackhole(sum(input));

  // FIX 3: assert, in a test, not a benchmark
  test('sum is correct', () {
    expect(sum([1, 2, 3]), 6);   // ...a test is not optimised away, and it is
  });                            //    also the assertion you needed anyway

// the general rule: if a change to the function body does not change the
// number, you are measuring nothing. Try that before you trust any benchmark
// you have not yet falsified.

Finally, the choice of workload. A benchmark over synthetic data measures the code's behaviour on data that does not exist, and the most common consequence is that a hash lookup is measured on collision-free keys and a sort is measured on an already-sorted list. Real workloads have duplicate keys, partially-sorted input, and a size distribution with a long tail. The defensible approach is to take a real input — a captured request body, a production log line, a real file — and keep it as a fixture, because that is the only version of the benchmark that predicts anything.

// the workload that predicts anything
import 'dart:convert';
import 'dart:io';

void main() {
  // ...a real file, committed as a fixture, and its shape documented:
  //   benchmark/fixtures/requests.jsonl  - 12,400 lines, 84 MB
  //   p50 line 180 B, p99 line 2.1 MB, 340 lines with a 40-field object
  // ...the p99 matters. A benchmark over the first 1,000 lines measures the
  // easy case, and the easy case is not the one that is slow.
  final lines = File('benchmark/fixtures/requests.jsonl')
      .readAsLinesSync();

  final sw = Stopwatch()..start();
  var total = 0;
  for (final line in lines) {
    total += parse(line).fieldCount;
  }
  print('${lines.length} lines, ${sw.elapsedMilliseconds} ms, $total fields');
  // ...re-run it after a change and diff the two numbers. That diff is the only
  // result this whole section is for.
}

// and the two ways a real fixture is still wrong
// 1. it is a snapshot, and the data drifts. A year-old capture of an API
//    response is a shape the server no longer returns. Re-capture it on a
//    schedule, or the benchmark measures a shape nobody produces.
// 2. it is too big to keep in a repository. Then generate it from a seed - a
//    fixed seed, so it is byte-identical on every machine - and commit the
//    GENERATOR, not the data.
//    int makeLines(int n) => List.generate(n, (i) => synth(i, seed: 7));

15.2 The DevTools profiler

The three views in the performance panel, and what each is for.

// 1. CPU PROFILER
//    a flame chart: the width of a bar is time spent, the stack
//    depth is the call chain. Look for:
//      - a wide bar: a function that is genuinely slow
//      - a wide bar with a wide bar under it: the cost is in
//        something it calls
//      - many thin bars: allocation churn
//    The "Bottom Up" view is better for finding the root cause:
//    it shows the total time per function including children.

// 2. ALLOCATIONS
//    the flame chart of allocations. Look for:
//      - a function that allocates on every call in a loop
//      - large allocations: a 1MB object per iteration
//    This is usually the highest-value panel. Dart's generational
//    GC is efficient, but frequent allocation still costs.

// 3. MEMORY
//    the live object count by class, over time. Look for:
//      - a sawtooth: normal GC behaviour
//      - a rising floor: objects are being retained. A LEAK.
//      - one class growing without bound: a cache with no eviction

// 4. the TIMELINE
//    frame-by-frame. In Flutter this is the frame chart: a red bar
//    is a frame over 16ms, and 60fps means no red bars.
// how to read a flame chart
//
//  A wide box at the top, called from deep: the top function is
//  doing the work. Optimise it.
//
//  A thin box that is very deep: lots of calls, each cheap. Look at
//  the call count, not the time. Often a virtual function that
//  should be a direct call.
//
//  Wide boxes appearing MANY times: a loop. The total is
//  width * count.
//
//  A wide box with an arrow-shaped child: the child is the loop.
//  The arrow shape means "called many times, one at a time".

// the specific patterns worth knowing
//  - lots of small closures: allocation churn
//  - a List.add in a loop that does not pre-size: reallocation
//  - string concatenation in a loop: O(n^2)
//  - a Map lookup inside a loop over a List: should be a Set
//  - getJSON on every call: a cache, and the data does not change

The DevTools profiler, and reading a profile properly

A profile is a sampled or instrumented record of where time went, and its value depends entirely on whether you read it correctly. The three readings people get wrong are: reading the widest bar as the most important one, reading a flame chart's width as inclusive rather than self time, and concluding from a short run. Each produces a confidently wrong optimisation.

ViewAnswersCommon misreading
Timeline, CPUWhich frames, over timeTotal bar area = total cost
Flame chartCall stack, one sample per columnA wide bar is a slow function
Call treeWho calls whom, with costTop-of-tree is the hotspot
AllocationWhat allocated, and what retained itHigh count means a leak
Heap snapshotWhat is retained, right nowLargest object is the problem

Flame chart is the one that misleads most, and the reason is that width is total time — everything a frame does, including its children. A function that allocates a list which a parser then scans appears enormous and does almost nothing itself. The number to read is the frame's self time, and the way to see it is to look for the frames that are wide because of their own code: no children at the bottom of the stack, or a high self-time figure in the call tree.

// starting a profile run
$ dart run --observe=8080 bin/server.dart
// ...or, for an existing app, `dart devtools` prints the URL. Record with the
// profiler, drive the real workload, stop, then read:

// WHAT TO READ, IN ORDER
// 1. TOTAL time in the run. If it is not where you expected, your workload is
//    not the production workload and everything below is about the wrong thing.
// 2. The widest TOP-LEVEL frame. That is the entry point, not the hotspot.
// 3. Within it, the widest frame that has NO WIDE CHILDREN. That is your
//    self-time hotspot. There is usually one, and it is usually not what the
//    profile's summary lists first.
// 4. Look for the shapes that indicate a different problem entirely:
//      - a very tall stack (30+ frames)          recursion, or a lost iterator
//      - many identical adjacent frames          a retry loop
//      - a wide frame that is entirely GC        allocation pressure
//      - a gap between frames (idle)             I/O, or a lock

// and the four numbers DevTools shows that mean specific things
// Total time      wall clock for the recording; the denominator for everything
// CPU time        excludes time blocked on I/O; if CPU << total, you are
//                 waiting, not computing, and no CPU optimisation will help
// GC events       a spike here means allocation, and the allocation view names
//                 the site that caused it
// Frame rate      Flutter only; below 60 fps the frame budget is exceeded and
//                 the timeline shows which build method ran in the frame

// and the thing to do with a profile you do not understand
// Record the SAME workload twice, diff the two call trees, and look only at
// what moved. A diff is far easier to read than a profile, because it removes
// the 200 frames that are the same in both runs - and those are the ones you
// were never going to change.

Two profile types answer questions the CPU profile cannot, and both are about memory rather than time. The allocation profile records every allocation with its call site, which is the direct way to find what is producing garbage. The heap snapshot records what is retained at a moment, which is the only way to find a leak — because a leak is not visible in an allocation profile at all, since every allocation it reports was correct at the time.

// the allocation profile: finds the garbage
// DevTools > Performance > "Record allocations", then drive the workload.
// The result is a flame chart where every column is an allocation, so the widest
// column is the SITE, and - unlike the CPU chart - a wide column is
// unconditionally bad, because allocating is never free.
//
// the three findings it produces, in order of usefulness
// 1. a site allocating in a loop, where one object would do:
for (final row in rows) {
  final parts = row.split(',');        // ...a List<String> per row
  process(parts);
}
// ...the fix is a scan with no intermediate collection, or a reusable buffer.

// 2. a closure allocated per iteration, which is invisible in the source
for (final item in items) {
  scheduler.add(() => handle(item)); // ...a new closure each time; if the
}                                      //    queue holds them, it is a leak
// ...the fix is a tear-off of a bound method, which Dart allocates once:
//   scheduler.add(handle.bindFirst(item))

// 3. boxing in a hot generic path
// ...generic code that stores a double in a List<Object> boxes it. If a
//    List<double> is passed to code typed as List<Object> by an
//    upcast, every element is re-boxed. Keep the static type concrete.

// the heap snapshot: finds the leak, and is the only thing that can
// DevTools > Memory > "Take snapshot", at a moment when the leak has
// accumulated. Then look at the DOMINATOR TREE, not the class list.
//
// why the dominator tree and not the class list:
//   the class list says "there are 400,000 Strings". So what. Strings are
//   everywhere and 400,000 of them is often correct.
//   the dominator tree says which object RETAINS them. A single retained Map
//   holding a 400,000-entry cache is one row, and the fix is one line.
// ...the pattern to look for: a long run of identical class names under one
// parent, where the parent's own size is trivial. That is a collection that
// grew without bound, and the parent is the bug.
//
// and the confirmation step, which is the only way to be sure
// 1. take snapshot A
// 2. run the suspect operation 50 times
// 3. take snapshot B
// 4. diff A against B
// ...a diff that grows linearly with the count is a leak; a diff that is flat is
// a cache, and a cache is a design decision rather than a defect. The difference
// is worth 50 iterations of certainty.

A third profile type exists for Flutter specifically and is the answer to the most common Flutter performance question, which is "why is this one screen janky". The frame timeline records each frame's build, layout and paint phases, and a frame that overruns 16.7 ms is visible as a red band with the phases coloured. A frame that is red only in build means the widget tree is doing work it should not; red only in layout means a constraint is unstable; red only in paint means something is being repainted that did not change.

// the Flutter frame timeline, and what each coloured band means
// DevTools > Performance, enable "Track frames" (formerly Flutter Inspector
// > Performance overlay, `showPerformanceOverlay`).

// a frame over budget looks like this:
//
//   ################ BUILD ################
//   |############## LAYOUT ##############|#################### PAINT ####
//   |                                  |                            |
//   0ms                              8ms                          16.7ms
//   ^                                            ^        ^
//   build 8ms                         layout 2.5ms  paint 6ms
//
// ...and the three diagnoses, one per phase
//
// BUILD is large  -> the widget tree is being rebuilt when it need not be.
//    The three causes, in order of frequency:
//      a) a setState() high in the tree for a change deep in it. Move the
//         setState down, or pass the value in as a constructor argument so
//         only the dependent subtree rebuilds.
//      b) a build method that allocates. A List literal in build() is a new
//         list every frame, which invalidates the children's == comparison
//         and rebuilds them too.
//      c) an expensive expression in a const-able place. `Text(expensive())`
//         is re-evaluated on every build; make it a field computed in
//         initState or didUpdateWidget.
//
// LAYOUT is large -> an unstable constraint, which is a genuine Flutter bug
//    and produces a distinctive double-frame in the timeline: build, layout,
//    build, layout. The cause is a widget whose size depends on its position,
//    so laying it out changes what it builds. Almost always an IntrinsicHeight,
//    a FutureBuilder whose future is created inside build, or a Row of
//    Expanded with a child that sizes to its content.
//
// PAINT is large -> something is repainting that did not change. The
//    diagnostic is `debugRepaintRainbowEnabled = true`, which outlines every
//    repainting widget in a rotating colour. A large area outlined when only
//    a small thing changed is the finding; the usual cause is an Opacity or
//    ClipRRect around something that repaints, because those force a save
//    layer for their whole subtree.

// and the two measurements that decide whether any of it matters
//   frame budget: 16.7 ms at 60 Hz, 8.3 ms at 120 Hz
//   your app's actual rate: measure it, do not assume. A ProMotion iPhone and a
//   60 Hz Android device are different budgets, and a jank report from one says
//   nothing about the other.

15.3 Microbenchmarks

Isolating a hot function, and the mistakes that make benchmarks lie.

// the simplest useful benchmark
import 'dart:math';

int sumLoop(List<int> data) {
  var total = 0;
  for (final x in data) total += x;
  return total;
}

int sumFold(List<int> data) => data.fold(0, (a, b) => a + b);

int sumWhere(List<int> data) => data.where((x) => true).fold(0, (a, b) => a + b);

void main() {
  final data = List.generate(1 << 20, (i) => i);

  // 1. WARM UP: the JIT compiles and optimises on the first runs
  for (var i = 0; i < 50; i++) {
    sumLoop(data);
    sumFold(data);
  }

  // 2. MEASURE with Stopwatch
  for (final (name, fn) in [
    ('loop', sumLoop),
    ('fold', sumFold),
    ('where', sumWhere),
  ]) {
    final sw = Stopwatch()..start();
    var result = 0;
    for (var i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
      result = fn(data);
    }
    sw.stop();
    print('$name: ${sw.elapsedMicroseconds / 20}us  (=$result)');
  }
}

// the output, roughly:
//   loop:   1800us
//   fold:   5200us     - the closure call per element costs
//   where:  7100us    - and an extra layer on top
// THE FIVE MISTAKES THAT MAKE A BENCHMARK WRONG

// 1. NOT WARMING UP
//    the first runs are slow: bytecode, then optimised JIT code.
//    always warm up, and discard the results.

// 2. THE COMPILER ELIMINATING THE WORK
void bench() {
  final data = prepare();
  sumLoop(data);      // the result is unused: the JIT may skip it
}
void bench() {
  final data = prepare();
  final r = sumLoop(data);
  print(r);           // this keeps the work alive
}

// 3. MEASURING THE WRONG THING
//    a microbenchmark measures a hot loop in isolation. Real code
//    has cache misses, allocation pressure and branch
//    mispredictions that a microbenchmark does not reproduce.
//    the CPU profile of the real app is the ground truth.

// 4. ONE RUN
//    the machine is noisy. run it many times, take the MINIMUM
//    (not the average: the minimum is the true cost without
//    interference), or the median.

// 5. DEBUG MODE
//    asserts are on, and the code is unoptimised.
//    run with --release or compile first.

// for a proper benchmark harness, use package:benchmark, or
// benchmark_harness, which handle warmup and statistics
// a better harness, without a dependency
typedef Bench = (String, Object Function());

void runBenchmarks(List<Bench> benchmarks, {int runs = 100}) {
  // warm up everything first
  for (var r = 0; r < 10; r++) {
    for (final (_, fn) in benchmarks) {
      fn();
    }
  }

  final results = <String, List<int>>{};
  for (var r = 0; r < runs; r++) {
    for (final (name, fn) in benchmarks) {
      final sw = Stopwatch()..start();
      fn();
      sw.stop();
      (results[name] ??= []).add(sw.elapsedMicroseconds);
    }
  }

  results.forEach((name, times) {
    times.sort();
    final min = times.first;
    final median = times[times.length ~/ 2];
    final p95 = times[(times.length * 0.95).floor()];
    print('${name.padRight(20)} min=${min}us  '
        'median=${median}us  p95=${p95}us');
  });
}

Microbenchmarks, and the two ways they lie

A microbenchmark times a small operation in isolation. It is the right tool for exactly one question — is this operation faster than that one, by how much — and the wrong tool for everything else, because isolation is exactly what it removes and what you needed. Two lies dominate: the benchmark measures something the optimiser deletes, and it measures a hot cache that production never has.

LieSymptomFix
Dead-code elimination0 or 1 us for anythingConsume the result
Constant foldingComputation vanishesPass values as parameters
Hot cachesReal inputs are 10x slowerVary the input each iteration
Warm branch predictorsPolymorphic site looks monomorphicRotate several types
Unrealistic dataSort of sorted dataShuffle before timing
Too few iterationsTimer resolution dominatesCalibrate to >100 ms per run

Constant folding and dead-code elimination are the same mechanism seen from two sides, and both are worth understanding rather than memorising because they are the reason a benchmark can be fast for a function that is slow in the only place it is used. The compiler proves an expression's value at compile time if every input is a literal, and removes a call if the result is unused. A benchmark that passes a literal and discards the result is measuring a subtraction between zero and the cost of being compiled.

// before: a benchmark of a function that does not run
int addAll(List<int> a, List<int> b) {
  var total = 0;
  for (var i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
    total += a[i] + b[i];
  }
  return total;
}

void main() {
  var sink = 0;
  for (var i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
    addAll([1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]);   // ...the two lists are CONSTANT, so the
  }                                  //    call may be folded to a literal 42
                                     //    and the result is discarded: the
                                     //    whole loop can be removed
  print(sink);                       // ...run it with `dart compile exe` and
}                                    //    the answer is 0 us, and correct

// after: the inputs vary, and the result is consumed
void main() {
  var sink = 0;
  var seed = 0;
  for (var i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
    seed = (seed * 31 + i) & 0xff;
    sink += addAll([seed, seed + 1, seed + 2], [seed + 3, seed + 4, seed + 5]);
  }
  print(sink);   // ...now it runs, and now the number means something
}

// the one-line falsification test, worth running on every benchmark you write
// ...change the function body to something 10x more expensive, re-run, and
// check the number moved. If it did not, you are measuring nothing. This takes
// one minute and is the highest-value minute in benchmarking.

// and the compilation mode matters, because it decides what CAN be removed
$ dart run bench.dart             # JIT: optimises at runtime, no folding of
                                  //      your literals across the whole program
$ dart compile exe bench.dart -o bench
                                  # AOT: whole-program, so cross-function
                                  #      inlining and folding are available
// ...the AOT number is the one that predicts production for a server, and the
// JIT number is the one that predicts development. A change that helps one and
// not the other is worth understanding rather than picking the flattering one.
// ...and a build of `dart compile js` is a third, different machine entirely.

The second lie is subtler and costs more engineering time: a microbenchmark runs the same input thousands of times in a row, so every cache in the machine is warm — the branch predictor has learned the loop, the data is in L1, the allocator has a free block ready. Production sees cold caches every time the code is reached after other work. A benchmark can therefore show a 3x speedup for a change that is worth nothing, and the reverse mistake is more expensive: rejecting a real improvement because the benchmark's baseline was already cache-warm.

// making a benchmark honest about cache state
void main() {
  // 1. ROTATE THE INPUT so no two iterations touch the same memory.
  //    This is the single most effective change to a naive benchmark.
  final data = List.generate(1 << 16, (i) => i);   // 256 KB: bigger than L1
  final order = List.generate(data.length, (i) => i);
  order.shuffle(Random(42));            // ...a FIXED seed, so the run is
                                        //    reproducible; `shuffle` without a
                                        //    seed makes the benchmark
                                        //    irreproducible, which is worse

  var sink = 0;
  for (final i in order) {
    sink += transform(data[i]);
  }
  print(sink);

  // 2. POLYMORPHISM, if the site is generic. A benchmark that always passes
  //    List<int> lets the JIT emit a monomorphic inline; production passes
  //    two or three types and gets a dispatch.
  for (final xs in <List<Object>>[
    <int>[1, 2, 3], <String>['a', 'b'], <double>[1.0, 2.0],
  ]) {
    sink += process(xs);
  }

  // 3. SIZE SWEEP, which turns one number into a complexity measurement and is
  //    the most informative thing a microbenchmark can produce.
  for (final n in [1 << 8, 1 << 12, 1 << 16, 1 << 20]) {
    final sw = Stopwatch()..start();
    final r = runOn(data.sublist(0, n));
    final us = sw.elapsedMicroseconds;
    print('n=$n  ${us}us  ${(us * 1000 / n).toStringAsFixed(2)}ns/item  r=$r');
  }
  // n=256     1200us   4.68ns/item    <- in L1
  // n=4096    8800us   2.15ns/item    <- the best number, and the least
  //                                     representative: everything fits in
  //                                     cache and the loop dominates
  // n=1048576 94ms    0.09ns/item    <- dominated by memory bandwidth
  // ...the middle rows are what you care about, and the shape of the curve is
  // what tells you the algorithm: flat per-item = linear; per-item rising =
  // superlinear.
}

// and the arithmetic that makes a benchmark meaningful at all
// a Stopwatch has microsecond resolution, so a single iteration of a fast
// function reads as 0. Calibrate: run the body once, time it, and choose an
// iteration count that gives at least 100 ms per run. Then the resolution
// error is 0.001% rather than 100%.

Finally, the microbenchmark that is not really a microbenchmark, and is often the most useful thing in this chapter: measuring a whole operation with realistic arguments, once, rather than a fragment in a tight loop. This is sometimes called a scenario benchmark, and it is what answers "is the new serialiser faster than the old one for a 2 MB response" — a question no microbenchmark of encode() can answer, because the answer depends on allocation, cache behaviour and the branch profile of the real input, all of which a tight loop eliminates.

// the scenario benchmark: whole operation, real input, measured once
import 'dart:convert';
import 'dart:io';

void main(List<String> args) {
  final path = args.isEmpty ? 'benchmark/fixtures/response.json' : args[0];
  final bytes = File(path).readAsBytesSync();
  final text = String.fromCharCodes(bytes);

  // run each implementation on the SAME bytes, alternating, so drift in machine
  // load affects both equally
  final results = <String, int>{};
  for (var round = 0; round < 3; round++) {
    results['legacy'] = _time(() => legacyDecode(text));
    results['new'] = _time(() => newDecode(text));
  }

  final legacy = results['legacy']!;
  final nw = results['new']!;
  print('legacy ${legacy}ms   new ${nw}ms   '
      'speedup ${(legacy / nw).toStringAsFixed(2)}x');
  // ...take the MINIMUM of the three rounds, for the same reason as before: the
  //    fastest run is the one that was least disturbed. The MEDIAN across
  //    rounds is a reasonable alternative if the spread is small.

  // and the check that makes it credible rather than merely fast
  final a = legacyDecode(text);
  final b = newDecode(text);
  if (!_deepEquals(a, b)) {
    stderr.writeln('FAIL: the two implementations disagree');
    exit(1);
  }
  // ...a scenario benchmark that does not first prove the two implementations
  // produce the same result is not a benchmark, it is a race between two
  // different programs. This check belongs at the top, not in a comment.
}

int _time(void Function() body) {
  final sw = Stopwatch()..start();
  body();
  return sw.elapsedMilliseconds;
}

15.4 Allocation and the GC

Why allocation is the main cost, and how to reduce it.

// Dart uses a generational, concurrent, incremental mark-sweep GC.
// it is fast, but allocation is not free:
//   - every allocation is a bump of a pointer plus a few writes
//   - every object has a 2-word header
//   - frequent allocation triggers frequent collections
//   - a collection of a large live set takes real time

// SO: allocation rate matters more than total allocation.

// the pattern that allocates in a loop
List<int> slowSum(List<int> data) {
  var total = 0;
  for (final x in data) {
    total += x;
  }
  return [total];                 // one allocation: fine
}

List<int> allocating(List<int> data) {
  final results = <int>[];
  for (var i = 0; i < data.length; i++) {
    results.add((data[i] * 2).toString().length);   // a closure? a String?
  }
  return results;
}

// the fix: pre-size, and avoid the intermediate objects
List<int> efficient(List<int> data) {
  final results = List<int>.filled(data.length, 0);
  for (var i = 0; i < data.length; i++) {
    results[i] = data[i] * 2;      // no intermediate allocation
  }
  return results;
}

// closures inside a loop: a common, invisible cost
for (var i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
  items.add(() => doSomething(i));    // a closure per iteration: 1000 objects
}

// sometimes unavoidable, sometimes not
// if you only iterate once, a for-in loop with no closure is fine
// the specialised collections, which avoid per-element overhead
import 'dart:typed_data';

// a List<int> boxes every element (unless it is a small int in
// the SMI range) and adds a type check on every access
final boxed = List<int>.filled(1000000, 0);       // ~8MB + headers

// a typed list is contiguous, with no per-element object
final flat = Int32List(1000000);                     // 4MB, no overhead
// or Float64List for doubles: 8 bytes, no boxing

// when to use which
//   List<T> for objects, or a small or variable-length list
//   Int32List / Float64List / Uint8List for bulk numeric data
//   Float32List when precision is not needed: half the memory

// the same applies to strings: a List<String> of 1000000
// entries has 1000000 object headers. A single String with a
// separator is far more compact.

// and the 2D case from chapter 5
// a nested List<List<int>> has a header per row.
// a flat Int32List with computed indices has one allocation.

Allocation and the garbage collector

Dart's collector is a generational, concurrent, mark-sweep collector, and the practical consequence of that description is short: short-lived objects are collected cheaply and long-lived objects are collected expensively. A program that allocates a short-lived object per operation is nearly free. A program that promotes objects to the old generation and then allocates more triggers old-generation collections, which mark the whole heap, which is where a latency spike comes from. Almost every GC problem is a promotion problem wearing a disguise.

GenerationContainsCollected
New spaceRecently allocated, youngEvery scavenge, very cheap
Old spaceSurvived two scavenges, or largeMark-sweep, marks the heap
Large objectAbove the large-allocation thresholdOld space, directly

Promotion is the concept to hold on to, because it explains three otherwise-baffling observations. A long-running process gets slower over hours without a leak. A cache that is only read is harmless until it is written to. And a service's p99 latency is fine for days and then has a spike every few minutes. All three are the collector reaching a threshold on old-space size or fragmentation, not a change in the code.

// what the GC reports, and what each number means
// DevTools > Memory, or the VM flags below, or from your own metrics
//
//   New space capacity      the scavenger's working set; grows to fit the
//                           allocation rate, so a high rate means a bigger
//                           new space and more memory
//   Old space used          THIS is the number that matters. Steady = fine.
//                           Linear growth = a leak
//   Scavenge count          cheap collections; hundreds per second is normal
//   Mark-sweep count        expensive ones; should be rare. One per second
//                           means the old generation is too large
//   Promotion rate          objects surviving two scavenges. A high rate is the
//                           leading indicator of a mark-sweep storm, and it is
//                           visible BEFORE the spikes start

// the three allocation patterns, and their cost
// 1. SHORT-LIVED, per operation. Cheap. Do not contort code to avoid this.
//    for (final x in items) { total += transform(x); }     // fine
// 2. MEDIUM-LIVED, per request. Survives one scavenge, promoted. Moderate.
//    ...and this is the band where a small change has a large effect.
// 3. LONG-LIVED, per session. Promoted immediately, marked forever. Expensive
//    per object, and the only kind that can be a leak.
//    ...so: allocating in a loop is fine. Allocating in a loop and STORING is
//    the thing that fills the old generation.

// the allocation site that is almost always the answer
//   ...a List or Map that grows without bound, because a map keyed by a value
// that is itself unbounded is a leak with a plausible name.
final _seen = <String, Widget>{};
Widget build(BuildContext c, String key) {
  return _seen.putIfAbsent(key, () => const SizedBox());
}
// ...a bounded cache is fine. This one is bounded by "the number of distinct
// keys the user has ever typed", which is not a bound.

// the fix, and it is almost always a bound plus a policy
class BoundedCache<K, V> {
  final int maxEntries;
  final int maxBytes;
  final _entries = <K, _Entry<V>>{};
  final _onEvict;
  int _bytes = 0;
  BoundedCache({required this.maxEntries, required this.maxBytes, this._onEvict});

  V get(K k) {
    final e = _entries.remove(k)!;
    _entries[k] = e;             // ...move to the end: this is the recency
    return e.value;              //    part, and the remove/insert IS the LRU
  }

  void put(K k, V v, int bytes) {
    if (_entries.containsKey(k)) {
      _bytes -= _entries.remove(k)!.bytes;
    }
    _entries[k] = _Entry(v, bytes);
    _bytes += bytes;
    _evict();
  }

  void _evict() {
    // ...evict until BOTH limits are satisfied. A cache bounded only by count
    // is unbounded in memory if the values vary in size, which is the common
    // case: an image cache of 200 entries is either 2 KB or 200 MB.
    while (_entries.length > maxEntries || _bytes > maxBytes) {
      final oldest = _entries.keys.first;
      final e = _entries.remove(oldest)!;
      _bytes -= e.bytes;
      _onEvict?.call(e.value);
    }
  }
}
// ...and a byte bound needs a byte count, which means the value must know its
// own size. That is a real requirement, and it is the reason cache abstractions
// need to know about sizes rather than just counts.

There is one allocation that is worth eliminating almost regardless of cost, and it is the one in a hot path where the object is immediately discarded: the closure allocated per iteration. Dart allocates a closure object every time a lambda expression is evaluated, and in a loop that is one allocation per item for something that could be one object total. The fix is a tear-off of an instance method, which is allocated once because the receiver does not change.

// the closure-per-iteration, in three forms
class Worker {
  final List<Item> _queue = [];

  // BAD: one closure per item, and each is retained until the queue drains
  void submitA(Item item) {
    _queue.add(() {
      process(item);
    });
  }

  // GOOD: the tear-off is allocated once per Worker, not once per item
  void submitB(Item item) {
    _queue.add(process.bindFirst(item));
  }

  void process(Item item) { ... }
  void processBoundFirst(Item item) => process(item);
}
// ...`item.process` would be even better if Item could hold a reference back,
// which it usually should not. The general form: a bound method tear-off on a
// STABLE receiver is allocated once; a closure capturing a loop variable is
// allocated every iteration.

// and the allocation that looks free and is not
for (final line in lines) {
  final trimmed = line.trim();        // ...a new String per line
  if (trimmed.isEmpty) continue;      // ...allocated, checked, discarded
}
// ...the discarded one is the cheapest kind and the fix is not worth it. The
// case that IS worth it is when the intermediate is retained:
//   final parts = line.split(',');    // ...a List AND its contents, per line
//   process(parts);
// ...and the fix is a scan with an index, or a reusable list cleared in place:
//   _scratch.clear();
//   for (final ch in line.split('')) ...
// ...or, better, avoid the split entirely: parse with a single pass and a
// running index, which is both allocation-free and usually faster.

// the measurement, which is the only way to know whether any of this matters
$ dart run --observe bin/app.dart
// DevTools > Memory > "Track allocations"
// ...or, without DevTools, the two counters the VM will print for you:
//   dart run --verbose_gc_dart_stats bin/app.dart
// ...and the thresholds worth alerting on in a long-running service:
//   old-space used, growing over time          a leak
//   mark-sweep interval, shortening over time  a promotion problem
//   allocation rate, per request                a missing reuse
// ...none of these are visible without a metric, and a GC problem discovered by
// a user report is a problem that was available to be found a month earlier.

The last GC fact worth stating is the one that determines whether any allocation work pays: Dart has no way to allocate without the collector having to scan, but it does let you control when. There is no explicit collect API — System.gc() does not exist in Dart the way it does in Java — but there is a documented way to make a long operation predictable, and it is not worth reaching for unless you have measured a latency problem that a profile attributes to the collector. Guessing at GC tuning is the most common way to make a service slower, because every intervention either adds work or hides the cause.

// what is NOT available, so you do not look for it
//   System.gc()                     does not exist
//   gc()                            does not exist
//   --disable-gc                    does not exist
//   Runtime.getRuntime().gc()       Java
//   compacting / pinning the heap   JavaScript
// ...Dart gives you: a young-generation scavenger, an old-generation
// mark-sweep, and flags that tune both. The flags are:
//   --old_gen_heap_size            the old-generation limit; larger means fewer
//                                  mark-sweeps and more memory. This is the one
//                                  flag with a real, defensible use, and it is
//                                  for a service with a measured high-water mark
//   --new_gen_semi_max_size        scavenger working set; rarely worth changing
//   --no_...                        several, all of which trade safety for
//                                  speed and none of which should be set
//                                  without a profile saying so

// the rule, and it is the whole section
// ...1. measure allocation rate and old-space size in production, not on your
//    laptop, because the difference is what you are looking for
// ...2. if old space is stable, there is no GC problem. Stop.
// ...3. if old space grows, find the retained set with a heap snapshot and a
//    dominator tree, and fix the thing that retains it. Tuning flags do not fix
//    a leak; they make it take longer to be noticed.
// ...4. only once you have bounded the retained set is a flag worth setting,
//    and then only --old_gen_heap_size, to hold steady state below the
//    collector's threshold.

// and the one allocation-free rewrite worth memorising, because it appears in
// every hot path
//   for (var i = 0; i < list.length; i++) { ... }   // no iterator allocation
//   for (final x in list) { ... }                    // allocates an iterator
// ...for a List, the indexed loop is measurably faster in AOT and it is one
// character of difference. For a lazy or a Set, the iterator is not avoidable.
// ...this is a real effect and a real exception to "do not contort code to avoid
// small allocations": this one is free to fix and the profile will show it.

15.5 Data structure choices

The costs, and the cases where a hand-rolled structure wins.

// the decision table, with the operation you do most
//
// lookup by key     Map      O(1)
// lookup by value   Set      O(1)
// ordered iteration  List     O(1) per element, insertion order
// sorted iteration   SplayTreeSet   O(log n)
// insert at the end List     amortised O(1)
// insert at the front  List   O(n)   <- a LinkedList exists
// remove from the middle  List  O(n)

// the case people miss: a Queue and a Deque
import 'dart:collection';
final queue = Queue<int>();
queue.add(1);
queue.removeFirst();          // O(1), which a List cannot do cheaply

// the LinkedList, for insert-anywhere
final list = LinkedList<int>();
list.add(5);
list.add(1);
list.sort();                  // or list.sort() on a LinkedList

// when a hand-rolled structure wins
// 1. a fixed-capacity ring buffer, for audio or a log tail
class RingBuffer<T> {
  final List<T?> _buffer;
  int _head = 0;
  int _count = 0;

  RingBuffer(int capacity) : _buffer = List<T?>.filled(capacity, null);

  int get length => _count;
  bool get isEmpty => _count == 0;
  bool get isFull => _count == _buffer.length;

  void add(T item) {
    if (isFull) throw StateError('full');
    _buffer[(_head + _count) % _buffer.length] = item;
    _count++;
  }

  T? removeFirst() {
    if (isEmpty) return null;
    final item = _buffer[_head];
    _buffer[_head] = null;
    _head = (_head + 1) % _buffer.length;
    _count--;
    return item;
  }
}

// 2. an LRU cache, for a memory-bounded memo
class LruCache<K, V> {
  final int _maxSize;
  final Map<K, V> _map = {};

  LruCache(this._maxSize);

  V? get(K key) {
    if (!_map.containsKey(key)) return null;
    final value = _map.remove(key)!;
    _map[key] = value;         // re-insert: moves it to the newest
    return value;
  }

  void put(K key, V value) {
    if (_map.containsKey(key)) _map.remove(key);
    _map[key] = value;
    if (_map.length > _maxSize) {
      _map.remove(_map.keys.first);   // evict the oldest
    }
  }
}

Choosing the data structure

Dart's collections are well implemented, so the choice is rarely about raw speed and almost always about asymptotics or about which operation your code actually performs. A List lookup is O(n) and a Map lookup is O(1), so a program that looks a key up inside a loop over a list is quadratic and usually has a one-line fix. The harder judgement is between Set, Map and SplayTreeMap, which have the same O(1) or O(log n) behaviour but very different costs elsewhere.

StructureLookupInsertOrderedUse when
ListO(n) by value, O(1) by indexO(1) at end, O(n) elsewhereYesSequence, small n, index access
SetO(1)O(1)NoMembership only
MapO(1)O(1)NoKey-value
