LinkedHashMapO(1)O(1)InsertionThe Map default; order is usually wanted
HashMapO(1)O(1)NoWhen insertion order is noise
SplayTreeMapO(log n)O(log n)SortedRange queries, sorted iteration
Queue / ListQueueO(1) at endsO(1) at endsYesFIFO work queues
DoubleLinkedQueueO(1) at endsO(1) at endsYesLRU eviction from both ends

The quadratic lookup is the single most common performance defect in application Dart, and it has a distinctive signature: it is invisible in a test with ten records and catastrophic at a hundred thousand. The pattern is always the same — a loop over a list, and inside it a contains or a linear scan of another list.

// the quadratic lookup, and the one-line fix
// 10 records:   0.1 ms
// 100,000:      4.2 s
List<String> visibleTitles(List<Post> posts, Set<String> hiddenIds) {
  final out = <String>[];
  for (final p in posts) {
    if (!hiddenIds.contains(p.id)) {   // ...if hiddenIds is a LIST, this is
      out.add(p.title);                //    O(n) per post: O(n*m) overall
    }
  }
  return out;
}

// the fix, in preference order
// 1. use the structure the question needs
final out = posts.where((p) => !hiddenIds.contains(p.id)).map((p) => p.title).toList();
// ...where hiddenIds is a Set. One annotation, and the asymptotic changes.

// 2. if you must be given a list, build the index once, outside the loop
final hidden = {for (final id in hiddenIdsList) id};
for (final p in posts) {
  if (!hidden.contains(p.id)) out.add(p.title);
}
// ...this is the shape to use at a boundary: one O(n) pass to build the set,
// then O(1) per lookup. It is the most useful eight lines in this chapter.

// 3. if the SAME membership test runs over many collections, the index is
//    worth keeping as a field and invalidating on change
class VisibilityFilter {
  Set<String>? _cache;
  List<String> _source = const [];
  void update(List<String> ids) {
    _source = ids;
    _cache = null;                    // ...and the invalidation is the part
  }                                   //    that is easy to forget, which is
  bool isVisible(String id) {          //    why a stale cache is so common
    _cache ??= _source.toSet();
    return !_cache!.contains(id);
  }
}
// ...a cache without a defined invalidation point is a latent bug. If you
// cannot state when it is rebuilt, it is not a cache, it is a variable you
// forgot to update.

// the other common quadratic: indexOf inside a loop
var start = 0;
for (final id in orderedIds) {
  start += ids.indexOf(id);            // ...O(n) per lookup
}
// ...and the fix is a Map from id to position, built once:
// final pos = {for (var i = 0; i < ids.length; i++) ids[i]: i};
// start += pos[id]!;

// and the one that is NOT a bug: a linear scan over a small collection
// ...a `List.contains` over 8 elements is faster than a hash lookup, because the
// hash has to compute the hash, find a bucket, compare, and the linear scan is
// eight pointer-chases in contiguous memory. Below about 16 elements, linear
// wins. So `if (items.length < 16) return items.contains(x);` is a real
// optimisation in a genuinely hot path, and an absurd one anywhere else.

The second judgement is between the Map implementations, and the deciding question is almost never lookup speed. It is whether anything will iterate the collection, and if so, in what order. The default Map literal in Dart is a LinkedHashMap, which iterates in insertion order — and that is almost always what you want, since it means a map built from a document preserves the document's field order. HashMap iterates in an unspecified order that depends on hash values and insertion history, and code that depends on it produces output that changes between runs.

// the map, and the iteration-order question
final a = {'b': 1, 'a': 2, 'c': 3};      // LinkedHashMap: b, a, c
final b = HashMap.of({'b': 1, 'a': 2, 'c': 3});
// ...b's order is unspecified and may differ between runs, between SDK
// versions, and between platforms. A test asserting on `b.keys.toList()` will
// pass locally and fail in CI, and the error message will show an order that
// looks arbitrary.

// the rules that follow
// 1. never assert on the iteration order of a HashMap. Sort it in the test:
//      expect(b.keys.toList()..sort(), ['a', 'b', 'c']);
// 2. never rely on it in output. If a JSON body must be stable, build it from
//    a List or an explicitly sorted key sequence:
//      jsonEncode(Map.fromEntries(keys.map((k) => MapEntry(k, m[k]))));
// 3. use HashMap deliberately, and only where order is genuinely noise and the
//    memory matters. The saving is real - no linked list, no insertion-order
//    bookkeeping - and it is smaller than people expect for small maps.

// SplayTreeMap, for the case that actually needs it: sorted iteration and
// range queries, which is a different capability and not a different speed
final index = SplayTreeMap<String, Post>(
  (a, b) => a.compareTo(b),
  (k) => MapEntry(k, postFor(k)!),
);
// index.keys.toList()                          sorted
// index.keys.from(a).takeWhile((k) => k < b)  every key in [a, b)
// index.keys.between(a, b)                      the range directly
// index.firstKey(...) / lastKey(...)            bounds
// ...none of these have a hash equivalent. If you need "everything since last
// Tuesday, in order", this is the structure, and a sorted List with binary
// search is a worse answer than either.

// and the two collection classes that are not Map or List at all
final q = ListQueue<Task>();   // O(1) at both ends, backed by a circular
                                  // buffer. A growable List used as a queue
                                  // calls removeAt(0), which is O(n) per
                                  // dequeue - a genuinely quadratic queue.
final dq = DoubleLinkedQueue<Task>();  // O(1) at both ends, with a node per
                                          // element. Use when you need BOTH
                                          // ends; otherwise the circular buffer
                                          // is better.
final pq = HeapPriorityQueue<Task>();  // O(log n) push and pop, ordered by
                                          // comparator. A sorted List with
                                          // insert is O(n) per insert.
// ...and `SplayTreeSet` for a sorted set with the same range queries.
// ...These four exist because the naive version of each is quadratic, and the
// quadratic version is what everyone writes first.

One more decision belongs here because it is made constantly and is usually made by default: mutating an existing collection versus creating a new one. Dart has no persistent data structure in the standard library, so "functional" code rebuilds, and on a large collection inside a loop that is an allocation per iteration. But inverting it — mutating in place for performance — has a cost that is easy to forget: the collection is now aliased by anything that already held it, and Dart's copy-on-write iterators detect the mutation and throw rather than let you read a torn state.

// the aliasing rule, which is enforced but not prevented
final items = [1, 2, 3];
final view = items;                  // NOT a copy: the same List object
view.add(4);
print(items);                        // [1, 2, 3, 4]

// the failure, and it is loud rather than silent, which is deliberate
final snapshot = List<String>.of(names);
for (final name in snapshot) {
  if (name == 'skip') {
    names.remove(name);              // ...modifying while iterating
  }
}
// Concurrent modification during iteration
// ...this is a GOOD design decision by the library. The alternative — reading a
// collection that is being rewritten — produces a bug that appears in
// production, once, on a code path nobody tests. So the rule is:
//   - iterate over a copy if you intend to mutate
//   - or collect the victims first, then mutate:
//       final doomed = names.where(test).toList();
//       names.removeWhere(test);
// ...and `removeWhere` is the answer for almost every "delete while scanning"
// case, because it does the two-pass internally.

// the performance version of the same question
// BAD: rebuilds a 100,000-element list per iteration
List<int> doubled = [];
for (final x in huge) {
  doubled = doubled.map((y) => y * 2).toList();
}

// GOOD: one list, one pass
final doubled = [for (final x in huge) x * 2];

// GOOD, and in place, when the list is not aliased
final doubled = huge.map((x) => x * 2).toList(growable: false);
// ...`toList(growable: false)` avoids a reallocation if the length is already
// correct, and for a fixed-length result it is the form to use.

// and the case where mutation is the ONLY correct answer: a large accumulation
final counts = <String, int>{};
for (final w in words) {
  counts.update(w, (n) => n + 1, ifAbsent: () => 1);
}
// ...one map, mutated in place, with `update` doing the read-modify-write. The
// rebuild-per-iteration version of this allocates 400,000 intermediate maps,
// and the profile blames the GC rather than the code that caused it.

15.6 Async performance

The costs of the event loop, and the batching patterns that help.

// the event loop, in order
//  1. the current synchronous task runs to completion
//  2. the microtask queue is drained COMPLETELY
//  3. one event from the event queue is taken
//  4. back to 2
//
// the consequences
// - a long synchronous task blocks everything, including microtasks
// - a microtask that queues another microtask can starve the event
//   loop: await Future.delayed(Duration.zero) to break out

// AWAIT IS NOT FREE
Future<void> loop() async {
  for (var i = 0; i < 100000; i++) {
    await Future.value();        // 100000 microtask hops: SLOW
  }
}

void loopSync() {
  for (var i = 0; i < 100000; i++) {
    // no await: fast
  }
}

// if the work does not need to yield, do not await inside the loop
Future<void> better() async {
  for (var i = 0; i < 100000; i++) {
    if (i % 1000 == 0) {
      await Future.delayed(Duration.zero);   // yield every 1000
    }
    // do the work
  }
}

// BATCHING, when you have many small events
// BAD: one write per event
for (final event in events) {
  await file.writeAsString('$event\n', mode: FileMode.append);
}

// GOOD: one write for all of them
final buffer = StringBuffer();
for (final event in events) {
  buffer.writeln(event);
}
await file.writeAsString(buffer.toString());

// and for a stream of events that arrive faster than you can
// process, debounce or buffer:
final controller = StreamController<int>();
final buffered = controller.stream.buffered(100);
await for (final batch in buffered) {
  await processBatch(batch);      // 100 at a time
}
// the STREAM overhead, which surprises people
// a Stream has a real per-event cost: a subscription, a queue, a
// microtask. For a hot path, a plain loop is faster.

// BAD: a stream where a loop would do
final controller = StreamController<int>();
for (var i = 0; i < 1000000; i++) {
  controller.add(i);      // 1M stream events
}
controller.close();

// GOOD
for (var i = 0; i < 1000000; i++) {
  process(i);
}

// the exception: when the consumer is genuinely incremental, or
// the events come from outside, a stream is the right tool

// a sync controller, if the consumer cannot keep up
final syncController = StreamController<int>.broadcast(sync: true);
// sync: true delivers synchronously, which is faster but means a
// slow listener BLOCKS the producer. Use it only when both are
// in the same isolate and the consumer is fast.

Async performance

Async code is slow in a specific, measurable way, and the causes are not the ones people expect. An await is not expensive by itself — scheduling a continuation is tens of nanoseconds. What is expensive is everything an await makes possible: a microtask that runs the event loop, a future that crosses a stream, a retry timer, and a serial chain where each step waits for the last. A loop with an await per iteration is the pattern that produces a function which is correct, readable, and 40 times slower than the same loop without one.

// the serial chain, which is the most common async performance bug
// 200 records, one HTTP request each, fully sequential
for (final id in ids) {
  final record = await fetch(id);
  results.add(record);          // ...waits for id 1, then 2, then 3...
}
// ...200 requests x 80 ms = 16 seconds. Nothing is wrong with the code; it is
// simply one request at a time.

// the same work with bounded concurrency, which is the correct shape
Future<List<Record>> fetchAll(List<String> ids, {int limit = 8}) async {
  final pool = Pool(limit);
  final results = await Future.wait(ids.map((id) async {
    // ...`Pool` is a semaphore: at most `limit` of these bodies run at once,
    // and the rest wait for a permit. The map is lazy, so no 200 futures are
    // created up front either.
    return pool.withPermit(() => fetch(id));
  }));
  await pool.close();
  return results;
}
// ...200/8 x 80 ms = 2 seconds, and the server sees 8 concurrent requests rather
// than 200, which is usually as important as the wall clock.

// the unbounded version, which is the mistake people make instead
await Future.wait(ids.map(fetch));
// ...correct, and it opens 200 simultaneous connections. The server rejects
// them, the OS runs out of ephemeral ports, and the failure looks like network
// flakiness. Every `Future.wait` over I/O needs a bound.

// and the subtlety: a bound of 1 is a serial chain, so pick it deliberately
Future<List<Record>> fetchAllSerial(List<String> ids) async {
  return [for (final id in ids) await fetch(id)];
}
// ...this is faster than the for-loop version above it, because it does not
// create a closure and a Future per iteration, and it produces a growable list
// directly. When the work must be sequential, a for-in with await beats
// Future.wait with a concurrency of 1.

The second cause of slow async code is awaiting things that are already available. Every await yields to the event loop, so a chain of a hundred awaits of already-completed futures costs a hundred event-loop turns even though no work is pending. In a hot path — a serialiser, a validator, a per-row transformation — those turns are pure overhead, and the fix is to check before awaiting.

// awaiting a future that is already complete
Future<int> fast() async => 1;

var t = 0;
for (var i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
  t += await fast();     // ...1000 event loop turns for 1000 additions
}
// ...measured: ~1.1 ms, essentially all of it scheduling

// the fix, and it is not "make it sync" - it is "only await when pending"
var t = 0;
for (var i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
  final f = fast();
  t += f.isCompleted ? await f : await f;   // ...no, that is identical
}

// the actual fix: a synchronous fast path that returns the same type
class Maybe<T> {
  final T? _value;
  final Future<T>? _future;
  Maybe.value(T v) : _value = v, _future = null;
  Maybe.future(Future<T> f) : _value = null, _future = f;
  T get sync => _value ?? (_future == null
      ? throw StateError('not resolved')
      : throw StateError('use await'));     // ...an explicit, checked escape
  Future<T> get async => _future ?? Future.value(_value!);
}
// ...which is a real design with a real cost: two ways to do everything, and a
// runtime error when the wrong one is used. It is worth it only on a measured
// hot path, and the honest measurement is the one above: 1.1 ms for 1000
// iterations means this only matters if you are doing it millions of times.

// the much more common version of the same waste: awaiting inside a loop that
// does not need to be async
Future<List<Row>> toRows(List<Cell> cells) async {
  final out = <Row>[];
  for (final c in cells) {
    out.add(Row(await format(c)));   // ...one await per cell, no dependency
  }
  return out;
}
// ...and this one is genuinely necessary - format is async. The improvement is
// concurrency, not synchrony:
//   await Future.wait(cells.map(format))   // bounded, as above

// and the case where the loop IS dependent, which no amount of concurrency
// fixes, because there is only one thing to do at a time
// A workflow: fetch config, then use it to fetch data, then validate.
// ...this is a genuine serial dependency and the only correct answer is to
// await. The optimisation is to start what CAN be started concurrently:
//   final configFuture = loadConfig();
//   final staticAssetsFuture = loadAssets();   // ...independent of config
//   final config = await configFuture;
//   final data = await fetchData(config);
//   await uploadAssets(await staticAssetsFuture);
// ...two of the three I/Os now overlap, and the dependency graph says exactly
// which.

Streams have their own performance characteristic, and it is that a stream is a pipeline with per-event overhead that is invisible in the combinator count. Each operator in a chain adds a subscription, a closure invocation and an event delivery, so a ten-operator chain is ten times the per-event cost of one, on every event. For a stream of 10,000 events that matters; for a stream of 10 it does not. The measurement that tells you is items-per-second, not total time.

ShapePer-event costUse when
One mapOne closureAlways fine
Five operatorsFive subscriptionsUsually fine
Ten-plus operatorsDominates small per-event workFold into one
await for in a hot loopAn event loop turn per eventBatch it
Broadcast with several listenersDelivery to eachShare the work, not the stream
// folding a stream chain into one pass
// TEN operators on 10,000 events
source
  .where((e) => e.isMessage)
  .map((e) => parse(e))
  .where((p) => p.isValid)
  .map((p) => enrich(p))
  .distinct()
  .take(1000)
  .map((p) => serialise(p))
  .toList();

// ONE pass on 10,000 events, with the same semantics
final out = <String>[];
final seen = <String>{};
await for (final e in source) {
  if (!e.isMessage) continue;
  final p = parse(e);
  if (!p.isValid) continue;
  final enriched = enrich(p);
  final key = enriched.id;
  if (seen.contains(key)) continue;    // ...`distinct`
  seen.add(key);
  final s = serialise(enriched);
  out.add(s);
  if (out.length >= 1000) break;    // ...`take(1000)`
}
// ...same result, and the profile difference is the whole cost of the
// subscription machinery. Note this is not always better: the chain is far more
// readable, and a fold is easy to get subtly wrong. Fold when the profile says
// to, and keep a test asserting the two agree.

// `await for` and the per-event turn
await for (final row in csvRows) {
  await db.insert(row);      // ...one event loop turn per row, plus a round trip
}
// ...if the inserts do not need ordering or the transaction semantics are per
// batch, this is a Future.wait with a bound. If they do need ordering, the
// sequence is required and the cost is the database's, not Dart's.

// and the one measurement worth taking before optimising a stream at all
$ dart run --observe bin/pipeline.dart
// DevTools > Performance, look at the number of events and the total time, and
// compute us-per-event. Under about 10 us per event, the stream machinery is
// not your problem and you are optimising the wrong layer.
// ...under 10 us per event is roughly 100,000 events per second, which is more
// than most pipelines see. Most "the stream is slow" reports are a database
// round trip at 800 us per event.

15.7 Startup time

What happens before your first line of code runs, and how to shorten it.

// the phases, for a CLI tool or a Flutter app
//  1. OS process launch
//  2. Dart runtime initialisation (the AOT runtime is small: ~1ms)
//  3. loading the snapshot: AOT (fast) or kernel (slower)
//  4. your main() starts
//  5. your initialisation
//  6. first frame / first output

// measure it from the very first thing in main
void main() {
  final stopwatch = Stopwatch()..start();
  // ...
  stopwatch.stop();
  stderr.writeln('startup: ${stopwatch.elapsedMicroseconds}us');
}

// what makes it slow
//  1. large top-level initialisers: they run before main
final bigTable = buildTable();          // 500ms before main() starts
//    the fix: make it lazy
final bigTable = lazy(() => buildTable());

//  2. heavy imports: an import is loaded even if you never call it
import 'package:chart/chart.dart';      // 300KB of code, loaded always
//    the fix: a deferred import inside the function that needs it
Future<void> showChart() async {
  final chart = await import('package:chart/chart.dart');
  chart.render(...);
}

//  3. top-level static initialisers in a large package
//    the fix: move them into a function, called on demand

//  4. reading a big file or a big config before doing anything
//    the fix: do the work, then read the config

//  5. in Flutter: building the widget tree before the first frame
//    the fix: show a placeholder, then fill it in
// DEFERRED IMPORT, the tool for lazy loading
Future<void> main() async {
  print('startup: minimal');

  // the heavy library, loaded only when it is needed
  final analytics = await import('analytics.dart');
  await analytics.init();

  print('after analytics');
}

// on the web, a deferred import becomes a separate chunk that is
// fetched on demand. This is how you keep the initial bundle small.

// the rules
// - a deferred import is ASYNCENT: you must await it
// - the types are not available until it resolves
// - each deferred import is a separate compilation unit
// - a variable declared before a deferred import is typed as dynamic
//   if it uses types from the deferred library

// TOP-LEVEL: the cost of eager global state
final defaultConfig = Config.fromDefaults();   // runs at load time
late final defaultConfig = Config.fromDefaults();  // runs on first use

// so: use late final for anything expensive at the top level

Startup time, and what actually accounts for it

Startup is the first thing a user experiences and the last thing anybody optimises, because it is measured rarely and it is not a crash. A CLI that takes two seconds to print its version reads as broken even when it is correct, and for a mobile or serverless function the same two seconds is the difference between a responsive service and one that times out. The components are separable and each has a different fix.

ComponentTypicalFixed by
VM start + kernel load15-40 msNothing; it is the floor
Parsing your codePer KB, and it is superlinear in AOTLess code; deferred loading
Static initialisersWhatever they doMaking them lazy
Isolate/zone setupPer isolateFewer isolates
Config and I/O at startWhatever it costsMoving it after first output
Framework init (Flutter)100-300 msFramework; measure before fighting it

The measurement has to distinguish these, and the tool that does it is a timeline recorded from process start, not a Stopwatch in main — because a stopwatch in main starts after the VM has already loaded the program, which is usually the part you cannot change. So: timestamp at the very first line, and separately record the process's own wall clock, and the difference between them is the load time you did not measure.

// measuring startup, including the part before main()
import 'dart:io';

const _scriptStart = _ScriptStart();

@pragma('vm:entry-point')
class _ScriptStart {
  const _ScriptStart();
  // ...a const constructor initialiser runs during snapshot load, before main -
  // which is exactly the point. The alternative, ProcessInfo, does not report
  // process start, only VM start.
  static final int at = DateTime.now().microsecondsSinceEpoch;
}

void main(List<String> args) {
  final inMain = DateTime.now().microsecondsSinceEpoch;
  stdout.writeln('to main: ${(inMain - _scriptStart.at) / 1000} ms');
  // ...on a JIT run this is small; the interesting number is the AOT one, where
  // the snapshot must be loaded and the code deserialised.

  // the total, from the OS, which includes everything
  final rss = ProcessInfo.currentRss;
  stdout.writeln('rss: ${rss >> 20} MB');
}

// the two methods that measure it properly, for comparison
// $ time ./server --version
//   real 0m0.412s
// ...includes process fork/exec, dynamic linking, VM start, snapshot load, and
// main. This is the number a user experiences and the one to optimise.

// $ dart compile exe bin/server.dart -o server
// $ strace -f -tt -e trace=openat ./server --version 2>&1 | tail -30
// ...every file opened, in order, with timestamps. This names the 200 ms: a
// snapshot load of 9 MB, a dynamic library that is being searched for on the
// filesystem, or a config file on a slow path.

// and the definitive tool for a Dart program
$ dart run --observe --pause-isolates-on-exit bin/server.dart
// ...DevTools > Performance, record from launch, and the timeline's first
// frame includes the load. Compare a --version run against a real run: the
// difference is your application's own start-up work, and that difference is
// the only part you control.

Of the controllable parts, static initialisers are the most surprising and the most fixable, because they run before main and are therefore invisible in any in-process measurement. A top-level final in Dart is lazily initialised on first read — so it is not the problem — but a top-level const and a library-level initialiser in a dependency are not, and some packages do expensive work at import time.

// lazy vs eager initialisation, and how to tell which you have
// LAZY: a top-level final, initialised on first read
final _cache = Expensive();          // ...runs on first access, not at import
void use() { _cache.get(); }         // ...so this costs 40 ms HERE

// EAGER: a const, or a top-level statement that is not a declaration
const thresholds = computeThresholds();   // ...const requires a const
                                          //    expression, so this is a
                                          //    COMPILE-time value, not a cost
final registry = <String, Handler>{}       // ...cheap, and lazy
..add('a', A())
..add('b', B());                           // ...the cascade runs on first read

// how to find the real cost, since you cannot read it in main()
$ strace -f -tt -e trace=openat ./app --version 2>&1 | grep -c ENOENT
// ...a high count of failed file opens is a library search path problem: some
// package is probing for an optional native library at load time, and each
// probe is a filesystem miss. The fix is in the dependency, or a
// platform-conditional import so the probing code is not in the build.

// the fix for genuinely expensive startup work: move it after first output
void main() async {
  // 1. do the minimum that lets you print something useful
  final version = await readVersion();

  // 2. print
  stdout.writeln('myapp $version');

  // 3. NOW do the expensive part, concurrently where possible
  final results = await Future.wait([
    warmIndexes(),
    connectPool(),
    loadFeatureFlags(),
  ]);
  await runServer(results);
}
// ...and for a CLI, most of the work belongs behind a subcommand:
//   myapp --version      does nothing but read a version
//   myapp migrate        does the expensive thing
// ...so `myapp --version` in a shell prompt, a CI cache key check, or a
// container health check costs 20 ms instead of 400. This is the highest-value
// startup change available and it is not a performance technique, it is a
// command structure.

// the same idea for a server: bind the port before doing the work
final server = await HttpServer.bind(addr, port);   // ...listening now
await warmEverything();                              // ...still warming
// ...so a load balancer's health check succeeds immediately and traffic is not
// routed to a half-initialised process. On a rolling deploy this is the
// difference between no downtime and a burst of 503s.

Binary size and startup are the same problem for Flutter, because the AOT snapshot must be loaded and it is measured in megabytes. The relationships worth knowing: startup time grows roughly with snapshot size, and a tree-shaken snapshot is smaller. So the same three actions serve both goals — remove unreachable code, defer heavy initialisation, and split the entry point so the common path is small.

// the Flutter numbers, and what moves them
$ flutter build appbundle --release --analyze-size
  lib/arm64-v8a/libapp.so    9.8 MB    // your Dart AOT code
  lib/arm64-v8a/libflutter.so 6.1 MB   // the engine, not yours
// ...and startup time tracks libapp.so: roughly 100-150 ms per MB on a mid
// range device, so 9.8 MB is about a second, and 5 MB is about half that.

// what actually gets tree-shaken, and what defeats it
// REMOVED: code no exported entry point can reach
// KEPT: anything reachable through an exported API, transitively
// KEPT: a const value, because it is part of the program
// KEPT: anything reached by dart:mirrors
// KEPT: a class whose name appears as a STRING
// ...the last two are the reason a project is stuck at 12 MB, and both are
// avoidable:

// 1. reflection anywhere in the dependency graph
// ...json_serializable generates code and does not need it. build_runner, some
// DI containers, and most ORM layers do. Check the graph before blaming your
// own code:
//     dart pub deps | grep -i mirror

// 2. the string-referenced class, which is invisible to the analyser
static const _routes = {
  'home': HomePage,
  'settings': SettingsPage,   // ...a tear-off, so this IS reachable and kept
};
// ...that is fine. This is not fine:
Future<void&gt> open(String name) async {
  final cls = _registry[name];     // ...a runtime map, so every registered
  return cls!();                    //    constructor is retained
}
// ...the registry forces every page to be reachable. If the page count is what
// is driving the size, the fix is to build the registry from a generated file
// containing only the pages you ship, or to accept the cost deliberately.

// 3. a large generated table, which is CODE
const kCountryDialCodes = {
  'AF': 93, 'AL': 355, 'DZ': 213, /* ...250 entries... */
};
// ...250 map entries is real code in the snapshot. Moving it to an asset file
// costs an async load and saves a surprising amount of binary. The trade is
// only worth it for genuinely static data of genuinely large size.

// and the measurement that decides
$ size // the two numbers, in bytes
__TEXT           __DATA  __OBJC   others    decimal  hex
35878436  4294967295  1234432  1126461     4115  0x...
// ...compare before and after a change. "It got smaller" is the metric, and a
// size regression is as real a regression as a latency one, so it belongs in
// CI next to the tests, failing on a threshold.

15.8 Tree shaking and dead code

How the compiler removes unused code, and what defeats it.

// AOT compilation does tree shaking: unreachable code is removed,
// which is why a Dart executable is not enormous despite the
// large SDK.

// what defeats it
//  1. DYNAMIC: a call through `dynamic` is not statically known,
//     so the compiler must keep the target
//     final obj = something as dynamic;
//     obj.someMethod();          // the compiler cannot know what this is
//
//  2. MIRRORS: dart:mirrors can reach anything, so nothing can be
//     shaken. Do not use it in a release build.
//
//  3. A WIDE DYNAMIC: a value typed as dynamic, where every method
//     call is a dynamic dispatch

// 4. registerPlugin and similar runtime registration: the compiler
//     cannot see which plugin is registered

// 5. REFLECTION-BASED SERIALIZATION: which is why code generation
//     exists

// what you can do
//  - keep types precise; avoid dynamic
//  - avoid dart:mirrors
//  - use code generation, not reflection
//  - check the output size: if it is bigger than you expect,
//    something dynamic is pulling in a library
// measuring the size impact
// before and after removing a dependency
dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o before
# remove the import, rebuild
dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o after
ls -la before after

// for the web, which has its own tree shaker
dart compile js bin/main.dart -o app.js -O4
# check what is in the bundle
grep -o '[A-Za-z0-9_$]*' app.js | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -50

// the practical impact
//   a Dart hello world:      ~6MB (native), ~10KB (web, minified)
//   + 10 small packages:     ~8MB native, ~80KB web
//   + a heavy chart library: ~14MB native, ~450KB web
//   + dart:mirrors:          everything stays: 40MB+

// the size matters most on the web, and on mobile install size.
// on a desktop CLI, 14MB versus 8MB is not worth optimising.

Tree shaking, and what survives it

Tree shaking is the removal of code no entry point can reach. It is described as a single switch, and it is really a graph reachability problem with a dozen ways to make the graph wrong, most of which are invisible in the source. Understanding which of the twelve applies to your project is the whole skill; the flag is one argument.

Defeats shakingWhyDetectable?
dart:mirrorsAny type may be reflectively usedYes, in the dep graph
A class named in a stringNot a symbol, so not an edgeNo — search for it
A const tablePart of the programYes, in the size report
An exported APIReachable from the entry pointNo — that is the design
A subclass of a reachable typeOverrides may be dispatchedNo
An extension method on a core typeOnly if the name is usedYes

Shaking operates on reachability from the entry point, not on "is this class used anywhere". An exported symbol is reachable by definition, so a library that exports a hundred things keeps all hundred even if your program calls one — which is why a package that exports its entire internal surface is a package whose size cannot be reduced, no matter what flags you pass. That is a design property of the library, not a setting of yours.

// the mechanism, concretely
//   entry point:  main()
//   kept:         everything transitively referenced from it
//   removed:      everything else in the program and its dependencies
//
// so the question for any symbol is always: "is there a path from main() to it,
// through code the compiler can see?"
//
// a library that defeats shaking by being imported wholesale
//   import 'package:myapp/models.dart';   // exports 40 classes
//   // ...one is used, so the LIBRARY is imported, so all 40 are kept if the
//   // import is a wildcard, and the 39 unused ones are still retained because
//   // an exported symbol is a public API of the imported library.
//
// the fix, and it is a source-file change, not a flag
//   import 'package:myapp/models/user.dart';   // show, don't export
//   // ...so only the classes in that one file are reachable

// the string-reference, which no flag can see
class Route {
  const Route(this.path, this.builder);
  final String path;
  final WidgetBuilder builder;
}
const routes = <Route>[
  Route('/home', HomePage.new),        // ...a tear-off: a real edge, kept
  Route('/settings', SettingsPage.new),
];
// ...this is FINE. `HomePage.new` is a symbol reference and the tree shaker
// follows it. The problem is the other form:
final Map<String, WidgetBuilder> _registry = {};
void register(String name, WidgetBuilder b) { _registry[name] = b; }
// ...every `b` passed to register() is a real edge too. So the string map is
// actually fine.
//
// the genuinely untraceable case is a NAME as data, resolved by the framework:
//   const routes = {'/home': 'HomePage'};        // a string, not a symbol
//   final cls = routes[settings.name]!;
//   // (cls as dynamic)();                      // resolved at runtime
// ...now `HomePage` is only mentioned in a string, so the tree shaker has no
// edge to it, and the class is REMOVED. At runtime you get a null cast error.
// ...and this is worse than a size problem: it is a build that succeeds and
// breaks in production. If you do this, generate the map with build_runner,
// which writes `HomePage.new` as a real tear-off.

// the diagnostic: ask the compiler what it could not remove
$ dart compile exe bin/app.dart -o app --extra-gen-snapshot=unused.json
$ python -c "import json;d=json.load(open('unused.json'));u=d['unusedElements'];print(len(u));[print(x) for x in u[:40]]"
  1841
  {"kind":"class","name":"LegacyReportBuilder","library":"package:myapp/legacy"}
  {"kind":"function","name":"_debugPrintAll","library":"dart:core"}
// ...this is the only DIRECT evidence available: the compiler listing every
// declaration it proved unreachable. A large number is not itself a problem -
// core libraries contribute thousands. What you are looking for is a name you
// did not expect, which names a subsystem that should be dead, and a class from
// your own package, which is a reachability gap you can fix.

// and the reflection check, which is the one that must be automated
$ dart pub deps --style=compact | grep -iE 'mirrors|reflect'
  myapp 1.0.0
  |- build_runner 2.4.0       # dev only, so irrelevant to a release build
  |- provider 6.1.2
  |- get_it 7.7.0            # ...a DI container built on mirrors. This ONE
  #                          #    makes every type in your program reachable
  #                          #    and is, by itself, usually the answer
# ...so: a DI container that resolves by type at runtime will hold your entire
# object graph in the binary. Replacing it with explicit constructor
// parameters, or with a generated factory, is the single largest size win
// available in a Flutter project that has one.

Tree shaking interacts with optimisation level, and the interaction is not monotonic, which is why -O4 is the default and "let me try a higher level" is not a strategy. More aggressive optimisation can duplicate or unroll code, so a higher level can produce a larger binary that is not faster. This is worth knowing because the measurement you will make — size — is the one that moves in the wrong direction.

// the level sweep, which is cheap and settles the question
for level in 0 1 2 3 4; do
  dart compile exe bin/app.dart -o build/app-O$level -O$level
  printf 'O%s  %s
' "$level" "$(stat -c%s build/app-O$level)"
done
# O0  22400000
# O1  11800000
# O2   9600000
# O3  10100000    <-- LARGER than O2
# O4   9400000
# ...O3 unrolls a hot loop, and the unrolled copies are in the binary. The
# default is O4 and it is right; the sweep is worth running once per project to
// confirm, not once per build.

// what shaking does NOT remove, however good the graph is
// 1. const data. It is code, and code is kept.
// 2. anything a reachable function could reach dynamically through a virtual
//    call the compiler cannot resolve. Dart resolves most of these, so the
//    answer is "subclasses of a type you instantiate".
// 3. the runtime. dart:core, dart:async and the parts of the SDK you touch are
//    in every binary, and that is most of the floor.
// 4. resources. Images, fonts and audio are not code; they are assets, and they
//    are the reason a Flutter app's APK is 40 MB and its libapp.so is 10.
// ...so the honest framing: tree shaking optimises CODE SIZE, and code size is
// one of four things in the download. Report all four.

// and how to report it, so the optimisation is visible
// a size budget per release, failing CI on a regression
const budget = {
  'libapp.so': 10 * 1024 * 1024,     // ...and the number is a decision, made
  'apk': 40 * 1024 * 1024,           //    from a measurement, not a guess
  'startup_ms': 900,
};
test('release size is within budget', () {
  final actual = sizeOf('build/app/.../libapp.so');
  expect(actual, lessThanOrEqualTo(budget['libapp.so']!),
      reason: 'libapp.so grew by ${(actual - budget["libapp.so"]!) ~/ 1024} KB');
});
// ...a test that fails the build is the only kind of report that changes
// behaviour. A dashboard nobody opens is a number, not a control.

Attributing a size to a cause, and reviewing a size change

A size number on its own is not actionable. 9.8 MB is a symptom; the useful question is which of a dozen mechanisms produced it, and the way to answer is to change one thing and re-measure. That sounds obvious and is skipped constantly, because the measurement takes a few minutes and the change takes one line, so the size grows until something forces the question. Three comparisons make attribution cheap.

// 1. AGAINST THE PREVIOUS BUILD, per component. A total that grew 400 KB tells
//    you nothing; the breakdown tells you which file.
$ flutter build appbundle --release --analyze-size > after.txt
$ git stash && flutter build appbundle --release --analyze-size > before.txt
$ git stash pop
$ diff before.txt after.txt
  lib/arm64-v8a/libapp.so    9.4 MB -> 9.8 MB   +0.4 MB
    assets/                  1.1 MB -> 1.1 MB
  lib/arm64-v8a/libflutter.so 6.1 MB -> 6.1 MB
// ...one number narrows it to the Dart code, and then:

// 2. AGAINST A SINGLE SYMBOL, which is the version that names a cause. Pick the
//    component you suspect, remove it, and re-measure. The DELTA is its cost.
$ dart compile exe bin/app.dart -o without --extra-gen-snapshot=unused.json
// ...then, for each name the compiler reported unreachable, force it back in and
// see if the binary grows. That converts a guess into an arithmetic result:
//   libapp.so with and without the DI container      9.8 MB vs 6.1 MB
//   ...3.7 MB for get_it, which is a quarter of the binary, for a container that
//      resolves four services.

// 3. AGAINST A MINIMAL PROGRAM, which bounds the question. An empty Dart program
//    is the floor, and everything above it is yours.
// $ cat > empty.dart <<'EOF'
//   void main() {}
//   EOF
// $ dart compile exe empty.dart -o empty && stat -c%s empty
//   5803008      // 5.8 MB: the runtime, and nothing else
// ...so a 9.8 MB binary is 5.8 MB of floor plus 4.0 MB of your program and its
// dependencies. That 4.0 MB is the only number with any addressable content in
// it, and it is the number to put a budget on.

// and the three components of that 4.0 MB, in the order they usually appear
//   your own generated or handwritten code
//   a dependency that defeats shaking, which is one entry in `unused.json`
//   const data, which appears as unreachable nothing and is retained anyway
// ...and the test that separates the first two, which is to build a program
// that imports ONLY the suspect dependency:

import 'package:get_it/get_it.dart';
void main() {
  final g = GetIt.instance;
  g.registerSingleton<Clock>(SystemClock());
  print(g<Clock>());
}
// ...if that binary is 9.5 MB and yours is 9.8 MB, the dependency is the
// problem. If it is 6.0 MB, it is your code, and `unused.json` names it.

A size change in review is judged differently from a latency change, and the difference is that size is a permanent, cumulative cost while a latency regression can be tuned back. A 300 KB regression that ships and is never reverted grows to 3 MB over a year, and every individual step looked reasonable. So the review question is not "is 300 KB a lot" but "is this 300 KB accounted for", and the answer has to name a mechanism.

// the review question, and the two answers that are not
// "this adds 300 KB" -> unacceptable without a reason
// "this is faster"      -> irrelevant to a size review
// "this is required for
//   the feature"        -> accepted, and this is how binaries grow
//
// the answer that is accepted:
// "this adds 300 KB, all of it from `json_serializable`'s generated code for
//  the 14 new models. Regenerating with `checked: false` on 9 of them drops it
//  to 40 KB. Nothing else in the diff touches size."
// ...a mechanism, a magnitude, and a cheaper alternative already tried.

// the CI check that makes this a control rather than a report
// A single global threshold is weak: it passes while one important file grows
// 30% and a forgotten one shrinks 10%. Per-area budgets are the useful form.
const budgets = {
  'libapp.so': 6 << 20,        // ...the code you control
  'apk': 30 << 20,             // ...the delivered artefact
  'assets': 2 << 20,            // ...images and fonts, tracked separately
};

// ...and the reason assets are tracked separately: a designer replacing a
// screenshot is not a code problem, and a build that fails on a 300 KB asset
// change teaches people to ignore the failure. Split the budget so each failure
// has one cause.

// and the two changes that are NOT size regressions, so they should not fail the
// check
// 1. adding a feature that genuinely adds code. Raise the budget deliberately,
//    in the same commit, with the reason in the message. A budget that can only
//    go down gets worked around.
// 2. a dependency version bump. Compare before and after the bump, in
//    isolation, so a version change is never bundled with a feature.

// and what to do about a dependency that defeats shaking, in preference order
// 1. Remove it. Usually a DI container, a logging facade or a serialiser used
//    for one class. Replacing four uses with four constructor parameters is an
//    afternoon and can be a third of the binary.
// 2. Configure it to not use reflection, if it has such a mode. Several DI
//    containers can generate a factory file instead of resolving at runtime.
// 3. Fork it and cut the reflectively-reachable surface. A container that
//    registers types by `Type` retains every type you ever register; a fork
//    that registers factories does not.
// 4. Accept it, and record the size in the budget so the cost is visible
//    rather than discovered. This is a legitimate outcome and the only one of
//    the four that requires no work.

// and the honest summary of what tree shaking can and cannot do
// CAN: remove code no exported entry point reaches. This is most of a typical
//      application, and it is why a Flutter app is 10 MB rather than 40.
// CANNOT: remove anything reachable through reflection.
// CANNOT: remove const data, because const data is code.
// CANNOT: remove a type whose name is a string at runtime.
// CANNOT: remove the SDK, which is most of the floor at around 5.8 MB.
// ...so the honest summary of the whole optimisation: you are not making the
// binary small, you are not putting a third of it back. The realistic best case
// for an application with a DI container and 200 generated models is
// approximately half of what it is, and that half is worth having.

15.9 The optimisation checklist

An ordered list, so you optimise the right thing in the right order.

// 1. MEASURE. Always first. Get a CPU profile and a memory profile
//    on a real device, in a release build.

// 2. FIX THE ALGORITHM. An O(n^2) in a loop is a bigger win than
//    any micro-optimisation, and it is nearly free to fix.
//    - contains/indexOf in a loop: build a Set
//    - string concatenation in a loop: StringBuffer
//    - nested loops over the same data: a Map index

// 3. MOVE THE WORK OFF THE UI ISOLATE. If it takes longer than
//    16ms, it belongs in an isolate (chapter 9).

// 4. REDUCE ALLOCATION. Pre-size lists, use typed lists for bulk
//    numeric data, avoid closures in hot loops, avoid intermediate
//    objects.

// 5. CACHE, with a bound. Memoize expensive calls, with an LRU
//    so the cache cannot grow without limit.

// 6. USE THE RIGHT COLLECTION. Set for membership, Map for keys,
//    typed lists for numerics.

// 7. SPLIT THE BUNDLE. Deferred imports, so a rarely-used feature
//    is not in the initial download.

// 8. ONLY THEN: micro-optimise.
//    - avoid the bounds check with a for-in, or List.first in a
//      loop where you know the list is non-empty
//    - combine loops
//    - const-fold what you can
//    - write the hot function in a tighter form

// 9. DO NOT:
//    - hand-optimise assembly-like tricks; the AOT compiler is good
//    - sacrifice readability for a 2% win
//    - optimise a function that runs twice
// the practical example: a slow list screen
// before: 1.2s to render 10,000 rows
class SlowList {
  List<Row> get visible => _items
      .where((r) => matchesFilter(r))     // a closure per item
      .map((r) => transform(r))            // and another
      .toList();                             // a new list of 10,000

  bool matchesFilter(Row r) => r.status == selected;   // O(1), fine
}

// the same, in one pass, with no intermediates
class FastList {
  List<Row> get visible {
    final out = <Row>[];
    for (final r in _items) {
      if (r.status == selected) out.add(r);
    }
    return out;
  }
}

// and better still: do it once, not on every build
class CachedList {
  List<Row>? _cache;
  int _cacheVersion = 0;

  List<Row> get visible {
    if (_cache != null && _cacheVersion == version) return _cache!;
    _cacheVersion = version;
    return _cache = _computeVisible();
  }
}

// and for 10,000 rows, the real answer is to render 20 of them:
// virtualise. That is a bigger change than any of the above, and
// it is the one that actually matters at that scale.

The most valuable performance advice in this chapter is negative: most Dart code is fast enough, and an unmeasured optimisation makes the code worse without making it faster. Profile, find the one thing that matters, fix that, and stop. The second most valuable is to remember that a slow interface is usually an algorithmic or allocation problem, not a language problem - Dart compiles to efficient native code, and the GC is generational and incremental.

Exercises 16

  1. Build a benchmark harness with warmup, minimum and median. Compare a loop, a fold and a where chain on a million elements.
  2. Profile a real program with the DevTools CPU profiler. Find the top three functions and explain what each is doing.
  3. Use the allocation panel to find a hot loop that allocates. Rewrite it and compare the two.
  4. Replace a List<int> with an Int32List for a million elements. Measure the memory and the speed difference.
  5. Measure the cost of 100,000 await Future.value() hops. Then find how many yields a UI needs to stay responsive.
  6. Implement an LRU cache, and prove the eviction order is correct with a test.
  7. Move a slow function to an isolate, and measure the difference in total wall time and in UI responsiveness.
  8. Take a dart:mirrors dependency and measure the binary size before and after removing it.

The optimisation checklist

The order below is the order that works, and the reason for the order is that every step is cheap and every step after it is informed by what the previous step found. Most performance work done out of order produces a change that cannot be evaluated — you cannot tell whether it helped, so nobody reverts it, so it stays forever.

  1. Measure the thing a user does. Not a function, not a microbenchmark: the request, the screen, the command. If you cannot state the number in user-visible terms, you do not have a performance problem yet, you have an opinion.
  2. Profile it and find the hotspot. One frame, read for self time. If the profile does not point somewhere you did not expect, you have found something worth more than the optimisation you came for.
  3. Establish the complexity. Any loop nested inside another loop, or any contains/indexOf inside a loop over a collection, is O(n²) and grows. This is checked by reading, not by profiling, and it is where the largest wins are.
  4. Fix allocation, before anything else. It is the most common cause of a latency tail, it is visible in the profile as GC, and the fixes are mechanical: reuse, avoid the intermediate collection, use a tear-off.
  5. Then, and only then, micro-optimise. A tight loop, a redundant allocation, a string concatenation in a hot path. These are worth perhaps 20% together.

The step that is most often skipped is the last one, and it is the one that decides whether the work survives. An optimisation that is not measured after the change, and recorded, will be reverted by someone refactoring the code it sits in, because nobody knows it was load-bearing. The record is three lines in the commit message.

// the change record, and it is three lines
//   perf: replace per-row split with a single-pass scan in OrderParser
//   before: 1,200 rows 84 ms p50 / 310 ms p99  (ProfileParser.tokenize)
//   after:  1,200 rows  9 ms p50 /  21 ms p99  (ProfileParser.scan)
//   why:    split() allocated a List and 12 Strings per row; the scanner
//           allocates one and reuses a cursor. p99 improved 15x because the
//           GC pauses were the tail.
// ...the "why" is the line that survives the next refactor. A commit that says
// only the before and after numbers invites a reviewer to ask, and a reviewer
// who asks and gets "it seemed slow" will eventually simplify it away.

// and what to do when you find the profile disagrees with your expectation
// 1. you profiled the wrong workload - check that the profile's total time
//    matches the measurement from step 1
// 2. you profiled the wrong build mode - a JIT profile tells you about JIT
//    behaviour; production is AOT
// 3. the cost is in a dependency - very common, and the fix is a version, a
//    configuration flag, or a replacement
// 4. the cost is I/O, not CPU - then no CPU work will help, and the answer is
//    caching, batching, or a protocol change
// 5. it is genuinely fine and your expectation was wrong - which is a real
//    answer, and the most valuable one, because it ends the work

// and the three that are never the answer
// - micro-optimising before profiling        you will optimise the wrong code
// - guessing at GC or JIT flags              flags trade safety for speed; every
//                                            one of them hides a real problem
// - rewriting a hot function in a faster    this is a last resort with a real
//   language or hand-written assembly        maintenance bill, and the profiler
//                                            will tell you the ceiling is
//                                            rarely worth it

// and the review question, which is the durable form of all of this
//   "which measurement says this is faster, and where is that number?"
// ...a change that cannot answer it does not need to be in the branch, however
// plausible it looks. Most performance regressions are not malicious
// optimisations; they are changes nobody could evaluate.
SymptomLook atUsually the answer
Slow, flat CPUCPU profile, self timeOne real hotspot
Slow only in burstsGC events, old spaceAllocation or a retained set
Slow p99, fine p50Tail of the timelineGC, a retry, or a lock
Slow on big input onlyThe complexity, by readingAn O(n²) loop
Slow on a network callCPU << total timeNot CPU. I/O, batching, cache
Slow to start, fast afterStartup timeline, first frameCode size, static init
Slow in a loop, fast aloneRetries, repeated framesSomething is being redone
Slow only on one machineHost CPU features, archBuild target mismatch

The last row is worth a note because it is the one that is environment-specific rather than code-specific, and it produces a bug report that cannot be reproduced. A binary compiled on a machine with AVX-512 runs with an illegal instruction on one without it; a dart compile exe from a newer glibc fails to start on an older one; a Docker image built on arm64 and run on amd64 fails with an exec format error that names no file. All three are one flag or one base image, and all three are found by building on the least capable machine in the matrix rather than the most.

// the three environment-specific failures, and their one-line fixes
// 1. illegal instruction
$ dart compile exe bin/app.dart -o app --target-cpu=generic
// ...compiles for a baseline CPU rather than the build machine's. Costs
// perhaps 10% and removes a class of production-only crash.

// 2. GLIBC version
$ ./app
./app: /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6: version `GLIBC_2.34' not found
// ...built on Ubuntu 22.04, deployed on Debian 11. The fix is the build image,
// not the binary:
FROM dart:stable AS build
RUN dart compile exe bin/app.dart -o /app
FROM debian:bullseye-slim          // ...an OLDER base, matched to the target
COPY --from=build /app /app
// ...or a musl static build, which removes the dependency entirely.

// 3. wrong architecture
$ docker run myapp:1.2.3
exec format error
// ...a single-arch image on a multi-arch host. The fix is a manifest list:
$ docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t myapp:1.2.3 --push .
// ...and the check that catches it before production:
$ docker buildx imagetools inspect myapp:1.2.3 | grep Architecture
    Architecture: amd64
    Architecture: arm64

// and the rule that prevents the whole class: the build that ships is built on
// the least capable machine in the support matrix, not the fastest one
// available. Everything else is a build cache waiting to be a bug report.

Appendix A · Quick Reference

A.1 Language referenceA.2 Null safety rulesA.3 Async and concurrencyA.4 Collections quick referenceA.5 pubspec referenceA.6 Command referenceA.7 Compilation targetsA.8 Pattern syntaxA.9 Glossary

Lookup tables to keep open while you write Dart: the language, null safety rules, async, collections, pubspec, commands, compilation targets, pattern syntax and a glossary.

A.1 Language reference

// VARIABLES
var x = 1;                     // mutable, inferred
final y = 2;                   // assigned once
const z = 3;                   // compile-time, deeply immutable
late final w;                  // assigned later, exactly once
late int? maybe;               // assigned later, nullable
const f = final int Function(); // a const function reference

// FUNCTIONS
void f1() {}
int f2() => 1;
Future<void> f3() async {}
Stream<int> f4() async* {}
Iterable<int> f5() sync* {}
Never f6() => throw 'x';
T f7<T>(T v) => v;

// PARAMETERS
void p1(int a, [String? b]) {}                 // optional positional
void p2(int a, {String? b, int c = 0}) {}      // named
void p3(int a, {required String b}) {}         // required named
void p4(int a, [int b = 0]) {}                 // default positional

// CLASSES
class C {
  final int a;                 // final field
  int _b = 0;                 // private (library-level)
  static const int s = 1;     // static const
  static late final f;        // static late final
  C(this.a);                 // initialising formal
  C.named(int a) : this.a = a; // redirecting
  C.computed(int v) : a = v * 2;  // computed initialiser
  factory C.make() => C(0);      // factory
  const C.constant() : a = 0;     // const constructor

  int get b => _b;
  set b(int v) => _b = v;
  @override
  String toString() => 'C($a)';
  @override
  bool operator ==(Object other) => identical(this, other);
  @override
  int get hashCode => a.hashCode;
  static C? _instance;
  factory C.singleton() => _instance ??= C(0);
}

// INHERITANCE
class A { void m() {} }
class B extends A { @override void m() {} }
class C2 implements A { @override void m() {} }
class D extends A with M1, M2 {}
mixin M1 {}
abstract class E { void mustImplement(); }
sealed class S {}
class S1 extends S {}   // S is now closed to S1, S2

// OPERATORS
+ - * / ~/ %            arithmetic (~/ is integer division)
+= -= *= /= ~/= %=
== != < > <= >=     comparison
a is T, a is! T        type test
a as T                cast
a ?? b, a ??= b       null-aware
a?.b, a?.b(), a?..b()  null-aware member
a!, a?                assert non-null, null-aware
..                     cascade
? :                    conditional
..=                    spread? NO - use ... instead

// SPREAD AND COLLECTION IF
final a = [1, 2, 3];
final b = [...a, 4, ...?maybeList];     // spread, with ? for nullable
final c = {...mapA, ...?maybeMap};      // map spread
final d = [for (final x in a) x * 2];   // collection if
final e = [for (final x in a) if (x > 1) x];
final f = {for (final x in a) x: x * 2};

How to read this table

A language reference is a lookup, and a lookup is only useful if you can get to the right row. The rows below are grouped by construct rather than by purpose, which is the standard arrangement and the wrong one for a programmer holding a specific problem — the question is never "what is a record", it is "how do I destructure this". So each subsection here is a decision: which construct to reach for, and what it costs. The bare list stays above it as the exhaustive index.

// the four decisions in this section, and what picks the answer
// 1. Do I need a NAME for a value, or only its parts?
//      only parts        -> a record pattern, or destructuring in a declaration
//      a stable name     -> a local variable
//      a compile-time constant -> const, never final
// 2. Is the collection's length fixed?
//      fixed and known at compile time -> a record: (int, String)
//      fixed but a runtime value       -> a List of a fixed shape, typed
//      unbounded                       -> a List, and document the length
// 3. Am I describing a TYPE or a VALUE?
//      a type with no instances ever -> an extension type
//      a set of named constants       -> an enum, or a sealed class
//      a namespace for related code   -> a library, one export per file
// 4. Does the operation need to be lazy, repeatable, or cancellable?
//      lazy and short-lived            -> an iterable, and `for` over it
//      repeatable and side-effecting  -> a Stream
//      one value, computed on demand  -> a getter, never a cached field

Records, and when one beats a class

A record is an anonymous value with a fixed, positional shape. It is structural — two records with the same shape and equal fields are equal — so it has no identity and cannot have methods, and it is the right answer for "a pair of values that travel together" and the wrong answer for anything with behaviour or a name. The rule of thumb: if you would write class Point { final double x, y; } and never add a method, use a record.

// records: shapes, equality, and destructuring
(int, String) parse(String line) {
  final parts = line.split(':');
  return (int.parse(parts[0]), parts[1]);
}

void main() {
  // ...equality is structural, so this works without an == override
  print(parse('7:abc') == (7, 'abc'));      // true

  // ...destructuring in a declaration: the form worth remembering
  final (code, name) = parse('7:abc');
  print('$code -> $name');

  // ...destructuring with types, and ignoring positions you do not want
  final (int code, String name) = parse('7:abc');
  final (_, String name) = parse('7:abc');       // `_` skips

  // ...named fields, when position would be unreadable at three or more
  ({int code, String name}) parseNamed(String line) {
    final parts = line.split(':');
    return (code: int.parse(parts[0]), name: parts[1]);
  }
  final r = parseNamed('7:abc');
  print(r.name);          // ...and now the ORDER does not matter, which is
                          //    the whole reason named fields exist
  print(r.$1);            // ...and they coexist: r.$1 is the code

  // ...a record used as a map key, which a class instance cannot be
  final seen = <(int, int), String>{};
  seen[(3, 4)] = 'a point';

  // ...nested destructuring, which is where records start to pay
  final ((int, int), String) nested = ((1, 2), 'label');
  final ((x, y), label) = nested;
}

// and what a record CANNOT do, which is the reason to stop reaching for one
// - no methods, so no behaviour
// - no inheritance
// - no nullability of its own: `(int, int)` is not `(int?, int?)`. If you need
//   a nullable field, name it: `({int? code, String name})`
// - a field name cannot start with an underscore, so no private fields
// ...so the moment a record needs a method, it is a class. This is the whole
// rule.

Extension types versus classes

The three ways to give a primitive a type are separate mechanisms that are easy to confuse, and picking the wrong one costs either performance or clarity. An extension type is a compile-time wrapper with zero runtime cost — it is not a distinct type at runtime, so it does not appear in a generic signature as anything but its representation. An class is a real runtime type with a real object. An enum is a class with a fixed set of constant instances. Reach for the extension type when you want the type safety of a distinct type and none of the behaviour.

// the three, and what each actually costs
// 1. EXTENSION TYPE: a zero-cost wrapper. Erased at runtime.
typedef Meters = double;
typedef Seconds = double;

double speed(Meters d, Seconds t) => d / t;

void main() {
  print(speed(100, 4));        // 25.0
  print(speed(Seconds(100), Meters(4)));   // COMPILES, and is a bug
}
// ...`Meters` and `Seconds` are both `double` at runtime, so the swapped call is
// not a type error. An extension type fixes this ONLY if you declare it with a
// representation it can distinguish:
//
//   typedef Meters(int _m);
//   typedef Seconds(int _s);
// ...now the two are distinct types and the swap is a compile error, because
// the compiler knows the representations differ. With `typedef Meters = double`
// it does not, and the annotation is documentation only. This is the single most
// important thing to know about extension types and it is in the spec on one
// page.

// 2. CLASS: a real object, with behaviour and a real runtime type
class UserId {
  final String value;
  const UserId(this.value);
  @override
  String toString() => 'UserId($value)';
  @override
  bool operator ==(Object other) =>
      other is UserId && other.value == value;
  @override
  int get hashCode => value.hashCode;
}
// ...one allocation, an == and a hashCode to maintain, and the guarantee that a
// UserId is never an int. Correct, and heavier than the problem usually needs.

// 3. ENUM: a closed set of named constants
enum Status { pending, active, suspended }

void handle(Status s) {
  switch (s) {
    case Status.pending:    print('waiting'); break;
    case Status.active:     print('live'); break;
    case Status.suspended:  print('paused'); break;
  }
  // ...NO default, and the compiler is still satisfied, because the switch is
  // exhaustive over the enum. Add a fourth case and this function STOPS
  // COMPILING. That is the property an enum buys and it is worth a great deal.
}
// ...an enum with data, which is the form that replaces most sealed-class
// hierarchies that only carry a payload:
enum Result<T> {
  ok<T>(T value) : _value = value;
  error<T>(String message) : _value = message as T;

  final T _value;   // ...the awkward part: a union type, so this is a lie
  // ...`Result<int>.error('bad')` can hold 'bad' cast to int, which throws
  // at runtime. A SEALED CLASS is the correct construct for a tagged union:
//
//   sealed class Result<T> {}
//   final class Ok<T> extends Result<T> { final T value; Ok(this.value); }
//   final class Err<T> extends Result<T> { final String m; Err(this.m); }
//   String describe<T>(Result<T> r) => switch (r) {
//     Ok(:final value) => '$value',
//     Err(:final m) => 'error: $m',
//   };
// ...and this is the pattern from A.8, repeated here because the choice between
// an enum-with-data and a sealed class is the one most often made wrongly.

// and the decision, in one table
//   need a distinct type, no behaviour, no cost   -> extension type with a
//                                                    non-primitive representation
//   need behaviour or equality                    -> class
//   need a closed set of constants                -> enum
//   need a closed set that each carries data      -> sealed class + pattern switch
//   need to tag a value for later                 -> record with named fields

Functions: the seven forms and when each is right

Dart's function syntax has more surface than most languages because it encodes four things that could each have been separate keywords: required (positional parameters), optional positional (brackets), named (braces), and return type (the arrow). The arrangement is not arbitrary — each bracket type means something about what the caller may do — and reading the signature tells you the calling convention without any other information.

// the four bracket forms, and what each permits
int a(int x);                                  // required positional
int b(int x, [int y = 0]);                     // optional positional
int c({required int x, int y = 0});            // named; `required` if no default
int d(int x, {String? tag});                   // positional THEN named - legal
void e([int x = 0, int y = 0]);                // ...but two optional lists is
                                               //    not: `void e([int x], [int y])`
                                               //    is a syntax error

// and what the caller can do with each
b(1);              // yes
b(1, 2);           // yes
c(x: 1);           // yes - and c(1) is a compile error
c(1);              // COMPILE ERROR: named params need `name:`
d(1);              // yes
d(1, tag: 'x');    // yes

// the rule the brackets encode
//   []  the caller MAY vary these. Usually a small, fixed arity.
//   {}  the caller NEEDS these by name, or may omit them. Use when there are
//       more than about two optional parameters, because a caller of
//       b(1, 2, 3, true, 'x') cannot remember what the third one was.
// ...this is the single most useful thing about the syntax, and getting it
// wrong is the most common API design mistake in Dart.

// return types, and the arrow
int f() => 42;                 // expression body: the value is returned
void g() { print(1); }           // block body: no value
Iterable<int> h() sync* {     // `sync*` - a synchronous iterable, lazy
  yield 1;
  yield 2;
}
Stream<int> i() async* {      // `async*` - a stream, lazily produced
  yield 1;
}
Future<void> j() async {      // `async` - a future
  await Future.delayed(Duration.zero);
}
Future<List<int>> k() async {     // `async` with a value
  return [1, 2];
}
Never l() => throw StateError('x');   // `Never`: does not return normally

// and three things about these that are not obvious
// 1. `async` makes the function's WHOLE BODY asynchronous, including everything
//    before the first await. A 1,000-iteration loop that runs before an await
//    is 1,000 synchronous iterations, so the caller is blocked for its
//    duration. This is why `Future.microtask` and friends exist.
// 2. `async*` holds the caller's subscription open for the generator's life.
//    A `yield` inside a `try` whose `finally` cancels the subscription is the
//    standard resource-cleanup shape:
//      Stream<int> ticks() async* {
//        try { while (true) { yield 1; await Future.delayed(s); } }
//        finally { cleanup(); }        // ...runs on cancel, not on return
//      }
// 3. `Never` is not `void`. `void` says "this returns nothing"; `Never` says
//    "this does not return". A function declared `Never` may be used where a
//    `T` is expected WITHOUT an await, because it never produces one. That is
//    the whole reason the type exists:
//      int parse(String s) { ... throw ...; }   // ...a compiler complaint in
//      Never parse(String s) { ... }             //    strict-mode analysis
//      Never fail() => throw StateError('x');

// a tear-off, which is a first-class function value with no call
int add(int a, int b) => a + b;
void main() {
  final f = add;                  // ...a tear-off, a value
  final g = add;                  // ...note: a tear-off is NOT equality-
  print(f == g);                  //    comparable to a closure with the same
                                  //    body; two closures are different objects
  final h = (int a, int b) => a + b;
  print(f == h);                  // ...false. Do not rely on it either way.
  print(add.runtimeType);         // ...`void Function(int, int)`
  print(identical(f, add));       // ...false: a NEW closure object each time
  // ...so `identical(add, add)` is false, and a Map keyed by a function will
  // not find it. Use a top-level or static tear-off as a constant:
//   static final reducer = add;   // ...now it is one object
}

A.2 Null safety rules

// THE TYPES
T          never null
T?         may be null
Object     any non-null value
Object?    any value, including null
dynamic    no checking at all

// THE OPERATORS
x!             assert non-null, throws if null
x?.y           null if x is null
x?.y()         null if x is null
x ?? y         y if x is null
x ??= y        assign y if x is null
x?..y()        cascade, skipped if x is null

// PROMOTION: the compiler tracks your checks
if (x != null) { x.length; }              // promoted
if (x case final s?) { s.length; }        // pattern promotion
final y = x; if (y != null) { y.length; } // via a local

// PROMOTION IS REFUSED for:
// - a getter
// - a field (it could change)
// - a top-level or static field
// - a local captured and written by a closure
// FIX: capture in a local first

// THE CONVERSIONS
// T -> T?           automatic, always safe
// T? -> T           NOT automatic: check, or use !
// List<T> -> List<T?>  needs .cast<T?>()
// Map<K,V> -> Map<K,V?>  needs a new Map

// THE CHECKS
// late: a T that is assigned later. Throws LateInitializationError
//       if read first. ONE assignment, then it is final.
String? late String? cache;    // the honest version
late final String token;      // if it is really always there

// THE PATTERNS THAT AVOID NULL
List<T> get items => _items;              // never null
List<T> get items => _items ?? const [];  // never null, may be empty
T? find(String id) => _map[id];              // null is a real answer
Validated<T, E> validate(T input);           // a sealed result

// THE RULES TO REMEMBER
// 1. default to final
// 2. never use ! to silence an error you have not investigated
// 3. never validate user input with assert: it is stripped in release
// 4. never persist a token in a plain field: use late or a store

The four states, and why there are four

Null safety in Dart is a type-system property, and the useful way to think about it is that every reference has one of four states, only two of which are usually intended. The type annotation says which two are permitted; it says nothing about which one actually holds, which is why a null-safety error is a runtime error and not a compile error in every case. Understanding which of the four you are looking at explains most null-safety diagnostics.

// the four states of a reference
String a = 'x';        // 1. a valid string
String? b = null;      // 2. explicitly null - PERMITTED by String?
String c;              // 3. null - a COMPILE ERROR under sound null safety
String d;              //    ...and it is a compile error because the definite
                       //    assignment analysis cannot prove it happens
String? e = 'x';       // 4. a valid string, typed as nullable - PERMITTED

// so the type is about PERMISSION, and the value is about FACT
// ...which is the whole mental model, and it is why `String? s; if (x) s = 'a';`
// still does not compile: x does not prove assignment.

// the three operators, and each is a different claim
String? maybe;

print(maybe?.length);        // null-aware call: null PROPAGATES
print(maybe ?? 'default');  // null-aware value: null is SUBSTITUTED
print(maybe!.length);       // null-assert: null CRASHES
// ...three different intentions, and using the wrong one is a bug rather than
// a style question:

// `!` where `?.` belongs - crashes on exactly the input you were guarding
//   print(maybe!.length);        // throws if maybe is null
// `??` where `?:` belongs - eagerly evaluates the right side
final expensive = computeFallback();     // ...computed even when maybe is set
final cheap = maybe ?? computeFallback(); // ...and `??` is lazy: the right side
                                          //    is only evaluated if needed
//   ...but `??` has no short-circuit for a side effect on the LEFT:
//   maybe.length ?? 0        // COMPILE ERROR: `?.` needs the `??`
//   maybe?.length ?? 0      // correct, and lazy on both sides

// `!` in a constructor, which is the one legitimate use of `!`
class Point {
  final int x, y;
  Point(this.x, this.y);
  const Point.origin()
      : x = 0,
        y = 0;          // ...no `!` needed in an initialiser list, which is
                       //    why initialisers are the right place
  Point.fromString(String s) {
    final parts = s.split(',');
    x = int.parse(parts[0]);
    y = int.parse(parts[1]);
  }   // ...a body assignment: x and y are NOT promoted, because they are
       //    instance fields and a subclass could override a getter. So `x`
       //    cannot be used where an `int` is required. Initialise via the
       //    parameter list or the initialiser list and the promotion works.
}

Promotion, and the five things that stop it

Promotion is the compiler narrowing a T? to T after it has proved the value is not null. It is the mechanism that makes null safety ergonomic — without it you would write if (x != null) { x.length } where x.length needs a non-nullable — and it works on a fixed list of syntactic forms. Knowing the list is worth more than any heuristic, because every "the compiler should have promoted this" question resolves to "one of these five applies".

PromotesDoes not promote
if (x != null) { }A local captured by a closure that runs later
if (x is T) { }A public instance FIELD — a subclass can override the getter
x ?? throw ...A top-level or static variable
assert(x != null)A property with a user-defined getter
x!; as a statementAnything after an await or a function call in some cases
// 1. promotes: a local
String? s = maybe();
if (s != null) {
  print(s.length);          // ...s is String here
}

// 2. promotes: an is-test, which also narrows the TYPE
Object o = 42;
if (o is String) {
  print(o.length);          // ...o is String, not Object
}

// 3. promotes: the ?? throw idiom, which is the best one
final name = input ?? throw ArgumentError('name required');
print(name.length);         // ...non-nullable, and it throws at the boundary
// ...this is the shape to prefer over `!` at an API boundary: the error is
// raised once, at the point the invariant is established, and everything
// downstream is non-nullable with no assertion.

// 4. promotes: assert, which is checked in debug and stripped in release
assert(x != null);
print(x.length);            // ...works, and in a release build the check is
                            //    gone - so NEVER rely on it for an invariant

// 5. does NOT promote: an instance field
class Box {
  String? label;            // ...public: a subclass could override `label`
  int get safeLength {
    final l = label;
    if (l == null) return 0;
    return l.length;        // ...a LOCAL copy promotes; `label` would not
  }
}
// ...the fix is the local copy, and that single line is the answer to most
// "why is this not promoted" questions about fields.

// 6. does NOT promote: a closure that may run later
String? name;
void register(void Function(String) cb) {
  cb(() {
    print(name.length);     // ...COMPILE ERROR: `name` may change by then
  });
}
// ...and `final` does NOT fix it. `final String? name` is still not promoted
// inside a closure, because the closure is not guaranteed to run before any
// assignment. This surprises people who expect `final` to help.
// ...the fix is a local capture, or `name!`, or - better - pass the value in:
//   final captured = name;
//   cb(() { if (captured != null) print(captured.length); });

// 7. does NOT promote: a public getter
class Config {
  String? get endpoint;      // ...public getter: overridable, so not promotable
  int get port => _port ?? 0;
  int? _port;
}
// ...a PRIVATE field or getter (`_endpoint`) IS promotable, because a subclass
// in another library cannot override it. So the fix is often to make the
// member private, which is also better encapsulation.

// 8. a local IS promoted across an await, but only if it is not reassigned
String? s = maybe();
await Future.delayed(Duration.zero);
