print(s?.length);           // ...works: `s` is a local, not a field
// ...`await` was the one case where promotion used to lapse. It does not now,
// which is worth knowing because older answers say otherwise.

Late, required, and the migration flags

Three modifiers exist for nullability that are not annotations on a variable but restrictions on a declaration, and each exists for a specific case that ? cannot express. late means "not initialised yet, trust me, and check at runtime". required means "the caller must pass this, by name, there is no default". And a language version flag decides whether the whole library is checked.

// late: deferred initialisation, checked on first read
class Session {
  late final User user;          // ...`final` plus `late`: assigned once,
                                 //    on first read, never again
  late final int cacheSize = 64; // ...a default AND late: assigned on first
                                 //    read unless something assigns it first

  void restore() {
    user = loadFromDisk();       // ...without `late` this line would need a
  }                               //    null check, because a final field
}                                //    cannot be nullable-and-uninitialised

// the failure `late` converts from a compile error to a runtime one
late final int x;
print(x);          // LateInitializationError: field 'x' has not been
                   // initialized.
// ...which is strictly worse, and that is why `late` is a last resort:
//   - it turns a compile-time guarantee into a runtime crash
//   - it is UNSOUND: `late final List<int> a = [];` then `late final List<int>
//     b = a;` and a mutation through b is visible through a
//   - it does nothing at all for a TOP-LEVEL variable's initialisation ORDER,
//     which is why top-level `late final` referencing another top-level
//     `late final` is a real crash
// Use it for: a field initialised by the framework (after `initState`), a value
// computed once lazily, and dependency injection. Not for: anything that could
// be initialised in the constructor.

// required: a named parameter the caller must supply
class Server {
  Server({required this.host, required this.port, this.debug = false});
  final String host;
  final int port;
  final bool debug;
}
// Server(host: 'x')                 // COMPILE ERROR: port is missing
// Server(host: 'x', port: 80)       // correct
// ...`required` on a positional parameter is a compile error, which is the
// language telling you the bracket choice was wrong.

// the version flags, and why they still matter
// analysis_options.yaml
analyzer:
  language:
    strict-casts: true
    strict-inference: true
    strict-raw-types: true
// ...and in pubspec.yaml
environment:
  sdk: '>=3.0.0 <4.0.0'
// ...a library below Dart 3.0 is UNSOUND null safety: `String s;` may be null
// at runtime and the compiler will not stop you. So the SDK constraint in
// pubspec.yaml is the switch that turns the whole guarantee on, and a package
// with `sdk: '>=2.12.0'` is not null safe regardless of what its source
// looks like. Bumping it to `>=3.0.0` is the single most valuable change to
// an old package, and it is mechanical: the analyser tells you every site.

// and the two flags worth adding that are not about null safety
analyzer:
  errors:
    unused_import: error        // ...the two most common causes of a file that
    unused_local_variable: error //    compiles but is wrong
  exclude: [build/**, '**/*.g.dart']
// ...`unused_import` as an ERROR is what stops a dead import from hiding a
// dependency in pubspec that a reviewer cannot see.

What null safety does not give you

Null safety removes one class of error and creates one habit. It removes the NullReferenceException from the language, so a dereference of null is now a deliberate act rather than a consequence of a path nobody considered. The habit it creates is designing APIs so that "this is not present" is expressed in the type, which is worth far more than the exception it removes.

What it does not do is make your program handle absence. A nullable type says "absence is possible here"; it says nothing about what should happen when absence occurs. An empty optional string, a missing configuration key and an absent user record want three different behaviours, and the type system is silent on all three. This is why "null safety means no more null checks" is wrong — it means the checks move from everywhere to the boundaries, which is a much better place for them and also a place where somebody has to decide what to write.

// three nullable fields, three correct behaviours
class Settings {
  const Settings({this.locale, this.pageSize = 25, this.endpoint});

  final String? locale;         // ...null means "not set". Behaviour: fall back
  final int pageSize;           //    to a default, at the point of USE:
  final String? endpoint;       //    `locale ?? systemLocale()`
  // ...and null here is an ERROR, because a server with no address cannot run:
  //    `endpoint ?? throw StateError("endpoint required")`
}

// ...which means the distinction is not in the TYPE, it is in the SEMANTICS, and
// the type only records that you thought about it. Two `String?` fields with
// different fallbacks are indistinguishable to the compiler and completely
// different to the reader. This is the design work that null safety pushes
// onto you; it is not free and it is not automatic.

// and the three shapes a fallback can take, which the language does not choose
final a = settings.locale ?? "en-GB";          // 1. a constant default: always safe
final b = settings.locale ?? detectLocale();  // 2. a computed default: costs work
final c = settings.locale!;                   // 3. no default: asserts the invariant
// ...and the reason 2 deserves care is that `??` is lazy, so `detectLocale()` is
// called only when the field is null. Written as `detectLocale() ?? x` by mistake
// it would run on every call. The operator's short-circuit is easy to rely on
// and easy to lose by reordering.

// and the case that is neither: make absence impossible
final Set<String> required = {"host", "port"};
for (final key in required) {
  final v = json[key];
  if (v == null) throw FormatException("missing $key", json);
}
// ...once a field has no valid null value, a non-nullable type plus a validation
// step is strictly better than a nullable type plus a fallback at every use.
// Reach for `String?` only when absence is genuinely a legitimate state.

Why late is unsound, precisely

The previous section called late unsound, which is correct and needs saying properly, because "unsound" has a specific meaning: there is a program the compiler accepts that violates the declared type, and the violation is discovered at runtime rather than at compile time. For late the mechanism is aliasing.

// the unsoundness, in six lines
class Cache {
  late final List<String> entries = [];
  late final List<String> alias = entries;   // ...same object, not a copy

  void add(String s) => entries.add(s);
}

void main() {
  final c = Cache();
  c.add("x");
  print(c.alias);       // ["x"] - `alias` is NOT an independent copy, and the
                        // type `List<String>` says nothing about that
}
// ...a reader of `alias`'s declaration has every reason to believe it is a
// separate list. It is not. This is exactly the class of bug null safety was
// introduced to prevent, reintroduced through a modifier. It is worse, because
// the declaration reads as though the guarantee is present.

// and the second failure, which is order, and is NOT a null-safety issue
// two top-level late finals that reference each other:
//   late final Config config = Config(db: database);
//   late final Database database = open(config);
// ...Dart initialises top-level finals in DECLARATION ORDER, so `config` is built
// first, reaches for `database`, which has not been initialised, and throws
// LateInitializationError. The declaration order makes one of them wrong and
// there is no way to express a cycle between two top-level finals. A function
// with `late` locals, or a lazy accessor, is the fix — not reordering, which
// just moves the crash to the other one.

// so the honest summary: `late` means "the compiler cannot prove this is
// initialised, so I am promising, and the promise is checked on first read".
// That is a weaker guarantee than the type system gives you elsewhere, and it
// should be used where a genuinely stronger mechanism does not exist:
//   - a field the framework assigns after construction
//   - a value computed once and read many times, on a measured hot path
//   - a value obtained by reflection or deserialisation, which cannot appear in
//     a constructor parameter list
// ...and nowhere else. Every one of those three has a non-`late` alternative
// that is better in at least one dimension, and the dimension to check is
// usually "can the compiler check this".

A.3 Async and concurrency

// FUTURES
Future.value(x)                 a completed future
Future.error(e)
Future.delayed(duration, [callback])
Future(() => work())           runs on the event loop
Future.sync(() => work())      runs now
Future.wait([f1, f2])          all complete
Future.any([f1, f2])           first to complete
future.then(v => ...)
future.then(v => ..., onError: (e) => ...)
future.catchError((e) => ...)
future.whenComplete(() => ...)
future.timeout(duration)
future.asStream()
unawaited(future)              from dart:async, marks it deliberately

// SEQUENTIAL vs CONCURRENT
final a = await one();                 sequential
final b = await two(a);                dependent
final [x, y] = await Future.wait([one(), two()]);   concurrent

// STREAMS
Stream.value(x)               a stream with one value
Stream.fromIterable([1, 2])
Stream.periodic(duration, (i) => i)
StreamController()            single-subscription: buffers
StreamController.broadcast()  multi-listener: drops events
await for (final x in stream) {}
stream.listen(onData, onError:, onDone:, cancelOnError:)

// STREAM OPERATORS
stream.map / where / take / skip / distinct / expand
stream.asyncMap((x) async => ...)     the async transform
stream.transform(StreamTransformer.fromBind(...))
stream.takeWhile / skipWhile
await stream.toList() / toSet() / reduce() / fold() / length

// ISOLATES
Isolate.run(() => heavy())            the simple form
Isolate.spawn(entry, arg)             the long-lived form
TransferableTypedData.fromList([b])    move memory, do not copy
SharedArrayBuffer.fromList([b])       share memory between isolates

// ZONES
runZonedGuarded(body, onError)        app-wide error capture
Zone.current[...]                     ambient context

The four async kinds, and what each costs

Dart has four asynchronous constructs and they are not variations on one mechanism — they differ in when control returns, whether cancellation is possible, and what error handling they imply. Picking the wrong one is the most common async defect in Dart code, and the symptom is always the same: work that should have overlapped did not, or work that should have been cancelled was not.

KindReturnsCancellableUse for
async functionOne FutureNoA single result
async* functionA StreamYesZero or many, produced lazily
awaitWaits for a futuren/aSequencing
Future.waitOne future for manyNoConcurrency
Isolate.runOne future, off-threadKills the isolateCPU-bound work
// 1. async: exactly one value, ever
Future<User> load(String id) async {
  final res = await http.get(Uri.parse('/users/$id'));
  return User.fromJson(jsonDecode(res.body) as Map<String, Object?>);
}
// ...one Future, completes once, cannot be cancelled. If the caller loses
// interest, the work still happens.

// 2. async*: zero, one or many, produced only as fast as they are consumed
Stream<int> countTo(int n) async* {
  for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    yield i;                     // ...the consumer's pace governs production
    await Future.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 10));
  }
}
// ...and this is the cancellation point, which a Future has no equivalent of:
Stream<int> withCleanup() async* {
  final sub = registry.listen(handle);
  try {
    yield* sub;                  // ...cancelling the outer subscription
  } finally {                    //    cancels `sub` here
    sub.cancel();
  }
}
// ...so `async*` is the construct to reach for whenever there is a resource,
// because it is the only one that gives you a `finally` on abandonment.

// 3. Future.wait: concurrency, and its one trap
Future<List<User>> all() async {
  return Future.wait(ids.map(load));    // ...all concurrent, unbounded
}
// ...the trap is the second line: 10,000 ids opens 10,000 sockets. The correct
// form bounds it:
Future<List<User>> allBounded(List<String> ids, {int limit = 8}) async {
  final pool = Pool(limit);
  try {
    return await Future.wait(ids.map((id) => pool.withPermit(load)));
  } finally {
    await pool.close();
  }
}
// ...and the second trap: `Future.wait` with `eagerError: false` (the default)
// waits for ALL of them and then reports the FIRST error, having silently
// discarded the rest. `eagerError: true` fails fast. Neither is obviously right;
// the choice depends on whether you need all results or the first failure.

// 4. Isolate.run: CPU-bound work, off the event loop
Future<int> checksum(List<int> data) {
  return Isolate.run(() => data.fold(0, (a, b) => a ^ b));
}
// ...the closure is sent to a new isolate, run, and the RESULT is copied back.
// Three consequences:
//   - the argument is COPIED, so passing a 100 MB list copies 100 MB
//   - only values that are SENDABLE cross the boundary; a closure that captures
//     an open file or a controller does not
//   - the function must be a top-level or static, or at least not require
//     `this` - it runs in a different isolate with no shared state
// ...so for a large input, `Isolate.run` is wrong and a worker isolate with a
// TransferableTypedData buffer is right: that is a transfer, not a copy.

// and the ordering rules that cause the most confusion
// MICROTASKS before EVENTS, always:
void main() {
  scheduleMicrotask(() => print('microtask'));
  Future(() => print('event'));
  print('sync');
}
// sync / microtask / event
// ...every microtask drains completely before the first event runs, which means
// a microtask that schedules another microtask STARVES the event loop and the
// page - or the CLI - appears to hang. `Future(() {...})` is an EVENT, not a
// microtask, which is the difference people get wrong.

// and the scheduling primitives, in order of latency
//   print(...)                synchronous, and the cheapest
//   scheduleMicrotask(...)    after the current synchronous block, before I/O
//   Future(() {...})          after I/O and timers - the "event queue"
//   Future.delayed(d)         after at least d, and no earlier
//   Timer.periodic(d, f)      every d, and the callback must be re-entrant
// ...a general rule: a microtask that does real work delays I/O, and a loop of
// microtasks delays it indefinitely. A `Future.delayed(Duration.zero)` is the
// correct "let the UI breathe" and a microtask is the WRONG one, because it
// runs BEFORE the frame is painted.

Zones, and the one thing they are for

A zone is a context that every asynchronous callback executes inside. It is invisible in ordinary code and it is the mechanism behind two things you use constantly without knowing: package:test's fake time, and Flutter's BuildContext lookup in async gaps. Understanding what a zone actually does explains both, and also explains why zone-based error handling is a bad idea.

// what a zone carries: two maps and an error handler
final zone = Zone.current.fork(
  zoneValues: {#traceId: 'abc-123'},
  errorHandler: (error, stack) {
    logger.severe('unhandled in zone', error, stack);
  },
);

Future<void> main() async {
  // ...everything awaited INSIDE runs with that key, at any depth
  await zone.run(() async {
    await Future.delayed(const Duration(seconds: 1));
    print(Zone.current[#traceId]);        // ...abc-123, two frames later
  });
}
// ...this is how request-scoped context reaches code four call frames deep that
// has no parameter to receive it in. It is genuinely useful and it is also the
// reason `Zone.current` appears in so much third-party code.

// WHY fakeAsync works, which is the thing worth understanding
import 'package:fake_async/fake_async.dart';

// ...`fakeAsync` does not replace the clock. It forks a zone whose
// `createTimer`, `createPeriodicTimer` and `scheduleMicrotask` are captured, so
// every Timer and every future chain created inside the zone is recorded by the
// zone rather than by the real event loop. Then:
//   async.elapse(Duration(seconds: 30))   advances the virtual clock AND
//                                          flushes the microtask queue
// ...which is why a future chain resolves inside `elapse` with nothing else
// having yielded: the zone captured the continuation and `elapse` runs it.
// ...and why awaiting REAL I/O inside a fakeAsync zone HANGS: the real I/O
// completes on the real event loop, and nothing in the fake zone is driving it.
// For code with real I/O, inject a Clock instead — which is a parameter, not a
// zone, and therefore testable in ordinary async tests.

// WHY zones should not be used for error handling
void main() async {
  await Zone.current.fork(
    errorHandler: (e, s) {
      // ...this fires ONLY for errors in code that ran inside the zone AND that
      // had no listener. An awaited future's error is delivered to the awaiting
      // frame's own handler, so this never sees it:
      await mightFail();
    },
  ).run(() async {
    await mightFail();     // ...the error propagates here, to main, NOT to the
  });                      //    zone's errorHandler
}
// ...so a zone errorHandler is a LAST-resort net for genuinely unhandled async
// errors, not a place to put application error handling. It also makes control
// flow invisible: the function returns normally and something elsewhere handles
// the failure.

// and the two zone-adjacent things that ARE worth using deliberately
// 1. `runZonedGuarded` - the one correct use: a top-level net that logs and
//    does not rethrow, so an unhandled async error does not kill the isolate.
// 2. `package:logging`'s `Logger.runZoned` - which is (1) plus log retention.

// and what NOT to do
// ...a DI container that resolves from `Zone.current`. It works, it is
// untestable without a zone, and it makes the dependency graph invisible to
// every tool that reads source. Constructor parameters cost nothing and are
// greppable.

Why one await per iteration costs so much

The claim that awaiting inside a loop is expensive is true and the reason is not that the await itself costs anything. Scheduling a continuation is tens of nanoseconds. The cost is that each await ends the current turn of the event loop and hands control away, and getting control back means running every callback the loop has queued in the meantime — a timer that fired, a socket that became readable, a microtask that was scheduled. A loop with an await per iteration turns one turn into n turns, and each turn is an opportunity for unrelated work to run in the middle of yours.

That is why the magnitude of the effect scales with how busy the loop is, and why the same code is free in a test and expensive in a server. In a test nothing else is queued, so the extra turns cost the scheduler and nothing more. In a server handling a thousand connections, each turn drains a thousand ready callbacks, and your loop pays for all of them, a thousand times.

// the shape that costs the most, and why
Future<List<Row>> loadAll(List<int> ids) async {
  final rows = <Row>[];
  for (final id in ids) {
    rows.add(await db.fetch(id));   // ...1000 turns, each draining whatever
  }                                  //    else the loop has ready
  return rows;
}
// ...two independent costs here, and they are additive:
//   1. the database round trips are SERIAL. 1000 x 2 ms = 2 seconds.
//   2. 1000 event loop turns. In a test: negligible. In production: each one
//      lets another request's work run, so the request's own latency is now a
//      function of the server's load.
// ...the second cost is invisible in a benchmark and is often larger than the
// first. It is also the reason a "simple" batch job becomes a latency problem
// the day it is moved into a shared process.

// the fix has two independent parts, and applying only one still leaves you
// with the other
Future<List<Row>> loadAllBounded(List<int> ids, {int limit = 8}) async {
  final pool = Pool(limit);
  try {
    // 1. concurrency: the round trips now overlap, so 1000/8 x 2 ms = 250 ms
    // 2. ONE turn: Future.wait resolves after all complete, so the loop does
    //    not surrender the turn 1000 times
    return await Future.wait(ids.map((id) => pool.withPermit(() => db.fetch(id))));
  } finally {
    await pool.close();
  }
}
// ...applying only part 1 — `Future.wait` with a bound but the original serial
// dependency — is not possible, they come together. But applying concurrency to
// a loop that also does per-item work will NOT reduce the turn count, so the
// second cost needs the shape changed rather than just the concurrency raised.

// and the rule of thumb that follows, which is about dependencies not style
// ...concurrency is only possible between operations that do not depend on each
// other. An `await` in a loop is either a mistake (the items are independent)
// or a requirement (each depends on the last). Deciding which is the actual
// analysis, and there are three shapes:
//   independent       -> concurrent, with a bound
//   one depends on the next -> serial, and no concurrency helps
//   independent but ordered output -> concurrent internally, serial at the end
// The third is the one that is usually written as the first, and it is why some
// code cannot be made concurrent without a redesign: it does the expensive work
// serially and only sorts the results afterwards.

The microtask queue, and how it starves

The rule that governs all of this is one sentence long and everything surprising about Dart async follows from it: every microtask in the queue runs, in order, and no event runs until the microtask queue is empty. Not "no event runs until the next turn" — empty. A microtask that schedules another microtask appends it, and it runs too, before any event.

The consequence is that a microtask loop is indistinguishable from an infinite loop as far as I/O is concerned. The event loop is not permitted to reach the point where it would check for I/O, because there is always another microtask. A timer never fires, a socket never becomes readable, a Flutter frame is never painted, and the process appears to hang with no error and no crash.

// the starvation, and why it produces no diagnostic at all
void main() {
  var count = 0;
  void pump() {
    count++;
    scheduleMicrotask(pump);      // ...always another one queued
  }
  scheduleMicrotask(pump);

  Timer(Duration(milliseconds: 10), () => print("timer fired"));
  // ...never prints. The timer is due at 10 ms. The microtask queue is never
  // empty, so the event loop never reaches the timer phase. There is no
  // exception, no warning, and no stack trace: the process is spinning inside
  // the microtask drain and every other source of work is starved behind it.

// and the version that fails in production instead of in a demo, which is the
// one worth recognising
final queue = Queue<Task>();
Future<void> drain() async {
  while (queue.isNotEmpty) {
    await handle(queue.removeFirst());
  }
}
Future<void> handle(Task t) async {
  scheduleMicrotask(() {
    // ...deferred work that is not awaited and not returned
  });
  // ...an unawaited scheduleMicrotask here queues one callback per task. If
  // handle() resolves before those callbacks run, `drain` loops again and the
  // queue never empties from the event loop's point of view. The symptom is a
  // service that is 100% CPU with no work in it and no error anywhere.

// the three fixes, in order of preference
// 1. do the work IN the microtask. If it is quick, there is no reason to defer.
// 2. use Future(() {...}) instead, which is an EVENT. Events are bounded, so
//    starvation is impossible; you get fairness instead of priority.
// 3. use a Timer with Duration.zero, also an event, when you specifically want
//    "after the current frame".
// ...and the one that looks equivalent and is not: `await Future.delayed(Duration.zero)`
// is also an event, so it is safe, but it schedules a timer rather than an
// immediate callback, which is a different amount of work. Both are correct;
// knowing which one you meant is what matters.

// and the ordering rule, which is worth memorising because it determines what
// prints where
void main() {
  scheduleMicrotask(() => print("A microtask"));
  Future(() => print("B event"));
  Timer.run(() => print("C timer"));
  Future.delayed(Duration.zero, () => print("D delayed event"));
  print("E synchronous");
}
// E / A / B / C / D
// ...`E` first because nothing above it awaits. `A` second because microtasks
// drain before events. Then the three events, in the order their timers were
// registered with the same deadline — which is registration order, so `B` and
// `C` before `D` only because `D` was registered last.

A.4 Collections quick reference

// COMPLEXITY
//                 lookup  insert  order   dups    notes
// List             O(n)     O(n)*   yes     yes     the default
// Set              O(1)     O(1)    no      NO      membership
// Map              O(1)     O(1)    yes     NO      keyed
//   * insert at the END is amortised O(1); at the front it is O(n)

// LIST
[a, b, c]                      literal
List.filled(n, 0)              n copies
List.generate(n, (i) => i)     n values
List.unmodifiable([a, b])      read-only
.add .addAll .insert .insertAt .remove .removeAt .removeLast
.removeWhere .retainWhere .clear .sort .shuffle
.sublist(i, j) .take(n) .skip(n) .reversed
.first .last .firstWhere .single .elementAt
.contains .indexOf .forEach
// remove(v) removes ONE; removeWhere removes ALL

// SET
{a, b}                        literal, insertion order preserved
SplayTreeSet<T>()              sorted
LinkedHashSet.of(iterable)     explicit insertion order
.add (returns false if present) .remove .contains
.union .intersection .difference .symmetricDifference
// a set's iteration order is NOT numeric: it is insertion order

// MAP
{k: v}                         literal, insertion order preserved
HashMap<K, V>()                unordered, fastest
SplayTreeMap<K, V>()           sorted
m[k]                           read: V? - nullable!
m[k] = v                       write
m[k] ??= v                     write if absent
m.putIfAbsent(k, () => v)
m.remove(k) .containsKey(k)
m.keys .values .entries
m.forEach((k, v) => ...)
Map.fromEntries(pairs) .map((k, v) => MapEntry(...))
Map.from(m.where((k, v) => ...))

// ITERABLE
.map .where .whereType .expand .cast .followedBy
.any .every .contains .join .reduce .fold .count
.take .skip .takeWhile .skipWhile .first .last
.single .isEmpty .isNotEmpty .length
// lazy: map, where, take, skip, expand, followedBy
// eager: toList, toSet, fold, reduce, join, any, every, length
// add with package:collection: firstOrNull, lastOrNull,
//   elementAtOrNull, sortedBy, groupBy, whereNotNull, sumBy,
//   minOf, maxOf, averageBy, Equality, Permutation

Choosing between the four list types

Dart has four list types and the difference between them is not performance — it is whether the list can change length, and what happens to the memory when it does. Getting this right at the declaration removes a whole class of runtime error, because add on a fixed-length list throws UnsupportedError rather than silently reallocating.

DeclarationGrowableBackingDefault for
[]YesArrayAn empty growable list
List.filled(n, x)NoArrayA fixed-size list
List<T>.filled(n, x)YesArrayA pre-sized growable list
List.generate(n, f)YesArrayA computed list
List.unmodifiableNoCopy or wrapperA public API's return value
List.of(n)NoFixed arrayA length-only constructor
// the four, and what each does to a literal
// 1. [] - growable, empty, backed by a small array that grows by doubling
final a = <int>[];
a.add(1);              // ...works

// 2. List.filled(n, value) - FIXED length, all elements initialised
final b = List.filled(3, 0);
b[0] = 1;
b.add(4);              // ...UnsupportedError: Cannot add to a fixed length list
b.length = 5;          // ...also throws
// ...and this is the one that bites: a helper that does `result.add(...)` on
// whatever it is given will crash on a `List.filled`. Declare the parameter as
// `List<T>` (growable by default in the type) rather than passing a fixed list.

// 3. List<T>.filled(n, value) - growable BUT pre-sized
final c = List<int>.filled(1000, 0);
c.add(1);              // ...works, and never reallocates
// ...this is the form to use for a list you know the final size of. Building
// 10,000 elements by `add` does about 14 reallocations and copies; this does
// none. It is the single cheapest list optimisation in Dart.

// 4. List.unmodifiable - the one to return from a public API
List<int> snapshot() => List.unmodifiable(_internal);
// ...throws UnsupportedError on ANY mutation, rather than copying defensively.
// ...but be aware: `List.unmodifiable(existing)` COPIES. `UnmodifiableListView`
// wraps without copying, which is what you want for a large list where the
// caller should see later changes:
//   UnmodifiableListView(_internal)     // a view: reflects later mutations

// and the construction forms that do the work for you
final m = {'a': 1, 'b': 2};

// maps to entries, entries to values, values to keys
final names = m.keys.toList(growable: false);
final values = List<int>.filled(m.length, 0);
for (var i = 0; i < m.length; i++) {
  values[i] = m.values.elementAt(i);
}
// ...`elementAt` on a Map's values is O(n) for a LinkedHashMap, which makes the
// loop quadratic. Iterate `m.entries` instead:
//   for (var i = 0, e = m.entries.toList(); i < e.length; i++) values[i] = e[i].value;

// and the four that are almost always a mistake
final a = [1, 2, 3].map((x) => x * 2).toList();          // fine
final b = [for (final x in [1, 2, 3]) x * 2];            // better: one pass, no
                                                        //    intermediate iterable
final c = List.generate(3, (i) => i * 2);               // better still for a
                                                        //    computed sequence
final d = [1, 2, 3].where((x) => x.isEven).toList();    // fine, and readable

Sets and maps: the four decisions

Set and map selection has four independent decisions, and the defaults are right for three of them. The one that matters is iteration order, because it is the only one that changes program behaviour rather than performance — and a HashMap whose iteration order is unspecified produces output that differs between runs, which makes tests fail intermittently and JSON output uncompparable.

// 1. SET: membership, or de-duplication, or both
final seen = <String>{};              // ...a HashSet: unordered, O(1)
final ordered = <String>{};           // ...also a HashSet - the literal
                                          //    does NOT preserve insertion order
final linked = <String>{};            // ...to get insertion order:
final linked = LinkedHashSet<String>();
final sorted = <String>{}..toList()..sort().toSet();
final sorted = SplayTreeSet<String>((a, b) => a.compareTo(b));
// ...note the third line: `<String>{}` is a HashSet even though it looks
// like it should be ordered. If you iterate it and print, the order is
// unspecified and a test asserting on it will fail on someone else's machine.

// 2. MAP: the four implementations, chosen by one question each
//    LinkedHashMap (the default literal) - iteration in INSERTION order
final a = {'b': 1, 'a': 2};              // ...b, a
//    HashMap - iteration in an unspecified order
final b = HashMap.of({'b': 1, 'a': 2});  // ...a, b or b, a, and it may differ
                                         //    between runs
//    SplayTreeMap - iteration SORTED, and range queries
final c = SplayTreeMap<int, String>(
  (x, y) => x.compareTo(y),
  (k) => MapEntry(k, 'v$k'),
);
// ...c.keys.between(10, 20) is every key in [10, 20). There is no hash
// equivalent, which is the reason to choose it.

// 3. THE QUESTION THAT DECIDES: will anything iterate it?
//    No  -> HashMap. The memory saving is small but real.
//    Yes -> LinkedHashMap (insertion) or SplayTreeMap (sorted)
// ...and NEVER write a test asserting on a HashMap's key order. This is the
// single most common source of a test that passes locally and fails in CI:
//   expect(map.keys.toList(), ['a', 'b']);       // FRAGILE
//   expect(map.keys.toList()..sort(), ['a', 'b']);  // correct
// ...and never let a HashMap's iteration order reach output - a JSON body built
// from a HashMap has a key order that changes when the map grows.

// 4. THE OTHER QUESTION: is the key a plain value or an identity?
//    Value semantics (two equal keys are one entry):
final byName = {'ana': 1};                  // ...correct, and the normal case
//    Identity semantics (two objects are distinct even if == says otherwise):
class Entity {
  final int id;
  const Entity(this.id);
  @override
  bool operator ==(Object o) => o is Entity && o.id == id;
  @override
  int get hashCode => id.hashCode;
}
final byEntity = <Entity, String>{};
final a1 = Entity(1), a2 = Entity(1);
byEntity[a1] = 'first';
byEntity[a2] = 'second';
print(byEntity.length);     // ...1. They are equal, so the second assignment
                           //    OVERWRITES the first.
// ...so an entity map needs either a consistent == (as above) or an explicit
// identity key: `Map.identity()` — `Map<Entity, String>.identity()`, which
// uses identical() rather than ==. For a cache keyed by object where you mean
// "this exact instance", Map.identity() is the correct structure and it is
// almost never used.

// and the composite key, which is where records earn their place
// ...a Map<K, V> keyed on two values needs a composite, and a record is the
// only zero-cost way to do it:
final index = <(String, int), String>{};
index[('ana', 1)] = 'ana-1';
index[('ana', 2)] = 'ana-2';    // ...a distinct entry, correctly
// ...with a class key you would also write a composite == and hashCode; with a
// record both are structural and already correct.

Correcting the Set, and the distinction that matters

The first batch stated that a set literal is unordered. That is right of HashSet and wrong of the literal, and the correction matters because the wrong version is a rule people then apply to the right thing. In Dart, <String>{} and <String, int>{} both construct a LinkedHashSet and a LinkedHashMap respectively: the literals carry an implicit type parameter and the default is the order-preserving implementation. The unordered behaviour belongs to the explicitly-named HashSet and HashMap.

The distinction is worth making precisely because it is invisible at the call site. {} and HashMap<K,V>() look equally like "a map", and they differ in a way that changes program output, so the choice has to be deliberate rather than default.

// the same literal, both order-preserving
final s = <String>{}..addAll(['c', 'a', 'b']);
print(s.toList());                 // [c, a, b] - insertion order

final m = <String, int>{'c': 3, 'a': 1, 'b': 2};
print(m.keys.toList());            // [c, a, b] - insertion order

// and the same thing explicitly unordered
final hs = HashSet<String>()..addAll(['c', 'a', 'b']);
final hm = HashMap<String, int>()..add('c', 3)..add('a', 1);
print(hs.toList());                // unspecified: [a, b, c] on one run,
//                                   // [c, a, b] on the next, possibly

// so the practical rules, which are the corrected ones
// 1. a literal is ordered. You do not need to do anything to keep order.
// 2. naming HashMap/HashSet is a PERFORMANCE choice with a BEHAVIOURAL cost.
//    It is not a "faster shorthand" for the literal.
// 3. a test asserting on iteration order of a HashMap is testing an
//    implementation detail. Sort first, always.
// 4. the memory difference is real but small for the collection sizes typical
//    of application code. The order is worth more than the memory.

// and why the order is worth more: three things break without it
// a JSON response whose keys must be stable across runs, because a diff of two
//   responses is then meaningful
// a UI list that renders from a map, where reordering on every rebuild makes
//   selection and scroll position jump
// a log line assembled from a map, where field order is the only thing making
//   it greppable
// ...none of these is possible with a HashMap and all of them are common, which
// is why LinkedHashMap is the correct default and HashMap is the one that needs
// a reason.

Choosing between growable and fixed, and the cost of each

The growable flag is not a convenience; it changes the memory layout, and the difference is worth understanding because it is invisible at the call site and shows up only under load. A fixed-length list stores its elements contiguously with a known bound and cannot resize. A growable list stores a capacity separately from a length and reallocates when the length outgrows the capacity, copying everything.

// what growth actually costs
final a = <int>[];                      // capacity 0
for (var i = 0; i < 10000; i++) a.add(i);
// ...reallocations at roughly 1, 2, 4, ... 8192, 16384: fourteen of them, and
// the copies sum to about 32,000 element moves. Amortised, so each `add` is
// O(1) on average — and the constant is a full array copy every time the
// capacity is exhausted.

// the two forms that avoid it
final b = List<int>.filled(10000, 0);   // growable, PRE-SIZED: no
                                           // reallocation, and `.filled`
                                           // requires the TYPE ARGUMENT
final c = List.filled(10000, 0);          // FIXED length: same allocation,
                                           // but `.add` now throws
final d = List<int>.generate(10000, (i) => i);   // computed, one pass

// which of the three to use
//   List<T>.filled(n, v)  when you know the size and will still add to it
//   List.filled(n, v)       when the size is the contract: fixed buffers, table
//                           rows, and anything you hand to a C API
//   List.generate(n, f)     when the elements are computed and can be produced
//                           in order without an intermediate
// ...and the difference between the first two is one character of type
// argument and it is the difference between a working buffer and an
// UnsupportedError at runtime.

// the failure the fixed length produces, and why it is a good failure
final rows = List.filled(expectedCount, Row.empty());
for (final r in incoming) {
  rows.add(r);              // UnsupportedError: Cannot add to a fixed length
}                            // list
// ...thrown loudly, immediately, with the operation named. Compare the
// alternative: growing without a bound, and discovering at 3 a.m. that a
// misbehaving client sent 400 MB of rows and the process was OOM-killed. The
// fixed-length list turns a production outage into a caught exception at the
// boundary, which is the correct place for a size limit to live.

// and the length-only constructor, which is easy to miss
final buf = List<String>.filled(0, '');      // growable, empty: no better
final buf2 = List<String>.filled(10, '');     // ten NUL bytes, pre-sized
// ...`List.filled(0, '')` looks like an empty list and is a fine way to spell
// one, but it does not pre-size anything, so it is exactly equivalent to `[]`
// and slightly harder to read.

A.5 pubspec reference

name: my_package                    lowercase_with_underscores
description: >-                  60-180 chars, say what it DOES
version: 1.0.0                    semver, a number not a date
repository: https://github.com/... required by pub.dev
issue_tracker: https://...
homepage: https://...              optional
documentation: https://...

environment:
  sdk: ">=3.0.0 <4.0.0"           ALWAYS include the upper bound
  flutter: ">=3.0.0"                only for a Flutter package

dependencies:                     runtime: shipped to users
  http: ^1.2.0                    ^1.2.3 = >=1.2.3 <2.0.0
  path: ^1.8.0                    ~1.2.3 = >=1.2.3 <1.3.0
  collection: any                 avoid 'any'

dev_dependencies:                 development only: not shipped
  test: ^1.25.0
  lints: ^4.0.0
  build_runner: ^2.4.0
  json_serializable: ^6.8.0

executables:
  my_tool: my_tool                a CLI in bin/

flutter:
  plugin:
    platforms:
      android:
        package: com.you.my_package
        pluginClass: MyPlugin
    assets:
      - assets/data/
  uses-material-design: true

dependency_overrides:             FORCED versions: risky
  http: ^2.0.0

The fields, and the three that get misused

pubspec.yaml has about a dozen fields that matter, and three of them are misused often enough to be worth stating precisely: dependencies versus dev_dependencies, the SDK constraint, and the difference between an application and a library in what belongs in the lockfile. Getting the third wrong is a publishing mistake that cannot be taken back once the version is out.

name: myapp
description: A one-sentence summary for pub.dev.
version: 1.4.2+47
publish_to: none            # ...or 'https://pub.dev'
repository: https://github.com/you/myapp

environment:
  sdk: '>=3.4.0 <4.0.0'
  flutter: '>=3.22.0'        # ...Flutter apps only; a package omits it

dependencies:
  http: ^1.2.0
  json_annotation: ^4.9.0

dev_dependencies:
  build_runner: ^2.4.0
  test: ^1.25.0
  flutter_lints: ^4.0.0

flutter:
  uses-material-design: true
  assets:
    - assets/images/
  fonts:
    - family: Inter
      fonts:
        - asset: assets/fonts/Inter-Regular.ttf
          weight: 400
FieldMeansGotcha
versionSemVer, optional build number1.4.2+47 — the +47 is a build number
sdkThe supported Dart rangeBelow 3.0.0 means unsound null safety
^1.2.0>=1.2.0 <2.0.0Not "any 1.x above"; the major is a wall
anyAny versionUnpinned: the build changes without a commit
path: ../xA local directoryNever publishable; never in a released app
git:A repositoryMust also have a version constraint or pub warns
hosted:A private registryNeeds a token; breaks anyone without access
assets:Files bundled into the appA directory entry includes everything under it

Application versus library, and the lockfile

This is the distinction that matters for publishing and it is easy to get backwards. An application — anything you deploy — commits pubspec.lock, because its build must be reproducible: the same commit must produce the same binary. A library — anything someone else depends on — must not commit it, because the lockfile of a library is ignored by its consumers and committing it causes a pub warning and confuses contributors into thinking they control the versions.

// APPLICATION: commit pubspec.lock
// $ dart pub get
// ...resolves and writes pubspec.lock. Commit it. CI should use
// `dart pub get --enforce-lockfile`, which FAILS if the lockfile would change:
//   - run: dart pub get --enforce-lockfile
// ...so a transitive dependency cannot be bumped by a build, which is the
// supply-chain risk that makes this worth enforcing rather than defaulting.

// LIBRARY: do NOT commit pubspec.lock, and say so
//   # .gitignore
//   pubspec.lock
//   .dart_tool/
// ...and your CI must therefore resolve FRESH on every run, which is a feature:
// it means your package is tested against whatever is current, so a transitive
// release that breaks you is found by you rather than by your users.
//
// a `pub publish --dry-run` on a library with a committed lockfile prints:
//   warning: Your package has a pubspec.lock file. Libraries should not have
//   these files committed.
// ...and for an application it prints the opposite, so the warning is a reliable
// signal that you have the two backwards.

// and the constraint ranges, which are a compatibility decision
// dependencies:
//   http: ^1.2.0            # you work with 1.2-1.x. Correct.
//   http: '>=1.0.0 <2.0.0' # same thing, written longhand
//   http: any              # you have tested nothing and will break silently
//   http: ^1.2.0-beta.1     # a prerelease; pub will resolve prereleases only if
//                          #    explicitly asked, so your users get stable 1.x
// ...for a LIBRARY, widen your constraints as far as you honestly can. A
// library with `sdk: '>=3.4.0'` excludes every user on 3.0-3.3 for no reason.
// Narrow only where you genuinely use a newer API, and say so in the changelog.

// and dependency_overrides, which is for YOUR machine and nobody else's
dependency_overrides:
  my_package:
    path: ../my_package
// ...this is how you develop a package and its consumer together. It must NOT
// be committed to a published package (pub rejects it), and it is a common
// accident in an application: an override in main means the production build
// depends on a path that does not exist on the build machine, and the failure
// is at `dart pub get` rather than at build time.

// and the commands that read it
$ dart pub get              # resolve, write pubspec.lock
$ dart pub get --offline    # resolve from the cache only, no network
$ dart pub upgrade          # move to the newest allowed versions, rewrite the lock
$ dart pub upgrade --major-versions   # also move MAJOR versions, and expect breaks
$ dart pub deps             # the resolved tree
$ dart pub deps --style=tree
$ dart pub outdated         # what is behind, and what is constrained
$ dart pub publish --dry-run # every check pub will run, without publishing
$ dart pub add http         # adds the dependency AND the import in your source
// ...`dart pub add` is worth preferring over a hand edit: it writes the
// constraint at the currently-published version, and it edits the import so the
// two cannot drift.

Why the lockfile rule is not a style preference

The rule — commit the lockfile for an application, ignore it for a library — is usually presented as a convention, and it is not. It follows from what a lockfile is: a complete resolution of the dependency graph to exact versions, including every transitive dependency, recorded at one moment in time.

That description immediately explains both halves. An application needs a specific resolution, because its artefact must be reproducible: the same commit has to produce the same binary, or a rollback does not roll back. A library has no such need, because it does not produce an artefact — its consumer resolves the graph, and the consumer's own lockfile is the authoritative record of what they got. A library's committed lockfile describes a graph that no user will ever see.

// what the lockfile actually contains - this is why the rule follows
# pubspec.lock
packages:
  http:
    dependency: "direct main"
    version: "1.2.1"            # ...an EXACT version, resolved on one day
    source: hosted
    url: "https://pub.dev"
  async:
    dependency: transitive
    version: "2.11.0"           # ...and transitive: something you never
                                 #    mentioned and cannot see in pubspec.yaml
sdks:
  dart: ">=3.4.0 <4.0.0"
// ...so the file is a snapshot of a graph nobody chose deliberately: pub
// resolved what was newest-compatible on the day you ran get. That is exactly
// what you want frozen for an application and exactly what you do not want
// frozen for a library.

// the failure the rule prevents, in each direction
// APPLICATION, lockfile NOT committed:
//   git clone && dart pub get        # resolves to LATEST today
//   ...and next month the same clone resolves to something newer. Your "same
//   commit" now builds differently, and the difference is a transitive package
//   you have never heard of. The regression report will not mention it, because
//   nobody changed your code.
//
// LIBRARY, lockfile COMMITTED:
//   pub publish warns, and your contributors get confused. The deeper problem is
//   that it is actively misleading: the file looks authoritative and it is not,
//   because pub ignores it for consumers. Someone will try to bump a version by
//   editing it.

// and the CI enforcement, which is the part people skip
// for an APPLICATION:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
- run: dart pub get --enforce-lockfile
// ...`--enforce-lockfile` FAILS if resolution would change pubspec.lock. So a
// transitive release that your constraint allows cannot alter your build
// without a human editing the lockfile and committing that edit, where it is
// reviewable. This turns a supply-chain change from invisible to visible, and it
// is the single highest-value line in a Dart CI file.
//
// for a LIBRARY, the opposite:
- run: dart pub get
- run: dart pub outdated --no-dev-dependencies   # ...so a transitive release
                                                  //    that breaks you is
                                                  //    found by you, in this
                                                  //    run, rather than by your
                                                  //    users

Constraint ranges, and what they promise

A version constraint is a promise in one direction only. What ^1.2.0 means is "I will accept any 1.x from 1.2.0 upward", and it does not mean "I have tested every 1.x". It also does not mean "any 1.x will work", because your own code might use something that a later 1.x removed, though that is not supposed to happen within a major version.

The consequence is that the constraint is a statement about your willingness, and the tests are the statement about your knowledge. They are different things and conflating them produces the two errors people actually make: a wide constraint on untested code, and a narrow one for no reason.

ConstraintAcceptsUse when
^1.2.0>=1.2.0 <2.0.0The normal answer. A library you depend on heavily
^1.2.0-beta.1>=1.2.0-beta.1 <2.0.0You need a pre-release feature; pub prefers stable unless asked
>=1.0.0 <2.0.0Same as ^1.0.0When you want the reader to see the bound
>=1.0.0 <3.0.01.x and 2.xA library: you accept a breaking change you have not tested
>=3.4.0 <4.0.0Any 3.4+You use a feature added in 3.4
anyEverythingAlmost never. You have tested nothing and will break silently
1.2.0Exactly thatA known-broken patch. Pin exactly, and comment why
// the two mistakes, and what each costs

// MISTAKE 1: a narrow constraint on a LIBRARY
// environment:
//   sdk: '>=3.4.0 <4.0.0'
// ...every user on 3.0 to 3.3 is excluded from your package for no reason. If
// the library does not actually use a 3.4 feature, this costs you users and
// gains you nothing. The check is mechanical: raise the constraint, run the
// tests, and if they pass, the narrower bound was arbitrary.
//
// MISTAKE 2: a wide constraint on untested code
// dependencies:
//   json_annotation: '>=4.0.0 <6.0.0'
// ...you have tested 4.9. pub resolves 5.x for a new user, 5.x changed a
// behaviour you depend on, and their `pub get` succeeds. The report is "your
// package broke with no code change", which is the hardest kind to diagnose
// because nothing in your repository changed.

// and the two that are correct and look like mistakes
//   http: '>=1.0.0 <3.0.0'    // accepting a range you have not tested
// ...correct for a library whose surface to `http` is one function call. The
// compatibility cost of a narrow bound is paid by your users; the maintenance
// cost of a wide one is paid by you only if you actually use what changed.
//   http: '1.1.0'                  // pinned exactly, with a comment
// ...correct when a known patch version is broken. Pin it, and put the reason
// and the tracking issue in a comment, because an unexplained exact pin is
// removed by the next person who tidies up dependencies.

// and the one that is neither of these: your own SDK constraint is the single
// most consequential line in the file
//   sdk: '>=2.12.0 <4.0.0'
// ...2.12 is where null safety became AVAILABLE. Below 3.0, the library is
// marked as not sound-null-safe, and a dependent that IS null safe cannot
// depend on it without the unsafe code being reachable. So this one line
// determines whether your library can be used from modern code at all, and it is
// usually left behind from a mechanical version bump years earlier.

A.6 Command reference

// PROJECT
dart create -t console my_app
dart create -t package my_package
dart create -t web my_web_app
flutter create my_flutter_app
dart run bin/main.dart
dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o app

// QUALITY
dart analyze                     errors, warnings, lints
dart analyze --fatal-infos       fail on infos too (for CI)
dart fix                         apply the safe automated fixes
dart format .                    the formatter: non-negotiable
dart format --set-exit-if-changed .
dart doc                         generate API docs

// DEPENDENCIES
dart pub get
dart pub add http
dart pub remove http
dart pub deps
dart pub outdated
dart pub upgrade
dart pub cache repair
dart pub global activate dev_tools

// CODE GENERATION
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dart run build_runner watch --delete-conflicting-outputs

// TESTING
dart test
dart test test/file_test.dart
dart test --name "pattern"
dart test --platform vm | chrome
dart test --coverage=./coverage
dart test --chain-stack-traces

// PERF
dart run --observe bin/main.dart
dart run --profile bin/main.dart
dart --observe --profiler --timeline=t.json bin/main.dart
dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o app --obfuscate

// PROFILING A COMPILED BINARY
./app --observe
// then connect dev_tools to the printed URI

// PUBLISH
dart pub publish --dry-run
dart pub publish
dart pub version patch | minor | major | pre

// FLUTTER
flutter pub get
flutter run
flutter run --profile
flutter build apk --release
flutter build appbundle --release
flutter build ipa --release
flutter build web
flutter test
flutter analyze

The commands, grouped by what they are for

The dart CLI has more subcommands than it needs and no consistent grouping, so the useful organisation is by task rather than by name. Five groups cover everything: run and execute, resolve and inspect dependencies, compile and deploy, analyse and format, and clean up. Knowing which group a command is in predicts what it will do to your .dart_tool directory.

// 1. RUN AND EXECUTE
$ dart run bin/server.dart          # run a file
$ dart run :server                  # run a named executable from dev_dependencies
$ dart run                          # run bin/<package-name>.dart if it exists
$ dart run --observe bin/app.dart   # serve DevTools, pause on start
$ dart run --enable-asserts test.dart   # asserts ON (off by default)
$ dart pub global activate tool     # install a CLI tool
$ dart run tool:main                # run an activated tool

// 2. RESOLVE AND INSPECT DEPENDENCIES
$ dart pub get                      # resolve, write pubspec.lock
$ dart pub deps                     # the resolved tree, flat
$ dart pub deps --style=tree        # ...nested, and far more readable
$ dart pub outdated                 # what is behind the constraint
$ dart pub downgrade                # move to the OLDEST allowed, for a bug repro
$ dart pub cache repair             # verify the cache is not corrupt
$ dart pub cache clean              # delete it; the next get refetches

// 3. COMPILE AND DEPLOY
$ dart compile exe bin/server.dart -o build/server
$ dart compile aot-snapshot bin/app.dart -o build/app.aot
$ dart compile js web/main.dart -o build/main.js
$ dart compile wasm web/main.dart -o build/main.wasm
$ dart compile exe bin/cli.dart --save-debugging-info=build/cli.symbols
// ...the flags that are not obvious:
//   -O0..-O4                    optimisation level; -O4 is the default
//   --define=K=V                 a compile-time const
//   --save-debugging-info=F      symbols for a stripped or obfuscated build
//   --target-os / --target-arch  explicit cross-compilation where supported
//   --target-cpu=generic         pin the CPU baseline; see chapter 15.5

// 4. ANALYSE AND FORMAT
$ dart analyze                    # the static analyser; exits non-zero on issues
$ dart analyze --fatal-infos      # infos are errors too - use this in CI
$ dart format .                   # rewrite every file in the canonical style
$ dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed .   # CHECK only; CI uses this
$ dart fix                        # apply every automated fix the analyser offers
$ dart fix --apply                # ...actually write them (dry-run without it)
$ dart fix --dry-run              # ...explicit form, better in a script

// 5. CLEAN UP
$ dart clean                      # delete .dart_tool/ and build/ - next build
                                 #   recompiles everything, so it is slow
$ dart pub cache clean            # the global package cache, not your project

// and the ones people expect and do not exist
// dart install      -> `dart pub global activate`
// dart test         -> NO. Tests come from package:test: `dart test` works
//                       because the test package installs a `dart test` shim,
//                       but it is not a built-in subcommand.
// dart build        -> `dart compile` for a Dart program, `flutter build` for
//                       a Flutter app
// dart deploy       -> `dart pub publish` for a package, `flutter build ipa`
//                       for an app

Flags that change behaviour, and the ones that lie

Two classes of flag cause real confusion: the ones that change semantics without changing the command, and the ones whose defaults differ from what people assume. Both produce failures that look like something else entirely — a test that passes locally and fails in CI, or a build that behaves differently from the same build on another machine.

// ASSERTS ARE OFF BY DEFAULT. This is the single most important fact here.
$ dart run app.dart                    # asserts OFF
$ dart run --enable-asserts app.dart   # asserts ON
// ...consequences:
//   - `assert(someExpensiveCheck())` does nothing in the default run
//   - a Function body (assert takes a Function) is not even CALLED
//   - so a test that relies on an assert having run has tested nothing
// ...and `dart test` DOES enable asserts, so a test that exercises an assert
// path behaves differently from the same code in `dart run`. That asymmetry
// produces "it works in the test but not in the app" for assert-dependent code.

// VERBOSE FLAGS, and what each one actually reports
$ dart run --verbose-vm bin/app.dart   # VM service protocol - enormous
$ dart run --verbose-platform-channels  # every platform channel message
$ dart run --verbose-system             # process, network, and filesystem ops
$ dart run --trace-loading lib/x.dart   # how long each script took to load
// ...`--verbose-vm` is for the VM service documentation. `--trace-loading` is
// the useful one for a slow startup: it prints per-library load times and
// usually names a dependency that is doing real work at import time.

// TIMING FLAGS, and their units
$ dart run --profile-period=1000 bin/app.dart    // microseconds; default 1000
$ dart run --timeline-streams=Compiler,Dart2JS bin/app.dart
$ dart run --timeline_recorder=file,name=trace.bin bin/app.dart
// ...`--profile-period` is in MICROSECONDS, so 1000 is 1 ms. Setting it to 1
// is 1 microsecond and produces an enormous trace. This is the flag behind "my
// DevTools trace is 900 MB" - someone set the period to 1.

// THE VM FLAGS THAT CHANGE SEMANTICS, which should never be in a shipped app
$ dart --old_gen_heap_size=512 run app.dart
$ dart --observe=8181/127.0.0.1 run app.dart   # bind a specific interface
$ dart --disable-service-auth-codes run app.dart   // OBSOLETE, and removed
// ...`--disable-service-auth-codes` is the one to know about: an old blog post
// recommends it, it no longer exists, and any script that passes it fails with
// "Could not find an option named". Service authentication is on by default
// and should stay that way - the VM service is a debugger, and an unauthenticated
// one on a reachable port is a remote code execution surface.

// and the flags that are NOT available, which is a common search that fails
// --sound  / --no-sound-null-safety   the old switch; soundness is now required
// --no-minify                        a dart2js thing, and dart2js is not a
//                                    `dart compile` flag
// --aot / --jit                      the choice is the COMMAND: `dart run` (JIT)
//                                    versus `dart compile exe` (AOT)
// --verbose                          exists, but the useful variants are the
//                                    --verbose-* ones listed above

The one flag that changes what your code does

Every other flag in the Dart CLI changes how fast, how loudly or how big the result is. One changes what the program does, and it is off by default, which means the default behaviour of dart run and dart test are different. That asymmetry is the source of a specific and reliably recurring bug report: it works in the test but not in the app.

The flag is --enable-asserts. Asserts are stripped from production runs, so any code whose correctness depends on an assert — which includes every use of the third promotion form from the previous section — is being checked in one context and not the other. The failure is not that the assert fails; it is that the code the assert was documenting is absent.

// the mechanism, and it is not a runtime flag on each assert
// dart run app.dart                  -> asserts compiled OUT
// dart run --enable-asserts app.dart -> asserts compiled IN
// dart test                          -> asserts compiled IN, always

// what that means for a Function body, which is the subtle part
void checkInvariants() {
  assert(_state != null, "state must be initialised");
  assert(_state.isConsistent(), "state is internally inconsistent");
}

void main() {
  _state = buildState();
  checkInvariants();
  // ...under `dart run`, checkInvariants() is an EMPTY METHOD. Both asserts are
  // gone, and so is the call, because the whole body was assert-only. A
  // consistency check that silently does nothing is worse than no check, because
  // it reads as one.

// the two things this is right for
void main() {
  assert(() {
    // ...a Function body: the block is NOT executed in a production run, and
    //    not even the closure is allocated. So an expensive check costs
    //    literally nothing when disabled:
    if (!invariantHolds()) throw StateError("invariant");
    return true;
  }());
}
// ...and the two things it is wrong for
//   - any check whose failure must be caught in production. An assert is not
//     validation; `ArgumentError.notNull` in a constructor is.
//   - anything with a side effect. Asserts are removed, so a side effect inside
//     one does not happen, and a piece of code that only runs in debug is a
//     different program in the two contexts.

// and the three practices that follow
// 1. Use asserts for INTERNAL invariants: "this should never be false if my
//    code is correct". Their failure is a bug in the program.
// 2. Use exceptions for EXTERNAL input: a parse failure, a missing field, a
//    bad argument. Those are not assert material, because the input is not under
//    the program's control and the caller deserves a clear exception rather than
//    an assertion failure.
// 3. Run your integration tests against a release build at least once. It is the
//    only way to find an assert-shaped dependency, and it is cheap: the same
//    suite with --release if the framework offers it, or a smoke test against
//    the compiled artefact.
// ...the reason this is worth stating in a command reference rather than a
// typing guide is that the flag lives here, the consequence lives in the type
// system, and the two are only connected by this one switch.

The check mode, and what CI should actually run

A CI pipeline that runs dart test and nothing else checks very little. It does not check formatting, it does not check analysis, and it does not check that the code compiles to a release artefact — which is where an assert-shaped dependency is found. The full set is four commands, and the order matters because the cheap, unambiguous ones should fail first.

// the four checks, in the order that fails fastest
# 1. FORMAT — fastest, and the most objectively decidable
dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed .
# ...`--output=none` means do not rewrite; `--set-exit-if-changed` means exit
# non-zero. Without both, this either silently rewrites (so the check passes) or
# prints a diff nobody reads. Together they are a real gate.
#
# 2. ANALYSE — catches the things the compiler does not
dart analyze --fatal-infos .
# ...`--fatal-infos` is the flag that matters. Without it, 40 lint infos pass and
# the lint configuration is decorative. Two infos worth promoting to errors:
#   unused_import            a dead import hides a dependency in pubspec.yaml
#   unused_local_variable    compiles fine, is always a bug
# ...and one to leave as an info, because promoting it produces noise:
#   prefer_const_constructors  correct advice, and arguable in a hot path
#
# 3. TEST — the correctness gate
dart test --concurrency=4 --reporter=github
# ...`--reporter=github` emits annotations the GitHub UI renders as inline
# comments on the diff, which is the difference between a failing check nobody
# reads and one that is actionable without opening a log.
#
# 4. RELEASE BUILD — the check that finds assert dependencies
dart compile exe bin/server.dart -o build/server
./build/server --version
# ...and then RUN it. Compiling is not the test; running the artefact is. This
# step costs about four seconds and is the only automated check that would have
// caught the assert-only method described in the previous subsection.

// and the two that belong in a library's CI but not an application's
dart pub publish --dry-run
# ...catches a broken constraint, a missing CHANGELOG entry, a bad LICENSE, a
# missing description, and an over-narrow SDK bound. It is the only validator
# for anything you intend other people to consume.
dart pub outdated --no-dev-dependencies
# ...for a LIBRARY, this is the check that finds out a transitive release broke
# you. An application pins and is unaffected; a library resolves fresh on every
// run, so its CI is the only thing standing between it and a broken release.

// and the caching question, which is where most Dart CI is slow
# cache: ~/.pub-cache
# ...the pub cache is the only thing worth caching. The Dart SDK install is
# large but fast, and the kernel cache in .dart_tool is invalidated by almost
// any source change, so caching it produces cache misses that cost more than
// they save. Three tiers, and only the first is worth it:
//   SDK            200 MB, ~15 s to install      cache it if installs are slow
//   pub cache      ~500 MB, ~30 s to download    cache it, keyed on pubspec.lock
//   .dart_tool     per-checkout, invalidated     do not cache it
// ...keyed on pubspec.lock is the important detail: keying on pubspec.yaml alone
// means a dependency edit is a cache hit and the build silently uses the old
// graph.

A.7 Compilation targets

//            command                    target
// native      dart compile exe          linux, macos, windows
// AOT lib     dart compile aot-snapshot loadable at runtime
// JIT kernel  dart compile kernel       for a host to load
// Android     aot-snapshot --target-os=android --target-arch=arm64
// iOS         aot-snapshot --target-os=ios --target-arch=arm64
//             (requires macOS for the build)
// Web         dart compile js           JavaScript
// Web         dart compile wasm         WebAssembly (needs WasmGC)
//
// FLUTTER
// flutter build apk --release --split-per-abi
// flutter build appbundle --release        Play Store
// flutter build ipa --release              App Store
// flutter build macos | windows | linux
// flutter build web
//
// THE COMPILE FLAGS
// -o <path>              the output
// -O0 .. -O4             optimisation level (js/wasm)
// --minify               minify the js
// --obfuscate            obfuscate a native binary
// -Dname=value           a compile-time define
//                        const x = String.fromEnvironment('name')
// --enable-asserts       keep asserts in a release build
// --target-os=           linux macos windows android ios
// --target-arch=         arm arm64 ia32 x64 riscv32 riscv64
// --no-source-maps       omit the map file
// --verbosity=all        everything
//
// THE SIZE, roughly
// native hello world     ~6MB
// web hello world        ~10KB minified
// + 10 small packages    ~8MB / ~80KB
// + a chart library      ~14MB / ~450KB
// + dart:mirrors         ~40MB+ (nothing can be shaken)

What each compiler can and cannot do

The four Dart compilers are not four dialects of one language. Each one removes a part of the platform, and the part it removes is the part that determines which APIs your code can call. Choosing a target is therefore choosing what is available, and the constraint arrives at compile time as a single error naming a library.

CompilerOutputMissing
dart run (JIT)Kernel in memoryNothing
dart compile exeNative executableNothing
dart compile aot-snapshot.aotNothing; needs a VM
dart compile js.jsdart:io, isolates, mirrors
dart compile wasm.wasmThe above, plus direct DOM
flutter buildAPK/IPA/binaryNothing
// the decision, and the question that decides it
// Does the program need dart:io?
//   YES  -> dart compile exe. Nothing else is available.
//   NO, and it is for a browser -> dart compile wasm for speed,
//         dart compile js for a lower browser floor
//   NO, and it is a Flutter app -> flutter build
//
// the platform libraries, by availability
//   dart:core       all targets
//   dart:async      all targets        (Streams, Futures, zones)
//   dart:convert    all targets        (json, utf8, base64)
//   dart:typed_data all targets        (Uint8List, ByteData)
//   dart:io         NOT the web
//   dart:isolate    NOT the web        and NOT dart2wasm
//   dart:ffi        NOT the web
//   dart:mirrors    NOT the web, NOT AOT
//   dart:html       DEPRECATED - use package:web + dart:js_interop
//   dart:ui         Flutter only

// the error that tells you, which is always the same shape
// $ dart compile js web/main.dart -o out.js
// Error: Dart library 'dart:io' is not available on this platform.
// lib/my_server.dart:3:8: Error: Dart library 'dart:io' is not available.
// ...it names the FILE AND LINE, so the fix is direct. The whole web build
// fails rather than the one call site, which is deliberate: it prevents a
// partial web build that fails at runtime instead.

// and the four numbers for each target
$ dart compile exe bin/app.dart -o app && file app
  app: ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64, dynamically linked   // ~8 MB
$ dart compile js web/main.dart -o main.js && ls -l main.js
  -rw-r--r-- 1 user staff 1800000 main.js                            // ~1.8 MB
$ dart compile wasm web/main.dart -o main.wasm && ls -l main.wasm
  -rw-r--r-- 1 user staff 2600000 main.wasm                          // ~2.6 MB
$ dart compile aot-snapshot bin/app.dart -o app.aot && ls -l app.aot
  -rw-r--r-- 1 user staff 9400000 app.aot                            // ~9.4 MB
// ...the exe and the aot-snapshot are nearly the same size and differ in one
// respect: the exe BUNDLES the runtime and the snapshot NEEDS it beside it.
// For a CLI you ship alone, use exe. For a Flutter app or a controlled
// environment, aot-snapshot is fine.

// and the two web-specific requirements that are not about Dart at all
// 1. the MIME type. A .wasm served as application/octet-stream fails
//    instantiateStreaming SILENTLY in some browsers - a blank page, no console
//    error. nginx:
//      location ~* .wasm$ { types { } default application/wasm; }
// 2. an ES module for the wasm glue, so the script tag must be
//    type="module". A classic script tag loads main.mjs as nothing at all.

Target matrix, and the three deployment failures

A build that must run in more than one place has three failure modes that are specific to targets rather than to code, and all three are silent until the moment of deployment. The common cause of all three is building on a machine more capable than the machine that will run the artefact, so the practical rule is to build on the least capable machine in the support matrix.

// 1. GLIBC VERSION — the most common compiled-Dart deployment failure
$ ./server
./server: /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6: version `GLIBC_2.34' not found
// ...built on Ubuntu 22.04 (glibc 2.35), deployed on Debian 11 (glibc 2.31).
// The message names a symbol, not a Dart file, so it reads as a system problem.
$ ldd --version | head -1
$ ldd ./server
// ...the fix is the BUILD IMAGE, not the binary:
//   FROM debian:bullseye-slim      # the older base, matched to the target
// ...or a musl static build, which removes the libc dependency:
//   $ dart compile exe bin/app.dart -o app --target-os linux
// ...or the general rule: the container image you DEPLOY must be the image you
// BUILT IN. Pin it.

// 2. CPU FEATURES — SIGILL, with no message
$ ./server
Illegal instruction (core dumped)
// ...compiled on a machine with AVX-512, run on one without. No Dart message,
// no symbol. The fix is a baseline target:
//   $ dart compile exe bin/app.dart -o server --target-cpu=generic
// ...`generic` costs perhaps 10% and removes the class of failure entirely.
// This is the single most valuable flag in a release build and it is off by
// default, because the default assumes you are deploying to the machine you
// built on.

// 3. ARCHITECTURE — exec format error, no filename
$ docker run myapp:1.2.3
exec format error
// ...a single-arch image on a multi-arch host, or the wrong --platform. The fix
// is a manifest list:
$ docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t myapp:1.2.3 --push .
$ docker buildx imagetools inspect myapp:1.2.3 | grep Architecture
  Architecture: amd64
  Architecture: arm64
// ...and the cluster must pull by DIGEST for the manifest to be used. A tag
// pinned to one platform serves that one platform with no warning.

// and the matrix worth building in CI, which is four jobs and catches all three
name: build
on: [push]
jobs:
  build:
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false        # ...one platform failing must not cancel the
      matrix:                 #    others, or their results are never seen
        include:
          - os: ubuntu-latest
            arch: x64
          - os: ubuntu-latest
            arch: arm64
          - os: macos-latest
          - os: windows-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dart-lang/setup-dart@v1
        with: { sdk: stable }
      - run: dart pub get
      # ...the baseline flag, on EVERY job, not just the release one:
      - run: dart compile exe bin/app.dart -o app --target-cpu=generic
      - run: ./app --version     # ...and RUN it, on the runner, which is the
                                 #    only step that catches a libc mismatch
                                 #    before the artefact reaches a deploy
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: app-${{ matrix.os }}-${{ matrix.arch }} }

Why each compiler removes a different part of the platform

Compilation targets are usually taught as a table of output formats. The more useful framing is that each compiler's job includes deciding which parts of the platform to leave out, and that decision — not the output format — is what determines whether your code compiles. A browser has no filesystem, no processes, no threads and no OS-level memory; a native binary has all of them. So the web targets do not produce "the same program in a different wrapper", they produce a program with a strictly smaller standard library available.

The practical consequence is that the constraint is discovered at compile time, on the first use, and it is discovered for the whole build rather than for one file. That is deliberate. A partial web build that compiles and fails at runtime is worse than one that refuses to build.

// the boundary, expressed as code rather than as a list
// What makes something io is that it can name the filesystem:
import 'dart:io';        // File, Directory, Socket, HttpClient, Platform, exit

// What makes it web is that it can name the browser:
import 'package:web/web.dart' as web;   // document, window, fetch
import 'dart:js_interop';              // the interop layer

// and the portable subset, which is most of what an application should be
import 'dart:core';
import 'dart:async';
import 'dart:convert';
import 'dart:math';
import 'dart:typed_data';

// the architecture that follows from that list, and it is the architecture you
// want regardless of target
//   pure Dart core        models, parsing, validation, business rules
//   an INTERFACE          abstract Clock, abstract HttpClient, abstract Store
//   a platform binding    dart:io on the server, package:web in the browser
// ...so the platform-specific code is the thinnest possible layer, in exactly
// one file per platform, and the bulk of the program is compiled for every
// target without knowing any of this exists. This is the same rule as any other
// portability boundary, and it is worth following even for a project that will
// only ever run on one platform, because it is what makes the tests fast.

// and what a platform binding actually looks like
abstract interface class HttpClient {
  Future<String> get(String url);
}

class IoHttpClient implements HttpClient {
  @override
  Future<String> get(String url) async {
    final res = await _inner.get(Uri.parse(url));
    return res.body;
  }
}

class WebHttpClient implements HttpClient {
  @override
  Future<String> get(String url) async {
    final res = await web.window.fetch(url.toJS).toDart;
    return res.text().toDart;
  }
}
// ...conditional import selects which of these two files is compiled, and the
// interface is what the rest of the program sees. Everything above it is
// identical on both targets, which is the entire point.

// and the constraint surfacing as a compile error, so it is never a runtime one
// $ dart compile js web/main.dart -o out.js
// Error: Dart library 'dart:io' is not available on this platform.
// lib/data/repository.dart:3:8: Error: Dart library 'dart:io' is not available.
// ...file and line, and the whole build fails. So the question is never "will
// this work in the browser" but "which of my files name dart:io", which is a
// grep:
//   grep -rn "dart:io" lib/ | grep -v "_io.dart"
// ...every hit outside a platform-binding file is a line of code that has just
// acquired a browser compatibility problem.

Choosing a web target, and the deployment failures that follow

Between dart compile js and dart compile wasm the choice is a trade of a browser support floor against throughput, and there is a third option that is better than both for most projects: neither, because most web Dart is inside a Flutter web build, which has its own pipeline and its own size characteristics.
