Whichever you pick, three things must be true of the deployment or the application will not start, and all three fail silently — a blank page, a console error in a language you are not reading, and no exception in your code.

// 1. THE MIME TYPE. This is the most common wasm failure and it fails silently.
# nginx, for a .wasm file
location ~* \.wasm$ {
  types { }
  default application/wasm;
}
// ...`instantiateStreaming` REQUIRES that content type. Served as
// application/octet-stream it throws a TypeError that most logging setups drop,
// and the page renders empty. The diagnostic when a wasm app is blank:
//   fetch('/main.wasm').then(r => console.log(r.headers.get('content-type')))
//   null           <- wrong; and for some CDNs also requires no charset
//   application/wasm   <- correct

// 2. THE SCRIPT TYPE. The wasm glue is an ES module.
<script type="module" src="main.dart.js"></script>
<!-- NOT: <script src="main.dart.js"></script> -->
// ...a classic script tag evaluates the file as a script and a module's
// `import` statements are a syntax error. The error names a file nobody
// recognises as generated.

// 3. CORRECT HEADERS for SharedArrayBuffer, if you use dart2wasm with threads
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp
// ...without both, SharedArrayBuffer is undefined and the failure is usually
// reported as a hang rather than an error. This is the single most confusing
// wasm deployment problem, because the two headers also break third-party
// iframes and embeds.

// and the choice, stated as the decision it actually is
//   dart2js    : every browser that can run ES5. Larger output, slower compute,
//                no threads. The right answer when you must support Safari 14
//                or a WebView in an old Android.
//   dart2wasm  : Chrome/Edge/Firefox recent, Safari 16.4+. Faster compute,
//                smaller output. The right answer for a compute-heavy app on a
//                modern browser fleet.
//   flutter web: neither flag. Uses the engine's own compiler and a
//                CanvasKit or skwasm renderer. The right answer for a Flutter
//                app, and it is a different size conversation entirely -
//                CanvasKit is several MB of WebAssembly downloaded before
//                anything renders, which is why the HTML renderer exists for
//                small apps.

// and the honest size comparison, because the numbers are the deciding factor
//   dart compile js    main.dart.js    ~1.8 MB, gzipped ~450 KB
//   dart compile wasm  main.wasm + .mjs ~2.6 MB, gzipped ~700 KB, then
//                      main.mjs        ~120 KB
//   flutter web        CanvasKit      ~6 MB, and the app's own code on top
// ...so wasm is larger on the wire before compression and often faster after.
// The break-even is compute, not size: if the app spends its time parsing and
// transforming rather than drawing, wasm wins; if it is mostly paint, the
// difference is not measurable and the js target's reach is worth more.

A.8 Pattern syntax

// PATTERN KINDS
literal            42, 'text', [1, 2], {'k': 1}
variable           final x
wildcard           _
type               final String s, final num n
object             Circle(:final radius)
logical-or         1 || 2 || 3
relational         < 0, <= 10, > 100
cast               final num n
null-check         final String? s
null-assert        var x!
constant pattern   42, 'a', Color.red
guarded            pattern when condition

// DESTRUCTURING
final (a, b) = (1, 2);
final (:x, :y) = (x: 1, y: 2);
final (n, :name) = (1, name: 'a');
for (final (k, v) in map.entries) { ... }

// SWITCH EXPRESSION (exhaustive, no default needed)
return switch (shape) {
  Circle(:final radius) => 3.14 * radius * radius,
  Square(:final side) => side * side,
  Rect(:final w, :final h) => w * h,
};

// SWITCH STATEMENT (needs break)
switch (value) {
  case 0: print('zero'); break;
  case < 0: print('negative'); break;
  default: print('other');
}

// IF-CASE
if (value case final List<int> list when list.isNotEmpty) {
  print(list.length);
}

// SEALED + PATTERN = the compiler checks completeness
sealed class Result<T> {}
class Ok<T> extends Result<T> { final T value; Ok(this.value); }
class Err<T> extends Result<T> { final String message; Err(this.message); }

String describe<T>(Result<T> r) => switch (r) {
  Ok(:final value) => '$value',
  Err(:final message) => 'error: $message',
};
// add a variant to Result: describe() stops compiling

The pattern kinds, and which ones earn their keep

There are twelve pattern kinds and a working programmer uses about five of them. The other seven exist for completeness, and a reference that lists all twelve without saying which matter is a worse reference than one that lists five and explains the choice. So this subsection starts with the five that carry nearly all real code, and the full table above remains for lookup.

// 1. DESTRUCTURING — the most useful by a wide margin
final (a, b) = (1, 2);
final (x, y) = (width, height);           // ...on a tuple
final MapEntry(:key, :value) = entry;     // ...on a record with named fields
final (:name, :age) = person;             // ...pulling only two of five
// ...and in a pattern, which is the form that reads well in a switch:
switch (point) {
  case (0, 0):     print('origin');
  case (0, final y): print('on the y axis at $y');
  case (final x, 0): print('on the x axis at $x');
  default:         print('somewhere else');
}

// 2. TYPE — the workhorse, and usually as an `is` or `if-case`
if (json is Map<String, Object?>) { ... }
if (x case final int n when n > 0) { ... }
// ...`if-case` is better than `is` when you need BOTH the test and a binding,
// because it does not need a second statement to extract the value.

// 3. LOGICAL-OR — collapsing cases, which is where switches get readable
return switch (status) {
  200 || 201 || 204 => 'success',
  400 || 422 => 'client error',
  >= 500 => 'server error',
  _ => 'unexpected',
};
// ...which is much better than a long list of `case 200: case 201:` labels, and
// it mixes patterns and constants in one list.

// 4. NULL-CHECK and NULL-ASSERT — the two places a pattern mentions null
final String? maybe;
// ...`case final String s:` matches only a NON-NULL String
if (maybe case final String s) print(s.length);   // ...one statement, s bound
// ...whereas `if (maybe != null) print(maybe.length)` needs two, because `maybe`
// is a final local rather than a pattern variable. With a FIELD it is worse:
// the field is not promoted, so you need `maybe!` or a local copy.

// 5. OBJECT — pulling fields out of a class, which is the form that replaced
//    most `is` + cast chains
final area = switch (shape) {
  Circle(:final radius) => 3.14159 * radius * radius,
  Square(:final side) => side * side,
  Rect(:final w, :final h) => w * h,
};
// ...`:final radius` is shorthand for `:radius` when you want the field's
// value; `:final var r = radius` gives you a new name.

// AND THE ONES YOU CAN SKIP, with the reason
//   `var x!` as a pattern   -> `!` on a variable is clearer
//   relational alone         -> only useful with a constant: `case < 0:`
//   guarded alone            -> only useful after another kind
//   a constant alone         -> `case 42:` works, but `final int x when x == 42`
//                               does not, because a variable pattern binds
//   cast `final num n`      -> redundant with `final int n` unless you mean
//                               "an int that arrived as a num", which is not a
//                               thing patterns express

Switch: statement versus expression, and exhaustiveness

The most important thing about Dart patterns is not the destructuring — it is that a switch over a sealed hierarchy is checked for completeness. Add a case to the type and every switch that handles it stops compiling. That converts a class of runtime bug (the unhandled variant, which reaches production as a StateError("unhandled case")) into a compile error, and it is the strongest argument for sealed classes in the language.

// sealed + final makes the hierarchy CLOSED, so the switch is total
sealed class Shape {}
final class Circle extends Shape { final double radius; Circle(this.radius); }
final class Square extends Shape { final double side; Square(this.side); }
final class Rect   extends Shape {
  final double w, h;
  Rect(this.w, this.h);
}
// ...`sealed` permits subtypes only in the same LIBRARY; `final` permits none.
// So this set cannot grow without a compile error in this file, and the
// compiler knows the set is exactly these three.

double area(Shape s) => switch (s) {
  Circle(:final radius) => 3.14159 * radius * radius,
  Square(:final side) => side * side,
  Rect(:final w, :final h) => w * h,
};
// ...no `default`, no `_`, and it is complete. Add:
//   final class Tri extends Shape { ... }
// ...and THIS LINE STOPS COMPILING:
//   error: Non-exhaustive switch expression.
// ...which is the whole point. The compiler names the missing type.

// and the EXPRESSION form, which is a different tool from the STATEMENT form
// EXPRESSION (a switch expression, returns a value, must be exhaustive):
double a = switch (s) { Circle() => 1, Square() => 2, Rect() => 3 };
double b = switch (s) {
  Circle() => 1,          // ...no break needed - each arm is a value
  Square() => 2,
  Rect() => 3,
};

// STATEMENT (a switch statement, no value, falls through unless you break):
switch (s) {
  case Circle():
    print('circle');
    break;                  // ...REQUIRED, and its absence is a compile error
  case Square():
  case Rect():              // ...an empty fall-through group is allowed
    print('not a circle');
    break;
  default:                  // ...and `default` is optional if the cases cover
    print('unreachable');  //    a sealed type completely
}

// and the three rules that differ between them
//   1. a switch EXPRESSION must be exhaustive, with no default
//   2. a switch STATEMENT may be non-exhaustive, and falls through without break
//   3. `case` patterns in a statement cannot use variable bindings that are
//      unused; use `_` instead of a name you ignore

// and the `if-case` form, which is a STATEMENT with a pattern test
void log(Object? value) {
  if (value case final String s when s.length > 10) {
    print('long string: $s');
  } else if (value case final int n) {
    print('int: $n');
  } else {
    print('something else');
  }
}
// ...the `when` clause is the guard, and it is the difference from `is`: `is`
// gives you a bool, `case` gives you the bound value, and `when` narrows the
// test without a separate statement. Three alternatives in eight lines, with no
// casts and no `!`.

Why exhaustiveness is the point

Of everything in the patterns reference, one property is worth more than all the syntax together, and it is easy to miss because it is an absence of errors rather than a presence of a feature. A switch over a sealed hierarchy is checked for completeness by the compiler. Add a variant to the hierarchy and every switch that handles it stops compiling, at the exact line that needs attention, with the name of the missing type.

Compare that with the three alternatives, which all fail silently. A default clause that logs "unhandled" and returns a zero value compiles forever and produces a wrong answer in production. A chain of is tests followed by a cast throws a TypeError at a call site far from the type that changed. An if/else chain does the same.

// the mechanism, and the exact compiler message
sealed class Shape {}
final class Circle extends Shape { final double r; Circle(this.r); }
final class Square extends Shape { final double s; Square(this.s); }

double area(Shape shape) => switch (shape) {
  Circle(:final r) => 3.14159 * r * r,
  Square(:final s) => s * s,
};
// ...now add a variant:
final class Triangle extends Shape { final double b, h; Triangle(this.b, this.h); }
// ...and this line stops compiling:
//   lib/geometry.dart:24:11: Error: Switch expression of type
//   'Shape' must be exhaustive.
//   - 'Triangle' isn't matched.
// ...that is the whole argument for sealed classes: a change to a type system
// propagates to every place that switches on it, as a build failure rather
// than a runtime surprise. No amount of test coverage gives you that
// guarantee, because the test does not exist until somebody writes it.

// and the three levels of strictness, in increasing order
// 1. `switch` on an enum: exhaustive without `sealed`, because an enum's set
//    is closed by construction. Add a constant and every switch breaks.
// 2. `switch` on a sealed class: exhaustive because `sealed` closes the set of
//    direct subtypes. Add a variant and every switch breaks.
// 3. `switch` on an abstract class: NOT exhaustive. The compiler allows a
//    `default`, and you need one, and adding a variant changes nothing.
// ...so the rule is: if you want the compiler to check completeness, the type
// must be an enum, or sealed, or a primitive. An open class cannot provide it,
// and that is the difference between an abstraction that documents its own
// variants and one that does not.

// and why `final` on the subclasses matters separately
sealed class Result {}
final class Ok extends Result { final Object? value; Ok(this.value); }
class Err extends Result { final String m; Err(this.m); }
// ...if `Err` is NOT final, a subclass of `Err` is possible, and a switch on
// Result with an `Err` case is exhaustive over Result's DIRECT subtypes — which
// the compiler accepts, because `Err` covers itself and its subclasses. So
// `final` is about preventing extension, not about exhaustiveness. Use `final`
// unless there is a reason to extend, and expect the compiler to require it if
// you later seal the parent.

// and the cost, stated honestly: exhaustiveness is compile-time only
double total(List<Shape> shapes) {
  var sum = 0.0;
  for (final s in shapes) sum += area(s);
  return sum;
}
// ...`area` is total, so this is safe. But a switch that returns a default of
// 0.0 for an unhandled variant is exhaustive to the compiler and WRONG to the
// caller, because the type system has no way to say "this function may return a
// meaningless answer". The compile-time guarantee is exactly as strong as the
// domain: it guarantees the cases are handled, and it cannot guarantee the
// handler is right. That is the limit of every exhaustiveness check in every
// language, and it is why a test per variant is still worth having.

Choosing between is, if-case, and a switch

These three forms overlap almost completely, and picking the wrong one costs either readability or a runtime error. The differences are narrow and each has a case where it is the only correct answer.

FormBinds a valueMultiple alternativesExhaustive
isNoNon/a
if-caseYesNo (use else if)No
switch statementYesYesOptional
switch expressionYesYesRequired
// `is`: a bool, no binding, and therefore always followed by a second step
void a(Object o) {
  if (o is String) {
    print(o.length);        // ...promotion makes this work: o IS String here
  }
}
// ...`is` on a LOCAL promotes, so it is complete on its own. On a FIELD it does
// not, and then you need the copy, which is why the form below exists.

// `if-case`: a bool AND a binding, in one statement
void b(Object? o) {
  if (o case final String s when s.length > 3) {
    print(s.toUpperCase());  // ...s is bound, non-null, and guarded
  } else if (o case final int n) {
    print(n * 2);
  }
}
// ...this is the case where `if-case` is strictly better than `is`: a FIELD,
// where promotion fails.
//   if (config.endpoint case final String e) use(e);   // works
//   if (config.endpoint is String) use(config.endpoint!);  // needs the !
// ...and the `when` clause, which is what `is` cannot express at all. It is a
// guard, not a type test, and it is evaluated only after the pattern matches.

// a switch statement: multiple alternatives over one value
void c(Status s) {
  switch (s) {
    case Status.active when s.canEdit:
      print("editable");
    case Status.active:
      print("read only");     // ...a guarded case plus an unguarded one: order
    case Status.pending:       //    matters, and the guard is tried first
      print("waiting");
    case Status.suspended:
      print("paused");
  }
  // ...no default and no error: the enum is exhaustive, so this is complete.
//    Remove one case and the compiler requires either a default or that case.

// a switch EXPRESSION: when the value is the point
String describe(Status s) => switch (s) {
  Status.active => "live",
  Status.pending => "waiting",
  Status.suspended => "paused",
};
// ...no break, no default, must be exhaustive. When a switch assigns or returns,
// this form is strictly better: it cannot fall through, and the compiler
// enforces completeness. Prefer it always for a value.

// and the rule that resolves almost every case
//   returning or assigning? -> switch EXPRESSION
//   several tests in sequence on one value? -> switch STATEMENT
//   one test, and you need the value? -> if-case
//   one test, on a local, and you do not need the value? -> is
// ...and one form to avoid: `o is String` followed by `o as String`. The cast
// is always redundant after a successful `is` on the same variable, because
// promotion has already happened. It appears in a great deal of older code and
// in code ported from a language without promotion, and removing it is one of
// the highest-value mechanical changes to an untyped codebase.

A.9 Glossary

Isolate            the unit of concurrency: one thread, one event loop
Event loop         the queue that runs microtasks and then events
Microtask          work that runs before the next event
JIT                just-in-time compilation; the development mode
AOT                ahead-of-time compilation; the release mode
Kernel snapshot    the compiled Dart code, loadable by a VM
Sendable           a value that can cross an isolate boundary
TransferableTypedData  memory moved between isolates, not copied
SharedArrayBuffer  memory shared between isolates
Zone               a context async callbacks run inside
Null safety        T is never null; T? may be null
Promotion          the compiler narrowing T? to T after a check
Records            an anonymous fixed-shape value
Sealed class       an abstract class with a closed set of subtypes
Exhaustive         a switch that handles every case, with no default
Tree shaking       removing unreachable code at compile time
Deferred import    an async import that becomes a separate chunk
Dynamic            no static checking; an escape hatch, use sparingly
Extension method   a method added to a type you do not own
Extension type     a zero-cost wrapper giving a primitive a new type
Part / part of     splitting one library across files
Barrel file        a file that only re-exports
Path dependency    a dependency by filesystem path (not for release)
Dependency override  forcing a version, at the cost of compatibility
AOT snapshot       a compiled library for a mobile/desktop app
dart2js            the JavaScript compiler for the web
dart2wasm          the WebAssembly compiler for the web
WasmGC             garbage-collected WebAssembly, needed by dart2wasm
FFI                the Foreign Function Interface: calling C directly
Method channel     a Dart-to-native message channel in Flutter
Fuzzing            testing with random inputs to find crashes
Golden test        a test that compares rendered output to an image
Fake vs mock       a fake works; a mock records calls
fakeAsync          a test zone with virtual time
